title: Computational Analysis of K-Ras Gene Expression in Dendritic Mouse Cells (DC2.4)
authors: K'Yana Edwards, University of South Florida, United States; Dr Michael Shamblott, University of South Florida, United States
abstract: The K-Ras oncogene drives immune evasion in cancers, but its role in dendritic cells (DCs) remains underexplored. This study investigated K-Ras expression in the murine DC line DC2.4 using PCR, gel electrophoresis, DNA sequencing, and BLAST alignment. The findings confirmed robust K-Ras expression in DC2.4 cells, with high sequence homology to reference transcripts (Mus musculus KRAS variant 8). These results establish DC2.4 as a relevant model for studying K-Ras-mediated immune modulation in cancer. Further research should assess how oncogenic K-Ras mutations alter DC function, potentially revealing new immunotherapy targets.

title: FunGI, Functional Genomics Interpreter, and Computational Chemical Genomics
authors: Abolfazl Arab, UCSF, United States; Thomas O'loughlin, Mount Sinai, United States; Nick Youngblut, Arc Institute, United States; Nianzhen Li, Arc Institute, United States; Luke Gilbert, Arc Institute / UCSF, United States; Kevan Shokat, UCSF, United States
abstract: Advances in CRISPR technology have greatly enhanced our capacity for precise genetic modifications and large-scale functional genomics screening. Beyond single-guide approaches, multiplexed genetic perturbations are essential for studying interactions among coding and non-coding elements. An adaptable screen design and data processing framework is critical and computational tasks varying based on platform and research goals. This study introduces several genome-scale CRISPRi loss-of-function drug screens using chemical compounds activating or inhibiting their target proteins. First, we introduce a database of screens performed using inhibitors targeting DNA methylation enzyme DNMT1 and core constituents of the DNA damage response (DDR) machinery PARP, ATR, ATM, DNAPK, and WEE1. Then, we introduce a screen using small molecule targeting the p53-Y220C mutant to restore wild-type conformation and rescue tumor-suppressor activity. These experiments identify >1000 genes whose perturbation modifies the targeted treatment effects and provides a rich resource to the cancer therapeutics community. In addition, this compendium of functional genomics data reveals opens computational challenges to query specific chemical-genetic interaction for further studies. “Computational Chemical Genomics” approaches can integrate high-resolution functional genomics, sequence-informed predictive modeling, and rational chemical probe design to find novel therapeutic strategies in cancer.

title: Discovering Biological Signals in the Noise
authors: Sophia Cheng, University of Michigan, United States
abstract: Like astronomers who have only ever known a star by its light, biologists studying individual cells face a fundamental observational constraint - they cannot directly witness a cell's decisions, only interpret its signals. Single-cell RNA sequencing provides researchers with a snapshot of individual cells from which they can infer what the cell is, what it is doing, and what it might do next. This research focuses on the preprocessing that occurs before analysis begins. Current standards flag cells as noise to be filtered out if they fall outside any single quality control threshold. From a data quality standpoint, this is sound practice. However, the thresholds are often defined using the same set of assumptions that are being analyzed, introducing causal ambiguity. To investigate this further, I performed my own analysis on the discarded noise data from a high-impact 2021 paper (Pal et al., 2021). Using their provided supplementary data, I separated the samples into cells that would be discarded (noise) or analyzed (real). I identified 3 potential biological signals (PBS) when analyzing the latent space of the noise. Using these signals, I then built a decision tree classifier on the noise cells. The classifier has a high sensitivity to ER+ tumors (94.5%) with a moderate overall accuracy (69.3%). This research provides preliminary evidence that there are signals in what is discarded. Investigating these cells more carefully may matter most in cancers where heterogeneity is highest and treatment resistance is hardest to explain, such as breast cancer.

title: Single-Seed Benchmarks Are Unreliable for LLM Coding Agents on Bioinformatics Tasks
authors: Rikhin Kavuru, Independent Researcher, United States
abstract: LLM-based coding agents are now used for end-to-end bioinformatics workflows, but the benchmarks used to compare them rarely quantify their own measurement error. We present a pre-registered evaluation of three coding-agent configurations on fourteen analytical tasks spanning bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, functional genomics, clinical survival modeling, and rare-disease variant prioritization. Across 630 agent runs (fourteen tasks × three configurations × fifteen random seeds), we decompose three previously uncharacterized sources of measurement noise: seed variance within a fixed configuration, intra-session non-determinism in the LLM judges that score agent outputs, and judge sensitivity to evidence ordering. We find that within-seed standard deviation (median 0.13) systematically exceeds between-configuration differences (median 0.06), rendering single-seed comparisons structurally underpowered to detect plausible configuration effects. LLM judges at temperature zero exhibit a 6% per-call flip rate and a 10% upper bound on artifact-section ordering sensitivity, concentrated on borderline items. Cross-family judge calibration on 189 items shows that same-family judges agree on agent-capability criteria (Cohen's κ = 0.87) but disagree at chance level on documentation-style criteria (κ = 0.00); the disagreement replicates under a cross-family Llama judge, generalizes across rubric items, and is adjudicated against a 60-item blinded human annotation. We argue that agent benchmarks must be reported as measurement systems — with pre-registered hypotheses, modal-of-multiple judging, variance-aware power analysis, and criterion-behavior classification — and release a reusable evaluation harness, full reproducibility artifacts, and pre-registration commits to support the practice.

title: OpenChallenges: A FAIR-Aligned, Centralized Platform for Crowdsourcing in Biological Research
authors: Verena Chung, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Rongrong Chai, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Hallie Swan, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Jake Albrecht, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Jay Hodgson, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Solveig K Sieberts, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Luca Foschini, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Susheel Varma, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Thomas Schaffter, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Gaia Andreoletti, Sage Bionetworks, United States
abstract: Rigorous benchmarking is a critical bottleneck in the responsible development of AI agents for biomedical applications. Community challenges, where teams evaluate models on held-out data, provide the gold standard for objective, scalable AI assessment. Yet over 2,000 such challenges are scattered across hosting platforms without a centralized registry, fragmenting the landscape and preventing it from meeting FAIR data principles at the metadata level. We developed OpenChallenges (OC), a centralized, FAIR-aligned repository that aggregates and standardizes challenge metadata from 26 hosting platforms into a unified, searchable registry. OC is built on the Minimal Information About a Challenge (MIAC) schema, derived from an analysis of 47 DREAM challenges and enriched with ontologies for semantic search. The platform currently indexes 836 biomedical challenges spanning oncology, genomics, imaging, and drug discovery, with challenge creation accelerating markedly: 80 launched in 2025, 68 in 2024. Critically, 38.5% of indexed challenges originate from long-tail and independent platforms which are competitions lacking the inherent visibility of major hubs like Synapse or Kaggle, for which OC provides the greatest discoverability benefit. A metadata completeness scoring framework assigns each challenge one of four tiers (Baseline, Standard, Comprehensive, Gold Standard), revealing mean FAIR dimension scores of Findable 80.0%, Accessible 50.2%, Interoperable 45.7%, and Reusable 11.0% with the latter driven by sparse coverage of evaluationMetric (6.5%), submissionLicense (14.6%), and dataLicense (11.8%), the primary targets of ongoing curation. By consolidating a fragmented ecosystem into a FAIR-aligned knowledge base, OC provides essential infrastructure for transparent, reproducible benchmarking of AI agents across the biomedical sciences.

title: Unbiased Evaluation of Computational Biology Models in the AI Era
authors: Gaia Andreoletti, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Verena Chung, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Luca Foschini, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Susheel Varma, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United Kingdom; Solveig Sieberts, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States
abstract: Rigorous assessment and benchmarking via crowdsourcing are essential in advancing computational biology by promoting unbiased evaluations and fostering innovation. However, the field often encounters the ""self-assessment trap,"" leading to biased comparisons that frequentlyâ€”if unintentionallyâ€”favor their own algorithms. This bias, driven by selective reporting or narrow evaluation criteria, compromises the reliability of results and hinders unbiased scientific advancement. Community-driven challenges like DREAM (Dialogue on Reverse Engineering Assessment and Methods) and CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction) have become essential for promoting unbiased evaluations and fostering open, reproducible research. These initiatives emphasize transparent evaluations using diverse metrics and independent datasets to ensure robust method development. Continuous adoption of such benchmarking practices strengthens computational reliability and accelerates innovation across biomedicine. Given the increasing availability and rapid improvement of coding agents and specialized co-scientists, unbiased evaluation of models and understanding the performance of AI-generated solutions is especially important. The recently completed SEA-AD DREAM Challenge, which focused on single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas, offered an opportunity to test AI agents on tasks designed for human scientists. For the first time in DREAM Challenge history, a dedicated agentic track ran alongside traditional participant submissions using the same tasks and datasets. While agentic participation was nascent (2 and 1 submissions for subchallenges 1 and 2, versus 11 and 10 from traditional teams), this experiment establishes a framework for benchmarking AI agents in biomedical research, a capability that will become critical as autonomous systems become increasingly incorporated and deployed in scientific workflows.

title: VMGB: An Autonomous Multi-Agent Framework for Rare Disease Genomics
authors: Abhay Rastogi, University of Utah, United States; Kendell Clement, University of Utah, United States
abstract: Motivation: Diagnosing rare diseases requires integrating heterogeneous data, including phenotypes, genomic variants, transcriptomics, and regulatory annotations. This process demands complex manual curation and multi-domain expertise, motivating the development of agentic AI systems for structured, comprehensive clinical reasoning. Methods: We developed the Virtual Molecular Genetics Board (VMGB), a locally deployable framework for automated rare disease analysis. VMGB uses a LangGraph-based blackboard architecture to coordinate specialized modules for clinical feature extraction, genomic prioritization, database validation, and literature retrieval. The system constructs a dynamic case representation linking phenotypes, Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, genes, variants, and expression signals. Modules iteratively update this shared state, enabling traceable, multi-step reasoning. VMGB incorporates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground conclusions in curated biomedical databases and supports human-in-the-loop interaction for hypothesis exploration. All components operate within a closed environment using open-source large language models to ensure privacy-preserving handling of protected health information. Results: We evaluated VMGB on a skeletal dysplasia case. The system prioritized a splice donor variant in EFL1 under a compound heterozygous inheritance model. Agent-driven reasoning linked the variant to disrupted protein production, supported by concordant gene expression changes (log2FC = 0.76). This top-ranked hypothesis matched the causative variant identified through independent clinical evaluation, demonstrating concordance with expert interpretation. Conclusions: VMGB introduces a privacy-preserving, knowledge-driven framework for LLM-assisted diagnosis. By combining structured evidence integration and database-grounded reasoning within a closed environment, it provides a practical path toward augmenting molecular genetics boards while maintaining clinical data security.

title: Large Scale ‘Omics: An interactive data explorer platform for multi-omics data analysis and visualization
authors: Andrew Caruso, AbbVie, United States; Lauren Wasson, AbbVie, United States
abstract: The rapid advancement of high-throughput omics technologies has generated unprecedented volumes of biological data, presenting both opportunities and challenges for biomedical research. Data modalities such as single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq), mass cytometry (CyTOF), and targeted proteomics platforms have enabled researchers to profile biological systems at multiple molecular layers with remarkable resolution. However, the complexity, scale, and heterogeneity of these datasets pose significant barriers to effective integration, visualization, and interpretation. Existing tools often focus on single data modalities or require substantial computational expertise, limiting accessibility for researchers across diverse backgrounds. To address these challenges, we developed Large Scale â€˜Omics, an innovative web-based platform that transforms the integration and exploration of complex multi-omics datasets for biomedical research. Large Scale â€˜Omics is a comprehensive data exploration platform that unifies genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, and proteomics data from diverse studies into a single integrated framework. The platform enables seamless visualization and comparative analysis of molecular information across multiple modalities and data layers, facilitating the discovery of biomarkers, mechanistic pathways, and therapeutic targets. The application leverages a modern technology stack combining a React 18 frontend with TypeScript, and a high-performance FastAPI backend powered by Python and SQLAlchemy interfacing with a PostgreSQL database. This architecture ensures responsive, real-time interactive visualizations while efficiently managing large-scale datasets through cloud-based storage solutions. It also builds a framework that allows constant ingestion of new datasets and modalities with minimal changes to the backend architecture.

title: EmbedGen: Applying the FAIR principles to embed data
authors: Inês Duarte, National Cancer Institute, United States; Jeya Balaji Balasubramanian, National Cancer Institute, United States; Lee Mason, National Cancer Institute, United States; Arlindo Oliveira, INESC-ID, Portugal; Jonas Almeida, National Cancer Institute, United States
abstract: This work presents a comprehensive technical analysis of EmbedGen, a client-side JavaScript web application designed to convert user input data into file formats with embeddings compatible with TensorFlow Projector. The application supports multiple embedding providers including Voyage AI, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and in-browser inference via HuggingFace Transformers.js. We assess the architectural decisions, implementation methodology, data processing pipeline, embedding model characteristics, and visualization integration. The system demonstrates a modern approach to building privacy-preserving, client-side machine learning applications while maintaining compatibility with established visualization tools and adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) data principles. Key technical components include comprehensive data parsing, OAuth-based GitHub persistence enabling Findable and Accessible embeddings through shareable URLs, Interoperable export formats conforming to TensorFlow Projector specifications, and Reusable modular architecture supporting integration with dimensionality reduction visualization workflows. By combining client-side processing with standardized output formats and public repository hosting, EmbedGen ensures that generated embeddings are discoverable, programmatically accessible, compatible with existing analysis tools, and transparently documented for reuse across research and production environments.

title: Enabling Researchers to Quickly Find Useful Controlled-Access Data through View-Only Data Access Requests (VODAR)
authors: Jonathan Lawson, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Sofia Labrecque, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States
abstract: The secondary use of genomic and phenotypic data is governed by participant consent and local regulations, requiring Data Access Committees (DACs) to review research use statements (RUS) before granting access. This traditional Data Access Request (DAR) process creates a significant technical and administrative conundrum for researchers and developers alike: researchers cannot determine if a dataset is suitable for their specific computational analysis without first obtaining full access, while research data infrastructure (RDI) developers must choose between building complex, dataset-specific search interfaces or risking oversharing controlled-access data. To resolve this, we propose the View-Only Data Access Request (VODAR)--a paradigm shift that permits researchers to inspect participant-level data without authorization to analyze, download, or publish it. This provides researchers with sufficient insight to confirm that the data is useful for their research while maintaining strict compliance with the NIH Data Use Certification and institutional legal frameworks. Taking this a step further, by leveraging standardized, immutable terms for VODAR-specific RUS and integrating with the Data Use Ontology (DUO), we can transform the DAR into a discrete set of machine-readable inputs, enabling the automation of DAC responses. Combined, VODAR and automatic DAR review drastically reduce time-to-science and eliminate the need for costly, schema-specific search UIs. Ultimately, VODAR provides a scalable infrastructure solution that balances data transparency with ethical compliance, ensuring that participant altruism is honored through more efficient and findable secondary research.

title: Streamlining Controlled-Access Data Governance with DUOS: An Ontology-Based Review and Oversight System
authors: Jonathan Lawson, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Sofia Labrecque, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States
abstract: The rapid growth of genomic and health datasets has increased the administrative burden on Data Access Committees (DACs), who must ensure that secondary data use aligns with complex participant consent, institutional policies, and regulatory requirements. Traditional manual review processes are often time-intensive, inconsistent, and difficult to scale. To address these challenges, we developed the Data Use Oversight System (DUOS), an open-source platform designed for scalable, standardized data access governance. DUOS operationalizes the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) Data Use Ontology (DUO) to enable the structured representation of both dataset use restrictions and researchers' proposed purposes. The platform features an end-to-end workflow including ontology-based decision support, where semi-automated matching algorithms generate structured recommendations to support, but not replace, human decision-making. Implementation in diverse controlled-access environments has demonstrated improved consistency, reduced administrative burden, and shorter review times. By providing transparent and reproducible determinations through ontology-based matching, DUOS maintains human oversight for ambiguous cases while supporting interoperability with modern authentication and authorization standards for federated governance. As a scalable governance infrastructure, DUOS enhances efficiency and compliance in data access review, facilitating timely, ethically aligned biomedical research across global institutions and large-scale genomic programs.

title: Harmonizing Toxicology Data: An LLM-Driven Framework for Creating Machine Learning-Ready Resources
authors: Joan Saurina-i-Ricos, EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute, Spain; Aleix Puig-Barbe, EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute, Spain; Jessica Ewald, EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute, Canada
abstract: Background: The US EPA’s Toxicity Values Database (ToxValDB) contains historical in vivo toxicology data from over 40 international sources. However, inconsistent terminology across these sources creates a significant barrier to utilizing this data as structured training labels for predictive machine learning. To address this, we developed a framework using locally deployed Large Language Models (LLMs) to standardize and harmonize these descriptions into a unified, machine-readable resource. Method: Our pipeline maps unstructured toxicity outcomes to established frameworks, primarily the Mammalian Phenotype (MP) and Histopathology Ontology (HPATH), while rigorously retaining metadata links. Source terms are first converted into embedding vectors, followed by candidate retrieval via a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. An LLM then performs explicit reasoning that leverages the hierarchical structure of the ontologies, ensuring the most precise biological fit when validating the semantic match between the retrieved terms and the original toxicological effects. Finally, a subset of these mappings was expert-validated to establish a consensus-driven ground truth. Results: The automated pipeline successfully processed 15,000 unique toxicity effects in under 24 hours using a 120B parameter model (a >4-fold speedup over manual curation) and in only 10 hours using a 20B parameter model (a >11-fold speedup). Notably, inter-annotator variability between human experts was found to be higher than both human-vs-LLM and LLM-vs-LLM variability. The system achieved strong performance, obtaining an average Jaccard similarity index of over 70% between human consensus and LLM-generated mappings. Conclusion: This methodology successfully transforms legacy, unstructured text into high-quality training data, enabling the direct benchmarking of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) against historical in vivo outcomes. By quantifying the reproducibility of animal testing data and structuring historical knowledge, this framework accelerates early toxicity identification, supports the transition toward replacing specific preclinical in vivo studies with in vitro screening, and guides future NAM development.

title: AI Enablement for Biocuration: Evaluating Training Impact and Emerging Workflow Patterns in Biomedical Data Curation
authors: Michelle Holko, Computercraft, United States; Anne Ketter, Computercraft, United States; Monideep Charkraborti, Computercraft, United States; Alexa Salsbury, Computercraft, United States; Carl Leubsdorf, Computercraft, United States
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to augment biocuration and biomedical data workflows, but adoption remains limited by gaps in training, trust, and integration into domain-specific practices. We describe an AI enablement initiative designed for biomedical data professionals, focused on practical application of generative AI in curation tasks. Participants were primarily data wranglers, curators, and scientists (9/13 respondents). Pre-training results indicated minimal applied use of AI, with no participants reporting regular use in real workflows. Key barriers included lack of knowledge (8/13), uncertainty about output accuracy (7/13), and unclear policies (5/13). Following a structured training program combining asynchronous learning, synchronous sessions, and a mini-project, post-training results showed substantial increases in confidence and adoption. Ninety percent of participants reported confidence using AI responsibly in real workflows, and 70% reported a significant increase in AI use. Eighty percent indicated they were likely or very likely to continue using AI in their work. Participant feedback highlighted emerging applications in literature triage, metadata generation, and knowledge extraction. It also revealed growing interest in more advanced capabilities, including agent-based task orchestration, retrieval-augmented approaches, and modular tool integration. While these workflows are still under development, they represent a key direction for enabling scalable, human-in-the-loop biocuration. These findings suggest that targeted AI enablement can accelerate responsible adoption in biocuration while maintaining the rigor required for high-quality biomedical data stewardship.

title: Standardizing Cross-Species Transcriptomics Experimental Metadata using OBI and spaCy
authors: Moya Zouhon, Smith College, United States; Hayley Ma, Smith College, United States; Jade Lilian Palosky, Smith College, United States; Halie Rando, Smith College, United States
abstract: Repository-scale analyses often use metadata to select relevant projects. However, because metadata is semi-structured with many sections entered as free text, representations similar ideas can be represented very differently in different entries. In particular, we noticed that different terminology is used to describe experiments in humans compared to animal models. To address this problem, we developed an approach to classify and standardize descriptions of sequencing methods in human and mouse transcriptomics experiments that are uploaded to the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The first step was to construct a KnowledgeBase using the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (OBI). The OBI was filtered to identify sequencing-related root terms, and those terms and their descendants were integrated into a spaCy KnowledgeBase to facilitate disambiguation. Each OBI concept was represented in the KnowledgeBase as a single entity, along with associated synonyms, vector representations, and a prior probability of 1.0. Next, study metadata was combined into a single text corpus per study and preprocessed. We used two complementary strategies to match terms: first, the KnowledgeBase was loaded into the spaCy pipeline with an entity_ruler placed before named entity recognition (NER), allowing us to annotate each entity by matching study text to KnowledgeBase aliases; then, we also used Pythonâ€™s difflib package to implement fuzzy matching that captured near-misses. For each entity detected, the GSE ID, matched text, label, OBI ID, and confidence score of the match were recorded. Finally, annotated entities were mapped back to studies, allowing us to group studies by shared OBI identifiers and for the identification of similar experimental methods across differences in terminology. Mapping metadata back to OBI IDs is an important first step towards standardizing and quantifying the methodological similarity of studies that may use very different terminology. Our method allows us to compare metadata across species, with the goal of improving our understanding of model organism research and its limitations.

title: ChEBI 2.0: A robust foundation for future development
authors: Adnan Malik, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Muhammad Arsalan, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Carlos Moreno, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Juan Mosquera, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Eloy Félix, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Tevfik Kizilören, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Barbara Zdrazil, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Andrew R Leach, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom; Noel M O'Boyle, EMBL-EBI, United Kingdom
abstract: ChEBI (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chebi/) was first released in 2004 and is widely used by numerous biological databases and ontologies as a chemical registration system and for compound identification and information. The resource serves as a human-expert curated source for chemical structures, nomenclature, metabolite species data, and database cross-references. It provides links to several domain-specific data resources including Gene Ontology, PDBe, UniProt, MetaboLights, Reactome, Rhea, BioModels, and Europe PMC, amongst several others. ChEBI's ontology defines a hierarchical classification system for chemical entities, where relationships between chemical entities or classes of chemical entities are specified. Here we describe work carried out since 2022 to fundamentally overhaul and update the underlying infrastructure of ChEBI in order to address performance and stability issues, and difficulties in maintaining the existing architecture and codebase. This includes its website, web-services, search capabilities, downloadable files, and submission/curation interfaces. New data pipelines were deployed that leverage GitLab CI/CD for improved automation and issue detection. In 2025, the new ChEBI infrastructure went live replacing the legacy system, a critical step in ensuring the long-term sustainability of the resource for the global bioinformatics community and beyond. As of release 251, ChEBI 2.0 contains >202,000 entries of which 62,000 are manually curated, consisting of natural products, synthetic compounds, atoms, subatomic particles and mixtures.

title: Biomarker Knowledge Graph for Multi-Disease Biomarker Discovery and Translational Insights
authors: Maria Kim, George Washington University, United States; Jeet Vora, George Washington University, United States; Cyrus Au Yeung, George Washington University, United States; Rene Ranzinger, University of Georgia, United States; Raja Mazumder, George Washington University, United States
abstract: Biomarker data is dispersed across data sources, impeding discovery and hypothesis generation. To address the lack of standardization and data integration of biomarkers, we have developed BiomarkerKB, a Common Fund Data Ecosystem (CFDE) sponsored knowledgebase designed to harmonize, integrate, and contextualize biomarker data under a standardized data model. The current BiomarkerKB release covers more than 200K unique biomarkers, spanning over 1100 conditions. In parallel, we have developed a Biomarker Knowledge Graph, a CFDE-supported knowledge graph focused on clinically relevant biomarkers from BiomarkerKB and integrating molecular, cellular, and clinical-level biomarker data to support translational research and hypothesis generation across disease areas. The knowledge graph comprises more than 300,000 nodes and 1.2 million edges, enabling structured exploration of biomarker relationships within CFDE data. Biomarker Knowledge Graph allows the user to deduce new facts from existing relationships rather than just recalling stored data. A controlled vocabulary was developed to avoid duplication of biomarker data, and we used our standardized data as nodes and edges to construct the knowledge graph, thus enabling the data to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). Thanks to Biomarker Knowledge Graph (https://github.com/clinical-biomarkers/Knowledge-Graph), clinicians and researchers can identify biological patterns of biomarkers (freely available at data.biomarkerkb.org), their interconnections, and use this knowledge in clinical and research practices, such as identifying biomarkers shared across multiple diseases, uncovering complex multi-biomarker disease signatures, and linking biomarkers to pathways, immune responses, and potential therapeutic targets.

title: CAMERA: A Centralized Public Resource for Validated Alternative Methods to Support Regulatory Decision-Making
authors: Trey Saddler, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Alexander Cole, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Katie Needham, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Prince Osei-Akyeampong, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Tubosun Abioye, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Ricardo Tieghi, US National Institutes of Health, United States; Jeremiah Mensah, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Caleb DeGroote, Dynanet Corporation, United States; Helena Hoegberg-Durdock, US National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: The Collection of Alternative Methods for Regulatory Application (CAMERA) is a publicly accessible bioinformatics platform providing streamlined access to validated new approach methodologies (NAMs) for chemical and biological safety assessment. Federal agencies identified a critical need for a unified computational resource integrating validated alternative test methods to support reduced animal testing initiatives. CAMERA consolidates validated NAMs for human-relevant endpoints including skin sensitization, irritation, eye irritation, and corrosion from OECD-accepted test guidelines. We developed a structured ontological knowledge representation system extracting and harmonizing key metadata from validation reports: test method type, predicted endpoint, measured effect, test system, related key events, chemical applicability domain, validating organization, reference chemicals, and performance metrics. Controlled vocabularies and semantic mappings across alternative terminology enable consistent knowledge organization and cross-system interoperability. The platform architecture enables filtered searches by method type, endpoint, and regulatory agency, with side-by-side method comparisons. Custom visualization options are available for comparing reference chemicals and performance metrics. Interoperability with the Integrated Chemical Environment and the Adverse Outcome Pathway Wiki provides enhanced chemical characterization and mechanistic toxicity information, linking CAMERA's structured knowledge graph to broader regulatory and biological ontology ecosystems. User testing demonstrated strong support for CAMERA's ability to streamline NAM identification and enable method comparison. The platform significantly enhances transparency and facilitates consistent NAM application in chemical safety evaluation. Ongoing development will expand method domains, strengthen interoperability with computational toxicology tools, integrate large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence to enhance ontology-driven data extraction and user experience, and incorporate feedback from stakeholders to enhance utility for regulatory decision-making and modernized toxicology approaches.

title: dbCAN-HGM: CAZyme gene clusters in gut microbiomes of diverse human populations
authors: Yuchen Yan, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, United States; Yanbin Yin, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, United States
abstract: CAZymes (Carbohydrate Active EnZymes) play key metabolic functions in human gut microbiomes (HGM). Genes of glycan degrading CAZymes often form physically linked CAZyme Gene Clusters (CGCs) in gut bacterial genomes. Here we developed dbCAN-HGM (https://pro.unl.edu/dbCAN_HGM), a comprehensive data repository for human gut bacterial CGCs and CAZymes. dbCAN-HGM has the following unique features: (i) 121 883 CGCs are identified in 6031 high-quality species-level representative metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs), from a wide range of human populations, especially the under-studied African population; (ii) Each CGC page includes metagenomic read mapping results from different diets (vegan, vegetarian, omnivore, flexitarian) and disease statuses (ulcerative colitis [UC and Crohns disease), with interactive coverage plot and Jbrowse alignment tracks; (iii) CGCs are clustered with 1358 polysaccharide utilization loci into CGC families (CGC-Fs) to infer glycan substrates; (iv) Metadata and visualization are available for CGC-Fs by substrate, taxonomy, host geographic distribution, and top abundant CAZyme families; (v) CGCs are fully annotated with CAZymes, transporters, signal transduction proteins, transcriptional factors, sulfatases, peptidases, Pfam families, and protein 3D structure comparison results for unannotated proteins; and (vi) User-friendly and highly interactive web interface is provided for easy browsing and downloading of HGM genomes, CGCs, CGC-Fs by glycan substrates and continents.

title: KoMbine: statistical and systematic uncertainties on Kaplan-Meier curves
authors: Jeffrey Roskes, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Every measurement comes with statistical uncertainties, arising from the finite data sample, and systematic uncertainties, from errors in the measurement or model. Biomedical analyses typically account only for the statistical uncertainty from the number of patients. These are reported as p-values, power calculations, and other similar metrics. As datasets grow and this statistical uncertainty shrinks, it is not necessarily the dominant uncertainty anymore. For example, if patients are stratified by a density of a certain cell type, that measurement is affected by both the Poisson error on the number of cells and various systematic errors in the measurement of the cell density, which can move patients across the threshold. We developed the KoMbine package to propagate these uncertainties to Kaplan-Meier survival curves. KoMbine uses a mixed integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) formulation to find the best-fit Kaplan-Meier curve and its error bands. We processed mIF slides using the AstroPath platform and found two biomarkers whose densities predict patient response and survival. We estimated the statistical uncertainties from the number of patients and from the number of cells, as well as the systematic uncertainty from flatfielding, both before and after correction, and propagated them to the Kaplan-Meier curves. Our work in this area has been adopted as part of the "best practices" recommendations in imaging by the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer, and our goal is to bring a greater awareness and formal treatment of systematic uncertainties into the broader bioinformatics community.

title: nf-report: A highly customizable reporting plugin for Nextflow
authors: Junxuan Gao, Roche, Canada
abstract: Nextflow is a powerful workflow system used by researchers and institutions across the world to enable scalable and reproducible workflows. However, while Nextflow is exceptional at orchestrating tasks, its native reporting and logging capability can sometimes be insufficient especially when processing multiple samples in the same run. We present nf-report, a Nextflow plugin that enables a sample-oriented view of your pipeline run. While standard Nextflow reports provide information on each individual tasks and processes, the critical question in a production environment is often ""What happened to Sample A"". With only the task status report, bioinformaticians often have to manually comb through the execution logs to gather information related to each sample. nf-report automates this by grouping execution data by sample identity, providing an immediate view of which samples have completed, failed, or retried. The plugin can extract sample information from both the tag associated with a task and the meta map - a common idiom used in many Nextflow pipelines where the sample information is provided in a map that is passed to a process along with the data. The nf-report plugin is also highly customizable with support for JSON, TSV, and HTML report formats. Contents within the report can be further customized via a template so both the content and the graphical interface of report can be tailored to the technical and branding needs of each institution. In conclusion, the nf-report plugin provides pipeline developers with a ""plug-and-play"" way to add sample-level monitoring to their Nextflow pipelines without cluttering the workflow code. Developers can keep their pipeline scripts focused on the data logic while still providing users with high-quality summaries.

title: Opening the Data Journey: Making Data Harmonization Transparent and Reproducible
authors: Mete Akdogan, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Matthew Horridge, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Marcos Martínez-Romero, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Mark Musen, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States
abstract: Reproducibility in biomedical research depends not only on open code, but on open processes. Data harmonization, that is, aligning datasets to a common schema, is a prerequisite for data reuse and integration, yet is an often opaque step in research pipelines. When harmonization logic relies on custom undocumented scripts or domain specific tools, the decisions made are invisible to consumers. This opacity conflicts with the bioinformatics communityâ€™s shift toward open science. We present an open-source, integrated environment for transparent and reproducible data harmonization (https://github.com/bmir-radx/harmonization-ui-angular). The system represents transformations as primitive operations defined as discrete, composable, and human-readable functions. Crucially, every transformation decision is audit-logged and serialized, making the entire harmonization journey open and inspectable alongside the code itself. This approach guarantees the reproducibility of the entire workflow, from the software to the data transformations. An interactive interface allows data wranglers to define mappings between source and target data dictionaries, construct and preview harmonization rules, and apply them without custom scripting. The environment handles any tabular data and has been deployed within the NIH RADx Data Hub â€“ a production-level platform that integrates data from more than 100 US organizations across nearly 200 distinct studies â€“ demonstrating real-world biomedical impact. The implementation is fully documented and runnable. Ongoing work includes expanding the library of primitives, formal usability evaluation, and testing on diverse biomedical datasets. We welcome community contributions from researchers working on data interoperability, and we see this work as a contribution to open science infrastructure beyond just open code.

title: bsaseq: A Python package for bulk segregant analysis and QTL mapping from pooled sequencing data
authors: Arun S. Seetharam, Purdue University, United States; Adedayo O. Adeyanju, Purdue University, United States; Tesfaye T. Tesso, Purdue University, United States
abstract: Background: Bulk segregant analysis (BSA) combined with whole-genome sequencing has become a standard approach for rapid QTL mapping in plant genetics and model organism research. However, existing software tools present significant barriers including complex installation requirements, lack of command-line interfaces, and limited support for modern workflow management systems. These limitations hinder reproducibility and accessibility for researchers with varying computational expertise. Results: We present bsaseq, a Python package providing a complete workflow for BSA from variant call format (VCF) input to ranked candidate genes. The package implements sliding window analysis with tricube kernel smoothing, calculates both Z-scores and G-statistics for significance testing, and generates publication-quality visualizations. bsaseq features a comprehensive command-line interface with input validation, progress reporting, and informative error messages. The tool supports multi-sample bulk pooling, both recessive and dominant inheritance modes, and optional functional annotation via snpEff integration. We validated bsaseq using two data sets from the male sterility trait Sorghum bicolor and nematode resistance in Oryza sativa, successfully identifying the ms8 causal locus on sorghum chromosome 4 (Xiao et al. 2025) and the nematode resistance QTL on rice chromosome 11 (Lahari et al. 2019). The package is distributed via PyPI, Bioconda, and Docker, with integration templates for Nextflow and Snakemake workflow managers. Conclusions: bsaseq provides an accessible, reproducible, and actively maintained solution for BSA that addresses key limitations of existing tools. Its modern packaging, comprehensive documentation, and workflow manager integration make it suitable for both interactive analysis and large-scale production pipelines on high-performance computing systems.

title: Governance as a Service: A GA4GH-Compliant Open Platform for Federated Biomedical Data Access
authors: Susheel Varma, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Ann Novakowski, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Orion Banks, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Alberto Pepe, Sage Bionetworks, United States; John Wilbanks, John Wilbanks, United States; Christine Suver, Sage Bionetworks, United States
abstract: Researchers navigating multi-institutional biomedical studies face fragmented data access governance: each repository maintains distinct Data Access Committee (DAC) processes, bespoke request forms, and incompatible authorisation systems. This fragmentation creates significant barriers to cross-institutional research, particularly across Accelerating Medicines Partnership (AMP) programmes requiring approvals from multiple independent DACs. We present Governance as a Service (GaaS), an open-source platform designed to decouple data access governance from underlying storage infrastructure, enabling federated policy execution across institutions. GaaS implements GA4GH standards throughout: Data Use Ontology (DUO) for machine-readable access conditions, GA4GH Passports and Visas for portable researcher credentials, and a novel Data Access Request Service API and a Visa Issuer Service API filling critical gaps in the current specification landscape. The platform introduces a unified Data Access Request form structured around the Five Safes framework (Safe People, Safe Projects, Safe Data, Safe Settings, Safe Outputs), replacing institution-specific forms with a single standardised interface. A matchmaking algorithm routes requests to appropriate DACs based on DUO-annotated dataset metadata, while supporting single, consortium, and fully federated DAC governance models. The platform architecture comprises four interoperable microservices, with three accompanying draft GA4GH specifications proposed for community adoption: Visa Issuer Service, Data Access Request Service, and Agent Passports. Pilots are planned across Sage data portals (ADKP, ALSKP, CCKP, NF) with SDE/TRE integrations. GaaS will enable institutions to retain full governance authority while researchers experience a unified access process. By making governance computable through open standards, the platform transforms data access from an administrative bottleneck into a scalable, auditable service.

title: Microsatellites Made Accessible: An Open-Source Tool for Microsatellite Data Analysis
authors: Nargiz Akhmetova, Smith College, United States; Ruize Qin, Smith College, United States; Halie Rando, Smith College, United States
abstract: Microsatellites, or short tandem repeats, are repetitive sequences of DNA (e.g., AGAGAG). Repetitive sequences are prone to errors during DNA replication, and this high rate of mutation means that the number of repeats can change on a short time scale, making microsatellites useful for illuminating relationships between populations. Additionally, microsatellites can be amplified from low-quality samples and at low cost, making them an attractive option for non-invasive sampling, especially in wildlife studies and conservation genetics. Analysis of microsatellites typically involves annealing a fluorescent probe onto a fragment that is analyzed alongside a control sample of known sizes, known as a size standard. The positions of fluorescent peaks relative to the peaks of the size standard are used to estimate the number of repeats at a given locus. However, the format used to encode these peaks presents challenges to open and reproducible research. Typically, these data are analyzed using proprietary software such as GeneMapper. The data must be manually inspected by trained researchers to call the fluorescent peaks. This type of closed, platform-specific workflow is expensive and difficult to automate, while limiting reproducibility. Existing open-source tools only partially decode or visualize the data. Here, we present a Python pipeline that decodes binary ABIF files from Applied Biosystems capillary sequencers and exports raw fluorescence traces, size standards, and run metadata into a stable CSV format for downstream quantitative analysis and machine-learningâ€“based allele calling. Our aim is to provide an open-source tool that exposes the full electropherogram and metadata to allow integration with standard data-science and machine-learning workflows. Methodologically, we treat each ABIF file as a structured binary stream with a header, directory entries, and data blocks. The program parses the header, walks the directory to locate data, and decodes blocks into numeric and character values, retaining intensity traces, size-standard channels, and technical metadata such as batch identifiers. The extraction logic is modular so that the same code can run across many files in a project, and the decoded structures are assembled into data frames, written to CSV, and optionally plotted to visualize peak shapes and size-standard alignment. The current implementation successfully decodes representative ABIF files and exports machine-readable tables suitable for automated analysis. We are now using these outputs to engineer features from individual peaks and to train and evaluate machine-learning classifiers that predict alleles directly from raw fluorescence patterns. By replacing proprietary, manual allele calling with an open, automated pipeline, this work has the potential to reduce cost and human effort and to improve reproducibility of studies using microsatellites.

title: EGAfetch: an ultra-fast download client for the European Genome-phenome Archive
authors: Aziz Khan, MBZUAI, United Arab Emirates
abstract: The European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA) (https://ega-archive.org/) is one of the largest repositories of controlled-access human genomic and phenomic data, hosting thousands of datasets comprising petabytes of sequencing data. The official Python-based download client, pyEGA3, processes files sequentially over a single network stream, resulting in slow data transfers. Here we present EGAfetch, a command-line tool written in Go that enables fast, parallel, and resumable downloads from EGA. EGAfetch implements a two-level parallelism strategy, simultaneously downloading multiple files, with each file split into independently fetched chunks, achieving faster downloads than pyEGA3. A deterministic state machine governs each file's lifecycle with atomic state persistence, ensuring that interrupted downloads resume precisely from the last downloaded byte without data loss or corruption. Additional features include automatic OAuth2 token refresh, checksum verification, bandwidth throttling, adaptive chunk sizing, file filtering, batch identifier file input, structured metadata export compatible with Portable Encapsulated Project (PEP), and a persistent configuration file. EGAfetch is open source and distributed as a single statically linked binary with no runtime dependencies, making it particularly well-suited for deployment on HPC clusters and cloud environments. EGAfetch source code is freely available at https://github.com/khan-lab/EGAfetch under the Apache 2.0 license, and documentation is available at https://khanlab.bio/EGAfetch.

title: The Bioinformatics Resource Centers (BRC) for Infectious Diseases Program: Accelerating Infectious Disease Research through Bioinformatics
authors: Wiriya Rutvisuttinunt, National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases, United States; Inka Sastalla, National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases, United States; Keehwan Kwon, National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases, United States; Liliana Brown, National Institute of Allergies and Infectious Diseases, United States
abstract: The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) has supported innovative infectious disease research through the Bioinformatics Resource Centers (BRC) program since 2004. By providing access to advanced computational tools, knowledgebases, and expertise, the BRC program has enabled researchers to share data, collaborate on projects, and drive innovation in infectious disease research. Focusing on NIAID's priority research areas, the BRC program has fostered innovation, flexibility, and community feedback through publicly accessible infectious disease knowledgebases. This has led to the development of novel algorithms, facilitated collaboration, and accelerated the discovery of new treatments, vaccines, and diagnostics. In response to emerging needs and outbreaks, the BRC Program continues to provide critical infrastructure for integrated infectious disease knowledgebases, advanced bioinformatics technologies, training, community outreach, and bioinformatics support. In 2024, The program has awarded funding to three institutions in 2024: the University of Chicago's Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), Pennsylvania State University's Bioinformatics Resource Analytics Center (BRC.analytics), and the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics' The Pathogen Data Network (PDN). These new centers will expand the program's bioinformatics resources and expertise, supporting infectious disease research and public health initiatives. The BRC Program has made significant contributions to infectious disease research, with over 17 million annotated microbial genomes, thousands of transcriptomics datasets, and billions of genes and proteins. Through extensive outreach activities, including 160 workshops, online resources, and open forums, the BRC Program has delivered over 9 million bioinformatics services, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration across academia, industry, and government. This has enabled the development of novel algorithms, facilitated collaboration, and accelerated discoveries in infectious disease research. With a global user base of over 71,000 and 30,000 publication citations, the BRCs have become a vital resource, driving scientific progress for infectious disease research.

title: ad-kg: An Open-Source Knowledge Graph Pipeline for Alzheimer's Disease Drug Repurposing
authors: Leonardo Apolonio United States
abstract: Drug repurposing for Alzheimer's disease (AD) is hindered by the fragmentation of biomedical evidence across pharmacovigilance databases, clinical trial registries, genetic association catalogs, and the primary literature. We present ad-kg, a fully open-source Python pipeline that integrates four public data sources into a queryable Neo4j knowledge graph to surface drug repurposing candidates - with an initial focus on GLP-1 receptor agonists and metabolic pathway drugs. The pipeline runs in five reproducible stages. The ingest stage fetches biomedical abstracts (PubMed / NCBI E-utilities), trial metadata (ClinicalTrials.gov API v2), genetic associations (GWAS Catalog / EBI REST), and adverse event reports (FDA FAERS / OpenFDA). The extract stage applies scispaCy (en_core_sci_lg + UMLS linker) for named entity recognition followed by Claude-powered relation extraction with prompt caching for throughput efficiency. The resolve stage embeds entities with allenai/specter2 and canonicalizes synonyms via HDBSCAN (cosine threshold 0.88) to produce a deduplicated entity inventory. The load stage merges nodes and edges idempotently into Neo4j 5 using APOC. The query stage exposes 11 named Cypher queries for drug repurposing analysis, including a whitespace_opportunity pattern - drugs with a protective FAERS signal and GWAS genetic support but no active AD trial - and a triple_convergence pattern requiring concordant evidence across all three sources. The entire stack runs locally via Docker Compose with no proprietary dependencies beyond an optional NCBI API key. All data sources are openly licensed. The pipeline is tested, type-annotated, and designed for extension to other disease areas or additional ingestion sources. Applied to AD, the pipeline recovers known GLP-1 candidates (semaglutide, liraglutide) that now have Phase 2-3 clinical trial support, and proposes additional metabolic pathway drugs with multi-source signal convergence but no current AD trial - a set not captured by literature search alone. ad-kg is available at https://github.com/leo-explainml/ad-kg/tree/main under the MIT license.

title: A conformationally metastable subproteome drives aging in C. elegans
authors: Xiaojing Sui, Northwestern University, United States; Rick Morimoto, Northwestern University, United States
abstract: Aging and neurodegeneration are characterized by protein homeostasis (proteostasis) decline. While the accumulation of aberrant proteins is a hallmark of aging, it remains unclear whether protein metastability is a passive byproduct of aging or an active, systemic driver of proteome-wide failure. Here, we employ state-of-the-art quantitative structural proteomics to map the conformational landscape of the proteome during early aging. We show that even before the onset of physiological decline, approximately one-third of the proteome undergoes significant structural changes. These conformationally altered proteins are preferentially ubiquitinated and accumulate on proteasomes, suggesting that stalled degradation is a primary bottleneck in age-associated proteostasis failure. Strikingly, we demonstrate that the expression of a single metastable protein is sufficient to trigger a global conformational collapse that mirrors the signature of natural aging. This systemic vulnerability is most pronounced in high-abundance proteins and those enriched in Î²-sheets or intrinsically disordered regions. Finally, we show that polyglutamine-mediated protein instability is sufficient to directly accelerate organismal aging. Our results reveal that the proteome is a highly interconnected structural network where localized metastability can act as a tipping point for systemic decline, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the onset of age-related proteotoxicity. We developed ProteinWhisper (https://proteinwhisperapp-g949efa9imn35reycubkov.streamlit.app/), an interactive web application designed for the comprehensive visualization and analysis of this complex proteomics dataset.

title: How important are dark kinases?
authors: Marzieh Ayati, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, United States; Mark Chance, Case Western Reserve University, United States; Mehmet Koyuturk, Case Western Reserve University, United States
abstract: Protein kinases play central roles in all aspects of cellular regulation, and are major drug targets, particularly in oncology and inflammatory diseases. Despite their biological significance and functional diversity, research attention across the kinome remains highly uneven. This raise concerns on the role of computational biology in driving biological discoveries, as algorithms may perpetuate existing bias in kinase biology. A major contributor to bias in kinase biology is the number of known phosphorylated substrates per kinase. While some kinases are extensively studied with hundreds of known substrates, many others are considered "dark" due to having few annotated substrates. Because To investigate the biological significance and therapeutic potential of "dark" kinases, we systematically analyze 522 human kinases, by integrating multiple datasources including kinase-substrate associations, disease associations, and drug-target interactions. Our analysis demonstrates that many dark kinases exhibit regulatory features, show disease or phenotype associations, and are linked to drugs or chemical perturbagens. These findings suggest that limited substrate knowledge of kinase often reflects limited phosphoproteomic coverage rather than biological or therapeutic insignificance. Our results highlight how the design and validation of algorithms based on substrate-centric metrics systematically bias research focus and limits the ability of algorithms in discovery of novel kinases. We conclude that integrating heterogeneous data is key to overcoming bias and uncovering the full potential of the human kinome.

title: HLA Class I Presentation is Independent of Protein Abundance
authors: Badri Mishra, UCLA- Department of Biological Chemistry, United States; Hee Jong Kim, UCLA -Department of Biological Chemistry, United States; James Wohlschlegel, UCLA- Department of Biological Chemistry, United States
abstract: HLA Class I molecules present peptides to CD8+ T cells for immune surveillance. A common assumption in antigen prediction is that proteins harboring more binding motifs or expressed at higher abundance would contribute disproportionately to the immunopeptidome. We tested this hypothesis using mass spectrometry-based immunopeptidomics. We performed immunopeptidomics using data-dependent and data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry on 293F cells expressing defined HLA alleles. We analyzed 6 HLA Class I alleles including A01:01, A02:01, A11:01, and A23:01, identifying over 20,000 unique peptides mapping to more than 5,000 source proteins. For each allele, we derived position-specific binding motifs from 9-mer peptides based on anchor residue frequencies. We then scanned the human proteome to calculate motif density per protein and integrated matched whole-cell proteomic abundance data from 9,934 quantified proteins. Across all 6 HLA alleles tested, we found no significant correlation between binding motif density and protein abundance. Proteins with high predicted motif counts showed similar abundance distributions to those with few motifs. Mean motif density remained flat across abundance bins spanning four orders of magnitude. This pattern held consistently regardless of allele-specific anchor residue preferences. HLA Class I peptide presentation is not driven by simple relationships between motif availability and protein expression. Factors including antigen processing, protein turnover, and subcellular localization likely determine which peptides reach the cell surface. These findings suggest that neoantigen prediction algorithms should not weight candidates primarily by expression level alone.

title: Comprehensive Single-Cell Atlas Reveals Cellular Signatures Across Skin Immune Diseases
authors: Siqi Sun, AbbVie, United States; Yu Hu, AbbVie, United States; Shweta Yadav, AbbVie, United States; Yujia Wang, AbbVie, United States; Kathleen Smith, AbbVie, United States; Neha Chaudhary, AbbVie, United States; Elizaveta Leshchiner, AbbVie, United States; Jing Wang, AbbVie, United States; Dan Chang, AbbVie, United States; Naim Mahi, AbbVie, United States
abstract: Understanding cellular heterogeneity is critical for elucidating the pathogenesis of immune-mediated skin diseases. Here, we address the critical lack of large-scale, consistently annotated reference datasets by assembling a comprehensive, integrated single-cell skin atlas comprising approximately one million cells across six immune-related diseases: atopic dermatitis (AD), hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), psoriasis (PsO), alopecia areata, systemic sclerosis (SSc), and vitiligo. We curated 53 granular cell types encompassing immune, stromal, and epithelial compartments. Leveraging this well annotated atlas, both shared and disease-specific cellular features were identified, providing high-resolution insights into pathogenesis and immune dynamics across anatomical regions. We also developed skin-specific, fine-tuned models to facilitate robust and scalable cell type annotation. The annotation tools achieved high accuracy and strong precision, recall, and F1 performance across multiple datasets. Collectively, these resources provide a strong foundation for discovery of novel mechanisms, candidate biomarkers, and therapeutic targets in dermatological and immunological research.

title: Elucidating Immune Dysregulation in Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder through Bulk and Single-Cell RNA-seq Characterization of Interferon-Related Gene Expression
authors: Yi-Jen Chen, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taiwan; Kuo-Hsuan Chang, Chang Gung Memorial Hospital and Chang Gung University, Taiwan; Yu-Chao Wang, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taiwan
abstract: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system characterized by recurrent optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, often resulting in persistent neurological disability. Although type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling has been implicated in NMOSD pathogenesis, its dysregulation across specific immune cell subsets remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrated bulk RNA sequencing (bulk RNA-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) to characterize IFN-I–related transcriptional dysregulation and intercellular communication in NMOSD. Differential expression analysis across a discovery PBMC cohort and an independent whole-blood cohort, using limma-voom, edgeR, and DESeq2, identified seven cross-cohort IFN-I–related differentially expressed genes (DEGs): ISG15, IFI6, CMPK2, LY6E, and OASL were upregulated, whereas AKAP12 and TNFRSF13C were downregulated. ScRNA-seq analysis further mapped these IFN-I–related DEGs to specific immune cell subsets, showing increased ISG15 in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, increased CMPK2 and OASL in CD8+ central memory T cells, and increased LY6E in CD8+ naive T cells in NMOSD. Notably, TNFRSF13C showed the strongest increase in naive B cells despite being downregulated in bulk RNA-seq. To investigate this discrepancy, we performed CellChat analysis and found enhanced BAFF–BAFFR signaling toward naive B cells, with conventional dendritic cell 2 (cDC2) identified as a prominent inferred upstream sender. Overall, our findings define a cross-cohort IFN-I–related gene signature, localize its dysregulation to specific PBMC subsets, and highlight the BAFF–BAFFR axis and inferred cDC2-to-naive B-cell communication as candidate contributors to immune dysregulation in NMOSD.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning Reveals Sex-Biased Immune Gene Signatures for Pre-Exposure Prediction of Symptomatic Influenza
authors: Tsung-Hsien Lin, National Taiwan Ocean University, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Taiwan; Zhi-Jian Cheng, National Taiwan Ocean University, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Taiwan; Kuan Y. Chang, National Taiwan Ocean University, Taiwan
abstract: Motivation Seasonal influenza A viruses (H1N1 and H3N2) cause between 3 and 5 million severe cases and up to 650,000 deaths annually. Despite widespread exposure, only 40% to 45% of individuals develop symptomatic infection, a variation partially governed by host transcriptomic states prior to viral exposure. While the DeepFlu model—a six-layer deep learning architecture—predicts symptomatic outcomes from pre-exposure gene expression with high accuracy, its "black-box" nature often obscures the underlying biological logic. This study utilizes SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) method, to systematically decipher the individual gene impacts driving DeepFlu's predictions for H1N1 and H3N2 infections. Methods The analysis used pre-exposure peripheral blood transcriptomic profiles from two public datasets, GSE52428 and GSE73072, representing healthy volunteers who were challenged with influenza. Symptomatic infection was defined as a cumulative modified Jackson score of at least 6 points over 5 days. We tested various multi-layer perceptron configurations using leave-one-person-out (L1PO) cross-validation to simulate a clinically realistic predictive scenario. Feature attribution was performed via DeepExplainer to assign importance scores to each gene, followed by Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment and differential expression analysis to validate the biological relevance of the top SHAP-selected features. Results L1PO cross-validation on pre-exposure data demonstrated robust predictive performance, with the optimal H3N2 model achieving an AUROC of 0.847. SHAP analysis consistently identified a core signature of five genes across independent datasets: HLA-DQA1, HLA-DQB1, XIST, RPS4Y1, and KDM5D. These markers are fundamentally linked to immune function and biological sex. Higher expression of the female-specific marker XIST, combined with lower expression of the male-specific markers RPS4Y1 and KDM5D, was associated with high SHAP values, suggesting that females may have a greater transcriptomic susceptibility to symptomatic influenza. Furthermore, low HLA-DQB1 expression was associated with an increased risk, and GO enrichment analysis revealed a significant enrichment in the MHC class II protein complex and antigen presentation pathways. Crucially, the top SHAP-identified genes did not align with traditional univariate differential expression at the pre-exposure baseline. This disconnect highlights the deep learning model's distinct capacity to capture nonlinear, high-order interactive biological signals that standard transcriptomic analyses overlook. Conclusion This study demonstrates that the decision-making logic of deep learning models in infectious disease research can be rendered transparent and biologically grounded through XAI. Our findings reveal that pre-exposure sex-linked transcriptional markers and immune response genes are critical determinants of influenza susceptibility. The integration of SHAP with the DeepFlu model provides a testable genetic signature for symptomatic risk, paving the way for personalized risk stratification and targeted prophylactic interventions. This approach bridges the gap between black-box computational prediction and actionable systems immunology.

title: Decoding the Adipose-Cutaneous Axis: Computational Multi-Organ Integration Reveals Obese Subcutaneous Adipose Tissue as a Systemic Incubator for Psoriatic Th17 Cells
authors: Sai Nikhith Cholleti, University of Hyderabad, India; Prof. Vaibhav Vindal, University of Hyderabad, India
abstract: Epidemiological data strongly link obesity to psoriasis severity and biologic therapy resistance, yet the cellular mechanisms driving this metabolic-autoimmune comorbidity remain obscure. We hypothesized that obese subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) actively manufactures pathogenic immune effectors rather than passively leaking generalized inflammation. To test this, we performed a large-scale computational integration of independent single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) cohorts, encompassing lean and obese human SAT alongside a continuum of cutaneous biopsies (healthy, non-lesional, and lesional psoriasis). By applying advanced receptor-ligand network modeling and targeted module scoring, we mapped conserved inter-tissue immunological trajectories. Our in silico models revealed a profound, myeloid-driven restructuring within the obese SAT microenvironment. Intercellular communication analysis identified a specific adipokine-mediated signaling circuit (CAP1/LEPR) that triggers recruited monocytes and dendritic cells to synthesize a Th17-polarizing cytokine triad (IL6, TGFB1, IL23A). Consequently, the adipose T cell compartment undergoes massive pathogenic polarization; we quantified a more than two-fold expansion of the localized Th17 reservoir (from 2.5% in lean to 5.4% in obese SAT). Crucially, these adipose-generated effectors acquired a definitive skin-homing transcriptomic signature, robustly co-expressing CCR6 and IL17A. This systemic, generative expansion within the fat directly parallels the pathogenic effector accumulation observed in the active psoriatic skin cohorts. By computationally resolving this cross-organ crosstalk, we uncover that obese SAT acts as a primary, systemic manufacturing hub for autoimmune effectors. These findings fundamentally reframe the therapeutic landscape for obesity-associated autoimmune diseases, establishing the adipose microenvironment as a critical target for durable clinical remission.

title: Extending PARAFAC2-RISE to scATAC-seq Reveals Immune Programs Governing Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Response in Melanoma
authors: Andrew Ramirez, Rutgers University-New Brunswick, United States; Jackie Yang, Rutgers University-New Brunswick, United States
abstract: Standard single-cell analyses rely on matrix factorization, which flattens the natural multi-dimensional structure of data across cells, samples, and modalities, conflating biologically meaningful sources of variation. RISE, an unsupervised tensor decomposition framework based on PARAFAC2, addresses this limitation by preserving multi-dimensional structure and identifying cell- and sample-specific patterns without requiring predefined annotations or reference atlases. Previously validated for scRNA-seq, we extend RISE to scATAC-seq. We apply this extended single-cell tensor framework to investigate immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) resistance in metastatic melanoma, where survival has improved dramatically yet the majority of patients still fail to respond. We leverage a unique cohort comprising of tumor samples from metastatic melanoma patients stratified by ICI response. Using RISE maximizes the potential to discover novel cell states that would be missed by annotation-dependent methods. By applying RISE to scATAC-seq of these melanoma samples, we identify immune cell states and their epigenetic drivers linked to ICI outcome, uncovering coordinated immune cell programs that matrix-based approaches would obscure, with prioritized candidates poised for experimental validation.

title: Expanding the Human T-Cell Receptor Germline Reference through Pangenome-Based Discovery of 778 Novel Alleles using the gAIRR Suite
authors: Yu-Hui Lin, Department of Medical Genetics, National Taiwan University Hospital, Taiwan; Pei-Lung Chen, Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics, College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taiwan; Yu-Hsuan Yang, Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics, College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taiwan; Kuan-Ta Huang, Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics, College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taiwan; Mao-Jan Lin, Department of Computer Science, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: The adaptive immune receptor repertoire (AIRR) is central to adaptive immunity, yet accurate AIRR profiling depends on comprehensive germline gene references. To systematically identify germline genes encoding AIRR (gAIRR), we developed the gAIRR Suite, a framework integrating computational allele discovery from phased diploid genome assemblies (gAIRR-annotate) with orthogonal validation through targeted sequencing (gAIRR-seq) and variant calling (gAIRR-call). Applied to 47 Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) Release 1 assemblies, this framework yielded 335 novel T-cell receptor (TR) alleles with full orthogonal validation. We next applied gAIRR-annotate to 232 HPRC Release 2 assemblies, a superset encompassing all Release 1 samples with expanded global representation. Core-region analysis identified 305 novel alleles (277 TRV, 27 TRJ, and 1 TRD). Integration of flanking-sequence context further discovered an additional 138 alleles (84 TRV, 52 TRJ, and 2 TRD) that were indistinguishable by core sequence alone, bringing the Release 2 total to 443. Orthogonal validation for Release 2 alleles is ongoing. Across Releases 1 and 2, we identified 778 novel TR alleles, substantially expanding known TR germline diversity and increasing TRV, TRJ, and TRD representation by 200.6%, 113.4%, and 50.0% over the current International ImMunoGeneTics (IMGT) reference, respectively. We also established a comprehensive database of flanking sequences and recombination signal sequences (RSS) to optimize downstream immunogenomic analyses. As pangenome projects continue to expand, the gAIRR Suite provides a scalable framework for iterative reference updates toward a more complete catalog of human TR germline variation.

title: Host proteins associated with strong neutralizing SARS-CoV-2 antibody responses in a South African cohort
authors: Afrah Khairallah, Africa Health Research Institute, South Africa
abstract: High-dimensional biological data are increasingly central to health research, enabling the identification of biomarkers, immune correlates of protection, and molecular mechanisms underlying disease. In African research settings, where cohorts are highly diverse and burdened by endemic infectious diseases, scalable bioinformatics approaches are critical for integrating and analysing such data to advance discovery. Here, we investigated host proteins associated with SARS-CoV-2 neutralising antibody responses in a South African cohort during first infection. Seventy-one participants were enrolled, including individuals with moderate disease severity, 17 of whom required supplemental oxygen, but none were critically ill. Participants were stratified into high and low neutralisers based on convalescent plasma neutralisation capacity, with anti-spike antibody levels measured in parallel. Using large-scale SomaScanÂ® plasma proteomics generated early after diagnosis, we applied bioinformatics workflows to assess associations between host proteins and neutralisation, anti-spike responses, and disease severity using differential expression, pathway enrichment, and predictive modelling. The analyses identified host proteins associated with neutralisation capacity, spike-binding antibodies, and disease severity. Proteins linked to neutralisation showed strong concordance with spike-binding antibody responses (87%), but only partial overlap with disease severity (36%), highlighting the importance of separating protective immunity from clinical severity signals. Predictive modelling demonstrated that neutralisation status could be inferred from individual protein markers, with HSPA8 emerging as the strongest signal. HSPA8 is a molecular chaperone involved in viral protein interactions and antigen cross-presentation, highlighting a biologically plausible pathway shaping humoral immunity. This study revealed a distinct host proteomic program underlying neutralising antibody capacity that is strongly aligned with spike-binding responses and largely independent of disease severity.
