These findings provide new insights into host pathways that influence protective antibody responses and demonstrate the power of integrative computational analyses to extract biologically meaningful signals from high-dimensional omics data.

title: Benchmarking Differential Abundance Methods for Detecting Convergent Antibodies
authors: Caroline Sullivan, Program in Computational Biology and Biomedical Informatics, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA, United States; Zhaochen Ye, Program in Computational Biology and Biomedical Informatics, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA, United States; Gur Yaari, Department of Pathology, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, CT, USA, United States; Gisela Gabernet, Department of Pathology, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, CT, USA, United States; Steven H. Kleinstein, Department of Pathology, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, CT, USA, United States
abstract: B cells generate a diverse array of receptors through V(D)J recombination which then improve their affinity for antigen targets through affinity maturation. In individuals with a common immune exposure, such as infection, vaccination, or autoimmune disease, highly similar B cell receptors (BCRs) rare or absent in control populations have been observed, referred to here as â€œconvergentâ€ BCRs or antibodies. However, most existing approaches to identify convergent antibody sequences in BCR repertoire sequencing data lack statistical grounding and have not been validated on datasets containing ground-truth signal. Here we adapt two computational methods designed for identifying differentially abundant (DA) cell states in scRNA-Seq data to find convergent antibodies in BCR repertoires. We benchmarked these methods against an existing sequence similarity-based approach to identify convergent antibody sequences in ground-truth synthetic and publicly available experimental data. We show that DA methods applied to antibody representations based on large language models (LLMs) can effectively identify convergent antibodies in BCR repertoires. All three methods produce AUROC >= 0.9 given high frequency of convergent sequences in the repertoire but vary in sensitivity with decreased frequency, uneven sequencing depth, and decreased prevalence in the disease population. Our results highlight the potential for antibody LLM-based representations to widen the scope of computational methods that can be applied to find disease-enriched sequences in BCR repertoires. Identifying convergence may aid in the discovery of disease-specific antibodies, opening new opportunities in pathology research, drug discovery, and vaccine development.

title: Single-Cell Multi-Omics Reveals Subpopulation-Specific Transcriptomic Reprogramming of Pulmonary Monocyte/Macrophages Following Particulate Matter Exposure
authors: Rengul Cetin Atalay, University of Chicago, United States; Angelo M Meliton, University of Chicago, United States; Parker S Woods, University of Chicago, United States; Kun Woo D Shin, University of Chicago, United States; Robert Hamanaka, University of Chicago, United States; Gokhan M Mutlu, University of Chicago, United States
abstract: Particulate matter (PM2.5) air pollution causes 4.2 million premature deaths annually, primarily through cardiopulmonary disease. While PM dysregulates pulmonary immunity via mitochondrial ROS-dependent NF-ÎºB/NRF2 activation and IL-6-mediated thromboinflammation, the subpopulation-level transcriptional regulatory mechanisms underlying macrophage responses remain unresolved. How PM reshapes the heterogeneity and regulatory state of the pulmonary monocyte/macrophage compartment across exposure durations is unknown. Methods: C57BL/6J mice were exposed to ambient Chicago PM2.5 via a Versatile Aerosol Concentration Enrichment System (VACES) for 8 hours/day, 5 days/week at 3-day or 3-week durations. Filtered air (FA) controls received particle-free air through a Teflon-filtered VACES circuit. Two complementary transcriptomic approaches were employed: bulk RNA-seq from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) processed with Kallisto/EdgeR, and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) of CD45 enriched pulmonary immune cells processed with Cell Ranger, Seurat, and Scanpy. Transcription factor activity and pathway-level regulon analysis were inferred using DoRothEA and DecoupleR. Results: Unbiased scRNA-seq clustering resolved four transcriptionally distinct myeloid subpopulations: tissue-resident alveolar macrophages (TR-AMs), monocyte-derived alveolar macrophages (MoAMs), classical monocytes, and interstitial macrophages. Each exhibited unique, duration-dependent transcriptomic signatures with differential activation of inflammatory, metabolic, and oxidative stress programs. Bulk BAL RNA-seq corroborated these findings. Notably, MoAMs displayed the most pronounced transcriptional response, implicating them as key drivers of PM-induced pulmonary immune dysregulation. Conclusions: Integrating scRNA-seq with computational regulon inference, we identify subpopulation-specific regulatory mechanisms underlying PM-driven pulmonary immune remodeling, establishing a high-resolution framework for dissecting how environmental exposures perturb innate immune cell states with translational relevance to pollution-associated cardiopulmonary disease.

title: Blimp-1 shapes germinal center B cell clonal diversity by gating chromatin accessibility during light-to-dark zone transition
authors: Steven Gierlack, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Germinal center (GC) B cell responses are defined by many positive regulators of affinity maturation, but few components that restrain clonal dominance, notably Nr4a1, are known. We reveal an unsuspected role for PRDM1 (Blimp1), a plasma cell determinant, as a feedback regulator of affinity maturation. Single cell RNA-seq and B cell receptor (BCR)-seq showed that B cell specific Prdm1 loss drives an exaggerated GC reaction with larger clones, increased somatic hypermutation, and greater clonal dominance, independent of Nr4a1. Single cell chromatin profiling with base-resolution modeling indicated that Blimp-1 represses expression of BCR-signaling genes, gating chromatin accessibility at ISRE, EICE, NF-ÎºB, and Oct motifs. In the absence of Blimp-1, enhanced BCR signaling augments activities of transcription factors that promote G1â€“S transition during light-zone (LZ) selection and fuel dark-zone (DZ) expansion. Thus, Blimp-1 attenuates BCR signaling and constrains the LZ to DZ transition, fine-tuning clonal competition thereby maintaining repertoire diversity.

title: Single-cell long-read atlas of hippocampal SIV infection, antiretroviral treatment and chronic morphine exposure reveals cell-type-resolved splicing dysregulation
authors: Anoushka Joglekar, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Hagen Tilgner, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Lishomwa C Ndhlovu, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Teresa A Milner, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Howard Fox, University of Nebraska Medical Center, United States; Scott Bowler, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Matthew Parsons, Walter Reed Army Institute of Research, United States; Shaun Pollard, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Alina Pang, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Justine Hsu, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Careen Foord, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Yi He, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Shannon Callen, University of Nebraska Medical Center, United States; Julien Jarroux, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Shilpa Buch, University of Nebraska Medical Center, United States; Michael Corley, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Wen Hu, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States
abstract: Alternative splicing generates transcriptomic diversity in the brain and shapes cell-type-specific regulatory programs. For HIV, opioid exposure, and antiretroviral therapy (ART), prior studies often focus on the gene level, leaving splicing defects unresolved. We profile single-cell isoforms from macaque hippocampus upon SIV infection with/without ART, with/without chronic morphine exposure. We find >100 splicing events dysregulated by SIV, morphine, or their combination across neurons and glia. In contrast to similar work in Alzheimer's, SIV-induced splicing defects are of similar magnitude across neuron types and oligodendrocytes. In most brain cell types, most SIV-associated splicing dysregulation is rescued by ART. Strikingly, microglia show only a limited rescue effect. Importantly, a microglial sub-population associated with activation of interferon-stimulated genes harbors SIV-induced splicing dysregulation. Although ART rescues many SIV-dysregulated exons, it also produces widespread ART-specific splicing changes, including cryptic exon inclusion. These RNA defects occur on exons similarly used in human hippocampi. Chronic-morphine-induced splicing changes tend to converge with SIV on shared exons, with exon sets dysregulated by both SIV and morphine exhibiting distinct splicing patterns compared with those altered by SIV alone. Our findings establish a foundation for potentially complementing ART and place splicing at the forefront of HIV, ART and drug research in the brain.

title: Humora: Assessing Immune Repertoire Coverage in a Function-Aware Embedding Space
authors: Jiazheng Miao, Duke University, United States; Rohit Singh, Duke University, United States
abstract: B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire records an individual's history of immune exposures, and recent sequencing advances facilitate profiling them at scale. In principle, this enables antigen-agnostic discovery of disease-relevant antibodies by comparing repertoires between exposed and naive individuals. However, in practice, direct comparison is confounded by extensive clonal diversity across individuals, arising from genetics, exposure history, and batch effects. To address this challenge, we propose that the appropriate unit of analysis is the distribution rather than individual clones: responses to similar antigens may share little sequence overlap but occupy similar regions in a structure-function space. Here, we present Humora, a framework for analyzing BCR repertoire, which embeds BCRs using protein language models and represents each repertoire as a density over this function-aware manifold. Cross-individual comparison is performed by normalizing subject-specific variation through alignment to a reference panel of healthy donors using Gaussian mixture model signatures, and optimal transport between cohorts to identify regions of the embedding space associated with disease. We evaluate Humora on SARS-CoV-2 across diagnosis and antibody discovery tasks. In leave-one-cohort-out diagnosis, Humora achieves a mean AUROC of 0.72, outperforming the best existing method (0.66), indicating an immunological signal rather than cohort-specific artifacts has been learned. For antibody discovery, Humora identifies candidate sequences without using antigen information: among 94 selected antibodies, 10 bind the receptor binding domain, and 12 bind the nucleocapsid protein, achieving substantial enrichment over random expectation. Overall, Humora establishes a function-aware framework for analyzing immune repertoires, enabling disease diagnosis and antibody discovery independent of antigen information.

title: Comparing cell type annotation methods in thymus scRNA-seq datasets
authors: Yury Bukhman, Morgridge Institute for Research, United States; Bethany Moore, Morgridge Institute for Research, United States; Wesley Blashka, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States; Matthew Brown, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States; Li-Fang (Jack) Chu, University of Calgary, Canada; Ron Stewart, Morgridge Institute for Research, United States
abstract: We are applying two distinct and potentially complementary approaches to the annotation of single cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) datasets. One approach uses a specialized deep learning model, scVI, to project a dataset into an embedding computed on a large compendium of previously annotated scRNA-seq data, CellxGene. This is followed by annotating the cells based on a reference cell atlas projected into the same embedding. The other approach, CASSIA, uses LLM agents to annotate cell clusters based on the information about their differentially expressed markers available in scientific literature. We test both methods on a representative subset of a pre-annotated dataset, the Yayon et al. thymus cell atlas, and other available data. Although both approaches can by and large reproduce the original Yayon et al. annotations, there is also a degree of uncertainty. Methodological variations result in non-identical outcomes due to the complex and noisy nature of single cell transcriptomics data.

title: STAG-LLM: Multimodal TCR-pHLA binding prediction
authors: Jared Slone, Rice University, Brown School of engineering, United States; Minying Zhang, MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States; Peixin Jiang, MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States; Amanda Montoya, MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States; Emily Bontekoe, MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States; Barbara Rausseo, MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States; Alexandre Reuben, MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States; Lydia Kavraki, Rice University, United States
abstract: Strong binding between T cell receptors (TCRs) and peptideâ€“HLA (pHLA) complexes plays a key role in the adaptive immune response. Accurately predicting which TCRs will bind to which pHLAs is central to advancing personalized immunotherapies such as TCR-T. Many machine learning (ML) approaches to TCR-pHLA binding prediction rely only on amino acid sequences, limiting their ability to capture the full complexity of binding interactions. Recent advances in protein structure modeling provide a unique opportunity to integrate 3D structural information into ML pipelines. We developed TAG-LLM, a multimodal deep learning framework that combines protein language models with geometric deep learning to jointly leverage sequence information and computationally generated 3D structures of TCRâ€“pHLA complexes. STAG-LLM integrates transformer-derived sequence embeddings with graph neural networks that encode structural geometry and intermolecular interactions within modeled complexes. Our results show that STAG-LLM outperforms existing sequence and structure methods, even when trained on datasets three times smaller. Our findings demonstrate that integrating modeled 3D structural information with protein language modeling substantially improves TCR-pHLA binding prediction and provides a promising foundation for next-generation structure-aware immunoinformatics tools. The STAG-LLM framework was recently published in Volume 27 of the Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal in the article, â€œSTAG-LLM: Predicting TCR-pHLA binding with protein language models and computationally generated 3D structures.â€

title: AlphaFold3 Enables Scalable Screening of Antibody-Antigen Interactions in Autoimmune Disease
authors: Monica Dayao, Biohub, United States; Aaron Bodansky, University of California, San Francisco, United States; Vida Ahyong, University of California, San Francisco, United States; Joseph DeRisi, Biohub, United States
abstract: High-throughput identification of antibody-specific epitopes remains a major challenge in immunology. We developed PAIRIS (Prediction of Antibody-antigen Interaction at high Resolution In Silico), a computational framework using AlphaFold3 and Rosetta to model patient-derived B cell receptors and map their epitopes. Applied to a pediatric autoimmune disease cohort, we modeled 81 patient IgG antibodies against tiled peptides spanning a candidate autoantigen, generating >60,000 structural predictions. Using AlphaFold3 confidence scores and binding energy calculations, PAIRIS identified 14 high-confidence antibody-epitope pairs, with significant enrichment in cerebrospinal fluid clones. Experimental validation via PhIP-seq and biolayer interferometry confirmed predictions for multiple candidates, with AlphaFold3 models accurately recapitulating critical contact residues at single-amino acid resolution. This approach enables scalable BCR repertoire screening while simultaneously mapping antibody-specific epitopes, reducing experimental burden and accelerating antigen discovery across diverse applications.

title: A Statistical Framework for Modeling TCRβ Chain Sharing within Human Cohorts
authors: Michael Toomey, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Understanding patient immune response is critical for improving the development and deployment of novel immunotherapies. In particular, the ability to identify therapeutically-relevant T cell clonotypes present in multiple different patients may provide useful biomarkers of therapeutic response, as well as the basis from which to build novel vaccines and cell therapies. However, distinguishing biologically meaningful sharing from sharing expected by chance remains a challenge, as many clonotypes are shared between individuals due to commonalities in environmental and evolutionary pressures. Here, we present a proof-of-concept statistical framework for identifying public TCRβ sequences shared between patients beyond stochastic expectation in a given cohort, built and benchmarked on a dataset of TCRβ repertoires from 658 individuals with known cytomegalovirus serostatus. Our approach leverages a model of TCRβ recombination probabilities, enabling detection of clinically-relevant public clonotypes linked to disease state and patient immune response.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: AI-Based Functional Annotation of Novel Protein Sequences
authors: Tsviya Olender, Weizmann Institute, Israel; Tomer Antman, Weizmann Institute, Israel; Sagi Eppel, Weizmann Institute, Israel; Dvir Gur, Weizmann Institute, Israel
abstract: We investigate molecular mechanisms of bio-organic crystal formation across diverse organisms. We isolated a novel fungal strain that forms guanine crystals and generated a complete genome assembly for functional analyses. We identified over 5,000 protein-coding genes. Traditional functional annotation relies on homology-based methods, which often leave many genes uncharacterized. To address this limitation, we evaluate AI-based methods for large-scale functional. We first applied DeepGoPlus, a convolutional neural network-based tool to assign GO terms, and compared the results with those of EggNog, an orthology-based tool considered the gold standard. DeepGOPlus predictions overlapped with EggNOG annotations in 76% of proteins with identified orthologs, whereas this overlap decreased to 66% for proteins lacking orthologs. Importantly, 11.3% of proteins were predicted exclusively by DeepGOPlus. Next, we evaluated the performance of ESM2 and ProtT5, two protein language models trained on millions of sequences. Embeddings were extracted for each novel protein and compared against a reference sequence library, and the closest match was identified using cosine similarity. Both methods performed similarly, with 88.6% accuracy for ESM2 and 89.1% for ProstT5, but ESM2 is faster and offers models with varying depths. Clipping the most variable components improved the performance of both methods and increased the separation of the true/false hits. Importantly, both methods assigned orthology to 40% of proteins without orthologs. To summarize, our results demonstrate that AI-based approaches, particularly protein language models, can uncover distant homology relationships that remain undetected by traditional methods, substantially expanding the functional annotation landscape for non-model organisms and

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Performance analysis of AI-Based and Structure-Based Methods for Enzyme Function Prediction
authors: Asaf Salamov, DOE Joint Genome Institute, United States
abstract: Accurate prediction of enzyme function is a critical challenge in genome annotation, with direct implications for the correct reconstruction of metabolic pathways. In recent years, a growing number of prediction methods have emerged, leveraging either AI approaches â€”such as large language models (LLMs) â€” or those exploiting predicted protein structures, generated by tools such as AlphaFold2 o r ESMFold, which can subsequently be searched against structural databases using structural alignment tools such as TM-Ali gn or Foldseek. To rigorously evaluate these methods, we benchmarked their performance on a curated ""hard"" dataset comprising enzymes for which the top BLASTp hit fails to match the correct EC number, thereby excluding trivially solved cases. Our results demonstrate that current AI- and structure-based methods still underperform relative to established traditional sequence-based approaches, such as EggNOG, on this challenging benchmark. Nevertheless, our findings point to promising avenues for improvement. Specifically, gene family models built on embeddings derived from protein language models (PLMs) have shown greater sensitivity than conventional sequence-based methods (e.g. HMM profiles), suggesting that more accurate PLM-based predictors could be developed for individual enzyme families. Furthermore, we demonstrate that high-confidence computationally predicted protein structures can aid in the discovery of otherwise missing enzymes in poorly characterized genomes. We illustrate this utility in algal genomes, where structure-based approaches successfully identified enzymes absent from otherwise incomplete metabolic pathways. These results highlight both the current limitations and the untapped potential of next-generation enzyme function prediction methods.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Annotate Eukaryotic Genomes with NCBI EGAPx
authors: Pooja Strope, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Institutes of Health, United States; Terence Murphy, National Center for Biotechnology Information, United States; The Egapx Development Team Team, National Center for Biotechnology Information, United States
abstract: The NCBI RefSeq project provides high quality gene model annotations for more than 1300 eukaryotic organisms using NCBI's Eukaryotic Genome Annotation Pipeline (EGAP). To enable researchers to annotate assembled eukaryotic genomes locally and to accelerate annotation for large scale sequencing projects, we developed EGAPx (EGAP external), a public implementation of the EGAP methodology. EGAPx is an evidence based pipeline implemented as a Nextflow workflow with containerized applications. It produces structural and functional genome annotation for most metazoan and plant genomes, with outputs suitable for GenBank submission. EGAPx integrates multiple evidence types, including short read and long read RNA seq data and protein sequences, to support prediction of protein coding genes and ncRNA genes. Gene and protein naming is derived from orthology and homology comparisons to reference datasets, promoting consistent and interpretable annotations. EGAPx is designed to be straightforward to configure and portable across compute environments, supporting execution on cloud platforms such as AWS and on multiple local HPC schedulers. In mock annotations of human and Drosophila genomes, EGAPx demonstrates high sensitivity and precision. EGAPx is part of the NIH Comparative Genomics Resource (CGR), which supports reliable comparative genomics for eukaryotic organisms through the NCBI Toolkit and community collaboration. Workflow and documentation: https://github.com/ncbi/egapx Supported by NCBI, NLM, NIH.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Improving Protein Post-Translational Modification Prediction with Label Collision Resolution and Discriminative Fine-Tuning of Generative Protein Language Model
authors: Bhawana Prasain, Rochester Institute of Technology, United States; Pawel Pratyush, Rochester Institute of Technology, United States; Stefan Schulze, Rochester Institute of Technology, United States; Dukka B Kc, Technology, United States
abstract: Post-translational modification (PTM) prediction is a residue-level task, yet decoder-only protein language models (PLMs) mostly rely on byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenization, which merges multiple amino acids into a single token. This reduces the number of tokens required to represent a protein sequence; however, in some cases, individual tokens can combine both modified and unmodified sites. This leads to token-level label conflicts and limits the ability of such PLMs to accurately localize modification sites. We propose LCR-PTM, a residue-aware discriminative fine-tuning framework that resolves token-level label conflict by explicitly isolating the target residue using marker-based tokenization, combined with parameter-efficient adaptation via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). By repurposing the autoregressive objective as discriminative-guided fine-tuning, we enable the model to learn an explicit separation between positive and negative class labels while reducing the influence of tokens in the generative model's vocabulary. This formulation helps align token representations with residue-level downstream tasks in the protein domain while retaining the contextual modeling strengths of autoregressive PLMs. LCR-PTM outperforms on various PTM prediction tasks, with MCC gains varying across PTM sites. Along with MCC, we observe consistent gains in F1-score, AUROC, and AUPR on all tasks. The gain in residue-centered tokenization is higher in PTMs where there is a larger amount of conflict at token-level. These results highlight the importance of token-residue alignment while adapting autoregressive protein language models for residue level tasks in the domain of protein.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Prot-B-GAN: Generative Adversarial Network with Reinforcement Learning for Graph Completion in Protein Function Prediction
authors: Jaylin Dyson, Meharry Medical College, United States; Aize Cao, Meharry Medical College, United States; Bishnu Sarker, University of North Texas, United States
abstract: Proteins govern virtually every cellular process, yet a critical annotation gap persists: over 252 million sequences in UniProtKB/TrEMBL remain functionally uncharacterized, compared with only 573,000 manually curated entries in Swiss-Prot. Experimental methods are too slow and costly to close this gap at scale, and existing sequence-based computational models often fail to capture the multi-relational biological context essential for accurate protein function prediction. We present a Generative Adversarial Network with Reinforcement Learning (GAN-RL) framework that emulates human biocurator reasoning to predict protein functions directly over a biological knowledge graph. Initially, CompGCN, a composition-based graph convolutional network, generates context-aware protein node embeddings by jointly encoding sequence-derived features, molecular interactions, and ontological relationships. These embeddings are combined with relation embeddings and stochastic noise to generate candidate protein functions. Then, training proceeds in two stages: a pre-training phase optimizing a composite loss across mean squared error, cosine similarity, ranking, and manifold alignment, followed by an adversarial phase where a generator and a label-smoothed binary cross-entropy discriminator engage in structured competition. A composite reward integrating structural plausibility via a DistMult scorer, reinforcement learning signals, and adversarial feedback steers predictions toward biologically coherent protein-function links, evaluated via Hit@10 under filtered ranking. Preliminary results confirm a stable adversarial dynamic: semantic alignment between predicted and known protein functions improves monotonically while output diversity is preserved. This framework establishes a scalable, constraint-extensible foundation for automated functional annotation, advancing beyond simple sequence homology toward principled inference over an incomplete biological landscape.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: TD2+: a universal method for recognizing protein-coding regions in RNA
authors: Nikola Zadorozhny, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Mihaela Pertea, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Steven Salzberg, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Accurately identifying protein-coding regions in transcripts assembled from RNA sequencing data is essential for annotating newly sequenced genomes, interpreting de novo transcriptome assemblies, and separating genuine coding sequence from short or spurious open reading frames. TransDecoder and TD2 address this problem by identifying and scoring candidate open reading frames, where TD2 uses PSAURON as its protein-coding scoring model. Here we introduce TD2+, a coding-region recognition pipeline that identifies candidate open reading frames in RNA and scores them with a deep learning model trained on coding sequences from diverse eukaryotic species. TD2+ is designed to generalize across species without organism-specific retraining. We benchmarked TD2+ against TD2, TransDecoder, and related approaches using reference transcripts from diverse eukaryotic species, a human RNA assembly derived from nearly 10,000 GTEx RNA-seq datasets, and human lncRNA genes. Across reference transcripts, TD2+ exceeded TD2â€™s true-positive rate while maintaining low false-positive counts. On the set of assembled GTEx transcripts, TD2+ reduced non-matching predictions by 31.0% relative to TD2 without reducing reference-supported coding predictions. In human lncRNA genes, which should not contain protein-coding regions, TD2+ reduced false-positive rates relative to TD2/PSAURON from 23.2% to 10.0%, 14.8% to 5.9%, and 15.1% to 5.5% at minimum ORF lengths of 50, 98, and 150 amino acids, respectively. Together, these results suggest that TD2+ can improve RNA-based protein annotation across diverse eukaryotes without requiring organism-specific model retraining.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Balanced and Evolutionary Context-Aware Representation Learning for Robust Protein Function Prediction
authors: Jiaqi Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Shitong Dai, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Yunan Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Accurate protein function prediction is critical for interpreting the rapidly expanding volume of sequence data, but existing computational approaches often struggle with proteins linked to rare functions or distant from annotated homologs. These limitations arise from highly imbalanced annotation distributions and from the difficulty of capturing informative evolutionary context for remote homologs. To address these challenges, we introduce two complementary sequence-based representation learning methods, MSRep and EPERep, for robust protein function annotation. MSRep improves the prediction of underrepresented functions by refining pretrained protein language model embeddings using a neural collapse-inspired objective, encouraging a more balanced and separable representation space across function classes. EPERep enhances functional inference by retrieving homologous sequences from large unlabeled databases and integrating them with the query sequence to construct a contextualized evolutionary profile. Across four major annotation tasks, including Enzyme Commission numbers, Gene3D domains, Pfam families, and Gene Ontology terms, both methods consistently outperform strong machine-learning and alignment-based baselines. MSRep achieves particularly large improvements for rare function classes while maintaining competitive performance across functions with varying training frequencies. EPERep is most effective for proteins with low sequence identity to the training set, improving remote homology detection by leveraging unlabeled evolutionary neighborhoods. Together, our results demonstrate that balanced representation learning and retrieval-based evolutionary profiling provide complementary strategies for improving protein function prediction under challenging real-world conditions. These approaches offer scalable solutions for annotating understudied proteins and reducing the gap between sequence discovery and functional characterization.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Alternative Splicing Impact on Ligand Binding Across Human Proteome
authors: Ziyang Gao, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Dmitry Korkin, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States
abstract: Protein-ligand binding is a fundamental mechanism governing cellular signaling, metabolic regulation, and pharmacological response. Traditionally, functional annotations have relied on a gene-centric paradigm, assuming a singular correspondence between a gene and its biochemical role. However, alternative splicing (AS) frequently expands proteomic diversity by generating multiple isoforms with distinct structural properties. To bridge this gap, we developed the Alternative Splicing Impact Factor for Ligand Binding(ASIFLIG), a quantitative framework designed to model the impact of AS on protein-ligand interactions across the human proteome. By integrating isoform-resolved transcriptomic data from the Human Protein Atlas with structure-resolved binding annotations from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), the ASIFLIG model maps experimentally resolved binding sites onto alternative isoforms. This approach identifies three principal modes of modulation: Functional Robustness, where binding is preserved; Functional Silencing, where splicing acts as a binary switch to abolish recognition; and Functional Plasticity, where pocket remodeling alters binding affinity or specificity. Applying this model genome-wide across 40 tissues and 3,245 receptor genes, we generated a high-resolution functional map of the human ligand-binding proteome. Our results reveal that a gene's functional identity is highly plastic and dependent on the local splicing scenario. Notably, we identified divergent regulatory patterns between sexes for identical ligand-target pairs, suggesting a structural basis for sex-specific therapeutic responses. In a summary, ASIFLIG, provides a mechanistic foundation for explaining tissue-specific drug responses and improving the precision of therapeutic targeting by accounting for isoform-level functional diversity.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Single-Cell Transcriptomics Reveals Divergent Interferon Programs Associated with DMARD Response in Rheumatoid Arthritis
authors: Euijeong Sung, Department of Biotechnology, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University, South Korea; Ilseok Choi, Department of Biotechnology, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University, South Korea; Insuk Lee, Department of Biotechnology, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University, South Korea; Sungsoo Ahn, Division of Rheumatology, Yonsei University College of Medicine, Yongin, South Korea, South Korea
abstract: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitors, are central to the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), yet clinical responses remain highly heterogeneous. This study aimed to elucidate the cellular and molecular determinants underlying differential DMARD treatment responses. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from RA patients at baseline, before clinically indicated DMARD treatment, and compared cytokine signaling between responders and non-responders using single-cell transcriptomics, gene network analysis, and in silico perturbation. Our integrative analysis revealed divergent interferon axes between outcome groups: responders were dominated by type I IFN programs, whereas non-responders exhibited type II IFN and TNF-linked circuits. Interferon-classical monocytes were enriched in responders and showed strong activation of interferon-stimulated genes such as SIGLEC1 and IFI6. In contrast, non-responders exhibited elevated IFN-γ signaling in MAIT and NK cells, consistent with persistent inflammation. Co-expression networks also diverged, with more coherent myeloid networks in responders and aberrantly convergent lymphoid networks in non-responders, where IRF8 emerged as a hub associated with poor clinical improvement. In silico perturbations further suggested that SIGLEC1 may be involved in sustaining responder-associated type I IFN programs, as its perturbation was associated with a partial shift toward a non-responder-like state. These findings suggest that differential engagement of type I versus type II interferon pathways shapes the baseline peripheral immune landscape associated with clinical response after DMARD treatment, providing a basis for biomarker development and therapeutic stratification in RA.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: PrimerDesigner: Designing efficient primers for synthesizing large protein libraries without cross-hybridization
authors: Jonathan Mandl, Bar-Ilan University, Israel; Yaron Orenstein, Bar-Ilan University, Israel
abstract: Efficient synthesis of large protein libraries is key to making high-throughput biochemistry scalable. Advances in DNA microarray technology now allow more than 170,000 designed oligonucleotides to be synthesized in a single array, dramatically reducing cost and enabling pooled amplification for downstream mutagenesis reactions. Effective amplification of short oligonucleotides into long coding sequences requires efficient primer design without cross-hybridization. However, no primer-design method currently guarantees complete coverage of the protein-coding sequences with maximum efficiency and no cross-hybridization over multiple proteins or multiple variants of the same protein. Here, we present PrimerDesigner, a suite of methods to design the most efficient primers for synthesizing large protein libraries with complete protein-coding sequence coverage and without cross-hybridization. We first prove that primer design with complete coverage and without cross-hybridization is NP-hard, even for a single protein. As a solution, we formulate the primer-design problem as an integer linear program (ILP). When no cross-hybridization is possible, we solve the primer-design problem for a single protein in linear time. Moreover, we extend our ILP formulation to handle multiple variants of the same protein. We demonstrate that the methods in PrimerDesigner produce an optimal solution in only a few minutes for a single protein and within a couple of hours for multiple proteins while achieving higher efficiency than a greedy baseline approach. We expect PrimerDesigner to enable the synthesis of large protein libraries at an unprecedented scale and efficiency.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Characterizing isoform expression and mutation using bulk and single-cell long-read RNA sequencing
authors: Jia-Jun Liu, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Qingqi Lin, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Wenjia Wang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Mengying Xia, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Jian-Hua Luo, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Sungjin Ko, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Silvia Liu, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Long-read RNA-seq has emerged as a powerful technology for characterizing transcriptome complexity through the capture of full-length transcripts. Compared with short-read sequencing, long-read platforms provide the opportunity to quantify isoform-specific expression and to study transcript-level variations that are critical for understanding gene regulation and disease mechanisms. However, existing computational tools typically do not emphasize the annotation of individual long reads, and truncated long reads with multiple possible alignments are frequently discarded or inaccurately quantified, leading to potential bias in downstream analyses. Moreover, only a limited number of computational approaches have been developed to quantify RNA mutation and editing events at isoform resolution using long-read data. To address these challenges, we developed a novel computational approach for the comprehensive analysis of long-read RNA-seq data. Our algorithm first annotates individual long reads with all the possible isoform assignments. Next, it estimates the expression level of known isoform, alternative splicing, and fusion transcripts by explicitly modeling ambiguous read assignments, allowing truncated or multi-mapped reads to contribute probabilistically to transcript quantification. Building upon this framework, the second stage of the method estimates RNA mutation and editing expression at the isoform level, enabling integrated characterization of transcript structure and sequence variation. The proposed algorithm was systematically evaluated using multiple simulated and real long-read RNA-seq datasets. The results demonstrate improved accuracy in transcript quantification and robust detection of RNA mutation events. Importantly, the method is compatible with both bulk and single-cell long-read RNA-seq data. Overall, this work provides a generalizable computational tool that facilitates comprehensive isoform-resolved transcriptome analysis for a wide range of biomedical applications.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Genome size and complexity are major drivers of sequencing requirements for assembling fungal genomes
authors: Gabriel Silva, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States; Temitope Folorunso, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States; Lori Eckhardt, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States; Janna Willoughby, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States
abstract: High-quality genomes are essential for comparative, functional, and evolutionary studies, yet although fungal genomes vary widely in size, structural rearrangements, and gene architecture, the effects of assembly algorithms and sequencing strategies on fungal genome reconstruction remain little explored. Most assembly benchmarks have focused on bacterial genomes, leaving uncertainty about how sequencing depth, assembly algorithm, and genome structure interact in fungi. Here, we benchmarked fungal genome assembly performance using both simulated and empirical short- and long-read sequencing datasets. Simulated reads were generated from 66 complete fungal genomes spanning broad ranges of genome size, GC content, and gene density. We evaluated short-read, long-read, hybrid, and long-read-plus-polishing workflows across sequencing depths from 10x to 100x and validated key trends using sequencing data from 10 field-collected fungal isolates. Genome architecture significantly modulated assembly performance across all metrics. Genome size was the dominant architectural driver: larger and structurally complex genomes required substantially greater long-read depth to reach contiguity and base-accuracy plateaus, whereas compact genomes achieved near-maximal performance at low coverage. These effects were assembler-specific and were reproduced in the empirically sequenced isolates. A model-based threshold analysis translated these relationships into architecture-dependent sequencing recommendations. These results show that genome architecture, not assembler choice alone, governs how much sequencing a fungal genome requires, providing a quantitative framework for matching sequencing design to genome characteristics..

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Transcriptomic subtypes in high-grade serous ovarian cancer are driven by tumor cellular composition
authors: Stephanie Tanis, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA, United States; Manoel Lixandrao, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA, United States; Adriana Ivich, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA, United States; Laurie Grieshober, Department of Population Health Sciences, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT 84108, USA, United States; Katherine A. Lawson-Michod, Department of Epidemiology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98109, USA, United States; Lindsay J. Collin, Department of Epidemiology, Rollins School of Public Health, Emory University, Atlanta, GA, 30322, USA, United States; Lauren C. Peres, Moffitt Cancer Center and Research Institute, Tampa, FL 33612, USA, United States; Lucas A. Salas, Department of Epidemiology, Geisel School of Medicine, Dartmouth, Lebanon, NH 03784, USA, United States; Jeffrey R. Marks, Department of Surgery, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC 27707, USA, United States; Benjamin G. Bitler, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA, United States; Casey S. Greene, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA, United States; Joellen M. Schildkraut, Department of Epidemiology, Rollins School of Public Health, Emory University, Atlanta, GA, 30322, USA, United States; Jennifer Anne Doherty, Department of Population Health Sciences, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT 84108, USA, United States; Natalie R. Davidson, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA, United States
abstract: Background High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSC) is an aggressive malignancy with high recurrence rates and lim-ited targeted treatment options. Bulk transcriptomic subtypes are being investigated to stratify HGSC tumors but are interpreted as reflecting malignant-intrinsic transcriptional states. Because bulk tumors comprise mix-tures of malignant, stromal, and immune cells, it remains unclear whether subtype structure reflects tumor cell state or cellular composition, or both. Approach We quantified contributions of cellular composition and tumor-intrinsic expression to HGSC subtype identity. We combined 1,900 single-cell-informed pseudobulk simulations, varying epithelial, stromal, and immune fractions, with deconvolution-based modeling of 1,834 primary HGSC tumors across eight cohorts. Results In simulated tumors, subtype probabilities were determined by cellular composition alone, with MES increasing with fibroblast abundance and IMR/PRO varying along an opposing immune axis. These dependencies were reproduced in primary tumors, where inferred cell-type proportions associated with subtype probabilities and aligned with the principal axis separating subtypes. Subtype separation aligned with PC2 (Î·Â²=0.463; ~46% vari-ance) but not PC1 (Î·Â²=0.005; Conclusions HGSC transcriptomic subtypes are largely explained by tumor ecosystem composition rather than stable tumor-intrinsic states. This framework enables disentangling compositional and intrinsic signals in bulk tumor transcriptomics.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Spatial and Long-Read Transcriptomics Reveal the Microenvironment in Mixed Liver Tumors
authors: Qingqi Lin, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Mengying Xia, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Jia-Jun Liu, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Minwook Kim, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Joseph Kwon, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Jian-Hua Luo, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Sungjin Ko, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Silvia Liu, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Mixed liver tumors, particularly combined hepatocellularâ€“cholangiocarcinoma (cHCC-CCA), are highly aggressive malignancies characterized by pronounced cellular heterogeneity and complex tumor microenvironments (TME). A defining feature of these tumors is the coexistence of hepatocytic and biliary cell populations within the same lesion, suggesting intricate cellular interactions and lineage plasticity. However, current transcriptomic approaches are largely limited to gene-level measurements and fail to capture alternative splicing, an important regulatory layer in cancer biology. While spatial transcriptomics preserves tissue architecture, it lacks isoform-level resolution, whereas long-read RNA sequencing resolves full-length transcript isoforms but loses spatial context. To address this limitation, we analyzed clinical specimens from patients with mixed liver tumors using a dual-technology framework combining imaging-based spatial multi-omics (CosMx) and long-read RNA sequencing (PacBio). We developed a hierarchical Bayesian meta-integration framework to link spatial gene expression with isoform-level transcript information. In this model, latent isoform abundances are inferred from spatial gene expression through a probabilistic geneâ€“isoform mapping constrained by long-readâ€“derived references. This framework enables the inference of spatially structured isoform usage and cell-type composition across the TME. By integrating transcriptomic, proteomic, and spatial information, we identify spatially variable isoform patterns and their associations with distinct cellular states and microenvironmental contexts. Furthermore, leveraging long-read sequencing, we characterize spatial patterns of mutation and splicing variation across tumor subpopulations. Together, this study provides a framework for integrating spatial multi-omics with long-read transcriptomics, offering new insights into tumor organization and heterogeneity at the isoform level.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Quality Control of Single-Cell ATAC-seq data without peak calling using Chromap
authors: Omar Ahmed, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Haowen Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Benjamin Langmead, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Li Song, Dartmouth College, United States
abstract: Single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq) profiles the heterogeneity of chromatin accessibility across thousands of cells rather than only getting a single, bulk view. The common practice of ATAC-seq data analysis based on features defined by bulk peaks can miss rare cell types in the single-cell setting. This inspires the development of highly efficient methods, such as SnapATAC and ArchR, that use the features defined by the fixed-size genome intervals. However, the skipping of peak calling disenables several important quality control (QC) steps, like filtering low-quality cells based on the fraction of reads in peak regions (FRIP) score. We previously developed the method Chromap for ultrafast read alignment and preprocessing of scATAC-seq data. Chromap utilizes a sketch, which we call cache, to reuse alignment information for reads from peak regions to save running time. In this work, we augmented this cache structure to report important QC metrics, such as approximate FRIP score and cache occupancy. In particular, the FRIP score for a cell is predicted by a linear regression model considering the fraction of reads in the cache and other factors, like the number of duplicate reads in the cell. Cache occupancy is the number of distinct cache slots, inferred by the k-MinHash sketch, containing reads from the cell, which reflects the number of peaks for a cell. We show that these metrics capture additional low-quality cells missed by methods like SnapATAC2, and these metrics can be obtained without sacrificing running speed. The source code of Chromap is available at https://github.com/haowenz/chromap.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: HelixForge: Evidence-Based Reconciliation of Deep Learning Gene Predictions with RNA-seq and Protein Homology
authors: Arun Seetharam, Rosen Center for Advanced Computing, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47906, USA, United States; Laura Tibbs-Cortes, USDA-ARS, Corn Insects and Crop Genetics Research Unit, Ames, IA 50011, USA, United States; Margaret R. Woodhouse, USDA-ARS, Corn Insects and Crop Genetics Research Unit, Ames, IA 50011, USA, United States
abstract: Genome annotation of large, repeat-rich plant genomes such as maize remains challenging. Traditional pipelines combining ab initio predictors, transcript evidence, and homology require species-specific training and extensive manual curation. Deep learning predictors like Helixer bypass training requirements but produce single-isoform predictions with uncharacterized failure modes, making them insufficient as standalone annotation sources. No existing tool systematically reconciles deep learning predictions with experimental evidence while preserving the predictor's strengths. We present HelixForge, an open-source pipeline that produces publication-quality gene annotations by reconciling Helixer predictions with RNA-seq transcript assemblies and protein homology alignments. HelixForge implements a nine-step workflow: baseline scoring of every predicted locus before modification, PASA-inspired classification of transcript evidence overlaps, TSEBRA-inspired quality gating, pairwise competition where evidence-based modifications must outscore the original prediction to be accepted, a CDS assignment cascade that preserves predictor boundaries when possible, and score-gated splice site correction informed by the predictor's own per-base confidence signals. The pipeline supports parallel execution across HPC clusters via genome chunking. We validated HelixForge using a six-phase error profiling analysis on Arabidopsis thaliana (Araport11 reference), where it improved exact CDS match rate from 73.8% to 76.9% (+874 genes), gene-level F1 score from 74.30 to 77.44, and intron chain F1 from 60.03 to 63.30, with a 5.6:1 improvement-to-regression ratio. Error profiling revealed that the predictor's minimum CDS confidence is the dominant error discriminator (AUC 0.862), directly informing HelixForge's confidence-based triage. We are now applying HelixForge to annotation of maize NAM founder genomes, where complex gene families, large introns, and paleopolyploidy present additional challenges beyond the Arabidopsis validation.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Quantifying Phenotype-Associated Cell State Differences from Case-Control Single-Cell Data with scCST
authors: Anil Prakash, Virginia Tech, United States; Shenglin Mei, Virginia Tech, United States
abstract: The emergence of single-cell technologies has provided unprecedented views into the cellular and regulatory mechanisms of disease. However, identifying robust biological divergence at the single-cell level remains a statistical challenge due to technical noise, heterogeneous cell states, and the trap of pseudoreplication. We present scCST, a localized, biological-replicate-aware framework designed to extract high-confidence phenotype-associated cell state differences from case-control single-cell data. scCST leverages a latent-neighborhood matching strategy that transforms sparse single-cell profiles into batch-aware local pseudobulks around focal anchor cells. By performing condition comparisons within specific cellular niches and aggregating evidence across matched biological-replicate neighborhoods, scCST identifies local expression shifts that are consistent across batches. A central feature of this model is the calculation of signed gene-level scores that integrate both the magnitude of disease-control expression difference and statistical support from directional rank aggregation. This enables ranking of genes that drive local cell state divergence. When applied to case-control single-cell datasets, scCST identifies differentially shifted genes that are consistent across biological replicates and localized to specific regions of cell state space. The resulting cell-divergence scores provide a quantitative landscape of how specific cell types deviate from healthy baselines in response to disease or stimuli. By prioritizing replicate-consistent local expression shifts rather than simple cell-level comparisons, scCST offers a more nuanced interpretation of phenotype-associated transcriptional heterogeneity. This framework provides a useful tool for researchers to pinpoint local disease-associated cell states and candidate genes in complex single-cell atlas data.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: The NeuroBioBank Whole-Genome Catalog : sequencing from human brain donors with nervous system disorders
authors: Daniel Hupalo, Uniformed Services University, Bethesda, MD, United States; Jacob McCauley, Miller School of Medicine, University of Miami, United States; Matthew Wilkerson, Uniformed Services University, Bethesda, MD, United States; Clifton Dalgard, Uniformed Services University, Bethesda, MD, United States; William Scott, Miller School of Medicine, University of Miami, United States
abstract: Nervous system disease is a prevailing cause of morbidity and death worldwide. This set of neurological and psychological diseases have diverse causes aided by unknown genetic risks. Here we generated genome-wide genetic data on a large cohort of brain tissue donors with well annotated medical histories, allowing for broad investigations into the genetic risk of developing these neurological, neurodevelopmental, and psychological conditions. This resource consists of 9,663 donors with whole-genome genotyping and 9,543 donors with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) completed. The clinical diagnoses of these donors include 148 nervous system diseases clustered in 15 broad categories by ICD-10 coding. These donors were collected by six repositories comprising the NIH NeuroBioBank, with an average participant age of 60 years old. While primarily older individuals of European descent, the cohort also contains younger donors and individuals from non-European backgrounds. Full demographic and phenotypic descriptions for all donors are available via the NeuroBioBank Portal (neurobiobank.nih.gov). Variants detected by WGS were jointly called genome-wide and annotated to describe their functional impact; this identified 1,047,815 non-silent mutations. To illustrate applications of this resource, we replicated the strong associations observed in previous studies for single variants, structural variants, and burden tests for diseases such as Huntingtonâ€™s disease and Alzheimerâ€™s disease. The views expressed in this manuscript are solely of the authors and do not reflect the official policy of the Departments of Army/Navy/Air Force, Department of War, USUHS, HJF, or the United States government. We report no conflicts of interest.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Population-Structure-Aware SNP Threshold Derivation Improves Outbreak Resolution in Escherichia coli
authors: Minh Le, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center School of Health Professions, United States
abstract: Pairwise single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) distances derived from whole genome sequencing (WGS) data are the quantitative measure for inferring potential pathogen transmission. However, SNP thresholds are often applied arbitrarily across bacterial species, causing false positive or false negative transmission calls. With the increasing accuracy of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT), we sought to develop an ONT-only approach to derive population structure aware SNP thresholds for Escherichia coli subtypes. We evaluated long-read variant calling on simulated data and found Clair3 with a bacteria- finetuned model showed the highest SNP calling accuracy. For benchmarking, we sequenced 12 indexâ€“recurrent pairs using Illumina and ONT. Clair3 long-read calls were highly concordant with Snippy short-read calls, and long reads resolved SNPs in repetitive regions where short reads could not map uniquely. We applied the ONT only workflow to 500 clinical isolates, including 180 indexâ€“recurrent pairs as a surrogate for â€œtransmitted strains.â€ Core genome MLST allele distances were used for hierarchical clustering and split decomposition to identify genomic substructure without imposing a fixed tree. We delineated subgroups within ST131, a highly prevalent and clinically relevant lineage. Within each subgroup, recombination masked SNP distances showed clear separation between within patient and between patient comparisons. SNP thresholds at the 75th or 90th percentile yielded higher sensitivity and specificity within subgroups compared to thresholds applied to ST131 as a whole. These results show that ONT only WGS can accurately quantify SNP distances and that population structure aware thresholds improve ST131 subgroup-specific transmission inference, suggesting clustering-based approaches may improve genetic relatedness measurements across diverging bacterial lineages.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: DipSVFilter: filtering false-positive structural variants through cluster-aware diploid hypothesis modeling
authors: Rohit Khurana, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Yichen Henry Liu, Department of Computer Science, Vanderbilt University, United States; Xin Maizie Zhou, Vanderbilt University, United States
abstract: False positives remain a major limitation of long-read structural variant (SV) callsets, especially in complex loci containing clustered, overlapping, or interacting SV candidates. Such errors reduce the reliability of downstream analyses and make post-calling refinement an important bottleneck for accurate SV discovery. Existing SV filters typically evaluate candidate SVs independently using local alignment-derived features, without explicitly modeling alternative diploid sequence explanations for clustered SV signals. We present DipSVFilter, a cluster-aware post-calling SV filtering framework for long-read data. DipSVFilter first groups nearby candidate SVs into local clusters. Within each cluster, it constructs alternative pseudo-contigs by inserting candidate SVs into the reference sequence and enumerates possible diploid pseudo-contig combinations. It then prunes implausible configurations by comparing candidate-derived k-mers with k-mers observed in reads aligned to the local genomic region, excluding hypotheses that imply unsupported sequence content. For the remaining hypotheses, DipSVFilter realigns local reads to candidate diploid sequences and applies a time-distributed CNN-Transformer classifier to quantify residual SV signal after realignment. The best-supported diploid configuration is selected by minimizing residual SV signal, and the implied SVs are retained as the filtered SV set. Initial experiments suggest that DipSVFilter improves F1 on complex SV clusters relative to existing SV filtering methods, including CSV-Filter and Samplot-ML, while reducing false positives in clustered loci. These results highlight the value of jointly modeling clustered SV candidates as alternative diploid sequence hypotheses and suggest a practical strategy for improving the reliability of long-read SV callsets in structurally complex regions.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Structural Variant Mapping Enhances Genetic Discoveries for Pigmentation in Daucus carota
authors: Liangliang Gao, Plants for Human Health Institute, North Carolina State University, USA, United States; Romit Seth, Plants for Human Health Institute, North Carolina State University, USA, United States; Kopalli Venkataramana, Department of Agrobioinformatics, Liebig University, Germany, Germany; Agnieszka Golicz, Wageningen University & Research, Netherlands, Netherlands; Dariusz Grzebelus, Department of Plant Biology and Biotechnology, University of Agriculture in Krakow, Krakow, Poland, Poland; Phillip Simon, Dept of Plant and Agroecosystem Sciences, UW-Wisconsin and USDA-ARS, Vegetable Crops Research Unit, Madison, WI, USA, United States; Massimo Iorizzo, Plants for Human Health Institute & Department of Horticultural Science, North Carolina State University, USA, United States
abstract: While single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are the standard markers for trait mapping, they often fail to capture the linkage with important traits. Recent work in plants highlighted the value of Structural Variants (SVs) to address this challenge. Despite their significance, no study has addressed the genome-wide effects of SVs on GWAS in carrot. This study integrates a large resequencing dataset to resolve the genetic basis of root carotenoids and anthocyanin using SVs. Based on a single reference genome, over 100,000 high-quality SVs were identified across a diverse panel of 630 carrot accessions. Comparative SV-GWAS and SNP-GWAS reveal that structural variants capture significant "missing associations" for alpha carotenoid content and purple root pigmentation that were not detected by point mutations. Closer inspection of the region spanning the SVs association with purple root pigmentation identified a well-known anthocyanin related transcription factor, which support the effectiveness of the SVs association. These results demonstrate that SVs provide a critical, complementary strategy to uncover the genetic mechanisms underlying complex traits. Ongoing work will leverage a wider set of germplasm and a pangenome graph-based SVs to expand and refine the dissection of metabolite traits in carrots.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: From Raw Sequences to Taxonomic Inference: An End-to-End Hybrid Framework for Uncovering Cryptic Viral Elements
authors: Yu-Nong Gong, Chang Gung University, Taiwan
abstract: Identifying uncharacterized viruses in high-throughput sequencing datasets remains a significant computational bottleneck. Traditional homology-based tools depend heavily on reference genomes, often failing to detect cryptic viral elements that lack significant sequence similarity to known pathogens. Furthermore, conventional pipelines yield complex tabular data that require extensive manual curation. To address this, we developed an automated Snakemake pipeline designed to maximize viral rescue through a hybrid diagnostic architecture. The framework integrates: (1) geNomad for neural network-driven pattern recognition; (2) HMMscan for identifying conserved protein domains in Pfam; and (3) CheckV for genome completeness estimation and host contamination filtering. To streamline analysis, a Large Language Model (LLM) module leverages these quantitative metrics to derive evidence-based conclusions, linking detected biological features to taxonomic assignments. We benchmarked the pipeline using a mock dataset of 2,500 sequences, including 500 uncultivated viral and 2,000 non-viral entries. This simulates the challenge of discovering highly divergent or novel zoonotic pathogens, such as undiscovered members of the Coronaviridae family. While standalone tools demonstrate baseline sensitivities within the 90.4%–96.0% range, this hybrid framework yielded a 98.8% recovery rate, successfully rescuing divergent sequences that would otherwise be lost. By integrating compositional, functional, and genomic signatures into a reproducible workflow, this framework provides the high sensitivity required for uncovering cryptic viral elements in complex metagenomic datasets where reference homology is limited.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Resolving Novel Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron Genomes Using Hybrid Assembly and Assembly Graph Analysis
authors: Raighen Ly, Hope College, United States; Robert Glowacki, Hope College, United States; Catherine Welsh, Hope College, United States
abstract: Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (B. theta) is widely used as a model organism for studying host-microbiome interactions, yet most genomic analyses rely on the reference strain Bt-VPI-5482 despite substantial strain-level variation. Two additional strains, Bt-5951 and Bt-0940-1, currently lack publicly available closed genome assemblies, limiting comparative analyses and interpretation of strain-specific phenotypes. These strains along with Bt-3164 and Bt-VPI-5482 were sequenced and their genomes were assembled using a hybrid assembly workflow combining short- and long-read sequencing with Unicycler. Short reads were quality filtered and resulting assembly graphs were analyzed to identify unresolved repeats and ambiguous paths preventing chromosome closure. Assembly quality was evaluated using metrics from Quast and visually inspected with Bandage. Our current assemblies have reduced each strain to three to five contigs and assembly graph analysis suggests that the remaining breaks are associated with repeated regions and plasmids. Ongoing finishing is expected to produce complete circular chromosomes prior to presentation of this work. Preliminary comparisons to Bt-VPI-5482 indicate both conserved genomic structure and candidate strain-specific differences. The resulting assemblies will provide new genomic resources for studying strain-level diversity in B. theta and illustrate practical strategies for closing challenging bacterial genomes.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Guiding structural gene prediction with long-read transcriptomics using SQANTI Evidence
authors: Pablo Atienza, Genomics of Gene Expression Lab, Spain; Ana Conesa, Institute for Integrative Systems Biology, Spanish National Research Council, Spain
abstract: Despite the rapid advancement of long-read transcriptomics, current genome annotation methods often struggle to fully capture the structural complexity of the transcriptome. While long-read sequencing provides high resolution of full-length isoforms and alternative splicing events, integrating these data into traditional annotation workflows remains a significant bottleneck. Existing pipelines frequently rely on short-read data or generalized ab initio models, which can result in fragmented gene structures and the mischaracterization of novel transcripts. To address this limitation, we present SQANTI Evidence: a novel, evidence-driven genome annotation pipeline that directly integrates long-read sequencing data to accurately guide structural gene prediction. By incorporating transcript-level features to validate and refine gene models, our tool produces high-fidelity, comprehensive reference annotations. Our approach builds on the findings of Paniagua et al. (2025), where we demonstrated that using long reads as a guiding scaffold, rather than the sole source of evidence, yields superior results. SQANTI Evidence has been implemented using Snakemake (MÃ¶lder et al., 2021) as the workflow control tool. Built upon the established framework of AUGUSTUS (Stanke et al., 2008), the pipeline uses an IsoSeq3 transcriptome derived from long-read sequencing, curated using the SQANTI suite, as external evidence to guide the gene discovery process. This integration enables the generation of annotations that accurately reflect alternative splicing and isoform diversity. In addition to structural gene annotation, SQANTI Evidence produces a comprehensive quality report using GAQET2, a novel quality control pipeline that allows the user to obtain multiple parameters for a single annotation and benchmark against currently available state-of-the-art methods. SQANTI Evidence has been benchmarked against a set of model eukaryotic organisms, including human, mouse, fish, and yeast. The data for each annotation were taken from public datasets, and the reference genomes from ENSEMBL. In human datasets, perhaps the most well-studied of the organisms tested, the annotation benchmark achieved higher levels of sensitivity and structural resolution than standard annotation tools like BRAKER3 (Gabriel et al., 2024), which was run on the recommended mode for long-read RNA data. It should be mentioned, that this â€œmodeâ€ requires of proteomics data to be run, thus using a slightly different input from SQANTI Evidence, which solely relies on transcriptomic input and the reference genome. Using the whole human genome as a benchmark due to its massive scale and high transcriptomic complexity, SQANTI Evidence showed a substantial increase in sensitivity and overall F1 score at the exon level, as can be seen in Table 1. While BRAKER3 achieved an exon-level sensitivity of 39.2% and a precision of 89.3% (F1 score: 54.5%), SQANTI Evidence boosted sensitivity to 52.0% and achieved a superior F1 score of 60.9%, despite a trade-off in precision (73.5%). Furthermore, the direct integration of long-read transcriptomic evidence substantially reduced the number of false negatives. BRAKER3 failed to capture 40.2% (123,206) of the known reference exons; in contrast, SQANTI Evidence nearly halved this error rate, missing only 24.3% (74,516). These results highlight the capacity of SQANTI Evidence to resolve complex splicing events and capture a more complete picture of the transcriptome compared to traditional methods. SQANTI Evidence provides a robust framework for generating high-quality genome annotations that capture the full complexity of transcriptomic data, establishing accurate gene models to support downstream functional genomics across a wide range of species. Future benchmarking will be expanded to include non-model organisms and more annotation tools, especially in matters of speed and resource usage. track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Exploring the Spatial Transcriptome at Subcellular Resolution via Visium HD
authors: Zhenhua Shang, University of Louisville, United States; Jae Yeon Hwang, University of Louisville, United States; Ming Song, University of Louisville, United States; Juw Won Park, University of Louisville, United States
abstract: Background Spatial transcriptomics preserves gene expression within intact tissues, revealing organization lost in traditional sequencing. While bulk RNA-seq averages signals and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) requires tissue dissociation, both sacrifice spatial context. Visium HD addresses these gaps through unbiased, whole-transcriptome profiling at subcellular resolution, enabling precise mapping of cellular niches and microenvironmental dynamics. Methods Fresh-frozen mouse small intestine sections were processed using the Visium CytAssist workflow. Data were binned at 8 Âµm to balance sensitivity and resolution. To mitigate challenges like sparse transcript counts and partial volume effects, we employed a biology-driven annotation strategy. Cell types were manually identified using canonical markers validated by immunohistochemistry (IHC), in situ hybridization (ISH), and histological cross-referencing, ensuring more robust assignments than purely computational deconvolution. Results The analysis successfully resolved the crypt-villus architecture, identifying ten major cell populations with precise localization. Clustering revealed spatial domains that align with histological layers, capturing fine-scale signaling gradients and immune-stromal interactions. These insights represent biological details typically lost through bulk averaging (RNA-seq) or scRNA-seq dissociation. Statement of Significance This study demonstrates that combining 2 Âµm feature capture with rigorous manual annotation mitigates artifacts in high-resolution data. By bridging the gap between transcriptomic density and biological validation, this framework provides a high-fidelity map of cellular niches. This methodology offers a reliable approach for investigating tissue organization and spatial reprogramming in complex biological systems.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Smooth Muscle Klf4 Promotes Spp1⁺ Macrophage Accumulation in Obese Adipose Tissue
authors: Gamze Bulut, Virginia Commonwealth University, United States; Isabella Napoli, Virginia Commonwealth University, United States; Lavanya Sharma, Virginia Commonwealth University, United States; Johana Johnson, Virginia Commonwealth University, United States
abstract: Background: Obesity remodels adipose tissue macrophages (ATMs), but how they respond to signals from neighboring smooth muscle cells (SMCs) is less clear. Here we re-analyzed multiple single-cell RNA-seq experiments to build a unified view of adipose immune and stromal cells in a mouse model with SMC-specific Klf4 deletion. Methods: We combined 16 10x Genomics libraries from three experiments, including chow and diet-induced obesity (DIO) as well as wild-type (WT) and smooth-muscle Klf4 knockout (Klf4-SMC-KO) mice on DIO. After quality control, 27,398 cells remained. Datasets were integrated with SCTransform and canonical correlation analysis (Seurat v5), using experiment as a batch variable. We then subsetted 12,045 macrophage and mural cells based on marker gene expression and reclustered them using 12 principal components. We curated markers from the adipose macrophage literature (Itgax/CD11c, Cd9, Cd63, Lpl, Steap4, Mafb, Cybb, Pdgfra, Jam2, Prox1, Myocd) and used those to annotate clusters and assess diet- and genotype-dependent changes. Results: Single-cell RNA-seq of adipose SVF revealed 18 transcriptionally distinct clusters including macrophages and mural cells. Cluster 0, the largest cluster, contained an Spp1-high macrophage population previously linked to pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic functions, crown-like structures, and insulin resistance. In our dataset, Spp1âº macrophages increased in DIO vs chow and were more abundant in Klf4 WT than in Klf4-SMC-KO mice, suggesting that SMC Klf4 may promote accumulation of this potentially maladaptive macrophage population, which has also been implicated in vascular dysfunction. Conclusion: This integrated analysis, built collaboratively with undergraduate students, defines a macrophage- and mural-cellâ€“focused atlas of adipose stromal vascular cells across sorting strategies, diets, and SMC-Klf4 genotypes, and provides a foundation for targeted differential expression and pathway analyses.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Systematic Identification of Translated Circular RNAs through Integrated RNA-seq and Ribo-seq Analysis
authors: Jae Yeon Hwang, University of Louisville, United States; Zhenhua Shang, University of Louisville, United States; Abdelrahman Mahmoud, University of Louisville, United States; Juw Won Park, University of Louisville, United States
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed RNA molecules generated through back-splicing and are increasingly recognized as important regulators of gene expression. Recent studies suggest that a subset of circRNAs can be translated into functional peptides; however, systematic identification of actively translated circRNAs remains challenging due to the lack of computational frameworks that integrate transcriptomic and ribosome profiling data. We developed an automated and modular pipeline to detect ribosome-associated circRNAs by integrating RNA-seq and Ribo-seq datasets.
