The workflow identifies circRNAs from rRNA-depleted RNA-seq or circRNA-seq data and constructs back-splice junction (BSJ) reference sequences. Ribosome-protected fragments from Ribo-seq are aligned to both the genome and BSJ references to detect junction-spanning reads that provide direct evidence of circRNA translation. To ensure high-confidence results, the pipeline applies standardized filtering to retain uniquely mapped reads and reduce false positives commonly observed in junction-based analyses. Application of the pipeline to publicly available datasets identifies hundreds to thousands of circRNA candidates per dataset, with a subset showing strong translational signatures supported by BSJ-spanning ribosome footprints. Compared to naÃ¯ve junction-mapping approaches, the pipeline reduces ambiguous mappings and improves specificity while maintaining high sensitivity for detecting candidate coding circRNAs. The approach provides a reproducible framework for screening translated circRNAs across diverse biological conditions. This work offers a scalable computational solution for studying circRNA translation and facilitates deeper investigation into the functional roles of circRNAs and their contributions to proteomic diversity.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Transcript-Informed Cell Segmentation for Sequencing-Based Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: James Lubkowitz, University of Utah, United States; Kendell Clement, University of Utah, United States
abstract: Cell segmentation is central to spatial transcriptomics (ST), as accurate transcript-to-cell assignment impacts downstream analyses. In sequencing-based platforms such as Visium HD, cell segmentation remains challenging due to transcript sparsity, reliance on histological imaging, and spatial binning of transcript capture without single-molecule resolution. Traditional segmentation approaches depend on image-derived features; however, imaging-based ST has shown that incorporating spatial transcript maps improves boundary detection and cell definition. Here, we present a transcript-informed cell segmentation framework for sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics that integrates image-based nuclei detection with transcript-derived boundary inference. First, we construct a transcriptomic boundary confidence map. At multiple resolutions (e.g., 4 Î¼m, 8 Î¼m, â€¦), we partition the tissue into uniform tiles, aggregate transcripts within each tile, and cluster tiles by expression profiles. These cluster assignments define transcriptional similarity boundaries that capture tissue structure and cell organization. Boundaries across resolutions are combined into a unified map. Next, nuclei are identified and used as seeds for cell reconstruction. Cell boundaries are inferred by assigning each pixel to the nucleus that minimizes a cost function penalizing distance and crossing transcriptomic boundaries. We additionally estimate segmentation uncertainty by perturbing boundary penalties, yielding pixel-level and cell-level confidence scores. We show that this approach improves boundary delineation and reduces transcript misassignment in Visium HD data, with improved separation of marker gene expression between cells, while providing uncertainty-aware cell segmentations. By combining multiresolution transcriptomic information with image-based priors and explicitly modeling boundary uncertainty, this framework enables more accurate and reliable cell-resolved analysis in sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: scModCompare: Disentangling Shared Identity and Modality-Specific Regulatory Programs in Multimodal Single-Cell Data
authors: Hechen Li, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Xiuwei Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Paired multimodal single-cell assays promise to trace information flow across the central dogma, yet current computational frameworks (consensus VAEs, graph-based methods, and matrix factorization) prioritize merging modalities into a single representation. This treats biologically meaningful discordance, such as epigenetic priming, post-transcriptional buffering, and RNA velocity, as technical noise to be erased. Existing disentanglement approaches either target batch effects rather than cross-modality biology, rely on linear assumptions ill-suited to developmental manifolds, or validate private spaces only through indirect surrogate metrics. We present scModCompare, a multimodal variational autoencoder that explicitly partitions latent representations into shared and modality-private subspaces through a two-stage training scheme. Stage 1 trains shared encoders via cross-modal reconstruction with an alignment penalty, mathematically restricting the shared space to mutual information; Stage 2 freezes shared encoders and trains private encoders to capture residual modality-specific variance, preventing collapse between subspaces. We further introduce a Pointwise Log-Likelihood Ratio attribution score that quantifies, for every feature in every cell, the information gain contributed by each latent subspace on a unified information-theoretic scale across heterogeneous data distributions (ZINB, Gaussian, Bernoulli). Across three benchmark datasets, scModCompare resolves hidden CD4+ T cell subsets and flags doublets and ambient-RNA contamination in CITE-seq bone marrow data; reconstructs trajectory of epigenetic lineage priming in SHARE-seq hair follicle differentiation, decoupling enhancer accessibility from transcriptional activation; and recovers the complete kinetic lifecycle of master regulators from spliced/unspliced RNA without predefined kinetic equations, with private unspliced attribution scores achieving Spearman Ï = 0.92 against scVelo-inferred RNA velocity. On a human lymph node spatial multi-omics dataset, the private drivers identified canonical marker genes for each without supervision. By transforming multimodal discordance into an interpretable, quantitative signal at both cell and feature levels, scModCompare enables systematic discovery of temporal lags, modality-exclusive functions, and technical artifacts that integration-focused methods obscure.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Label-Free Detection of Epigenetic Modifications from Raw Nanopore Signals
authors: Bhargav Srinivasan, University of Maryland, United States; Simon Ambrozak, University of Maryland, United States; Can Firtina, University of Maryland, United States
abstract: Epigenetic modifications such as 5-methylcytosine (5mC), 5-hydroxymethylcystosine (5hmC), and N6-methyladenine (6mA) play crucial roles in gene regulation, biological signaling, and other downstream biological processes. Profiling and detecting these modifications at the single-base resolution is required to understand a full scope of genomic function across contexts beyond just the canonical base pair space. While nanopore sequencing offers a powerful platform for this purpose, existing epigenetic modification tools are limited to a small set of modifications and rely on costly machine learning models or articulate algorithms for each set of modifications. We present ProMURS (Profiling Modifications Using Raw Signals), a label-free framework for epigenetic modification detection directly from raw nanopore signals. ProMURS constructs a custom event pileup by aligning signal with a shared subsequence across reads and then performs downstream analyses to differentiate between modified and unmodified reads. These approaches entail a K-Means clustering on vectorized pileup values, a Principal Component Analysis based separation between modification types, and Dynamic Time Warping cost based error function as a differentiation between modified and unmodified reads. Epigenetic modifications such as 5-methylcytosine (5mC), 5-hydroxymethylcystosine (5hmC), and N6-methyladenine (6mA) play crucial roles in gene regulation, biological signaling, and other downstream biological processes. Profiling and detecting these modifications at the single-base resolution is required to understand a full scope of genomic function across contexts beyond just the canonical base pair space. While nanopore sequencing offers a powerful platform for this purpose, existing epigenetic modification tools are limited to a small set of modifications and rely on costly machine learning models or articulate algorithms for each set of modifications. We present ProMURS (Profiling Modifications Using Raw Signals), a label-free framework for epigenetic modification detection directly from raw nanopore signals. ProMURS constructs a custom event pileup by aligning signal with a shared subsequence across reads and then performs downstream analyses to differentiate between modified and unmodified reads. These approaches entail a K-Means clustering on vectorized pileup values, a Principal Component Analysis based separation between modification types, and Dynamic Time Warping cost based error function as a differentiation between modified and unmodified reads. On Oxford Nanopore Technologies Open Source Modification Benchmarking Dataset, ProMURS successfully differentiates unmodified and modified reads from 5mC, 5hmC, and 6mA modifications. Results show clear differentiation, with a PCA accuracy of up to 96% determined by 1-NN classification. ProMURS key contribution to the field is a modification pipeline that does not require labeled training data or prior modification knowledge.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Kmer-db: latest improvements in k-mer-based sequence indexing and comparison
authors: Adam Gudys, Silesian University of Technology, Poland; Andrzej Zieleziński, Adam Mickiewicz University, Poland; Sebastian Deorowicz, Silesian University of Technology, Poland
abstract: The exponential growth of sequence databases results in a need for fast, alignment-free sequence comparison algorithms. Most existing methods employ k-mers, often combining them with MinHash sketching to reduce representation size (e.g., Mash, Dashing). Kmer-db, our tool for k-mer-based sequence analysis, has confirmed its usability in many applications, with Vclust, a state-of-the-art package for large-scale viral genomes clustering, being the paramount example. Here we present a new version of Kmer-db. The algorithmic improvements result in substantial reduction of execution times, particularly on multicore architectures. An automatic split of data into batches based on sequence count or memory requirements, removes practical barriers for the dataset sizes that can be processed. The support of protein sequences with an optional alphabet reduction further increases the usability. Kmer-db database stores by default all the k-mers, thus can be accurately queried for their presence in the sequences. This is an advantage over data structures with a non-zero false positive rate employed by some packages (BIGSI, COBS). However, when one is interested only in identity estimation, the MinHash-based filtering is also available. When evaluated across different modes and configurations, Kmer-db was 70% to 5 times faster than its predecessor. For example, the comparison of over 15 million viral genomes from IMG/VR v4 repository at 0.95 nucleotide identity level required less than half an hour. We believe that superior performance combined with multiple usability features make Kmer-db ready for future challenges in genomics and proteomics.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Empirical Bayes inference in circadian omics
authors: Thomas Brooks, University of Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Empirical Bayes has widespread use in omics as part of packages such as DESeq2 and limma. However, most users only make use of its variance shrinkage properties which enable more robust p-values but do not affect effect-size estimates. Here, we introduce a software package that enables flexible empirical Bayes models. We demonstrate this by applications to complex circadian datasets which have time courses in multiple conditions. Importantly, this approach addresses a need for high-level summaries of differential expression or differential rhythms, improving on the widespread, but questionable, use of Venn diagrams. Our system improves the interpretability of results over existing empirical Bayes frameworks and is tailored to be sufficiently flexible to accommodate typical complex study designs.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: A systematic evaluation of the sources of non-uniform coverage in RNA-Seq
authors: Antonijo Mrcela, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Thomas Brooks, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Nicholas Lahens, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Jianing Yang, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Souparna Purohit, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Amruta Naik, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Emanuela Ricciotti, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Shaon Sengupta, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Peter Choi, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Gregory Grant, University of Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Extreme non-uniformity of transcript coverage remains one of the central unresolved technical artifacts in short-read RNA-Seq. These large-scale coverage biases substantially limit isoform-level quantification and impact a wide range of downstream analyses, including alternative splicing detection, transcript abundance estimation, benchmarking studies, and realistic simulation of RNA-Seq data. Despite extensive prior work, the dominant sources of this non-uniformity remain unclear. We performed a systematic evaluation of candidate sources of RNA-Seq coverage bias using both public datasets and newly generated libraries with controlled variation in ribosomal depletion strategy, fragmentation conditions, PCR ramp rate, fragment length, and PCR amplification. Coverage profiles were highly reproducible across technical replicates and reasonably consistent across biological replicates, demonstrating that the observed patterns are not primarily driven by stochastic fragment sampling. We show that several previously proposed explanations fail to substantially improve uniformity, including reduced PCR ramp rate, fewer PCR cycles, omission of ribosomal depletion, shorter fragment lengths, and use of thermostable reverse transcriptases. In contrast, PCR duplicate rates correlated with local coverage in a library-dependent manner, implicating amplification efficiency as an important contributor to coverage variation. However, decreasing PCR cycle number alone did not substantially improve uniformity, suggesting that molecular abundance and saturation-related effects may be more important than cycle count itself. Overall, our results demonstrate that RNA-Seq coverage non-uniformity arises from multiple interacting technical factors rather than a single dominant mechanism, with important implications for transcript quantification, benchmarking methodology, and RNA-Seq simulation frameworks.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: GRAINS: Enabling High-Performance and Low-Cost Graph-Based Genome Analysis via Storage-Aware Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design
authors: Nika Mansouri Ghiasi, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Harun Mustafa, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Talu Güloglu, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Rakesh Nadig, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Konstantinos Kanellopoulos, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Susana Rebolledo Ruiz, ETH Zurich, University of Cantabria, Switzerland; Marc Rautmann, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Furkan Eris, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Mohammad Sadrosadati, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Jisung Park, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), South Korea; Onur Mutlu, ETH Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: Graph-based representations of genome sequences have emerged as a powerful approach for representing massive genomic databases expressively and efficiently. However, analysis on large-scale genome graphs incurs significant data movement overhead from the storage system due to accessing large amounts of low-reuse data. Processing data directly inside the storage device, where data originally resides, can fundamentally mitigate this overhead. However, no existing tool for graph-based genome analysis can be efficiently used inside storage due to the limited hardware resources in modern SSDs. We propose GRAINS, the first system for analysis with large-scale genome graphs in storage. Through our detailed examination of typical analysis pipelines that operate on genome graphs, we perform storage-aware algorithm-architecture co-design to (i) make these pipelines more storage-friendly and (ii) further improve performance, energy-efficiency, and cost via in-storage and in-flash processing. GRAINS has three key aspects. First, we propose a new batching technique and execution flow, based on unique features of genome graphs, that reduces random accesses. Second, via in-flash and in-storage processing, we avoid transferring low-reuse or unused flash pages, preventing bandwidth waste. Third, to leverage the full parallelism of flash dies, we design a lightweight scheduling technique, enabled by re-purposing the existing SSD structures. GRAINSâ€™s design is versatile and flexible as it supports key operations on genome graphs and can be integrated into various analysis pipelines. GRAINS provides 2.7Ã—â€“47.8Ã— speedup (4.4Ã—â€“31.6Ã— energy reduction) over the state-of-the-art software baselines, and 1.5Ã—â€“17.0Ã— speedup (3.1Ã—â€“20.7Ã— energy reduction) over a hardware-accelerated baseline.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Quantum Closest-Pair Search for Biological Sequences via k-mer Distribution Statistics
authors: Zhezheng Xander Song, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Carl Kingsford, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Finding highly similar pairs of biological sequences is a fundamental task in bioinformatics, with applications in redundancy reduction, clustering, database cleaning, comparative genomics, and metagenomic analysis. Many practical sequence-search tools avoid exhaustive all-pairs comparison through heuristics, sketches, filters, or threshold-based clustering, thereby trading the exact closest-pair objective for scalability. For alignment-free \(k\)-mer distributional similarities, the induced feature space is high-dimensional and lacks the low-dimensional geometric structure used by classical exact closest-pair algorithms. Thus, in the exact pairwise-score setting, exhaustive evaluation over the \(\binom{N}{2}\) candidate pairs is the natural classical baseline. We present the first quantum framework targeting exact alignment-free closest-pair search in biological sequence collections using distributional \(k\)-mer statistics. It encodes empirical \(k\)-mer distributions as square-root amplitude states, estimates squared Bhattacharyya overlap using SWAP-test-based quantum amplitude estimation, and uses this estimate inside a D\"urr--H{\o}yer maximum-finding procedure. For \(N\) sequences of length at most \(L\) and additive precision \(\varepsilon\), we assume an idealized qRAM-style data-access model in which indexed state-preparation data can be queried coherently with polylogarithmic overhead. Under this assumption, our method performs closest-pair search in \(\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{NL}{\varepsilon}\right)\) time, where \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This reduces the leading dependence on the number of sequences from quadratic to linear compared with the classical exhaustive baseline \(O(N^2L)\). Without this qRAM assumption, our concrete Q\# implementation uses sparse prefix-tree state-preparation and explicit multiplexed indexed loading over the stored sequence states. Including this loading cost, its running time is \(\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{N^2L}{\varepsilon}\right)\), which matches the classical exhaustive scaling for constant precision while making the coherent data-loading cost explicit.

title: Relational Graph Convolutional Networks for Glioblastoma Biomarker Discovery via ceRNA and Copy Number Variation Analysis
authors: Samarth Khandelwal, Walnut Hills High School; Department of Computer Science, University of Cincinnati, United States; Nick Jarvis, Department of Computer Science, University of Cincinnati, United States; Justin Zhan, Department of Computer Science, University of Cincinnati, United States
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor with an extremely poor 5-year survival rate of 6.9%, largely attributable to the lack of reliable biomarkers. While competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) and copy number variation (CNV) analyses offer unique biomarker identification potential, current approaches neglect the integration of multiple regulatory mechanisms for biomarker detection. To address this limitation, we applied relational graph convolutional networks (RGCNs) to ceRNA and CNV knowledge graphs through a novel late fusion ensemble architecture. The proposed architecture outperformed baseline models and identified five novel biomarkers, including hsa-miR-196a and hsa-miR-224. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox regression indicated that the identified genes hold significant prognostic and diagnostic power. The early stratification of the Kaplan-Meier curves indicates the potential these genes hold for patient survival prediction. The results illustrate that RGCNs effectively capture complex gene interactions that current methods overlook, providing a framework for biomarker discovery. Ultimately, the novel biomarkers serve as prospective targets for future GBM therapeutic development and candidates for non-invasive diagnostic assays.

title: Structure-Conserved, Sequence-Divergent RNA Motifs in Nipah Virus Reveal Mutation Resistant Therapeutic Targets Missed by Protein Centric Design
authors: Abhinav Iyer, Dougherty Valley High School, United States; Vidya Subramanian, Independent Mentorship, United States
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a pathogenic paramyxovirus emerging in South and Southeast Asia with mortality rates ranging from 40â€“70%. It is listed by the World Health Organization as a priority pathogen. Despite its impact, the regulatory potential of the NiV genome remains incompletely understood. Most antiviral targeting focuses on viral proteins; however, RNA secondary structures can serve regulatory roles that make them promising targets. Functional RNA structures may remain conserved even as the nucleotide sequence diverges, making them difficult to detect using sequence-based analyses alone. In this study, we applied a computational framework to identify structurally conserved RNA elements across the NiV genome. Eighty-eight NiV sequences were aligned using Multiple Alignment Fast Fourier Transform (MAFFT), followed by analysis with a 120-nucleotide sliding window. Sequence variability was quantified using Shannon entropy. Structural conservation used the Conservation Index (SCI) derived from RNAfold and RNAalifold. We defined candidate regions as genomic windows exhibiting both moderate-to-high sequence variability and high structural conservation. Our analysis identified four candidate regions where SCI remained in the top 5% (SCI: 0.98 â€“ 1.0) of the data and sequence divergence in the top 50% (Shannon entropy: 0.65 â€“ 0.76). These regions represent conserved RNA structural elements that may play regulatory roles in the viral life cycle. These findings highlight conserved RNA structures as promising targets for further functional validation. Such elements may be particularly amenable to RNA-targeted therapeutic strategies, including antisense oligonucleotides and small-molecule RNA-binding compounds, offering a potential pathway toward the development of mutation-resistant antiviral interventions.

title: 3’UTR exitron splicing reshapes the 3’ regulatory landscape in cancer
authors: Joshua Fry, Northwestern University, United States; Rendong Yang, Northwestern University, United States
abstract: Alternative splicing of 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs) represents an underexplored dimension of post-transcriptional regulation in cancer. Here, we uncover a novel and prevalent splicing mechanismâ€”3'UTR exitron splicingâ€”where internal segments of 3'UTR exonic sequences are spliced out, reshaping transcript stability and regulatory potential. Utilizing a newly developed and rigorously validated computational pipeline, ScanEPIC, we systematically identify high-confidence 3'UTR exitrons across multiple RNA sequencing platforms. Analysis of paired tumor-normal samples reveals that 3'UTR exitron splicing is frequently dysregulated in tumors and associated with poor clinical outcomes. Single-cell analysis highlights cancer cell-specific exitron splicing patterns associated with aggressive cellular phenotypes. Functionally, we show that tumor-specific exitron splicing events, such as those in JAG2, attenuate tumor suppressor activity in lung cancer models. In castration-resistant prostate cancer, high exitron burden defines a molecular subtype with significantly worse survival outcomes. We further demonstrate that 3'UTR exitron splicing disrupts post-transcriptional regulatory networks by removing RNA-binding protein binding sites. In particular, 3'UTR exitron splicing of the tumor suppressor N4BP2 eliminates binding sites for the mRNA-stabilizing factor KHSRP, thereby destabilizing the transcript and abolishing tumor suppressive function. We show that 3'UTR exitron splicing represents a new paradigm of splicing-mediated tumor suppressor inactivation through post-transcriptional destabilization.

title: Short-read total RNA-Seq data reveals thousands of recursive splicing events in human introns
authors: David Bass, Department of Biology, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Steven Salzberg, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Recursive splicing (RS) is a process in which an intron is removed from a nascent RNA molecule in two splicing events, as if it were two adjacent introns lacking an intermediate exon. We describe a novel approach for detecting recursive splice sites (RSSs), the intronic loci at which RS constitutively occurs, based on alignment of total RNA-seq data to short, bespoke pre-RNA â€œtargetâ€ sequences. Our method proves to be reliable under changes to sample size, tissue, and transcript expression. While maintaining a low false discovery rate, we report 3,022 RSSs, which appear in 2,775 unique introns in 2,407 unique genes. 4% of these RSSs overlap with candidate RSSs reported by four recent studies of human RS, which is exciting considering the egregious lack of consensus among these prior studies. We find that the median RS intron length is 13,250 base pairs, which is nearly an order of magnitude greater than the median human intron, but is drastically shorter than average RS intron lengths reported in the majority of prior studies that limit their analysis to extremely long introns. We reconcile our annotation of RS in a large, but not abundant, set of human introns with claims by Wan et al. (2021) that recursive splicing is the near-ubiquitous result of stochastic splice site selection. Our work dramatically increases the number of known RSSs in the human genome and provides a bioinformatic pipeline for annotating RSSs only from total RNA-seq data.

title: Bifunctional lncRNA SNHG16 with antagonistic RNA and peptide functions in colorectal cancer malignancy
authors: Minwook Lee, Hanyang University, South Korea; Sang-Ho Yoon, Hanyang University, South Korea; Yeongwon Kim, Hanyang University, South Korea; Junho Choe, Hanyang University, South Korea; Jin-Wu Nam, Hanyang University, South Korea
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are emerging as key regulators of gene expression with cell type-specific functions, yet their roles in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain poorly defined. Bulk RNA-sequencing obscures cell-level heterogeneity, and the bifunctionality of lncRNAs, as both regulatory transcripts and sources of functional peptides, has been largely overlooked. Here, we integrated TCGA bulk RNA-seq with single-cell transcriptomes from Korean and Belgian CRC patients, and applied long-read sequencing, ribosome profiling, and functional assays to resolve isoform- and cell typeâ€“specific lncRNA functions. Among 20,971 novel lncRNAs, SNHG16 was enriched in malignant cells and encoded two micropeptides (MP20 and MP33). These isoforms localized to light polysomes and showed translation potential. Functional studies revealed that MP33 enhanced migration, invasion, and tumor growth, while untranslated SNHG16 RNA suppressed these traits. Inserting stem-loop structures abolished translation-dependent effects, confirming the functional role of the peptides. Furthermore, SNHG16 expression was upregulated by JAK/STAT3 signaling from tumor-associated macrophages. Collectively, these findings redefine SNHG16 as a bifunctional lncRNA with opposing roles at the RNA and peptide levels, highlighting the need to resolve lncRNA isoform-specific functions. This work provides a framework for investigating lncRNA bifunctionality and developing isoform- or peptide-targeted therapies in cancer.

title: Designing mRNA coding sequence via multimodal reverse translation language modeling with Pro2RNA
authors: Bian Bian, Kitasato University, Japan; Yiming Zhang, The University of Tokyo,; Jichen Zhang, The University of Tokyo,; Kiyoshi Asai, Institute of Science Tokyo,; Yutaka Saito, Kitasato University,
abstract: mRNA coding sequence design is a critical component in the development of mRNA vaccines, nucleic acid therapeutics, and heterologous gene expression systems. While large language models have recently been successfully applied to protein design and RNA modeling, designing optimal mRNA coding sequences for a given protein, particularly in a species-specific manner, remains a major challenge. Here, we present Pro2RNA, a multimodal reverse-translation language model that generates mRNA coding sequences from their corresponding protein sequences while explicitly conditioning on host organism taxonomy information. Pro2RNA integrates multiple pretrained language models across different modalities, including ESM2 for protein representation, SciBERT for taxonomy understanding, and a generative RNA language model for mRNA codon-level sequence generation. By training on mRNA-protein pairs from eukaryote and bacteria datasets respectively, Pro2RNA learns species-dependent genetic codes and codon usage patterns, enabling the generation of host-adapted and natural-like mRNA coding sequences. Across multiple benchmark evaluations, Pro2RNA matches or surpasses existing optimization methods, demonstrating its potential as a powerful and flexible framework for species-aware mRNA coding sequence design.

title: Prediction of non-canonical base pairs using structural constraints from sequence comparison
authors: Megan Miaro, Department of Biochemistry & Biophysics and Center for RNA Biology, University of Rochester, United States; David Mathews, Department of Biochemistry & Biophysics and Center for RNA Biology, University of Rochester, United States
abstract: Non-coding RNA (ncRNA) have many roles including carrying genetic information, catalyzing reactions, and regulating gene expression. Around 98% of the human genome is made up of non-protein-coding sequences with ncRNA making up most of the transcriptional output. The majority of these ncRNA have yet to be characterized. ncRNA 3D structure predictions can provide key insights on the function of an RNA. These predictions currently suffer from a lack of accurate modeling, particularly in loop regions that contain non-canonical base pairs. Current methods in RNA secondary structure prediction focus on the prediction of canonical base pairs using thermodynamic parameters. There are no thermodynamic parameters available for predicting non-canonical base pairs. Additionally, predicting conserved structural elements from homology is the most accurate approach to predict RNA secondary structures as homologous RNAs can share high structural similarity, even with low sequence identity. We developed a program to predict RNA secondary structures including non-canonical base pairs using a sequence comparison approach. TurboFold, from the RNAstructure package, predicts conserved secondary structures and a sequence alignment given a set of homologous sequences. Using TurboFold, we implemented a preexisting set of parameters named Nucleotide Cyclic Motifs (NCMs) that allow for the prediction of non-canonical base pairs. We demonstrated that the NCMs perform worse than thermodynamic parameters at predicting conserved canonical base pairs. To address this, we use accurate predictions of canonical base pairs with thermodynamic parameters to constrain the search for non-canonical base pairs with NCMs. This correctly predicts on average 61% of conserved non-canonical base pairs.

title: SamplingDesign: RNA design via continuous optimization with coupled variables and Monte-Carlo sampling
authors: Wei Yu Tang, University of Southern California, United States; Ning Dai, Oregon State University, United States; Tianshuo Zhou, Oregon State University, United States; David Mathews, University of Rochester, United States; Liang Huang, Oregon State University, United States
abstract: This paper has just been published in Nature Communications (2026): https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67901-3 RNA design aims to find a sequence that can fold into a target secondary structure. It can create artificial RNA molecules for specific functions, with wide applications in medicine. It is computationally challenging due to two levels of combinatorial explosion: the exponentially large design space and the exponentially many competing structures per design. Popular methods such as local search cannot keep up with these combinatorial explosions. We instead employ two techniques from machine learning, continuous optimization and Monte-Carlo sampling. We start from a distribution over all valid sequences, and use gradient descent to improve the expectation of an arbitrary objective function. We define novel coupled-variable distributions to model the correlation between nucleotides. We then use sampling to approximate the objective, estimate the gradient, and select the final candidate. Our work consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in key metrics including Boltzmann probability and ensemble defect, especially on long and hard-to-design structures.

title: Characterizing the interplay between genetic variants and the splicing of alternative terminal exons
authors: Étienne Fafard-Couture, Boston University, United States; Ana Fiszbein, Boston University, United States
abstract: Alternative terminal exon usage, a type of alternative RNA processing, shapes proteomic diversity in human genes by controlling the choice of transcription start and polyadenylation sites. We recently characterized hybrid exons, a novel class of exons that act as terminal exons, internal exons or both, depending on the tissue in which they are expressed. By modulating the composition of untranslated regions, hybrid exons influence transcript stability and translation. While defects in RNA processing are a major cause of human diseases, the effects of genetic variants on the regulation of terminal and hybrid exons remain poorly understood. Therefore, we applied the hybrid-internal-terminal (HIT) index, a pipeline we developed to quantify hybrid and terminal exon usage from RNA-seq data, to the Genotype-Tissue-Expression (GTEx) cohort across 49 human tissues. Using tensorQTL, we integrated these measurements with genotype data to identify 5,010 significant RNA-processing quantitative trait loci (rpQTLs), defined as genetic variants associated with terminal or hybrid exon usage. We classified these rpQTLs as predominantly tissue-specific (~80%), displaying either an additive, dominant or recessive effect. rpQTL variants are enriched in promoter regions and near splice sites, suggesting coordinated regulation between transcription and splicing of terminal and hybrid exons. Interestingly, rpQTL genes contain significantly more exons and shorter introns, suggesting that compact gene architecture may favor the emergence of finely tuned RNA-processing regulatory programs for terminal exons. Overall, our work shows that genetic variation broadly modulates tissue-specific usage of terminal and hybrid exon and highlights how variants influence RNA processing to expand proteomic diversity.

title: MICA: A Variational Autoencoder Learns Cohort-Invariant Microbiome Signatures of Colorectal Cancer
authors: Xueyao Wang, Karolinska Institutet, Sweden; Amir Ata Saei, Karolinska Institutet, Sweden
abstract: Motivation: Gut microbiome alterations have been repeatedly associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), but microbiome based prediction models often generalize poorly across studies because cohorts differ in geography, host composition, sequencing protocols, and preprocessing. Our hypothesis is that representation learning can recover CRC relevant structure while reducing cohort driven variation. Methods: We developed MOSAIC-CRC, a domain-adversarial variational autoencoder that learns low dimensional latent representations from stool metagenomic taxonomic profiles. To better reflect biological relationships among taxa, the model uses a phylogeny aware input representation derived from the microbial tree. We evaluated the approach on approximately 4000 stool metagenomic samples from 18 curated CRC cohorts using leave one cohort out cross validation and compared latent feature classifiers against strong baselines trained on taxonomic features, including batch correction based pipelines. Results: Latent representations learned by MOSAIC-CRC achieved CRC prediction mean AUROC of 0.785 Â± 0.073, comparable to a vanilla VAE baseline (0.780 Â± 0.071), while showing reduced cohort separability in the embedding space (0.287 vs 0.387), consistent with improved transfer across unseen cohorts. Interpretation of the latent dimensions linked CRC associated regions of the embedding space to increased contributions from known CRC enriched taxa, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, Parvimonas micra, and other oral associated pathobionts, whereas control associated regions were linked to commensal taxa more typical of a healthy gut microbiome. This pattern suggests that the model captures shared diseass related community restructuring rather than only study specific variation. Conclusion: These results support cross cohort representation learning as a promising strategy for deriving more transferable and interpretable microbiome signatures of CRC from heterogeneous metagenomic studies.

title: Toward a systematic method of database enrichment for reference-based metagenomics
authors: Henry Secaira-Morocho, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health, United States; Xiaofang Jiang, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health, United States; Qiyun Zhu, Center for Fundamental and Applied Microbiomics, Arizona State University, United States
abstract: Tracing millions of shotgun metagenomic sequencing reads to their source requires mapping them to a database of reference microbial genomes. While most efforts have improved the efficiency and accuracy of sequence aligners and taxonomic profilers, the engineering of reference databases has received inadequate attention. On the one hand, databases with few genomes yield a highly incomplete picture of the community because multiple taxonomic groups are missing. On the other hand, databases with the most comprehensive genome collections can introduce inaccuracies and misidentifications in the inferred community due to a highly skewed distribution, in which most sequenced genomes belong to a handful of microbial species of biomedical interest. Therefore, striking a balance between under- and over-represented taxa is essential for reference-based metagenomics, as database composition determines which taxa are inferred to be present in the community. Here, we explore whether database composition can be adaptively enriched for each sample. For this, we developed an iterative enrichment method that traverses a distance-based tree connecting all genomes to identify microbial genomes likely to be the sources of sequencing reads. Using simulated metagenomic datasets, we demonstrate that enriched databases improve metagenomic classification at the genome level and can recover microbial community composition with accuracy comparable to that of larger databases. Although enrichment generates false positives, these genomes are closely related to true positives, and abundance-weighted $\beta$-diversity metrics indicate that they do not increase the distance between the inferred and ground-truth profiles. Our results indicate that database engineering has a significant impact on metagenomic analysis, and incorporating enriched databases can yield a more accurate description of microbial communities.

title: A Multi-Layer Workflow for Low-Biomass Airway Metagenomics Integrating Signal Attrition, Site Confounding, and Database-Aware Resistome Interpretation
authors: Mashael Alghuraybi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Norah Alharbi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Aisha Alamri, Department of Clinical Laboratory Sciences, College of Applied Medical Sciences, Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Saudi Arabia; Aroob Alhumaidy, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Othman Aljurayyad, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Muruj Tukruni, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Muhayla Alanazi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Nouf Alharb, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Saidan Alotaibi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Nuha Bin Tyyash, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Hend Alotaibi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Shahad Alsalman, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Yara Altuwaijri, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Hatim Almutairi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia
abstract: Shotgun metagenomic analysis of the upper airway presents a distinct computational challenge due to low microbial biomass, where host DNA dominates sequencing output and reduces usable microbial signal. In addition, anatomical heterogeneity across sampling sites (nasal versus oropharyngeal) introduces a strong ecological structure that can obscure disease-associated variation, while resistome inference remains sensitive to reference database choice. Here, we present a structured, multi-layer workflow that integrates signal-aware preprocessing, site-stratified analysis, and database-aware resistome interpretation for robust analysis of low-biomass airway metagenomes. A total of 98 pediatric airway samples were processed, of which 69 retained sufficient signal for taxonomic analysis and 43 for functional profiling, highlighting substantial signal attrition. Taxonomic profiles and diversity metrics were computed using standard approaches, with all analyses stratified by anatomical site to control for confounding. Functional profiling was performed using HUMAnN, and resistome analysis was conducted on de novo assemblies using AMRFinderPlus and ABRicate across multiple databases. Anatomical site was the primary driver of variation in both taxonomic and functional profiles, with oropharyngeal samples exhibiting higher richness and diversity than nasal samples. Differential signals were dominated by housekeeping and translation-related functions. Resistome analysis showed variability across databases, with AMRFinderPlus identifying more resistance genes and detecting additional clinically relevant targets. Together, these results demonstrate that airway metagenomic interpretation is shaped by signal availability, site structure, and database choice, and support a confounder-aware workflow that improves robustness and interpretability in low-biomass studies.

title: Amplicon-Based Stool Microbiome Proﬁling for Predicting Gut Health
authors: Yimeng You, IBMI, University of Tübingen, Germany; Anupam Gautam, IBMI, University of Tübingen; Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany; Vinod Gupta, Mayo Clinic, Center for Individualized Medicine, United States; Wenhuan Zeng, Berlin Institute of Health at Charité, Germany; Daniel Huson, IBMI, University of Tübingen; IMPRS ""From Molecules to Organisms"", Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany
abstract: The gut microbiome plays a critical role in human health, contributing to numerous physiological functions and showing strong associations with a wide range of diseases. Recent indices such as the Gut Microbiome Health Index (GMHI) and its successor GMWI2 have demonstrated promising performance in predicting host health status. However, these approaches rely on high-resolution shotgun metagenomic sequencing, which remains costly and less accessible for routine applications. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of predicting human health status using amplicon-based stool microbiome profiling. We compiled a large-scale 16S rRNA dataset comprising 43,564 samples from 187 independent studies. Applying LASSO regression to a rarefied feature table, we identified 85 key microbial taxa at the genus and species levels associated with health status. These features were subsequently used to train an XGBoost classification model, achieving an accuracy of 79.87% on our 16S-based dataset. Our findings highlight the potential of cost-effective amplicon sequencing approaches for microbiome-based health assessment, offering a scalable solution for clinical and hospital settings. Future work will focus on translating model outputs into a novel microbiome-based health index and validating its performance on independent datasets.

title: Bacterial Community Structure and Functional Potential of Fermented Pearl Millet Revealed by 16S rRNA Amplicon Sequencing
authors: Akriti Dhakal, Morgan State University, United States; Bahram Faraji, Morgan States University, United States; James Wachira, Morgan State University, United States; Roshan Paudel, Morgan State University, United States
abstract: Spontaneous cereal fermentations represent complex microbial ecosystems that contribute to food preservation, safety, and nutritional enhancement, yet their microbiome dynamics and functional potential remain insufficiently understood. This study employed a bioinformatics-driven microbiome approach to characterize the temporal microbial community structure and predicted metabolic functions during spontaneous fermentation of pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and PICRUSt2-based functional inference. Fermentation was conducted under controlled conditions, and samples were collected at 72 h and 144 h. Microbial DNA was extracted, sequenced (V3â€“V4 region), and analyzed using the DADA2 pipeline to infer amplicon sequence variants, assign taxonomy, and assess diversity metrics. Results showed progressive acidification during fermentation, with pH decreasing from 6.50 to 3.59, indicating active microbial metabolism. Microbial community analysis revealed a clear successional pattern, with Pediococcus dominating at early stages and a relative increase in Lactobacillus at later stages, alongside consistent representation of Weissella spp. Species-level profiling identified predominant lactic acid bacteria including Weissella paramesenteroides, Lactobacillus coryniformis, and Lactobacillus sakei, while a substantial proportion of reads remained unclassified, suggesting the presence of uncharacterized taxa. Alpha diversity decreased over time, reflecting selective enrichment of acid-tolerant microorganisms. Functional prediction analysis indicated temporal shifts in metabolic potential, with early-stage communities enriched in nucleotide degradation and central carbon metabolism pathways, whereas later stages showed increased representation of amino acid biosynthesis, cofactor metabolism, and cell wall-associated processes. These findings demonstrate dynamic microbiome succession and functional adaptation during fermentation, providing insights into microbial ecology and the potential for leveraging fermentation-associated microbiota to enhance nutritional and functional properties of cereal-based foods.

title: Linking Microbial Abundance to Gene Content with a Robust and Scalable Phylogeny-Aware Comparative Framework Using Phylogenize2
authors: Kathryn Kananen, Department of Microbiology, The Ohio State University, United States; Nghi Tran, Department of Microbiology, The Ohio State University, United States; Patrick Bradley, Department of Microbiology, The Ohio State University, United States
abstract: To move beyond microbiome association studies toward mechanisms, researchers need to identify microbial genes underlying these associations. However, because related species tend to share genotypes and phenotypes, most existing methods are biased towards discovering clade markers with weak evidence for functional relevance. Phylogenetic comparative methods can address this problem, but remain underutilized in metagenomics for two main reasons: they require genomes from the environment being studied and pose statistical challenges for metagenomic data. We present Phylogenize2, a major revision of a phylogeny-aware tool linking microbial abundance changes to specific genes. Phylogenize2 integrates modern, biome-specific assembly databases from MGnify and applies consistent functional annotation, allowing the tool to be applied to an expanding set of environments, including the human gut, mouse gut, and ocean. Furthermore, to handle noisy differential abundance measurements, Phylogenize2 uses a new, non-parametric statistical test called robust permutration. Robust permutration controls the false positive rate when outliers are present, while retaining superior power to previously published approaches. Finally, Phylogenize2 is easier to install. When we apply Phylogenize2 to commensal gut Lachnospiraceae in a human liver cirrhosis study, we find that Lachnospiraceae with higher abundance tend to have homologs of a transcription factor likely to sense nitrosative stress. When applied to a mouse study of high-fat diets, Muribaculaceae with higher abundance tend to have additional thioredoxins, possibly reflecting diet-induced host free radical release. Finally, in a study of polar marine samples, Flavobacteriaceae from the mesopelagic zone are enriched for an aryl aldehyde oxidoreductase that may help metabolize lignin-like compounds.

title: Probing decision boundaries in bioinformatics classifiers using mutation path analysis
authors: Dinithi Wickramaratne, University of Maryland College Park, United States; Mihai Pop, University of Maryland College Park, United States
abstract: Machine learning is widely used in bioinformatics, yet the robustness of machine learning algorithms to errors in the data is poorly understood. An approach used to understand the robustness of machine learning systems to errors is defining the decision boundary, since the data points that are closer to the decision boundary are more likely to be affected by errors. In this work, we explore the decision boundaries by constructing mutation paths between closely related sequences with divergent labels and by tracking changes in predicted labels along these paths. As an example, we used VirFinder, a k-mer based machine learning method that identifies viral sequences within genomic sequence data. The dataset used for the experiment consisted of metagenomic sequences from the DIABIMMUNE study of infant gut microbiomes. In the analysis of these data, we find that decision boundaries can lie extremely close to sequence endpoints, with label flips occurring after a single mutation. Many paths exhibit a single, stable change in label, whereas others oscillate between classes which may indicate locally unstable regions of the decision boundary. Our approach also assesses whether certain positions in a sequence are more prone to inducing label flips than others, potentially revealing sequence features relevant for classification. Beyond viral classification, we have applied this framework to taxonomic classification, and believe our work represents a general framework for assessing the robustness to errors of a broader range of bioinformatics sequence classifiers.

title: Characterization of the Gut and Oral Microbiomes in Egyptian Patients with Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder
authors: Rana Salah Khalel, The American University in Cairo, Egypt; Khlood Abdelaal, The American University in Cairo, Egypt; Ahmed Moustafa, The American University in Cairo, Egypt
abstract: The gut-oral-brain axis positions the human microbiome as a pivotal modulator of neuropsychiatric health; yet population-specific, multisite investigations remain scarce, particularly in underrepresented regions. This study addresses that gap by presenting the first, to our knowledge, integrative computational characterization of gut and oral microbiome alterations in Egyptian patients with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD). Fecal and saliva samples were collected from patients with SZ (gut n=54; oral n=55), BD (gut n=53; oral n=57), and healthy controls (n=20 per site). Extracted DNA underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing followed by standardized bioinformatic processing. Microbial community structure was assessed through alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, differential abundance testing, and predictive functional profiling. Both gut and oral microbiomes in SZ and BD exhibited significant dysbiosis, with reduced alpha diversity observed in the oral microbiome and distinct beta-diversity clustering across both sites compared to controls, indicating consistent microbial alterations. Differential abundance analysis identified both shared and disorder-specific taxonomic signatures, including depletion of short-chain fatty acidâ€“producing bacteria and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa, suggesting a shift toward a pro-inflammatory microbial state. Functional predictions revealed convergent disruptions in amino acid and lipid metabolism, immune-related pathways, and neurotransmitter-associated functions. Notably, schizophrenia-associated gut microbiomes showed enrichment of dopamine degradation pathways, supporting a potential microbial contribution to dopaminergic dysregulation. Together, these findings provide population-specific evidence linking microbiome composition and function to neuropsychiatric disorders and identify candidate microbial signatures. This work establishes a foundation for microbiome-informed, data-driven approaches to personalized neuropsychiatric diagnostics and therapeutics and highlights the significance of including underrepresented populations in microbiome research.

title: Structural Motifs in Metagenomic Assembly Graphs Reveal Novel Phage and Plasmid Diversity
authors: Anning Cui, University of Maryland at College Park, United States
abstract: The human microbiome harbors a large variety of mobile genetic elements, including bacteriophages and plasmids, whose roles in strain-level adaptation of the microbial community remain poorly characterized. Standard metagenomic pipelines fragment assembly graphs in ways that obscure these elements. Here we present an integrated graph-based framework built on tools developed in the Pop lab for recovering phages and plasmids directly from metagenomic assembly graphs across multiple body sites sampled during the Human Microbiome Project (HMP). We identified circular segments and other structural motifs that had high confidence classifications as plasmids and/or phage when annotated with Platon and Virsorter2. These tools detect genomic elements associated with plasmids and phages. More structural motifs were classified as phage in stool samples in comparison to other body sites. Our samples are DNA derived, therefore dsDNA dominate across body sites which should be considered when interpreting diversity estimates. Several samples exhibited high hallmark gene scores from Virsorter2, indicating these structural motifs may represent complete or near-complete phage genomes. A portion of phage-classified structural motifs show little similarity to known phages, suggesting the potential for discovery of novel phages. Our presentation will also highlight body-site specific patterns of phage diversity and plasmid content. These results demonstrate that assembly graph-aware methods can link graph topology to biologically meaningful mobile element recovery. Future work will focus on assessing the functional implications and adaptations associated with mobile elements identified in the human microbiome. Together, these analyses lay the groundwork for a comprehensive, graph-aware understanding of genetic exchange within the human microbiome.

title: Evaluation of Hybrid-Sequencing Metagenomics Analysis to Capture the Rare Biosphere of Greenhouse Gas Consumers within Wetlands and Rice Soils
authors: Shu Ying Wee, University of Southern California, United States; Morgan Lindback, University of Southern California, United States; Jeremy Alexander, University of Southern California, United States; Raven Althouse, University of Southern California, United States; Cameron Thrash, University of Southern California, United States; Adam Smith, University of Southern California, United States
abstract: Soils represent one of the most biodiverse ecosystems in the world and play an important role in global biogeochemical cycles. Wetland soils and rice field soils are major sources of greenhouse gases, particularly methane and nitrous oxide. Interestingly, found within the same soils are methanotrophs and nitrous oxide reducers that act as biofilters, partially consuming the greenhouse gases produced. Metagenomics analyses of these soils often highlight the predominant members of the microbial community. This inadvertently overlooks the rare biosphere that may be as functionally significant as the more abundant communities. Rare taxa may also harbor functional genes such as methane monooxygenase and nitrous oxide reductase that have diverged from known genes present in databases. Recent applications of hybrid metagenomic sequencing strategies involving both long- and short-reads have improved the resolution of soil microbiome studies. Investigations to further elucidate the rare soil biosphere may be advanced by a strategic combination of available and recent bioinformatics tools. Here, we evaluate a hybrid-sequencing metagenomics workflow that aims to capture the rare soil microbiome, with an emphasis on microorganisms involved in greenhouse gas cycling. This workflow involves optimizations of tools used in assembly, binning, and gene annotation. Characterizing the microbial community composition and functional potential of the rare greenhouse gas consumers is essential to assess the capacity of microbial-driven attenuation of methane and nitrous oxide into the atmosphere. Furthermore, the workflow outlined here provides a replicable framework for rare biosphere exploration in other complex and diverse microbial ecosystems of ecological importance.

title: PlasRAG: comprehensive plasmid characterization and retrieval through sequence-text alignment
authors: Yongxin Ji, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Jiaojiao Guan, City Univesity of HongKong, China; Herui Liao, Institute for Medical Engineering and Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, United States; Jiayu Shang, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Yanni Sun, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Plasmids play a pivotal role in the emergence of multidrug-resistant and pathogenic bacteria, posing significant clinical challenges. However, the rapidly growing number of unannotated plasmids necessitates comprehensive characterization of their diverse properties. Here, we present PlasRAG, a tool that integrates multi-faceted property characterization of query plasmids and plasmid DNA retrieval based on textual queries. PlasRAG employs a bidirectional multi-modal information retrieval model that aligns DNA sequences with textual data, effectively overcoming the limitations of traditional approaches. Rigorous experiments demonstrate that PlasRAG delivers robust performance and enhanced analytical capabilities, underscoring the effectiveness of its architectural design.

title: MicroGlot: a taxonomy-informed microbial foundation model enabling effective sequence annotation in microbiome
authors: Yuxuan Du, Department of Electrical Engineering, The University of Texas at San Antonio, United States
abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on DNA are increasingly used for microbial sequence prediction, yet existing designs underuse a freely available global signal, namely the taxonomic background of each sequence. We present MicroGlot, a taxonomy-informed gLM with 479 M activated parameters, whose sparse, lineage-conditioned architecture is motivated by recent findings on language-specific expert specialization in multilingual neural language models. A sequence-based species encoder maps raw DNA to the same lineage embedding, extending taxonomy-informed inference to unlabelled environmental contigs. MicroGlot is pretrained on 3.7 million sequences from 100,574 species across the six major microbial categories, the broadest taxonomic coverage reported for a gLM. Across nine linear-probing benchmarks spanning sequence categorization, viral taxonomy, species classification, regulatory elements, growth rate, and bacterial phenotypes, MicroGlot matches or exceeds established baselines with the largest gains on genome-scale tasks.

title: Denoising Genomes with a Phylogenetically Informed Empirical Bayes Model
authors: Stephanie Majernik, The Ohio State University, United States; Patrick Bradley, The Ohio State University, United States
abstract: Large-scale metagenomic assembly efforts have dramatically increased the number of documented species with available genomes. However, Metagenome Assembled Genomes (MAGs) are sourced from mixed communities, and can therefore introduce contamination, defined as genes from the wrong species or strain. The most common methods for addressing this issue simply remove genomes with significant estimated contamination (e.g., above 5%), but this still leaves some contamination in the remaining high-quality MAGs, which may be underestimated by common tools. Worse, gene-level analyses enrich for contaminants: in our prior analysis of a metagenomic case-control study of cirrhosis, we found that 38% of genes with significant differential detection were likely contaminants. We previously developed a tool, PanSweep, that predicted contamination by (1) using each gene's predicted taxonomic range and (2) correlating gene and species counts across samples. While effective (AUROC > 0.9), the second method only applies within a specific dataset. In contrast, predicting taxonomic range requires no additional data other than existing phylogenetic databases. However, our previous tool was limited to coarse-grained, approximate taxonomic information, and did not incorporate other potentially-informative data, such as gene presence rates or the predicted quality of the genomes containing the gene. To incorporate this missing data, we are designing and validating a phylogenetically informed empirical Bayes model to predict whether genes are contaminants. We can apply this model to existing MAG collections to "denoise" these contaminants and thus improve the reliability of downstream analyses.

title: dbcan-nf: a scalable Nextflow pipeline for CAZyme annotation in metagenomes
authors: Xinpeng Zhang, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, United States; Haidong Yi, St.Jude Children's Research Hospital, United States; Jinfang Zheng, Zhejiang Lab, China; Yanbin Yin, University of Nebraska - Lincoln, United States
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing has greatly expanded our understanding of complex microbiomes, particularly in the human gut, where carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) drive carbohydrate metabolism and host-microbe interactions. However, accurate and reproducible profiling of CAZyme abundance from whole-genome shotgun (WGS) data remains challenging due to fragmented analytical workflows and inconsistent tool configurations. Here we present dbcan-nf, a scalable and reproducible Nextflow pipeline built within the nf-core framework for automated CAZyme annotation from metagenomes. The pipeline integrates commonly used metagenomic processing steps, including read quality control, assembly (MEGAHIT/Flye), gene prediction (pyrodigal), CAZyme annotation (run_dbcan), and read mapping-based CAZyme abundance quantification. dbcan-nf supports multiple analytical modes, including individual sample assembly, co-assembly, and assembly-free analysis, and processes both short reads and long reads. We evaluated dbcan-nf using simulated reads of synthetic mock community as well as reads from an ultra-deep sequencing dataset from Hadza hunter-gatherer microbiome samples. Benchmark analyses revealed that assembly-based modes provided higher CAZyme annotation accuracy, while the assembly-free mode significantly overestimated CAZyme abundance despite lower computational cost. dbcan-nf produces interpretable and publication-ready outputs, including CAZyme abundance table/plot, substrate-level summary table/plot, and read mapping plots for CAZyme gene clusters (CGCs). dbcan-nf provides a standardized and scalable solution for functional characterization of microbiome carbohydrate metabolism and facilitates reproducible analysis of CAZyme repertoires across large metagenomic cohorts. The source code is freely available at: https://github.com/bcb-unl/dbcan-nf.

title: Phylogenetic Placement Enables Near-Haplotype Resolution of Metagenomic Samples using metaWEPP
authors: Pranav Gangwar, University of California, San Diego, United States; Qiwen Xu, University of California, San Diego, United States; Jaden Seangmany, University of California, San Diego, United States; Pratik Katte, University of California, Santa Cruz, United States; Yatish Turakhia, University of California, San Diego, United States
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing is transforming diverse areas of health and biological sciences, including pathogen surveillance, clinical diagnostics, and microbiome research. However, the inherent complexity of metagenomic data limits most existing computational tools to species-level classification and abundance estimation, overlooking intra-species genetic diversity that drives key phenotypes. In this talk, we present metaWEPP, a novel computational pipeline that overcomes this limitation by achieving near-haplotype resolution in metagenomic analysis. Specifically, metaWEPP first assigns sequencing reads to species using standard taxonomic classifiers, and then leverages WEPP to phylogenetically place them onto species-specific mutation-annotated trees of publicly available sequences and select the subset of haplotypes that best explain the sample. It also reports unaccounted alleles indicative of novel variants and includes an interactive dashboard for detailed, read-level visualization. Applied to diverse metagenomic and mixed-genome samples from prior studies, metaWEPP produced concordant species-level results, while also revealing finer lineage- and haplotype-level insights beyond the capabilities of existing tools. For instance, across various clinical samples, in addition to identifying the pathogens infecting patients, metaWEPP provided credible lineage- and haplotype-level information that can support clinical decision-making by identifying mutations in haplotypes associated with key phenotypes. In wastewater samples, metaWEPP uncovered previously undetected, epidemiologically relevant haplotype clusters of human-infecting pathogens, as well as clusters associated with plant-infecting pathogens. These findings demonstrate metaWEPP's ability to advance various clinical, epidemiological, and research applications by providing deeper, actionable insights.

title: Medival Can Detect Mobile Genetic Elements Without a Reference Database
authors: Grace Oualline, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Sakshi Pandey, University of Florida, United States; Christina Boucher, University of Florida, United States; Yun William Yu, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Motivation: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are DNA sequences that move within or between genomes, driving horizontal gene transfer and accelerating bacterial evolution. Detecting MGEs is crucial for understanding their evolution and managing antibiotic resistance. Existing tools rely on reference databases or trained models, imposing a fundamental ceiling on what they can find, as they are structurally unable to detect MGEs absent from their reference data. Results: We present Medival (https://github.com/graceoualline/Medival), a method that identifies MGEs by comparing against databases of unannotated bacterial genomes. Our previous work, skandiver, identified large intercellular MGEs by detecting genomic regions with high sequence similarity to phylogenetically distant species. Medival extends this divergence-based approach to small and fragmented MGEs. Medival uses BLAT against the Genome Taxonomy Database to get short alignments, filtered by divergence or average nucleotide identity, providing strong statistical evidence for horizontal transfer. On a synthetic benchmark of 100 plasmid insertions, Medival detected 66 MGEs, recovering an average of 7.7% of each element while reporting 1.1% of the host genome as signal. By comparison, geNomad detected 10 MGEs with higher per-element recovery (84.1%) but flagged 5.02% of the host genome, and MobileElementFinder detected 24 MGEs with 20.5% average recovery and no host-genome signal. Reference-based tools thus achieve higher coverage of recognized elements, but miss the majority of MGEs entirely. Medival also recovered 55% of a plasmid from newly discovered species Photobacterium toruni, a species absent from existing reference databases and undetected by the existing tools.

title: ICICLE: Transformer-Based Detection of Integrative and Conjugative Elements from Genomic and Metagenomic Sequences
authors: Sakshi Pandey, University of Florida, United States; Noelle Noyes, University of Minnesota, United States; Yun William Yu, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Christina Boucher, University of Florida, United States
abstract: Integrative and Conjugative elements(ICEs) are potent agents of bacterial evolution, combining stable chromosomal maintenance with autonomous conjugative transfer to disseminate antimicrobial resistance, virulence, and symbiosis genes across species. For instance, the SXT system in the bacteria Vibrio cholerae can transform susceptible strains into multi-drug resistant pathogens in a single transfer event. However, despite being one of the most abundant mobile genetic elements(MGEs) in nearly all prokaryotic clades, ICEs remain difficult to detect. Their modular, mosaic architecture lacks any single conserved backbone, and current tools relying on rigid heuristics often truncate large elements and miss divergent families. To address this we present ICICLE, a ~126M-parameter transformer-based classifier that learns compositional signatures of ICE directly from nucleotide sequences as short as 2000bp. Unlike existing methods, ICICLE does not require annotation, or a curated database, enabling ICE detection in metagenomic reads, draft genomes, and fragmented assemblies where current tools falter. Benchmarked against five state-of-the-art methods across 131 genomes (191 ICEs), ICICLE outperformed all competitors with 99% detection and 95% mean sequence coverage. This coverage marks an 8% improvement over the next-best tool, scaling to a 22% advantage for elements exceeding 100 kbp, highlighting ICICLE's superiority for large ICEs. Beyond standard benchmarks, ICICLE detected a novel, experimentally validated 61.6 kbp composite ICE unseen in its training data with 92% coverage. Leveraging its short sequence context, ICICLE also enables extraction of a dynamic "ICE burden" metric from metagenomic datasets, offering a proof of concept for real-time, culture-free surveillance of ICE prevalence across microbial communities.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Evaluating Fidelity of Protein LLM Embeddings for Host-Association Analysis
authors: Maliha Aziz, The George Washington University, United States; Lance Price, The George Washington University, United States
abstract: Host-adaptive genes in the accessory genome enable bacterial colonization and persistence across diverse animal hosts. Many of these genes are carried on mobile genetic elements (MGEs), which can be rapidly gained or lost during host transitions, accelerating antimicrobial resistance dissemination and pathogen evolution. Detecting host-associated multigene MGE modules remains challenging because classical alignment-based pangenome and GWAS approaches are computationally expensive and often fail to capture modular gene co-mobilization patterns. We developed a reproducible and memory-efficient Transformer-based pipeline to systematically discover host-enriched MGE gene modules using protein language model embeddings and graph-based clustering. We extracted MGE-associated proteins from 49 Escherichia coli genome assemblies sampled from four vertebrate hosts and encoded 114,682 amino acid sequences into fixed-length embeddings using the ESM-2 protein language model. Embeddings were generated in streamed mini-batches and stored in a scalable format to support downstream analysis without excessive memory requirements. We constructed a sparse similarity graph using approximate nearest-neighbor search (FAISS; cosine similarity; k=10) and applied Leiden community detection to identify protein communities without requiring predefined cluster counts. Cluster host association was quantified using host purity and diversity metrics, and cluster coherence was validated using BLAST-based sequence identity summaries and functional annotation profiles. Application of this workflow to a multi-host MGE dataset, including poultry-adapted ColV plasmid modules previously linked to zoonotic E. coli urinary tract infections revealed distinct gene clusters and co-mobilization patterns supporting a sequence alignment free approach. Embedding-driven clustering captured broad evolutionary and structural signals while reducing dependence on computationally expensive all-vs-all alignments, though some clusters merged functionally distinct proteins with shared structural signatures. This framework provides a scalable, alignment-light approach for host-association analysis of MGEs while maintaining interpretability and transparent provenance for public health surveillance.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PENNE measures live-cell transcriptomes from phase contrast microscopy images using domain adaptation and gated attention
authors: Richard Zhi Fei Dong, University of Toronto, Canada; Shreya Mishra, University Health Network, Canada; Maha Tageldein, University of Toronto, Canada; Shane Harding, University Health Network, Canada; Chris McIntosh, University Health Network, Canada; Gregroy Schwartz, University Health Network, Canada
abstract: Introduction: Capturing temporal dynamics of cellular states is critical for understanding development and disease. While non-invasive methods like phase contrast microscopy (PCM) can capture morphological changes in live cells, longitudinal molecular profiling at the global transcriptome level remains a major challenge, as RNA sequencing fundamentally alters or destroys cells. Methods: We introduce PENNE, a deep-learning framework that infers whole-transcriptomic profiles directly from live-cell PCM images. Utilizing gated attention mechanisms, PENNE trains on spatial transcriptomic datasets to align morphological features with gene expression. To enable PCM inferences, our model performs domain adaptation to eliminate discrepancies between stained and unstained modalities, effectively transferring molecular knowledge from tissue sections to live-cell imaging. Results: PENNE accurately identifies cell-type-specific and radiation-response markers via differential expression analysis across images of various cell types and treatment conditions. Furthermore, using temporal PCM images of cells with a G2/M cell cycle marker, the model captures temporal gene dynamics, evidenced by strong correlations between predicted markers and both ground-truth cellular confluency and cell cycle progression. Finally, interpretability analyses confirm that PENNEâ€™s gated attention mechanism correctly associates specific morphological features with distinct organelle-related gene programs, demonstrating successful mapping between morphology and underlying biology. Conclusion: By bridging the gap between data-rich spatial transcriptomics and widely accessible PCM, PENNE provides a powerful new method for monitoring molecular temporal dynamics directly through morphological information. This approach enables a paradigm-shifting workflow, fusing transcriptome-wide data with live-cell microscopy to fuel the discovery of novel gene programs via scalable, non-invasive, real-time interrogation of cellular states.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Transforming bioinformatics algorithms into federated learning pipelines using skill-based AI agents
authors: Chao-Chun Chuang, NATIONAL CENTER FOR HIGH-PERFORMANCE COMPUTING, Taiwan; Zhi-Han Wang, Chang Gung University, Taiwan; Yen-Jung Chiu, Chang Gung University, Taiwan
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a transformative paradigm for collaborative biomedical research, enabling multiple institutions to jointly train AI models while keeping sensitive patient data private and on-site. However, a critical barrier to widespread adoption is the substantial engineering effort required to convert existing, well-tested bioinformatics algorithms into federated workflows. This work proposes an innovative agent-driven framework that automatically transforms standalone, single-machine bioinformatics code into privacy-preserving federated learning pipelines, dramatically reducing development complexity and time-to-deployment. Our approach encapsulates bioinformatics algorithms as reusable, composable skills and leverages automated skill-tuning to optimize computation, communication, and data partitioning strategies across distributed participants.
