The framework enables researchers to take their existing proven algorithmsâ€”without substantial code modificationsâ€”and instantly convert them into federated versions ready for multi-institutional deployment. In evaluation experiments, algorithms converted through our framework executed successfully in federated settings on first deployment, eliminating the iterative debugging cycles typically required for FL implementation. By providing this seamless pathway from single-machine to federated execution, our work democratizes collaborative biomedical AI, enabling institutions of all sizes to rapidly share models and collectively advance biomedical research while maintaining rigorous data privacy and regulatory compliance.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ARCADE: Controllable Codon Design from Foundation Models via Activation Engineering
authors: Jiayi Li, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Hong-Sheng Lai, Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University, Taiwan; Litian Liang, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Shiyi Du, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Shijie Tang, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Carl Kingsford, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Codon sequence design is crucial for generating mRNA sequences with desired functional properties for tasks such as developing mRNA vaccines or gene editing therapies. Yet existing methods lack flexibility and controllability to adapt to various design objectives. We propose a novel machine learning-based framework, ARCADE, that enables flexible and controllable multi-objective codon design. Leveraging inherent knowledge from pretrained genomic language models, ARCADE extends activation engineering, a technique originally developed for controllable text generation, beyond discrete feature manipulation such as concepts and styles, to steering continuous-valued biological metrics. Specifically, we derive biologically meaningful semantic steering vectors in the model's activation space, which directly control properties such as the Codon Adaptation Index, Minimum Free Energy, and GC content. Experimental results demonstrate the flexibility of ARCADE in designing codon sequences with multiple objectives, underscoring its potential for advancing programmable biological sequence design.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Integrating Spatial Transcriptomics and Digital Pathology to Decipher Tumor Microenvironment and Spatial Biomarkers of Treatment Response in Rectal Cancer
authors: Chen-Pei Chiang, National Health Research Institutes, Taiwan; Shang-Hung Chen, National Health Research Institutes. National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Yi Hsuan Huang, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Yi-Jing Huang, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Ying-Tzu Huang, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Bing-Syuan Chung, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Yu-Min Yeh, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Po-Chuan Chen, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Ren Hao Chan, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Chun-Hsien Wu, National Cheng Kung University Hospital., Taiwan; Ren-Hua Chung, National Health Research Institutes, Taiwan
abstract: Rectal cancer (RC) is a highly prevalent and lethal malignancy globally, with a notably decreasing age of onset. While neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) followed by surgery is the standard of care, clinical responses vary significantly among individuals. Some patients achieve a pathological complete response (CR), while others exhibit poor sensitivity and high recurrence risk. Growing evidence suggests that spatial architecture and molecular interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) are pivotal in determining treatment resistance. To overcome the loss of spatial context in traditional sequencing and the lack of morphological validation in computational clustering, this study establishes a dual-track analytical framework integrating spatial transcriptomics (ST) and digital pathology. The pipeline utilizes the STAIG model to identify spatial domains with similar molecular signatures, complemented by Hover-Net deep learning for nuclei segmentation and Tumor Region of Interest (ROI) identification. This approach ensures that clustering results possess both biological and pathological credibility. Cell types are precisely annotated using CellTypist, and spatial autocorrelation analysis via Moranâ€™s I is employed to investigate the local clustering patterns of key genes. By comparing differential gene expression (DEGs) and functional enrichment (GO/KEGG) between CR and non-CR samples within tumor and immune regions, this study identifies potential spatial molecular markers associated with varying treatment sensitivities. This high-confidence spatial omics workflow provides deep molecular insights into the spatial mechanisms of the RC microenvironment, translating complex data into interpretable evidence to advance personalized precision medicine.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Scalable latent-factor modeling for omics: out-of-core PCA and PLS for reproducible systems biology
authors: Myriam Maumy, UTT and EHESP, France; Frederic Bertrand, UTT and National Conservatory of Crafts and Arts, France
abstract: Systems biology pipelines often start with PCA for QC and structure discovery and PLS regression for phenotype prediction and multi-omics integration. These steps are increasingly limited by data scale and by the need for cross-validation and resampling without copying large matrices into RAM. We present two R packages designed to keep these analyses scalable and reproducible on large biological matrices. bigPCAcpp provides PCA/SVD routines that operate directly on file-backed bigmemory::big.matrix objects, with centering/scaling and blockwise computation, plus utilities to compute and export PCA diagnostics (e.g., loadings and explained variance) while keeping memory bounded. Complementing this, bigPLSR implements fast PLS regression for dense and out-of-core data, offering SIMPLS and NIPALS solvers, kernel-style PLS variants, and streamed cross-products with chunked BLAS. A key feature is automatic algorithm selection (XtX SIMPLS vs XXt wide SIMPLS vs NIPALS) based on (n, p) and a configurable memory budget, enabling scalable model fitting and cross-validation across regimes common in omics. We illustrate how these memory-aware primitives support cohort-scale expression/proteomics analyses and downstream network-oriented interpretation through latent scores and stable feature contributions.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: MiLaSol: Modeling Protein Solubility by Mixing Up Multiple Protein Language Models
authors: Weiwei Lou, Tufts University, United States; Mert Erden, Tufts University, United States; Lenore Cowen, Tufts University, United States
abstract: Motivation: Protein solubility is a critical property that significantly impacts therapeutic efficacy and protein reengineering applications. Recent advances in machine learning and deep learning techniques provide unprecedented opportunities to develop predictive models for solubility, enabling more efficient protein design and optimization. This work is motivated by the potential of leveraging deep learning to address the solubility prediction challenge and to accelerate protein engineering workflows. Results: Leveraging and combining multiple protein language model representations, our MiLaSol model attains 81% accuracy, outperforming prior methods, with the highest Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) score of 0.63 demonstrating balanced performance across both soluble and insoluble proteins. The model achieved 86.2% agreement with experimental annotations on deleterious mutations, validating its predictive reliability. Through simulated annealing optimization coupled with the Raygun model, we also present a computational method to reengineer insoluble protein variants into soluble forms, with predictions confirmed by multiple independent solubility prediction methods. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining machine learning-based solubility prediction with generative optimization for protein engineering.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: An Adaptive Feedback Framework for Cell-Type-Deconvolved Transcriptional Brain Aging Clock
authors: Ghada Abdelhady, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Andreas Pfenning, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Gene expression patterns of a given cell are a product of both intrinsic factors -reflective of the cell's identity or current state and systemic factors imposed by the tissue environment surrounding the cell. Disentangling these influences is essential for understanding cell-autonomous aging and vulnerability, particularly in neurodegenerative diseases. Here, we present a transcriptional brain aging clock that resolves cell type heterogeneity and serves as a neuronal vulnerability metric in aging and neurodegeneration. Through an adaptive feedback-based representation learning framework, we are able to decompose cell-specific (intrinsic) transcriptional aging signals from tissue-wide (systemic) in the human prefrontal cortex. Our approach is based on an iterative elastic net regression model (iENR) that begins with a standard ElasticNet predictor of chronological age, capturing dominant systemic aging effects. The model then iteratively refines age predictions by using outputs from previous iterations as targets, progressively enriching for gene programs that explain cell-specific deviations from the shared aging trajectory. Using this adaptive approach, we identify an intrinsic aging signature that is predictive of cell-type-specific vulnerability. This signature highlights stress-response and metabolic pathways, including FKBP5, and oxidative phosphorylation dysregulation, as key cell-autonomous regulators of molecular aging. In Alzheimer's disease, the intrinsic aging signature more strongly predicts cell-type-specific vulnerability than systemic aging signals. To gain insight into whether the intrinsic aging signature drives longevity divergence within and across species, we identify regulatory elements under differential selective pressure in longer- versus shorter-lived mammals that overlap with the intrinsic aging signature, highlighting shared mechanisms of selective vulnerability and lifespan variation, and implicating CTCF. This framework offers a generalizable and interpretable approach for decomposing shared and cell-specific aging signals in single-cell data, enabling resolution of cellular heterogeneity across disease contexts and revealing that transcriptional aging signatures encode biologically meaningful differences in vulnerability, with insights into evolutionary pressures on the regulatory landscape.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: RiceExFormer: Learning Tissue-Resolved Gene Expression Representations in Rice through Multi-Task Pre-Training
authors: Joo-Seok Park, Gyeongsang National University, South Korea; Yang Jae Kang, Gyeongsang National University, South Korea
abstract: Understanding gene expression across different tissues is essential for studying plant development and adaptation. In rice (Oryza sativa), large-scale bulk RNA-seq datasets have been generated across diverse tissues and developmental stages, but methods to integrate these heterogeneous datasets and extract shared regulatory patterns remain limited. Here, we present RiceExFormer, a Transformer-based model pre-trained on 2,798 bulk RNA-seq samples from 54 rice tissue types to learn generalizable representations of gene expression. Instead of treating each sample independently, the model is trained with three self-supervised objectives: masked expression reconstruction, masked gene identity prediction, and contrastive learning across augmented transcriptomic views. This allows the model to capture both expression levels and co-regulation patterns. The learned representations reflect meaningful biological structure: tissues with similar developmental origins cluster together, and the model's gene attention concentrates on tissue-variable genes. Notably, the representation generalizes across independent studies, organizing samples from unseen datasets by tissue more consistently than raw expression. In addition, experiments with different gene vocabulary sizes (1,000–20,000 genes) show that using highly variable genes leads to better tissue discrimination than using the full transcriptome, indicating that expression variability is more important than gene coverage. RiceExFormer shows that self-supervised learning on bulk RNA-seq data can capture biologically meaningful patterns and provides a useful representation framework for downstream tasks such as phenotype prediction, regulatory analysis, and gene function annotation

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Querying structural and functional niches on spatial transcriptomics data
authors: Mo Chen, Tsinghua University, China; Minsheng Hao, Research & Early Development, Genentech, China; Xinquan Liu, Tsinghua University, China; Lin Deng, Tsinghua University, China; Peng Liu, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China., China; Chen Li, Tsinghua University, China; Dongfang Wang, Peking University, China; Kui Hua, University of Cambridge, United Kingdom; Xuegong Zhang, Tsinghua University, China; Lei Wei, Tsinghua University, China
abstract: Cells in multicellular organisms coordinate to form functional and structural niches. With spatial transcriptomics (ST) enabling gene expression profiling in spatial contexts, it has been revealed that spatial niches serve as cohesive and recurrent units in physiological and pathological processes. These observations suggest universal tissue organization principles encoded by conserved niche patterns, and call for a query-based niche analytical paradigm beyond current computational tools. In this work, we defined the Niche Query Task, which is to identify similar niches across ST samples given a niche of interest (NOI). We further developed QueST, the first niche-centric subgraph representation learning framework for solving this task. Unlike existing cell-centric methods that derive niche embeddings indirectly from individual cell representations, QueST models each niche as a subgraph, uses contrastive learning to learn discriminative niche embeddings, and incorporates adversarial training to mitigate batch effects. In simulations and benchmark datasets, QueST outperformed existing methods repurposed for niche querying, accurately capturing niche structures in heterogeneous environments and demonstrating strong generalizability across diverse sequencing platforms. Applied to tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) in renal and lung cancers, QueST identified three functionally distinct TLS subtypes with divergent prognostic associations, and uncovered conserved and divergent spatial architectures across cancer types through cross-cancer niche retrieval. We further demonstrated QueST's capacity for de novo discovery of niches of interest without prior biological knowledge. These results demonstrate that QueST enables systematic, quantitative profiling of spatial niches across samples, providing a powerful tool to dissect spatial tissue architecture in health and disease.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Reconstructing biologically coherent cellular profiles from imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
authors: Long Yuan, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, United States; Youyun Zheng, Harvard Medical School, United States; Shuming Zhang, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Rameen Beroukhim, Broad Institute/Dana-Farber, United States; Atul Deshpande, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: In imaging-based spatial transcriptomics, transcript-to-cell assignment shapes downstream biological interpretation including cell typing, ligand-receptor inference, and niche characterization. However, two-dimensional segmentation of volumetric tissue often yields mixed cellular profiles, while cells without detected nuclei are missed entirely, distorting the aforementioned downstream analyses. We present TRACER, which refines cellular representations in imaging-based transcriptomics by leveraging geneâ€“gene coherence and spatial co-localization of transcripts observed directly in the data, without requiring external annotations or reference atlases. TRACER resolves mixed cellular profiles and reconstructs partial cells whose nuclei are not detected, enabling more complete representation of cells within the tissue section. We also introduce coherence-based metrics that quantify transcriptional purity and conflict, enabling platform-agnostic benchmarking of segmentation quality. Across diverse platforms, tissues, and segmentation methodologies, TRACER consistently and reproducibly improves the coherence of cellular profiles and the quality of downstream analyses.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: STPBench: Benchmarking Spatial Transcriptomics-to-Proteomics Prediction Models
authors: Yimeng Qiao, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China; Zijie Fang, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China; Ran Liu, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China; Jihong Tang, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China; Yuyan Ruan, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China; Zhidong Yang, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China; Jiguang Wang, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, China
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics provide complementary insights into tissue organization by capturing gene expression and protein abundance in situ. Predicting spatial proteomic profiles from spatial transcriptomic data offers a promising strategy to model the translation processes within spatial context while alleviating the high cost and limited throughput of current proteomic technologies. However, the performance of existing Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome (STP) prediction models remains poorly characterized across diverse platforms and experimental settings. In this study, we present STPBench, a comprehensive benchmark of STP prediction models across diverse spatial omics platforms. We curate a large-scale collection of 44 paired spatial transcriptomicsâ€“proteomics datasets, including 29 public and 15 in-house samples, spanning nine state-of-the-art spatial multi-omics technologies with heterogeneous resolutions and disease states. We systematically evaluate representative modelsâ€”covering expression-only, spatial-aware, and morphology-integrated approachesâ€”using complementary metrics that assess both expression accuracy and spatial structure preservation. Our results reveal pronounced performance heterogeneity across datasets and platforms, with no single method consistently dominating. Importantly, we uncover regime-dependent behavior, where model performance varies substantially with data characteristics such as spatial structure, modality alignment, and feature sparsity. We further observe that incorporating spatial and histological image information improves performance and generalization in specific settings, while simpler models can outperform more complex approaches under certain regimes. In addition, the predictability of protein markers varies markedly across technologies, highlighting intrinsic biological and technical constraints. Overall, STPBench provides a systematic resource for evaluating STP prediction and offers insights into the limitations of current models and when they succeed or fail in real-world applications.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PLM-GUARD: Diagnosing protein search in the era of language models
authors: Han Zhou, The University of Waterloo, Canada; Yifan Yang, University of California, Davis, United States; Yang Lu, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States
abstract: Protein language model (PLM) based sequence search is increasingly used as a fast alternative to classical alignment, especially for remote homology retrieval. However, it remains unclear whether high embedding similarity scores truly reflect biological evidence, raising concerns about interpretability and trustworthiness. To investigate this, we introduce PLM-Guard, a set of six controlled sanity checks spanning biological fidelity, semantic validity, and manipulation safety, designed to probe what similarity scores actually capture. These checks examine whether similarity follows evolutionary and structural principles, behaves coherently when evidence is duplicated or removed, and remains resistant to data- or model-level manipulation. Our evaluation reveals that, across eight representative search engines, classical alignment-based methods satisfy most or all applicable checks, whereas current PLM-based search methods exhibit systematic inconsistencies between embedding similarity and biological evidence despite strong empirical adoption. These findings suggest that protein search in the PLM era requires not only higher retrieval performance but also explicit diagnosis of what similarity scores mean and when they can be trusted.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Intrinsic Geometric Tests for Biological Foundation Model Representations
authors: Sinan Ozbay, Duke University, United States; Rohit Singh, Duke University, United States
abstract: The power of foundation models in biology derives in substantial part from their latent representations, which are intended to capture meaningful biology in a low-dimensional space. However, for reasons that remain unclear, these representations often fail to outperform simple baselines on downstream tasks. To investigate this, we take a geometric view of learned representations, seeking to evaluate their information content independent of downstream tasks. We compare the distribution of distances in the latent space versus the original input space, reasoning that a good representation will strike a delicate balance between distance preservation and rearrangement. Consequently, this reveals two failure modes for representation learning: First, if distances are largely scrambled (as in a hash) then any latent structure in the data will be destroyed. Second, if distances are too-well preserved, then the possibility of learning novel structure relative to raw inputs is slim. In fact, when nearly-isometric mappings are learned, simpler, cheaper methods, like PCA, deliver similar performance on nearly any task. Crucially, these properties of representations can be tested without reference to downstream tasks. With this insight, we evaluate representations of several single-cell foundation models on a number of datasets, finding they fall into two categories. On the one hand, models like Transcriptformer tend to preserve large scale distances and scramble small-scale distances. On the other hand, scGPT and scFoundation tend to strike a better balance between distance preservation and rearrangement at both scales. These findings support the hypothesis that reconstruction objectives should balance compression and feature-learning. These geometric tests can be used to guide further exploration of the use of foundation model representations by enabling practitioners to identify task-appropriate representations and investigate optimal scales for distance representations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: GenomeOcean-Sentinel: A Dual-Modality Framework for Detecting Synthetic DNA Signatures of Genome Foundation Models
authors: Zhong Wang, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab; The Joint Genome Institute, United States; Guang Yang, Department of Communication, University of California, Los Angeles, United States; Rob Egan, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab; The Joint Genome Institute, United States; Fengchen Liu, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, United States
abstract: BACKGROUND: Modern genomic foundation models (gFMs) generate synthetic DNA sequences that evade standard quality filters and alignment-based checks, creat- ing urgent data-integrity and biosecurity risks for public repositories such as NCBI, ENA, and IMG. METHODS: We present GenomeOcean-Sentinel (GOS), a dual-modality cascade framework exploiting two universal generative artifacts: (1) Noticeable Tokenizer Fingerprint (NTF) â€” rigid autocorrelation signals imprinted at BPE/k- mer token boundaries (5â€“6 bp intervals) that are absent in natural sequences; and (2) Collapse of Attention Variance (CAV), that distinguishes evolutionarily optimized from computationally sampled sequences. Five complementary signals (GO-100M semantic score, 1D-CNN motif anomaly, BPE periodicity, gzip/LZMA compression ratio, GO-4B attention distance variance) are fused by a 3-layer stacking MLP. RESULTS: GOS achieves AUROC 0.971, with 100% sensitivity on low-complexity sequences and 81% on DustMasker-filtered high-complexity outputs. Extended evaluation across diverse gFMs â€” spanning BPE trans- formers (GenomeOcean-100M/500M/4B, GENERator-v2) and character-level models (Genos-1.2B, evo-1-131k, evo2- 7B) â€” achieves 100% detection on all seven architectures (24,000 independent sequences). Specificity against hold- out assembled metagenome is over 90%, with the majority of false positives traced to naturally low-complexity se- quences. SIGNIFICANCE: GenomeOcean-Sentinel provides the first cross-architecture validated, mechanistically inter- pretable framework for AI-generated DNA detection, di- rectly applicable to genomic database integrity monitoring and biosecurity surveillance.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CC-SPR: Sparse and Geometry-Aware Persistent Representatives for Interpretable Omics Feature Selection
authors: Chimdi Walter Ndubuisi, University of Missouri-Columbia, United States; Dotun Olaoye, University of Missouri-Columbia, United States
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the multiscale topology of point-cloud data, but its standard output discards the geometric identity of detected cycles, limiting biological interpretability. Harmonic persistent homology recovers cycle identity via an L2-minimizing representative, yet the resulting dense edge support dilutes downstream feature attribution. We introduce CC-SPR (Cycle-Consistent Sparse Persistent Representatives), which replaces the dense harmonic objective with a convex elastic-net formulation that concentrates cycle support on fewer edges, yielding sparser, more interpretable representatives. CC-SPR further formalizes the sample-space metric as a selectable backend, implementing five geometry families: Euclidean, Ollivier-Ricci curvature-adjusted, diffusion, PHATE-like potential, and distance-to-measure (DTM) robust distances. Bootstrap-aggregated Topological Influence Profiles (TIP) convert sparse representatives into per-feature stability scores. We benchmark all five backends on three cancer-genomics datasets (TCGA-LUAD, GSE161711, GSE165087) and perform a targeted cross-domain validation on Arabidopsis root scRNA-seq. Backend ranking is dataset-dependent and scale-sensitive: DTM leads on pilot LUAD (F1=0.53); Ricci overtakes DTM at full scale (F1=0.63 vs 0.58); Euclidean is the best-performing CC-SPR backend on GSE161711 (F1=0.75). DTM uniquely recovers xenobiotic metabolism by cytochrome P450 (adjusted p=7e-4), and zero genes are shared across all six LUAD backend configurations, confirming that geometry choice controls biological signal extraction. CC-SPR produces 2.8x sparser sample-bar matrices than harmonic representatives while preserving comparable clustering structure. Cross-domain generalization to Arabidopsis shows DTM outperforming Euclidean (F1=0.67 vs 0.59) with biologically coherent top genes. Standard baselines remain strongest on raw F1; CC-SPRâ€™s contribution is a geometry-sensitive topological framework for interpretable, pathway-validated feature selection.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: DeepMalignant: Multi-modality Graph Representation Learning for Tumor Cell Identification from scRNA-seq
authors: Pankaj Bhattarai, Department of Computer Science, Florida State University, United States; Weiman Yuan, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Hongmei Chi, Department of Computer Science, Florida Agricultural & Mechanical University, United States; Xin Maizie Zhou, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Xian Mallory, Department of Computer Science, Florida State University, United States
abstract: Distinguishing malignant from normal cells in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is a critical yet challenging task in cancer genomics. Existing methods often suffer from poor precision, limited generalizability across cancer types, and lack of robustness across different sequencing platforms. We developed DeepMalignant, an unsupervised multimodal graph attention autoencoder for tumor cell identification that jointly integrates gene expression and copy number alteration information. In DeepMalignant, RNA-derived cancer signature features define cell-level node attributes, while CNA-based cosine similarity defines weighted edges in a cell-cell graph. A graph attention encoder then performs CNA-informed message passing to learn embeddings that capture both transcriptional state and genomic similarity. To stabilize representation learning and prevent collapse, the model is trained with a joint reconstruction and Information Noise-Contrastive Estimation (InfoNCE) objective. Cells are first clustered in the learned latent space using the Leiden algorithm, and each cluster is then assigned as tumor or normal by a two-component Gaussian mixture model applied to cluster-level CNA burden scores. We applied DeepMalignant to five datasets covering 26 samples and and four cancer types (breast, colorectal, pancreatic, and ovarian cancers), generated by three platforms (10x Genomics, inDrop, and Drop-seq). DeepMalignant achieved the best overall balance of precision and recall and consistently outperformed five established methods in F1 score. Ablation studies showed that both CNA-based edge weighting and graph attention aggregation contribute independently to performance, and attribution analysis further indicated that the learned embeddings capture biologically meaningful malignant programs. Specifically, in the Moncada et al. pancreatic dataset, DeepMalignant was the only method that was robust to the pancreatic dataset generated by inDrop seq, showing the importance of incorporating multiple modalities of both gene expression and CNAs. We further show that the framework extends to a sample sequenced by spatial transcriptomics, where it accurately identifies tumor-enriched spots. Finally, the identification of the tumor cells enabled us to analyze the tumor microenvironment and the cell-cell communication on the spatial transcriptome data .

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Inferring virtual cell environments using multi-agent reinforcement learning
authors: Noah Cohen Kalafut, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States; Chenfeng He, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States; Jie Sheng, University of Wisconsin- Madison, United States; Pramod Bharadwaj Chandrashekar, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States; Jerome J Choi, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Daifeng Wang, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States
abstract: Single cells interact continuously to form a cell environment that drives key biological processes. Cells and cell environments are highly dynamic across time and space, fundamentally governed by molecular mechanisms, such as gene expression. Recent sequencing techniques measure single-cell-level gene expression under specific conditions, either temporally or spatially. Using these datasets, emerging works, such as virtual cells, can learn biologically useful representations of individual cells. However, these representations are typically static and overlook the underlying cell environment and its dynamics. To address this, we developed CellTRIP, a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that infers a virtual cell environment to simulate the cell dynamics and interactions underlying given single-cell data. Specifically, cells are modeled as individual agents with dynamic interactions, which can be learned through self-attention mechanisms via reinforcement learning. CellTRIP also applies novel truncated reward bootstrapping and adaptive input rescaling to stabilize training. We can in-silico manipulate any combination of cells and genes in our learned virtual cell environment, predict spatial and/or temporal cell changes, and prioritize corresponding genes at the single-cell level. We applied and benchmarked CellTRIP on various simulated and real gene expression datasets, including recapitulating cellular dynamic processes simulated by gene regulatory networks and stochastic models, imputing spatial organization of mouse cortical cells, predicting developmental gene expression changes after drug treatment in cancer cells, and spatiotemporal reconstruction of Drosophila embryonic development, demonstrating its outperformance and broad applicability. Interactive manipulation of those virtual cell environments, including in-silico perturbation, can prioritize spatial and developmental genes for single-cell-level changes, enabling the generation of new insights into cell dynamics over time and space.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: GeneCAD: structure-aware plant gene annotation with biologically constrained decoding and DNA foundation models
authors: Zong-Yan Liu, Cornell University, United States; Ana Berthel, Cornell University, United States; Eric Czech, Open Athena AI Foundation, United States; Michelle Stitzer, Cornell University, United States; Sheng-Kai Hsu, Cornell University, United States; Matt Pennell, Cornell University, United States; Edward S. Buckler, Cornell University; USDA-ARS, United States; Jingjing Zhai, Cornell University, United States
abstract: High-quality plant genome assemblies are accumulating faster than reliable gene annotations, especially in repeat-rich and polyploid genomes where splice boundaries and complex loci remain difficult to resolve. Existing scalable sequence-only annotation methods help address this gap, but often produce inaccurate transcript structures and excessive false positives. We present GeneCAD, a DNA-only annotation framework that combines long-context representations from a plant foundation model with biologically constrained decoding to generate structurally coherent transcripts directly from genomic sequence. GeneCAD predicts base-level gene structure states and decodes them under explicit constraints on feature order and splice-phase consistency. To improve robustness to imperfect training annotations, we prioritize supervision using conservation-informed motif signals and further refine predictions with a protein-based filter that suppresses transposable-element-derived open reading frames. Across five held-out angiosperm genomes, including the allotetraploid Nicotiana tabacum, GeneCAD improves exact-match transcript F1 by approximately 9% over both Helixer and the RNA-seq-supported BRAKER3 pipeline. In maize, GeneCAD recovers valid transcripts for 87% of curated classical genes and 57% of challenging NLR immune receptor genes, while producing zero spurious isoforms in this benchmark; among matched loci, 96% of classical gene predictions and 76% of NLR predictions are exact. These results show that biologically constrained decoding can substantially improve the fidelity and structural validity of plant gene annotation from DNA alone, providing a scalable solution for newly assembled genomes and pangenomes.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: TissueNarrator: Generative Language Modeling of Cellular States in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Sizhe Liu, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Junjie Tang, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Jian Ma, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Shaoheng Liang, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: The intricate spatial organization and molecular communication among cells are fundamental to multicellular systems. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables gene expression profiling while preserving spatial context, providing rich data for studying cellular interactions and tissue dynamics. However, most existing computational methods remain largely descriptive, focusing on embedding-based analyses rather than generating context-dependent cellular states or simulating perturbations in situ. Here, we present TissueNarrator, a text-native framework that reformulates spatial omics analysis as a generative language modeling problem. By representing tissue sections as spatial sentences, composed of rank-based gene lists augmented with spatial coordinates and metadata, TissueNarrator leverages pretrained large language models (LLMs) to learn spatially conditioned cellular states. The model generates realistic, context-aware cellular profiles, captures intercellular interactions, and supports in silico perturbation analyses. Across multiple ST technologies (MERFISH, Perturb-FISH, and CosMx SMI), TissueNarrator outperforms baseline methods in cell generation, recovers biologically meaningful ligandâ€“receptor and signaling pathways, predicts transcriptional responses to unseen perturbations, and models immune infiltration programs in cancer. Moreover, a conversational inference mode enables natural-language querying of tissue organization. TissueNarrator establishes a scalable generative paradigm for modeling, simulating, and interrogating tissue systems in native and counterfactual spatial contexts.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: The LD Motif Mystery: Transcription Activation Domains
authors: Keely Roe, Butler University, United States; Hassan Hashmi, Butler University, United States; Aayan Ansar, Butler University, United States; David Cooper, Butler University, United States; Caleb Class, Butler University, United States; Alexandre Erkine, Butler University, United States
abstract: Transcription activation domains (ADs) are key regions in transcription factors required to regulate transcription, but their protein sequences can vary wildly, and their structures and binding preferences are relatively unknown. Previously determined residue grammar rules assisted in the discovery of a sequence motif consisting of leucine and aspartic acid residues enriched in highly active ADs, with a short motif LDDLL and long motif LDLDDLL. In this work, we investigate how these LD motifs contribute to AD function by potentially influencing structure and interactions. We prepared a library of protein sequences with duplications, truncations, and substitutions within the LD motif to test the requirements for functionality. Structural analysis was performed using AlphaFold 3, and the RMSD and surface area/accessibility was calculated for each sequence as compared to the motif controls using bio3D and evo3D in R. The control motifs tend to form an amphipathic helical structure. Preliminary results show that ~30% of sequences composed solely of L and D residues are functional, while replacing aspartic acid with glutamic acid is usually detrimental unless the LD motif is present. Substituting variable positions (LXXLL, LDLXXLL) within the motif with aromatic, aliphatic, or acidic residues can generally enhance functionality by contributing to the amphipathic helical structure of the motif. The motif is more functional when multiple copies of the motif are present in one sequence. We hypothesize that the amphipathic nature of the motif contributes to the interaction of the ADs with DNA and histones for transcription activation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Bridging the negative data gap in bioactivity prediction using InertDB
authors: Seungchan An, Princeton University, United States; Minsoo Noh, Seoul National University, South Korea
abstract: Small molecule bioactivity prediction is frequently limited by "publication bias," where the scarcity of negative data hinders model reliability. To address this gap, we present InertDB, a comprehensive database of 3,205 Curated Inactive Compounds (CICs) and 64,368 Generated Inactive Compounds (GICs). CICs were identified from 4.6 million PubChem records using a natural language processing (NLP)-based bioassay diversity metric to ensure consistent inactivity across diverse biological contexts. Remarkably, 97.2% of CICs adhere to the Rule of Five, with a minimal pan-assay interference compounds (PAINS) rate of 1.2%, offering superior drug-like properties compared to general chemical sets. To further navigate sparsely populated chemical space, we employed a recurrent neural network-based generative AI to produce GICs, providing unique scaffolds (e.g., dioxaspiroundecane) absent from existing datasets like Dark Chemical Matter. Validation on LIT-PCBA and MUV benchmarks shows that models trained with InertDB significantly outperform those using random sampling or property-matched decoys. By integrating extensive curation with generative AI, InertDB serves as a pivotal resource for robust virtual screening and bioactivity prediction.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CLCluster: a redundancy-reduction contrastive learning-based clustering method for cancer subtype identification from multi-omics data
authors: Mengyuan Yang, Xi‘an Jiaotong University, China
abstract: Identifying robust cancer subtypes from multi-omics data remains challenging due to data heterogeneity and high dimensionality. Existing contrastive learning approaches rely on negative sampling, which is often ill-defined in multi-omics settings and can introduce bias. We propose CLCluster, a redundancy-reduction contrastive learning framework that eliminates negative sampling and enforces feature-wise decorrelation to capture independent biological signals. CLCluster integrates multiple omics layers, including gene expression, DNA methylation, copy number variation, miRNA, and alternative splicing (AS). Across 33 TCGA cancer types, CLCluster consistently outperforms existing clustering methods in terms of cluster separability and robustness. The identified subtypes show stronger associations with patient survival, indicating improved clinical relevance. Ablation analysis demonstrates that incorporating AS provides complementary information that enhances subtype discrimination. CLCluster provides a robust and generalizable framework for multi-omics integration and highlights the importance of redundancy-reduction representation learning in capturing biologically meaningful signals.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Cross-Species Generative Reconstruction of Atherosclerosis Progression Cell Atlas
authors: Yuzhuo Li, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China, China; Yongxin Zhou, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Beijing 100730, China., China; Lei Wei, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China, China; Jinmeng Jia, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China, China; Xuegong Zhang, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China, China
abstract: Human atherosclerosis (AS) progression spans from a long asymptomatic phase to sudden clinical events. In single-cell studies, human samples are highly discrete and limited to healthy or end-stage states, missing the critical stable-to-unstable transition. Mouse models, while differ from humans in pathological outcomes, provide controllable, continuous, and full-cycle omics trajectories. To leverage this cross-species complementarity, we propose a generative framework that utilizes the temporal depth of mouse models to reconstruct latent human AS stages. We first constructed a 1.2-million-cell cross-species AS atlas, one of the largest resources in this field. Utilizing a cross-species unified feature space on this atlas and a VAE-Diffusion architecture, we established a pseudo-time coordinate system using the dynamic trajectory of mice, which allows us to generate corresponding human cell states by shifting mouse-derived conditions. Experiments validate the modelâ€™s potential in extracting conserved signals. We observed consistent expressions in key genes such as MYH11 and TAGLN within generated human smooth muscle cells (SMC). The model also successfully replicated the initial activation of Lipid-Associated Macrophage (LAM) features, including TREM2 and APOE. Generated human early stages are also showing promising differential signals, providing evidence for identifying key transition points before plaque instability. This study provides a systematic solution to the dynamic blind spots prevalent in chronic diseases. For AS research, this framework facilitates the discovery of early diagnostic biomarkers and the precise location of transition windows before plaque rupture. Beyond AS, this generative paradigm has significant potential for other chronic progressive diseases with similar sampling challenges.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Representation Matters: How Molecular Encodings Shape Deep Learning Performance for rAAV Capsid Fitness Prediction
authors: Yann Vander Meersche, WhiteLab Genomics, France; Dylan Serillon, WhiteLab Genomics, France
abstract: Predicting the manufacturability of recombinant AAV (rAAV) capsids remains a major bottleneck in gene therapy vector engineering. The sequence space is vast, and experimental validation is costly, making machine learning a promising approach to accelerate capsid design. However, predictive performance depends not only on how molecular information is represented, but also on whether the downstream architecture preserves that information. In this work, we systematically evaluated deep learning methods for AAV2 production fitness prediction, focusing on the impact of molecular encoding. We benchmarked physicochemical descriptors, chemical fingerprints, one-hot encodings, and protein, peptide, and genomic language model embeddings, paired with two prediction heads. By decoupling representation from architecture, we aimed to establish a principled foundation for model development. Robustness was assessed using strict train-test splits based on sequence-identity clusters. Our results show that the discriminative signal lies in position-specific amino-acid identities of the variable region: any setup preserving them (large CNN kernels, flattened encodings, or context-rich PLM tokens) reaches the same performance ceiling, while operations that dilute them (embedding mean-pooling, small-kernel pooling, invariant flanking context) hurt. Under representation-preserving conditions, very different encodings converge within ~0.03 AUPRC, with only modest drops under cluster-based splitting. This representation-independent ceiling points to the limited diversity of publicly available AAV datasets as the dominant remaining bottleneck. These findings motivated the generation of internal datasets focused on the most complex-to-modify and functionally critical positions of the capsid, designed to improve generalization and support our end-to-end AI-guided capsid engineering platform.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Cell Type Annotation with Covariate Shift Robust Uncertainty Metrics
authors: Matthew Mollerus, George Washinton University, United States; Ali Rahnavard, George Washinton University, United States
abstract: Tools and models to classify cell types from RNA-seq gene expression data vary widely in their underlying architecture and reference datasets, resulting in a lack of rigorous uncertainty measures, valid comparison between tools, and ability to handle covariate shift. We address these issues with a modular framework to calibrate conformal classifiers that account for covariate shift and can be applied to any cell type annotation tool. This framework consists of a conformal risk control classifier that can incorporate hierarchical cell ontologies into its loss function, a reweighting of calibration data to ensure coverage in the presence of covariate shift, and decision algorithms that enable both no-label and higher level classifications in the case of increased uncertainty. We evaluate these methods on a variety of commonly used annotation tools and datasets that represent the varying degrees of covariate shift in real world data. They consistently provide prediction sets with statistically guaranteed coverage, including in situations where existing uncertainty methods give miscalibrated results. Prediction sets and uncertainty metrics also provide performance comparisons beyond top-line classification metrics. Moreover, tracking the uncertainty of different tools across datasets and degrees of covariate shift demonstrates which methods are more robust to variations inherent in experimental data. This work provides a framework for researchers to rigorously estimate uncertainty in single cell data and highlights the need for evaluation of annotation tools in a variety of situations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Efficient Spatial Domain Identification from Spatial Transcriptomics via Gaussian Mixture Models
authors: Giorgio Venturin, University of Padova, Italy; Fabio Vandin, University of Padova, Italy
abstract: Spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) measures gene expression at many spots within a tissue slice while preserving spatial information. Identifying spatial domains-- subregions where cells share specific traits--is key to studying tissue organization and function. Among others, graph and deep-learning-based approaches brought consistent improvements over previous approaches but are computationally expensive and sensitive to hyperparameters, causing inconsistent performance across different datasets. We propose GaMMA-ST, an efficient method for spatial domain identification using Gaussian Mixture Models and graph-based label smoothing. Experiments show that GaMMA-ST consistently improves over the state-of-the-art on multiple SRT datasets, scales to hundreds of thousands of spots while remaining accurate, and provides an uncertainty measure for its domains at no extra computational cost. We further illustrate how this uncertainty can be used to improve GaMMA-ST's results in practice.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Predicting evolutionary rate as a pretraining task improves genome language model representations
authors: Micaela Elisa Consens, University of Toronto, Canada; Kevin K. Yang, Microsoft Research, United States; James Hall, Microsoft Research, United States; Ashley Conard, Microsoft Research, United States; Bo Wang, Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto, Canada; Lorin Crawford, Microsoft Research, United States; Alan Moses, Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto, Canada; Alex Xijie Lu, Microsoft Research, United States
abstract: Genome language models (gLM) have the potential to further understanding of regulatory genomics without requiring labeled data. Most gLMs are pretrained using sequence reconstruction tasks inspired by natural language processing, but recent studies have shown that these gLMs often fail to capture biological signal. To overcome this, we introduce pretraining tasks that predict the rate of evolution. These tasks are designed so that they can be composed with sequence reconstruction, enabling a controlled comparison of predicting sequence only, evolutionary rate only, or both. To address gaps in existing evaluations, we developed a suite of biologically grounded benchmarks. Across these tasks, and for established variant effect prediction benchmarks, models pretrained on both sequence and evolutionary rate outperform those trained on sequence alone, and training on evolutionary rate can make the even the relatively small models in our work competitive with much larger existing gLMs for some tasks. These results establish evolution as a key training target for genome-scale models.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Multi omics Analysis of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Treatment Resistance and Derivation of a Treatment Associated Gene Signature
authors: Jianfang Liu, Chan Soon-Shiong Institute of Molecular Medicine at Windber, United States; Praveen-Kumar Raj-Kumar, Chan Soon-Shiong Institute of Molecular Medicine at Windber, United States; Anupama Praveen-Kumar, Chan Soon-Shiong Institute of Molecular Medicine at Windber, United States; Mariano Russo, Chan Soon-Shiong Institute of Molecular Medicine at Windber, United States; Craig Shriver, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, United States; Xiaoying Lin, Chan Soon-Shiong Institute of Molecular Medicine at Windber, United States; Hai Hu, Chan Soon-Shiong Institute of Molecular Medicine at Windber, United States
abstract: Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies with substantial heterogeneity in tumor and variation in clinical outcomes following standard therapy. Whereas a subset of patients achieves complete response (CR), others develop progressive disease (PD). The intrinsic molecular determinants underlying these divergent therapeutic responses remain incompletely understood. Method: We selected 41 CR and 45 PD cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma cohort as a discovery set and performed multi-omics analysis on the omics data to explore treatment resistance mechanism. Applying machine learning approaches, a prognostic signature was constructed using LASSO Cox regression model, evaluated using random forest, and validated using independent datasets. Results: PD tumors were characterized by activation of proliferative signaling pathways, enhanced cell cycle progression, chromosomal instability, etc., consistent with intrinsic resistance phenotypes. In contrast, CR tumors exhibited enrichment of immune-related pathways and a stroma- and immune-enriched tumor microenvironment marked by immune checkpoint upregulation and increased myeloid and B-cell infiltration, suggestive of a pre-existing inflamed state associated with therapeutic sensitivity. A robust 12-gene predictive and prognostic signature was derived and validated that stratifies PDAC patients into treatment resistance high- and low-risk groups prior to therapy initiation. Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that intrinsic molecular states present before treatment critically determine therapeutic response and survival in PDAC and provide a clinically actionable framework for biology-driven patient stratification to optimize frontline treatment selection and advance personalized therapeutic strategies. track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Integrating knowledge graphs for machine learning-enabled prediction of response to therapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
authors: George Acquaah-Mensah, Massachusetts College of Pharmacy and Health Science, United States; Kawther Abdilleh, Pancreatic Cancer Action Network, United States; Boris Aguilar, Institute for Systems Biology, United States
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a deadly cancer with low survival. Knowledge graphs (KGs) have been used for a variety of biomedical applications including in prediction of response to chemotherapy, survival, and biomarker discovery. Here, we explore the utility of embeddings derived from KGs based on PDAC patient response to therapy which remains an area of intense interest because of the need to tailor treatments to patients. Data for this study was derived from the Pancreatic Cancer Action Networkâ€™s (PanCAN) Know Your Tumor program in the PanCAN SPARK platform. Somatic mutation data were used to generate patient-specific embeddings from the Hetionet KG using algorithms within the KarateClub python package including Graph2vec, NetMF, RandME. The patient-specific embeddings were then associated with available responses to chemotherapy regimens that included 5-fluorouracil, a widely-used compound in oncology. The embeddings we used were associated with data on response to therapy and used to build models for machine-learning (ML) classification schemes. The Waikato Environment for Knowledge Analysis (WeKa) ML workbench was used to predict response to therapy. To mitigate bias, we balanced the class sizes generating synthetic instances using Synthetic Minority Over-sampling technique (SMOTE). Patients were grouped by their response to therapy for the following classes: â€œComplete Responseâ€, â€œProgressive Diseaseâ€, â€œAbsence of Therapeutic Responseâ€. These data were used as input for ML classification. Among the ML classifiers, modified logistic regression and RandomForest approaches performed best in predicting response to therapy. Combining KG embeddings with mutation and clinical data provide a robust model for predicting response.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Pre-Training Dataset Deduplication Improves Genomic Language Models
authors: Mahler Revsine, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Alex Ostrovsky, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States; Daniel Khashabi, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States; Michael Schatz, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States
abstract: State-of-the-art genomic language models (gLMs) make use of increasingly large volumes of pre-training data in their efforts to advance the field. However, the substantial redundancy in genomic data from repetitive and conserved sequences creates the potential for more efficient training. In natural language, the removal of redundant samples from pre-training data (deduplication) improves model performance, increases training efficiency, and decreases pretraining data regurgitation (Penedo et al., arXiv, 2024; Lee et al., ACL, 2022, Kandpal et al., PMLR, 2022). In this work, we tested whether deduplicated pre-training improved model performance on biologically-relevant tasks. We pre-trained a collection of BERT-based models on unfiltered or deduplicated versions of five genomic corpora: GRCh38 (3Gb), the HPRC v2 (1.4Tb), a multi-species collection of vertebrates (27Gb) and organisms (30Gb), and a closely-related T2T ape pangenome (20Gb). We then fine-tuned each of our models to assess their accuracy on a suite of widely-employed gLM tasks from the GUE and DART-Eval benchmarks (Zhou et al., arXiv, 2024, Patel et al., arXiv, 2024). Deduplication reduced pretraining data volume by 50% to 99%+ while preserving key coding and regulatory regions, allowing for more thorough training under the same compute budget. Deduplicated models outperformed their unfiltered counterparts across nearly all tasks, demonstrating improved understanding of splice sites (4% improvement), epigenetic marks (5%), and variant effects (6%). Partial deduplication by permitting some repeated samples back into the dataset further improved performance under certain settings. These results highlight an inefficiency in state-of-the-art gLM training and demonstrate the utility of pre-training dataset deduplication.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: SHAPTURE: Integrated Adaptive Scoring for Robust Marker Prioritization in Single-Cell Data
authors: Max Alimadadi, Augusta University, United States; Onyekachi Nwogu, Augusta University, United States; Ruibo Cai, Augusta University, United States; Catherine'Lynn' Hedrick, Augusta University, United States
abstract: Identifying robust and biologically meaningful features from high-dimensional single-cell data remains challenging. While machine learning models provide powerful tools for feature selection, most approaches rely on a single dimension of importance and do not integrate statistical evidence, reproducibility, and biological signal. We present SHAPTURE, an integrated adaptive scoring framework for robust feature prioritization using SHAP. SHAPTURE combines complementary signals, including model-derived importance, statistical significance, stability across iterations, confidence interval strength, expression-based metrics, and the relationship between feature values and SHAP contributions. Each component is scaled and adaptively weighted based on its distribution across features, enabling data-driven integration without manual tuning. The framework generates interpretable outputs, including ranked feature lists, multi-layer visualization plots (e.g., SHAP-based volcano, bubble, and decomposition plots), and consistency analyses that relate model attribution to expression patterns. The resulting Integrated Adaptive Score prioritizes features that are not only predictive but also statistically supported, reproducible, and biologically interpretable. In addition, SHAPTURE evaluates the alignment between model-derived signals and expression-based directionality, enabling identification of both consistent and biologically discordant features. We demonstrate that SHAPTURE improves the identification of robust markers across conditions and cell populations, outperforming single-metric ranking approaches in stability and interpretability. The framework is flexible and applicable to diverse data types, including single-cell transcriptomics, cytometry, and other high-dimensional omics data.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Data-Driven Longitudinal Pathway Inference in Metabolomics via Sparse Multi-Output Gaussian Processes
authors: Allen Ross, The George Washington University, United States; Ali Reza Taheriyoun, The George Washington University, United States; Jason Lloyd-Price, Google, United States; Ali Rahnavard, The George Washington University, United States
abstract: Longitudinal untargeted metabolomics captures the dynamic biochemical state of human disease, but the majority of detected features lack chemical identification or pathway membership. Conventional methods rely on static databases and collapse temporal dynamics to a per-metabolite score, rendering them blind to transient signals and unannotated features. We propose a sparse multi-output Gaussian process (MOGP) framework for data-driven discovery of dynamic metabolic modules in longitudinal metabolomics. The model represents metabolites as outputs of shared latent GP functions via a coregionalization matrix, with a horseshoe prior inducing sparse module assignments and a Negative Binomial likelihood for overdispersed count data. Each factor is defined by a kernel encoding a functional hypothesis, enabling simultaneous inference of dose-response, peri-event, periodic, and group-level metabolic programs. Downstream inference proceeds in three tiers: signed GSEA for pathway enrichment, probabilistic annotation transfer for metabolites lacking database membership, and projection of unnamed features onto the latent space for structural prioritization. We apply this method to stool metabolomics from the iHMP IBD Crohnâ€™s disease cohort (459 metabolites, 238 samples, 49 participants). The model recovers a 10-factor structure, identifies a transient peri-flare signature in which 71 glycerolipid and glycerophospholipid species, including 32 TAGs, 22 PCs, 6 DAGs, and 11 lysophospholipids, load on the peri-event factor, and detects 58 significant factor-pathway pairs via signed GSEA (vs. 18 unsigned). Annotation transfer achieves 61% precision at 0.20 confidence, and projection of 41,967 unnamed features yields m/z-matched HMDB candidates consistent with named findings.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Beyond transcriptomics: predicting cellular phenotypic changes caused by perturbations
authors: Peng Liu, Tsinghua University, China; Chen Li, Tsinghua University, China; Lei Wei, Tsinghua University, China; Xuegong Zhang, Tsinghua University, China
abstract: Understanding how cells respond and their fate changes after perturbations is crucial for studying biological mechanisms and screening drug targets. Current research mainly focuses on changes at the transcriptome level after perturbation, which cannot be directly mapped to cell fate.Changes in cellular phenotype, such as cell fitness, division potential, and morphology, represent functional outputs that directly reflect cell fate. We introduce Phenopert, a multi-task model to predict cellular phenotypic changes after perturbations. Taking gene expression and perturbation embedding as inputs, we use different heads to predict various phenotypic changes. We construct perturbation embedding by fusing semantic information regarding perturbation responses with gene structural information to enable generalizability to unseen perturbation. We use multi-layer perceptrons to build multi-task prediction heads, enabling the prediction across diverse phenotypic tasks. We used Phenopert to predict three phenotypes after perturbation: cell fitness, division potential and morphology, and we conducted experiments on 3 recent datasets to validate the prediction preformance. In the cellular fitness prediction task, Phenopert achieved strong performance across various scenarios in Depmap datastet, including unseen cell contexts, unseen perturbations, and combinations of perturbations. In predicting division potential, Phenopert successfully captured the perturbation-induced changes in division capacity. In the task of predicting morphological changes, Phenopert elucidated the changes in cellular morphology following perturbation. Furthermore, we demonstrated that Phenopert can capture the intrinsic connections among different phenotypes, thereby revealing the possible biological mechanisms of cellular fitness. In summary, Phenopert demonstrates capabilities in predicting cellular phenotypes after perturbations, offering a phenotypic perspective for cellular perturbations modeling.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: LatentGEE: Unsupervised Microbiome Batch Effect Correction via Latent Space Residualization
authors: Seungrin Yang, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Yeonsu Jeon, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Dongyoon Lee, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jimin Ahn, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jong-Hwan Kim, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jongbum Jeon, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jin Ok Yang, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Haeyoung Jeong, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea
abstract: Background: Multi-study integration of microbiome data is essential for achieving sufficient statistical power in large-scale analyses, but introduces substantial batch effects arising from differences in sequencing protocols, study designs, and population characteristics. Existing correction methods, including ComBat, MMUPHin, and ConQuR, require known batch labels and strict preprocessing, limiting their applicability when annotations are incomplete or unreliable. Methods: We propose LatentGEE, an unsupervised batch effect correction method that operates without batch labels or cleanset preprocessing. LatentGEE integrates a Zero-Inflated Log-Normal Variational Autoencoder (ZILN-VAE) with a semi-parametric Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) layer. The ZILN-VAE encodes high-dimensional microbiome profiles into a low-dimensional latent representation, explicitly modeling zero-inflation and compositional properties of microbiome data. Unsupervised density-based clustering (HDBSCAN) discovers pseudo-batch structure from the latent space, and GEE residualization removes pseudo-batch effects while conditioning on biological covariates. Hyperparameters, including the zero-prevalence cutoff, are jointly optimized via Bayesian search (Optuna, 2,000 trials per setting). Results: We evaluated LatentGEE on the HIV Re-analysis Consortium (HIVRC) dataset (1,032 samples, 17 studies) across five experimental settings varying in taxonomic level, normalization strategy, and cohort composition. LatentGEE achieved 91–96% reduction in study-associated variance (PERMANOVA R²) under normalized input conditions, with kBET acceptance rates reaching 1.000 (Setting IV). In direct comparison with baseline methods, LatentGEE outperformed all evaluated methods under normalized conditions and achieved competitive performance with ConQuR under raw count conditions, despite requiring no batch annotations. Study label classification analysis demonstrated that LatentGEE was the only method to substantially reduce study discriminability (AUC: 0.611–0.620), while all baseline methods retained near-perfect study discriminability (AUC > 0.999) even after correction. Conclusions: LatentGEE demonstrates that meaningful batch effect correction can be achieved from intrinsic data structure alone, without relying on batch labels or extensive preprocessing. These results open new possibilities for integrative microbiome analyses across heterogeneous cohorts where batch annotations are unavailable or unreliable.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Protein-informed single-cell embeddings preserve biological signal across large evolutionary distances
authors: Lena Trnovec, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia, Slovenia; Mariko Katoh-Kurasawa, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA, United States; Rachel N Arey, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA, United States; Gad Shaulsky, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA, United States; Blaž Zupan, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia, Slovenia
abstract: Foundation models trained on mammalian single-cell atlases promise broad transfer, but their behavior at large evolutionary distance remains unclear. We benchmarked five embedding strategies in a zero-shot setting on developmental single-cell RNA-seq atlases from Dictyostelium discoideum (~1.2 billion years from humans) and Caenorhabditis elegans (~600 million years): PCA, scVI, Geneformer, scGPT, and Universal Cell Embedding (UCE). We quantified gene coverage for each method and evaluated downstream biological signal using diffusion pseudotime agreement and preservation of curated organism-specific annotations. Methods that rely on one-to-one human ortholog mapping retained only ~32-33% of genes in both species, whereas UCE, which encodes genes using protein-sequence embeddings, retained 97.4-97.5%. UCE delivered the most consistent overall performance: in C. elegans it achieved the strongest pseudotime agreement, and across both organisms it ranked first on five of six annotation families, including large gains for Dictyostelium cAMP-responsive programs and C. elegans lineage and developmental-marker panels. Importantly, the benchmark also shows where strong species-native baselines remain competitive: PCA gave the best pseudotime in Dictyostelium. Together, these results argue that gene representation, not pretraining alone, is the key determinant of zero-shot cross-species transfer. Protein-based gene representations preserve substantially more biological signal than ortholog mapping across large evolutionary distances.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A Multi-Strategy Rank-Based Framework for Robust Cancer Drug Sensitivity Prediction
authors: Yen-Jung Chiu, Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Taiwan; Yen-Hua Huang, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan
abstract: Predicting cancer drug response from patient transcriptomic profiles remains a central challenge in precision oncology, particularly due to domain shifts between preclinical models and clinical tumors. Here, we present a robust, rank-based multi-strategy gene signature framework that enables transferable drug sensitivity prediction from pharmacogenomic datasets to patient cohorts. Drug-specific sensitivity and resistance signatures were derived from Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) data using complementary strategies, including differential expression and correlation-based approaches. These signatures were projected onto The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) tumor transcriptomes using a signed single-sample, rank-based scoring scheme, which mitigates batch effects and cross-platform variability. To enhance robustness, predictions from multiple strategies were integrated into a unified sensitivity score for each patientâ€“drug pair. Across 31 shared drugs and over 1,200 TCGA patientâ€“drug records, the integrated scores demonstrated significant separation between responders and non-responders, with selected drugâ€“cancer contexts achieving strong discriminative performance (AUC > 0.80). Notably, predictive performance exhibited substantial heterogeneity across drugs and cancer types, highlighting context-specific transcriptional determinants of drug response. The framework avoids reliance on binary classification and instead provides continuous, interpretable sensitivity scores suitable for downstream statistical and clinical analyses. This study demonstrates that multi-strategy integration and rank-based scoring provide a scalable and biologically interpretable approach for bridging preclinical pharmacogenomics and clinical prediction. Our method complements existing machine learning models by emphasizing robustness, transferability, and mechanistic interpretability, offering a practical solution for precision oncology applications.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: EliteST: A ViT-Structured Multi-Channel Model for Learning Spatially Interpretable Latent Feature Representations in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Tianjie Wang, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Lingyu Li, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Yuanhua Huang, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables mapping of gene expression within tissue contexts, offering critical insights into cellular heterogeneity and microenvironmental interactions. Existing foundation models for ST largely employ graph-based or multi-modal neural architectures that integrate spatial coordinates, histology images and gene expressions but seldom leverage the unique advantage of treating genes as distinct channels akin to image processing. Here, we propose a novel multi-channel foundation model for spatial transcriptomics, pre-trained on 422 human Visium (10x) ST datasets with ~1.15 million ([4Ã—4]-scale) patches to learn spatially structured latent feature representation. It directly treats genes as channels in a computer vision framework, enabling application of potential advanced vision strategies. This modelling paradigm unlocks powerful feature extraction techniques developed in computer vision, facilitating robust spatial gene expression pattern recognition and multi-scale integration without requiring external modalities. Although various previous models have been developed and exhibited strong performance in common downstream tasks, they typically leverage graph neural network (GNN) as the core architecture for feature extraction. Our method distinguishes itself by defining genes explicitly as image channels, modelling spatial transcriptomics data as multi-channel images, enabling direct utilization of novel architectural designs borrowed from computer vision, granting the learned representation better interpretability. We deployed a masked autoencoder (MAE)structure with vision transformer (ViT) as backbone and trained the model on Hest-1kdataset , consisting of 4,162 genes overlapping with all Visium datasets, Visium HD, and Xenium 5k panel, after appropriate preprocessing. Our model demonstrated its capability to learn meaningful representations through its latent embedding, significantly enhancing cell type deconvolution. Compared to the TransImp baseline, this approach raised the Adjusted Rand Index from 0.07 to 0.37 and from 0.09 to 0.19 on two unseen datasets.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: MEMOL: Mixture of experts for multimodal learning through multi-head attention to predict drug toxicity
authors: Jong-Hoon Park, Yonsei University, South Korea; Jae-Woo Chu, Yonsei University, South Korea; Young Rae Cho, Yonsei University, South Korea
abstract: Modeling molecular toxicity requires integrating heterogeneous representations that capture complementary structural and chemical properties. We present MEMOL, a multimodal learning framework for drug toxicity prediction that combines molecular images, graphs, and fingerprints through mixture-of-experts-guided attention. Unlike conventional fusion strategies, MEMOL incorporates sparse mixture-of-experts routing directly into both self-attention and cross-attention modules, enabling adaptive expert selection during intra- and inter-modality representation learning. In MEMOL, molecular images are encoded by a Vision Transformer, molecular graphs by a hybrid GIN-GAT architecture, and molecular fingerprints by the encoder of an autoencoder. These modality-specific embeddings are refined through self-attention and subsequently fused through cross-attention, allowing the model to capture both modality-specific patterns and cross-modal dependencies. This design supports more expressive and efficient multimodal learning than conventional static feature fusion. We evaluated MEMOL on five toxicity benchmark datasets covering cardiotoxicity, drug-induced liver injury, skin reaction, carcinogenicity, and an extended liver injury dataset. MEMOL consistently outperformed conventional machine learning and recent deep learning baselines, with improvements of up to 8.33% AUROC and 9.11% AUPRC over the strongest competing model. Additional analyses showed that integrating all three modalities yielded the most robust performance, and ablation studies confirmed that sparse expert routing in both self-attention and cross-attention was more effective than standard attention or dense expert configurations. Our results highlight sparse expert-guided attention as a promising multimodal representation learning strategy for molecular property prediction.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
