title: AbFuseNet: A Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Predicting Pharmacokinetic Properties of Therapeutic Antibodies
authors: Ji Hye Park, CHA University, South Korea; Hyo Young Kim, Tech University of Korea, South Korea; Hyeong Gyu Choi, CHA University, South Korea; Gyu Seong Lee, CHA University, South Korea; Dae Keun Park, CHA University, South Korea
abstract: Predicting the pharmacokinetic (PK) properties of therapeutic antibodies â€” bioavailability (F), clearance (CL), and volume of distribution (Vd) â€” remains a critical challenge in early drug development. Existing computational approaches rely primarily on sequence-level features, overlooking structural and formulation context. We present AbFuseNet, a multimodal framework that jointly encodes three information streams: antibody sequence embeddings from ESM2, three-dimensional structural features from AlphaFold2, and formulation variables including excipient composition and route of administration. Using a curated dataset of approximately 400 FDA- and EMA-approved antibody products, a two-axis ablation study â€” varying embedding modality and classifier type â€” demonstrates that each additional modality yields consistent improvements in AUROC across all three PK endpoints. The full model with stacking ensemble achieves the best overall performance, confirming that sequence, structure, and formulation information are complementary rather than redundant. AbFuseNet provides a scalable framework for early-stage antibody developability assessment and establishes a rigorous evaluation protocol for future computational PK models.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Machine Learning for Viral Inference in Metagenomes: Progress, Pitfalls, and Emerging Directions
authors: Sadaf Raoufi, North Carolina State University, United States; Mery Touceda-Suárez, North Carolina State University, United States; Alise Ponsero, Quadram Institute of Biosciences, United Kingdom; Xinge Jeng, North Carolina State University, United States; Bonnie Hurwitz, North Carolina State University, United States
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing has transformed virus discovery by revealing vast viral diversity beyond isolate genomes. Viral identification workflows have evolved from homology-based tools relying on known viral genes and hallmark proteins (e.g., VirSorter2) to machine learning (ML) approaches, including k-merâ€“driven deep learning classifiers (DeepVirFinder), gene-content and marker-based hybrid systems (geNomad), and genome foundation modelâ€“based methods (ViraLM). Despite rapid progress, viral inference from real metagenomic data remains challenging when target sequences are rare, fragmented, or highly divergent. Three core problems compound this difficulty. First, most pipelines operate on assembled contigs, meaning low-abundance viruses may fail to assemble or appear only as short fragments, reducing detectable signal. Second, many ML models are trained on curated viral references but deployed in host-dominated, noisy metagenomes with different error profiles, conditions unfavorable for novel virus discovery. Third, the boundary between mobile genetic elements (MGEs) is not clean: plasmids, phages, and phageâ€“plasmid hybrids share sequence and gene-content features, complicating detection and motivating explicit modeling of hybrid biology over binary labels. We synthesize how these factors bias viral inference and reduce sensitivity for rare virusesâ€”low-abundance, novel, or both. We argue rare-virus discovery should be framed as an extreme class-imbalance and weak-signal detection problem rather than a conventional classification task. This motivates evaluation schemes that vary contig length and coverage to reflect nearâ€“detection-limit scenarios, and modeling strategies incorporating coverage and cross-sample recurrence alongside sequence features. These directions clarify why current tools struggle with low-abundance and novel viruses, and why distinguishing them from MGEs like phage-plasmid hybrids remains an open challenge.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Systematic evaluation of gene expression marker selection approaches in single-cell tissue atlases
authors: Ajith Viswanathan Asari Pankajam, National Institutes of Health, United States; Bingfang Xu, National Institutes of Health, United States; Matthew Diller, National Institutes of Health, United States; Daniel Pintard, National Institutes of Health, United States; Beverly Peng, J. Craig Venter Institute, United States; Yun Zhang, National Institutes of Health, United States; Richard Scheuermann, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: The development of single-cell sequencing technologies has significantly enhanced our understanding of cell populations in complex tissues. This increase in sequencing data has led to the creation of numerous tissue-specific single-cell atlases, serving as valuable resources for studying cellular diversity and function. Identifying reliable marker genes is essential for accurately classifying cell types in these atlases, serving as signatures of specific cell identities. To ensure their reliability, marker genes must undergo rigorous evaluation, including assessments of specificity, sensitivity, and reproducibility. For systematic evaluation of marker genes, we used a single-cell tissue atlas of the human retina that includes a broad range of cell types, including bipolar cells (BCs), retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), amacrine cells, endothelial cells, and their subtypes. We created various marker gene setsâ€”local-markers, global-markers, class-markers, and combined-markersâ€”to assess their specificity and sensitivity across cell types. Global-markers are derived from the entire dataset, encompassing all cell types, while local-markers originate from a subset of cells within a broader cell class. Class-markers combine granular cell types within a broader category into a single cell class within the global dataset. Using NS-Forest v4.1, we evaluated these marker sets across retinal cell types. Results indicated that local markers do not always perform well globally, nor do global markers perform well locally. Combining local-markers with global class-level markers improved performance. Thus, we propose this combined approach as an alternative method when robust global markers are unavailable.

title: Introducing EndotyPy: A Python Package for Network-Based Disease Endotyping
authors: Chloé Bucheron, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Iker Núñez-Carpintero, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Mathilde Meyenberg, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Enes Sakalli, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Julia Guthrie, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Jörg Menche, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria
abstract: Dissecting diseases into molecular-based subtypes, so called endotypes, offers a more molecularly accurate and therapeutically actionable understanding of the pathomechanisms of diseases and their potential therapeutic interventions. However, identifying these subtypes within complex biological networks remains a significant computational challenge. We present EndotyPy, a versatile Python package designed for network-based disease endotyping. EndotyPy integrates network medicine principles into a streamlined workflow to identify mechanistically cohesive disease modules. Starting from user-provided seed genes and a given biological network of interest (e.g. networks based on transcriptomic or protein-protein interaction data), the pipeline employs a Random Walk with Restart-based algorithm to construct expanded, fully connected submodules. Pre-analysis optimizes network integration strategies, followed by functional annotations that drive unsupervised hierarchical clustering to partition the subnetworks into distinct endotypes. EndotyPy performs the hierarchical clustering on functional enrichment profiles generated via GSEApy, allowing users to leverage over 100 biological libraries (e.g., GO, KEGG, MSigDB) for highly customizable, high-dimensional biological characterization and interpretation of disease endotypes. By bridging the gap between network topology and functional modularity, EndotyPy enables the identification of subgroups of disease-related genes or proteins that are both molecularly and phenotypically cohesive. EndotyPy is available as an open-source library, providing a robust framework for discovering precision therapeutic targets and optimizing patient stratification in heterogeneous diseases.

title: Beyond Pathway Boundaries: A Degree-Aware Network Clustering Test for Gene Sets
authors: Bryan Queme, Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science, University of Southern California, United States; Paul Marjoram, Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science, University of Southern California, United States; Huaiyu Mi, Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science, University of Southern California, United States
abstract: Traditional over-representation analysis assumes pathway independence and compares genes of interest against predefined pathway definitions. An alternative is to test directly whether a gene set clusters on a biological interaction network more than expected by chance, capturing cross-pathway signals without being limited to pathway definitions. However, the heterogeneous degree distribution of biological networks confounds naÃ¯ve permutation nulls: randomly sampled genes are unlikely to match the degree profile of the test set, potentially producing spurious significance regardless of true clustering. We present MANGO (Moran's Autocorrelation for Network Gene Over-representation), a framework that pairs Global Moranâ€™s I with degree-stratified permutation nulls. MANGO operates on an integrated experimental interaction network (Reactome, PANTHER, KEGG) and constructs null distributions by sampling genes from empirical degree-percentile bins, conditioning on degree. We benchmarked MANGO against join count analysis and a fragmentation-based connectivity score across real pathway gene sets with varying set sizes and degree-control stringencies, as well as synthetic planted-cluster simulations. MANGO maintained strong detection power while eliminating false positives in scenarios where degree-naÃ¯ve methods failed. A second step, graph decomposition of the induced subgraph into connected components with leave-one-out analysis, identifies which genes and modules drive the signal, which summary statistics alone cannot provide. MANGO was tested on a colorectal cancer gene set from FIGI consortium GWAS data (115 network-mapped genes) and detected significant clustering at all degree-control levels. Graph decomposition recovered a dominant module with genes known to play roles in colorectal cancer. Ongoing work targets functional characterization of signal-driving modules.

title: Development of a Genotype Specific Multi-Omics Framework for Precision Modeling in NGLY1 Deficiency
authors: Soukaina Amniouel, Postdoctoral Fellow, United States; Zeenat Shyr, Scientist, United States; William Borschel, Scientist, United States; Wei Zheng, Leader, United States
abstract: Rare diseases affect more than 300 million individuals worldwide, yet fewer than 10 percent have approved therapies due to limited understanding of genotypeâ€“phenotype relationships. Monogenic disorders are often assumed to be molecularly uniform, yet distinct mutations in the same gene can produce substantial clinical variability, as exemplified by N-glycanase (NGLY1) deficiency. This ultra-rare autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder results from loss of function mutations in a cytosolic deglycosylating enzyme involved in endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation. Its deficiency disrupts proteostasis and causes neurological dysfunction. To address this gap, I developed a mutation resolved systems framework integrating multi-omics profiling with knowledge-based pathway modeling and predictive analytics. We generated glutamatergic neurons from three independent patient derived induced pluripotent stem cell lines representing distinct biallelic genotypes and included control lines. The genotypes included a homozygous null mutation, a compound heterozygous nonsense and splice disrupting mutation, and a homozygous catalytic domain missense mutation. We generated RNA sequencing and quantitative proteomic datasets and identified concordant alterations across platforms. The null genotype showed the greatest overlap with approximately 120 shared changes, compared to approximately 80 in the missense genotype and fewer than 50 in the compound heterozygous genotype. Pathway integration revealed genotype specific enrichment. The null genotype showed synaptic, calcium, and glutamatergic pathway enrichment. The compound heterozygous genotype showed endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial stress pathways, and the catalytic domain missense genotype showed secretory pathways. A conserved pathogenic core was shared across genotypes. Ontology-based phenotype mapping and validation against published case reports demonstrated that shared clinical features arise from distinct molecular drivers. Protein-protein interaction analysis identified central regulatory nodes that recapitulated endoplasmic reticulum stress and neuronal signaling abnormalities experimentally validated in independent NGLY1 models. I am advancing supervised machine learning to prioritize genotype specific regulatory drivers for targeted validation. This framework offers a scalable strategy for precision therapeutic target prioritization in NGLY1 deficiency and other rare diseases.

title: A Bayesian Network-Based Framework for Causal Cancer Drug Target Discovery Integrating Patient and Cell Line Data
authors: Seok Hwan Yoon, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), South Korea; Ye Rin Park, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), South Korea; Hyun Uk Kim, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), South Korea
abstract: Drug target discovery in cancer has relied largely on cell line-based perturbation data, such as CRISPR screens and pharmacological assays. While these approaches enabled systematic identification of genes affecting cell viability, translation of findings to patient tumors remains limited due to differences in biological context, including tumor microenvironment. In this study, we propose a Bayesian network (BN)-based framework to bridge this gap by integrating observational patient data and interventional cell line data for causal target discovery in breast cancer. Using TCGA-BRCA and DepMap datasets, we constructed a layered causal model incorporating transcriptomic and pathway-level activities and phenotypic endpoints such as gene dependency scores. We constructed domain-specific BNs from patient and cell line data and derived a consensus network by retaining shared edges. Prior biological knowledge was incorporated via structural constraints, and robustness was ensured through bootstrap aggregation. Multiple combinations of transcriptomic and pathway-level activity calculation methods were compared using log-likelihood (LL) and mean squared error (MSE) to identify the optimal configuration. Using do-calculus-based intervention simulations, we estimated causal effect sizes of candidate genes and pathways on cell viability and ranked potential drug targets based on effect magnitude, stability, and druggability. Prioritized targets and their upstream regulators were supported by existing literature, providing biological validation of the resulting network. Our framework provides a systematic and scalable approach for causal target discovery in cancer, bridging observational and interventional datasets to prioritize biologically meaningful and clinically actionable therapeutic candidates.

title: TCDD PROMOTES PDAC THROUGH SUPPRESSION OF INTERFERRON REGULATORY FACTOR 6 AND CLOCK EXPRESSION
authors: George Acquaah-Mensah, Massachusetts College of Pharmacy and Health Science, United States; Kawther Abdilleh, Pancreatic Cancer Action Network, United States; Boris Aguilar, Institute for Systems Biology, United States
abstract: Survival rates for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are low. Early detection remains a challenge. The Endocrine Disrupting Chemical, 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD), a byproduct of some combustion and manufacturing processes, promotes metastases in certain cancers. The mechanisms by which TCDD does this remain only partially resolved. In this work, we employ a Transcriptional Regulatory Network (TRN) for insights. Gene expression data capturing all PDAC cell lines available from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia were retrieved. The trees-based machine learning algorithm, GEne Network Inference with Ensemble of trees (GENIE3), was used to reverse-engineer a TRN. Furthermore, a mouse model (GSE144765) was used for the identification of genes whose expressions in pancreatic islets are altered by a 12-week treatment with TCDD and High-fat Diet (HFD). Human ortholog expression data were superimposed on the TRN. Expression of IRF6, a hub in the TRN, is suppressed in the TCDD-HFD group. Its regulatory targets include genes whose products participate in the epithelial-mesenchymal transition. They also include LAD1, SMIM22, and ARHGAP8, all of which have elevated expression in the TCDD-HFD group. LAD1 and SMIM22 are associated with progression and metastasis in colorectal, non-small cell lung cancer, or other cancers. ARHGAP8 expression is elevated in colorectal tumors. The circadian clock is known to be disrupted in pancreatic cancer. CLOCK, another TRN hub, with suppressed expression in the TCDD-HFD group, targets EXOC1, whose expression is elevated in the TCDD-HFD group. EXOC1 variants have been associated with cervical or breast cancer. Thus, we posit plausible TCDD links to carcinogenesis and PDAC.

title: Identification of metastasis drivers from multi-omics primary tumor data via graph representation learning
authors: Yang Luo, Xidian University, China; Liyu Huang, Xidian University, China; Xiaobo Zhou, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States; Jiajia Liu, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States
abstract: Metastasis is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality, making the identification of metastasis-driving genes critical for improving prognosis and therapeutic intervention. However, this task is fundamentally challenged by tumor heterogeneity, high-dimensional multi-omics data, and the difficulty of distinguishing causal drivers from correlated molecular signals. Here, we present a transformer-based graph representation learning framework to identify candidate metastasis drivers from primary tumor data. We curated 177 experimentally validated metastasis driving genes as positive nodes. Graph structure is defined using six curated biological interaction networks, including CPDB, IREF9, IREF15, MULTINET, PCNET, and STRINGdb, capturing complementary regulatory relationships. Node features were constructed from TCGA multi-omics data across 14 cancer types, integrating somatic mutation, gene expression, DNA methylation, and copy number variation. We proposed a structure-aware graph Transformer framework (GTF) for representation learning on multi-omicsâ€“informed biological graphs, with attention-based message passing over edges and normalized Laplacian positional encodings incorporated into node representations. GTF was benchmarked against GCN, GAT, DeepWalk, and Laplacian Eigenmaps (LAP). Performance was evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) as the primary metric. Across all six biological networks, GTF achieved the best performance on all networks, with a mean AUPRC of 0.778, outperforming GCN (0.709), GAT (0.695), DeepWalk (0.655), and LAP (0.692). These results demonstrate that integrating multi-omics features with structure-aware graph representation learning substantially improves the interpretable identification of metastasis drivers.

title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell multiomic data: a novel framework for cell-level analysis
authors: Eric Moeller, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Karamveer Karamveer, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Hannah Valensi, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Ewura-Esi Manful, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Yasin Uzun, Penn State College of Medicine, United States
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) underlie how cells sense, interpret, and respond to their environment. Composed of transcription factors (TFs) and the target genes (TGs) that they regulate, changes in normal GRN signaling can dysregulate cell behavior and contribute to disease. While molecular techniques for mapping GRNs are advancing rapidly, GRNs vary between species, cell types, and disease states. This variability and specificity makes GRNs difficult to map comprehensively using experimental techniques.Single-cell multiomic RNA and ATAC sequencing provides a promising avenue for overcoming these challenges. Single-cell multiomics now allows researchers to measure both gene expression and chromatin accessibility in individual cells. Researchers are beginning to develop GRN inference methods that can make predictions at the cell-level from multiple data sources. Despite these advances, current models struggle to accurately detect true TF-TG regulatory relationships. We have developed MultiomicTransformer, a new attention-based deep learning method for GRN inference. We utilize the rich context of single-cell multiomic data to create a model that can predict TG expression from TF expression and ATAC accessibility. We then use this trained model to generate GRNs by averaging the loss gradient between the TF inputs and the TG outputs across all cells in the dataset. Our method avoids the limited availability of direct TF-TG regulatory interaction data for training TF-TG edge classifier models by instead training a model to predict TG expression, then using the learned model to predict regulatory interactions.

title: Perturb-Seqr: Comprehensive Signature Search Engine Integrating Connectivity Maps from Multiple Sources
authors: Lily Taub, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; John Gardner, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Avi Ma'Ayan, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States
abstract: Connectivity Mapping was significantly expanded via the NIH Common Fund LINCS program that produced a massive drug and single gene knockout perturbations followed by expression resource with the L1000 assay. These efforts set the stage for a new wave of Connectivity Mapping datasets that recently emerged due the availability of the DRUG-seq and Perturb-seq biotechnologies. However, as far as we know, no efforts were made to integrate multiple Connectivity Mapping resources for an integrative search. Motivated by this opportunity, we have developed Perturb-seqr, a comprehensive Connectivity Mapping search engine that integrates nine small molecules transcriptomics Connectivity Maps and nine single gene perturbation Connectivity Maps. Specifically, Perturb-seqr contains processed data from LINCS (L1000), Tahoe-100M, NIBR (DRUG-seq), the original CMap (cDNA microarrays), Ginkgo Bioworks (DRUG-seq), SciPlex, DeepCover MoA (Proteomics), Perturb Atlas (Perturb-seq), Replogle et al. (Perturb-seq), CM4AI (Perturb-seq), CREEDS (cDNA microarrays), and RummaGEO (RNA-seq). To serve these datasets in one unifying search engine, we assembled over 400,000 sets of up- and down-regulated genes measuring the effects of over 11,000 unique drugs, and over 12,000 unique gene perturbations, targeting over 4,000 cell lines, cell types, and tissues. Users of Perturb-seqr can submit their own up and down gene sets to identify small molecules and gene perturbations that produce the most similar or opposite effect on gene expression. Perturb-seqr also provides interactive UMAP visualizations for exploring the clustering of signatures from each dataset, as well as programmatic access to Perturb-seqr via a GraphQL API. To demonstrate how Perturb-seqr can be used for drug and target discovery, we applied it to a dataset that seeks to identify drugs that would maximize insulin secretion from pancreatic islets. Overall, Perturb-Seqr introduces the most comprehensive up-to-date Connectivity Mapping search engine and database to date, enabling the discovery of new drugs and targets. Perturb-Seqr is accessible from: https://perturbseqr.maayanlab.cloud/.

title: MethScope: Ultra-fast Analysis of Sparse DNA Methylome via Recurrent Pattern Encoding
authors: Hongxiang Fu, Center for Computational and Genomic Medicine, The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Hao Xu, Center for Computational and Genomic Medicine, The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Chin Lee, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Cameron Cloud, Center for Computational and Genomic Medicine, The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Yanxiang Deng, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Wanding Zhou, Center for Computational and Genomic Medicine, The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, United States
abstract: DNA methylation is a key epigenetic mark with broad applications in biology and medicine, but its high dimensionality and sparsity hinder analysis. We introduce Most Recurrent Methylation Patterns (MRMPs), which capture long-range, punctate methylation correlations beyond conventional region-based methods. MRMPs reveal higher-order epigenetic organization and provide a compact, interpretable representation of global methylation variation. Using this framework, we developed MethScope, a fast and interpretable machine learning approach that encodes sparse methylation data via additive combinations of MRMP signals. This representation enables mini-bulk deconvolution of spatial methylation maps, whole-genome upscaling, rapid cell type annotation, and improved cell embedding with enhanced lineage resolution. MethScope reconstructs cell-type-specific methylomes from as little as ~0.1% randomly sampled CpGs with high accuracy, including for unseen cell types and conditions.

title: High-throughput Decoding of Transcription Factor Binding Site Grammar for Synthetic Promoter Design In Vivo
authors: Camilla Belamarich, MeiraGTx, United States; Chenjin Jin, MeiraGTx, United States; Jared Sills, MeiraGTx, United States; Gavin Lagani, MeiraGTx, United States; Casey Lutnick, MeiraGTx, United States; T.D. Barbara Nguyen-Vu, MeiraGTx, United States; Josefa M. Sullivan, MeiraGTx, United States; Enrico Mossotto, MeiraGTx, United States
abstract: Utilizing transcription factor binding sites (TFBS) to design compact, tissue-specific promoters is important for optimizing vector payload and expression for genetic medicines. However, decoding TFBS grammar and predicting combinatorial effects remains a significant challenge. We used a massively parallel reporter assay comprised of synthetic promoters (182 bp; n=244,000) to evaluate TFBS influence on promoter activity in vitro (N2A cells) and in vivo (mouse muscle). We systematically varied regulatory regions upstream of six core promoters (JeT, AdML, MCK, DES, mTTR, AAT) to model individual and combinatorial TFBS effects. Activity was quantified as expression fold change relative to the parent promoter to classify TFBS as activators, repressors, or neutral. In N2A, a minority of designs revealed improving activity across core promoters. JeT showed the highest baseline activity, further enhanced >4-fold by specific TFBS while the brain-inactive AAT promoter was boosted 20-fold (Validation RPearson=0.64). In vivo, we identified robust activators and repressors, defined by consistent magnitude and directionality across all five animals, comprising 8.7% and 8.3% of designs, respectively. Robust activators increased activity of JeT, MCK, and DES up to six-fold. Notably, the myocyte-specific MEF2A TFBS emerged as a consistent activator across promoters. However, regulatory logic was highly context-dependent: N2A and muscle activity showed poor correlation (RÂ²=0.01) and no shared universal activators or repressors. Additionally, individual TF effects rarely predicted combinatorial performance. This scalable platform enables engineering potent, tissue-specific promoters. Our findings demonstrate in vitro screening is a poor predictor of in vivo logic, necessitating large-scale in vivo datasets for accurate regulatory modeling.

title: Improving Structure-Based Prediction of Protein–DNA Binding Specificity using AlphaFold 3-Predicted Complexes
authors: Wei Yu Tang, University of Southern California, United States; Jinsen Li, University of Southern California, United States; Peijun Lin, University of Southern California, United States; Yueshan Liang, University of Southern California, United States; Kalie Uberti, University of Southern California, United States; Remo Rohs, University of Southern California, United States
abstract: Predicting proteinâ€“DNA binding specificity is a fundamental challenge in understanding gene regulation, with broad implications for decoding transcription factor function. The diversity of protein folds that recognize DNA, combined with binding-associated conformational changes, motivates approaches that leverage 3D structural information beyond sequence alone. Previous work, DeepPBS, addresses this by predicting binding specificity as a position weight matrix (PWM) directly from proteinâ€“DNA complex by encoding their physicochemical and geometric interactions. However, DeepPBS is limited by the scarcity of transcription factors with both experimental crystal structures and characterized PWMs, restricting training to only hundreds of complexes. Here, we present several extensions that improve the predictive accuracy and generalizability of DeepPBS. First, we incorporate predicted complexes from AlphaFold 3 as a data augmentation strategy. Second, we reformulate the model's output to predict a dinucleotide PWM, allowing the model to explicitly capture inter-base dependencies during training. Third, we introduce architectural improvements, including separate processing pathways for inter- and intra-base pair DNA shape features and residual connections that enable deeper networks. Across two complementary metrics, mean absolute error (MAE) and cross-entropy, our extensions yield substantial improvements on predicted structures while maintaining accuracy on experimental ones. We further show that some predicted structural quality metrics, such as average pLDDT, steric clashes, and the number of close contacts, correlate with model performance. Finally, we apply the model to predict binding specificity changes in transcription factor mutants using AlphaFold 3-generated structures, illustrating its potential for studying the effects of mutation in protein sequences.

title: Multi-layered regulatory networks for discovery of causal interactions in complex-traits
authors: Qingbo Wang, Calico Life Sciences, United States; Eugene Melamud, Calico Life Sciences, United States; Anastasia Baryshnikova, Calico Life Sciences, United States
abstract: Human diseases arise as a consequence of complex-network of interactions from genetics through all layers of biology, yet we lack network understanding of influence between each layer. Identifying causal factors that drive these networks is challenging, requiring methods for reconstructing the underlying regulatory network structure. Here we utilize a combination of genetics and high-throughput plasma proteomics to enable discovery of genetically driven protein interactions and causal pathways. We apply our method on ~50,000 individuals in UKBB with proteomics measurements, and show that the derived networks are highly enriched for known gene interactions, co-expression, tissue and cellular co-localization with directional interpretations (e.g. ANGPTL3 on PCSK9). Utilizing the network, we re-construct the gene regulatory hierarchy for >100 complex traits including >60 biomarkers, to define the core genes as well as distance from the core-gene in the regulatory network. We show that the genes upstream of core-genes are highly enriched for trait-heritability (e.g. >10x for top 1% genes in LDL level), while those downstream, even if in proximity, are not, thereby classifying causal versus consequential genes. We also utilize the upstream distance to core genes (UDON) for gene-prioritization in GWAS locus, achieving an enrichment comparable to the fieldâ€™s standard (1.27x compared to when using the PoPS score alone). Finally, we integrate UDON for >60 biomarkers to estimate the impact on human mortality for ~3,000 plasma proteins, highlighting known and potential novel key drivers of human physiological decline, such as TP53 and SIRT1.

title: Airqtl dissects cell state-specific causal gene regulatory networks with efficient single-cell eQTL mapping
authors: Matthew Funk, UMass Chan Medical School, United States; Yuhe Wang, UMass Chan Medical School, Boston University, United States; Lingfei Wang, UMass Chan Medical School, United States
abstract: Single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sceQTL) mapping offers a powerful approach for understanding gene regulation and its heterogeneity across cell types and states. It has profound applications in genetics and genomics, particularly causal gene regulatory network (cGRN) inference to unravel the molecular circuits governing cell identity and function. However, computational scalability remains a critical bottleneck for sceQTL mapping, prohibiting thorough benchmarking and optimization of statistical accuracy. We present airqtl, an efficient method to overcome these challenges through algorithmic advances and efficient implementations of linear mixed models. Airqtl achieves superior time complexity and over 108 times of acceleration, enabling objective method benchmarking and optimization. Airqtl offers de novo inference of robust, experimentally validated cell state-specific cGRNs that reflect perturbation outcomes. Our results dissect the drivers of cGRN heterogeneity and underscore the value of natural genetic variations in primary human cell types for biologically relevant single-cell cGRN inference.

title: Shank3∆C differentially impacts the molecular response to sleep deprivation across development
authors: Elliot Wald, Washington State University, United States; Elizabeth Medina, University of Nebraska Medical Center, United States; Caitlin Ottaway, Washington State University, United States; Christine Muheim, Washington State University, United States; Kaitlyn Ford, Seattle Children's Hospital, United States; Kristan Singletary, Washington State University, United States; Hannah Schoch, Washington State University, United States; Taylor Wintler, Seattle Children's Hospital, United States; Ashely Ingiosi, Ohio State University, United States; Lucia Peixoto, Washington State University, United States
abstract: Insomnia is prevalent in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), worsening core symptoms and negatively impacting quality of life. We previously showed that mice with a mutation in the high-confidence ASD gene Shank3 (Shank3∆C) recapitulate the clinical insomnia phenotype. Specifically, Shank3∆C mice do not respond properly to sleepiness after acute sleep deprivation (SD) starting as early as postnatal day 24 (P24, ~1 year old infant). However, the molecular basis of sleepiness and how ASD-associated mutations impact it remains unclear. In this study, we used RNA-sequencing to define the effect of Shank3∆C on the molecular basis of sleepiness by comparing cortical gene expression following SD in Wild-Type (WT) and mutant mice between P24 and P90 (adults). We found that at P90, the typical WT response involves upregulating DNA damage repair systems and neuronal activity-dependent transcription. At P24, WT animals upregulate neuronal growth and development pathways. The Shank3∆C mice do not show these changes, with the mutation largely repressing the transcriptional response to SD. However, mutants do consistently upregulate oxidative stress/neurodegeneration after SD regardless of age. We conclude that mutant mice are unable to accumulate sleepiness at the molecular level, instead showing an aberrant oxidative stress response. Enhancing the recruitment of neuronal growth and DNA repair pathways while diminishing the impact of oxidative stress following SD may therefore be actionable strategies to improve sleep in ASD. Future studies will focus on validating top candidates using low-throughput spatial transcriptomics to identify key targets and cell-types for further investigation.

title: Identifying causal pathways of immune-mediated diseases and traits using genetic variation from single cell RNA-seq studies
authors: Xiaoyu Gui, University of California, San Diego, United States; Tiffany Amariuta, University of California, San Diego, United States
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of disease-associated variants, and colocalization with eQTLs via transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) have been helpful for interpreting their regulatory impacts. Single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNAseq) provides unprecedented resolution of gene expression in disease-critical cell types, but stratifying genetic association analyses by discrete cell types attenuates power to identify disease-critical genes. To address this, we developed Pathway-TCSC (Pathway-level Tissue Co-regulation Score Regression), a framework that scores single cells based on expression of pathway-specific marker genes and then constructs gene expression prediction models for high scoring cells, abandoning discrete cell type annotations and enhancing power to identify disease-critical genes. We applied Pathway-TCSC to scRNAseq of immune cells from OneK1K and 312 immune-related and hallmark MSigDB pathways. We found gene expression levels in cells involved in T cell maturation and interferon-driven B cell dysregulation to be strongly regulated by genetic variation (across ~12K genes, cis-heritability h²=0.135 (se=0.033), 0.125 (se=0.033), respectively). Across 21 autoimmune GWAS summary statistics, we performed TWAS for ~624K gene-pathway-disease trios and recovered established disease risk genes, such as GPX1 (p=5.57e-32) in cells involved in interferon signaling with IBD. Finally, we used TCSC to partition disease heritability into causal pathways; T cell differentiation and TNF-alpha/NF-kB pathways were nominally causal for lupus (h²=0.064 (se=0.037), h²=0.036 (se=0.019), respectively), while natural killer cytotoxicity and antigen processing were identified as non-causal, tagging pathways, further clarifying the regulatory context of disease-critical genes.

title: PathwayCCA: Jointly Linking Multiomic Alterations in Cancer to Pathway Dysregulation
authors: Yuqi Zhang, Department of Computer Science; Lewis-Sigler Institute of Integrative Genomics, Princeton University, United States; Sara Geraghty, Center for Advanced Genomic Technologies, Duke University, United States; Yaojie Hu, Department of Mathematics, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Mona Singh, Department of Computer Science; Lewis-Sigler Institute of Integrative Genomics, Princeton University, United States
abstract: Cancer genomes accumulate diverse somatic alterations, including mutations, copy number alterations, and DNA methylations, that drive tumor initiation and progression. Understanding how these alterations collectively perturb biological pathways is essential for elucidating cancer progression. While pathway-level effects of individual alterations are routinely assessed using gene set enrichment analyses, determining the joint influence of multiple alteration types on pathway-level gene expression remains challenging. Here we propose PathwayCCA, a framework based on canonical correlation analysis (CCA) that tests whether multiple somatic alterations jointly affect the expression of a given pathway. A key challenge is accounting for structured confounders such as cancer subtypes, which can dominate the biological signal of interest. PathwayCCA addresses this using group-regularized CCA, enabling stronger regularization of confounding covariates relative to genomic features, thereby better isolating signals from genomic alterations. To mitigate spurious correlations common in high-dimensional settings, we further develop a sampling-based hypothesis test. We adopt CCA visualization methods to reveal relationships between specific alteration types and pathway genes. We evaluate PathwayCCA in two settings: modeling multiomic alterations for single driver genes and for multiple drivers jointly. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that PathwayCCA markedly increases the ability to detect perturbed pathways comparing to approaches that analyze each alteration individually. Applying our method to breast cancer cohorts from TCGA and METABRIC, we identify common pathways in both associated with recurrent genomic alterations. In sum, by modeling the combined effects of genomic changes on pathway expression, PathwayCCA provides a principled framework for linking multiomic alterations to functional dysregulation in cancer.

title: Lineage-Specific Enhancer Networks Organized by IKAROS Establish Lineage Bias in Hematopoietic Stem Cells
authors: Daniela Salgado Figueroa, La Jolla Institute for Immunology and UC San Diego, United States; Charlie Mazof, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Toshimi Yoshida, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Kate Graham, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Brock Dean Tweedy, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Halley Emmons, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Mariko Kashiwagi, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Bruce A Morgan, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Ferhat Ay, La Jolla Institute of Immunology, United States; Katia Georgopoulos, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States
abstract: A central question in hematopoiesis is whether lineage bias arises only after hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) differentiate into downstream multipotent progenitors (MPPs) or whether it is already embedded within the regulatory landscape of long-term HSCs. Classical models have largely described HSCs as functionally unbiased; however, accumulating evidence suggests that individual HSCs can exhibit stable lineage preferences. The molecular basis for this fate bias, and whether it arises from transcriptional priming or is encoded within a deeper regulatory chromatin configuration, remains unclear. We hypothesized that IKAROS, a key regulator of lymphocyte differentiation, functions earlier in hematopoiesis to maintain multipotent regulatory states by organizing enhancer landscapes and constraining regulatory networks involving these enhancers and their upstream transcriptional factors. Through single-cell multiome profiling, we identified that IKAROS deficiency results in a progressive loss of lymphoid-associated chromatin programs starting at the HSC stage and extending through MPPs, leading to complete depletion of lymphoid-primed progenitors. In parallel, myeloid-associated regulatory programs were elevated, accompanied by increases in myeloid and megakaryocyte-biased progenitors, whereas erythroid progenitors remained largely unchanged. Topic modeling of enhancer co-accessibility further revealed modular regulatory programs aligned with specific lineage trajectories. IKAROS loss selectively attenuated lymphoid-associated topic modules, amplified an intermediate MPP regulatory program, and induced myeloid-associated enhancer programs. Our study shows that IKAROS remodels chromatin accessibility and enhancer networks prior to the substantial changes in gene expression that occur during differentiation. This provides a mechanistic link between early chromatin deregulation in hematopoiesis and the development of myeloid dysplasia and related hematological disorders.

title: flex: GNN-Based Metabolic Flux Estimation from Transcriptomics Data
authors: Dennis Kostka, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Background: Cellular metabolism is a key determinant of phenotype; yet, measuring metabolic fluxes at single-cell resolution at scale remains elusive. While single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics can quantify enzyme abundance, there is a scarcity of methods to reliably infer underlying reaction-level fluxes that drive cellular physiology and disease. Existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained pathway abstractions, and/or lack integration with modern single-cell analysis ecosystems. Methods: We developed flex (FLux Estimation from eXpression), a graph neural network (GNN) framework that models genome-scale metabolic networks as explicit graphs to infer reaction-level fluxes from expression data. flex leverages three main inductive biases, grounded in thermodynamics and biophysics: protein structure, compound chemistry, and metabolic network topology. Metabolic maps are reduced to reaction/gene networks where node embeddings for enzymes are derived from ESM2 protein language model representations, and reaction embeddings are based on Morgan molecular fingerprints of substrates and products. Repeated heterogeneous convolutions propagate expression information through the network. The model is trained using a composite objective incorporating flux balance, thermodynamic plausibility, pathway-level expressionâ€“flux correlation, and a similarity learning term preserving expression-based cell-cell relationships. Results: Expression-independent validation confirms that the model's inductive biases are mutually coherent: compound fingerprint embeddings alone predict reaction-reaction edges with AUC 0.92, and a gated compatibility function over ESM2 and fingerprint embeddings predicts gene-reaction associations with AUC 0.88 on held-out gene nodes. Trained on Tabula Sapiens atlas data, flex demonstrates strong generalization on a held-out set of 10,000 cells. Applied to pancreatic cancer cell line data, flex identifies elevated glycolysis fluxes under hypoxia and reveals reaction-level variation within pathways masked by module-level summaries. In zero-shot application to Visium spatial transcriptomics breast cancer data, flex produces flux estimates that clearly separate cancer subtypes and distinguish cancer from non-cancer spots, with metabolic enzyme-based principal components showing higher spatial autocorrelation than those derived from all genes. Conclusions: flex provides biologically grounded, reaction-level metabolic flux estimates from transcriptomic data, generalizes across tissues and data modalities, and reveals metabolic heterogeneity in disease contexts.

title: 5-Hydroxymethylcytosine QTL Mapping in Human CD4+ T Cells via Long-Read Sequencing
authors: Bolutito Babatunde, La Jolla Institute for Immunology, United States; Rosan Wang, Salk Institute for Biological Studies, United States; Nirmalya Dasgupta, La Jolla Institute for Immunology, United States; Abhijit Chakraborty, La Jolla Institute for Immunology, United States; Ferhat Ay, La Jolla Institute for Immunology, United States
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) link thousands of loci with complex disease, but most risk alleles map to noncoding DNA within dense haplotypes, making causal regulatory variants difficult to pinpoint. Molecular quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping links polymorphisms to intermediate phenotypes, prominently gene expression QTLs (eQTLs) and histone QTLs (hQTLs) on enhancer-associated chromatin marks, yet these layers capture only part of the cis-regulatory architecture and cannot uncouple causality from linkage disequilibrium. Work from our group and others suggests that DNA demethylation can precede chromatin accessibility and active histone deposition, motivating 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), a stable TET-mediated oxidation product enriched at active and poised enhancers, as an early enhancer readout. Conventional bisulfite assays, including methylation arrays, conflate 5hmC with 5-methylcytosine (5mC), leaving population-scale 5hmC QTL mapping uncharacterized. We applied Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing to nCD4+ from 39 healthy donors, combining standard basecalling with nano-NOMe-seq (enzymatic GpC labeling of accessible DNA on the same reads) to define cis-5hmC and 5mC QTLs genome-wide. Our analyses reveal abundant cis effects, opposing 5hmC versus 5mC genetics consistent with oxidative demethylation, and, where loci overlap, alignment with DICE/ImmunexUT eQTLs (nCD4+) and Blueprint/WP10 hQTLs (T cells), while exposing eQTL-colocalized 5hmC signals without matching hQTLs and 5hmC-led loci without eQTL/hQTL overlap, with allele-resolved validation from long reads. 5hmC QTL mapping establishes a demethylation-focused regulatory genotype-phenotype layer orthogonal to array and histone QTL maps, cross-validating shared programs while uncovering cis-associations hidden to those assays, broadening enhancer hypotheses for noncoding GWAS interpretation in T cells and immune disease mechanisms.

title: Quantitative Frameworks for Studying Replication Timing Changes Upon Transcription Factor Loss
authors: Laura Hinojosa, La Jolla Institute for Immunology, United States; Jesse Turner, San Diego Biomedical Research Institute, United States; Takayo Sasaki, San Diego Biomedical Research Institute, United States; David Gilbert, San Diego Biomedical Research Institute, United States; Ferhat Ay, La Jolla Institute for Immunology; Bioinformatics and Systems Biology PhD Program, UCSD; Department of Pediatrics, UCSD, United States
abstract: DNA replicates during S phase following a defined temporal program, called Replication Timing (RT), which helps establish the correct epigenetic state in the genome. Although we previously showed that specific Transcription Factor (TF) Binding Sites (TFBS), enriched in histone acetyltransferase P300, are necessary to maintain early replication and an active chromatin state, the regulatory role of TFs in RT is still not fully understood. Here, we employed auxin-inducible degron systems to knockdown (KD) the master TFs Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC), and three bromodomain-containing proteins (Brd), which recognize and bind to acetylated histones. We established two complementary statistical frameworks in order to accurately measure the effects of KDs on RT, and account for spontaneous differentiation of mESC into Trophoblast Stem Cells induced upon loss of these TFs. We first employ a multivariate distance measurement to determine affected regions, and then build a randomized background for significance calculation of each site. We observed that KD of Oct4 and Sox2 trigger widespread delays across the genome, with increased delays when jointly depleted. Similarly, joint Sox2 and Nanog KD increased RT delays compared to their individual degrons. Inhibition of the transcriptional activators CBP/EP300 also caused widespread RT delays. In contrast, the RT program was robust to Brd KDs. Most perturbation-sensitive loci fall within developmentally regulated replication domains containing multiple Oct4-Sox2-Nanog TFBSs, although not all loci with these characteristics are equally delayed. This suggests that TF binding in each locus helps determine precise RT control, coordinated with lineage commitment and transcriptional regulation.

title: Multi-tiered integration of gene regulatory networks in cancer cell lines
authors: Marouen Ben Guebila, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA, United States; Camila Lopes-Ramos, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA, United States; John Quackenbush, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA, United States
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) control how, when, and where genes are expressed, yet their complexity puts them out of reach of direct measurement across all transcription factors (TFs) and cellular contexts. The Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) includes measurements for gene expression, promoter methylation, copy number variation, protein and metabolite levels, but does not capture TF binding activity, which cannot be assayed across all TFs and cell lines systematically. To address this, we used Network Zoo (netZoo) methods to re-analyze CCLE data and extend it by inferring genome-scale, sample-specific GRNs for 1,376 cell lines, thereby estimating TF-gene regulatory interactions as a new multi-omic layer. We then used DRAGON, a method for efficient multi-omic integration based on Gaussian Graphical Models with covariance shrinkage, to compute partial correlation networks between TF targeting scores and nine types of omics measurements. This allowed us to identify direct associations between TF regulatory activity and molecular phenotypes while controlling for spurious correlations across data types with different underlying distributions. We crossed these regulatory networks with drug sensitivity data from PRISM and gene knockout fitness screens from the Dependency Map, and found correlations between drug response and gene dependency that recapitulate known pharmacogenomic interactions, such as the association between sensitivity for tyrosine kinase inhibitors and knockout effects in the BRAF-MAPK signaling pathway. These results demonstrate that computational inference of unobserved regulatory layers combined with multimodal statistical methods can extend multi-omic data analysis beyond the limits of experimental assays to find meaningful biological associations.

title: LIY Deletion in SH2 Domain Alters STAT5A Function and Disrupts Mammary Gland Development and circRNA Expression
authors: Ethan McCrary, Georgetown University, United States; Markus Hoffmann, Georgetown University, United States; Lothar Hennighausen, NIH, United States; Hye Kyung Lee, NIH, United States; Priscilla Furth, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Mammary gland development during pregnancy is regulated by lactogenic hormones acting through the JAK2â€“STAT5 signaling pathway. STAT5 is activated via JAK-mediated phosphorylation and subsequent binding to the SH2 domain. In this study, we introduced a LIY (leucine-isoleucine-tyrosine) deletion within this domain, revealing significant functional effects. To investigate the consequences of this mutation, mammary tissue was collected at lactation day 1 (L1) and pregnancy day 18 (P18). The lack of LIY in the SH2 domain resulted in the inability for female mice to feed their pups. Histological analysis revealed underdeveloped mammary glands in mutant mice. A transcriptomic analysis showed that the L1 LIY samples clustered more closely with P18 groups than with L1 wildtype (WT) controls. At both time points, LIY samples exhibited significant downregulation of circular RNAs derived from milk protein genes, WAP and CSN, alongside upregulation of genes associated with transcriptional regulation. Gene set enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment in organ and tissue development pathways in the P18 RNA-seq data. Analysis of circRNA profiles revealed similar patterns. Collectively, these findings indicate that the LIY deletion alters the function of STAT5, disrupts mammary gland development, and highlights a potential role for STAT5 in the regulation of circular RNAs.

title: Are Circular RNAs Uncoupled from Their Host Genes in Breast Cancer Models?
authors: Lin Liu, Georgetown University, United States; Priscilla Furth, Georgetown University, United States; Markus Hoffmann, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Motivation The estrogen receptor (ER) is a transcription factor activated by estrogen. Its overactivity is highly associated with breast cancer development. Clinically, the estrogen pathway can be inhibited in two ways: by targeting the receptor using selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) Tamoxifen, or by reducing estrogen production using aromatase inhibitors (AIs) Letrozole. We treated ESR1 and CYP19Y1 mice with Tamoxifen and Letrozole separately and investigated circular RNAs (circRNAs) expression changes. Methods In this study, single-ended RNA-seq data are from GSE70440 and GSE201767. FASTQ files were obtained from mammary tissue of MMTV-rtTA/tet-opâ€“Esr1 and MMTV-rtTA/tet-opâ€“CYP19A1 mice (C57BL/6 background), under conditions of age variation, gene overexpression (Esr1 or CYP19A1), and treatment with Tamoxifen or Letrozole (n=3 per condition) We use DESeq2 and clusterProfiler to analyze the mice. Especially the differentially expressed circRNAs during treatment. Results We found that doxycycline can change the ratio between circRNAs and host gene expression. In many cases, circRNAs expression decreases relative to the host gene when using doxycycline to activate ESR1 or CYP19Y1, but exceptions exist (e.g., SENP1). We observe different types of circRNA regulation. circRNAs are not always co-regulated with their host genes. Some circRNAs increase simply because the host gene increases, but others increase without corresponding increases in host gene expression, suggesting independent regulatory mechanisms. Conclusion/Meaning We investigate the relationship between circRNAs and their host genes after Tamoxifen or Letrozole treatment. As a result, these circRNAs could be used as new biomarkers for breast cancer for a larger female group.

title: Benchmarking component choices for unpaired single cell RNA and epigenomic integration
authors: Fnu Naqing, Institute for Human Genetics of Clemson University, United States; Qiuyue Yuan, Department of Human Cell Biology and Genetics, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, China; Zhana Duren, Indiana University School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Background: Single-cell multi-omics sequencing technologies enable profiling various cellular aspects, offering valuable biological insights. Integrating unpaired multi-omics data, which involves profiling different modalities from distinct cells within the same overall population, remains challenging yet crucial for a comprehensive understanding of cell states and molecular dynamics. Although numerous computational methods for integrating such unpaired data exist, a systematic evaluation of the choices at each step is lacking. The recent emergence of technologies simultaneously profiling multiple modalities within the same cell provides paired datasets, allows for the systematic evaluation of unpaired pipelines. Method: We leverage paired scRNA-seq with scATAC-seq and histone modifications to systematically evaluate methods for unpaired scRNA and peak-based epigenomic (ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq) data integration to establish a robust, general pipeline. We benchmark individual steps, including feature linking, dimension reduction, and clustering, and evaluate their combinatorial effects on pipeline performance by testing various choices at each stage. Results: Our findings reveal that while gene activity scores show limited correlation with gene expression, they effectively preserve cellular neighborhoods for clustering. Dimension reduction emerges as the most critical step, with non-linear methods generally offering better performance and linear methods providing robustness. Optimal transport (OT)-based label transfer consistently outperforms other strategies across various embeddings. Conclusions: This benchmark of unpaired integration provides valuable insights for developing methods suited for increasingly complex multi-omics study designs.

title: PRIUS decodes BRD4-mediated chromatin remodeling driving fibroblast activation
authors: Yeting Li, Boston University, United States; Michael Alexanian, Gladstone Institutes, United States; Pawel Przytycki, Boston University, United States
abstract: Excess fibroblast activation induced by stress contributes to cardiac dysfunction and pathological remodeling of the heart. However, the regulatory mechanism governing this process remains unclear. BRD4, a stress-responding protein, plays a widespread role in remodeling the chromatin landscape across various cell types. In Cx3cr1-expressing monocyte-derived macrophages, BRD4 induces transcriptional secretion of IL-1Î² to drive pathological fibroblast activation in heart failure. Pharmacological inhibition of BRD4 using the small molecule JQ1 has shown protective effects on stress-induced heart failure with improving cardiac function. However, the broad inhibition of BRD4 poses challenges due to its widespread binding sites across chromatin regions, highlighting the need for more precise cell-type-specific targeting strategies. We hypothesize that dynamic distal regions regulated by BRD4 in Cx3cr1-expressing macrophages are the primary driver of IL-1Î² production to induce fibroblast activation in response to stress. To address this, we developed a robust, cell-type-specific scoring system named PRIUS, Perturbed Regulation Indicator in cells Under Selection, to quantify stress-induced chromatin accessibility dynamic changes regulated by BRD4 in Cx3cr1-expressing macrophages. PRIUS integrates single-cell ATAC-seq and CUN&RUN datasets to quantify the regulatory potential of 23,520 BRD4-regulated distal regions in this subset of macrophages under stress. PRIUS successfully captures dynamic chromatin accessibility changes regulated by BRD4 in response to cardiac stress, as well as identifies BRD4-regulated enhancer regions. The top 100 genes regulated by those distal regions highlight their potential role in regulating the immune response in macrophages and contributing to cardiac fibrosis, further validating the capability of PRIUS. PRIUS informs novel, cell-type-specific therapeutic strategies for pharmacological intervening to reverse pathological cardiac remodeling at the cellular level.

title: Integrating Deep Learning-Based Modeling and Design of Transcription Factor–DNA Interactions
authors: Jinsen Li, University of Southern California, United States; Yingfei Wang, University of Southern California, United States; Tsu-Pei Chiu, University of Southern California, United States; Beibei Xin, China Agricultural University, China; Remo Rohs, University of Southern California, United States
abstract: Transcription factor (TF)-DNA binding specificity arises from both sequence and DNA shape features. Deep learning models such as CNNs and self-attention transformers have improved prediction accuracy, yet challenges remain in modeling low-affinity binding and integrating sequence-structure relationships. Using SELEX-seq data for Exd-Hox heterodimers in Drosophila, we show that reverse-complement-aware models outperform conventional approaches and enable improved characterization of low-affinity binding sites. Model interpretation further reveals potential biophysical mechanisms underlying Exd-Ubx binding. In addition, we present DNAdesign, a framework for feature-aware in silico DNA design that integrates sequence and shape information via Deep DNAshape. The platform enables systematic exploration of mutations and their effects on DNA structure, supporting applications in gene regulation and synthetic biology. (https://dnadesign.usc.edu/)

title: SpiderNet reveals a meta-interaction basis for cell-cell communication in tissues
authors: Junjie Tang, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Shaoheng Liang, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Shahul Alam, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Jian Ma, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Cell-cell communication in tissues emerges from spatially organized, directional signaling programs that couple sender state, intercellular ligand--receptor interactions, and receiver transcriptional responses, yet these programs remain difficult to resolve in situ. Here we present SpiderNet, an interpretable framework for learning cell-cell meta-interactions (MIs) from spatial transcriptomics. Each MI represents a directional communication module linking sender-side regulators, ligand--receptor bridges, and receiver-side target genes, thereby connecting intercellular coupling to intracellular regulatory consequences. SpiderNet models ordered neighboring cell pairs and is trained end-to-end to jointly reconstruct ligand--receptor co-expression and gene expression, yielding a compact and mechanistically interpretable representation of multicellular regulation. Across simulations and diverse spatial transcriptomic datasets, SpiderNet robustly recovers biologically coherent meta-interactions, more faithfully links intercellular signaling to curated regulatory activity than existing approaches, and supports downstream analyses including cell-subtype discovery, in silico spatial perturbation, phenotype prediction, and multi-hop communication cascade detection. In ovarian cancer, SpiderNet identifies a thrombospondin (THBS)-associated fibroblast--tumor program coupled to an upstream osteopontin (SPP1) monocyte--fibroblast relay marking aggressive tumor states. In aging brain, it resolves a T cell-associated pro-aging communication module linked to local transcriptional remodeling and transferable age prediction across regions and platforms. In perturbation-resolved melanoma, it uncovers coordinated remodeling of melanoma--T cell communication following NF-KB perturbation. By organizing tissue communication into a small set of reusable meta-interactions, SpiderNet provides a general framework for resolving, comparing, and perturbing multicellular regulatory programs across tissues and experimental settings.

title: Developing a methylation and SNP-aware DNA large language model
authors: Dante Bolzan, La Jolla Institute for Immunology; University ofCalifornia, San Diego, United States; Ferhat Ay, La Jolla Institute for Immunology; University ofCalifornia, San Diego, United States
abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA language models, such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained on reference genomes, thereby omitting sequence variation and epigenetic base modifications. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and methylated cytosine (5mC) are associated with gene expression and genome function. We hypothesize that a single model that incorporates both SNPs and 5mC during pretraining would learn representations that better capture functional genomic contexts. To test this hypothesis, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model that was pretrained on the human reference genome with the addition of SNP and CpG methylation information from the 1000 Genomes Long Read Sequencing Consortium. ModBERT takes as input a probabilistic representation of the genome where each locus is a probability distribution over A, C, G, T, M (5mC). The probabilities reflect the frequency of alleles for each SNP and the percent methylation of each CpG site. We show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, outperforming ab initio models and models pretrained on sequences without methylation. Furthermore, ModBERT demonstrated predictive power on prediction tasks in heldout donors, suggesting that ModBERT has learned associations of SNPs and 5mC with gene regulation. We also show that ModBERT may be extended to include additional base modifications. This work paves the way for in silico assessment of genetic variants and their epigenetic status in their prioritization for experimental validation.

title: Chromatin-informed inference of cell-type-specific regulatory programs in Alzheimer’s disease using single-cell multi-omics
authors: Jiahui Hou, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Hatice Osmanbeyoglu, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Computational inference of transcription factor (TF) regulatory programs from single-cell data remains challenging due to sparsity and the weak coupling between chromatin accessibility and gene expression. To address this, we develop a chromatin-informed multitask framework that integrates single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq data for cell-type-resolved TF activity inference. Our approach extends PSIONIC by combining pseudobulk aggregation with multitask learning across cell typeâ€“sample pairs, enabling robust estimation of TF activity while sharing information across contexts. We further improve regulatory specificity by incorporating ChIP-seqâ€“derived priors, replacing motif-based features with empirically informed TFâ€“gene regulatory potentials. Applied to Alzheimerâ€™s disease (AD) data, our framework recovers biologically coherent regulatory programs that distinguish neuronal and glial identities and identifies cell-type-specific TF activity changes across disease stages. These include known AD-associated regulators as well as novel candidate TFs, highlighting disease-specific regulatory rewiring. Overall, our method improves TFâ€“target inference through chromatin-informed priors and multitask learning, providing a scalable and generalizable framework for dissecting regulatory mechanisms in complex diseases.

title: Chorus: An Agentic Framework for Comparative Regulatory Genomics with Sequence-to-Function Oracles
authors: Dmitry Penzar, Vavilov Institute of General Genetics, Gubkin 3, 119991, Moscow, Russian Federation, Russia; Lorenzo Ruggeri, Department of Computer Science, University of Verona, Verona, 37134, VR, Italy, Italy; Rosalba Giugno, Department of Computer Science, University of Verona, Verona, 37134, VR, Italy, Italy; Luca Pinello, Harvard University, United States
abstract: "Sequence-to-function deep learning models â€”Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome, ChromBPNet, Sei, LegNetâ€” predict chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, histone modifications, gene expression, and splicing from DNA sequence across hundreds of human cell types. Yet each model inhabits its own ecosystem with unique dependencies, input requirements (2 kb to 1 Mb), output resolutions, and prediction formats. Cross-model comparison requires heroic engineering effort, leaving these tools underutilized. We present Chorus, a unified framework addressing these barriers through three innovations: a standardized oracle abstraction, a multi-layer analysis framework, and an agentic AI interface. Chorus treats each model as an ""oracle"" returning predictions for genomic coordinates or sequences. Each oracle runs in an isolated environment with automatic dependency management, yet all are accessed through a single Python API. Predictions across thousands of tracks are organized into regulatory layers with modality-specific scoring and quantile-based contextualization against empirical backgrounds. Integrated modules support causal variant prioritization from GWAS loci, cell-type discovery, saturation mutagenesis, and sequence engineering. Most transformatively, Chorus exposes its capabilities as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, letting AI agents orchestrate regulatory genomics from natural-language requests such as ""score rs12740374 across AlphaGenome, Borzoi, and Enformer in liver cell types and report convergent evidence."" The agent autonomously selects oracles, picks cell-type-matched tracks, runs reference and alternate predictions, and synthesizes multi-oracle evidence into an interactive report. This turns cross-oracle variant interpretation from a specialist engineering task into a conversational one, letting clinicians, biologists, and synthetic biologists use state-of-the-art models without code. Chorus is freely available at https://github.com/pinellolab/chorus."

title: FIREFate: Functional and Interpretable Regulatory Encoding of Fate determination
authors: Swapnil Keshari, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Zarifeh Rarani, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Akanksha Sachan, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Nicholas Pease, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Jingyu Fan, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Harinder Singh, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Jishnu Das, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Cell fate determination integrates gene regulatory programs with epigenetic signals to coordinate differentiation and functional specialization across tissues. Yet how fate decisions are encoded in regulatory programs, how these programs dynamically rewire during transitions, and whether fate bias can be detected prior to phenotypic divergence remain unresolved. Existing approaches are insufficient: GRN methods miss transition-driving dynamics, differential expression is univariate, ML models sacrifice interpretability, and co-expression frameworks cannot resolve causal regulation. We introduce FIREFate (Functional and Interpretable Regulatory Encoding of Fate determination), which integrates interpretable ML with mechanistic regulatory modeling through high-resolution static and dynamic GRNs to identify regulatory programs that define and drive cell states. Applied to primary human B cells, FIREFate resolves the bifurcation between plasmablast (PB) and germinal center (GC) fates, recovering canonical regulatorsâ€”PAX5, PRDM1, and IRF4â€”without prior knowledge, and identifying CREB3L2 as a central hub linking ER stress to PB commitment. Benchmarking against SCENIC+ confirms more compact, higher-specificity regulatory modules with improved mechanistic interpretability. To resolve dynamic regulation, FIREFate reconstructs time-resolved TF activity integrating expression, regulatory edge strength, and downstream regulatory force, uncovering sequential regulatory waves: a CREB3L2â€“RUNX2â€“PRDM1 activation cascade for PB commitment and a repression-dominated IRF4/NFKB1â€“PAX5 program locking in GC identity. Finally, perturbation-guided transfer learning predicts fate bias prior to phenotypic commitment, revealing GC-primed subsets within early activated B cells and identifying IKZF2 and RBPJ as episodically active regulators invisible to conventional analyses. FIREFate shifts cell fate inference from descriptive characterization to predictive, mechanistic resolution across biological systems.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Modeling Cellular State Transitions: An RNA Velocity–Guided Neural Stochastic Framework for Forward Simulation
authors: Bob Zhao, The Webb Schools, United States
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) can represent each cell as a high-dimensional gene expression vector and enables computation of RNA velocity, which estimates short- term directional change. However, existing methods primarily infer fate probabilities rather than simulate explicit future trajectories. In this project, I model cellular transitions as a stochastic process in gene expression space and develop an RNA velocityâ€“guided stochastic simulation framework to simulate forward evolution. Tran- sitions are proposed using local similarity and velocity alignment, and accepted via a Metropolisâ€“Hastings inspired criterion. Terminal states are treated as absorbing states. This approach generates explicit simulated trajectories from a single snapshot,shifting scRNA-seq analysis from static inference toward dynamic prediction of cellular evolution.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Modeling Macrophage Polarization in Wounds: A Heterogeneity Perspective
authors: Prateek Gupta, Purdue University, United States; Doraiswami Ramkrishna, Purdue University, United States
abstract: Macrophages are specialized immune cells with very high plasticity and extreme diversity. Equipped with super-sensing capabilities, they can rapidly sample their milieu and polarize into functionally distinct subsets. This work studies their remarkable heterogeneity through the lens of a population balance framework and shows how a distribution of cell states emerges from intracellular metabolic dynamics. Under the postulate that each macrophage cell purposefully allocates its limited internal resources to drive the correct metabolic pathway, we recover phenotypic heterogeneity even under a fixed cytokine stimulus. This addresses a fundamental question: although LPS/IFNÎ³ and IL4/IL13 are known to push macrophages toward opposing M1- and M2-like phenotypes, respectively, how do macrophages resolve conflicting cytokine cues in the wound milieu and adopt a phenotype? We further study the consequences of this postulate on the number densities of different macrophage subsets and show how they evolve as a wound resolves. We also demonstrate how macrophage populations use biochemical noise to their advantage and accelerate the process of wound healing. Finally, we reproduce experimental flow-cytometry trends, including the relaxation and convergence of FACS-sorted iNOS^low and iNOS^high macrophage subpopulations toward an overlapping distribution over time. The modeling framework presented herein is modular and extensible to any immune cell and can seamlessly integrate detailed immune profile data (e.g., scRNA-seq, flow cytometry etc.). Moving forward, such model features are desirable as we embrace the complexity of human disease in the single-cell era.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Exploring Resource Constraints for Modeling Pairwise Microbial Metabolic Interactions in the Hydra-associated microbes
authors: Natchapon Srinak, Research Group Medical Systems Biology, Institute of Experimental Medicine, Kiel University, Germany; Peter Deines, Institute for Zoology and Developmental Biology, Kiel University, Kiel, Germany, Germany; Christoph Kaleta, Research Group Medical Systems Biology, Institute of Experimental Medicine, Kiel University, Germany; Jan Taubenheim, Research Group Medical Systems Biology, Institute of Experimental Medicine, Kiel University, Germany
abstract: Microbe-microbe metabolic interactions are primary determinants of community composition and ecosystem function. Despite advances in omics technologies, resolving the mechanistic basis of these interactions remains a significant challenge. In this study, we combined experimental and computational approaches to investigate the interactions of the microbial community associated with Hydra. We conducted cell-free supernatant (CFS) experiments to characterize pairwise interactions and their impact on microbial growth.
