Our experimental results revealed that Curvibacter-CFS generally inhibited the growth of most taxa except Pelomonas, while Acidovorax-CFS consistently promoted the growth of several species, including Pseudomonas, Undibacteria, and Duganella. To elucidate the underlying metabolic mechanisms, we performed in metabolic modeling simulations of both CFS environments and pairwise microbial communities, implemented with metabolic models using classical stoichiometric and Resource Allocation Constraints (RACs). Stoichiometric Flux Balance Analysis (FBA) omits enzymatic capacity, potentially leading to inaccurate predictions of nutrient consumption and byproduct secretion. Models using RACs are more difficult to reconstruct and rely on more assumptions, leading to potentially wrong simulation prerequisites. Here we compare both modeling approaches and their capability to predict microbial interactions and to recapitulate growth rates from a defined experimental system. This study provides a foundational step toward more reliable mechanistic modeling of complex microbe-microbe interactions, bridging the gap between simplified metabolic flux and the biological phenotype.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: In silico comparison of three genome-scale models (GEMs) of Bacillus subtilis using Flux Balance Analysis (FBA)
authors: Gabriel Granados, Pontificia Universidad Javeriana, Colombia; Óscar Sánchez Pontificia Universidad Javeriana; César Vargas Colombian Agriculture Corporation (AGROSAVIA); Juan David Tibocha Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) are key tools for studying microbial metabolism through in silico simulations such as Flux Balance Analysis (FBA). Although several GEMs exist for Bacillus subtilis, they differ in structure, annotation quality, and predictive performance. This work presents the first curated repository compiling B. subtilis GEMs and introduces GEMcompare, a computational pipeline to prepare and compare metabolic models. Three GEMs (iYO844, iBB1018, and iBsu1147R) were evaluated through structural analysis, model quality assessment, FBA simulations under different carbon sources and comparisons with experiments from the literature. Additional comparisons included central carbon flux distributions and essential gene prediction. Also, a experimental validation in glucose, lactose and arabinose showed that models are useful to predict general in vitro behaviors but not precise ones. iYO844 provided the best predictions at higher glucose uptake rates, while iBB1018 showed the most conservative flux behavior, particularly in the TCA cycle. iBsu1147R exhibited better performance in essential gene prediction. Overall, this study enables researchers to find B. subtilis GEMs in a single place, compares three of them and establishes a comparison pipeline, and highlights the complementary strengths of existing GEMs for future systems biology and strain engineering applications.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Transcriptomic Profiling of Fanconi Anemia Subtypes Reveals Splicing and Expression Dysregulation
authors: Hua Tan, Kelly, United States; Shivatheja Soma, NIH, United States; Valer Gotea, NIH, United States; Frank Donovan, NIH, United States; Kinjal Bhadresha, NIH, United States; Oliva Alston, NIH, United States; Jeremy Amen, NIH, United States; Arleen Auerbach, The Rockefeller University, United States; Agata Smogorzewska, The Rockefeller University, United States; Laura Elnitski, NIH, United States; Settara Chandrasekharappa, NIH, United States
abstract: Fanconi anemia (FA) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous disorder caused by mutations in at least 23 genes within the DNA repair pathway. Beyond their established roles in maintaining genomic stability, the broader molecular consequences of FA gene deficiency remain incompletely understood. In this study, we performed comprehensive transcriptomic profiling of 189 cell lines to characterize both gene expression and alternative splicing dysregulation in FA-deficient cells across ten FA subtypes. Global analyses revealed that transcriptomic patterns can distinguish tissue types and experimental conditions, while also uncovering both shared and distinct molecular features across FA genetic subtypes. Restoration of FA gene function led to widespread changes in gene expression and splicing, highlighting coordinated yet partially independent regulatory layers. Differentially expressed and alternatively spliced genes converged on key biological processes, including cell cycle regulation, extracellular matrix (ECM) organization, and apoptosis, while also showing pathway-specific distinctions, with expression changes enriched in immune and inflammatory signaling and splicing alterations enriched in RNA processing. Notably, FA subtypes exhibited both common and exclusive transcriptomic signatures, suggesting diverse functional contributions to disease pathology. These findings indicate that FA deficiency disrupts cellular homeostasis through combined effects on transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation. Importantly, the results provide insight into potential therapeutic strategies, including targeting immune signaling, ECM remodeling, and splicing regulation. Overall, this study highlights the dual impact of gene expression and alternative splicing dysregulation in FA pathogenesis and offers a broader framework for understanding the molecular complexity of this disease.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Data selection significantly impacts automated reconstruction of genome-scale metabolic networks
authors: Blaine Bates, University of Virginia, United States; Jason Papin, University of Virginia, United States
abstract: Genome-scale reconstructions of metabolic networks are powerful tools for studying metabolism at a systems level. The process of generating reconstructions involves several steps (e.g., gene annotation, compiling a draft network, gap-filling, etc.), all of which rely heavily on prior genetic and/or biochemical data. This reconstruction data can be obtained from multiple sources, and each source has its own advantages and limitations which affect the reconstruction process; however, the impact of data selection on the quality of reconstructed networks has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we generated different sets of reconstruction data with varying levels of annotation accuracy or taxonomic coverage. We used each set of data to produce metabolic networks for several strains of bacteria. We compared these networks to manually curated ones for the same strains to assess reconstruction quality. Despite having different methods, two reconstruction tools, CarveMe and Reconstructor, perform similarly when they use the same reconstruction data. Additionally, while data with misannotated genes consistently worsened reconstruction quality, the magnitude of this impact varied considerably from one organism to another. Finally, adjusting which species were represented in the reconstruction data significantly affected reconstruction. When the data included species that were closer to the target organism, both precision and recall improved. Conversely, greater taxonomic coverage had little impact on recall and decreased precision. These results emphasize the importance of data selection and demonstrate principles to improve automated reconstruction of metabolic networks.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Spatiotemporal modeling of developmental architecture guides engineering scalable hPSC-derived esophageal mucosa.
authors: Sadhana Gaddam, Program in Epithelial Biology, Stanford University, United States; Ying Yang, Program in Epithelial Biology, Stanford University, United States; Ian Glass, Birth Defects Lab, University of Washington, United States; Anthony Oro, Program in Epithelial Biology, Stanford University, United States
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived tissue engineering is a promising approach for patient-specific cell therapies, genetic diseases, and tumor pathogenesis and helps better understanding how cells coordinate at the tissue level through spatial organization and cell-cell signaling. We previously established a scalable manufacturing protocol for an ectoderm-derived stratified epithelium for cell replacement therapy but there is a clinical need to manufacture tissue replacements for endodermal-derived tissues like the esophagus. Even though endoderm-derived esophageal epithelium shares broadly similar structure to ectoderm-derived cells the signaling interactions differ, making manufacturing difficult. To bridge this gap, here we integrate single-cell and spatial profiling to build a spatiotemporal, multi-omics atlas of human esophageal development. This atlas delineates the evolving cellular composition of the developing esophageal epithelium and its surrounding stroma. We then use a machine-learning strategy to infer and rank combinations of candidate human developmental signals to derive in vitro specification of esophageal basal progenitors from pluripotent stem cells. This framework helps accelerate human tissue manufacturing to support regenerative therapies, genetic defects, and chronic wounds. Because esophageal mucosa stability depends on the local stromal niche, we have extended our work to focus on understanding the tissue architecture at the gastroesophageal junction using spatial transcriptomics. This work will help identify how epithelial and stromal niches align in this junction and how we can harness this information to investigate disease states such as Barrettâ€™s esophagus and other metaplastic condition associated with an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Integration of aged brain multi-omics reveals cross-system mechanisms underlying Alzheimer’s disease heterogeneity
authors: Ricardo Vialle, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Lucas Scheidemantel, Universidade Federal do Parana, Brazil; Katia de Paiva Lopes, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Chris Gaiteri, SUNY Upstate Medical University, United States; Vilas Menon, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Philip De Jager, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Julie Schneider, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Aron Buchman, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Yanling Wang, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Shinya Tasaki, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Roberto Raittz, Universidade Federal do Parana, Brazil; David Bennett, Rush University Medical Center, United States
abstract: The molecular correlates of Alzheimerâ€™s disease (AD) are increasingly being defined by omics. Yet, the findings from different data types or cohorts are often difficult to reconcile. Collecting multiple omics from the same individuals allows a comprehensive view of disease-related molecular mechanisms, while addressing conflicting findings derived from single omics. Such same-sample multi-omics can reveal, for instance, when changes observed in the transcriptome share distinct but coordinated signals in epigenetics and proteomics, relationships otherwise unclear. Here, we apply a data-driven multi-omic framework to integrate epigenomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and cell-type-specific population data from up to 1,358 aged human brain samples from the Religious Orders Study (ROS) and Rush Memory and Aging Project (MAP). We demonstrate the existence of sprawling cross-omics cross-system biological factors that also relate to AD phenotypes. The strongest AD-associated factor (factor 8) involved elevated immune activity at the epigenetic level, decreased expression of heat shock genes in the transcriptome, and disrupted energy metabolism and cytoskeletal dynamics in the proteome. We also showed immune-related factors (factors 2 and 3) with discordant enrichments, reflecting reactive-like glial subpopulations and protective contributions from surveillance microglia. Finally, unsupervised clustering of participants revealed eleven molecular subtypes of the aging brain, including three clusters strongly associated with AD but displaying distinct molecular signatures and phenotypic characteristics. Our findings provide a comprehensive map of molecular mechanisms underlying AD heterogeneity, highlighting the complex role of neuroinflammatory processes, and yielding potential novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets for precision medicine approaches to AD treatment.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Thermodynamic modelling of multimeric protein complexes in yeast
authors: Xavier Castellanos-Girouard, Wellcome Sanger Institute, United Kingdom; Stephen Michnick, Université de Montréal, Canada; Adrian Serohijos, Université de Montréal, Canada
abstract: Cells are organized into structured networks of functionally interdependent biomolecules. These networks are integrators of genetic information and environmental context, shaping cellular phenotype. Therefore, accurate models of biological networks and their dynamics is key to understanding the molecular basis of genotype-phenotype relationships. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are among the most comprehensively mapped biological networks, benefiting from large-scale experimental screens across model organisms. These datasets have subsequently driven the construction of theoretical kinetic and thermodynamic models of PPI networks. Advances in quantitative mass spectrometry have enabled the measurement of interaction stoichiometry (a ratio analogous to fraction of protein bound in a complex). However, no comprehensive kinetic models to date have incorporated this variable. We previously used measurements of interaction stoichiometry to generate the first proteome-wide estimation of dissociation constants (Kd). Building on this foundation, we now integrate interaction stoichiometry, total protein abundances, and known subunit stoichiometries to estimate intracellular numbers of multimeric protein complexes, free (unbound) protein abundance, and effective equilibrium constants (Kds) for multimeric complexes in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We find reasonable concordance between our estimates of complex abundances and those from low-throughput experiments in the literature. Further, building on previous models of reversible heterodimeric PPI networks, we construct a thermodynamic model of the yeast protein interactome to evaluate how perturbations in specific protein abundances propagate through neighbouring complexes. Finally, we systematically investigate whether gene pairs demonstrating high network sensitivity to abundance changes also exhibit genetic interactions.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Identifying translatable axes of drug resistance in NSCLC via integration of patient and PDX single-cell transcriptomics
authors: Paulina Eberts, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, United States; Zachary Rogers, Massachusetts Institute of Technology,; Toshio Fujino, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School,; J. Christopher Love, Massachusetts Institute of Technology,; Aaron Hata, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School,; Douglas Lauffenburger, Massachusetts Institute of Technology,
abstract: Understanding drug resistance in NSCLC is critical for improving patient outcomes; however, the sparsity of single-cell data from patients on treatment makes it difficult to ascertain cellular state transitions at this resolution. Mechanistic insights therefore rely on patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, which lack the complex cues present in patients. Discerning which PDX-derived phenotypes reflect patient biology versus model-specific artifacts remains a fundamental challenge limiting translational utility. Here we employed our TransComp-R (Translatable Components Regression) framework to identify gene covariance structures conserved between patient and PDX tumor cells. We integrated scRNA-seq data from TKI-treated patients at three timepoints (treatment-naive, minimal residual disease (MRD), progressive disease) with snRNA-seq data from seven PDX models collected at analogous stages. Differentially expressed genes distinguishing patient treatment populations were used to construct PDX-derived principal components at the pseudobulk level. Patient samples were projected into the PDX PC spaces to identify components along which treatment groups separated in both systems with consistent directionality. Principal components meeting these criteria, reflecting shared gene covariance structures, were designated translatable axes, and the proportion of original patient variance preserved along these axes after projection was used to approximate the amount translatable information retained by each model. Projecting the single-cell PDX data along the translatable axes resolved subpopulations and identified treatment-relevant transcriptional programs with conserved covariance across patients and models. This framework bridges PDX and patient biology to identify the transcriptional transition into drug resistance, nominating perturbation candidates and predicting which PDX-derived findings are poised to translate clinically.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: A Generative Model for the Synthesizing of Single-Cell Proteomic Datasets for Dynamic Modeling of Cell Signaling Pathways.
authors: Carolina Ribeiro, UNICAMP, Brazil; Cristiano Campos, UNICAMP, Brazil; Marcelo Reis, UNICAMP, Brazil
abstract: Motivation Biological processes are dynamic and time-resolved cellular profiling is essential for understanding changes in cell states, signaling pathways and regulatory mechanisms during differentiation, stimulus response, and disease progression. While time-series gene expression data provide rich insights into these dynamics, the scarcity of comprehensive protein-level perturbation data limits systems-level modeling. In particular, single-cell proteomic measurements are often destructive and constrained in depth and coverage, hindering temporal reconstruction and the availability of longitudinal ground-truth datasets for robust algorithm evaluation. Results We introduce a reusable pipeline for generating synthetic single-cell proteomic (scProteomic) datasets from ODE-based biochemical models. The pipeline provides modular components for simulating signaling dynamics through numerical integration, enabling controlled variability across cell lines and treatments through randomized initial conditions and parameters. Using four ODE-based signaling models (EGFR, IL-6, Insulin, and MAPK), we generated benchmark datasets whose global statistical properties, including mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, skewness, and kurtosis, closely matched those of the DREAM experimental dataset, with low Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics and moderate Wasserstein distances (0.2–0.6). Evaluation was performed using Ridge regression and Random Forest models under static, temporal, and generalization settings, including unseen cell lines and treatment conditions. The synthetic datasets produced prediction tasks of comparable or greater difficulty than the DREAM dataset. Comparison against known ground-truth trajectories demonstrates the utility of the framework for simulating realistic scProteomic time series and systematically benchmarking modeling strategies. Availability and Implementation The pipeline is freely available at https://github.com/cristiano-campos/scProteomics-GenerativeModel Contact c184298@dac.unicamp.br, msreis@unicamp.br

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Temporal multi-omics modeling resolves sex-specific regulatory mechanisms governing cardiac metabolic adaptation to endurance exercise
authors: Blake B. Rasmussen, University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio, TX, United States; Mary Anne S. Amper, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Matthew Wolf, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Charlottesville, VA, United States; Mital Vasoya, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Nasim Bararpour, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Navid Zebarjadi, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Nikolai G. Vetr, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Roxanne Chiu, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Si Wu, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Venugopalan D. Nair, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Yongchao Ge, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Krista M. Hennig, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Martin J. Walsh, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Michael P Snyder, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Stephen B Montgomery, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Stuart C. Sealfon, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; William E Kraus, Duke University, Durham, NC, United States; Zhen Yan, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Charlottesville, VA, United States; Euan Ashley, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Matthew T. Wheeler, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Daniel H. Katz, Division of Computational Biology, Department of Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Bingqing Zhao, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Joyce Njoroge, Stanford University, Stanford CA, United States; Samuel Montalvo, Stanford University, Stanford CA, United States; Malene E. Lindholm, Stanford University, Stanford CA, United States; Sasha Gladkikh, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Gregory R. Smith, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Gina Many, Biological Sciences Division, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, United States; David Jimenez-Morales, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Hasmik Keshishian, Proteomics Platform, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, United States; Nicole R. Gay, 23and ME, Sunnyvale, CA, United States; Pauline Brochet, Stanford University, Stanford CA, United States; Chia-Jui Hung, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Christopher A. Jin, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Clarisa Chavez, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Daniel Nachun, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Elena Zaslavsky, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; German Nudelman, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Hanna Pincas, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City, NY, United States; Jose Juan Almagro Armenteros, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Kevin S Smith, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States
abstract: Endurance exercise improves cardiac metabolism and reduces cardiovascular risk, yet the molecular programs that drive cardioprotection remain incompletely understood. Here, we applied a systems biology approach to the MoTrPAC rat cardiac dataset, integrating eight omic layers measured after 1-8 weeks of endurance training in males and females. Using a temporal multi-omic factor analysis framework (MOFA/MEFISTO) that models time as a continuous covariate, we identified 7 latent factors capturing coordinated temporal molecular variation across multi-omic layers. Factor 2 emerged as the most robust multi-omic signature (transcript-protein weight correlation r=0.49, pâ‰¤2.2e-16). This sex-consistent factor revealed a progressive shift toward enhanced glycolysis and reduced lipid transport, correlating with systemic VO2max improvements (r>0.8 in both sexes). Conversely, Factor 1 identified an early sex-divergent epigenetic signal. Females exhibit chromatin closure at 1w while males show opening at 4w (Pâ‰¤0.05) at the promoters of critical glucose-glycogen regulators (Pdk4, Ppp1r3d, Ppara). Epigenetic motif analysis identified the metabolic transcription factor KLF15 as the top candidate driver of this divergence. Furthermore, Factor 6-associated proteins were enriched in fatty-acid (FA) metabolism (FDRâ‰¤0.05), with a maximal expression at 2w in males, but 4w peak in females. Kinase enrichment confirmed these divergent strategies through GYS1 regulation, where male-specific dephosphorylation at 2w (Factor 7) promotes its glycogen storage function. These results identify a temporal divergence in metabolic substrate preference, where early female adaptation is characterized by oxygen-efficient glucose utilization while males favor fastest FA adaptation. Ultimately, this analysis establishes a cross-omic mechanistic chain linking early epigenetic regulation to downstream signaling and proteomic dynamics.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Percolation and lifestyle transition in microbial metabolism
authors: Rydberg Supo, Columbia University, United States; Dennis Vitkup, Columbia University, United States
abstract: Microbial species exhibit a remarkable diversity in their metabolic properties, genome composition, and ecological distribution. However, it is currently not well understood how the structure of metabolic networks defines and reflects the lifestyle and phenotypic properties of diverse bacterial species across the tree of life. By analyzing thousands of genome-scale metabolic models of bacteria, we found a percolation-like transition characterized by a sharp increase in metabolic network functional connectivity. This transition â€“ primarily associated with the completion of central carbon metabolism and the TCA cycle â€“ occurs at a threshold of approximately 800 metabolic reactions or about 2000 protein-coding genes. Strikingly, species with metabolic network sizes below the transition are typically obligate symbionts, while species above it, are predominantly free-living generalists. The observed percolation transition is also reflected in multiple other genomic properties, such as a substantial decrease in the fraction of regulatory genes below the transition and increased evolvability for new metabolic phenotypes above the transition. Furthermore, we found that the distribution of bacterial genome sizes from unbiased environmental metagenomic sequencing also reveals two regimes corresponding to the observed transition. Overall, our work identifies two qualitatively different regimes in microbial metabolism and lifestyles, characterized by distinct structural and functional properties of their metabolic networks.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Learning HLA ligand regulation via link prediction in multilayer biological networks
authors: Guangyuan Li, University of Notre Dame, United States; Ian Mersich, University of Notre Dame, United States; Aktar Ali, University of Notre Dame, United States; Xin Lu, University of Notre Dame, United States
abstract: Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) presents a dynamic snapshot of cellular proteome as short peptides on the cell surface, enabling T cell-mediated immune surveillance and forming the basis of T cell-based immunotherapies, including TCR-T and CAR-T. Despite its central role, the upstream mechanisms governing HLA ligand density remain poorly understood. Inspired by Gene Regulatory Network (GRN), we hypothesize that integrating HLA ligand presentation with its source genes and upstream regulators will enable quantitative modeling of this complex system, reveal key post-translational mechanisms, and inform therapeutic strategies to modulate antigen presentation. To this end, we developed the Ligand Regulatory Network (LRN) framework that integrates context-specific transcriptomic data with prior-curated large-scale cancer immunopeptidomic data to capture empirically derived gene-ligand relationships. We propose a three-layer approach by first constructing transcription factor-gene and kinase-substrate networks using generalized linear models, followed by extending network edge weights informed by immunopeptidomic evidence to account for HLA presentation dynamics, and finally training a graph neural network on the prior graph, formulated as a link prediction task to infer regulatory strength between upstream regulators and HLA ligands. Applied to 12 RNA-Seq data from KRAS G12D pancreatic cancer samples, the model achieved 92.3% accuracy on the validation set and 91.0% accuracy on independent test datasets. Notably, LRN identified druggable targets, including Cdk4, Cdk6 and Ezh2, whose inhibition is associated with increased presentation of G12D derived neoantigen, highlighting its potential for prioritizing pharmacological targets. Overall, we envision LRN will be broadly applicable to any cancer transcriptomic datasets to uncover novel antigen presentation mechanisms and guide immunotherapeutic intervention strategies.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: ChatGEM: An Agentic System for In Silico Genome-Scale Metabolic Engineering
authors: August George, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Niaz Bahar Chowdhury, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Paul Rigor, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Sumit Purohit, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Abby Jerger, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Angela Cintolesi, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Jaydeep Bardhan, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States
abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) are widely used tools for rational metabolic engineering but often require significant programming expertise, limiting their use by experimental researchers. To address this challenge, we present ChatGEM, an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot and coding agent that converts natural-language instructions into executable programs for GEMs. ChatGEM is guided by expert-curated workflow examples, supporting flux balance analysis (FBA) for tasks such as predicting growth rates and production fluxes. Advanced approaches including OptKnock (growth-coupled strain design), OptMDFPathway (thermodynamically constrained pathway optimization), and ecGEM (enzyme-constrained modeling) are also supported. Using Pseudomonas putida as a case study, ChatGEM autonomously executed multi-step workflows involving growth maximization, succinate production, targeted reaction deletions, and succinate production re-evaluation â€“ with significantly reduced programming time required. In follow-up case studies, ChatGEM successfully designed a strain of Escherichia coli for succinate overproduction and predicted absolute proteomics and metabolomics that support a growth phenotype of Pseudomonas putida. Overall, this work demonstrates that natural language interfaces and AI coding agents can accelerate and democratize in silico metabolic engineering tasks.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Predicting Receptor-Transcriptional Signaling Paths via Hopfield Backpropagation: with AXL receptor activated induced Preeclampsia
authors: Charlie Chou, Brigham Young University, United States
abstract: Axl (Tyrosine-protein kinase) receptor is an oncogenic gene that plays a pivotal role in pregnancy disease. Axl is directly associated with the development of preeclampsia, the most prevalent mid-gestation disease that can lead to seizure and miscarriage. In our previous research with a mouse model, we discovered that activation of the Axl receptor led to the development of symptoms of preeclampsia with high blood pressure and proteinuria, and our primary bulk RNA-seq analysis shows that Axl-induced preeclampsia does not possess the gene signature of canonical preeclampsia. To illustrate how the activation of a receptor can lead to phenotypical observation, we built a bioinformatic framework where we emulate every possible receptor-to-transcriptional factor (TF) and transcriptional factor-to-differentially expressed gene (DEG) path. Different from conventional pathways, our algorithm hypothesizes signaling transmission at the path level where the proteins are connected in a linear fashion to build a comprehensive narrative. Our resource, Threads, is a 42GB database that stores all possible receptor-to-TF paths. Via the permutation test, we can enrich the bulk RNA-seq DEGs against it. Afterward, we can simulate the signal propagation effects based on existing data to quantify literature alignment. By identifying high literature-logical alignment paths, we can effectively and systematically search through all possible signaling paths and direct our focus to the major causal relationships for investigation. We have identified 2 driver signaling axes and 1 passenger axis that has profound implications in Axl-induced preeclampsia.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Mechanistic ODE Modeling of MAPK/AKT Signaling Reveals Scheduling-Dependent Control of Persister Dynamics in BRAF-Mutant Melanoma
authors: Ethan Wang, Independent Researcher, United States; Aayan Alwani, Independent Researcher, United States
abstract: "Melanoma relapse is frequently associated with drug-tolerant persister cells, rare tumor subpopulations that survive targeted therapy through adaptive signaling rather than stable genetic resistance. Because these cells remain dependent on MAPK and RTK/AKT signaling, combination strategies that disrupt both pathways may improve control of drug-tolerant populations. Here, we present a mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based model to investigate treatment scheduling strategies combining a PROTAC degrader targeting mutant BRAF with an RTK inhibitor. The model integrates MAPK and AKT signaling dynamics, downstream transcriptional programs, and tumor population behavior, with drug action represented through two-compartment pharmacokinetics, bolus dosing, and Hill-type pharmacodynamics. Treatment performance was evaluated using a persister index (PI) together with a composite optimization score (COS) that balances persister burden and drug exposure. Screening across a large set of candidate regimens identified scheduling strategies that reduce simulated persister populations relative to baseline conditions. Regimens incorporating early PROTAC exposure followed by sustained RTK inhibition achieved the largest reductions in PI while maintaining lower modeled toxicity penalties. Additional analysis across simulated tumor phenotypes revealed variability in optimal schedules, reflecting differences in underlying signaling dynamics. Overall, this framework demonstrates that, within a mechanistic modeling context, treatment scheduling can substantially influence persister dynamics and comparative performance metrics. These results provide a basis for exploring combination treatment strategies and generating hypotheses for future experimental validation of scheduling-based approaches to targeting melanoma persister cells. "

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: LitGraph: Leveraging large language models to derive high-value knowledge graphs from literature
authors: Tyler Beck, National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, NIH, United States; Christine Colvis, National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, NIH, United States
abstract: Over the past several years, large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly important for data science projects because of the power and ubiquity of their use. The ability to analyze and accurately summarize free text is a particular strength for models of this type, and this has created an opportunity to modernize the typical biomedical publishing pipeline. The biomedical literature is an incredible resource for researchers, but it is anything but AI-ready. To this end, NCATS created the LitGraph program with the goal of building the transformation to graphs from literature into the process that researchers already use to share their outcomes. LitGraph allows researchers to derive high-level knowledge assertions from the free text of research abstracts into a convenient and sharable knowledge graph format which follows well-established standards such as the Biolink ontological framework, then presents these assertions to the researcher for curation to ensure accuracy. Future work on this program will expand the corpus of publications that LitGraph supports to include many rare disease-focused publications found on PubMed, and will automatically generate a publication-quality graphical abstract for use by the researcher and on webpages associated with the work. The knowledge generated by LitGraph will also be made available to data scientists to build tools for hypothesis generation and other use cases where highly-accurate publication-based knowledge graphs can help bring more treatments to all people more quickly.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: An AI-Powered Trisomy 21 Research Assistant
authors: Sutanu Nandi, Department of Pharmacology, University of Colorado AnschutzMedical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Zenitha Sundararajan, Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome, University ofColorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Marc Subirana-Granés, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University ofColorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Milton Pividori, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University ofColorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Kelly D. Sullivan, Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome, University ofColorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Matthew D. Galbraith, Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome, University ofColorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; James C Costello, Department of Pharmacology, University of Colorado AnschutzMedical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States
abstract: Background/Motivation: Down syndrome (Trisomy 2; T211) affects multiple biological systems, causing co-occurring conditions including congenital heart defects, immune dysfunction, thyroid disorders, leukaemia, and early-onset Alzheimer's disease. With over 34,000 PubMed-indexed publications as of early 2026, keeping pace with this literature is an ongoing challenge. General-purpose large language models are trained on broad corpora and may not reflect peer-reviewed Down syndrome evidence. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses this by grounding responses in a curated corpus at query time. However, standard RAG implementations treat all manuscript sections equally, allowing introductory background to rank as highly as Results sections reporting primary experimental findings. Method: We developed the T21 Research Assistant, a domain-specific, section-aware multi-agent RAG system that retrieves information exclusively from 363 NIH INCLUDE (Investigation of Co-occurring conditions across the Lifespan to Understand Down syndromE) project publications, ranks retrieved chunks by section priority, and generates structured responses with inline citations. The pipeline integrates retrieval, reranking, synthesis, citation checking, safety monitoring, and quality review using open-source NVIDIA Nemotron models. Results: Evaluated against a 12-question expert-written benchmark using BERTScore, semantic similarity, UMAP-based retrieval visualization, and a blinded expert preference survey (COMIRB No. 26-0596), the system achieved a BERTScore F1 of 0.76 Â± 0.06 and semantic similarity of 0.69 Â± 0.08, performing comparably to or better than proprietary models, with statistically significant improvements in specific metrics (one-sided Wilcoxon test, p Significance: The T21 Research Assistant provides the Down syndrome research community with a freely accessible, evidence-grounded tool for querying primary literature, available at https://bioinformatics.cuanschutz.edu/t21-res-assi/.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Forecasting Clinical Risk from Textual Time Series: Structuring Narratives for Temporal AI in Healthcare
authors: Sayantan Kumar, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes on Health, United States; Shahriar Noroozizadeh, Machine Learning Department, School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA, United States; Jeremy C. Weiss, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes on Health, United States
abstract: Clinical case reports encode temporal patient trajectories that are often underexploited by traditional machine learning methods relying on structured data. In this work, we introduce the forecasting problem from textual time series, where timestamped clinical findings---extracted via an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline---serve as the primary input for prediction. We systematically evaluate a diverse suite of models, including fine-tuned decoder-based large language models and encoder-based transformers, on tasks of event occurrence prediction, temporal ordering, and survival analysis. Our experiments reveal that encoder-based models consistently achieve higher F1 scores and superior temporal concordance for short- and long-horizon event forecasting, while fine-tuned masking approaches enhance ranking performance. In contrast, instruction-tuned decoder models demonstrate a relative advantage in survival analysis, especially in early prognosis settings. Our sensitivity analyses further demonstrate the importance of time ordering, which requires clinical time series construction, as compared to text ordering, the format of the text inputs that LLMs are classically trained on. This highlights the additional benefit that can be ascertained from time-ordered corpora, with implications for temporal tasks in the era of widespread LLM use.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: LLM-Based Agentic Workflow for Large-Scale Extraction of Glycan Structure Terms and Biomarker Associations from Biomedical Literature
authors: Jeet Vora, The George Washington University, United States; Cyrus Au Yeung, The George Washington University, United States; Maria Kim, The George Washington University, United States; Raja Mazumder, The George Washington University, United States
abstract: Aberrant glycosylation patterns are hallmarks of numerous disease states, particularly cancer, yet systematic cataloging of glycan biomarkers has been hindered by inconsistent nomenclature across publications. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new avenues for large-scale structured knowledge extraction from biomedical literature. Building on a previously established manually curated Glycan Structure Dictionary (GSD) designed to harmonize glycan names and synonyms, we developed an LLM-based agentic workflow to expand this resource and systematically associate glycan structures with functional and clinical roles, including disease-biomarker status. The workflow extracts and organizes biomarker evidence from glycobiology publications, enforcing sentence-level citation grounding for each claim. A dedicated post-extraction validation module filters out unsupported or inaccurate entries. Extracted entities are mapped to established biomedical ontologies and reference databases, including the GSD, Disease Ontology, Uberon, UniProtKB, and Cellosaurus via retrieval-augmented generation. When applied to 4,787 PubMed abstracts identified through targeted keyword queries, the workflow yielded 1,578 unique glycan structure terms and 1,441 annotated biomarker associations that conform to the BiomarkerKB data model (https://biomarkerkb.org). The results demonstrate that structured biomedical data can be extracted with high precision using a mid-sized open-weight model through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, and that rigorous post hoc validation effectively adapts general-purpose LLMs to domain-specific curation tasks. The curated glycan structure term list is publicly accessible via the GlyGen Wiki (https://wiki.glygen.org/Glycan_Structure_Dictionary_v2), and biomarker associations are integrated into BiomarkerKB, addressing a critical gap in glycobiology and biomarker research, thereby enabling downstream discovery and clinical translation.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: BV-BRC Literature RAG: Scalable Structured Knowledge Extraction and Hypothesis Generation for Infectious Disease Research
authors: Ozan Gokdemir, Consortium for Advanced Science and Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637, USA, United States; Clark Cucinell, Consortium for Advanced Science and Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637, USA, United States; Andreas Wilke, Consortium for Advanced Science and Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637, USA, United States; James Davis, Consortium for Advanced Science and Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637, USA, United States; Maulik Shukla, Consortium for Advanced Science and Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637, USA, United States
abstract: The explosive growth of biomedical literature has created a critical bottleneck in transforming unstructured knowledge into actionable insights for infectious disease research. Within the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center, this challenge is particularly acute given the need to continuously integrate knowledge extracted from the latest scientific literature with large-scale pathogen genomic data. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual grounding of Large Language Models (LLMs), its application at the scale of millions of scientific articles, remains dependent on tremendous computational resources and manual metadata labeling efforts. We present a scalable Literature RAG framework integrated into BV-BRC that combines high-performance computing (HPC) with domain-adapted retrieval and generation strategies to enable structured knowledge extraction, hypothesis generation, and continuous knowledgebase enrichment. Open-access publications from PubMed Central are indexed into a vector database using a high-throughput document parsing pipeline, followed by fine-tuning of a query-aware encoder to improve retrieval accuracy for pathogen-specific queries. A straightforward user interface allows researchers to specify organism scope, data types of interest (e.g., hostâ€“pathogen interactions, sequence features, antimicrobial resistance phenotypes), and desired output formats. For each user query, the system retrieves the most semantically relevant document fragments from tens of millions of candidates. It then generates structured outputs, such as tables and machine-readable records, with explicit provenance and literature references. This enables dynamic and precise population and expansion of BV-BRC knowledgebase while minimizing manual curation effort. We demonstrate the framework on priority pathogens through a prototype for literature-informed viral host-protein interaction (HPI) discovery. By integrating retrieved evidence in a multi-strategy generation pipeline, the system both consolidates existing knowledge and generated novel, testable viral-host protein-protein interaction hypotheses. Built on scalable HPC infrastructure capable of indexing and querying millions of articles, this framework supports continuous knowledge integration tightly coupled with BV-BRC genomic data, analysis services, and user workflows. Beyond HPI discovery, it enables extensible applications such as mining sequence determinants of pathogenicity and linking genotypes to antimicrobial resistance phenotypes. By bridging large-scale literature mining with structured knowledge extraction and automated knowledgebase population, this work reduces the cost of manual curation while accelerating data-driven discovery and hypothesis generation across the BV-BRC ecosystem.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Reconstruction Of Spatial Expression Topologies Through Alignment via Fused Gromov–Wasserstein Optimal Transport
authors: Bryan Cheng, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory/Great Neck South High School, United States; Austin Jin, Tulane University/Great Neck South High School, United States
abstract: Model organism atlases provide rich cell-type annotation of spatial tissue organization, yet transferring this knowledge to unannotated human data requires aligning transcriptomes across species â€” a problem existing tools cannot solve. Batch-correction methods discard spatial coordinates entirely, while within-species spatial methods offer no inter-species capacity. We present ROSETTA (Reconstruction Of Spatial Expression Topologies Through Alignment), which frames cross-species alignment as a structured optimal transport problem: Fused Gromovâ€“Wasserstein (FGW) simultaneously matches feature similarity and spatial geometry, exploiting the fact that tissue topology â€” how cell types arrange into functional domains â€” is conserved across species even where orthologous gene expression diverges. ROSETTA learns spatially-informed spot embeddings via a self-supervised position-aware GNN (CHISEL), aligns species through a shared projection head with joint BatchNorm and MMD regularization (BRIDGE), discovers conserved gene programs via joint NMF (COMPASS), and transfers annotations with conformal prediction uncertainty (ATLAS). Evaluated on three humanâ€“mouse tissue pairs and a held-out mouseâ€“zebrafish brain pair, ROSETTA achieved mean class ARI = 0.420 Â± 0.148 (95% CI: [0.347, 0.492]) across 15 random seeds â€” 210Ã— above the permutation null and significantly above all baselines including Harmony (0.061), Scanorama (0.030), and SAMap (0.210) (Welch's t, all p

title: Design and validation of a Xenium spatial transcriptomics viral panel for virome profiling in Sjögren’s Syndrome
authors: Federica Bichicchi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Natalie Atyeo, National Institutes of Health, United States; Danny Yi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Jay Chiorini, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: glands, leading to severe dryness and systemic complications. While its exact cause remains unknown, genetic predisposition and environmental triggers are thought to contribute to disease onset and progression. Several viruses are known to infect salivary gland cells, and emerging evidence suggests that persistent infections may drive immune dysregulation and chronic inflammation in SjD. However, the specific viruses involved and their impact on disease pathology remain unclear. To address this, we developed and validated a spatial transcriptomics viral probe panel. We implemented a computational pipeline to retrieve viral genomes, perform multiple sequence alignment, and quantify sequence conservation using normalized Shannon entropy. Conserved regions were selected to guide probe design across genomes with varying variability, resulting in a panel of 258 viral targets. For experimental validation, representative viral fragments were cloned into plasmids and embedded in tissue microarrays (TMAs) enabling controlled benchmarking of probe performance within a Xenium spatial transcriptomics framework. Control experiments demonstrated robust detection of viral and host transcripts with consistent signal across replicated cores. Integration of probe-level expression with known ground truth enabled quantitative assessment of sensitivity and specificity, revealing strong performance for targets and identifying potential cross-reactivity in variable genomes. This study establishes a scalable framework for the design and validation of spatial viral panels, supporting accurate virome profiling in salivary gland tissues. Future work will apply this approach to SjD patient samples to investigate virusâ€“host interactions and their role in disease pathogenesis

title: Spatial Profiling Reveals Significant Tumor-Border Immune Differences Across Multiple Cancer Types
authors: Leia Huang, Rancho Bernardo High School, United States
abstract: The tumor-border is an invasive belt which defines the boundary between malignant and adjacent healthy tissue; understanding the location of the tumor-border is important for defining patient prognosis, recurrence rate, achieving maximal survival and quality-of-life. Although the tumor-border is essential for understanding the tumor microenvironment, definitions of the tumor boundary remain unclear, requiring further study using quantitative approaches. H-Plot, a novel graph-based spatial-profiling plot, allows researchers to analyze immune-cell infiltration using an empirically defined tumor-border. H-Plot assigns each cell a spatial layer index relative to the tumor boundary using k-hop traversal of a Delaunay cell graph constructed from H&E WSIs, without requiring manual annotation. The algorithm compares the proportion of immune-cell infiltration with distance from the tumor border. A dataset of 1,500+ pretreatment cases was obtained from TCGA, including BRCA, STAD, UCEC, CESC, and CRC repositories. Using an image analysis platform, researchers classified cells into various cell subtypes. This study revealed that immune-cell tumor stromal infiltration differs most significantly near the tumor-border across multiple cancer types. We observed that group-level differences reached peak statistical significance within approximately 0 to 275 Î¼m toward the tumor core, with p-values as low as 10^-33 across multiple cancer types. These findings support the tumor-border as a key spatial compartment for the evaluation of different immune microenvironment states across various cancer types. Furthermore, this study may lead to a biologically driven method for tumor-border identification, leading to a better understanding of oncological studies for future developments of cancer immunotherapies.

title: Hypothesis-Driven Analysis of Gut Microbiome in Subclinical ASCVD
authors: Shreya Chindepalli, Duke University, United States; Anita Shlesinger, Duke University, United States; Joshua Granek, Duke University, United States; Francois Haddad, Stanford University, United States; Jessilyn Dunn, Duke University, United States
abstract: Host-microbe interactions contribute to pathways relevant to atherosclerosis pathogenesis, including lipid metabolism, bile acid metabolism, and vascular inflammation. Alterations in human gut microbial composition have been reported in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), though evidence in early, subclinical stages remains limited. Subclinical ASCVD is characterized by measurable plaque burden prior to onset of symptomatic cardiovascular disease. Studying this stage enables investigation of biological processes associated with disease development. This study examines associations between gut microbiome taxonomic composition and subclinical ASCVD. Stool metagenomic sequencing data from 485 samples across 136 participants (68 with subclinical ASCVD, defined as coronary artery calcium score > 100; 68 matched controls with no coronary artery calcium) was obtained from the Project Baseline Health Study. Participants were propensity-matched on age, sex, race, ethnicity, BMI, hypertension, ASCVD risk score, and type 2 diabetes status. Species-level taxonomic profiles were generated using MetaPhlAn v4. Based on published findings linking specific gut taxa to ASCVD, four genera were selected for prespecified hypothesis-testing: Collinsella, Roseburia, Eubacterium, and Streptococcus. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with multiple testing correction identified higher relative abundance of genera Collinsella and Roseburia in the subclinical ASCVD group. Species-level tests identified three taxa, Eubacterium ventriosum, Eubacterium ramulus, and Streptococcus gordonii, as significantly associated with subclinical ASCVD status after multiple testing correction. These findings suggest that some microbial associations with ASCVD reported in the literature are also detectable in subclinical ASCVD. This work represents an initial hypothesis-testing analysis within an ongoing investigation of this longitudinal data from the Project Baseline Health Study cohort.

title: Therapeutic Target Discovery for Rare Diseases via Machine Learning Integrating GWAS and TWAS
authors: Satoko Namba, Nagoya University, Japan; Michio Iwata, Kyushu Institute of Technology, Japan; Shin-Ichi Nureki, Oita University, Japan; Noriko Otani, Nagoya University, Japan; Yoshihiro Yamanishi, Nagoya University, Japan
abstract: Identifying therapeutic targets for diseases is important in drug discovery. However, the depletion of viable therapeutic targets has a major bottleneck, contributing to the recent stagnation in drug development, especially for rare and orphan diseases. Here, we propose a disease signature, TRESOR, which characterizes the functional mechanisms of each disease through genome-wide association study (GWAS) and transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) data. Based on TRESOR and target perturbation signatures (TGPs)—i.e., gene knockdown and overexpression profiles of target-coding genes—we develop machine learning methods for predicting inhibitory and activatory therapeutic targets for various diseases. TRESOR enables highly accurate identification of target candidate proteins based on inverse correlations between TRESOR and TGPs. Furthermore, Bayesian integrative method combines TRESOR-based inverse correlations and omics-based disease similarities, providing more reliable predictions for rare and orphan diseases with few or no known targets. We make comprehensive predictions for 284 diseases with 4,345 inhibitory target candidates and 151 diseases with 4,040 activatory target candidates. These predictions were validated through literature-based cross-referencing and independently assessed using human cohort data, supporting their therapeutic potential. For instance, multiple endocrine neoplasia, a rare disease with only one known inhibitory target, was predicted to have new candidate targets such as FHL2, whose downregulation correlated with improved survival in independent cohorts. The proposed method was also applied to orphan diseases lacking any known targets, such as tauopathies, identifying promising candidates including RAB1B. Proposed methods are expected to be useful for understanding disease–disease relationships and identifying therapeutic targets for rare and orphan diseases.

title: Benchmarking Virtual Cell Perturbation Reasoning: A Comprehensive Dataset for Drug Response Prediction
authors: Hiufung Yip, Institute of Systems Medicine and Health Sciences, Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong; Aiping Lyu, Institute of Systems Medicine and Health Sciences, Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong; Lu Zhang, Department of Computer Science, Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong
abstract: Accurately predicting how drugs alter gene expression across different cell types remains a core challenge in virtual cell biology. Large language models offer new possibilities for reasoning through these perturbation questions, yet no standard benchmark exists to measure whether their predictions reflect genuine biological understanding. We introduce PerturbReason, a dataset of 32,667 drug-gene-cell triplets for evaluating model reasoning on transcriptional perturbation tasks. The training set contains 24,000 samples spanning 922 drugs, 1,635 genes, and 1,084 cell lines with balanced perturbation labels (50% YES/NO) and mechanism-based annotations. For testing, we construct three out-of-distribution splits totaling 8,667 samples: OOD-Drug (3,000 samples featuring 17 unseen drugs), OOD-Gene (2,667 samples targeting 45 genes absent from training), and OOD-Cell (3,000 samples from 57 novel cell lines). Every entry pairs a perturbation question with mechanistic reasoning and supporting PubMed references, enabling evaluation of both prediction accuracy and reasoning quality across six dimensions: research depth, analytical rigor, source quality, practical value, balance & objectivity, and writing quality. An evaluation of five state-of-the-art models, DeepSeek-V3/R1, Qwen2.5/3, and MiniMax, found that while they achieve 50–70% accuracy, reasoning quality assessments yield normalized scores of only 0.36 to 0.63, with particularly poor performance on research depth from 0.32 to 0.59 and analytical rigor from 0.32 to 0.69, indicating superficial understanding rather than mechanistic reasoning. PerturbReason reveals that current general-purpose LLMs lack robust generalization to novel perturbation contexts, highlighting the urgent need for specialized architectures and training strategies tailored to biological reasoning rather than relying on pre-trained knowledge alone.

title: BioArena: A Community-Driven Platform for Trusted Benchmarking of LLMs in Biomedicine
authors: Rongrong Chai, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Thomas Schaffter, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, Switzerland; Gaia Andreoletti, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Serghei Mangul, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Susheel Varma, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United Kingdom; Alberto Pepe, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Jay Hodgson, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Solveig Sieberts, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States; Luca Foschini, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted rapidly in biomedical research, yet available evaluation approaches often rely on static benchmarks or general-purpose leaderboards, with limited support for trusted, domain-specific biomedical assessment. This has become a bottleneck for responsible AI adoption in biomedical research. We introduce BioArena (https://bioarena.io/), an open-source benchmarking platform purpose-built for community-driven evaluation of LLMs on biomedical topics. BioArena enables blinded, head-to-head human evaluation of model responses to biomedical questions. Users input a biomedical query, BioArena randomly selects two LLMs to pose the query to, and users select their preferred answer. BioArena leverages Synapse, a research-oriented biomedical community platform, for trusted participation, with account verification and two-factor authentication reinforcing integrity in the evaluation process. The platform combines AI-based validation of submitted questions for biomedical relevance with expert human review to improve evaluation data quality. Model rankings are computed using Bradley-Terry modeling with bootstrap confidence intervals, supporting a statistically rigorous and continuously updated leaderboard. To sustain engagement, the platform includes a community quest in which valid evaluations contribute to a collective, publicly tracked milestone. The platform currently evaluates 32 frontier proprietary and open-weight models, including GPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, and Qwen, with capacity to expand to more than 300 models through OpenRouter integration. Early deployment has produced hundreds of evaluations from verified users. BioArena provides the biomedical community an open-source, trusted, living benchmark and a reliable reference for selecting and evaluating biomedical AI on real scientific questions.

title: varLens: functional track–driven deep learning for allele-specific variant effect prediction using genome language models
authors: Dezhao Fu, Ph.D. Candidate at George Washington University, United States; Ali Rahnavard, Associate Professor at George Washington University, United States
abstract: Predicting the functional impact of single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) is a fundamental problem in genomics, yet remains challenging due to the complexity of regulatory mechanisms and the difficulty of translating learned representations into actionable scores. Recent genome language models (gLMs) provide powerful sequence representations, but existing strategiesâ€”such as embedding distanceâ€“based scoring or task-specific fine-tuningâ€”either lack interpretability or require substantial retraining. We present varLens, a functional trackâ€“aware deep learning framework that explicitly models allele-specific perturbations in regulatory signals. Leveraging nucleotide-resolution functional tracks derived from the Nucleotide Transformer v3, varLens constructs a delta representation between reference and alternative alleles and applies locality-aware weighting centered on the variant. A hybrid architecture combining convolutional layers and attention modules is used to capture both local sequence patterns and long-range dependencies. To enable scalable training without curated labels, we introduce a weakly supervised pretraining strategy using 9.7 million variants from gnomAD, where allele frequency serves as a proxy for evolutionary constraint. The model is evaluated across diverse benchmark datasets spanning expression quantitative trait loci, pathogenic variants, and complex trait associations, using chromosome-held-out splits to prevent local sequence leakage. varLens consistently improves AUROC over classical machine learning baselines and deep neural architectures, and outperforms both zero-shot and fine-tuned gLM-based approaches.

title: Visual Analytics for Genomic and Epidemiological Integration in Livestock Pathogens
authors: Norah Alharbi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Hatim Almutairi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Mohammed Alarawi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Sulaiman Alajel, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Maha Alsayegh, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Muhayla Alanazi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Nuha Bin Tyyash, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Saidan Alotaibi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Areej Almuhayya, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Shahad Alsalman, National Livestock And Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Hend Alotaibi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Muruj Tukruni, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Aroob Alhumaidy, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Alaa Aljohani, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Nouf Alharbi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Othman Aljurayyad, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia; Mashael Alghuraybi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Saudi Arabia
abstract: The increasing availability of whole genome sequencing (WGS) data in livestock pathogen surveillance presents challenges in integrating high-dimensional genomic data with epidemiological context in a coherent and interpretable manner. Existing approaches often lack effective visual frameworks to support interactive exploration and interpretation, particularly within the livestock sector. The Livestock Pathogen Tracker Platform, developed under the National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP) in Saudi Arabia, which integrates genomic and epidemiological data within an interactive visual analytics environment. The platform combines local and global WGS datasets with structured metadata curated according to Minimum Information about any (x) Sequence (MIxS) standards. Scalable bioinformatics workflows generate outputs including phylogenetic relationships, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles, virulence factors, and immunologically relevant epitopes and antigens profiling. A central contribution of this work is the design and implementation of coordinated visual analytics dashboards that enable multi-dimensional exploration of pathogen data. Built using Python-based frameworks (Dash and Plotly), the system provides linked views across geographic, temporal, and genomic dimensions, including interactive phylogenetic trees, geospatial maps, temporal trend visualizations, and AMR profiling with drill-down capabilities. These visualizations support dynamic filtering, comparative analysis, and real-time interrogation of large-scale datasets. The platform is demonstrated using Salmonella in poultry and Brucella in livestock, highlighting its ability to reveal patterns in pathogen distribution, lineage dynamics, and resistance trends. By bridging genomic analysis and visual interpretation, the platform enhances data accessibility and supports more effective surveillance and decision-making in livestock health systems.

title: Pseudotime graph diffusion for post hoc visualization of inferred single-cell trajectories
authors: Brandon Lukas, University of Illinois Chicago, United States; Jingbo Pang, University of Illinois Chicago, United States; Timothy J. Koh, University of Illinois Chicago, United States; Yang Dai, University of Illinois Chicago, United States
abstract: Background: Single-cell trajectories are often visualized using low-dimensional embeddings (e.g., UMAP) even if inference is performed in a higher-dimensional feature space. Due to information loss, these embeddings sometimes fail to represent the inferred trajectory structure, compromising interpretation of cellular dynamics and downstream layout-dependent analyses. Existing trajectory-aware visualization methods (e.g., PAGA, PHATE) construct embeddings that encode global structure but are not suitable when an inferred trajectory already exists and the goal is to improve its visualization. Methods: We introduce Pseudotime Graph Diffusion (PGD), a lightweight, interpretable, post hoc framework that smooths per-cell features along inferred pseudotime. PGD constructs a cell graph using a sliding window along the pseudotime ordering of each branch and propagates features via lazy random-walk diffusion controlled by a single mixing parameter. Results: Using a scRNA-seq dataset of 2,848 monocytes and macrophages from murine skin wounds at days 3, 6, and 10 post-injury, we inferred increasingly complex trajectories (5â€“10 clusters) with Lamian and applied PGD. Compared to UMAP, PGD-smoothed embeddings produced complexity-specific layouts with continuous pseudotime gradients and resolved branch structure. Two clusters at opposite ends of the pseudotime continuum overlapped in UMAP but became separated while their global neighborhood remained preserved. We further show that PGD extends naturally to trajectory-aware gene expression smoothing. Conclusion: PGD operates post hoc on any pseudotime estimate and embedding, integrating with existing workflows without re-inference, and enables faithful interpretation of cellular dynamics by aligning visual representations with inferred trajectories.

title: Navigating the NIH Data Ecosystem: A Landscape Analysis of the 105 NIH-Funded Data Resources and the Path Toward Federation
authors: Bronwyn Walsh, Baylor College of Medicine, United States; Jonathan Lawson, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Sofia Labrecque, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Vasiliki Rahimzadeh, Baylor College of Medicine, United States
abstract: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) invests heavily in data resources to drive scientific discovery guided by FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) principles. However, a proliferation of overlapping repositories introduces significant operational challenges for data findability and reusability. To characterize this landscape, we conducted a cross-sectional inventory of 105 NIH-funded, domain-specific data resources as of April 2026. We categorized their primary classifications, species scopes, and access controls while estimating 2015–2025 financial investments using official NIH dashboards and NIH REPORTER transaction logs. The results reveal that genomic (n=54) and clinical (n=41) data predominate, clustering heavily within computational and neuroscience fields. These platforms provide significantly more metadata than direct access to raw datasets. Furthermore, while 55% of the resources utilize open-access models, only 53% of these open platforms permit external data submissions. Total estimated funding represents a conservative $6 billion investment that peaked at $517 million in 2024. Concurrently, the average listed institutional affiliations per resource dropped by 45.18% between 2025 and 2026, signaling administrative catalog consolidation rather than active funding cuts. Ultimately, the current NIH ecosystem prioritizes data preservation over active interpretation, leading to redundant software implementations. Transitioning toward a federated "hub and spoke" architecture will maximize FAIR compliance, reduce operational duplication, and liberate critical funding for next-generation molecular biology analysis tools.

title: Integrating Protein Knowledge Network (ProKN) into NSF Prototype Open Knowledge Network (Proto-OKN) for Cross-Domain Knowledge Discovery
authors: Chuming Chen, University of Delaware, United States; Manju Anandakrishnan, University of Delaware, United States; Karen Ross, Georgetown University Medical Center, United States; Pratim Ugale, University of Delaware, United States; Elena MacDonald, University of Delaware, United States; Sravya Buddha, University of Delaware, United States; Cathy Wu, University of Delaware, United States
abstract: The NSF Prototype Open Knowledge Network (Proto-OKN) is designed to establish a national-scale data infrastructure that facilitates cross domain knowledge discovery across scientific disciplines. As a key biomedical contribution to this effort, the Protein Knowledge Network (ProKN), developed within the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem (CFDE), harmonizes diverse protein-centric data. This includes post-translational modifications (PTMs), functional pathways, drug-target interactions, and associated genomic and variant datasets. ProKN comprises over 100 million Resource Description Framework (RDF) triples organized across 41 classes and 220 properties. These triples represent more than 114,778 proteins, 38,372 genes, 89,904 variants, 295,694 sites and 220,229 PTM annotations. This structured knowledge model allows researchers to directly connect molecular events to broader biological and environmental contexts. Integration of ProKN into Proto-OKN enables novel cross-domain discovery via SPARQL queries that operate across interconnected knowledge graphs. For example, users can retrieve protein associations from the Open Annotations for Rare Diseases (OARD) Knowledge Graph while simultaneously accessing protein variants causally linked to diseases influenced by social determinants of health (SDOH) from resources such as the Scalable Precision Medicine Oriented Knowledge Engine (SPOKE) and BioHealthKG. Such queries reveal how socioeconomic factors and associated phenotypes interact with molecular variants that are associated with SDOHâ€‘related conditions, effectively linking proteinâ€‘level biology to realâ€‘world health disparities. ProKN serves as a model for integrating domain-specific knowledge graphs into national infrastructure, acting as a biomedical pillar within Proto-OKN while demonstrating an approach readily extensible beyond biomedicine to enable cross-domain discovery across the broader scientific landscape.

title: A Generative AI-Extracted Mechanistic Knowledge Graph for mAb Stability: Construction, Analysis, and Prediction with mAb-GATED
authors: Gyu Seong Lee, CHA University, South Korea; Hyo Young Kim, Tech University of Korea, South Korea; Hyeong Gyu Choi, CHA University, South Korea; Dae Keun Park, CHA University, South Korea; Ji Hye Park, CHA University, South Korea
abstract: The transition of monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutics from intravenous (IV) to subcutaneous (SC) formulations has heightened the need to understand how stability indicatorsâ€”including aggregation, viscosity, and oxidationâ€”interact through shared mechanisms. Most prior work, however, has examined these indicators in isolation, and systematic efforts to map the mechanistic network among them remain scarce. In this study, we applied generative AI-based structured extraction and term normalization to PubMed abstracts to construct a mechanistic knowledge graph (KG) encompassing thousands of nodes, directed edges, and over twenty relation types. Here, mechanistic relationships refer to directional associations explicitly described as such by the original authors, rather than statistically inferred interventional effects. Graph structure analysis identified aggregation, stability, and conformational stability as dominant hub nodes. To assess whether the mechanistic patterns within this KG are learnable, we developed mAb-GATED (Graph-Aware Transformer with Encoder-Decoder), a model that initializes node representations with PubMedBERT embeddings and refines them through a graph-based learning architecture. On a sub-category-constrained classification task across canonical stability indicators, mAb-GATED substantially surpassed frequency-based and DistMult baselines. These results demonstrate that literature-derived mechanistic relationships in mAb stability can be effectively captured through graph-based learning. This work provides a foundational framework for knowledge-driven reasoning over protein stability networks, with broader applicability to formulation design and biologics development.

title: Multi-DWPC: A many-to-one pathfinding approach for subgraph extraction in biomedical knowledge graphs
authors: Lucas Gillenwater, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Sutanu Nandi, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; James Costello, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Casey Greene, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States
abstract: A path through a biomedical knowledge graph (BKG) can provide a mechanistic hypothesis for an observed but unexplained association. The Degree-Weighted Path Count (DWPC) algorithm prioritizes informative path types, or metapaths, by downweighting high-degree nodes, but is designed for one-to-one relationships. Many biological questions instead involve a set of source features converging on a shared phenotype. To account for many-to-one associations, we extend DWPC to Multi-DWPC, a method for prioritizing metapaths connecting gene sets to targets by filtering metapaths to those whose signal exceeds degree-aware null models. We validated Multi-DWPC in the Hetionet BKG by testing whether metapaths prioritized from 2016 Gene Ontology (GO) gene annotations and updated 2024 annotations remained consistent.
