Multi-DWPC similarly ranked metapaths across annotation snapshots (Ï = 0.91). Among genes driving DWPC scores (top 75th percentile) in selected metapaths, 2024-added genes showed low intermediate node overlap with each other (Jaccard = 0.21), comparable to 2016 genes (Jaccard = 0.16). This result suggests that genes may reach shared phenotypes through largely distinct intermediates. We also applied Multi-DWPC to three gene sets from pathway-informed matrix decomposition with associated phenotypes. One of the three gene setâ€”phenotype pairs discriminated from null models (LV246-adipose tissue). For this gene set, top-scoring genes showed similar intermediate node overlap (mean Jaccard = 0.12 across 68 metapaths). Taken together, the results indicate that Multi-DWPC recovers the diffuse signal of pairwise relationships through aggregation. Multi-DWPC recovers stable biological structure and generates many-to-one mechanistic hypotheses. Code is available at https://github.com/greenelab/multi-dwpc.

title: Transforming Biomedical Literature into Structured Gene-Disease Knowledge Through Agentic AI
authors: Dongyu Liu, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Mario Pandolfi, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Emanuele de Rinaldis, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Shameer Khader, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Franck Rapaport, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States
abstract: The exponential growth of biomedical literature has made it increasingly difficult for researchers to comprehensively map gene-disease relationships. We previously developed SciLinker â€” a biological relationship extraction framework that mines gene-disease, gene-cell, disease-cell, and other associations from 39 million PubMed abstracts, spanning 29,459 genes, 1,586 cell types, 32,171 drugs, and 14,219 diseases. Yet the sheer volume of extracted information remains a barrier: the lack of structured categorization, combined with many associations having hundreds of supporting sentences, makes it challenging for researchers to synthesize what is known about specific relationships. To address this, we developed an agentic summarization pipeline that harnesses Large Language Models to transform raw extracted sentences into coherent, structured gene-disease summaries. Built on the LangGraph orchestration framework and deployed via AWS Bedrock within Sanofi's OneAI platform, the pipeline aggregates disease-relevant excerpts from SciLinker and organizes knowledge across four dimensions: (1) genetic evidence (variants and inheritance patterns), (2) expression profiles (tissue-specific expression, transcriptomic changes), (3) molecular mechanisms (pathways, protein interactions, pathological associations), and (4) therapeutic implications (treatment associations, clinical applications). A built-in critic feedback loop enforces summarization quality and consistency by validating the accuracy of each knowledge category and eliminating hallucinations, ensuring that generated summaries remain faithful to the original literature evidence. Applied to 350,000 gene-disease association sentences across 10 immune diseases relevant to Sanofiâ€™s therapeutic portfolio, the pipeline transforms fragmented literature into structured summaries for each gene-disease pair, reducing volume by 80% while preserving scientific depth, For example, the TNF-Asthma association was condensed from over 500 sentences to just 22 structured summary sentences. The summaries have been integrated into Sanofi's Target Engines platform, giving researchers rapid access to structured insights. By presenting evidence across genetic, expression, mechanistic, and therapeutic dimensions in a unified view, researchers can identify mechanistic gaps missed in fragmented literature reviews and discover novel gene-disease associations that reveal previously unexplored therapeutic targets. This integration of traditional NLP with modern LLM capabilities represents a significant advancement in biomedical knowledge synthesis, accelerating translation of literature evidence into target discovery.

title: GlyGen: An Integrated Knowledgebase for Glycoscience Data Discovery and Data Sharing
authors: Rene Ranzinger, University of Georgia, United States; Raja Mazumder, The George Washington University Medical Center, United States; Michael Tiemeyer, University of Georgia, United States
abstract: Glycosylation is a fundamental and diverse biological process that influences protein structure, cellular communication, development, and disease. However, glycoscience research is often hindered by the structural complexity of glycans and the fragmentation of relevant data across multiple databases. GlyGen was developed to address these challenges by serving as an integrated, interoperable knowledgebase that enables exploration of glycans, glycoproteins, glycosylation enzymes, and their biological context. GlyGen aggregates and harmonizes glycoscience data through collaborations with major international resources, including EBI, NCBI, PDB, GlyTouCan, and GlyCosmos, as well as direct contributions from the research community. Data is standardized, integrated and cross-referenced to support seamless navigation across multiple domains. The GlyGen knowledgebase is freely accessible through a user-friendly web interface (https://glygen.org), alongside programmatic access via APIs, a dataset archive, and a SPARQL endpoint, supporting both data exploration and computational workflows. Each glycan and protein in GlyGen is represented by an interlinked summary page that integrates structural, functional, and biological annotations from multiple sources. These views are complemented by dedicated summary pages for glycosylation sites, diseases, biomarkers, publications, and glycan motifs, providing multiple entry points for exploring and contextualizing GlyGen data. In addition to serving as a data discovery platform, GlyGen supports data producers through integration with GlyTableMaker, a web-based repository that facilitates standardized submission of glycomics and glycoproteomics datasets. By combining data integration with data deposition, GlyGen promotes FAIR data practices and accelerates data sharing, reuse, and discovery.

title: LLM-Assisted Evaluation of Biomedical Ontologies using OntoClean
authors: William Duncan, University of Florida, United States; Robert Hoehndorf, KAUST, Saudi Arabia
abstract: OntoClean provides a principled methodology for detecting awkward taxonomic decisions in ontologies, but its application requires manual annotation of every class with five modal meta-properties, a cost that has kept it out of routine use on biomedical ontologies. Here, we present a workflow that uses a fine-tuned large language model to assign the meta-properties automatically, an OWL reasoner to classify the hierarchy, and an OntoClean constraint checker over every inferred (sub, super) pair. Applied to the Emotion Response Ontology (EMRO, 64 classes) the workflow surfaces 303 violations; an LLM auditor and a manual review identify plausible modelling issues, including a rigidity conflict on sweat secretion âŠ‘ secretion by tissue and a contested unity assignment on phenomenal cognitive experience. The review also exposes the central limitation: 83.5% of the violations cascade from a small number of upstream meta-property mislabelings on GO/BFO process classes, where the model over-assigns identity to occurrents. This limitation is reducible at zero training cost: re-running inference with a BFO-grounded system prompt drops the violation count from 303 to 72 (âˆ’76.2%), removes every R2 conflict, and collapses the residue to four specific class mislabelings. LLM-assigned OntoClean is a viable, if not yet sufficient, route to scaling principled ontology evaluation across biomedicine.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ImputeVAE: Translating Single-Nucleus to Single-Cell Expression Profiles via Cross-Reconstructive Variational Autoencoders
authors: Suchen Zheng, Yale University, United States
abstract: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) enables transcriptomic profiling of frozen and archived tissues, but systematic differences from single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) including nuclear transcript enrichment and reduced complexity limit direct comparability. Existing approaches typically treat these discrepancies as batch effects, assuming noise-like or gene-independent variation. However, nucleusâ€“cell differences are structured, nonlinear, and directional. We present ImputeVAE, a variational autoencoder framework that explicitly models the transformation from nucleus to cell expression. Instead of removing differences, ImputeVAE learns a translation function via a shared latent space and cross-reconstruction objective. The model integrates three key components: (1) latent alignment using Jensenâ€“Shannon divergence to enforce modality mixing within cell types; (2) a conditioned decoder with modality embeddings to generate modality-specific outputs; and (3) a translation objective, where nuclei are encoded and decoded to produce cell-like expression profiles, directly optimizing the mapping from nucleus to cell. Training proceeds in two stages, starting with a cell-only model followed by progressive integration of nuclei data. Using the Allen Brain Cell Atlas (71k cells, 40k nuclei across 17 cell types), ImputeVAE substantially improves reconstruction fidelity. Nuclei translated into cell-like expression profiles achieve 94.1% cell-type classification accuracy (+10.6% over raw nuclei), with strong gene-level agreement (Pearson r = 0.963) and improved preservation of coexpression structure. These results demonstrate that nucleusâ€“cell differences are better modeled as learnable biological transformations rather than batch effects, enabling principled integration of large-scale datasets derived from frozen tissues.

title: Open-Source Harness Engineering for Molecular Informatics-Aware AI
authors: Scott Reed, University of Colorado Denver, United States
abstract: Accurate AI for science will depend less on model scale alone and more on harness design: structured prompting, deterministic validation, tool use, and automated improvement loops. This work describes an open-source approach to building chemistry-aware AI systems that are more reliable for cheminformatics and bio-related workflows by combining large language models with deterministic checks, modular tools, and evidence-driven iteration. The project focuses on cheminformatics capabilities that are useful at the chemistry-biology interface, including structure validation, molecular property calculation, format conversion, and interactive handling of biologically relevant small molecules within chat and agentic environments. Rather than treating the AI model as a standalone interface, the system treats it as one component within a constrained workflow in which chemical and biological operations can be checked, traced, and improved over time. This is especially important in scientific settings, where chemically invalid outputs can silently undermine downstream interpretation. A second focus is a collaborative method for improving scientific AI harnesses. We have developed repository-based workflows with contribution templates, structured evaluation, and guardrail-protected review processes that enable distributed community input on harness design. This supports training of the harness itself: not only improving model behavior, but also evolving the surrounding workflow through shared examples, benchmark cases, and evidence-backed revisions. The broader goal is to build open infrastructure for more trustworthy AI in science, with particular relevance to cheminformatics applied to bioinformatics, chemical biology, and molecular informatics.

title: From hacking to preprint; open science and expanding commons
authors: Sung Won Lim, Binomica labs, United States
abstract: Research tools underlying key aspects of modern biology went through a period of dramatic improvements in the last ten years. These changes often came with explicit promise of democratizing science through new technologies. Here, I draw from both a decade long experience as a blue collar laborer who transitioned from hackerspace DIYBio to publishing amateur biologist focused on sequencing and comparative genomics, and works of contemporary historians of science to suggest democratization of science depends on expansion of the intangible idea of the commons. Broader participation in the commons of knowledge led by the modern day open access and open source movements is intimately linked to continuous refinement of the idea of science and the scientist, both of which might be dynamic and evolving descriptions of practices rather than static social status. I support these suggestions with presentation of research data and usage patterns of open source tools alongside published preprints, produced both independently and in equal collaboration with other academic scientists. I hope to impart to the participants that their open source works are at the forefront of broader changes to how science is defined and practiced, changing lives for the better.

title: Customizing Canopy for Domain-Specific Data Hubs with CEDAR Templates and BioPortal Ontologies
authors: Yan Cao, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Attila L. Egyedi, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Matthew Horridge, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Mete Akdogan, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Martin O'Connor, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Marcos Martínez-Romero, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States; Mark Musen, Division of Computational Medicine, Stanford University, United States
abstract: Canopy is an open-source platform for building FAIR-aligned scientific data hubs that supports data sharing, harmonization, discovery, and reuse across research studies. Canopy is derived from the NIH RADx Data Hub (https://radxdatahub.nih.gov/), a cloud-based platform originally developed for the NIH Rapid Acceleration of Diagnostics (RADx) program. Rather than presenting a one-size-fits-all data hub, Canopy enables customization of RADx Data Hub technology for the needs of specific scientific domains. Support for customizable metadata templates and ontologies was central to adapting the RADx Data Hub into Canopy. This capability allows communities to configure Canopy for their own domain-specific metadata models while supporting standardization, interoperability, and FAIR-aligned metadata across study domains. Communities can tailor the platform to their own metadata needs without infrastructure changes. This poster highlights how Canopy achieves domain-specific customization through integration with the CEDAR Workbench and the BioPortal ontology repository. Communities define metadata standards as structured CEDAR templates that specify study attributes and link them to ontologies or value sets that provide controlled terms. By using ontologies in BioPortal to constrain field values, CEDAR templates support metadata standardization and machine-actionability. Within Canopy, metadata is structured according to these customizable templates, enabling metadata validation and visualization without application code changes. Canopy is available as open-source software at https://github.com/canopy-datahub. By combining reusable RADx Data Hub-derived infrastructure with customizable, ontology-enabled metadata specifications, Canopy supports the development of domain-specific, FAIR-aligned data hubs for open science.

title: Reactome: Scalable, Computable Knowledge Representation of Human Biological Pathways for Systems Biology and AI Applications
authors: Nancy Li, OICR, Canada; Reactome Consortium Consortium, OICR, Canada
abstract: The increasing scale and heterogeneity of omics data require structured biological knowledge representations that are both human-interpretable and computationally tractable. Reactome is an open-source, expert-curated pathway knowledgebase that models human biological processes as a computable graph of molecular interactions, reactions, and regulatory events. Reactome integrates literature-supported mechanistic knowledge across signaling, metabolism, gene regulation, immune biology, and disease processes within a unified data model grounded in biological semantics. All pathway content undergoes expert authoring and peer review, followed by computational inference to orthologous species, enabling comparative systems analysis across diverse organisms. Reactome provides programmatic access through APIs, graph exports, and standards-compliant formats including BioPAX and SBML, supporting interoperability with network analysis, enrichment workflows, and machine learning pipelines. Recent developments focus on scaling knowledge accessibility and reuse. These include AI-assisted curation workflows that accelerate literature integration while preserving expert oversight, and a new AI-conversational interface that lower barriers for non-specialist users while maintaining provenance transparency. Reactome pathways increasingly serve as structured priors for network modeling, knowledge graphs, and foundation models in computational biology. By combining rigorous biocuration with computable representation, Reactome functions as a reference framework linking molecular mechanisms to large-scale biological data analysis. Ongoing work emphasizes reproducibility, interoperability, and integration with emerging AI methodologies, positioning Reactome as critical infrastructure for data-driven biology.

title: WILDS WDL Library: Modular Bioinformatics Components for Researchers and Developers
authors: Emma Bishop, Fred Hutch Cancer Center, United States; Taylor Firman, Fred Hutch Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Reproducibility and scalability are challenges for many bioinformatics analyses. Workflow languages, such as Nextflow and Workflow Description Language (WDL), address this by defining analyses as portable, version-controlled scripts paired with containerized environments. Our team at Fred Hutch Cancer Center has adopted WDL for its readability and approachable learning curve. However, the upfront investment of writing workflows from scratch remains a significant barrier for many bench researchers. To lower this barrier, we developed the WILDS WDL Library, a rigorously tested, well-documented collection of modular WDL scripts. The scripts are organized into two tiers: modules, that wrap popular commands for over 40 bioinformatics tools into reusable tasks, and pipelines, which use the tasks in end-to-end workflows. Modules can be imported via their GitHub URLs and combined in numerous ways. With developmental guardrails in place, we have begun exploring the use of large language models to assist with prototyping new modules, with all generated code undergoing thorough review and validation by human researchers. At Fred Hutch, this library has encouraged workflow adoption by researchers and in some cases reduced computational wait times from weeks to hours. Since releasing the library in January, weâ€™ve had contributions from twelve researchers across six labs and been cited in a manuscript. We have built this community through an introductory workshop and a workflow development program. The WILDS WDL Library serves as a resource for the distributed development of WDL workflows and as an example of how to build an open source community among biologists from scratch.

title: Building Bridges: Academia-Industry Hackathons for Open Biomedical Data Science
authors: Beryl Rabindran, AWS, United States; Ben Busby, NVIDIA, United States
abstract: Background: Researchers face a growing gap between the computational skills taught in traditional graduate programs and the technical skills increasingly required for cutting-edge biomedical research. While cloud computing and AI are transforming how large-scale biological data are analyzed, most researchers lack hands-on experience with these technologies. Method: In Oct 2025, the AWS Open Data team partnered with NVIDIA to organize an intensive 3-day Knowledge Graph hackathon bringing together academic researchers and industry experts. In Jan 2025, NVIDIA and Carnegie Mellon University organized a Federated Learning hackathon which AWS Open Data supported. Both events provided participants with access to over 225 open life sciences datasets from the Registry of Open Data on AWS, cloud computing resources, access to NVIDIA resources for PyTorch Geometric (PyG) RAG and NVIDIA FLARE, and technical mentorship from AWS solutions architects and NVIDIA scientists. Results: Over 150 participants across the two events successfully developed 17 open-source prototypes spanning knowledge graphs and federated learning. Projects demonstrated practical solutions for data integration across siloed datasets, and trustworthy AI systems grounded in verifiable evidence. All code, documentation, and methodologies were published as open-source repositories, with open preprints enabling reproducibility and extension by the broader research community. Conclusion: These hackathons demonstrate an effective model for building technical capacity and fostering academia-industry collaboration in computational biology. By providing hands-on experience with production-scale infrastructure and real-world datasets, this approach closes the gap between skills learned in graduate programs and those needed for real-world data exploration in biomedical research.

title: UniFORM: Toward universal immunofluorescence normalization for multiplex tissue imaging
authors: Kunlun Wang, Oregon Health and Science University, United States
abstract: Multiplex tissue imaging (MTI) enables high-dimensional spatial profiling of tissue microenvironments, but slide-to-slide and batch-to-batch intensity variability can obscure biological signal and distort downstream analyses. Existing normalization approaches often rely on restrictive distributional assumptions and may fail on the heterogeneous, right-skewed (often bimodal) marker patterns that are common in fluorescence-based MTI, leading to misaligned marker distributions and altered marker-positive population characteristics. Here, we present UniFORM, a non-parametric, Python-based normalization pipeline that operates at both the single-cell feature level and the pixel level. UniFORM uses an automated rigid-landmark registration strategy tailored to MTI intensity distributions, aligning biologically invariant negative populations to remove technical variation while preserving tissue-specific signal in positive populations. UniFORM supports unimodal and bimodal marker patterns and includes an optional guided fine-tuning mode for complex or highly heterogeneous datasets. Across benchmarks on multiple MTI platforms (including CyCIF, ORION, and COMET), UniFORM consistently improves batch alignment while maintaining biological fidelity, reflected by better marker distribution agreement and preservation of marker-positive behavior. Downstream, UniFORM improves quantitative integration metrics (e.g., kBET and silhouette scores) and yields more coherent embeddings and clustering results (UMAP/Leiden), supporting more reliable cell phenotyping and spatial analyses. UniFORM is released with reproducible tutorials and reference datasets to facilitate adoption and benchmarking.

title: Graph-Native Modernization of Pharos: A Configurable ETL Framework for Target Knowledge Integration
authors: Keith Kelleher, National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, United States; Jessica Maine, National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, United States; Steven Mathias, University of New Mexico, United States; Timothy Sheils, National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, United States; Tudor Oprea, Expert Systems Inc, United States; Ewy Mathé, National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, United States
abstract: Pharos is an integrated resource for exploring the human proteome, especially understudied targets, across target development level, disease, ligand activity, pathway, expression, and Gene Ontology annotations. To support continued growth of the resource, including expanded transcript- and variant-oriented representations, we developed a configurable ETL framework that makes data integration more automated, traceable, and maintainable across heterogeneous biomedical sources. The updated system uses YAML-based configuration to orchestrate source ingestion, identifier resolution, graph construction, post-processing, and downstream export through reusable pipelines. A central design feature is support for multiple graph views over the same integrated knowledge, including a target-centric graph optimized for Pharos-style exploration and a more explicit biological graph in which proteins, transcripts, genes, and future variant-level entities can be represented as distinct node types. This flexibility supports richer relationship modeling and graph-based analyses and prediction workflows. For users, these updates strengthen Pharos for target prioritization, hypothesis generation, and translational discovery. The integrated graph supports narrowing candidate target lists based on disease associations, or ligand activities, in addition to pathways and expression context, and enabling downstream applications including target prioritization and drug repurposing. The framework also preserves operational continuity by converting the target-centric graph into the legacy TCRD-style MySQL schema used by the current Pharos GraphQL API and user interface. This work provides a graph-centered, configurable, and extensible foundation for consistent Pharos updates and a practical bridge from graph-native integration to the existing Pharos application ecosystem.

title: BioFmt: Spec-Referenced Validation and Interactive Previews of Bioinformatics File Formats in VS Code
authors: Jeremy Fan, Independent Researcher, Canada
abstract: Bioinformaticians and computational biologists typically work with dozens of structured file formats across their data pipelines. While malformed fields and spec violations can be caught as inputs/outputs of softwares, there are few options to visually inspect these fields. While existing editor tools support syntax highlighting, they do not offer support for cross-field errors or indexed files. Furthermore, as autonomous coding agents begin driving the development of bioinformatics pipelines, the need for machine-readable validation and human visual inspection harnesses becomes critical. BioFmt is a VS Code extension that provides a set of differentiated features. For instance: spec-reference diagnostics, which references documentation on the reason for malformed file types. Beyond single-field errors, BioFmt validates relationships across fields and records. For instance, in GFF3, child features (e.g., exons) may reference a non-existent parent transcript that may have been filtered out or merged. These orphan elements could be silently dropped by downstream tools, leading to incorrect gene models, read counts, or annotations without warning. BioFmt also integrates other features like syntax highlighting, hover tooltips, and interactive previews for genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics on file formats extending what existing editors cover. BioFmt supports a planned declarative plugin system will allow contributors to add new formats and validation rules without modifying core code based on public specs, lowering the barrier for community-driven format support.

title: Clinical Dataset Structure: A Universal Framework for Structuring Clinical Research Datasets
authors: Aydan Gasimova, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, San Diego, CA, USA, United States; Sanjay Soundarajan, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, San Diego, CA, USA, United States; Nayoon Gim, Department of Ophthalmology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA, United States; Jamie Shaffer, Department of Ophthalmology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA, United States; Julia Owen, John F. Hardesty MD Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences, Washington University, St. Louis, MO, United States; Aaron Lee, John F. Hardesty MD Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences, Washington University, St. Louis, MO, United States; Bhavesh Patel, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, San Diego, CA, USA, United States
abstract: Clinical studies collect rich multimodal data, such as surveys, wearables, and eye images. There is currently no consensus on how to structure that data into a consistently organized dataset. As a result, clinical datasets are hard to reuse, and datasets from different studies are not readily interoperable. To address this challenge in the AI Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights (AI-READI) project, we developed the Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS). The CDS is an open-source (CC-BY-4.0), standardized framework for organizing multimodal clinical research data and metadata developed by unifying existing domain-specific standard structures (e.g., Brain Imaging Data Structure), metadata schemas (DataCite, ClinicalTrials.gov), and AI/ML-focused standards (Datasheet, Healthsheet). The CDS recommends organizing multimodal clinical research datasets into one folder per data type, named as per a set convention, where applicable standard structure must then be followed within each folder. It also recommends including multiple metadata files at the root level in human-friendly (e.g., README, Healthsheet) and machine-friendly (e.g., dataset_description.json, study_description.json) formats that collectively capture over 80 metadata elements. The CDS specification is documented openly at cds-specification.readthedocs.io. We are also building tooling to lower the barrier to adoption. The AI-READI dataset, which is structured following the CDS, has already been downloaded over 950 times and contributed to multiple publications, demonstrating real-world impact. In this presentation, we will introduce the CDS, present its implementation in the AI-READI dataset, and explain how the community can adopt and build on it.

title: What are the key pretraining parameters for self-supervised models on tandem mass spectra for improved performance on structure retrieval
authors: Ehud Herbst, Princeton University, United States; Chencheng Xu, Princeton University, United States; Vishu Gupta, Princeton University, United States; Lucas Ayres, Princeton University, United States; Michael Skinnider, Princeton University, United States
abstract: Mass spectrometry is one of the leading analytical methods for metabolite analysis in biological samples. However, for the vast majority of metabolites detected by mass spectrometry in a typical sample, the chemical structure is unknown. The availability of billions of unlabeled tandem mass spectra in public repositories poses the question whether self-supervised models learning from these spectra can enhance chemical structure annotation rates. In this study we set out to answer this question by thoroughly examining self-supervised pretraining parameters such as mass spectra encoding, masking ratio, what values to predict and loss type. With our model's pretrained embeddings we report retrieval rates on MassSpecGym of 12.3% and 11.8% for the mass and formula candidates (Bonus challenge), respectively, a 21.7% and 9.2% improvement relative to 10.1% and 10.8% rates with DreaMS pretrained embeddings. Through a detailed ablation study we report the key pretraining parameters responsible for enhanced retrieval performance.

title: Benchmarking Strategies for Phosphopeptide Discovery in Non-Enriched Proteomes
authors: Shannon Marshall, AstraZeneca, United States; Jana Zecha, AstraZeneca, United States; Ben Pullman, AstraZeneca, United States; Matthew Glover, AstraZeneca, United States; Sonja Hess, AstraZeneca, United States
abstract: Phosphopeptide detection by mass spectrometry typically relies on enrichment strategies that are impractical for low input and limited sample types. Furthermore, standardized workflows for phosphopeptide identification directly from non-enriched global proteome datasets remain underdeveloped. To address this gap, we systematically assessed phosphopeptide detection from DIA-PASEF data acquired on a timsTOF Ultra mass spectrometer analyzing matched global proteome and IMAC enriched phosphoproteome preparations from cultured Jurkat and HCT116 cells. We further compared peptide centric identification (DIA-NN) with spectrum centric workflows (diaTracer/FragPipe) to establish practical guidance for phosphosite discovery without enrichment. Using DIA-NN, we identified 16,303 class I phosphopeptides from IMAC enriched samples while global proteome analysis using project-specific spectral libraries identified 1,005 phosphopeptides. In contrast, a spectrum-based approach using the diaTracer workflow in FragPipe to deconvolute DIA spectra before database searching identified 856 phosphopeptides. 303 phosphopeptides were detected in both the DIA-NN and FragPipe workflows. Comparative analysis of the DIA-NN results showed that phosphopeptides detectable without enrichment overrepresent high abundance species with 65% of unenriched identifications corresponding to the top 20% most intense precursors from the enriched dataset. Our analysis reveals the fraction of phosphopeptides detectable in unenriched samples and establishes phosphopeptide abundance thresholds below which enrichment remains necessary for reliable detection. This framework provides critical guidance for researchers seeking to leverage enrichment free strategies for PTM discovery while understanding the trade-offs between sensitivity, specificity, and phosphoproteome coverage.

title: Intron Variant Identification in Mass Spectrometry
authors: Benjamin Krummenacher, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, United States; David Koes, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, United States; Robin Lee, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Intron retention (IR) is a major mechanism of post-transcriptional regulation under cellular stress. Beyond controlling cytoplasmic mRNA availability, retained introns can encode new domains or premature termination codons, contributing to induced proteomic diversity. Despite several known examples of IR-derived proteins, the extent to which IR transcripts are translated into proteins is unknown. Current proteomics methods are unsuited for IR-derived protein detection in complex mixtures without prior transcriptomic evidence. Here we present Intron Variant Identification in Mass Spectrometry (IVIMS), a de novo sequencing approach which uses learned spectral relationships between canonical and IR-derived peptide spectra to selectively detect intron-variant peptides at proteome scale.

title: Proteome-Wide Identification of Differentially Abundant Plasma Proteins Implicates Tretinoin-Driven Regulation in Asthma
authors: Soheil Farid Azar, NIH, United States; Subrata Paul, NIH, United States; Brittany Dulek, NIH, United States; Rasika Mathias, NIH, United States
abstract: Asthma is a complex chronic airway disease with heterogeneous endotypes. Proteomic studies improve endotype characterization but have largely focused on European populations. Plasma proteomics were generated in African ancestry participants from the Consortium on Asthma among African-ancestry Populations in the Americas (CAAPA) using the SomaScan 11k Assay. SomaScan data were normalized using hybridization control normalization, intraplate median normalization, plate scaling/calibration, and ANML. Quality control revealed variation driven by the fedâ€“fasted state, which was modeled using a novel protein-derived score; samples that were identified as having an outlier state were dropped. Differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) were identified by comparing asthma cases (N=200) to controls (N=220) using limma on log_2 (protein abundances) adjusting for age, sex, and genetic ancestry. DAPs were defined at FDR We identified 169 DAPs. IgE (immunoglobulin E), 6PGDH (pentose phosphate pathway enzyme), EMBP (eosinophil granule protein involved in allergic inflammation), and ARRB1 (beta-arrestin involved in GPCR signaling and immune regulation) were the top proteins. IPA identified tretinoin (an active form of vitamin A) as a top upstream regulator (p = 9.64Ã—10â»Â¹âµ). Clustering based on the 84 tretinoin-target proteins revealed two asthma subgroups; one had higher neutrophil/ lower eosinophil levels, and the second group had the opposite pattern suggesting non-T2 and T2 leaning endotypes, respectively. These findings identify proteomic signatures of asthma in African-ancestry populations and highlight tretinoin as a key regulatory signal with a potential role for vitamin A biology in asthma severity and heterogeneity.

title: Prediction of nivolumab clinical response using tumor microenvironment-related multi-omics features across diverse cancer histologies
authors: Kai-Wen Cheng, Institute of Biomedical Informatics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan; Yu-Chao Wang, Institute of Biomedical Informatics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) have shown clinical benefit across multiple cancer types, yet robust biomarkers for predicting response to nivolumab remain limited. Here, we developed a multi-omics machine learning framework to predict nivolumab response across diverse tumor histologies using tumor microenvironment-related features. Five datasets were collected from the database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGaP) and the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), including patients with advanced melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, and several rare cancers. A total of 149 patients treated with nivolumab monotherapy were included, and their whole-exome sequencing and bulk RNA sequencing data were processed through a standardized preprocessing pipeline. To reduce inter-dataset variation, ComBat-seq was applied for batch correction. Candidate features were first screened using random forest, Fisherâ€™s exact test, and DESeq2, yielding 303 mutation-based and 45 expression-based features from protein-coding regions. These were further refined using LASSO logistic regression to build the final predictive model, which retained 43 features (13 mutation-based and 30 expression-based). The model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.8613 in the training set using 5-fold cross-validation and 0.7273 in the test set. Notably, COL6A1 mutation, DAPL1 downregulation, and altered expression of ATP1A3 and ATP12A were associated with extracellular matrix instability, enhanced CD8+ T-cell activity, and ion transport regulation, respectively. These findings suggest that tumor microenvironment-related multi-omics features may serve as informative biomarkers for predicting nivolumab response across cancer types and help characterize immunologically relevant determinants of response to PD-1 blockade.

title: Spatial Topology Analysis Reveals Spatial Recurrent Motifs Colorectal Cancer
authors: Jia Yao, QBRC, Peter O’Donnell Jr. School of Public Health, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas, United States; Yuqiu Yang, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Qin Zhou, QBRC, Peter O’Donnell Jr. School of Public Health, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas, United States; Munir Buhaya, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Zhikai Chi, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Guanghua Xiao, QBRC, Peter O’Donnell Jr. School of Public Health, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas, United States; Emina Huang, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Yang Xie, QBRC, Peter O’Donnell Jr. School of Public Health, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas, United States
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables systematic characterization of tumor microenvironment (TME) organization, yet methods for discovering recurrent multi-cellular configurations across patients remain limited. We present a STORM (Spatial Topology Of Recurrent Motifs) that models cell-cell spatial relationships as graphs to discover reproducible spatial motifs from single-cell resolution Xenium data. Applied to 32 colorectal cancer specimens (16 early-onset, EOCRC; 16 average-onset, AOCRC), STORM identified ten recurrent spatial motifs spanning tumor, stromal, and immune compartments. Systematic spatial analysis revealed that the Desmoplastic Fibrotic Barrier (DFB) motif physically demarcates immune-excluded zones. Comparative analysis demonstrated that EOCRC tumors harbor significantly greater DFB abundance and myofibroblastic CAF enrichment relative to AOCRC, independent of disease stage, mechanistically linking early-onset aggressiveness to enhanced immune exclusion. To enable clinical translation, we further developed a histology retrieval framework that predicts spatial motif identity directly from routine H&E images, accurately recovering motifs burden from morphological features without requiring spatial transcriptomics. Finally, these findings establish STORM as a powerful discovery engine for tumor microenvironment biology with immediate clinical relevance.

title: Integrated Spatial and Single-Cell Framework for Tumor–TME Characterization and Drug Sensitivity Mapping in NSCLC
authors: Milad Rafiee Vahid, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Jason Dobson, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Konstantinos Mavrakis, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Yilin Zhao, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Yue Ren, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Amy Hung, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Vladislav Uzunangelov, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Yulong Bai, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Shradha Srinivasan, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Diana Wiesnoski, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Brian Rabe, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Andrew Fisher, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Lauren Giampapa, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Alba Font-Tello, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Aparna Chhibber, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States; Bettina Nadorp, Bristol Myers Squibb, United States
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide, with heterogeneous responses to immunotherapy-based treatments and their combinations. Understanding the spatial tumor microenvironment (TME) is critical for identifying clinically relevant therapeutic targets and resistance mechanisms. Here, we present an integrated computational framework that combines single-cell and spatial transcriptomics with large-scale pharmacogenomic resources, including DepMap, LINCS, and CCLE to dissect the TME organization in situ. We leverage 10x Visium spatial transcriptomics data from Bristol Myers Squibb CheckMate 817 trial (CA209-817; 21 baseline samples treated with nivolumab + ipilimumab), including both adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma combined with a curated NSCLC single-cell reference atlas. We first systematically benchmark widely used spatial deconvolution methods, e.g., Cell2location, RCTD, and CARD, evaluating their robustness, reproducibility, and biological consistency in the context of NSCLC. We utilized immune- and tumor signature-based approaches as well as histopathological annotations to evaluate model performance. Across all major cell types, RCTD consistently outperforms the other methods. Then, using CytoSPACE and leveraging RCTD-derived cell type fractions as input, we map individual cells onto spatial coordinates to enable single-cell resolution spatial analyses and downstream spatial gene set-level investigations. Finally, we perform spatial drug sensitivity mapping using a BeyondCell-inspired approach, leveraging sensitivity-derived signatures to identify tumor and TME cell states and spatial niches associated with drug sensitivity or resistance. In summary, our novel approach enables the discovery of transcriptional programs driving therapeutic response and the identification of spatially resolved TME-vulnerabilities to guide precision cancer immunology strategies.

title: Unmasking Immunoglobulin Germline Diversity: Discovery of 1,556 Novel Alleles in the Human Pangenome
authors: Yu-Hsuan Yang, Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics,College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taiwan; Yu-Hui Lin, Department of Medical Genetics, National Taiwan UniversityHospital, Taiwan; Kuan-Ta Huang, Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics,College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taiwan; Mao-Jan Lin, Department of Computer Science, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Pei-Lung Chen, Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics,College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taiwan
abstract: The Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) is encoded by T-cell receptor (TR) and immunoglobulin (IG) germline genes (gAIRR), pivotal for elucidating adaptive immune mechanisms. While the International ImMunoGeneTics (IMGT) database remains the most comprehensive repository for germline genes encoding AIRR, the rate of allele discovery and incorporation remains relatively modest, not yet fully reflecting the potential of the NGS and genomics era. To address the incompleteness of current references, we utilized the gAIRR Suite to identify novel IG alleles—specifically encompassing IgH, IgK, and IgL loci—within 232 high-quality, phased, diploid assemblies from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC). To ensure identification of germline rather than rearranged sequences, we extracted sequences with 50 bp flanking regions encompassing recombination signal sequences (RSS) and characterized variants relative to IMGT reference alleles (assessed as of March 20, 2026). Through this pipeline, we identified 1,556 novel alleles (1,472 V, 13 D, and 171 J), representing a 130% increase in known IG diversity. Of these, 397 alleles were observed in more than three haplotypes, underscoring their prevalence. Although these assemblies originate from EBV-transformed lymphoblastic cell lines, which may result in missed alleles due to somatic rearrangements, the novel alleles identified with available flanking sequences are highly credible. Future validation using independent samples or experiments will further strengthen these findings. Expanding the IG catalog, this work provides a more complete reference for AIRR analysis, reducing misannotation. Furthermore, our scalable pipeline enables continuous refinement of the gAIRR references, advancing our understanding of immune-related diseases.

title: A pipeline for influenza A(H3N2) vaccine design and characterization using protein language models
authors: Victoria Howard, Vanderbilt University, United States; James Allen, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Matthew Thomas, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Ted Ross, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Ivelin Georgiev, Vanderbilt University, United States
abstract: Seasonal influenza A viruses impact millions of people around the globe. Although vaccines provide the best protection against infection, their efficacy has been limited in recent years due to frequent antigenic drift. Vaccine strains are typically selected based on predictions of dominant or emerging clades from global surveillance data, but this method can often lead to the selection of antigenically mismatched strains that induce limited antibody protection against co-circulating viral variants. In particular, the rapid evolution of influenza A(H3N2) viruses has required frequent vaccine updates that result in only low to moderate effectiveness, highlighting the need for innovative strategies to design vaccines that induce both broad antibody reactivity against co-circulating strains and neutralization across future influenza seasons. Here, we present a computational framework for engineering broadly reactive influenza A(H3N2) vaccines using protein language models (pLMs). pLMs learn generalizable sequenceâ€“function relationships from large-scale protein data and have shown strong performance in protein design tasks. Here, we leverage pLMs to generate candidate hemagglutinin antigens and develop a machine learning model to predict their antigenic properties relative to circulating strains. In a proof-of-concept study, candidates were designed using sequence data from 2013â€“2018 and evaluated against subsequently circulating strains. Notably, multiple vaccine candidates conferred protection against influenza strains circulating in 2019 and 2020. These results highlight the potential of an integrated generation-selection computational strategy to improve vaccine coverage across both current and future influenza A(H3N2) seasons. This approach can also be used for the development of seasonal influenza vaccines against other subtypes.

title: Convergent B-cell receptor sequence features point toward shared neoantigen targets in colorectal cancer
authors: Eujin Hong, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon, South Korea; Ping Lu, Krantz Family Center for Cancer Research, MGH and Harvard Medical School, Boston, United States; Hyun Uk Kim, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon, South Korea; Lloyd Bod, Krantz Family Center for Cancer Research, MGH and Harvard Medical School, Boston, United States; Doga Gulhan, Krantz Family Center for Cancer Research, MGH and Harvard Medical School, Boston, United States
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Despite recent advances in immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy, its efficacy in CRC is largely limited to mismatch repair-deficient (MMRd) tumors, highlighting the need for alternative immunotherapies. B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoires and tumor neoantigens are key components of anti-tumor humoral immunity, yet their landscape in CRC remains incompletely characterized. We systematically profiled BCR clonotypes and somatic mutationâ€“derived neoantigen candidates across CRC and investigated their potential immunological links. Using single-cell RNA-seq data from CRC patients, we reconstructed tumor-infiltrating BCR sequences and quantified BCR diversity and its association with clinical variables. Although exact clonotype sharing across patients was minimal, k-merâ€“based CDR3 analysis revealed convergent sequence features, suggesting shared antigen-driven B-cell responses across individuals. To investigate potential antigenic drivers, we identified and characterized recurrent somatic mutations across tumors from different patients. These shared mutations represent candidate sources of common tumor-derived neoantigens. CRC patients exhibit convergent BCR sequence features despite largely private clonotypes, potentially reflecting antigen-driven selection by shared tumor-derived neoantigens. This integrative framework provides a foundation for the rational design of broadly applicable B-cell-directed therapies in CRC.

title: Soft-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Switch Transformers for Peptide-MHC Binding Prediction in the JANUS Framework
authors: Alan Perez-Rathke, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, United States; Justin Balko, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, United States; Jens Meiler, Vanderbilt University, United States
abstract: Accurate prediction of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (MHC) binding supports neoantigen discovery and interpretation of immunopeptidomics data. We extend JANUS, a transformer-based model for joint peptide and MHC sequence modeling, to evaluate a soft-gated mixture-of-experts (MoE) switch transformer. The architecture augments transformer feed-forward blocks with shared experts and routed experts selected through differentiable gating applied to token-level representations. We integrate MoE layers into JANUS and train on single- and multi-MHC allele immunopeptidomics data. We compare the MoE model with (i) dense feed-forward transformer baselines and (ii) NetMHCpan and NetMHCIIpan on MHC class I and class II benchmarks. Performance is evaluated using precision-recall area under the curve (PR AUC) and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC). We also investigate ranking performance for each MHC allele to determine whether MoE routing improves ranking of candidate peptides relative to dense transformer baselines and NetMHCpan and NetMHCIIpan.

title: Evaluating Physicochemical Metrics for Clustering Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoires
authors: Ludmila Danilova, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Bahman Afsari, National Cancer Institute, United States; Elana Fertig, University of Maryland, United States; Neeha Zaidi, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Elizabeth Jaffee, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Erika Darrah, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Clifton Bingham, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Jonathan Schneck, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Alexander Favorov, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Alexander Girgis, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Lvovs Dmitrijs, University of Maryland, United States; Janelle Montagne, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Luciane Kagohara, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Hanzhi Wang, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Theron Palmer, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Emily Davis-Marcisak, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Amanda Huff, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Predicting antigen reactivity from adaptive immune receptor repertoires (AIRRs) remains a central challenge in computational immunology. Most methods infer antigen specificity by clustering receptors according to sequence similarity, commonly using substitution matrices such as BLOSUM62. However, these matrices were developed for detecting homology in evolutionarily related proteins rather than in V(D)J-recombined immune receptors, and their suitability for AIRR analysis has not been systematically established. We developed Homolig (Homol-Ig), a unified software framework for AIRR clustering and receptor sequence characterization under user-specified similarity metrics. In addition, we introduce new similarity measures derived by matrix factorization of amino acid physicochemical properties, providing interpretable alternatives to traditional substitution matrices. Using this framework, we compared sequence-only distances, conventional substitution matrices, and our new physicochemical similarities across 383 simulated and biological TCR and BCR repertoires. Physicochemical and traditional approaches showed broadly similar overall clustering performance. However, the membership of antigen-enriched clusters differed substantially across metrics, indicating that similar aggregate performance can lead to different inferred immune responses. We further applied these similarity matrices to pancreatic cancer and rheumatoid arthritis repertoires to identify disease-associated antigen signals. These inferences varied markedly across matrix choices, highlighting a lack of consensus among current similarity-based AIRR methods. Although no single similarity consistently outperformed the others, our new similarities improved interpretability by linking receptor clusters to explicit physicochemical properties. These results identify metric choice as a major source of variability in AIRR analysis and highlight the value of multiâ€‘metric benchmarking for robust immune repertoire discovery.

title: Gland-centric spatial multi-omics profiling uncovers distinct microenvironment trajectories and early predictors of prostate cancer progression during active surveillance
authors: Kunlun Wang, Oregon Health and Science University, United States
abstract: Active surveillance reduces overtreatment in low- and intermediate-risk prostate cancer, yet a subset of lesions progress despite apparently similar baseline histology. We hypothesized that progression risk is encoded in baseline epithelialâ€“stromalâ€“immune ecosystem organization that is not captured by routine H&E assessment. We analyzed longitudinal paired biopsies collected from the same lesion at two timepoints (A and B), separated by a median interval of 24 months, in an active surveillance cohort (n=56), integrating 40-plex cyclic immunofluorescence (CyCIF), matched H&E gland pathology annotations, and bulk TempO-seq transcriptomics. After image quality control and CyCIF preprocessing, we performed MESMER single-cell segmentation, UniFORM normalization across batches, and CellCharter and Leiden Clustering to delineate epithelial, stromal, and immune subtypes. To anchor CyCIF spatial features to pathology, we registered CyCIF to adjacent H&E using VALIS and quantified intragland and periglandular (20â€“80 Âµm) cell-type densities around annotated gland types. Pathologist-annotated gland masks (including benign glands, glandular atrophy, and Gleason grade 3â€“5 glands) enabled gland-resolved analyses to interrogate mechanisms of prostate cancer progression during active surveillance, revealing gland gradeâ€“specific shifts in epithelial and stromal cell density and distance-dependent immune gradients, including myeloid and mast cellâ€“associated patterns concentrated near gland boundaries. To further link microenvironment organization to progression, we quantified cellâ€“cell spatial interactions using complementary neighborhood frameworks (GraphCompass and i-Niche), identifying recurrent interaction programs and observing substantially stronger time-dependent neighborhood remodeling in progressors than in non-progressors. Finally, we assembled baseline (timepoint A) multimodal features spanning tissue-level composition, gland-centric density and architecture metrics, neighborhood enrichment signatures, and TempO-seq programs, and trained predictive models for progression classification while highlighting interpretable early-indicator features. Together, these results support gland-centric spatial multi-omics as a path toward improved early risk stratification in active surveillance.

title: Multi-omic Characterization of the FOXD3-Mediated Immune Microenvironment in Melanoma
authors: Colette Trouillot, Drexel University, United States; Dan Erkes, Jefferson University, United States; Diana Melissaratos, Jefferson University, United States; Scott Varney, Jefferson University, United States; Will Madden, Jefferson University, United States; Timothy Purwin, Jefferson University, United States; Andrew Aplin, Jefferson University, United States
abstract: Advances in immune checkpoint (IC) and mitogen activate protein kinase (MAPK) pathway inhibitor therapies have improved progression free survival and overall survival for cutaneous melanoma patients in part due to changes in tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). Roughly 50% of melanomas have activation mutations in v-Raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B (BRAF) and MAPK inhibitor (MAPKi) treatment is approved for treating BRAF V600E. The neural crest transcription factor Forkhead box D3 (FOXD3) is primarily active in early embryoblast formation but increases during MAPKi treatment and downregulates the immune checkpoint protein V-domain Ig suppressor of T cell activation (VISTA); however, additional downstream impact on the TIME is not fully clarified. We used RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from inducibly expressed FOXD3 melanoma cell lines to identify activated and repressed gene signatures for FOXD3. Enrichment analysis confirmed the repressed gene signature in bulk and single cell RNA-seq data. Gene signature scoring of additional publicly available RNA-seq data confirmed FOXD3 expression increases with MAPKi treatment in cell lines and patient data. We analyzed the downregulated signature of malignant tumors against proportions of immune cell types and found CD8+ T-cells were correlated with FOXD3 levels. Concurrent in vivo mouse experiments and RNA-seq gene-set activity scoring analyses found that higher levels of FOXD3 are associated with decreased levels of myeloid derived suppressor cells, dendritic cells, and CD8+ T-cells. These findings reveal FOXD3â€™s role in modulating the TIME which we will expand using single cell transcriptomic analyses to understand FOXD3-driven TIME changes in MAPKi and IC inhibitor therapeutics.

title: Similarity-based counts weighting improves differential T cell clonotype abundance analysis
authors: Thomas C. Smits, Radboudumc, Netherlands; Franka Buytenhuijs, Radboudumc, Netherlands; Ankur Ankan, Radboudumc, Netherlands; Radu-Florian Diaconescu, University of Göttingen, Germany; Johannes Textor, Radboudumc, Netherlands
abstract: Differential T cell clonotype abundance analysis can give insight into clonal expansion following vaccination, infection, and other immune responses. However, because the majority of T cell receptor (TCR) sequences are private, data is highly sparse and overdispersed, causing both the sensitivity and specificity of differential abundance analysis to be limited. It has been shown that TCRs that bind the same antigen are highly similar in sequence and structure. Based on this, we propose a similarity-based weighting strategy to increase true positive detection in differential abundance analysis, by first finding TCR neighbourhoods and subsequently weighting the read counts of sequences. This preprocessing step can be combined with any downstream differential analysis. Using both simulated and real datasets, we show that similarity-based weighting can improve the true positive rate (TPR) while controlling the false positive rate (FPR). We simulated datasets using immuneSIM and incorporated sequences from the VDJ database in the treatment group, enabling assessment of the TPR and FPR. We observe increases in TPR from under 20% without weighting to over 90% with similarity-based weighted counts, while the FPR remains under 5%, using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and DESeq2. We also show the power of similarity-based weighting in TCR data from SRBC-infected mice, using permutation testing to assess false positive control. This simple preprocessing step can be integrated in existing pipelines through our accompanying R package (https://github.com/thomcsmits/simweightR). We examined local neighbourhoods with the Hamming distance and BLOSUM62 alignment, although this can easily be extended towards other similarity metrics.

title: Learning Interpretable Disease-relevant Gene Programs for Predicting Personalized Disease Risk
authors: Tala Sadat Yasenpoor, University of Connecticut, United States; Marjan Hosseini, University of Connecticut, United States; Alyssa Matz, University Of Connecticut, Department of Immunology, United States; Beiyan Zhou, University of Connecticut, Department of Immunology, United States; Derek Aguiar, University of Connecticut, Institute for Systems Genomics, United States
abstract: Early prediction of disease risk can inform interventions that delay onset or reduce severity. Single-cell gene expression profiles capture immune cell heterogeneity and coordinated molecular programs not reflected in traditional clinical risk scores, but existing expression-based risk models either ignore the coordinated gene activity underlying cellular processes, discard cell-type composition, or produce uninterpretable predictions. Here, we introduce a Bayesian supervised Poisson factorization model that jointly learns disease-relevant gene programs (DRGPs), quantifies the contribution of individual immune cell types to disease risk, and predicts disease status from single-cell RNA-seq data. The model decomposes the expression matrix into latent factors representing gene programs, optionally informed by prior pathway knowledge, while an L1 -penalized logistic regression provides an interpretable link between sample-level factors, auxiliary clinical covariates, and cell-type composition to disease labels. We derive variational Bayes algorithms for efficient inference under both pathway-informed and de novo configurations. We evaluate our DRGP method on synthetic single-cell data and a COVID-19 single-cell atlas. On simulations, DRGPs recover ground-truth programs and gene subsets driving the outcome label; on the experimental data, the model achieves competitive predictive performance while recovering biologically coherent programs and cell-type contributions consistent with validated COVID-19 severity biomarkers, demonstrating that joint supervision yields interpretable, immune-relevant structure without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

title: Ontogenesis and Development of Circadian Leukocyte Trafficking in Humans
authors: Andrew Kwon, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Thomas Brooks, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Greg Grant, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Shaon Sengupta, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States
abstract: Background and purpose: The ontogeny of circadian regulation in early human development remains incompletely understood. For example, while central-clockâ€“driven sleepâ€“wake rhythms begin to appear around 16 weeks, the developmental timing of peripheral clock maturation is far less well understood. Circadian regulation of the immune system has a crucial role in effective immune response. One of the most salient features of this temporal organization is the rhythmic trafficking of leukocyte subpopulations between blood and peripheral tissues across the 24-hour cycle. Daily rhythms in leukocyte trafficking offer a sensitive and quantifiable readout of circadian timing mechanisms, and thus may serve as an early marker of clock emergence. Methods: We analyzed a retrospective dataset of 501,275 complete blood counts (CBCs) from infants aged 0-11 months at the Childrenâ€™s Hospital of Philadelphia. To minimize confounding physiological stress, a stringent filtering pipeline was applied, yielding a final cohort of 25,933 individuals with single blood draws and no significant medical complications. For this pseudo-longitudinal study, CBCs were binned by collection hour and stratified by age to identify potential developmental shifts in immune cell distribution. We also consider normal body temperature readouts when available (10,193 individuals) as a positive control. Cosinor analysis via glmmTMB was used for quantification of rhythmicity. Results: For newborns more than two months old, population-level rhythmicity of leukocyte trafficking, as well as for subpopulations, is statistically significant, mirroring the emergence of cortisol rhythms. Interestingly, lymphocyte trafficking rhythms differ significantly from known biology in adults, suggesting possible relevance for chronotherapy in infants and children. Conclusion: Our findings point to leukocyte trafficking as a tractable measure of the emergence of peripheral circadian rhythms. Future research should focus on the mechanisms by which this control is established, as well as on how these rhythms may be clinically harnessed.

title: Tracing Class-Switch Recombination (CSR) Introns in long-read BCR Sequencing Data
authors: Chinmay Vaidya, Dartmouth College, United States
abstract: Targeted long-read single-cell sequencing (TLR-SC) of immune receptors captures full-length receptor transcripts directly, providing sequences of V(D)J regions, constant regions, secreted/membrane-anchored regions, and large gene insertions that standard short-read sequencing cannot. These additional regions are a potentially rich source of information about cell dynamics in response to perturbations. For example, TLR-SC can reveal switch regions within a B cell receptorâ€™s constant region that indicate a B cell lineageâ€™s history of class-switch recombination events. However, each protocol typically uses a unique read structure and requires protocol-specific computational pipeline for tasks like barcode demultiplexing and immune receptor annotation. To address these issues, we developed a Read-structure Agnostic Demultiplexer (RAD), a C++ package versatile enough to handle existing TLR-SC sequencing protocols. We then apply RAD to TLR-SC data of single-cell in vitro class-switched human B cells and targeted long-read sequencing from spatial transcriptomic data of the human tonsil. Analysis of these TLR-SC datasets captures transitions of individual BCR clones from membrane-anchored to secreted, and class-switched antibodies within a tonsil section. Taken altogether, we can utilize the â€œscarsâ€ of B cell receptor recombination as unique historical barcodes of CSR, allowing novel insights into single-cell genetic determinants of class-switch recombination.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Machine learning–guided characterization of peptide toxicity for safety-aware design of antimicrobial peptides
authors: Nicole Soto-García, Departamento de Ingeniería en Computación, Universidad de Magallanes, Chile; David Medina-Ortiz, Departamento de Ingeniería en Computación, Universidad de Magallanes, Chile
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics, but their clinical translation is limited by safety issues, as many peptides with strong antimicrobial activity also exhibit adverse effects such as hemolysis, cytotoxicity, or immunogenicity. Current computational approaches have improved activity prediction, yet toxicity modeling remains fragmented across heterogeneous datasets, independent prediction tasks, and inconsistent annotations, preventing the development of reliable design strategies. In particular, the lack of unified toxicity-aware models limits the ability to identify peptides that simultaneously satisfy activity and safety constraints. Here, we present a machine learning framework for the systematic characterization of peptide toxicity using curated multi-source datasets and unified modeling strategies. Peptide sequences were integrated from public databases and literature reports and standardized using controlled annotations covering multiple toxicity types, including hemolysis, cytotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and general toxicity. Using these datasets, we evaluated multiple representation strategies, including physicochemical descriptors, sequence-derived features, and protein language model embeddings, to train predictive models for multi-label and multi-task toxicity prediction. Preliminary analyses reveal the existence of both global and local patterns associated with peptide toxicity, which can be captured through embedding-based representations, interpretable models, and clustering approaches. These patterns are being used to derive empirical rules linking sequence properties with adverse effects, providing the basis for safety-aware peptide design. Ongoing work focuses on integrating these predictors into conditional and multi-objective generation strategies to guide the exploration of peptide sequence space under simultaneous activity and toxicity constraints. This work-in-progress highlights the importance of unified toxicity modeling and suggests that machine learning can enable rule-guided and safety-aware discovery of antimicrobial peptides against multidrug-resistant bacteria.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Interpretable protein function predictions with deepFRI2
authors: Paweł Szczerbiak, Sano Centre for Computational Personalised​ Medicine,Kraków, Poland, Poland; Rund Tawfiq, Sano Centre for Computational Personalised​ Medicine,Kraków, Poland, Saudi Arabia; Adam Nowak, Sano Centre for Computational Personalised​ Medicine,Kraków, Poland, Poland; Witold Wydmański, Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, JagiellonianUniversity, Kraków, Poland, Poland; Jakub Wojciechowski, Sano Centre for Computational Personalised​ Medicine,Kraków, Poland, Poland; Valentyn Bezshapkin, Institute of Microbiology and Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, Ukraine; Jakub Adamczyk, Faculty of Computer Science, AGH University of Kraków,Kraków, Poland, Poland; Lukasz Szydlowski, Sano Centre for Computational Personalised​ Medicine,Kraków, Poland, Poland; Tomasz Kosciolek, Sano Centre for Computational Personalised​ Medicine,Kraków, Poland, Poland
abstract: Protein function prediction remains a key challenge in biology due to the rapid growth of sequence and structure data enabled by high-throughput technologies and recent advances in protein structure prediction. While deep learning methods and protein language models have improved predictive performance, effectively integrating sequence and structural information for large-scale function prediction remains an open problem. Here, we introduce deepFRI2, an upgraded framework of deepFRI (Deep Functional Residue Identification) for predicting protein function using Gene Ontology terms and Enzyme Commission numbers. Like its predecessor, deepFRI2 operates in two complementary modes: sequence-based and sequence+structure-based. Architecturally, the model consists of two main components: a structural prober, which leverages shallow convolutions over distograms for improved interpretability, and a sequence analyzer, powered by ESM with lightweight attention, to capture evolutionary and sequence-derived signals. This dual design enables robust functional inference in metagenomic settings, where protein structures are unavailable, as well as high-precision annotation when structural information is known. Moreover, its modular architecture allows disentangling structure- and sequence-driven signals while maintaining interpretability. Guided by principles of simplicity and robustness, deepFRI2 uses only a few million parameters yet achieves strong performance across all evaluated benchmarks, improving upon deepFRI and reaching state-of-the-art results. At the same time, it preserves a high level of interpretability and scalability â€” two often overlooked, but crucial features.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: CB-Search: A method that improves searching for similar protein motifs with biased compositions
authors: Patryk Jarnot, Silesian University of Technology, Poland
abstract: Traditional protein similarity search algorithms have historically prioritized homology detection, leaving motifs with biased composition, such as compositionally biased regions, low-complexity regions, short tandem repeats, and homopolymers, largely underaddressed. Standard similarity measures, such as e-value, are often unreliable for these sequences because of their unusual amino acid distributions and distinct evolutionary pathways. To bridge this gap, we introduce CB-Search, a novel computational method designed to identify similar protein motifs based on physicochemical similarity rather than homology. CB-Search implements three distinct alignment strategies (local, global, and globalâ€“local) and SimiComp, a new algorithm utilizing dynamic window sizing and relative composition thresholds to identify compositionally similar regions. Additionally, the method accelerates computation time by using a 2-mer filtering step and introduces a similarity score that normalizes results and that is independent of the lambda parameter known from e-value. We validated our method against BLAST using transmembrane domains, RGG boxes, and keratin type II head domains which demonstrated that CB-Search's similarity score identifies significantly more true positive alignments than e-value. Furthermore, the 2-mer pre-alignment filter significantly reduced search execution time without compromising accuracy. In conclusion, our new CB-Search method is an efficient and specialized tool for the discovery, clustering, and functional analysis of proteins motifs with biased compositions.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Distilling evolutionary context into single-sequence protein language models through phylogeny-aware fine-tuning
authors: Ziyi Wang, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Whiting School of Engineering, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA, United States; Harsh Srivastava, Center for Genomics & Systems Biology, Department of Biology, New York University, New York, NY, USA, United States; Jane Carlton, Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute, Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, USA, United States
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) trained on millions of protein sequences produce feature-rich embeddings that encode structural, functional and physiochemical properties. However, during inference, each sequence is embedded independently, with no awareness of phylogenetic context. While multiple sequence alignment (MSA)-based transformer architectures can incorporate evolutionary context, running inference over full MSAs is computationally rate-limiting, making them impractical for large-scale applications. To address both limitations, we propose a novel phylogeny-aware pLM that distills evolutionary signals derived from MSAs at training time while retraining single-sequence inference efficiency. Using a frozen ESM-MSA-1b encoder, we extract and aggregate homolog representations from 3,395 eukaryotic MSAs sourced from OpenProteinSet via a learned attention mechanism that jointly weighs sequence content and phylogenetic distance. This phylogeny-weighted signal is then used to condition ESM-2 150M backbone through layer-wise FiLM modulation. Evaluated on 43,559 non-redundant Swiss-Prot eukaryotic sequences sharing no greater than 30% sequence similarity to the training set, our phylogeny-aware pLM outperforms the baseline ESM-2 150M model across all measures of cluster quality. Across Pfam domains and protein family annotations, our model yields tighter, better-separated clusters, reflected in gains in k-NN purity, logistic regression accuracy, and Calinskiâ€“Harabasz score, alongside a reduction in Daviesâ€“Bouldin index. These gains indicate that the model more effectively captures evolutionarily conserved sequence relationships with downstream benefits for pattern-recognition tasks, including homology detection, motif discovery, domain identification, and protein function prediction. Overall, our phylogeny-aware fine-tuning strategy improves functional grouping of proteins and provides a parameter efficient approach for enhancing biological interpretability of pLM embeddings.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Systematic classification and annotation of polymorphic toxin domain Families
authors: Yongjun Tan, Saint Louis University, United States; Huan Li, Saint Louis University, United States; Theresa Schneider, Saint Louis University, United States; Dapeng Zhang, Saint Louis University, United States
abstract: Bacteria have evolved a diverse repertoire of molecular conflict systems that mediate kin discrimination and enable competition for ecological niches.
