Among these, polymorphic toxin systems (PTSs) represent one of the most widespread and functionally diverse classes, characterized by multiple secretion pathways, numerous functionally diverse toxin repertoires, and structurally distinct cognate immunity proteins. Over the past 15 years, we applied a domain-centric â€œguilt-by-associationâ€ genome-mining pipeline to systematically identify hundreds of thousands of PTS-related components, characterize their domain architectures, and predict key toxic determinants. Despite these advances, the functional annotation and structural diversity of PTS toxin domains remain incompletely resolved. This limitation is largely driven by extreme sequence divergence and limited experimental characterization, which hinder accurate functional inference. To address this challenge, we developed an integrative computational framework, combining sensitive profile-based homology searches, two-stage network clustering to define domain families and superfamilies, and structure-informed comparisons using AlphaFold-based predictions. This approach enables comprehensive characterization of PTS toxin domain diversity and improves functional annotation by integrating sequence and structural information. Our analyses reveal previously unrecognized relationships among domain families and refine their classification within major structural fold superfamilies, including HNH nucleases, restriction endonuclease-like folds, BECR nucleases, deaminases, VOC enzymes, and ADP-ribosyltransferases. Compared with conventional annotation tools, our approach demonstrates improved performance and detects distant, previously unrecognized relationships. Overall, this work provides a scalable and robust framework for protein function annotation in highly diverse and rapidly evolving systems, offering a generalizable strategy for annotating deeply divergent protein families and guiding future experimental validation.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Comparing machine learning approaches for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) in gene activation
authors: David Cooper, Butler University, United States; Dina Zidan, Butler University, United States; Elizabeth Durbin, Butler University, United States; Kelly Van Busum, Butler University, United States; Alexandre Erkine, Butler University, United States; Caleb Class, Butler University, United States
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins play an important role in the process of gene activation, as transcription activation domains (ADs) are highly disordered, lacking a specific structure or consensus sequence. In this study, we developed and evaluated machine learning models in order to classify protein sequences as functional ADs. The training data included over a million random sequences published from Hahn et. al and ~19K natural sequences with mutations published from Sanborn et al. The testing data included a held-out division of both training sets (20% of each), in addition to two independent datasets. Classification models predicting AD functionality (binary) were trained using a feedforward neural network, logistic lasso regression, and random forest methods based on physicochemical properties, as well as a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network developed to make predictions from the sequences themselves. All models performed well on heldâ€‘out random sequences (AUROC 0.92â€“0.97) and natural ADs (AUROC 0.95â€“0.97), except Lasso regression, which performed worse on natural sequences. Performance declined on an independent random screen (AUROC 0.80â€“0.84) and was poor on designed sequences (AUROC 0.57â€“0.65), likely due to their atypical composition. Models favored high specificity over sensitivity, though LSTM achieved the best sensitivity while achieving reasonable precision. Analysis of the feature-based models indicated a focus on simple biochemical features like isoelectric point and hydrophobicity, while LSTM captured both similar and more complex patterns directly from sequence data.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Uncovering genes involved in un(der)studied functions and phenotypes across species using graph learning of molecular networks and biomedical ontologies
authors: Keenan Manpearl, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Alexander McKim, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Arjun Krishnan, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus, United States
abstract: Accurately predicting new links between genes and biological functions, phenotypes, and diseases is crucial for closing gaps in our understanding of human health and disease. Machine learning methods have been successful at predicting these links, however most approaches require labeled training data, thus they are not suitable for biological context for which no genes/proteins are already known to be associated. Recent methods aim to overcome this limitation by incorporating representations of biological contexts derived from terms in biomedical ontologies into the prediction process, and/or by incorporating training data from multiple species. However, most methods use representations of proteins derived from their primary sequences and consistently underperform for prediction of biological processes, which requires more contextual information, compared to, say, molecular function which is mostly intrinsic to the protein. Methods that use representations derived from molecular networks overcome this limitation by incorporating interactions between genes/proteins, but, to our knowledge, no network-based method exists that uses both zero-shot techniques and multi-species features. We present a novel framework for making and evaluating few- and zero-shot predictions using a multi-species feature space that captures both within-species interactions and cross-species orthology. While most state-of-the-art prediction methods are only evaluated on The Gene Ontology, through a rigorous evaluation scheme, we show that our approach can make predictions in the Gene Ontology Biological Process Branch and Unified Phenotype Ontology, for terms with and without known annotations, using a feature space representing genes from humans and five model organisms.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Identifying targets of chemical compounds using multi-modal chemical-genetic interaction screens
authors: Hamid Safizadeh, UMN Twin Cities, ECE & CSE, Minneapolis, MN, USA; UW–RiverFalls, Comp., Info. & Data Sci., River Falls, WI, USA, United States; Sheena Li, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science, Saitama, Japan; Donnelly Centre for Cell. & Biomol. Res., Toronto, Canada, Canada; Luis Alberto Vega Isuhuaylas, Donnelly Centre for Cellular and Biomolecular Research, Toronto, ON, Canada, Canada; Mami Yoshimura, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science (CSRS), Wako, Saitama, Japan, Japan; Yoko Yashiroda, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science (CSRS), Wako, Saitama, Japan, Japan; Hiroyuki Hirano, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science (CSRS), Wako, Saitama, Japan, Japan; Hiroyuki Osada, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science, Saitama, Japan; Institute of Microbial Chemistry, Shinagawa, Tokyo, Japan, Japan; Minoru Yoshida, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science (CSRS), Wako, Saitama, Japan, Japan; Charles Boone, RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science, Saitama, Japan; Donnelly Centre for Cell. & Biomol. Res., Toronto, Canada, Canada; Chad Myers, Univ. Minnesota–Twin Cities, Comp. Sci. Eng. & Bioinformatics Comput. Biol., Minneapolis, MN, USA, United States
abstract: Chemical-genomic approaches provide a powerful, unbiased approach for characterizing the modes of action of chemical compounds. In a recent study, we demonstrated the feasibility of scaling this technology to screen thousands of compounds using a high-throughput yeast chemical-genomic system, generating chemical-genetic interaction profiles for >13,000 compounds and predicting their modes of action at the biological process level. Our predictions enabled the prioritization of ~1500 compounds for further study, but they lack the precision required to identify individual protein targets. We developed a multi-modal yeast chemical-genomic pipeline where compounds are subjected to parallel mutant sensitivity profiling against complementary mutant collections spanning non-essential genes (haploid deletion mutants) and essential genes (haploid temperature-sensitive and diploid heterozygous deletion mutants). We also developed novel computational pipelines for integrating multi-modal chemical-genetic interaction data to derive confident predictions of specific protein-level targets. Our computational approach is based on methods previously developed for identifying the source of rumors in a social network. Specifically, we model protein targets of compounds as rumor sources that spread inhibitory signals to neighboring nodes in a functional network and identify the single source most likely to explain the observed, diffused chemical-genetic interaction signal. We applied these pipelines to ~1000 compounds from the RIKEN Natural Product Depository and other compound libraries and identified several compounds with high-confidence putative targets. We confirmed the accuracy for a subset of these predicted targets by generating drug-resistant mutants and using whole-genome sequencing to identify genetic loci where resistance-associated mutations emerged. Overall, our new approach enables the translation of chemical-genetic profiling data into more precise hypotheses about specific molecular targets of compounds.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Disentangling functional and stability effects of protein mutations with disentangled protein language models
authors: Kerr Ding, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Ziang Li, Georgia Institute Of Technology, United States; Tony Tu, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Jiaqi Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Yunan Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Understanding how evolutionary constraints shape protein sequences is fundamental to deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying protein stability and function, with broad implications for protein engineering and therapeutic development. Recent advances in protein language models (pLMs) have enabled accurate prediction of mutation effects, capturing the evolutionary pressure that governs protein sequence variation. A critical challenge, however, remains in disentangling the intertwined mutation effects on protein stability and function, as evolutionary signals conflate stability-driven and function-driven pressures, obscuring the mechanistic basis of mutation effects. In this work, we introduce DETANGO, a deep learning framework that explicitly deconvolves the mutation effects on protein functions by removing components attributable to stability perturbations from pLM-predicted mutation effects. DETANGO estimates a functional plausibility score for each single-point mutation that is the component of the mutation effect not accounted for by changes in stability. Single-point mutations with low functional plausibilities are predicted to be stable-but-inactive (SBI) variants, whose compromised activities are caused by direct perturbations on functional mechanisms rather than stability. Residues enriched for such variants are inferred to be functionally critical, as indicated by the strong pressures to maintain protein function. Through extensive benchmarking experiments, we show that DETANGO accurately identifies SBI variants and pinpoints functional sites across contexts, including ligand binding, catalysis, and allostery. Moreover, extending DETANGO from individual proteins to homologous protein families reveals shared and distinctive functional patterns across protein families. Collectively, these results establish DETANGO as a biologically grounded framework for disentangling evolutionary constraints and advancing mechanistic understanding of protein function.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Massively parallel analysis of coding mutations with CodonPrime
authors: Xiaoyu Zhao, University of California San Diego, United States; Isabella Panagiotou, University of California San Diego, United States; Francisco Sánchez-Rivera, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, United States; Marcus Kelly, University of California San Diego, United States; Trey Ideker, University of California San Diego, United States
abstract: Most coding mutations are of unknown function, limiting their biological and therapeutic interpretation. While prime editing enables precise genomic alterations, mutations often reside in sequence contexts unfavorable to current prime-editing guide RNA (pegRNA) designs. Here we develop CodonPrime, a prime-editing framework that exploits codon degeneracy surrounding a mutation site to substantially expand its targeting set of pegRNAs. We use CodonPrime to screen ~2500 amino acid mutations spanning 298 cancer-associated genes, yielding an 11.4-fold increase in per-mutation editing efficiency relative to conventional pegRNA designs. Approximately 10% of these mutations enhance cell growth, validating known oncogenic hotspots and uncovering 30 previously uncharacterized mutations with oncogenic potential (e.g. HNF1AR272C). Our analysis uncovers dominant effects in paralogous genes (e.g. RHOBTB1/2) and organization of mutant phenotypes in functional pathways (e.g. PI3K-MTOR signaling). We formulate a general-purpose transformer for design of codon-optimized pegRNAs, enabling scalable interrogation of human coding variants.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Long-Read Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Reveals Isoform-Level Transcriptional and Immune Repertoire Diversity in Influenza Infection
authors: Sehwa Hong, Research Institute, National Cancer Center; Interdisciplinary Program for Bioinformatics, Seoul National University, South Korea; Daejin Hyung, Research Institute, National Cancer Center, South Korea; Hyeyeong Hwang, Research Institute, National Cancer Center, South Korea; Yeonhui Lee, Research Institute, National Cancer Center, South Korea; Soo Young Cho, Department of Molecular and Life Science, Hanyang University, South Korea; Je Kyung Seong, Korea Model Animal Priority Center, Research Institute for Veterinary Science, Seoul National University, South Korea; Charny Park, Research Institute, National Cancer Center, South Korea
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) has advanced our understanding of molecular mechanisms underlying immune responses to viral infection; however, its reliance on short-read sequencing limits the characterization of isoform-level regulation and accurate reconstruction of immune receptor diversity. In this study, we performed PacBio long-read scRNAseq on lung tissues at multiple time points (days 0, 8, and 28 post-infection), enabling full-length transcriptome analysis and immune repertoire reconstruction simultaneously at single-cell resolution. Our analysis reveals that influenza infection triggers a widespread, cell-type-specific splicing program that is often invisible at the gene level. We identified splicing changes in genes involved in innate immune function and host-pathogen interactions, including a retained intron in Cd14 and a domain truncation in Dnm2, which may modulate macrophage signaling and viral entry efficiency during infection. Long-read sequencing also enabled the reconstruction of a paired, fully covered immune receptor repertoire, uncovering a distinct class-switch recombination toward IgG2a and IgG3 isotypes following infection, along with clonal expansion of specific VH subgroups such as IGHV1-14. Somatic hypermutation (SHM) patterns further confirmed plasma cell maturation during the post-infection phase. Together, our study demonstrates that long-read scRNAseq overcomes key limitations of conventional approaches by enabling simultaneous resolution of isoform diversity and immune receptor architecture, providing new insights into the molecular and clonal mechanisms underlying host antiviral immune responses. These findings also highlight the potential of this approach for identifying novel diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets by linking transcriptomic structural diversity with adaptive immune responses.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: ComFlow: An Optimal Transport Framework that Deciphers Intra- and Intercellular Signaling Landscapes in both 2D and 3D Tissue Systems
authors: Manfei Bella Xie, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Yuling Zhu, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Yunfei Hu, Department of Computer Science, Vanderbilt University, United States; Yiru Chen, Systems and Informatics of Zhejiang University-Universityof Edinburgh Institute, China; Bingshan Li, Department of Molecular Physiology Biophysics, VanderbiltUniversity, United States; Marjan Rafat, Department of Chemical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Shan Meltzer, Department of Pharmacology, Vanderbilt University, United States; Tae Hyun Hwang, Department of Surgical Research, Vanderbilt University, United States; Zixuan Cang, Department of Mathematics and Center for Research inScientific Computation, North Carolina State University, United States; Yanxiang Zhao, Department of Mathematics, The George Washington University, United States; Lu Zhang, Department of Computer Science, Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong; Xin Maizie Zhou, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Computer Science, andData Science Institute, Vanderbilt University, United States
abstract: Cell–cell communication (CCC) is fundamental to multicellular life, governing development, tissue homeostasis, and immune responses. Disease often arises when cells fail to communicate properly or misinterpret molecular signals. Understanding how CCC pathways are disrupted can therefore reveal new therapeutic opportunities. Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have transformed CCC studies from labor-intensive, low-throughput experimental approaches into scalable, data-driven analyses that probe diverse cell types and signaling interactions. However, scRNA-seq inherently lacks spatial context, despite the fact that most CCC events occur over short distances. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) offers a promising alternative, yet CCC inference from ST data remains underexplored—particularly in jointly modeling inter- and intracellular signaling and accounting for ligand–receptor competition. To address this gap, we introduce 2DComFlow, a novel optimal transport (OT)–based framework that models complex CCC dynamics, capturing global competition and cooperation among signaling molecules within and between cells or spatial spots. While most spatial assays provide 2D tissue sections, cellular communication can occur both within a section and across adjacent sections. Yet CCC in three-dimensional (3D) tissue architecture remains largely underexplored. We therefore extend our workflow to incorporate communication along the z-axis, yielding 3DComFlow, which enables CCC inference beyond conventional 2D analyses and uncovers spatial communication patterns that would otherwise remain undetected. We apply our framework across diverse datasets spanning species (human and mouse), varying cell numbers, gene panels, and biological conditions. Comparative analyses (e.g., disease vs. control) uncover both conserved and context-specific signaling networks, demonstrating the broad utility of our approach for advancing spatial systems biology and precision medicine.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Measuring the copy number and active fraction of 5S and 45S rDNA units using long-read nanopore sequencing
authors: Suhani Balachandran, NIH / NHGRI, United States; Steven Solar, NIH / NHGRI, United States; Adam Phillippy, NIH / NHGRI, United States
abstract: Human ribosomal RNA genes are organized as tandemly repeating arrays of a composite repeat structure known as ribosomal DNA (rDNA), with the 5S rDNA array located on Chromosome 1 and multiple 45S rDNA arrays located on the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes. Each genome contains hundreds of rDNA copies, and their copy number and transcriptional activity can vary widely between individuals, making them difficult to analyze from sequencing data alone. To enable the analysis of these important genes and uncover any associations with disease, we developed a method that can estimate rDNA copy number and activity using long-read nanopore sequencing. Rather than mapping reads to a reference genome, we instead identify individual rDNAs directly on the single-molecule sequencing reads and infer their transcriptional activity based on the observed methylation patterns. Application of our pipeline to thousands of brain- and blood-derived nanopore samples from the NIH Center for Alzheimer's and Related Dementias showed a weak positive correlation between the number of active 5S and 45S copies, no correlation between the total number of 5S and 45S copies, and a relatively consistent number of active rDNA units regardless of sample age or total rDNA copy number. We also detected lower than expected sequencing coverage across the rDNAs, with the degree of bias, as well as the estimated array size itself, varying by sequencing platform. Our work provides a new sequencing-based method for measuring rDNA copy number and transcriptional activity, helping to understand these less well characterized yet important regions of the genome.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Loss of local methylation coordination underlies structured intermediate methylation states in colorectal cancer
authors: Jacqueline Durney, University of Utah, United States
abstract: DNA methylation dysregulation is a hallmark of colorectal cancer (CRC), but how epigenetic instability is structured across individual cells and DNA molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we use single-cell bisulfite sequencing to characterize DNA methylation at both cellular and molecular resolution in primary CRC and matched normal colon tissue. We find that cancer-associated methylation changes extend beyond shifts in average methylation levels to include a pervasive loss of local coordination between neighboring CpGs. Across CpG islands, gene promoters, and large genomic domains, tumor cells exhibit increased methylation discordance alongside reduced methylation haplotype load, indicating disruption of coordinated methylation maintenance. By leveraging read-level metrics of methylation heterogeneity, we distinguish between intercellular variability and intramolecular discordance and show that intermediate methylation states in CRC primarily arise from mixtures of fully methylated and unmethylated cells rather than stable partial methylation within individual cells. Notably, observed methylation variability is significantly lower than expected under stochastic models, supporting a coordinated, non-random basis for epigenetic dysregulation. We further demonstrate that patient-specific methylation programs account for the majority of epigenetic variance and are conserved across tumor sites, while genomic regions that transition to intermediate methylation states exhibit elevated baseline variability in normal tissue, suggesting intrinsic susceptibility to dysregulation. Together, these results reveal that DNA methylation changes in colorectal cancer reflect a structured breakdown of coordinated epigenetic maintenance shaped by both patient-specific programs and region-specific properties, rather than purely stochastic processes.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Understanding Clinical and Genetic Features Associated with COVID-19 Disease Severity in Rhode Island
authors: Aley Abdel-Ghaffar, Brown University, United States
abstract: The rapid emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants has highlighted the need to understand how clinical and viral genetic diversity jointly influence disease severity. While host factors such as age, sex, and comorbidities are well-established determinants of COVID-19 outcomes, the contribution of viral genetic variation remains less characterized, partly due to the methodological challenges of population structure in viral genomics. Using a dataset of more than 11,000 SARS-CoV-2 sequences with linked clinical metadata provided by the Rhode Island Department of Health, we performed an integrated analysis of clinical and viral genetic determinants of hospitalization risk spanning March 2020 to August 2024. We first applied recursive feature elimination with cross-validation and permutation-based feature importance to identify key clinical predictors, finding that age, sex, vaccination status, and specific comorbidities, particularly cancer, diabetes, obesity, and lung disease, were the strongest predictors of severe disease. To identify viral genetic associations, we conducted a genome-wide association study correcting for clinical covariates and kinship using linear mixed models. To address viral population structure, samples were stratified into six genetic clusters via principal component analysis. An overall GWAS identified seven genome-wide significant variants; however, all were confirmed as Delta lineage-tagging artifacts concentrated in a single cluster. Cluster-stratified analyses revealed four genuine associations in three lineage groups, including missense variants in the nucleocapsid and ORF6 genes and synonymous variants in ORF1ab. Burden analyses further identified six genomic regions with cumulative rare variant signals, four mapping to ORF1ab. These results demonstrate that controlling for both clinical covariates and viral population structure is essential for distinguishing true genotype-phenotype associations from lineage confounding in viral GWAS.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Linking Genetic Risk to Disease-Relevant Cellular States via Metacell-Informed Modeling with ICePop
authors: Hao Yuan, Michigan State University, United States; Aishwarya Mandava, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Kewalin Samart, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Julia Ganz, Michigan State University, United States; Arjun Krishnan, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of loci associated with complex diseases, yet translating these population-level signals into specific cellular contexts remains a major challenge. Integrating GWAS with single-cell transcriptomic data enables systematic identification of disease-relevant cell types, but existing approaches face a fundamental tradeoff. Methods such as seismic achieve high statistical power by operating at the annotated cell-type level, but miss heterogeneous signals confined to specific cellular states. In contrast, single-cell-resolution methods like scDRS capture heterogeneity but often lack power to detect subtle associations. Here, we present ICePop (Informative Cell Populations), a framework that resolves this tradeoff by performing disease-cell association analysis at metacell resolution. By aggregating transcriptionally similar cells, ICePop achieves statistical power comparable to cell-type-level methods while retaining sensitivity to heterogeneous disease signals within cell types. In simulations, ICePop maintains appropriate false positive rates and demonstrates superior power when disease effects are concentrated in cellular subpopulations. Applying ICePop to 81 traits across cell types in Tabula Muris, we identify 2,178 disease-cell type associations, including preferential vulnerability of differentiated gut epithelial cells in ulcerative colitis and immune-stressed lung capillary endothelial states associated with lung capacities. Clustering diseases based on ICePopâ€™s metacell association profiles reveals disease groupings that diverge from genetic risk-based clustering, highlighting differences in cellular rather than genetic etiology. In autism spectrum disorder, ICePop implicates specific enteric neuron subtypes, suggesting a role for the enteric nervous system in gastrointestinal comorbidities. Together, ICePop enables resolution of disease-relevant cellular states and supports generation of testable, cell-state-specific hypotheses.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: CNVeil enables haplotype-resolved copy number inference and clonal analysis in single-cell tumor genomes from single-cell DNA sequencing data
authors: Weiman Yuan, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Can Luo, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, United States; Yunfei Hu, Department of Computer Science, Vanderbilt University, United States; Liting Zhang, Florida State University, United States; Zihang Wen, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Yichen Henry Liu, Department of Computer Science, Vanderbilt University, United States; Xian Mallory, Department of Computer Science, Florida State University, United States; Xin Maizie Zhou, Vanderbilt University, United States
abstract: Single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) enables copy number variation (CNV) analysis at single-cell resolution, providing insights into tumor heterogeneity and subclonal structure. While most existing methods focus on total copy number, haplotype-resolved copy number is critical for characterizing allelic imbalance and clonal evolution. However, accurate inference of both total and haplotype copy number from scDNA-seq data remains challenging due to low coverage, allelic dropout, and technical variability. We present CNVeil, a quantitative framework for joint inference of total and haplotype-resolved copy number from scDNA-seq data. CNVeil estimates total copy number by correcting systematic bias using normal cells identified via a PCA-based Gini coefficient, and performs robust ploidy estimation and segmentation through hierarchical clustering with cross-cell change rateâ€“based breakpoint detection to reduce noise. Building on these segments, CNVeil infers allele-specific copy number by leveraging unphased single-nucleotide polymorphism counts under constraints imposed by total copy number within an expectationâ€“maximization framework, thereby increasing statistical power. It further reconstructs chromosome-wide haplotype copy number profiles by phasing segments across the genome using a dynamic programming approach. Across extensive benchmarking against 12 state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real cancer datasets spanning diverse scDNA-seq technologies, including high-multiplexed single-nucleus sequencing, ACT, and 10x Chromium, CNVeil demonstrates strong performance in subclone identification, segmentation accuracy, and haplotype-resolved copy number inference. Together, CNVeil provides a unified framework for total and haplotype-resolved copy number analysis at single-cell resolution, enabling deeper characterization of tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Estimating a phylogenetic forest for single-cell RNA-sequencing data
authors: Shuyi Wang, THE CHINESE UNIVERSITY OF HONG KONG, China; Yingying Wei, THE CHINESE UNIVERSITY OF HONG KONG, China
abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies provide researchers with unprecedented opportunities to identify cell types and understand cell lineages. With the emergence of scRNA-seq studies that assay a large number of subjects, there is growing interest in aligning and comparing cell lineages between different individuals, especially for those with different clinical conditions. However, comparing cell lineages learned from scRNA-seq data collected from multiple individuals is challenging due to (a) scRNA-seq data can suffer from severe batch effects and (b) certain cell types may occur in some but not all individuals. In this study, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical model built upon Dirichlet diffusion tree to learn a phylogenetic forest for scRNA-seq data collected from multiple individuals. Our proposed model can automatically correct batch effects caused by multi-batch measurements and align the topologies of the phylogenetic trees of different individuals. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior inference. Real data analysis shows that the proposed method can effectively reconstruct and compare cell lineages across samples. Thus, we envision that the proposed method will greatly facilitate the study of development, cellular heterogeneity, and disease-related changes with population-scale scRNA-seq studies.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: A Robust and Computationally Scalable Method for Integrating a Large Number of Genomic Studies
authors: Zhiang Yuan, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Hongyuan Cao, Florida State University, United States; Yingying Wei, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: While individual genomic studies can suffer from weak signals, genomic studies spanning diverse conditions are becoming increasingly prevalent. For example, the integration of multi-ethnic genome-wide association studies is now essential to bolster power in underrepresented minority cohorts. Meanwhile, technologies like Perturb-seq have enabled genome-scale screens of transcriptional responses across hundreds of knockouts. However, conducting meta-analysis across numerous conditions presents significant challenges: the total number of association patterns 2^D grows exponentially with the condition number D. Moreover, existing meta-analysis methods typically rely on parametric assumptions that are not applicable to Perturb-seq studies, which usually adopt nonparametric tests for differential expression. Here, we propose a novel method that is able to (a) detect condition-specific signals while borrowing strength across conditions, (b) scale to a large number of conditions and (c) estimate non-null p-value distributions nonparametrically. We establish model identifiability and asymptotic false discovery rate control. Numerical studies show that our method outperforms existing methods.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Quality Control Metrics for Selecting Reference-grade Genomic Data for Medical Countermeasures and Diagnostic Use Cases
authors: Christie Rose Woodside, The George Washington University, United States
abstract: The rapid growth of genomic data in public repositories has enabled advances in infectious disease diagnostics and biosurveillance, but variability in genome assembly quality and inconsistent metadata limit the selection of reliable reference datasets. Current quality control (QC) approaches remain fragmented and lack standardized criteria for regulatory or clinical use. We present a scalable computational framework developed within the FDA-ARGOS initiative to standardize QC evaluation of genomic data. This framework integrates three complementary pipelines, ngsQC, assemblyQC, and biosampleMeta, within a reproducible workflow documented using BioCompute Objects to ensure provenance and FAIR-compliant data practices. A versioned data dictionary comprising 272 QC attributes was applied to 1,430 genome assemblies across 524 species from our NCBI BioProject and curated pathogen datasets. To evaluate redundancy and identify informative QC features, we performed principal component analysis with varimax rotation on both read-level and assembly-level metrics. Results show that a reduced subset of orthogonal QC metrics captures more than 85 percent of the variance in genome quality, enabling dimensionality reduction while preserving interpretability. Assembly-level metrics exhibited greater independence compared to read-level metrics, suggesting distinct contributions to overall quality assessment. This work provides a standardized and reproducible approach for evaluating genomic data quality and selecting reference-grade assemblies for diagnostic and regulatory applications. The resulting QC-annotated datasets are publicly available and enable researchers to identify and use high-quality reference genomes for biosurveillance, assay development, and next-generation sequencing diagnostics.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Detection of Somatic Point Mutations Directly from Spatial Transcriptomics Enables in vivo Spatiotemporal Lineage Tracing
authors: Yanmei Dou, Westlake University, China
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics reveals tissue organization but lacks in vivo lineage-tracing methods applicable to humans. We introduce SpaceTracer, a computational framework that accurately detects somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) directly from spatial transcriptomics data. By leveraging naturally occurring somatic SNVs, SpaceTracer reconstructs cellular phylogenies within native tissue architecture, enabling the mapping of lineage spread, migration, lineage-coupled expression changes and lineage-aware local interactions. Applied to human cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, it traced tumor initiation and progressions, uncovered widespread pre-invasive migration of dedifferentiated epithelial cells and characterized mutant B cells migrating from tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) into the tumor boundary. The framework also reconstructed developmental lineages across multiple tissues and identified tissue-resident mutant immune cells. SpaceTracer thus provides a perturbation-free platform for high-resolution spatiotemporal lineage tracing, offering a transformative tool for elucidating complex biological systemsâ€”especially tumor-immune ecosystemsâ€”with direct implications for advancing cancer immunotherapy.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: KIRP: Detecting allele-specific expression with k-mer analysis of RNAseq data
authors: Jason Miller, Hood College, United States; Karina Hornslien, University of Oslo, Norway; Paul Grini, University of Oslo, Norway
abstract: Epigenetic effects such as genomic imprinting have been shown to play a role in the endosperm of developing seeds of the model organism, Arabidopsis thaliana. Experiments on other plant species must overcome challenges of outcrossing, heterozygosity, and lower quality references. To expand the study of allelic expression to other Arabidopsis species, we present a new protocol that has low reliance on reference data. KIRP uses k-mer analysis of paired RNAseq read sequences from three individuals: two parents and their cross. It builds k-mer sets specific to each parent and deletes their intersection. It assigns cross reads to a parent, where possible, by set comparison. It bins reads by gene using a map to the nearest available annotated reference. It applies standard differential expression statistics to the binned read counts. KIRP was designed to avoid the pitfalls of map bias that arise when parental genomes differ by level of heterozygosity and similarity to the (single-haplotype) reference. We present KIRP results on crosses of two wild ecotypes of the species Arabidopsis arenosa. We replicated experiments on four crosses in each direction (i.e. swapping the pollen donor and acceptor), and we filtered for genes expressed in endosperm. Compared to a reference-based analysis of the same data, the KIRP results indicated greater resilience to the confounding factors of heterozygosity and map bias.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Accurate methylation calling from damaged DNA
authors: Xuecong Fu, Foundation Medicine Inc, United States; Yu Sun, Foundation Medicine Inc., United States; Neil Peterman, Foundation Medicine Inc., United States; Alex Robertson, Foundation Medicine Inc., United States
abstract: There are many applications of analyzing DNA methylation patterns in cell free DNA (cfDNA) in patients with cancer. They can inform on the epigenetic state of the primary tumor and its metastases, giving insight into how well the patient is responding to therapy and which therapies the tumor may be susceptible to. Methylation patterns are assayed by subjecting the cfDNA to a conversion process that converts each unmethylated cytosine into uracil which is read as thymine. Existing algorithms and code packages exist to analyze the raw data from such experiments. The majority of cfDNA molecules have characteristic jagged ends (double-stranded DNA molecules with protruding single-stranded ends) and accumulate DNA damage marks such as nicks (single-strand breaks in the DNA backbone) in circulation. However, library preparation methods often seek to fill in jagged ends or replace nucleotides downstream of nicks by incorporating unmethylated cytosines into the molecule. Such practice incorporates artifactual unmethylated cytosines in the template, resulting in "methylation bias" which confounds detection of true methylation patterns. We present computational methods to identify methylation signals in Watson/Crick strands of input DNA molecules likely introduced by jagged ends/nick repair or insufficient conversion in library preparation. By excluding these confounding regions in the analysis, we reconstruct a dependable portion of the original cfDNA molecule for downstream methylation calls. We also present data showing that these estimates are concordant with an orthogonal measure of cfDNA damage. Taken together, these methods could potentially improve the accuracy of methylation analysis in cfDNA.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: A multiomics and spatial atlas of mouse cloaca development reveals an early regulatory program governing bladder and genitalia tubular specification
authors: Atieh Abedin-Do, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, United States; Linbu Liao, Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology, China; Xing Ye, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, United States; Xue Li, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, United States
abstract: How the cloaca gives rise to the bladder and genital tubercle remains poorly understood, largely because cell-type–specific regulatory programs across developmental time have not been resolved. We generated a multiomic and spatially resolved atlas of mouse cloaca development spanning embryonic days E10.5–E15.5 by integrating single-nucleus RNA/ATAC sequencing , and Visium HD spatial transcriptomics. Across 113,989 cells, we identified epithelial and mesenchymal populations and reconstructed their developmental trajectories. Joint RNA/ATAC embedding enabled robust cell-type annotation and revealed stage-specific regulatory landscapes. We identified a bladder-directed mesenchymal population characterized by strong enrichment of Gata family motifs (Gata6/5) and coordinated transcriptional activation. Integrative analysis of chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and peak-to-gene associations prioritizes Gata6 and Gata5 as central regulators of bladder mesenchymal specification. This regulatory program is supported across modalities: motif accessibility, transcriptional expression, and enrichment of known Gata6 target genes. In contrast, genital tubercle mesenchyme follows a distinct regulatory trajectory during early development (E10.5–E12.5), marked by transient Lef1 activity and subsequent engagement of alternative transcriptional programs, such as Dlx5/3. Spatial transcriptomic mapping independently confirms that predicted bladder and genital tubercle populations localize to anatomically distinct regions, providing spatial validation of single-cell–derived identities in tissue context. This work establishes a stage-resolved multiomic framework for cloaca development and identifies a Gata6-driven regulatory program governing early bladder mesenchymal specification ; one that has not previously been characterized at this resolution.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: A Spatially Informed Cellular Reference Map of the Human Amygdala
authors: Kumar Arvind, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Laura Heinly, Human Brain Collection Core, NIMH-IRP, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Ningping Feng, Human Brain Collection Core, NIMH-IRP, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Anton Schulmann, Human Brain Collection Core, NIMH-IRP, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Ajeet Mandal, Human Brain Collection Core, NIMH-IRP, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Pavan Auluck, Human Brain Collection Core, NIMH-IRP, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Stefano Marenco, Human Brain Collection Core, NIMH-IRP, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Yun Zhang, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States
abstract: The human amygdala is a complex brain structure composed of approximately 13 anatomically distinct subnuclei, the major subnuclei being the central (CeA), basal (BA), and lateral (LA) nuclei. It is responsible for behavioral responses to emotional stimuli. Alterations in amygdala have been linked to several neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. Understanding the cellular organization of human amygdala is crucial to elucidating its role in disease states. To this end, we leveraged single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomic approaches to generate a spatially-resolved cell atlas of the human amygdala. Transcriptional profiles of approximately 30,000 spatially indexed nuclei were analyzed using standard snRNA-seq workflow. Broad cell classes identified were excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, microglia, and endothelial cells. Molecularly defined broad cell classes were visualized on the tissue sections using their respective Trekker spatial coordinates. Spatial projection revealed that neuronal and non-neuronal cell types were distributed uniformly at the broad cell class level across the tissue map. Notably, regions enriched in inhibitory neuron were identified on the spatial map, suggesting the potential location of Central Amygdala (CeA). Further analyses will characterize neuronal subtypes at granular level leveraging the NS-Forest machine learning framework. Future integration of PIP-seq (snRNA-seq) and Visium (spatial transcriptomics) datasets of the same region will be conducted to enable fine-grained spatial mapping of amygdala cell populations. Together, this study anticipates establishing a spatially informed atlas of human amygdala centered on CeA that would serve as a reference for localizing cell type-specific transcriptional changes in spatial structure.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Orbit: Bitpacked Move Structure Library for Efficient Pangenome Indexes
authors: Nathaniel K. Brown, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Benjamin Langmead, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Compressed indexes are increasingly used to answer pattern-matching queries within a memory budget, such as in pangenomics where users commonly need to search for substrings within large collections of related genome sequences. Even when a pangenome is on the level of terabytes, its Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT) can often be compressed to be much smaller. Examples which use the run length-encoded BWT (RLBWT) for their indexes include classification of DNA reads, sequence alignment, and haplotype similarity. Recently, the move structure has advanced both theory and practice for RLBWT based indexes, thanks to its cache efficient locality of reference. However, not all tools have transitioned to using a move structure, and those that do have been custom built for their use cases, even though the underlying structure is similar. Further, the â€œsplittingâ€ required for fast and small move structures with theoretical guarantees may invalidate the data users need to store alongside to support pattern matching. To this end, we introduce the Orbit C++ library, a header only plug and play implementation of move structures. Due to bitpacking, Orbitâ€™s index components are small, even when introducing user data types. The library also manages splitting regimes for ease of use. Further, we introduce length capping, a splitting optimization resulting in smaller and faster move structures in theory and practice. Evaluating on chromosome19 haplotypes, we find that length capping with Orbit results in faster and smaller data structures, sometimes much faster for certain queries, and at least 40% smaller on pangenomic scaled data.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Hypercube structure of local decycling set operations
authors: Aidan Jan, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Guillaume Marçais, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: The de Bruijn graph provides a one-to-one mapping between strings and graph walks, connecting string algorithms and graph theory. This connection serves as a foundation for many algorithmic methods in computational biology, including genome assembly, string matching, and sequence sketching. Cycles in a de Bruijn graph correspond to repetitive sequences, and their structure constrains the efficiency of k-mer-based sketching methods. We study Minimum Decycling Sets (MDS), smallest sets of k-mers that intersect every cycle, equivalently appearing in any sufficiently long sequence. Recent work introduced F-moves, local operations on MDSes that exchange selected k-mers for others while maintaining the decycling set property. This enables traversal over the space of decycling sets that permits optimization of underlying sketching methods with window guarantees. We modeled the network of MDSes joined by F-moves as a graph and identified a previously unreported structural organization. The graph admits substructures isomorphic to n-dimensional hypercubes, where n is the maximum number of independently applicable F-moves on a given MDS. This follows from the locality and commutativity of F-moves, which allow them to be executed in any order. This structure provides a new perspective on the organization of MDSes and suggests new methods for analyzing and constructing decycling sets with desirable properties.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: RNASeq analysis of the hyperprogressive tumor samples
authors: Howard Yang, National Cancer Institute, United States; Anish Thomas, National Cancer Institute, United States; Maxwell Lee, National Cancer Institute, United States; Lalage Wakefield, National Cancer Institute, United States; Brett Schroeder, National Cancer Institute, United States
abstract: We analyzed RNASeq data of tumor samples from a clinical trial of bintrafusp alfa, a bifunctional fusion protein targeting 48 PD-L1 and TGF-beta in patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Among the evaluable patients, 38% of them experienced hyperprogressive disease (HPD), marked by rapid clinical deterioration. The sequence reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38) using the STAR aligner (v2.7.8a). Gene-level read quantification was performed using the featureCounts function from the Rsubread package. Differential gene expression analysis was conducted using the DESeq2 R package on raw count data comparing HPD samples and the other tumor samples. Functional annotation and biological pathway enrichment analyses were conducted using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA v4.3.2). We applied 16 gene signatures in literature to analyze the samples and found that two signatures cell_cycle_progression and replication_stress were higher in HPD tumors based on after treatment samples. We applied the Cybersort analysis to these samples and found HPD samples were different from the rest samples in these 6 cell types: T cells gamma delta, NK cells resting, Dendritic cells activated, Macrophages M2, T cells CD8, Macrophages M1. We examined 16 stemness and neuroendocrine-ness signatures and found that 13 of them showed higher in HPD samples. These founding revealed some biology characteristics of the HPD samples.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Bramble: projection of spliced genomic alignments into transcriptomic space for improved transcript quantification
authors: Zoe Rudnick, Johns Hopkins University, Center for Computational Biology, Baltimore, MD, United States; Ales Varabyou, Johns Hopkins University, Center for Computational Biology, Baltimore, MD, United States; Rob Patro, University of Maryland, Department of Computer Science, College Park, MD, United States; Mihaela Pertea, Johns Hopkins University, Center for Computational Biology, Baltimore, MD, United States
abstract: Accurate transcript quantification is challenged by the complexity of alternative splicing and the presence of unannotated transcripts, divergent sequences, and pervasive transcriptional noise within RNA-seq data. Quantification methods such as Salmon and Oarfish traditionally rely on transcriptome mappings, leading to biased transcript assignments that depend on the genome annotation composition. Aligning to the genome with HISAT2 or minimap2 and then projecting the alignments into transcriptomic space may circumvent this problem, because reads best explained by unannotated genomic loci would not be constrained to the space of known transcripts during mapping. Despite the advantages of this approach, an efficient and comprehensive implementation has not yet been realized. To address this, we developed Bramble, a software tool for projecting spliced genomic alignments into transcriptomic space. Bramble was benchmarked against existing short- and long-read quantification pipelines using simulated data that incorporates realistic transcriptional noise and transcript-level subsampling to mimic annotation incompleteness. We demonstrate that pipelines using Bramble consistently yield superior transcript abundance estimates to those using other methods, and for long-read analysis, where reads contain considerable information about transcript origin via exon-exon junction coverage, Bramble provides particularly substantial improvements. We note that improvements to quantification accuracy become more pronounced as annotation incompleteness increases, indicating the benefit of Bramble to analysis of non-model organisms. Overall, Bramble provides an effective bridge between genome alignment and transcript quantification, improving the accuracy of expression estimates and increasing confidence in downstream findings across a wide range of experimental designs.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: offSCope: Primer and Amplicon Level Detection of Mispriming in Targeted Amplicon Single-Cell DNA Sequencing
authors: Samuel Coleman IV, University of Utah, Biomedical Informatics, United States; Kendell Clement, University of Utah, Biomedical Informatics, United States
abstract: High-throughput amplicon-based single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA) enables allele-specific sequence resolution in individual cells, supporting applications from investigating clonal heterogeneity in cancer to analyzing multiplexed CRISPR edit outcomes. However, these assays are dependent upon multiplexed PCR reactions which can introduce technical artifacts such as off-target mispriming and primer-dimerization. These technical artifacts create background noise which can impact the effective sequence depths of amplicon targets, obscure or hide biological signals, and decrease the reliability of downstream analyses. Without taking steps to measure and interpret these technical artifacts, additional sequencing capacity is wasted and primer libraries for future runs cannot be amended in a data driven manner. Here we introduce offSCope, a tool designed to analyze the quality of scDNA assays, locate misprimed reads, and identify the primers responsible. Using offSCope within a publicly available dataset, we detected mispriming rates between 2-3% on average within each cell. Additionally, the most common type of mispriming event was due to primers initiating reads that overlapped unintended amplicons which, at times, resulted in truncated amplicons that failed to cover targets of interest[KC1.1][SC1.2]. Finally, we observed an inverse relationship between read count and mispriming rate, with cells containing fewer reads exhibiting higher levels of mispriming, potentially indicating a role for the mispriming rate as a useful quality control metric in scDNA data. By enabling researchers to identify problematic primers within their sequencing data, offSCope supports informed primer redesign and assay optimization ultimately improving data quality and biological interpretation of single-cell data.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Multi-omic Profiling Reveals Cardiac Microenvironments and Cellular Diversity in iPSC-derived Cardiac Bioengineered Heart Muscle Organoids
authors: Muhammad Atif Sikandar, Institute of Pharmcology and Toxicology, University Medical Center Gottingen, Germany, Germany; Jingyu Wang, Institute of Pharmcology and Toxicology, University Medical Center Gottingen, Germany; Aagash Nedunchezhian, Institute of Pharmcology and Toxicology, University Medical Center Gottingen, Germany; Imran Ullah, Institute of Pharmcology and Toxicology, University Medical Center Gottingen, Germany; Wolfram-Hubertus Zimmermann, Institute of Pharmcology and Toxicology, University Medical Center Gottingen, Germany; Olaf Bergmann, Institute of Pharmcology and Toxicology, University Medical Center Gottingen, Karolinska Institutet, Sweden, Germany
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiac bioengineered heart muscle (BHM) organoids present a promising platform for recapitulating key aspects of cardiac development and disease in vitro. In this study, we combined temporal bulk RNA sequencing with high-resolution spatial transcriptomic analyses to systematically characterise the differentiation trajectory and structural maturation of BHM organoids. Integrated analysis revealed a heart-like architecture characterised by the spatial distribution of cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, epicardial cells, and other support cell types. Furthermore, spatial mapping revealed the organised arrangement of these cell types within in vivo-like microenvironments. Preliminary hypoxia experiments also highlight the potential of BHM organoids as a model for mechanistic studies of cardiac pathology and drug screening. Overall, our findings establish iPSC-derived BHM organoids as a versatile and functionally competent system for investigating human heart development, disease mechanisms and therapeutic evaluation.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Design and validation of a spatial transcriptomics viral panel for virome profiling in Sjögren’s Syndrome
authors: Federica Bichicchi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Natalie Atyeo, National Institutes of Health, United States; Danny Yi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Jay Chiorini, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: SjÃ¶grenâ€™s Syndrome (SjD) is a chronic autoimmune disorder affecting salivary and lacrimal glands, leading to severe dryness and systemic complications. While its exact cause remains unknown, genetic predisposition and environmental triggers are thought to contribute to disease onset and progression. Several viruses are known to infect salivary gland cells, and emerging evidence suggests that persistent infections may drive immune dysregulation and chronic inflammation in SjD. However, the specific viruses involved and their impact on disease pathology remain unclear. To address this, we developed and validated a spatial transcriptomics viral probe panel. We implemented a computational pipeline to retrieve viral genomes, perform multiple sequence alignment, and quantify sequence conservation using normalized Shannon entropy. Conserved regions were selected to guide probe design across genomes with varying variability, resulting in a panel of 258 viral targets. For experimental validation, representative viral fragments were cloned into plasmids and embedded in tissue microarrays (TMAs), enabling controlled benchmarking of probe performance within a Xenium spatial transcriptomics framework. Control experiments demonstrated robust detection of viral and host transcripts with consistent signal across replicated cores. Integration of probe-level expression with known ground truth enabled quantitative assessment of sensitivity and specificity, revealing strong performance for targets and identifying potential cross-reactivity in variable genomes. This study establishes a scalable framework for the design and validation of spatial viral panels, supporting accurate virome profiling in salivary gland tissues. Future work will apply this approach to SjD patient samples to investigate virusâ€“host interactions and their role in disease pathogenesis.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Generating correlated data for omics simulation
authors: Jianing Yang, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Gregory Grant, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Thomas Brooks, University of Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Simulation of realistic omics data is a key input for benchmarking studies that help users obtain optimal computational pipelines. Omics data involves large numbers of measured features on each sample and these measures are generally correlated with each other. However, simulation too often ignores these correlations. To alleviate this, we describe and implement three approaches for generating omics-scale data with correlated measures which mimic real datasets. These approaches are all based on a Gaussian copula approach with a covariance matrix that decomposes into a diagonal part and a low-rank part, which allows for extremely efficient simulation. We use these approaches to demonstrate the importance of including correlation in two benchmarking applications. First, we show that variance of results from the popular DESeq2 method increases when dependence is included. Second, we demonstrate that CYCLOPS, a method for inferring circadian time of collection from transcriptomics, improves in performance when given gene-gene dependencies in some circumstances.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: SAGe: A Lightweight Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Mitigating the Data Preparation Bottleneck in Large-Scale Genome Sequence Analysis
authors: Nika Mansouri Ghiasi, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Talu Güloglu, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Harun Mustafa, ETH Zurich and Johns Hopkins University, Switzerland; Can Firtina, University of Maryland, United States; Konstantina Koliogeorgi, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Konstantinos Kanellopoulos, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Haiyu Mao, King's College London, United Kingdom; Rakesh Nadig, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Mohammad Sadrosadati, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Jisung Park, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), South Korea; Onur Mutlu, ETH Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: Genome sequence analysis drives advances in many critical medical and biotechnological fields. Given its importance and the exponentially growing volumes of genomic sequence data, there are extensive efforts to accelerate genome sequence analysis. In this work, we demonstrate a major bottleneck that greatly limits and diminishes the benefits of state-of-the-art genome sequence analysis accelerators: the data preparation bottleneck, where genomic sequence data is stored in compressed form and needs to be first decompressed and formatted before an accelerator can operate on it. To mitigate this bottleneck, we propose SAGe, an algorithm-architecture co-design for highly-compressed storage and high-performance access of large-scale genomic sequence data. The key challenge is to improve data preparation performance while maintaining high compression ratios (comparable to genomic-specific compression algorithms) at low hardware cost. We address this challenge by leveraging key properties of genomic datasets to co-design (i) a lossless (de)compression algorithm, (ii) hardware that decompresses data with lightweight operations and efficient streaming accesses, (iii) storage data layout, and (iv) interface commands to access data. SAGe is highly versatile, as it supports datasets from different sequencing technologies and species. Due to its lightweight design, SAGe can be seamlessly integrated with a broad range of hardware accelerators for genome sequence analysis to mitigate their data preparation bottlenecks. Our results demonstrate that SAGe improves the average end-to-end performance and energy efficiency of two state-of-the-art genome sequence analysis accelerators by 3.0Ã—â€“32.1Ã— and 13.0Ã—â€“34.0Ã—, respectively, compared to when the accelerators rely on state-of-the-art software and hardware decompression tools.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: UniPhase: Joint Assembly-Based and Population-Level Haplotype Phasing
authors: Yifei Wang, Yale School of Medicine, BIDS, United States; Zezhen Du , Yale School of Medicine, BIDS, United States; Haoyu Cheng, Yale School of Medicine, BIDS, United States
abstract: De novo long-read genome assembly has become increasingly routine. However, because sequencing reads still do not span chromosome-scale haplotypes, current approaches remain unable to directly reconstruct fully phased diploid genomes from long-read data alone, limiting the power of many downstream applications. Existing approaches typically separate read-based phasing and population-based phasing into sequential steps, preventing joint optimization of sequencing evidence and linkage disequilibrium (LD) information under a unified weighted Minimum Error Correction (wMEC) framework. We present UniPhase, a haplotype phasing framework that jointly integrates assembly-derived unitigs and population-level LD information. UniPhase uses error-corrected unitigs generated from a hifiasm assembly as phasing fragments. Compared with raw reads, unitigs are substantially longer, less redundant, and locally low-coverage, enabling tractable exact wMEC optimization while reducing orientation ambiguity at biallelic heterozygous sites. To further incorporate population information, UniPhase embeds a PBWT-restricted Li-Stephens transition penalty directly into the wMEC dynamic program, allowing LD information to guide phase orientation only when unitig evidence is ambiguous. In a second stage, SHAPEIT4 uses phased block scaffolds to bridge inter-block gaps and refine long-range haplotypes using a population reference panel. Evaluated on 48× HG002 HiFi whole-genome sequencing data, UniPhase improves phasing continuity and accuracy relative to hifiasm dual assembly. Phased block N50 increases from ~1.1 Mb to ~3.9 Mb, switch error rate decreases from 0.7557%/0.7525% to 0.6518%/0.6105%, and Hamming error rate decreases from 23.71%/22.31% to 20.13%/19.15%. UniPhase also achieves over 5× runtime reduction compared with read-based phasing pipelines under the same computational setting (64 CPUs). These results demonstrate that assembly-derived unitigs provide an effective substrate for integrating exact phasing optimization with population-aware haplotype inference.

title: Systematic CRISPR Activation Screening Identifies Oncogenic LncRNAs That Sensitize Cancer Cells to CDK4/6 Inhibition
authors: Yueshan Zhao, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yifei Wang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Zehua Wang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Min Zhang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Da Yang, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are increasingly recognized as regulators of gene expression programs, yet their functions in cancer proliferation and therapeutic response remain incompletely characterized. To systematically identify oncogenic lncRNAs, we performed a two-stage CRISPR-SAM activation (CRISPRa) screen. First, we conducted a genome-wide screen targeting 9,744 lncRNAs to evaluate their effects on cancer cell proliferation. To reduce false positives, we designed an independent focused sgRNA library targeting the top-ranked candidates and performed a secondary validation screen. LncRNAs consistently selected across both screens were further validated through functional assays in vitro and in vivo. To investigate their potential as therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed a parallel CRISPRa screen under treatment with FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i). We observed a strong inverse relationship between lncRNA-driven proliferation and CDK4/6i resistance. Among the top hits, TENM3-AS1 was identified as a novel oncogenic lncRNA whose activation sensitized cancer cells to CDK4/6 inhibition. RNA sequencing revealed that TENM3-AS1 induces a hyperproliferative transcriptional program characterized by activation of the estrogen receptor (ER) signaling pathway, increasing dependence on CDK4/6-regulated cell cycle control. To assess clinical relevance, we derived a lncRNA activation signature and applied it to single-cell transcriptomes from serial tumor biopsies of 24 patients with early-stage breast cancer enrolled in the FELINE clinical trial. Patients who responded to combination therapy with letrozole and ribociclib exhibited higher lncRNA activation scores, suggesting predictive value for therapeutic response. These findings highlight a novel mechanism of lncRNA-mediated therapeutic vulnerability and the development of biomarkers for personalized cancer treatment.

title: IMPROVED TRANSCRIPTOME ANNOTATION FOR AFRICAN TURQUOISE KILLIFISH USING LONG-READ SEQUENCING
authors: Sohini Rebba, Washington University in St. Louis, United States; Van Schalkwyk Lianri, University College London, United Kingdom; Philip Ruzycki, Washington University in St. Louis, United States; Brian Clark, Washington University in St. Louis, United States; Ryan MacDonald, University College London, United Kingdom
abstract: Background: Ageing is a major risk factor for retinal neurodegenerative diseases that lead to progressive vision loss. Understanding retinal aging requires accurate transcriptomic profiling. The African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) is a valuable vertebrate model for aging research due to its short lifespan. However, incomplete transcriptome annotations in killifish limit transcript-level analyses. Improving transcriptome annotation using long-read sequencing enables accurate transcript-level analysis of gene expression and isoform diversity, helping better understand underlying molecular mechanisms in age-related retinal dysfunction. Computational pipeline: Long-read RNA sequencing of killifish retina was performed using PacBio Iso-Seq. Full-length cDNA libraries were prepared using the Kinnex protocol and sequenced on a PacBio Revio SMRT cell, producing HiFi reads. Full-length non-chimeric transcripts were identified using the Iso-Seq workflow to generate high-confidence transcripts, which were aligned to the existing killifish genome assembly. Isoforms were structurally classified using SQANTI3, coding regions predicted with TransDecoder, and ortholog annotation performed using eggNOG. Results: Long-read transcript reconstruction expanded the killifish reference transcriptome identifying 176,474 transcripts (>2.5-fold increase). Functional annotation assigned gene names to ~90% of predicted proteins and reduced uncharacterized (LOC) genes from ~45% to ~5%. Analysis of bulk retinal RNA-seq data profiling the entire lifespan of the organism retained significantly more transcripts after filtering and differential expression analysis revealed ~2x more isoforms that change with age. Significance: These results show that long-read transcript reconstruction improves transcriptome completeness in emerging model organisms. The updated killifish retina annotation provides a stronger reference for bulk and single-cell RNA-seq studies to investigate retinal aging.

title: General thermodynamics algorithm recovers the RNA structural dynamics and ensemble conformation
authors: Hyeonggon Cho, Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Sunghyun Ha, Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Juhyeon Kim, Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Yujin Park, Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Sungchul Yang, Graduate School of Engineering Biology, KAIST, Daejeon,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Young-suk Lee, Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon,Republic of Korea, South Korea
abstract: Computational modeling for RNA structure is key in understanding the function of RNA as it is largely determined by its structural dynamics. Chemical probing experiments have provided the necessary data to tackle this, yet existing computational methods often struggle with generality, reliability, and software portability. Here, we present a general thermodynamics algorithm that deconvolves its RNA ensemble conformation from chemical probing experiments such as SHAPE- and DMS-MaP. Our framework consists of two major steps: (1) Bayesian reactivity for robust estimation of single-stranded regions marked by the chemical probing reagent, and (2) a probabilistic latent mixture model that incorporates thermodynamic information as a prior to resolve discrete structural states. Benchmarking our methods with 311 publicly available datasets results in accurate prediction of RNA structure across different experimental conditions and technical platforms. For example, our framework successfully resolved the structural dynamics of the HIV-1 REE 5-stem and 4-stem loops (SL) from DREEMâ€™s synthetic DMS-MaP data where existing methods fail. These results suggest our framework as a generalizable tool for exploring the structural landscapes of functional RNAs and providing the foundation for RNA design and therapeutics.

title: Transcriptome-wide Profiling of Alternative Splicing in ADHD Brain Reveals Isoform-level Dysregulation
authors: Deepthi Nammi, Translational and Functional Genomics Branch, National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH, Bethesda, MD, 20892, USA, United States; Gutsavo Sudre, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, King’s College London, UK, United Kingdom; Valer Gotea, Translational and Functional Genomics Branch, National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH, Bethesda, MD, 20892, USA, United States; Kwangmi Ahn, Social and Behavioral Research Branch, National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH, Bethesda, MD, 20892, USA, United States; Philip Shaw, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, King’s College , London, UK, United Kingdom; Laura Elnitski, Translational and Functional Genomics Branch, National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH, Bethesda, MD, 20892, USA, United States
abstract: Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heritable neurodevelopmental condition that results in symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that impair daily functioning. About 5â€“7% of children worldwide are affected, often into adulthood. In the United States, roughly one in nine children (6.5 million) has been diagnosed. Despite its prevalence, the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. ADHD commonly co-occurs with anxiety, mood, autism spectrum disorder and conduct disorders, and learning disabilities, further impacting quality of life and increasing risk for adverse outcomes. Few ADHD studies have examined transcriptome-wide alternative splicing. We aimed to identify differential alternative splicing events (DASEs), associated genes, and enriched pathways to better understand ADHD molecular mechanisms. Methods: DASEs were identified using rMATS-turbo in postmortem brain transcriptomes from ADHD cases and controls. Five event types were analyzed: skipped exon (SE), alternative 5â€² splice site (A5SS), alternative 3â€² splice site (A3SS), mutually exclusive exon (MXE), and retained intron (RI). Analyses were performed in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; 24 cases, 29 controls) and caudate nucleus (CAU; 24 cases, 32 controls). Significant events met uniform filtering thresholds: average read count â‰¥ 10, false discovery rate (FDR) â‰¤ 0.05, and percent spliced-in (PSI) difference â‰¥ 0.05. Pathway enrichment was conducted using the cluster Profiler package. Results: In the ACC, 1,413,082 novel splicing events were detected within significant genes: SE (4,835), MXE (8,854), A3SS (1,623), A5SS (1,578) and RI (308). Pathway enrichment identified 1,620 significant pathways, including 75 neurological pathways. In CAU 1,647,033 novel splicing events were identified within significant genes: SE (5,572), MXE (10,481), A3SS (1,843), A5SS (1,768) and RI (329). Pathway analysis revealed 888 enriched pathways including 24 neurological pathways. Notably, 12 key splicing-related pathways were shared between regions. Conclusion: These results suggest that disruptions in RNA splicing are linked to ADHD. The enrichment of dopaminergic and glutamatergic pathways, consistent with previous RNA-seq studies, indicates that dysregulation of RYK, CLN3, GRIA2, PLCB1, and GRIA4 isoform processing is likely to play a key role in the underlying mechanisms of the condition.

title: HGCTSVG: Finding Single-Cell Resolution Cell-Type-Specific Spatial Domains and Spatially Variable Genes in Spot-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics using Neighborhood-Aware Hypergraph Embeddings
authors: Edgardo Felizmenio, Pusan National University, South Korea; Kibeom Kim, Pusan National University, South Korea; Giltae Song, Pusan National University, South Korea
abstract: Spatially-resolved transcriptomics (ST) enables the utilization of spatial information while investigating gene expression within a tissue, leading to a deeper understanding of cell function and tissue structure. An important task in ST analysis is the detection of Cell-Type-Specific Spatially-Variable Genes (ct-SVGs), genes with non-random spatial expression patterns within a cell type. These genes can reveal heterogeneity within cell types, providing insights into how tissue microenvironments influence cell type function and behavior, cell differentiation and development, tissue organization, and disease diagnostics. Despite their importance, ct-SVG detection is hindered by the limited resolution of ST data. Existing approaches do not achieve single-cell resolution and model gene expression independently, ignoring gene-to-gene and cell-to-cell interactions. We propose Hypergraph ct-SVG (HGCTSVG).
