Unlike existing methods that use cell-type proportions, HGCTSVG uses an annotated single-cell expression decomposition of ST data and transforms it into a hypergraph, where nodes represent single cells and hyperedges represent spatial neighborhoods. A hypergraph autoencoder then learns neighborhood-aware embeddings per cell, capturing gene and cell interactions at single-cell resolution. Clustering the embeddings reveals cell-type-specific spatial domains, each associated with a set of marker genes corresponding to ct-SVGs. Evaluation of HGCTSVG on a human kidney cancer dataset shows that an average of 96.5% of predicted ct-SVGs across 12 cell types exhibit significant spatial autocorrelation, indicating strong agreement between cell-type spatial domains and ct-SVGs. These results suggest that jointly modelling gene expression and neighborhood information at single-cell resolution captures non-random spatial structure within a cell type, providing a more detailed view of their spatial variation.

title: KnockRBP: an integrated multi-omics database of functional perturbation profiles for RNA-binding proteins
authors: Mengyuan Yang, Xi‘an Jiaotong University, China; Yungang Xu, Xi‘an Jiaotong University, China
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) regulate diverse post-transcriptional processes, yet their functional impacts across multiple molecular layers remain incompletely characterized. KnockRBP (https://knockrbp.xu-bioinfo.com) is presented as a comprehensive, multi-omics database systematically cataloging regulatory changes resulting from genetic perturbation of RBPs. The resource integrates 1453 datasets from GEO, ENA, and ENCORE, encompassing RNA-seq, Ribo-seq, microRNA (miRNA)-seq, and 3â€²RACE-seq across 639 RBPs, 182 cell lines, and 61 diseases. Regulatory outcomes covered include alternative splicing, alternative polyadenylation, RNA editing, transcript abundance, translation efficiency, and miRNA expression, with all events processed through standardized analytical pipelines and annotated with open reading frame consequences, predicted loss-of-function impacts, and established disease or drug associations. The web interface supports dataset browsing, RBP- and gene-centric multi-omics exploration, transcript structure visualization, and interactive regulatory network navigation, while integrated analytical modules enable prioritization of perturbation-responsive events, cross-layer regulatory inference, and evaluation of clinical relevance. In contrast to existing RBP resources, KnockRBP integrates multi-omics data with perturbation-aware functional annotation, enabling mechanistic investigation and identification of RBP-affected genes and events in post-transcriptional regulation. The database is freely accessible and intended for long-term maintenance, serving as a community resource to advance functional genomics research on RBPs and their roles in human disease.

title: Shared and Distinct Exonic Parts in Alternative Paths of Splicing Bubbles
authors: Daniel Witoslawski, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, United States; Jelard Aquino, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, United States; Chuanchuan He, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, United States; Mira Han, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, United States
abstract: Alternative splicing can be detected as ""bubbles"" in splicing graphs. Complex bubbles where more than two transcript paths compete are challenging for methods designed for simple binary events. We present a unified framework that compares more than two paths using distinct exonic parts observed directly from reads. We build a DAG called GrASE per gene, enumerate all bubbles, and quantify shared and distinct exonic parts across three comparison structures: (i) all-pairwise contrasts; (ii) multinomial n-way comparison; and (iii) valid bipartitions via lower-set enumeration. The lower-set enumeration runs in time linear to the number of paths in a bubble, substantially below exhaustive powerset search, making genome-wide application tractable. Applied to the human genome, GrASE finds 263,308 bubbles across 22,299 genes, and 844,184 valid bipartitions with shared and distinct exonic parts to test. These include alternative TSS/TTS events inaccessible to junction-based methods. Benchmarking on simulated data shows that bipartition with fixed empirical Bayes dispersion achieves the best precision-recall balance. GrASE shows higher precision while testing significantly more events compared to other methods.

title: Million-Scale Functional Profiling Enables Machine Learning for RNA Function Prediction and Design in ZTP Riboswitches
authors: Yuntong Zou, Northwestern Universtiy, United States; Julius Lucks, Northwestern University, United States; Eric Strobel, University at Buffalo, The State University of New York, United States; Skyler Kelly, University at Buffalo, The State University of New York, United States
abstract: Accurate function prediction and rational design of RNA remain central challenges in synthetic biology since RNA activity depends on complex relationships among sequence, structure, and biophysical context. Recent advances in machine learning for RNA modeling have been limited by the scarcity of large-scale datasets with quantitative RNA functional measurements; a challenge that high-throughput experimental assays are now beginning to overcome. Here, we leverage Transcription Elongation Complex display (TECdisplay) to obtain ZTP riboswitch sequence-function measurements at up to the million-sequence scale, providing a foundation for machine learning of RNA function. Using this dataset, we evaluated multiple sequence representations and model architectures in two complementary tasks: predicting RNA function from sequence and designing candidate sequences for desired functional outputs. Initial results suggest that compact predictive models can achieve useful accuracy for riboswitch function prediction, and that lightweight generative models can produce candidate sequences with biologically plausible characteristics at target functional levels. The in-vivo experimental validation further supports the reliability and predictive accuracy of the model. These findings indicate that relatively efficient architectures may capture important functional constraints in this system and provide a practical starting point for design-oriented RNA modeling. Together, this work provides a large-scale RNA functional dataset and a machine learning framework for RNA function prediction and design, with clear potential to incorporate structural and biophysical priors, knowledge distillation of pretrained RNA foundation models to build more advanced RNA models. In this context, ZTP riboswitches profiled by TEC Display offer a useful benchmark for investigating how RNA machine learning models can achieve both high precision within a specific system and useful generalizability across related RNAs and downstream tasks.

title: Evaluating Ovarian Cancer Subtypes Defined with Different Molecular Markers
authors: Hildana Shiferaw, Smith College, United States; Kira Hou, Smith College, United States; Beamlak Woldeab, Smith College, United States; Maisha Tasneem, Smith College, United States; Kaitlyn Cook, Smith College, United States; Halie Rando, Smith College, United States
abstract: High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), one of the deadliest gynecologic malignancies, is a global health problem. Current diagnostic approaches often rely on a combination of imaging and serum biomarkers. While these markers are useful for monitoring disease progression or recurrence, they have limited specificity and sensitivity for screening, especially in asymptomatic individuals. As a result, most cases of HGSOC are diagnosed at an advanced stage, when treatment options are more limited and prognosis is poorer, contributing to the diseaseâ€™s high mortality rate. In recent years, transcriptomic analyses have revealed molecular subtypes of HGSOC associated with differences in prognosis, although the exact number of subtypes varies across studies. In other cancers, microRNAs (miRNAs), small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally, have emerged as promising biomarkers. However, miRNAs have not been widely explored for HGSOC detection or diagnosis, despite being more biologically stable than mRNA. This project explores the potential for miRNAs to inform ovarian cancer screening by comparing molecular subtypes of HGSOC defined under different paradigms. Using patient data from TCGA-OV, a large publicly available transcriptomic dataset, we characterized patterns in sequencing data collected from biopsied ovarian tumors. We used consensusOV, an open-source R package for mRNA subtyping, to assign each patient to a subtype based on their pattern of mRNA expression. We then used k-means clustering and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to define clusters of miRNA expression and assign miRNA-based subtypes. Finally, we compared survival across subtype definitions using Kaplan-Meier curves and survival analyses. The analysis is currently underpowered because of the limited size of the TCGA-OV cohort, and we were therefore unable to detect significant differences in survival among any clusters, including mRNA-based clusters previously reported as clinically relevant in the literature. However, the clear emergence of distinct miRNA-based clusters, together with the greater biological stability of miRNAs, supports further investigation of this approach as a potential avenue for less-invasive detection of molecular signatures associated with HGSOC.

title: Assessing the Physiological Fate of Alternatively Spliced Protein Isoforms through Proteogenomic Machine Learning at Genome Scale
authors: Senbao Lu, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Ziyang Gao, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Oleksandr Narykov, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Gloria Sheynkman, University of Virginia, United States; Dmitry Korkin, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States
abstract: Alternative splicing of mRNA precursors is a fundamental mechanism to expand the functional capabilities of the genome by generating multiple protein isoforms from a single gene, greatly diversifying protein function. Approximately 70% of alternatively spliced isoforms are predicted to induce functional or structural protein alterations, whereas others may be unstable and subject to degradation. To date, large-scale experimental characterization of isoform-level physiological stability remains limited, where we refer to the isoforms that are expressed in biologically relevant amounts at both transcript and protein levels as physiological stable. In this work, we construct a novel multi-source dataset of 3,754 paired reference and alternative isoforms with annotated physiological stability, derived from a harmonized proteogenomic integration of four experimental datasets. We then train an integrative proteogenomic machine learning framework that combines biologically derived features with foundation models-based embeddings at both transcript- and protein-levels to predict physiological stability of alternative protein isoforms and reach 83% cross-validated F1 score. We further perform orthogonal validation using proteomics experiments and wide-range temperature-series molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to assess thermal stability differences among isoforms from the same gene. Finally, we apply our model at genome scale. Analysis of the Human Protein Atlas (filtered at â‰¥20 TPM) identifies 7,376 stable and 8,216 unstable alternative isoforms, and analysis of GENCODE basic annotation reveals that, among 44,684 protein-coding alternative isoforms across 19,411 genes, 31,936 are predicted to be stable and 12,735 unstable, suggesting that the functional human proteome is substantially shaped by isoform-level stability constraints.

title: Machine Learning Predicts Potential DprE1 Inhibitors for Mycobacterium tuberculosis using MtbPred
authors: George Hanson, Department of Parasitology, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana, Ghana; Miriam Eyram Lawson Gakpey, H3Africa Kidney Disease Research Network, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana, Ghana; Joseph Adams, Department of Parasitology, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana, Ghana; Richmond Kabutey Kudiabor, Department of Clinical Pathology, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana, Ghana; Emmanuel Ankomah Kissi, Department of Biomedical Engineering, School of Engineering Sciences, University of Ghana, Ghana; Maame Esi Annor-Apaflo, H3Africa Kidney Disease Research Network, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana, Ghana; Daveson Innocento Brank Kepgang, Department of Biochemistry, Faculty of Sciences, University of Douala, Cameroon; Clifford Seyram Yisufu, Department of Clinical Pathology, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana, Ghana; Edgar Sungwacha, Department of Medical Microbiology, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Kenya; Charles Ssemuyiga, Department of Biological and Environmental Sciences, School of Natural Sciences, Kampala International University, Uganda; Olaitan I. Awe, African Society for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology, South Africa
abstract: The emergence of extensive resistance to commonly used first-line drugs has posed a major challenge to Tuberculosis (TB) treatment. Thus, the discovery of new anti-TB drugs with no cross-resistance to existing drugs is urgently needed. We developed machine learning classifier models, Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN), Random Forest (RF), and NaÃ¯ve Bayes (NB), trained on high-throughput screening bioassay data (AID:1626) to predict compounds active against Mtb. Predictions were validated through a comprehensive computational pipeline targeting the microbial DprE1 enzyme. This included molecular docking of predicted actives from FDA-approved and AfroDb natural product libraries, followed by ADMET filtering, protein-ligand interaction analysis, and 200 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations coupled with MM/PBSA free energy calculations. The known DprE1 inhibitors BTZ043 and PBTZ169 served as experimental benchmarks. The SVM and LR models demonstrated superior performance (97% accuracy). From 2,328 predicted actives, molecular docking against the DprE1 binding site, followed by pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiling, identified 28 high-affinity lead compounds (binding energy â‰¤ -9.0 kcal/mol). These compounds formed stable, key interactions with the catalytic residues of the enzyme (Cys387, Lys418, His132), mirroring the binding mode of validated inhibitors. MD simulations confirmed the structural stability of the DprE1-lead complexes, and MM/PBSA calculations substantiated favorable binding free energies. The identified compounds, which potently engage the essential DprE1 enzyme, represent promising candidates for further experimental validation against drug-resistant TB. We deployed our pipeline, MtbPred as a web tool for targeted drug discovery for ongoing anti-mycobacterial research and it is publicly accessible (https://igmr.org/software/mtbpred).

title: An Exploration of Robustness to Data Artifacts in Hybrid Alignment–Deep Learning AMR Prediction Systems
authors: Nathalie Bonin, University of Maryland, United States; Kamala Varma, University of Maryland, United States; Nakyung Lee, University of Maryland, United States; Rain Haworth, University of Maryland, United States; Tudor Dumitraș, University of Maryland, United States; Mihai Pop, University of Maryland, United States
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a dynamic public health issue that annually provokes millions of hospitalizations and deaths. Efficient computational algorithms are constantly under development to improve upon the state of the art in resistance prediction accuracy. However, the robustness to data artifacts of deep learning AMR prediction models remains unclear. Consequently, we analyze DeepARG, a hybrid alignmentâ€“deep learning AMR prediction system, to understand how interactions between those two components impact such a systemâ€™s resiliency to data artifacts. By running DeepARG on whole-genome sequencing samples, we demonstrate that over 94% of DeepARG predictions agree with the most frequent class alignment hits, with some of the remaining deviation correlating with class imbalances and sequence homology in the reference database. Furthermore, by exploiting DeepARGâ€™s reliance on alignment bit-scores, we successfully generated input sequence perturbations capable of inducing prediction changes. However, after retraining DeepARG on a dataset injected with modified sequence, we did not find any significant changes in resistance predictions. Overall, we conclude that while hybrid alignmentâ€“deep learning AMR prediction systems may be resilient to training sequence perturbations, they are not robust to data artifacts that can arise from imbalance in the database between different drug classes or from input sequence processing errors.

title: Dual transcriptomic approaches characterize fungal community structure associated with brown spot needle blight symptoms across Pinus families
authors: Temitope Folorunso, Auburn University, United States; Gabriel Silva, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States; Rabiu Olatinwo, Southern Research Station, United States Forest Service, United States; Lori Eckhardt, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States; Janna Willoughby, Auburn University College of Forestry Wildlife and Environment, United States
abstract: Disease outcomes in forest systems often emerge from interactions among co-occurring microbial taxa rather than single pathogens. In brown spot needle blight (BSNB), a fungal disease affecting Pinus speciesâ€”previous studies have relied largely on culture-based methods to characterize the pathobiome, thereby overlooking unculturable taxa. In this study, we characterize the BSNB symptoms pathobiome, including both cultured and uncultured fungal taxa. We used complementary transcriptomic approaches, combining host-filtered de novo assembly with read mapping of total RNA to a targeted multi-species fungal reference panel. De novo assembly using Trinity generated 63,308 contigs, with significant fungal sequences identified based on BLASTX similarity to the NCBI RefSeq database. Functional annotation of fungal transcripts suggested pathways potentially involved in hostâ€“pathogen interactions. Among annotated fungal contigs, Neodothiora populina represented 5.05% of contigs, while previously cultured taxa such as Sydowia polyspora and Rhizosphaera spp. were represented at lower percentages. To support these matches and estimate species-level abundance, total RNA reads were mapped to a targeted fungal multi-reference panel, yielding alignment rates of 80â€“90% across samples. Species-level coverage analysis indicated that Rhizosphaera kalkhoffii had the strongest genome support (mean 4%, exceeding 20% in some host families), whereas other taxa such as Lecanosticta acicola (1.5%), Cladosporium spp. (0.5%.), and S. polyspora (0.5%.) were much lower. Both approaches recover taxa identified through culture-based isolation while also revealing additional species, providing a more comprehensive view of fungal community composition and establishing a foundation for downstream analyses of functional hostâ€“pathogen interactions.

title: Gut Microbiota Modulation by Anthocyanin-Rich Pigmented Maize under Protein Restriction: 16S rRNA Analysis.
authors: Kathleen Stephany Soto Sigala, Faculty of Medicine and Nutrition, Universidad Autónoma de Baja California (UABC), Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, Mexico; Diana Reyes-Pavón, Faculty of Medicine and Nutrition, Universidad Autónoma de Baja California (UABC), Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, Mexico; Edgar Torres Maravilla, Faculty of Medicine and Nutrition, Universidad Autónoma de Baja California (UABC), Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, Mexico
abstract: Protein malnutrition alters intestinal physiology and gut microbial ecology, contributing to dysbiosis and impaired nutrient absorption. Whole grain maize contains dietary fiber, phenolic compounds, and anthocyanins that may modulate gut microbiota. This study evaluated the effects of different maize varieties on gut microbiota composition under protein-restricted conditions. Male BALB/c mice were fed a 7% protein diet supplemented with 20% whole grain flour from white, pink, or purple maize varieties and compared with an unsupplemented protein-restricted control. Growth parameters, intestinal morphology, and gut microbiota were evaluated using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and bioinformatic analyses. All maize-supplemented groups displayed a distinct microbial composition compared with the protein-restricted control (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA, p = 0.001), with no significant differences in alpha diversity. Supplementation was associated with increased nasoanal length (7.6–9.6%) and crypt depth (17.1–32.5%), while the pink maize group showed a 17.7% increase in colon length. Differential abundance analysis revealed enrichment of Muribaculaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Oscillospiraceae-associated taxa, alongside a reduction of Helicobacteraceae and other taxa associated with altered intestinal homeostasis. Enriched genera included Adlercreutzia, Lachnospiraceae_NK4A136_group, and [Eubacterium]_xylanophilum_group. Co-occurrence networks showed greater connectivity and taxonomic complexity in maize-supplemented groups than in the fragmented network observed under protein restriction alone. These findings suggest that whole grain maize supplementation may promote a more favorable microbial profile under protein restriction while improving selected growth and intestinal morphology parameters. Pigmented maize varieties exhibited higher antioxidant capacity and distinct microbial interaction patterns.

title: CanisLupus2.0: An Open-Source Interactive Dashboard for Microbiome Data Analysis and Visualization
authors: Philip Appiah, George Washington University, United States
abstract: Background & Significance: The human microbiome plays a critical role in health and disease, yet comprehensive analysis of microbiome data remains a significant challenge for researchers without advanced bioinformatics expertise. Existing tools are often command-line dependent, computationally demanding, or require extensive programming knowledge, creating barriers to accessible microbiome science. There is a growing need for standardized, user-friendly platforms that simplify microbiome data analysis across research settings, particularly in clinical and translational health research. Purpose: This project aimed to develop CanisLupus2.0, a fully open-source, web-based interactive dashboard that enables students and researchers to upload, explore, analyze, and visualize microbiome datasets without requiring advanced programming skills. The central goal was that a simple standardized web-based platform could integrate multiple microbiome analytical workflows â€” from data quality control to community-level statistical analyses â€” within a single accessible interface. Methods: CanisLupus2.0 was developed using R, Shiny, and phyloseq, and containerized with Docker for reproducibility and portability. The application accepts user-uploaded amplicon sequence variant (ASV) tables, taxonomy tables, metadata, and phylogenetic trees. The pipeline integrates standardized preprocessing steps including singleton removal and sample filtering, followed by comprehensive analytical modules: taxonomic profiling via stacked bar plots and interactive heatmaps, alpha diversity estimation (Shannon, Simpson, Chao1), beta diversity ordination (PCoA, NMDS, Bray-Curtis, UniFrac), phylogenetic tree visualization, heat trees, dendrograms, correlation networks, differential abundance testing with Kruskal-Wallis and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and PERMANOVA for community-level group comparisons. The tool was validated using publicly available human skin microbiome and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) datasets. Findings & Conclusions: CanisLupus2.0 successfully integrates over ten standardized microbiome analytical workflows into a single interactive interface, with real-time visualization and point-and-click controls for taxonomic level, grouping variables, and statistical parameters. Validation analyses using skin microbiome data demonstrated that the tool accurately reproduces established findings including body-site-specific community differences and core microbiome identification. The application was recognized with First Place at the GW Open-Source Project Office competition, affirming its scientific and technical merit.

title: CleanSweep: Detecting strain-specific variation in culture-enriched metagenomes
authors: Marco Teixeira, Infectious Disease and Microbiome Program, Broad Institute of Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard, United States; Gabrielle M. Gussin, Division of Infectious Diseases, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, United States; Veda Khadka, Infectious Disease and Microbiome Program, Broad Institute of Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard, United States; Raveena D. Singh, Division of Infectious Diseases, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, United States; Thomas Abeel, Delft Bioinformatics Lab, Department of Intelligent Systems, Delft University of Technology, Netherlands; Susan S. Huang, Division of Infectious Diseases, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, United States; Colin J. Worby, Infectious Disease and Microbiome Program, Broad Institute of Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard, United States; Ashlee M. Earl, Infectious Disease and Microbiome Program, Broad Institute of Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard, United States
abstract: Plate sweeps - culture-enriched mixed strain communities - are an emergent alternative to single colony-purified isolates for genomic epidemiology because of their improved sensitivity and simplified workflows. But assessing variation within specific strains from plate sweep data is challenging due to closely related strains, with many regions of homology that can lead to spurious variants. Existing approaches for variant calling in complex communities ignore homologous regions, restricting analysis to a fraction of the genome, or require prior knowledge of strain diversity. This limits the use of plate sweeps for genomic epidemiology. We overcame these issues by developing a tool (CleanSweep) that leverages allele depths to call strain-specific single-nucleotide variants from short-read plate sweep data. CleanSweep outperformed existing tools for both semi-synthetic and real plate sweeps. Its improvement in performance was greater for more complex plate sweeps and for strains at lower coverages. Furthermore, variants detected by CleanSweep were concordant with data from isolates. To demonstrate its applicability in large-scale genomic epidemiology analyses, we used CleanSweep to analyze the spread of resistant bacteria in nursing homes. We found that inter-facility transmission is a major driver of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus spread, especially through more mobile residents. We also quantified the within-host diversity of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, finding that strains are circumscribed to a single body site and uncovering potential evidence of body site adaptation. Thus, CleanSweep enables the use of plate sweeps for large-scale analyses of bacterial transmission, providing an attractive alternative to resource-intensive and insensitive isolate collection.

title: PACK: A Scalable Pipeline for Standardized Functional Annotation of Large Microbial Genome Collections
authors: Anupam Gautam, IBMI-University of Tübingen/ Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany; Daniel H. Huson, IBMI, University of Tübingen; IMPRS ""From Molecules to Organisms"", Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany; James W. Marsh, Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany
abstract: The increasing availability of genome-resolved metagenomic data has created a demand for scalable and integrative workflows that go beyond basic genome annotation to enable functional and ecological interpretation. Existing solutions often focus on isolated tasks such as quality assessment or annotation, limiting their utility for comprehensive genome analysis. Here, we present PACK, a modular Nextflow-based pipeline for integrated genome annotation and downstream functional profiling. PACK combines sequence processing, taxonomic classification, and functional annotation within a unified and reproducible workflow. Starting from genomic sequences, the pipeline performs ORF prediction using Prodigal, followed by taxonomic classification with GTDB-Tk and multiple annotation layers, including defense system detection, methylation-related gene prediction, antibiotic resistance profiling, and auxotrophy inference. Beyond annotation, PACK extends analysis to metabolic and ecological interpretation by integrating species-level information and external databases. This enables predictions of cultivation conditions, metabolic capabilities, plasmid content, DNA transfer strategies, codon usage patterns, and promoter features. The pipeline is implemented using a modular DSL2 architecture in Nextflow, allowing flexible extension and seamless integration of additional tools and databases. We demonstrate that PACK enables scalable and reproducible analysis of diverse microbial genomes while significantly reducing manual integration efforts. By bridging genome annotation with functional and ecological insights, PACK provides a comprehensive framework for genome-centric studies in microbiome research and biotechnology.

title: Hypothesis-Driven Analysis of Gut Microbiome in Subclinical Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease
authors: Shreya Chindepalli, Duke University, United States; Anita Shlesinger, Duke University , United States; Joshua Granek, Duke University , United States; Francois Haddad, Stanford University, United States; Jessilyn Dunn, Duke University , United States
abstract: Host-microbe interactions contribute to pathways relevant to atherosclerosis pathogenesis, including lipid metabolism, bile acid metabolism, and vascular inflammation. Alterations in human gut microbial composition have been reported in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), though evidence in early, subclinical stages remains limited. Subclinical ASCVD is characterized by measurable plaque burden prior to onset of symptomatic cardiovascular disease. Studying this stage enables investigation of biological processes associated with disease development. This study examines associations between gut microbiome taxonomic composition and subclinical ASCVD. Stool metagenomic sequencing data from 485 samples across 136 participants (68 with subclinical ASCVD, defined as coronary artery calcium score > 100; 68 matched controls with no coronary artery calcium) was obtained from the Project Baseline Health Study. Participants were propensity-matched on age, sex, race, ethnicity, BMI, hypertension, ASCVD risk score, and type 2 diabetes status. Species-level taxonomic profiles were generated using MetaPhlAn v4. Based on published findings linking specific gut taxa to ASCVD, four genera were selected for prespecified hypothesis-testing: Collinsella, Roseburia, Eubacterium, and Streptococcus. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with multiple testing correction identified higher relative abundance of genera Collinsella and Roseburia in the subclinical ASCVD group. Species-level tests identified three taxa, Eubacterium ventriosum, Eubacterium ramulus, and Streptococcus gordonii, as significantly associated with subclinical ASCVD status after multiple testing correction. These findings suggest that some microbial associations with ASCVD reported in the literature are also detectable in subclinical ASCVD. This work represents an initial hypothesis-testing analysis within an ongoing investigation of this longitudinal data from the Project Baseline Health Study cohort.

title: 16S rRNA k-mer composition encodes microbial functional potential
authors: Jia Liu, Emory University, United States; M. Clara De Paolis Kaluza, Northeastern University, United States; Yana Bromberg, Emory University, United States
abstract: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing is widely used to profile microbiome taxonomic composition and functional potential. Most 16S rRNA-based methods compare reads against reference marker genes from previously characterized organisms, leading to accuracy declining in environments dominated by uncharacterized microbes, such as soil and ocean. We uncovered a direct link between 16S rRNA and genome-encoded functions. Using fully-sequenced bacterial genomes, we show that whole-genome k-mer composition predicts genome-encoded functions; and 16S rRNA k-mer profiles reflect their source genome k-mer compositions. Leveraging this relationship, we introduce embeRNA, a framework that predicts functions directly from 16S rRNA k-mer, without taxonomy assignment or phylogenetic placement. Per-function probability output allows users to adapt decision thresholds to match study goals, balancing precision vs. recall or accounting for community novelty. We trained embeRNA on a large collection of bacterial function-omes and evaluated it on a future-genomes benchmark where all test sequences were dissimilar to training data ( We further evaluated embeRNA on soil samples with paired 16S rRNA and whole metagenome shotgun (WMS) sequencing data. embeRNA recovered the majority of WMS-inferred functions and produced abundance profiles strongly correlated with WMS-derived values, consistently across all soil samples tested. These results indicate that 16S rRNA k-mer composition carries substantial functional signal, providing a reference-independent pathway to explore the uncultivated biosphere's functional dark matter, particularly in understudied environments.

title: Intermittent fasting improves bone health by impacting gut microbiota
authors: Abhirupa Ghosh, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Janani Ravi, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Honey Hendesi, Department of Orthopedics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States
abstract: Obesity is a risk factor for delayed fracture healing, posing a substantial financial and healthcare burden. Intermittent fasting (IF) emerges as an intervention that alleviates obesity-related pathologies, in part by altering the gut microbiome. We have previously shown that IF can augment bony callus and enhance fracture healing in obese mice; however, the potential role of gut microbiome in mediating IF effects remains unknown. To address this, we performed tibial fracture in obese mice on one of two diet regimes: 1) alternate-day fasting (IF) and 2) unlimited access to food (ad libitum; AL). At 21 days post-fracture, cecal samples were collected for metagenomics and targeted metabolomics. Alpha diversity analysis on metagenomics data revealed significantly higher species richness and evenness in the IF group, indicative of a more diverse gut microbiome, while beta diversity showed distinct community separation, confirming significant shifts in gut microbiome. Taxonomic profiling and differential analysis identified key microbial species in the IF cohort, such as beneficial gut bacteria Alistipes sp., Bacteriodes thetaiotaomicron, and Lactobacillus johnsonnii involved in anti-inflammatory function and energy metabolism. Principal component analysis on metabolomics data showed clear separation between groups; the IF group is enriched with multiple metabolite classes, including short- and medium- chain fatty acids, bile acids, and peptides, consistent with finding beneficial bacteria in the gut microbiome that improve metabolic health. Integrative multi-omics analysis identified significant correlations between specific metabolites and species (e.g., 7-hydroxyoctanoic acid and Evtepia sp.), suggesting that IF mitigates obesity-induced impairment of bone healing via coordinated microbiome-metabolome interactions.

title: PhaBOX2: an enhanced web server for discovering and analyzing viral contigs in metagenomic data
authors: Jiayu Shang, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Cheng Peng, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Jiaojiao Guan, City Univesity of HongKong, China; Dehan Cai, Department of Electrical Engineering, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong (SAR), China, Hong Kong; Donglin Wang, Key Laboratory of Drinking Water Science and Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China; Yanni Sun, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing has transformed virus discovery; however, downstream bioinformatic analyses for viral identification, classification, and host prediction remain fragmented across multiple tools. Here, we present PhaBOX2, a major upgrade that extends the platform from a specialized bacteriophage identification tool to a comprehensive and integrated suite for viral sequence analysis. PhaBOX2 broadens its detection, taxonomic, and host prediction scope beyond phages to enable the characterization of archaeal and eukaryotic viruses. The updated workflow incorporates rigorous quality control and quantitative analyses, automatically removes host contamination, clusters sequences into viral operational taxonomic units, and performs phylogenetic analysis based on marker genes. In contrast to traditional â€œblackâ€“boxâ€ deep learning approaches, PhaBOX2 combines alignmentâ€“based strategies with machineâ€“learning models under a â€œglassâ€“boxâ€ design philosophy, providing interpretable intermediate evidence alongside final predictions to improve transparency and biological interpretability. Powered by a dedicated highâ€“performance computing infrastructure, the server delivers a fully automated, endâ€“toâ€“end workflow, while achieving an ~80% reduction in processing time. PhaBOX2 thus provides a robust and userâ€“friendly ecosystem for viral metagenomic analysis and is freely available at https://phage.ee.cityu.edu.hk/.

title: Benchmarking Shotgun Metagenome Classification Pipelines for Low Microbial Biomass Samples
authors: Shan Sun, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, United States; Ivory Blakley, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, United States; Anthony Fodor, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, United States
abstract: Taxonomic classification of shotgun metagenomic data varies substantially across tools due to fundamental methodological differences. Marker geneâ€“based approaches such as MetaPhlAn4, k-merâ€“based methods such as Kraken2, and ANI-based strategies such as Sylph each exhibit distinct performance characteristics, particularly for low microbial biomass samples. To systematically evaluate these differences, we constructed a synthetic mock community of 82 genomes and simulated sequencing reads across a gradient of coverage levels and mixed with human genome sequences as a controlled background. At very low coverage, Kraken2 and Bracken maintained substantially higher sensitivity, whereas MetaPhlAn4 and Sylph detected near-zero taxa until ~0.078Ã— coverage. At higher coverage, all methods converged to ~0.9 sensitivity and F1 score. MetaPhlAn4 and Sylph achieved near-perfect precision once taxa were detectable, while Kraken2 and Bracken showed reduced precision at default settings but approached comparable performance at confidence thresholds â‰¥0.7. We extended this benchmarking framework to real environmental samples. Using hospital sink biofilm metagenomes, Kraken2 (confidence â‰¥0.7) identified taxa (>20 reads) not detected by other tools, spanning 7 phyla, 11 classes, 24 orders, 66 families, and 193 genera. To assess reliability, we developed a validation pipeline that maps Kraken2-classified reads back to reference genomes. Classifications supported by >20 reads, >1000 bp genome coverage, and >99% sequence similarity were considered strongly supported. Among 193 Kraken2-only genera (abundance >20), 147 (76%) demonstrated strong support. This work underscores how classifier performance varies in low microbial biomass samples and provides a practical framework for robust detection of low-abundance taxa in complex metagenomic datasets.

title: Understanding plant pathogen-mutualist interactions on urban trees using a differential equation model
authors: Emily Kim, Boston University, United States; Jennifer Bhatnagar, Boston University, United States; Daniel Segrè, Boston University, United States
abstract: Tree growth and survival depend on ectomycorrhizal (EMF) and arbuscular mycorrhizal (AMF) fungi to provide nitrogen in exchange for photosynthate, but these mutualistic interactions decline in urban areas while decomposers and plant pathogens increase. Synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) that reintroduce mutualists to tree roots provide a promising solution, but species selection remains a key bottleneck in implementation. To address this challenge, we are developing a differential equation model that combines elements of a consumer-resource model with additional biological processes. We model an urban tree-mycorrhizal-pathogen system in which both microbes and the host plant are represented as consumers that can exchange resources (carbon and nitrogen) with their surrounding environment. We further include specific environmental stressors that can affect tree growth, mortality, and microbiome health. We expect that the consumer-resource dynamics, coupled with these stressors, will allow us to model competition between microbial groups, nutrient deprivation during pathogenic attack, and other processes that could be added to the model through omics-based metabolic constraints. Preliminary simulations display interesting dynamical trajectories of the different species, with some parameters strongly affecting the final health of the plant. For example, at extremely large abundances of AMF and EMF, plant biomass decreases due to low availability of environmental nitrogen. The model also mimics real-world results, as a higher pathogen capacity for AMF/EMF antagonism results in lower plant biomass regardless of soil fertility. Our model represents a predictive mathematical tool that can be used to understand complex tree-microbiome-environment relationships and design SynComs for urban microbiome restoration.

title: Temporal stability and niche partitioning of bacterial communities in paired residential sink P-traps
authors: Megan Hill, Duke University, United States; Will Stiffler, Duke University, United States; Jorden Rabasco, NC State, United States; Ivory Blakley, UNC Charlotte, United States; Shan Sun, UNC Charlotte, United States; Anthony Fodor, UNC Charlotte, United States; Claudia Gunsch, Duke University, United States
abstract: Sink P-traps harbor microbial communities derived from environmental and human sources, yet longitudinal studies examining their stability and assembly dynamics remain limited. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the longest continuous characterization of bacteria collected from residential sink P-traps, with daily sampling over two months (n = 61 days). Samples were collected from paired sinks in a shared bathroom to identify dominant taxa, quantify temporal stability, and determine how occupant usage patterns influence community assembly. Using full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we identified 3,865 unique taxa, with both sinks dominated by common sink-associated genera, including Pseudomonas, Citrobacter, Klebsiella, and Arcobacter. Despite sharing identical plumbing, environmental conditions, and cleaning regimes, the two sinks maintained distinct communities (p

title: Modeling Scale Uncertainty Improves Microbiome Analysis
authors: Maxwell Konnaris, Pennsylvania State University, United States; Manan Saxena, Pennsylvania State University, United States; Gregory Gloor, University of Western Ontario, Canada; Nicole Lazar, Pennsylvania State University, United States; Justin Silverman, Pennsylvania State University, United States
abstract: Microbiome sequencing measures relative abundances, leaving total microbial load (scale) un-observed and confounding inference about absolute abundances. Existing approaches either fix scale through normalization (e.g. TSS, DESeq2, and ANCOM-BC2) or predict it from taxonomic profiles using machine learning (ML), thereby treating scale as identifiable and risk distorting effect sizes, false discovery rates, and predictive performance. To benchmark these strategies, we assembled mutt, a curated database of 35 studies comprising more than 15,000 samples with paired sequencing data and direct microbial load measurements across diverse study settings. Using mutt, we compared normalization-based methods, ML-based load prediction, and Bayesian Partially Identified Models (PIMs) using a Scale-Reliant Inference perspective under realistic cross-study heterogeneity conditions. ML predictors failed to generalize: sample correlations were near zero and R2 was frequently negative. Normalization-based methods yielded median FDR above 75% and PPV below 25%. By contrast, Bayesian PIMs achieved near-zero median FDR, PPV â‰ˆ99%, and NPV â‰ˆ97%. Re-analysis of 19 autism caseâ€“control cohorts showed that previously reported autism microbiome associations are study-specific and more consistent with scale misspecification than reproducible biology. Microbial load is not recoverable from sequencing data alone, and strategies that assume otherwise systematically inflate false discoveries. Bayesian PIMs, which model scale uncertainty rather than imputing a point estimate, substantially improve false-discovery control without loss of power and materially alter biological conclusions in a prominent multi-cohort application. These results argue that microbiome studies should treat scale as a source of uncertainty to be modeled explicitly, not a nuisance to be normalized or imputed away.

title: Metagenomic Strain-Resolved DNA Modification Patterns Link Extrachromosomal Elements to Host Strains
authors: Daniel Portik, PacBio, 1305 O’Brien Dr, Menlo Park, CA, USA, United States; Rohan Sachdeva, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Jillian Banfield, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Spencer Diamond, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Matthias Hess, Department of Animal Science, University of California, Davis, CA, USA, United States; Michael Morowitz, Department of Surgery, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, PGH, PA, USA, United States; Susan Lynch, Department of Medicine, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA, United States; Jeremy Wilkinson, PacBio, 1305 O’Brien Dr, Menlo Park, CA, USA, United States; Siyuan Zhang, PacBio, 1305 O’Brien Dr, Menlo Park, CA, USA, United States; Shuai Wang, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Holly Steininger, Department of Medicine, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA, United States; Marie Schoelmerich, Department of Environmental Systems Sciences, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, Switzerland; Ling-Dong Shi, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Ming Yan, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Pengfan Zhang, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Rebecca Garner, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Luis Valentin-Alvarado, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States; Allison Guitor, Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, United States
abstract: DNA modification is central to microbial defense against extrachromosomal elements (ECEs), consequently ECEs tend to adopt their hostâ€™s modification patterns. Shared ECEâ€“host modification patterns enable linking ECEs to their hosts, but modification detection tools are designed for single genomes and are ineffective at metagenome scale. Here, we present MODIFI, software for detecting DNA modifications in metagenomes. MODIFI assumes that each k-mer in a metagenome is mostly unmodified and calculates background signal levels for that k-mer from PacBio HiFi reads, eliminating the need for matched control experiments. MODIFI ECEâ€“host linkages were validated using >1,000 isolate and mock microbiome datasets. Illustrating the approach, we identified 315 strain-resolved, non-redundant ECEâ€“host linkages in environmental and human metagenomes. In infant gut microbiomes, a chromosomal inversion in Enterococcus faecalis alters host and associated plasmid methylation motifs simultaneously. Overall, MODIFI solves a major bottleneck in DNA modification analysis and provides a foundational tool for understanding microbial epigenomics.

title: WWBio: Control-Calibrated Multi-Evidence Inference for Robust Marker Detection in Long-Read Wastewater Metagenomics
authors: Ayesha Wasim, Universidade da Coruña, CITIC, Database Laboratory, A Coruña, Spain, Spain; Susana Ladra, Universidade da Coruña, CITIC, Database Laboratory, A Coruña, Spain, Spain; Margarita Poza, Microbiology Research G.,INIBIC–CICA–UDC–CIBERINFEC-ISCIII & UDC,Microbiome&Health ResearchG.,Dpto Biología,F.Ciencias, Spain; Todd Treangen, Department of Computer Science; Department of Bioengineering; Ken Kennedy Institute, Rice University, Houston, TX, USA, United States
abstract: Wastewater metagenomics enables population-level monitoring of disease-associated microbial signatures, but detecting predefined markers in long-read sequencing data remains challenging under low-depth and heterogeneous conditions. Sparse and fragmented signals cause nucleotide-only approaches to miss true markers or produce spurious alignments. We present WWBio, a control-calibrated multi-evidence inference framework that integrates nucleotide and protein signals while explicitly modeling background noise using matched shuffled controls. WWBio combines read support, coverage breadth, and translated protein homology into a unified confidence score, enabling robust and interpretable marker detection under realistic sequencing constraints. We evaluated WWBio on Oxford Nanopore wastewater metagenomic datasets at two sequencing depths (2 Gb and 5 Gb) against a nucleotide-only baseline (â‰¥2 reads and â‰¥10% coverage thresholds). At higher depth, both approaches detected established markers (bft, clbB, clbN), while WWBio additionally identified radD supported by protein evidence. At reduced depth, the baseline detected only bft, whereas WWBio recovered multiple markers (clbB, clbN, fap2, radD) by integrating complementary evidence sources. Shuffled-marker controls yielded no detections for either method, confirming that improved sensitivity does not arise from spurious alignments. These results demonstrate that explicit background calibration combined with multi-evidence integration substantially improves sensitivity and reduces false positives of marker detection in low-depth long-read metagenomic data, providing a scalable and interpretable framework for biomarker detection in complex environmental sequencing settings.

title: Multi-sample binning increases MAG recovery from Empty Quarter desert soils with minimal benefit from geographic sample grouping
authors: Alejandra Lopez-Velazquez, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Saudi Arabia; Robert Hoehndorf, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Saudi Arabia
abstract: Multi-sample metagenomic binning exploits co-abundance patterns to improve genome recovery, but two practical questions remain: the optimal configuration for low-biomass environments with fragmented assemblies, and whether geographically informed sample partitioning improves recovery when scaling to large cohorts. We benchmarked five SemiBin2 configurations on 20 hyperarid desert metagenomes (median N50: 1,796 bp) from Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter, selected from an ongoing collection of over 500 metagenomes, then compared geographic versus random grouping across 130 metagenomes. Multi-sample binning yielded 31% more high-quality bins than the best single-sample mode (465 vs 355 HQ), but was not strictly dominant: cross-mode dereplication at 95% ANI revealed that multi-sample uniquely recovered 293 MAGs (22.9%) while single-sample uniquely recovered 120 MAGs (9.4%), suggesting a union strategy may maximize recovery. A union of both methods yielded 1,280 dereplicated MAGs, of which 96.6% lacked GTDB species assignments. Geographic grouping showed no advantage over random assignment (TOST equivalence p

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: GANCODE: A Deep Learning Model to Identify Ganciclovir Incorporations in Viral DNA
authors: Dana Joseph, Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine, United States; Aaron McKenna, Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Direct, genome-wide detection of antiviral nucleotide analog incorporation remains an unresolved computational challenge. We present GANCODE (Ganciclovir Analysis of Nanopore Current for On-genome Drug Embedding detection), a deep learning framework for identifying ganciclovir (GCV) drug incorporations directly from raw Oxford Nanopore electrical current signal. To generate labeled training data, we designed a complex library of synthetic oligonucleotides containing site-specific GCV incorporations across diverse sequence contexts and sequenced these constructs using third-generation nanopore technology to capture drug-specific current perturbations. GANCODE integrates one-dimensional convolutional neural networks with bidirectional long short-term memory layers to jointly model local signal distortions and long-range context dependencies. By aligning raw current signal to basecalled sequence, the model learns to distinguish GCV from canonical guanine in native signal space. Across synthetic constructs, GANCODE achieves high-precision classification of GCV incorporations and generalizes across nucleotide contexts. Applied to cytomegalovirus (CMV)-infected fibroblasts harboring exonuclease mutations and to CMV-positive patient blood samples, the model reveals differential incorporation frequency and positional bias associated with resistance genotypes. GCV is a guanine nucleotide analog used to treat CMV and other herpesviruses. While GCV incorporation into the viral genome typically induces chain termination, resistant strains tolerate incorporation and continue replication. By enabling single-molecule detection of drug embedding within the genome, GANCODE provides a computational framework for mechanistic investigation of antiviral resistance and establishes a generalizable strategy for studying therapeutic nucleotide drug analogs in viral and cellular genomes.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: An ongoing study of novel techniques for predicting inhibitory ligand binding to prevent Androgen Receptor activation
authors: Harry Shaw, Xyngal Morph LLC, United States; Deborah Preston, Co-founder, United States; Kimberly Jackson, Spelman College, United States
abstract: The pathways leading to activation of the Androgen Receptor (AR) is an area of intense study. The motivation is the fact that AR activation is one of the principal causes of poor outcomes in castration resistant prostate cancer. Our methodology involves reducing a trade space of molecular interactions between AR, co-activators, ligands, and the cellular environment to a matrix of features and targets in an unsupervised learning AI model. Our research is focused on tautomers of dibenzoylmethane (DBM). The process starts with building and analyzing the information entropy of successive pentapeptide sequences in AR. Combinations of AR, DBM tautomers, water, and co-activators are subjected to MM2 energy minimization. Further modeling is performed using Density Functional Theory tools. We are developing AI models to cluster DBM tautomers with other AR binding ligands from databases like bindingDB and ZINC. Hydrogen bonding, Van der Waals forces, geometries, and a variety of other interactions are under analysis. Results are placed into a matrix with over fifty characteristics related to the interaction of ligands, AR binding domains, and co-activator binding domains for Principal Component Analysis, k-means clustering and other techniques. In this poster, the status and preliminary results will be displayed. Upon completion, simulation results for a series of binding ligands and binding sites to AR and co-activator proteins will be published. The results should provide a significant boost in the knowledge of mechanisms of AR activation inhibition.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: DeepFootprinting: Decoding the Combinatorial Transcription Factor Logic of Active Enhancers at Nucleotide Resolution
authors: Gaetano Manzo, NIH, United States; Ivan Ovcharenko, NIH, United States
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) regulate gene expression by binding enhancers in combinatorial and context-dependent configurations, yet the sequence-level logic underlying TF co-occupancy at active regulatory elements remains incompletely defined. Existing approaches either map TF occupancy at limited resolution using ChIP-seq or rely on motif enrichment analyses that do not integrate chromatin context or quantify the functional contribution of individual binding events. We present DeepFootprinting, an interpretable deep learning framework that resolves TF binding at nucleotide resolution while attributing each binding event to its predicted contribution to regulatory activity. Across 747 ENCODE TF ChIP-seq datasets, DeepFootprinting recovers known motif families, captures positional organization within peaks, and links nucleotide-level contributions to higher-order chromatin features. Application to 20,833 active HepG2 enhancers reveals a non-random and hierarchically organized TF architecture. Enhancers are enriched for ARID-family chromatin organizers, frequently co-occurring with liver identity regulators and pioneer factors. ARID5B-associated motifs are detected in the majority of enhancers containing LCOR, TCF7L2, or FOXP4, consistent with a scaffold-like role in enhancer organization. HNF4A and FOXA factors exhibit asymmetric co-occurrence and distinct positional distributions, supporting a model in which chromatin accessibility and transcriptional activation are spatially coordinated within enhancer cores.TF co-occupancy increases with enhancer activity, with signaling-responsive factors preferentially enriched at highly active elements. Proximal motif analysis further identifies recurrent AP-1 and FOXP family co-binding within short genomic intervals in HepG2 enhancers. In silico disruption of high-contribution nucleotides within HNF4A motifs markedly reduces predicted enhancer activity, illustrating single-nucleotide sensitivity of the inferred regulatory architecture. Independent validation using allele-specific binding and eQTL-associated variants demonstrates concordance between model-derived attributions and experimentally observed regulatory effects.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: BarCall: a deep-learning base caller for Optical Pooled Screens
authors: Daphne Kontogiorgos-Heintz, Paul. G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA, United States; Yuan Gao, Center for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA, United States; Sergio Hleap, Copoly.ai, Canada; David Richmond, Genentech, United States; Joshua Gould, Genentech, United States; Monica Ge, Genentech, United States; Bo Li, Genentech, United States
abstract: Motivation: Optical Pooled Screens (OPS) is a transformative technology that combines the scalability of pooled genetic screens with the rich phenotypic modalities enabled by high-content imaging. It is emerging as a key data source for training perturbation foundation models and enabling the construction of ``virtual cellsâ€™â€™, providing a complementary modality to Perturb-seq. However, the throughput of OPS is currently constrained by the computational challenge of base calling from \textit{in situ} sequencing (ISS) data. Standard analysis pipelines rely on \textit{ad hoc} spot detection and sequence decoding methods that struggle with tile edge effects, optical crowding, phasing, channel crosstalk, and signal decay, leading to substantial data loss (dropout) in high-cell-density regions. Results: We present DeepBase, an ensemble spot detection and deep-learning base calling approach and BarCall, a unified deep learning framework that performs joint spot detection and base calling. DeepBase improves upon the traditional â€œdetect-then-decodeâ€ approaches by maximizing spot detection capability via ensemble learning and optimizing sequence decoding accuracy via a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture. Improving upon DeepBase, BarCall jointly models the spot detection and sequence decoding steps using a spatiotemporal U-Net architecture with a bidirectional LSTM bottleneck. BarCall additionally utilizes a novel Barcode-Adjusted Dice (BAD) Loss, which uses a pseudo-labeling strategy to rescue spots missed in the ``weakly labeledâ€™â€™ training dataset. Benchmarked against the baseline method, SCALLOPS, on public OPS dataset of A549 CRISPR-KO screen, BarCall substantially improves barcode mapping rates (82.5% vs. 53.3%) and increases the yield of high-confidence phenotyped cells by approximately 18.5%, without sacrificing correlation with ``ground-truthâ€™â€™ NGS abundances (r~0.9). BarCall is computationally efficient, requiring fewer model parameters and offering faster inference time compared to DeepBase. Availability and implementation: Source code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Genentech/barcall.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Confidence-weighted network reconstruction from functional omics via stability and SelectBoost
authors: Frederic Bertrand, UTT and National Conservatory of Crafts and Arts, France; Myriam Maumy, UTT and EHESP, France
abstract: Network reconstruction in systems biology is often performed under â€œlarge p, small nâ€ constraints and pervasive correlation (co-expression modules, shared pathway activity, temporal coupling). When predictors are functionalâ€”time-course expression, trajectories summarized as curves, or longitudinal multi-omicsâ€”standard sparse regressions can yield unstable edge sets and inflated false positives. We present a workflow for confidence-weighted network inference that combines (i) functional representations (basis coefficients or discretized trajectories), (ii) selection-frequency estimation, and (iii) correlation-aware resampling to improve edge precision. Two baselines are considered: functional boosting with curve-level subsampling, and a generic basis/FPCA + grouped sparsity recipe producing selection frequencies for candidate regulators. We then enhance robustness with SelectBoost by perturbing predictors within correlation- or region-defined groups and aggregating edge selection proportions across perturbation levels. Edges are scored by persistence under increasingly stringent perturbations, yielding an interpretable edge confidence index. Region-aware grouping supports temporal interpretability (e.g., early vs late windows) and prioritizes biologically actionable hypotheses. We discuss how confidence-thresholded networks improve reproducibility across cohorts and support downstream enrichment and validation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Leveraging Persistent Mutation Representations for Interpretable Cancer Survival Modeling via Pathway-Constrained Neural Encoding
authors: Yen-Jung Chiu, Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Taiwan; Yen-Hua Huang, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan
abstract: Modeling the prognostic impact of somatic mutations remains challenging due to heterogeneous functional effects and limited interpretability. We propose a framework that leverages large language model (LLM)-derived mutation embeddings, combined with a pathway-constrained neural encoder, to capture biologically meaningful mutation effects for survival modeling. We define persistent mutations as alterations exhibiting sustained clonal presence or dosage impact, operationalized using variant allele frequency, multiplicity, and copy-number amplification, thereby approximating long-term regulatory influence. Mutation embeddings are generated via an external LLM embedding API using structured genomic descriptors (e.g., gene identity, mutation attributes), and subsequently integrated through a pathway-aware architecture derived from curated KEGG gene sets. Clinical and genomic covariates (e.g., pTMB, ploidy, age, stage) are jointly modeled. On TCGA-LIHC, the model achieves a cross-validated C-index of ~0.70. Ablation analysis shows that removing persistent mutation features degrades performance (0.710 â†’ 0.689), demonstrating their predictive contribution. Furthermore, representation probing indicates that persistent mutation signals are preserved within LLM-derived embeddings, supporting their biological relevance. Interpretability is achieved via multi-level SHAP analysis, including gene-, pathway-, and patient-level features. SHAP beeswarm plots reveal distinct contribution patterns between persistent and non-persistent mutations, and identify dominant prognostic factors such as pTMB, ploidy, and age. This work presents an interpretable and biologically grounded framework that leverages pretrained mutation representations, bridging LLM-based embeddings and cancer survival modeling.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Machine learning framework for mRNA alternative splicing analysis identifies a signature of progression in colorectal adenocarcinoma
authors: Uran Maimekov, Rutgers Health, United States; Antonina Mitrofanova, Department of Health Informatics, Rutgers School of Health Profession, United States
abstract: Despite recent advances in genome-wide profiling and the discovery of novel therapeutic options for colorectal adenocarcinoma (COAD), effective patient classification for the risk of cancer progression remains underdeveloped. Recent research has highlighted the crucial role of mRNA alternative splicing (AS) in the development and progression of COAD, yet a genome-wide comprehensive evaluation of the role of AS in COAD progression has not been implemented. In this study, we present a robust machine-learning framework designed to uncover clinically relevant AS events associated with progression-free survival (PFS) in COAD patients. For this, we analyzed RNA sequencing data from the TCGA-COAD cohort (n = 266). We employed a machine learning approach integrating Cox Proportional Hazards (PH) analysis and Robust Likelihood-Based Survival (RBSURV) modeling that identified a five-event AS-PFS signature (spanning AS events in OR52K1, SPIN3, NDUFV1, BMPR1A, and ARPC4 genes). By leveraging this signature, we defined a risk score for each patient, categorizing them into low and high-risk groups. This signature and its risk score were further validated through Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis in the TCGA-COAD test set and independent patient cohort AC-ICAM (n = 348). Comparison to other markers and methods further confirmed the independent predictive value of the AS-PFS risk signature. We propose that this signature could be utilized in clinical settings to enhance patient stratification at diagnosis and further inform personalized treatment strategies.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Multi-Modal Virtual Screening Identifies Candidate Inhibitors of Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells Across Breast Cancer Subtypes
authors: Huikang Ye, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Hsi-Chun Wang, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Ying-Ju Lai, Department of Biostatistics and Health Data Science, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Hsiao-Chun Chen, Department of Bioengineering, Swanson School of Engineering, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yu-Chiao Chiu, Department of Medicine, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yu-Chih Chen, Departments of Computational and Systems Biology & Bioengineering, UPMC Hillman Cancer Center, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) are increasingly recognized as key drivers of tumor therapeutic resistance, metastasis, and recurrence. However, systematic discovery of compounds that selectively inhibit PGCCs remains challenging due to their rarity, heterogeneity, and limitations of large-scale experimental screening. To address this, we developed a multi-modal machine learning framework to prioritize candidate anti-PGCC compounds by integrating diverse drug-related data. Our approach incorporates five complementary feature modalities: chemical structure, known targets and pathways, drug-induced transcriptomic profiles, drug-induced cell morphology responses, and text-derived biomedical knowledge. Each modality was modeled independently using machine learning methods, with representation learning applied to high-dimensional datasets. The best-performing models from each modality were integrated through ensemble blending to generate final predictions of PGCC-selective inhibition. We evaluated the framework across four breast cancer cell lines representing major subtypes: SUM159, MDA-MB-231, SKBR3, and MCF7. Multi-modal integration significantly improved predictive performance compared with individual modalities across all cell lines. The highest performance was observed in SKBR3 cells, where the ensemble model achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.462, compared to 0.305 for the best single modality (transcriptomic features). We further expanded virtual screening using 3,093 additional compounds from the PRISM dataset. Five top-ranked candidates, Selamectin, AV-412, Azeliragon, Lestaurtinib, and UCN-01, were experimentally validated, and all demonstrated inhibition of PGCC formation in MDA-MB-231 cells. These results demonstrate that multi-modal virtual screening provides an effective strategy for identifying anti-PGCC therapeutics and highlight the potential of integrated machine learning approaches to accelerate drug discovery targeting therapy-resistant cancer populations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Multistudy Multimodal Pretraining and Transfer Learning
authors: Chuxuan Gao, Cornell University, United States; Himel Mallick, Cornell University, United States
abstract: Machine learning has become integral to biomedical research, yet its success often depends on large, high-quality datasets that are rarely available. Transfer learning (TL) offers a principled way to leverage information from related large-scale datasets to improve prediction in a target study. However, existing TL methods are typically designed for single-view settings, limiting their use with complex multiview data collected across multiple cohorts. To address this gap, we propose a Multistudy Multimodal TL framework that enables integration-aware knowledge transfer across studies and modalities. The framework employs pretraining using cooperative learning followed by fine-tuning, yielding both general and context-specific predictions. Simulation studies and multi-omics analyses from cancer immunotherapy and inflammatory bowel disease cohorts demonstrate that our method improves predictive accuracy and cross-study generalization. Our method thus establishes a principled and scalable foundation for cross-study and cross-modality transfer learning, substantially outperforming published methods in estimation and prediction. An open-source implementation is publicly available at: https://github.com/himelmallick/GPTLasso

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Deep learning enabled prediction of nuclear lamina-associated chromatin
authors: Priyojit Das, Department of Molecular Biology, United States; Jeannie T Lee, Department of Molecular Biology, United States
abstract: Tethering of chromatin regions to nuclear lamina contributes to genome organization and gene regulation. Disruption of this lamina association has been found to be associated with different pathogenic conditions. Several studies have been performed to delineate the role of different molecular and epigenomic factors in mediating the chromatin lamina association. However, the influence of genomic sequences in lamina association has received much less attention. Here, we present LADDER, a multimodal deep leaning model to predict lamina association based on DNA sequence, gene density, LINE1 and SINE densities. The predictions made by LADDER are not cell-type specific in nature. By leveraging the predictive capability of LADDER, and performing in silico genome-wide random deletions, we established a background landscape of intrinsic genome lamina susceptibility, revealing that chromatin lamina perturbation is not uniformly distributed across the genome but is concentrated within boundary-centered architectural transition zones. Building on this landscape, we showed that clinically pathogenic structural variants and deletions of CTCF binding sites alter lamina tethering predominantly when they primarily localize to boundary-proximal structurally sensitive chromatin regions. Applying LADDER across species, we examined allele-specific differential lamina association of mouse escapee genes. We further demonstrated the effectiveness of integrating nonspecific lamina tethering data with the other cell-type-specific data to improve the modeling of 3D chromatin structures ranging from genome to gene level. Collectively, we showed how LADDER can be used to predict lamina tethering for different wild-type conditions and genetic disruptions across different species, thus providing avenues for generating new biological hypotheses.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: BreedAI: An open-source framework for fair and standardized machine learning-based genomic prediction in livestock
authors: Nuha Bintayyash, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Ministry of Environment, Saudi Arabia; Areej Almuhayya, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Ministry of Environment, Saudi Arabia; Hatim Almutairi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Ministry of Environment, Saudi Arabia; Mohammed Alarawi , National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Ministry of Environment, Saudi Arabia; Mashael Alghuraybi, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Ministry of Environment, Saudi Arabia; Aroob Alhumaidy, National Livestock and Fisheries Development Program (NLFDP), Ministry of Environment, Saudi Arabia
abstract: Genomic prediction is central to modern livestock breeding, yet existing workflows are difficult to compare, reproduce, and operationalize. Production pipelines often rely on GBLUP without systematic benchmarking, while research studies apply inconsistent preprocessing and validation strategies with limited fairness, traceability, and reproducibility. A unified framework is needed to standardize machine learning evaluation and enable reliable deployment across livestock populations. We present BreedAI, an open-source genomic prediction framework built on three principles: transparency, fair standardization, and a reproducible pipeline. BreedAI uses a shared backbone for learning and deployment: sample and SNP quality control, VanRaden genomic relationship matrix construction, fixed-effects modeling, and seed-controlled training, validation, and test partitions. This ensures fair and consistent model evaluation. The framework provides a literature-aligned GBLUP baseline and an extensible benchmarking engine that evaluates 18 genomic prediction models spanning Bayesian, regularized linear, kernel, tree-based, and neural approaches, together with ensemble strategies, including non-negative ridge stacking. BreedAI supports deployment through standardized prediction pipelines for new animals with SNP alignment and imputation. We evaluated BreedAI on the public Van den Berg simulated Holstein dataset where GBLUP achieved test Pearson r = 0.835-0.912. Systematic benchmarking revealed that penalized linear models outperformed GBLUP on moderately polygenic traits (up to r = 0.956), while stacking ensembles achieved the highest performance (r = 0.957), improving mean accuracy to 0.912 (+3.0% over baseline). Standardized reporting captured multiple metrics (R2, Pearson r, RMSE, MAE, bias) with fully reproducible outputs. BreedAI provides a standardized and reproducible framework for machine learning benchmarking and deployment in livestock genomic prediction. By enabling fair comparison across models and datasets, it supports scalable application to multiple species, including cattle, sheep, and goats, and facilitates future genomic prediction in under-represented populations such as camels and horses.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: EMTformer: A Pretrained Transformer Model for Hybrid EMT State Identification from Single-Cell Data
authors: Jiajia Liu, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States; Kexin Huang, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States; Xiaobo Zhou, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States
abstract: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a central driver of metastatic initiation and therapeutic resistance. Increasing evidence shows that EMT is not a binary process but a continuous spectrum of cell states, in which hybrid epithelial/mesenchymal phenotypes retain epithelial adhesion while acquiring mesenchymal traits. These hybrid states confer remarkable cellular plasticity, enabling tumor cells to migrate, adapt to hostile microenvironments, and dynamically interact with immune and stromal components. Critically, this phenotypic continuum cannot be fully captured by traditional binary classifications, posing a major challenge for accurately characterizing EMT dynamics in high-dimensional single-cell data. To address this challenge, we developed EMTformer, a transformer-based foundation model for single-cell representation learning and hybrid EMT state identification.
