We curated a large-scale compendium of ~950,000 single-cell transcriptomic profiles from primary tumors across 19 cancer types for pretraining, followed by fine-tuning on ~400,000 EMT cells. EMTformer enables precise resolution of intermediate EMT phenotypes and introduces a continuous scoring framework to quantify EMT plasticity at single-cell resolution. Validation on ~80,000 single cells shows that EMTformer outperforms traditional methods, including random forests and SVMs, achieving the highest accuracy in hybrid EMT state identification. Applying EMTformer to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) data, we successfully identified hybrid EMT subpopulations and uncovered evidence that specific subsets may serve as peritoneal metastasis-initiating cells. By integrating large-scale, heterogeneous single-cell data, EMTformer provides a robust and generalizable framework for dissecting EMT heterogeneity and highlights potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Identification of Atopic Dermatitis Endotypes and Machine Learning–Based Prediction Using RNA-seq of Minimally Invasive Skin Samples.
authors: Yujin Ko, Department of Animal Biotechnology, Jeju National University, South Korea; Jin-Muk Lim, Innowl Inc., South Korea; Yeonhee Park, Department of Animal Biotechnology, Jeju National University, South Korea; Kwang Hoon Lee, Cutis Biomedical Research Center, South Korea; Chang Ook Park, Department of Dermatology, Yonsei University College of Medicine, South Korea; Jong-Eun Park, Department of Animal Biotechnology, Jeju National University, South Korea; Jinhyun Ahn, Department of Management Information Systems, Jeju National University, South Korea
abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease with a complex pathogenesis and molecular heterogeneity. Diagnosis relies primarily on clinical presentation and physician judgment, limiting the identification of molecularly defined endotypes. To investigate AD heterogeneity, we analyzed skin transcriptome data to define endotypes and develop predictive models. Skin transcriptome profiles were generated from participants recruited at Severance Hospital using microneedle-based minimally invasive skin sampling, followed by RNA sequencing. A total of 67 samples were collected, of which 15 AD and 10 control passed quality control and were used for analyses. Consensus clustering using multiple clustering algorithms through a voting-based strategy identified three endotypes (A, B, C), with the number of clusters selected based on clustering stability. The Gene Ontology enrichment analysis revealed distinct biological programs: Endotype A showed enrichment of RNA processing and mRNA splicing, along with transcriptional regulation and viral life cycle-associated processes; Endotype B was enriched in immune activation and cytokine-mediated signaling, including cytokine production, immune effector processes, myeloid cell differentiation, and granulocyte migration; and endotype C was characterized by epidermal development and keratinocyte differentiation, reflecting skin barrierâ€“related processes. Machine learning models were applied for case-control and endotype classification, and evaluated using stratified and repeated stratified cross-validation, respectively. The best-performing model achieved 92.2% accuracy for case-control classification. For endotype classification, Support Vector Machines achieved 98% (A, B + C), and Random Forest achieved 86.1% (B, C) accuracy. This suggests that transcriptome-defined endotypes are biologically distinct and computationally predictable, highlighting their potential for molecularly informed AD stratification.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Demographic Bias in Single-Cell Foundation Models: Systematic Evaluation and Mitigation Through Synthetic Data Augmentation
authors: Fernando Peralta Castro, Moravian University, Brown University, United States; Jiaqi Zhang, Brown University Department of Computer Science, United States; Ritambhara Singh, Brown University, Department of Computer Science and Center for Computational Molecular Biology, United States
abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used in biomedical research, yet biases can enter at every stage of the analysis pipeline, from which donors are sampled, to how cohorts are composed, to how models amplify existing imbalances. Training datasets are often strongly imbalanced across demographic variables such as sex, age, and ethnicity, and these imbalances propagate into model representations, creating demographic representation gaps where minority groups are overlooked in downstream analysis. Such biases risk producing diagnostic errors that disproportionately affect underrepresented populations, particularly as foundation models begin to influence clinical decision-making. We address three questions in this work: Does demographic imbalance affect model learning? Which foundation model is most robust to that imbalance? And which rebalancing strategy most reliably restores equity? We evaluate three foundation models (scFoundation, Geneformer, scGPT) on three cohorts spanning a wide range of demographic imbalance: an interstitial lung disease cohort, a colorectal cancer atlas, and the Asian Immune Diversity Atlas. We compare four strategies for addressing data imbalance: proportional sampling, downsampling, upsampling, and realistic augmentation based on the scDesign3 model, and benchmark them against Harmony with the demographic group as the batch variable. We find that all models exhibit poor integration on proportional data, with representation gaps scaling with demographic imbalance, and provide practical guidelines for selecting rebalancing strategies in real-world settings.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A Causal Multimodal Mediation Framework for Multiomics Data
authors: Nalin Arora, Cornell University, United States; Sneha Das, University of Turku, Finland; Leo Lahti, University of Turku, Finland; Himel Mallick, Cornell University, United States
abstract: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) has matured considerably over the past decade, making multimodal endpoints integral to biomedical research. Yet most analytic approaches remain limited to association-based, single-modality modeling, with no unified framework for causal mediation analysis across biological layers. To address this gap, we present a population-scale multimodal mediation framework for characterizing causal relationships spanning multiomics data. The framework accommodates both parallel mediation structures (e.g., X â†’ Mâ‚ â†’ Y and X â†’ Mâ‚‚ â†’ Y) and sequential pathways (e.g., X â†’ Mâ‚ â†’ Mâ‚‚ â†’ Y), enabling systematic decomposition of how cross-modal interactions shape downstream outcomes. To build this approach, we first developed an unified multimodal AI engine that combines early, intermediate, and late fusion strategies to jointly model heterogeneous modalities. The engine supports continuous, binary, survival, and multiclass outcomes within a single estimation pipeline. Next, we embed this engine within a counterfactual causal mediation framework, enabling formal decomposition of total effects into natural direct and indirect components across arbitrarily structured mediation paths. Across large-scale multimodal datasets, including iHMP and FINRISK, our framework outperforms single-modality approaches and reveals biologically meaningful cross-modal relationships, while simulation studies further demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness over published methods. An open-source software implementation of our method is publicly available.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: An Ensemble-Based Multi-Omics Feature Selection Framework for Cross-Cancer Identification of Tertiary Lymphoid Structure Signatures
authors: Wei-Chen Chang, Institute of Biomedical Informatics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan; Yi-Chen Yeh, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Taipei Veterans General Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan; Yu-Chao Wang, Institute of Biomedical Informatics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, Taiwan
abstract: Identifying robust molecular signatures from high-dimensional multi-omics data remains a major challenge in computational biology, particularly for complex immune-related phenotypes such as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Here, we propose an ensemble-based multi-omics feature selection framework to identify stable and generalizable TLS-associated signatures across pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD), cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD). Multi-omics data, including RNA sequencing, DNA methylation, somatic mutations, and copy number variation (CNV), were integrated from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). To capture regional genomic effects, CNV features were further clustered based on shared alteration patterns. Our framework employs a two-stage feature selection strategy. First, minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) is applied independently to each omics layer to reduce dimensionality while preserving informative features. These features are then concatenated and refined using an ensemble of machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost). Features consistently selected across models are retained to enhance robustness and reduce model-specific bias. Across three cancer types, our approach identified TLS-associated signatures (24 in PAAD, 38 in CHOL, and 16 in STAD) and achieved consistent performance in cancer-specific classification tasks. Cross-cancer evaluation further demonstrated the transferability of cancer-specific models to held-out cancer types. Notably, CR2 (CD21) and CLEC17A were reproducibly selected across all datasets, supporting their biological relevance while demonstrating the stability of the proposed framework. Overall, this study presents a robust and generalizable strategy for multi-omics feature selection, providing a scalable computational approach for identifying immune-related biomarkers across cancer types, with potential for extension to other high-dimensional multi-omics prediction tasks.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Bridging Continuous and Discrete Generation for Protein Sequence Structure Co-Design
authors: Leo Tianlai Chen, Harvard Medical School, United States
abstract: Designing functional proteins remains one of the central challenges in computational biology, requiring joint reasoning over amino acid sequences and three-dimensional structures, two fundamentally different modalities that existing methods largely treat in isolation or through oversimplified unified representations. This disconnect limits the capacity of current models to capture the intrinsic bidirectional dependencies between sequence and structure that ultimately determine protein function. We present Centaur, a unified generative framework for protein sequence and structure co-design that reconciles continuous structural generation and discrete sequence modeling within a single coherent architecture. Centaur introduces a modality-aware design embedded within a shared latent space, enabling each modality to undergo tailored generative processing while retaining rich cross-modal interactions. We evaluate Centaur across a comprehensive suite of protein design benchmarks, encompassing unconditional co-design, structure prediction, inverse folding, and fitness prediction over a large-scale mutational landscape. A 200M parameter instantiation already demonstrates competitive performance relative to comparably scaled baselines across multiple evaluation axes, while exhibiting favorable diversity and novelty in co-design settings. Collectively, these results indicate that the longstanding representational divide between sequence and structure modeling can be systematically addressed within a unified generative paradigm. We posit that Centaur offers a principled and scalable foundation for general-purpose protein design, with potential impact spanning de novo protein engineering, structure-informed therapeutic discovery, and the broader scientific pursuit of decoding the sequence-structure-function relationship in biological macromolecules.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Latent Class Attribution Model: A Deep Learning Framework for Interpretable Subgroup Discovery and Interaction-conditioned Prediction in Heterogeneous Clinical Data
authors: Xiaoxu Deng, University of Kansas Medical Center, United States; Jeffrey Thompson, University of Kansas Medical Center, United States
abstract: Patient Heterogeneity is a fundamental challenge in precision medicine, where unobserved latent structures lead to different clinical outcomes despite similar observed features. Although deep learning models have some ability to capture latent structure through automated meta feature construction, existing approaches lack an explicit mechanism for capturing latent structure, which can impact model performance and fail to uncover interpretable latent subgroups and their associated feature interactions, which limits their utility for precision medicine. We propose the Latent Class Attribution Model (L-CAM), a supervised deep learning model that simultaneously performs outcome prediction, latent subgroup discovery, and subgroup-specific feature importance attribution in high-dimensional clinical data. L-CAM integrates latent class inference with feature interaction modeling via a cross-network, distance-based latent assignment, attention mechanisms, optimized through a structured loss function that balances predictive accuracy and latent structure learning within a unified and computationally efficient framework. Through extensive simulations under varying conditions (class separation, feature correlation, interaction strength, prevalence, and sample size), L-CAM achieves improved predictive performance over the baseline model (mean AUC 0.971 vs 0.944) with a lower mean binary cross-entropy (BCE 0.238 vs 0.296), while accurately recovering latent class membership (mean ARI 0.778) and interaction structures (mean pair recovery rate 0.882). Application to a real-world polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) dataset demonstrates that L-CAM identifies stable and interpretable latent subgroups with competitive predictive performance compared to both the baseline model and logistic regression (mean AUC 0.943 vs 0.938 vs 0.931) with a lower mean BCE (0.312 vs 0.472 vs 0.375). Stability test across cross-validation folds and falsification test under feature permutation further demonstrate that captured subgroups are consistent and meaningful latent structures rather than random artifacts. Overall, L-CAM is particularly suited for identifying latent structure within a single disease population with potential applications in precision medicine where heterogeneous treatment effects and complex feature interactions are prevalent.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: AI-based Characterization of Alzheimer’s Disease Phenotypes from Population Scale Single Cell Data
authors: Chenfeng He, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison, United States; Athan Li, Department of Computer Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53706, USA., United States; Kalpana Arachchilage, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA., United States; Chirag Gupta, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA., United States; Xiang Huang, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA., United States; Xinyu Zhao, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison; Department of Neuroscience, UW-Madison, United States; Carissa Sirois, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison; Department of Neuroscience, UW-Madison, United States; Kiran Girdhar, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; Georgios Voloudakis, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; Gabriel Hoffman, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; Jaroslav Bendl, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; John Fullard, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; Donghoon Lee, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; Panos Roussos, Center for Disease Neurogenomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, 10029, USA., United States; Daifeng Wang, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States
abstract: The complexity of Alzheimerâ€™s disease (AD) manifests in diverse clinical phenotypes, including cognitive impairment and neuropsychiatric symptoms. However, the etiology of these phenotypes remains elusive. To address this, the PsychAD project generated a population-level single-nucleus RNA-seq dataset comprising over 6 million nuclei from the prefrontal cortex of >1,000 individual brains, covering a variety of disease phenotypes. Leveraging this dataset, we developed a computational framework, called Phenotype Associated Single Cell encoder (PASCode), to score single-cell phenotype associations, and identified âˆ¼1.5 million phenotype associated cells (PACs) from 584 donors with AD-related phenotypes. PASCode ensembles multiple statistical methods into a graph neural model for robust scoring. Comparing PACs within 27 brain cell subclasses, we prioritized cell subpopulations and their expressed genes for various AD phenotypes. For instance, we identified microglia subpopulations implicated in AD pathology; reactive astrocyte subtypes with altered neuroprotective and neurotoxic gene expression that likely confer cognitive resilience; and enhanced excitatory/inhibitory imbalance and mitochondrial dysfunction in cognitively impaired AD donors. We also identified many PACs for multiple phenotypes, including the astrocytes between AD and depression showing specific gene expression patterns such as inflammation and Endoplasmic Reticulum stress pathways. These prioritized subpopulations, genes and pathways potentially offer valuable insights for precision diagnostic and therapeutic development. We also validated our findings in external population-scale datasets including AD and major depression disorder, compiled an AD-phenotypic single-cell atlas, and delivered the framework as an open-source tool with pre-trained models and a web application for community use.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: GRNFormer: Accurate Generalizable Gene Regulatory Network Inference Using Graph Transformer
authors: Akshata Hegde, University of Missouri Columbia, United States; Jianlin Cheng, University of Missouri - Columbia, United States
abstract: Motivation: Deciphering gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell transcriptomics data remains a fundamental challenge due to data sparsity, high dimensionality, and the lack of scalable, generalizable inference models. To address this, we present GRNFormer, a graph transformer framework for accurate GRN inference across species, cell types, and platforms without requiring cell-type annotations or prior regulatory information. Methods: GRNFormer integrates a transformer-based gene expression encoder (Gene-Transcoder) with a variational graph autoencoder (GraViTAE) employing pairwise attention to jointly learn gene (node) and co-expression (edge) representations. Using TF-Walker, a transcription factor-centered subgraph sampling strategy, it captures regulatory interactions from both single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data. Results: Benchmarking against nine state-of-the-art methods shows that GRNFormer outperforms both traditional and deep learning approaches in blind evaluations on unseen cell types and cross-dataset settings, achieving average Sampled Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (Sampled_AUROC) and Sampled Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (Sampled_AUPRC) of 0.90â€“0.98 and Sampled F1 scores of 0.87â€“0.98. The model demonstrates cross-species and cross-modality generalization, achieving strong performance on DREAM5 bulk RNA-seq datasets from Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Across both sampled and full-matrix evaluations, GRNFormer shows robust performance, with strong early precision (EPR) and an average win rate of ~84%. It recovers known and novel regulatory networks, including pluripotency circuits in human embryonic stem cells and immune modules in PBMCs, and enables scalable, biologically interpretable GRN inference across diverse datasets, cell types, and species, establishing GRNFormer as a robust and transferable tool for network biology.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: scMKL: Biology-Guided Kernel Learning for Interpretable and Scalable Single-Cell Multiomics
authors: Sam Kupp, Oregon Health and Science University, United States; Ian Vangordon, Oregon Health and Science University, United States; Mehmet Gonen, Koc University, United States; Ece Eksi, Oregon Health and Science University, United States; Sadik Esener, Oregon Health and Science University, United States; Çiğdem Ak, Oregon Health and Science University, United States
abstract: Single-cell multiomic technologies can profile gene expression and chromatin accessibility in the same cells, creating opportunities to identify regulatory programs associated with cancer phenotypes. However, many integrative machine learning approaches improve prediction at the cost of interpretability, limiting their use for biological discovery and translational research. We developed scMKL, a scalable and interpretable multiple kernel learning framework for single-cell multiomics. scMKL organizes features into biologically meaningful groups, including pathway-defined gene programs and transcription factor motif-associated chromatin programs, and learns how RNA, ATAC, and their combinations contribute to classification and transfer learning tasks. To scale kernel learning to large single-cell datasets, scMKL uses random Fourier feature approximations with sparse regularization, enabling efficient learning while preserving interpretation at the level of modalities, pathways, motifs, and regulatory programs. Across prostate, breast, and lung cancer datasets, scMKL accurately classified cancer-relevant cell states using RNA alone, ATAC alone, or integrated multimodal input. The model identified biological programs associated with clinically relevant phenotypes, including prostate tumor grade, estrogen-associated breast cancer states, and lung cancer subtype, and generalized across datasets in transfer settings. Unlike black-box predictors, scMKL links predictive performance to structured biological explanations, revealing which molecular programs drive classification and how complementary omic layers contribute. More broadly, scMKL provides a reusable framework for building biology-guided, interpretable machine learning models for multimodal single-cell data, with applications in reproducible cell-state annotation, regulatory program discovery, and translational cancer research. Code: https://github.com/ohsu-cedar-comp-hub/scMKL Paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-025-08533-7

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PertVI: Disentangling Intrinsic Cellular Manifolds to Discover Context-Specific Immunity Boosters in Single-Cell Pharmacology
authors: Yue Wang, UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH, United States
abstract: Massive single-cell perturbation screens provide unprecedented opportunities to map the cancer pharmacological interactome, yet extracting precise mechanistic insights remains computationally challenging. While current deep generative models excel at broad data integration and perturbation prediction, they often collapse highly entangled intrinsic cellular states into one single latent representation. This obscures whether a perturbation effect drives, or is driven by, a specific cellular state, limiting the discovery of context-specific therapeutic opportunities. To address this, we developed PertVI (Disentangled Perturbation Variational Inference), a multi-encoder architecture that partitions the standard monolithic latent space into perturbation-agnostic spaces for decoding intrinsic cellular states and perturbation-aware spaces for modeling perturbation effects. By applying structurally aware constraints and conditional transition networks, PertVI is designed to disentangle how perturbations interact with multi-layered cellular dynamics. We evaluated PertVI across two distinct pharmacological contexts. In a massive in vitro screen of human primary CD8+ T cells, PertVI reconstructed the effector differentiation trajectory and cell cycle dynamics while simultaneously isolating state-driving drug effects. This disentanglement prioritized T cell adjuvant agents capable of promoting IL7R+ memory-like phenotypes without distorting natural cellular functions. These include known CAR-T boosters (e.g., decitabine) and novel candidates with reported in vivo anti-PD-1 synergism that are slated for validation. Extending PertVI to the TAHOE-100M atlas further revealed that drug-induced tumoral immunogenicity is also highly gated by specific cellular states, cell cycle phases, and genomic backgrounds. These results demonstrate PertVI's capacity to translate highly entangled single-cell omics into context-aware immunomodulatory strategies in both tumor and immune cell populations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PhenoBridge: A Graph-Guided Contrastive Framework for Phenotype Mapping Across Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Caicai Zhang, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Frank Qingyun Wang, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Yao Lei, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Huidong Su, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Youming Guo, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Xinxin Chen, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Wanling Yang, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Chun Hing She, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Bulk transcriptomic cohorts often provide robust phenotype labels, whereas single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets offer much higher biological resolution but frequently lack reliable outcome annotation. This creates a key challenge for phenotype mapping: how to transfer phenotype-associated information learned from labeled bulk transcriptomes into cellular and spatial data while preserving biological structure and tissue context. Here, we present PhenoBridge, a graph-guided cross-modal learning framework for linking bulk-level phenotype supervision to single-cell and spatial observations (Fig. 1). PhenoBridge integrates supervised learning on bulk transcriptomes, graph-aware representation learning, and outcome-aware contrastive alignment to map cells or spatial units into a shared phenotype-informed latent space and assign observation-level phenotype association scores. By combining a bulk-derived gene graph, optional spatial graph fusion, and a graph-guided encoder, PhenoBridge supports phenotype classification, cross-modal alignment, and optional continuous outcome regression, enabling phenotype-consistent mapping across modalities without requiring direct cell- or spot-level labels. In semi-synthetic benchmarking across five complementary scenarios, including continuous, distributed, dominant, hidden-state, and rare-cell signal architectures, PhenoBridge showed robust and consistently strong recovery of phenotype-associated cells. It achieved the best overall mean cell-level ROCâ€“AUC in both binary and survival benchmarks, with particular strength in settings where phenotype signals were diffuse, distributed across cell types, or confined to subtle subpopulations. These results indicate that PhenoBridge remains effective under heterogeneous and challenging signal structures that are difficult for existing methods to resolve reliably. We further applied PhenoBridge to biologically and clinically relevant transcriptomic datasets. In heart failure, PhenoBridge identified adverse phenotype-associated cellular states enriched in cardiomyocyte and related compartments, with spatial analyses further localizing high-risk programs to anatomically structured ventricular regions. In breast cancer, the framework localized prognosis-associated states to stromal, vascular, and selected epithelial compartments, highlighting activated fibrovascular niches with coherent extracellular matrix and mesenchymal programs. Across applications, PhenoBridge revealed biologically interpretable cellular and spatial patterns and supported transferability to external bulk cohorts. Together, these results establish PhenoBridge as a flexible framework for linking bulk-level phenotype supervision to cellular and spatial mechanisms across transcriptomic modalities.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Personalized Single-Cell Transcriptomics Reveals Molecular Diversity in Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Athan Li, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Daifeng Wang, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States; Panos Roussos, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Donghoon Lee, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; John Fullard, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Jaroslav Bendl, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Gabriel Hoffman, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Georgios Voloudakis, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Kiran Girdhar, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Pramod Bharadwaj Chandrashekar, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States; Shuang Liu, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Xiang Huang, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Ryan Conway Burczak, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Chirag Gupta, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Ting Jin, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States; Noah Cohen Kalafut, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States; Sayali Alatkar, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States
abstract: Understanding the heterogeneity of brain diseases requires approaches that capture population-level variation in molecular and cellular mechanisms. Functional genomics has emerged as a key strategy for investigating these mechanisms from genotype to gene regulation and cellâ€“cell communication. While recent large-scale single-cell studies have revealed population-level gene expression trends, modeling functional genomic variation at the individual donor level remains challenging. We performed personalized functional genomics analysis on population-scale single-nucleus RNA-seq data, with cross-cohort validation across multiple cohorts comprising over 1900 individual brains, capturing donor-level cell type interactions and gene regulatory networks. Using a knowledge-guided graph neural network, we learned latent representations of functional genomics (embeddings) and scored the importance of cell types, genes, and their interactions for each donor. In contrast to population-averaged methods, our framework preserves individual donor variation across cell types, genes, and their interactions. The embeddings improved phenotype classification and identified molecularly defined subpopulations, and traced disease progression trajectories in AD. Our importance scores. Our importance scores, derived from graph attentions, identified significant inter-donor differences and prioritized personalized cell type genes and gene regulation. Finally, we identified gene regulatory QTLs (grQTLs) linking genetic variants to donor-level regulatory changes, providing novel insights into gene regulatory relationships beyond traditional eQTLs. We validated our findings in external cohorts, demonstrating robustness and generalizability. All results are summarized into a personalized functional genomics atlas for AD, including an open-source framework, iBrainMap. Our work provides a scalable approach to model population-scale functional genomic variation and offers a resource for mechanistic insights and precision targeting in brain diseases.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CHERRY: Computational Hybrid Engine for Regulatory Response in perturbed sYstems
authors: Jimyung Park, Department of Medicine, Division of Hematology/Oncology, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Lawrence Wu, Department of Medicine, Division of Hematology/Oncology, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Sung Joo Jang, Department of Surgery, Division of Surgical Sciences, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Ryan Moy, Department of Medicine, Division of Hematology/Oncology, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States
abstract: Background Recent advances in artificial intelligence have highlighted its potential to uncover cancer regulatory mechanisms. However, most approaches remain limited to single-modality analyses and fail to capture how genomic regulation drives transcriptional programs and clinically relevant phenotypes. Here, we present CHERRY (Computational Hybrid Engine for Regulatory Response in perturbed sYstems), a machine learning framework integrating multiple biological layers to discover cancer regulatory mechanisms. Methods CHERRY combines sequence-based regulatory inference using Alphagenome, perturbation-aware transcriptomic modeling using State-ST, and downstream correlation analysis with TCGA data. As a proof-of-concept study, we applied CHERRY to five prioritized regulator-target pairs in liver cancer: MYCâ†’BCAT1, MYCâ†’YTHDF1, MYCâ†’BIRC5, SP1â†’HMGA1, and HMGA1â†’GLUL. Each pair was evaluated across three evidence layers: Alphagenome binding score for sequence-based regulatory inference, log2 fold change and P-value for State-ST perturbation prediction, and Pearson correlation coefficient for TCGA cohorts. Results Among the five pairs, four corresponded to previously reported regulatory relationships: MYCâ†’BCAT1, MYCâ†’YTHDF1, MYCâ†’BIRC5, and SP1â†’HMGA1. Notably, MYCâ†’BCAT1 emerged as the strongest integrated example, showing consistent support across regulatory prediction (binding score, 67.0), perturbation-linked target response (log2FC=0.475 and P-value = 0.008), and positive correlation from TCGA-LIHC (Pearson r = 0.198 and P-value Conclusion Overall, CHERRY provides a generalizable framework for linking regulatory prediction, perturbational transcriptomics, and clinical relevance, enabling interpretable multi-omics discovery in cancer research.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Uncertainty-Aware Ensemble Learning for Bacterial sgRNA/Cas9 On-Target Activity Prediction
authors: Tyler Browne, Western University (Ontario), Canada; David Edgell, Western University (Ontario), Canada; Gregory Gloor, Western University (Ontario), Canada
abstract: Methods to predict sgRNA/Cas9 on-target activity in bacteria have advanced over the past decade, driven by pooled assays providing large datasets and increases in modelling methodology. Models typically focus on the target site sequence as an input, with a single activity score used as the target label for training. While these models perform well, the method, and single output prediction per site, ignore the uncertainty inherent to the process. In this work we break down the uncertainty in sgRNA/Cas9 activity prediction into two distinct variance sources: 1) label variance arising from biological and technical variability, and 2) model variance arising from the stochastic nature of model training. Using an ensemble approach, we capture these sources of variance through training sub-models on sampled log2 fold-change activity score estimates. Variance across sub-model predictions is then used as a filter to remove predictions of low confidence. With this approach, consistent best-in-class performance is attained for ensemble models across six distinct held-out and independent testing datasets. We show that this methodology extends to different Cas9-variants and is architecture-agnostic, allowing for its use as a plug-and-play system. Here we present a data-focused deep ensemble methodology and set of models for bacterial sgRNA/Cas9 activity prediction. For researchers needing reliable predictions of sgRNA/Cas9 activity, these tools provide a basis for more informed guide selection, closing the gap between best performance and best dependable performance.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Integration of Single-cell Transcriptomic and Neuroimaging Data Reveals Cellular-Level Molecular Programs Underlying Neurodegeneration and Clinical Heterogeneity in ALS
authors: Emily Cui, McGill University, Canada; Veronika Pak, McGill University, Canada; Tobias R. Baumeister, McGill University, Canada; Sanjay Kalra, University of Alberta, Canada; Yasser Iturria-Medina, McGill University, Canada
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a clinically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder characterized by spatially structured patterns of brain atrophy and variability in motor and cognitive decline. Single-cell transcriptomic studies in ALS have largely been confined to a limited set of brain regions, whereas neuroimaging has revealed widely distributed patterns of neurodegeneration. However, these two domains remain largely disconnected, hindering a mechanistic understanding of region-specific tissue vulnerability. Here, we present a multiscale framework integrating cell-type-specific region-resolved gene expression from the Allen Brain Cell Atlas with MRI-derived gray matter atrophy from ALS patients in the Canadian ALS Neuroimaging Consortium (CALSNIC), mapped to a shared anatomical space. Using partial least squares (PLS) regression, we identified molecular-structural vulnerability axes capturing shared spatial covariance between intrinsic cellular transcriptional organization and neurodegeneration. The leading axes explained a substantial proportion of covariance, with the first ten axes collectively explaining 94.9% of shared covariance. Subject-specific expression of these axes was associated with clinical heterogeneity, including differences in onset phenotype and longitudinal motor and cognitive decline. Biological interpretation revealed consistent contributions from inhibitory interneuron populations and enrichment of synaptic signaling and neuronal connectivity pathways. Gene signatures derived from top-ranked features accurately predicted ALS status in an independent transcriptomic cohort, supporting the generalizability of identified molecular programs. Together, these findings establish a whole-brain framework linking cellular transcriptional architecture to neurodegeneration and clinical progression in ALS, providing insight into mechanisms of selective vulnerability and potential targets for biomarker development and therapeutic investigation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Injecting biology on DNALMs through pre-training on SNP and Hi-C informed genomes
authors: Pablo Meyer, IBM, United States; Hongyang Li, IBM Research Healthcare and Life Sciences, United States; Sanjoy Dey, IBM Research Healthcare and Life Sciences, United States; Bum Chul Kwon, IBM Research, United States
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on text demonstrated remarkable results on natural language processing (NLP) tasks. These models have been adapted to decipher the language of DNA, where sequences of nucleotides act as â€œwordsâ€ that encode genomic functions. However, the human genome differs fundamen- tally from natural language, as it lacks clearly defined words or a consistent grammar. Although DNA language models (DNALMs) such as EVO, DNABERT, GENA-LM have achieved a high level of performance on genome-related biolog- ical tasks using DNA sequences as input, these models do not encode biological functions in the presence of DNA sequence variations. To address this problem, we pre-train foundation models that effectively integrate sequence variations, in particular Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) and Hi-C, as they underlie important biological functions and disease. Specifically, we use ModernBERT architecture to pre-train different Biomedical Foundation Models (BMFM), namely, BMFM-DNA-REF in which the model is trained with sequences of varying lengths along with their reverse complements derived from the reference genome, BMFM-DNA-SNP in which a model is trained with sequences created using a novel representation scheme that encodes reference genome along with sequence variations and also Hi-C derived sequences. Our findings indicate that integrating sequence variations into DNALMs and augmenting the token vocabulary helps capture the biological functions of specific DNA sequences, as seen in improvements on all fine-tuning tasks tested (GUE benchmark, MPRA, SNP to disease and eQTLs). To enable more comprehensive assessment in the future, we release our models through HuggingFace and the code to reproduce the results at https://github.com/BiomedSciAI/biomed-multi-omic and encourage the community to collaborate in developing richer benchmarking datasets.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Deduplication of Pangenomic Pretraining Data Enhances Genomic Language Model Efficiency
authors: Alex Ostrovsky, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States; Mahler Revsine, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States; Daniel Khashabi, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States; Michael Schatz, Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering: Computer Science Department, United States
abstract: Major genomic LLMs (gLM) such as Evo2 have continuously increased the size of their pretraining corpora over previous state-of-the-art models to prioritize performance (Brixi et al., 2026). While adding additional human and closely-related genomic data is a major opportunity to enhance human model performance, sheer data volume is becoming prohibitive in scope for many researchers, raising questions of possible efficiency enhancements. Previous non-genomic LLM studies have demonstrated deduplication of pretraining data by removing text with too-similar compositions results in both increased model training efficiency and decreased data regurgitation (Penedo et al., arXiv, 2024; Lee et al., ACL, 2022, Kandpal et al., PMLR, 2022). In our work, we demonstrate the effectiveness of k-mer-based deduplication of genomic data in condensing large pangenomic datasets while retaining or improving model accuracy. The data volume reduction is relative to the relatedness of data, with an ape pangenome of 6 T2T assemblies reducing by 85%, and a pangenome of the 466 human assemblies of the HPRC v2 reducing by 99.9%, while both maintaining similar ratios of base annotation to the original data. Despite a dramatic reduction in pretraining data volume, the resulting models maintained comparable or better performance across a range of fine tuning tasks to those trained on equivalent uncondensed data under the same computational budget (Zhou et al., arXiv, 2024, Patel et al., arXiv, 2024) . Our results demonstrate deduplicated pretraining datasets can permit efficient learning of patterns present in the original pangenome, and could allow larger pretraining data pools on an equivalent budget.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Mechanosensing-driven metabolic enterotypes shape organ-specific breast cancer metastasis
authors: Kexin Huang, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States; Jiajia Liu, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States; Xiaobo Zhou, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, United States
abstract: Breast cancer metastasis emerges in organ microenvironments with distinct extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness and oxygen tension, yet it remains unclear how these biophysical constraints are encoded in tumor-cell state and coupled to metabolic adaptation across metastatic sites. We present a mechanosensing-aware computational framework for reconstructing organ-specific mechanometabolic states from single-cell and spatial multi-omics. The framework first learns a stiffness-informed latent space from hydrogel-perturbed breast cancer cell lines using a variational autoencoder coupled with flow matching, and then transfers this representation to single-cell RNA-seq profiles from primary tumors and metastases to infer per-cell stiffness scores. We integrate these scores with single-cell metabolic pathway activities, transcription-factor regulons, CNV-derived subclones, spatial transcriptomics, and targeted metabolomics to quantify how biomechanical context shapes metabolic state, and to distinguish clonally selected from environmentally plastic phenotypes. Across metastasis scRNA-seq datasets from bone, brain, and lymph node, inferred stiffness scores stratified invasive states and were elevated in brain and bone lesions relative to primary tumors and lymph nodes. Topic modeling over 79 metabolic pathways identified three recurrent mechanosensing-associated metabolic enterotypes: an ECM/remodeling and cofactor program enriched in bone, an anabolic biosynthetic program dominant in brain, and an oxidative/energy-scavenging program prominent in lymph node. These computationally inferred programs were supported by targeted metabolomics, which showed enrichment of phenylalanine/taurine metabolites and lipid-oxidation intermediates in highly invasive cells, and by spatial transcriptomics, which localized cholesterol biosynthesis and fatty-acid Î²-oxidation hotspots to epithelial tumor regions. CNV-informed phylogenies resolved site-enriched subclones with distinct metabolic liabilities, enabling separation of selection-like versus plasticity-like metabolic states. In silico perturbation analysis prioritized stiffness-responsive regulators, including YAP/TEAD and SREBF1, as candidate drivers of brain-associated lipid metabolism, and a PPP1R1B-TCF7-PTS axis linked to phenylalanine metabolism and JQ1+paclitaxel sensitivity in bone-tropic clones. Finally, integrating mechanosensing features, metabolic enterotypes, and regulon activity yielded metastasis-propensity and mechanometabolic drug-sensitivity scores predictive of organotropism, adverse survival, and therapeutic response in retrospective cohorts. Together, this work provides a computational taxonomy of breast cancer metastasis that connects biophysical niche cues to metabolic programs and nominates organ-aware therapeutic vulnerabilities.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Multiscale and Structure-Constrained Deep Learning for Robust Enhancement of Sparse Single-Cell Hi-C Data
authors: Yichen Ma, Tianjin Normal University, China; Shaoqiang Zhang, Tianjin Normal University, China; Yong Chen, Rowan University, United States
abstract: Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) enables the characterization of 3D genome organization at single-cell resolution, but its widespread application is limited by extreme data sparsity and noise. Existing deep learning approaches have improved pixel-level reconstruction quality, yet often fail to simultaneously capture multi-scale chromatin structures and preserve biologically meaningful features such as distance-dependent decay patterns and topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries. We propose MSCHiCE, an end-to-end deep learning framework for scHi-C data enhancement that integrates multi-scale feature modeling with biologically informed structural constraints. The model is built on a U-Net-style encoder-decoder architecture augmented with distance-stratified convolution, which explicitly models interaction patterns across genomic distance scales, and a progressive diffusion-based denoising module to separate signal from noise. A high-frequency detail extractor and multi-head hierarchical attention further enhance the recovery of local structural features and long-range dependencies. To ensure biological fidelity, we design a multi-task loss function incorporating distance decay, TAD boundary consistency, interaction peak preservation and distributional constraints, combined with a progressive training strategy. Extensive evaluations on multiple public datasets demonstrate that MSCHiCE achieves superior performance than ScHiCEDRN, HiCDiff and LoopEnhance in both image-based metrics (PSNR, SSIM) and Hi-C-specific reproducibility measures (HiCRep, GenomeDISCO). The model shows strong robustness under extreme sparsity and generalizes effectively across cell types and species. Furthermore, it significantly improves TAD boundary detection accuracy, highlighting its ability to preserve biologically relevant structures. MSCHiCE provides a robust and interpretable solution for enhancing sparse scHi-C data and facilitates downstream analysis of three-dimensional genome organization.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: pertTF: context-aware AI modeling for genome-scale and cross-system perturbation prediction
authors: Lei Wang, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Danwei Huangfu, Sloan Kettering Institute, United States; Wei Li, University of Maryland-Institute for Health Computing, United States; Lumen Chao, Center for Precision Medicine and Genomics Research, Children’s National Hospital, United States; Hanrui Zhang, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Yarui Diao, Duke University Medical Center, United States; Seth Ament, University of Maryland School of Medicine, United States; Bharath Swargam, University of Maryland School of Medicine, United States; Gary Hon, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Mpathi Nzima, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Yangqi Su, University of Maryland-Institute for Health Computing, United States; Huan Zhao, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Nan Hu, Sloan Kettering Institute, United States; Jiahui Zhao, Sloan Kettering Institute, United States; Nan Zhang, Sloan Kettering Institute, United States; Alon Katz, University of Maryland College Park, United States; Samuel Boccara, University of Maryland College Park, United States; Bicna Song, Children’s National Hospital, United States; Vipin Menon, University of Maryland-Institute for Health Computing, United States; Dingyu Liu, Sloan Kettering Institute, United States
abstract: Predicting genetic perturbation responses at a single-cell level is central to building models for cell state and disease. However, existing approaches are limited on predicting phenotypic outcomes beyond expression changes and generalizing predictions across genome-scale perturbations in biologically relevant contexts. Here we introduce pertTF, a transformer-based single-cell genetic perturbation model. pertTF was trained from a unique dataset capturing single cell expressions profiles of 30 full gene knockouts across 14 relevant cell types during human pancreatic development and beta-cell differentiation. pertTF outperforms current methods in predicting expression changes of perturbing unseen genes in unseen cellular contexts. In addition, pertTF infers perturbation-induced shifts in cell identity and population composition, an important phenotypic outcome of perturbation in many physiology and disease settings. Through transfer learning, pertTF operates in physiologically relevant systems, including primary human islets, where large-scale perturbation experiments are challenging. The generalizability of pertTF is further demonstrated by in silico pooled and single-cell CRISPR screens, capturing critical regulators of stem cells and early pancreatic cell development. These results establish pertTF as a framework for integrating large-scale single-cell perturbation data with AI models to predict genetic perturbation effects across cellular systems and disease contexts.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Adjacent Token Prediction for Motif Scaffolding
authors: Rain Haworth, University of Maryland, United States; Samuel Kinstlinger, University of Maryland, United States; Mohammad Teli, University of Maryland, United States
abstract: Transformer-based deep learning models have seen widespread use in protein modeling and have advanced our understanding of the relationship between sequence, structure, and function. Recently, ESM3 introduced a new Transformer-based protein design paradigm that encodes sequence, structure, and function as a series of tracks that can be populated in any order. This is enabled by its representation of 3D protein structures as sequences of discrete tokens and its unconventional use of a bidirectional modeling objective within a generative model. Bidirectional modeling is particularly useful for motif scaffolding, a common protein design task in which a complete protein must be constructed around some core functional motif. However, we are concerned that ESM3's modeling objective introduces theoretical limitations by assuming that masked tokens are independent, reducing the model's understanding of local dependencies. We propose adjacent token prediction (ATP), a novel bidirectional modeling objective designed to improve performance on generative motif scaffolding. We characterize its theoretical advantages over ESM3's modeling objective. We design, implement, and train a small sequence-only prototype model that modifies ESM3's architecture to perform ATP. Finally, we apply this prototype to a motif scaffolding task and evaluate the structural validity of generated proteins with ESM3 and AlphaFold.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Graph neural network framework with cross-attention for transcription factor-ligand binding affinity prediction for synthetic biology applications
authors: Haechan Sung, Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, KAIST, South Korea, South Korea; Mun Su Kwon, Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, KAIST, South Korea, South Korea; Taeyoung Lee, Graduate School of Engineering Biology, KAIST, South Korea, South Korea; Hyun Uk Kim, Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, KAIST, South Korea, South Korea
abstract: Transcription factor (TF)-ligand binding plays a critical role as the first regulatory module in gene circuits by transducing external chemical signals into transcriptional responses. However, machine learning approaches for predicting TF-ligand binding affinity remain underexplored, primarily due to the scarcity of well-curated TF-ligand datasets. We propose a fine-tuning framework for TF-ligand binding affinity prediction based on a pre-trained protein-ligand binding model. The model was pre-trained on the PDBBind dataset and fine-tuned on a TF-ligand dataset constructed from BindingDB using TF annotations derived from UniProt GO terms. Proteins and ligands were represented as graphs, where node features were obtained by comparing three protein language models (ESM-C, ProtBERT, and ProtT5) as alternatives; ProtT5 achieved the best performance on the PDBBind v2016 benchmark and was selected for fine-tuning. Edge features incorporated ESM3-derived topological distance bins for proteins and chemical bond information for ligands. The model captures intramolecular interactions via graph neural networks and intermolecular interactions via cross-attention mechanisms, followed by multilayer perceptrons to predict binding affinity as âˆ’log(Kd) or âˆ’log(Ki). The pre-trained model effectively leverages structural information for general protein-ligand affinity prediction, while the fine-tuned model enables identification of potential TF-ligand pairs. This is particularly relevant to synthetic biology, where designing TFs responsive to user-defined ligands is central to constructing programmable gene regulatory circuits, and our framework provides a computational tool to screen and prioritize candidate pairs during gene circuit design.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CTFacTomo: Reconstructing 3D spatial structures of RNA tomography transcriptomes by collapsed tensor factorization
authors: Tianci Song, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, United States; Quoc Nguyen, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota, United States; Charles Broadbent, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, United States; Rui Kuang, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, United States
abstract: Cells are organized to form three-dimensional structures of complex tissues. RNA tomography, a microdissection approach, applies 1D transcriptomic profiling to consecutive slices of a tissue along orthogonal spatial axes of tomography, and is particularly useful for capturing such 3D organization. We introduce CTFacTomo to learn a Collapsed Tensor Factorization for RNA tomography data from cryosections to reconstruct 3D spatially resolved gene expressions. CTFacTomo combines tensor factorization with collapsing tensor entries to match the bulk gene expressions in each cryosection, enriched by graph Laplacian regularization that uses a product graph of a protein-protein interaction network and spatial graphs. In the experiments, CTFacTomo is first validated on three datasets projected from fully profiled 3D spatial gene expressions to demonstrate that CTFacTomo significantly outperforms the benchmark methods for predicting the ground-truth gene expressions based on the projected 1D spatial gene expressions of three orthographic views. CTFacTomo is then applied to two RNA tomography datasets from zebrafish embryo and mouse olfactory mucosa, respectively. In both datasets, CTFacTomo detects 3D spatial expressions of several marker genes that are consistent with the developmental or functional regions in comparison to accompanying ISH staining images. In addition, a qualitative comparison between the reconstructed zebrafish embryo gene expressions with a matched external 3D Stereo-seq dataset also suggests that CTFacTomo reconstructs more spatially coherent patterns in the whole transcriptome with state-of-the-art performance.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Biological knowledge-based neural network with pretraining for interpretable and robust prediction for herb-phenotype associations
authors: Jaehong Kim, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea; Sungjoo Han, University of California, Los Angeles, USA; Sunjae Lee, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea; Doheon Lee, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea
abstract: Herbs are multi-compound therapeutic entities whose phenotypic effects emerge from complex, coordinated biological pathways. However, predicting herb-phenotype associations remains challenging because herb-level data is sparse and heterogeneous, and purely predictive models provide limited mechanistic interpretability. Here, we propose a pretraining-enhanced biological visible neural network for interpretable and robust herb-phenotype association prediction. We represent each herb through its constituent compounds and initialize the network using compound and phenotype embeddings pretrained from abundant compound-phenotype associations. To overcome the limitations of conventional black-box architectures, we constrain our predictions through a visible hierarchical biological route spanning gene products (GPs), molecular functions (MFs), and biological processes (BPs). This pretraining strategy significantly improves data efficiency, achieving an AUROC of 0.8763 compared to 0.6986 for randomly initialized models under low-data regimes, while also enabling substantially faster convergence. Under stringent held-out evaluations targeting unseen clinical (UMLS semantic categories) and functional (Gene Ontology clusters) phenotype groups, the framework demonstrates robust out-of-distribution generalization. Our model consistently outperforms baseline methods, achieving a mean AUROC improvement of over 0.14 while maintaining strong precision-recall performance. Furthermore, DeepLIFT-based pathway analysis enables the extraction of mechanistically interpretable GP-MF-BP paths underlying model predictions. For representative conditions such as Type 2 Diabetes, these pathway mechanisms show strong attribution similarity across cross-validation folds and achieve statistically significant enrichment in PubMed literature validation. These results demonstrate that integrating pretrained molecular representations with biologically visible constraints provides an interpretable, data-efficient framework for natural product drug discovery, effectively bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and mechanistic insight.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Pathway-Derived Subnetworks Enable Cross-Cohort Survival Transfer in Rare Pediatric Brain Tumors
authors: Seher Zeynep Sonkaya, Department of Computer Engineering and Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, Acibadem University, Turkey; Osman Ugur Sezerman, Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, Acibadem University, Turkey
abstract: Rare pediatric brain tumors such as ependymoma and medulloblastoma lack sufficient samples and survival events for direct prognostic modeling, calling for cross-cohort transfer. Gene expression varies across adult and pediatric tumor types, and whether any representation bridges these differences remains unknown. Active subnetwork enrichment methods such as pathfindR identify mechanistically coherent pathway-level signals; representing tumors through these pathways discards gene-level noise unlikely to generalize, which we propose as a domain-invariant representation for cross-cohort survival transfer in rare pediatric brain tumors, offering a novel pathway-derived representation over raw genes. We compared six feature representations under two transfer settings: same-domain (PBTA pediatric glioma, N=342 to held-out ependymoma, N=81 and medulloblastoma, N=103) and cross-domain (TCGA adult glioma, N≈544 to PBTA targets). All methods used the top 1000 Cox-ranked genes, evaluated across 25 stratified folds. Representations included raw gene features, GSVA pathway scores, PCA projections, and pathfindR subnetworks at three enrichment thresholds (default, p In same-domain transfer, pathfindR outperformed GSVA and PCA on rare tumor types. Stricter thresholds (p Pathway-informed transfer improves survival modeling where direct training is infeasible, with gains scaling with enrichment selectivity. Consistently enriched subnetworks, including cell cycle, Hippo signaling, and focal adhesion, capture domain-invariant biology more effectively than gene-level features.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Construction of a Domain-Specific Knowledge Graph for LPMO Research Using Machine Learning-Based Named Entity Recognition
authors: Kishore Matheswaran, SASTRA deemed to be university, India; Vennila K Marimuthu, SASTRA deemed to be university, India; Ragothaman M Yennamalli, SASTRA deemed to be university, India
abstract: Lytic Polysaccharide Monooxygenases (LPMOs) play a critical role in biomass degradation and have significant applications in biofuel production and industrial biotechnology. These enzymes enhance the breakdown of complex polysaccharides, making them highly relevant in sustainable energy research. However, the rapidly growing volume of scientific literature in this domain makes it increasingly challenging to systematically extract, organize, and interpret relevant biological knowledge. In this study, we propose a pipeline for constructing a domain-specific knowledge graph from LPMO-related research articles using natural language processing (NLP) techniques. A curated dataset comprising titles and abstracts from research works of 14 authors was collected and manually annotated into four entity categories: enzyme, substrate, relation, and others. This annotated dataset served as the foundation for training a machine learning-based Named Entity Recognition (NER) model, enabling automated extraction of domain-specific entities from unstructured text. The extracted entities and their relationships were subsequently structured into a graph database using Neo4j, allowing biological interactions to be represented in a network format. The resulting knowledge graph facilitates improved visualization and exploration of enzymeâ€“substrate relationships within LPMO research, supporting better understanding of complex biological interactions. This work demonstrates the potential of integrating NLP and graph-based approaches to enhance knowledge discovery, scalability, and data-driven insights in specialized biomedical domains.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: AI-Augmented Graph-Based Gene Discovery for Unsolved Mendelian Diseases
authors: Niel Vanhamel, Ghent University, Belgium; Wim Van Criekinge, Ghent University, Belgium
abstract: Over 3,700 Mendelian phenotypes in OMIM remain molecularly unsolved. Existing prioritization tools are largely variant-centric, scoring coding mutations in known disease genes while overlooking the ~98% of the genome comprising regulatory elements. We present an unsupervised, element-centric discovery framework that scores 1.8 million genomic elements (19,869 genes, 1,718,628 cis-regulatory elements, 20,424 lncRNAs, and 1,918 miRNAs) for phenotype relevance using a heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph. Elements are ranked via phenotype-seeded Personalized PageRank combined with self-supervised graph neural network embeddings through Reciprocal Rank Fusion, without requiring disease-gene labels during training. Computational scoring is complemented by autonomous AI agents that investigate phenotypic blind spots, assess biological plausibility, and discover candidates invisible to graph topology: neither computational ranking nor literature reasoning alone determines the outcome, and candidates are validated through convergence of independent evidence streams. Application across unsolved OMIM diseases has generated high-confidence candidate genes with proposed pathogenic mechanisms, supported by converging evidence across population genetics, tissue-specific expression, model organism phenotyping, genome-wide association, chromatin architecture, protein interaction networks, clinical variant databases, and evolutionary conservation, producing testable hypotheses while honest null results prevent false discovery.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Functional Drug Representations Derived from Single-Cell Perturbation Signatures for Drug Response Prediction
authors: Manyan Huang, Yale University, United States; Youli Xia, Boehringer Ingelheim, United States; Bino John, Boehringer Ingelheim, United States; Mark Gerstein, Yale University, United States
abstract: Accurately predicting drug response remains a central challenge in precision oncology. Existing models predominantly treat drugs as static entities, represented by chemical structure or annotations, while relying on bulk transcriptomic profiles of the cell. This paradigm fails to capture the functional impact of drugs on cellular states, as it ignores treatment-induced transcriptional changes. Moreover, current approaches lack a principled way to represent drug effects in a shared space that generalizes across cell types and perturbations. In this work, we present a framework that represents drugs through treatment-induced transcriptional shifts measured in single-cell perturbation data and use these signatures to improve drug response prediction. As a first step, we fine-tuned two single-cell foundation models, scGPT and Cell2Sentence, on glioblastoma single-cell RNA-seq data and evaluated the quality of learned cell-state embeddings using cell-type local inverse Simpson's index (cLISI), Silhouette score, adjusted Rand Index (ARI), and normalized mutual information (NMI). Fine-tuning consistently improved clustering structure and batch integration compared to pretrained baselines. Building on these representations, we are extending the framework to encode treatment-induced transcriptional shifts (Î”X = X_treated - X_control) from large-scale perturbation experiments (MIX-seq) as drug-specific signatures via a learned embedding model. The combined cell-state and drug-signature embeddings will be used for drug response prediction, evaluated on held-out cell lines using standard drug response prediction metrics. This framework provides a biologically informed and functionally grounded representation of drug effects, with the potential to improve prediction accuracy, interpretability, and generalization across cell types and perturbations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Astra: A Mechanistic Multi-Task Learning Framework for Biochemically Consistent Enzyme Kinetic Parameter Prediction
authors: Maxim Kirby, University of Toronto, Canada; Rana Ahmed Barghout, University of Toronto, Canada; Lya Chiñas, University of Toronto, Canada; Radhakrishnan Mahadevan, University of Toronto, Canada
abstract: Accurate prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters (kcat, KM, Ki) is critical for metabolic engineering, synthetic biology, and drug discovery. Existing deep-learning approaches treat these observables as independent regression targets, ignoring their mechanistic interdependence and limiting performance on sparsely labeled data. We present Astra, a modular multi-task learning framework that directly predicts elementary rate constants from ESM-2 protein embeddings and ECFP4 substrate fingerprints. These rates are analytically recomposed into observable parameters via numerically stable log-sum-exp formulations of 3-rate and 5-rate Michaelis-Menten mechanisms, introducing a strong architectural inductive bias that enforces biochemical consistency by construction. Astra adapts backbone architectures from CPI-Pred (a recent deep-learning baseline for compound-protein interaction kinetics), implements uncertainty-weighted losses and masked MSE to fully exploit partial annotations, and uses MMseqs2-based sequence-similarity splitting to prevent data leakage. Preliminary benchmarks on curated kinetic datasets demonstrate that the mechanistic inductive bias can be incorporated without sacrificing performance. Astra achieves Pearson correlations of 0.45-0.65 across targets and 60-75% accuracy within one order of magnitude, remaining on par with single-task baselines and CPI-Pred. Linear projection heads consistently perform on par with or better than self-attention layers. Astra provides an open-source, extensible platform that bridges classical enzyme kinetics with modern representation learning, enabling researchers to enforce biochemical consistency by architectural design while testing new inductive biases through custom embeddings and architectures.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Structure Prompt Adapter (SPA): Flexible Structural Conditioning for RFdiffusion3
authors: Gregg Helt, Genomancer Consulting, United States
abstract: All-atom diffusion models like RFdiffusion3 excel at de novo protein design. However, RFdiffusion3 enforces 3D structural conditioning by explicitly keeping specified atomic coordinates fixed within the iterative diffusion loop. While precise for motif scaffolding, this rigid geometric constraint can limit higher level topological flexibility. Here we introduce the Structure Prompt Adapter (SPA), a parameter-efficient method enabling additional, more flexible structural conditioning when coupled with RFDiffusion3. Inspired by the Image Prompt Adapter (IP-Adapter) used in image diffusion workflows, SPA is a lightweight sidecar model that injects decoupled cross-attention into the RFdiffusion3 token track. It uses the Contrastive Learning Sequence-Structure (CLSS) encoder for encoding its additional structural prompts. This effectively guides coarser fold topology, while the native RFDiffusion3 cross-attention between atom level and token level tracks translates this guidance to the atom level track for positioning. Because RFdiffusion3 natively processes absolute Cartesian coordinates and CLSS encodes geometric topologies as invariant latent features, SPA can integrate these representations without computationally heavy geometric transformation layers. Trained on diverse 3D structures, SPA uses extensive data augmentation to learn spatial symmetries. We also train alternate versions of SPA that use only the outputs of CLSS or deeper layers within CLSS connected to trainable layers in SPA. To validate SPA-guided output, we utilize ProteinMPNN for inverse-folding sequence design, followed by in silico validation using OpenFold3. We compare and contrast specific examples of protein design using RFdiffusion3 with or without SPA. Source code and models are available at: github.com/GreggHelt2/structure-prompt-adapter.

title: How Resolution Shapes Modularity Clustering in scRNA-seq
authors: Sivan Leviyang, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Clustering nodes in a network is central to many computational biology workflows. In particular, modularity-based clustering was introduced in the network literature for community detection and is widely applied to single cell RNA-seq (scRNAseq) datasets for cell type identification. Modularity clustering depends on a resolution parameter that implicitly determines the number of clusters inferred, but few results exist describing clustering as a function of the resolution. I will present two recent results that characterize clustering as a function of the resolution parameter through the notion of a splitting resolution, the minimum resolution at which a graph or subgraph is split into multiple clusters. First, I will show that the splitting resolution of a weakly connected subgraph is inversely proportional to the relative size of the subgraph within the graph. This result extends the resolution limit result of Fortunato and Barthelemy in the network literature and has significant implications for cell type inference in scRNAseq. Second, I will consider k-nearest-neighbor graphs formed from cell embeddings distributed as a normal distribution. For such graphs, I will present formulas that describe modularity clustering as a function of the resolution parameter. I will show that these two results imply unavoidable specificity/sensitivity tradeoffs in modularity-based clustering of scRNAseq datasets.

title: A Novel ILP Framework to Identify Compensatory Pathways in Genetic Interaction Networks with GIDEON
authors: Jocelyn Garcia, Tufts University, United States; Kevin Yu, Tufts University, United States; Catherine Freudenreich, Tufts University, United States; Lenore Cowen, Tufts University, United States
abstract: In Baker's yeast, there exists a comprehensive collection of pairwise epistasis experiments that, for nearly every pair of non-essential genes, measure the growth of the double-knockout strain as compared to its component single knockouts. This data can be represented as a weighted signed graph termed the genetic interaction network, and we introduce a new ILP-based method named GIDEON to search for a diverse collection of Between-Pathway Models (BPMs) in this network, where BPMs are a graph motif signature that indicates potential compensatory pathways in the genetic interaction network. With both an improved distribution-informed edge weighting scheme and an improved ILP method, GIDEON produces BPM collections that are substantially larger and with better functional enrichment compared to previous methods. We find some interesting new BPM gene sets including one with potential insights into antifungal drug targets through ties between ergosterol and aromatic amino acid biosynthesis.

title: Statistically Enriched Interactome Routing Identifies Bridge Regulators Linking Eucommia ulmoides Targets to Osteoporosis Disease Modules
authors: Sheng An Lee, Department of Medical Informatics, Tzu Chi University, Taiwan; Ming Der Lin, Institute of Human Genetics, Tzu Chi University, Taiwan
abstract: Eucommia ulmoides has been widely reported to exhibit anti-osteoporotic activity; however, the network-level signaling mechanisms connecting its molecular targets to osteoporosis-associated disease modules remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present an interactome-based routing analysis framework to systematically reconstruct indirect signaling trajectories between herbal compound targets and disease genes within the human proteinâ€“protein interaction network. Experimentally supported compound targets were integrated with curated osteoporosis-associated genes from the CTD and Phenopedia databases. Using high-confidence STRING interactions (score â‰¥ 700), we constructed a targetâ€“disease interaction network and identified shortest-path routing structures linking the two layers. Intermediate proteins mediating indirect connectivity were defined as bridge regulators and prioritized using degree, betweenness centrality, shortest-path occurrence frequency, and diffusion-based propagation scores to capture both topological and signal-flow properties within the interactome. To evaluate statistical robustness, permutation-based null models and diffusion-based signal propagation analyses jointly confirmed that the observed routing architecture significantly exceeded random expectation, demonstrating enriched connectivity between compound targets and disease modules through a compact intermediate regulatory layer. Top-ranked bridge regulators included MAPK1, STAT3, EGFR, SRC, EP300, and CREBBP, forming a signaling bottleneck connecting Eucommia ulmoides targets to osteoporosis-associated pathways. Enrichment analysis of bridge-node subnetworks revealed strong convergence across MAPK, JAKâ€“STAT, estrogen receptor, FoxO, and TGF-Î² signaling pathways, suggesting coordinated mechanotransduction and hormone-responsive regulatory mechanisms underlying bone remodeling.
