These results support a model in which Eucommia ulmoides influences osteoporosis-related processes through statistically enriched indirect interactome routing rather than direct disease-gene overlap and demonstrate that interactome routing analysis provides a generalizable network-based framework for reconstructing compound-to-disease signaling relationships in complex therapeutic systems.

title: Microbiome-Integrated Network Pharmacology Uncovers Target Pathways Inaccessible to Parent-Centric Models of Herbal Medicine
authors: Minjun Jeong, College of Korean Medicine, Dongguk University, South Korea; Dongyeop Jang, Department of Physiology, College of Korean Medicine, Dong-Eui University, South Korea
abstract: Conventional network pharmacology of herbal medicines has focused on parent compounds meeting physicochemical absorption criteria, without accounting for metabolites generated through gut microbial biotransformation. Such exclusion likely underestimates the bioavailable chemical space, as some compounds failing absorption criteria can serve as substrates for microbial biotransformation whose metabolites meet absorption thresholds but remain uncharacterized. To address this gap, we propose a microbiome-integrated network pharmacology pipeline comprising microbial metabolite prediction via MicrobeRX, Lipinski–Veber absorption filtering, and target identification via SwissTargetPrediction against a unified gene set, using literature-validated thresholds. A threshold optimization method was developed to determine an optimal cutoff via composite pathway enrichment and Jaccard stability scoring, with standardized inputs applicable to other herbal medicines. Applied to Panax ginseng (49 compounds from TM-MC and TCMSP), the pipeline identified an optimal threshold of P > 0.13, augmenting 28 parent compounds with 601 metabolites meeting absorption criteria. Analysis revealed pathways enriched among metabolite-derived targets, including Notch signaling, Cadherin signaling, and Terpenoid backbone biosynthesis, absent from parent-only analysis. Notably, the pipeline computationally predicted the compound K–γ-secretase interaction, consistent with prior experimental findings, supporting predictive accuracy. PPAR signaling, enriched in both sets with similar gene coverage, suggests metabolite-derived targets contribute to this pathway comparably to parent compounds. Our findings suggest microbiome-integrated network pharmacology as a potential strategy for identifying target pathways beyond parent-centric models, allowing more comprehensive characterization of orally administered herbal medicines by accounting for gut microbial biotransformation. These results highlight gut microbial biotransformation as an emerging factor in herbal pharmacology that warrants further study.

title: Integrated Proteomic and Phosphoproteomic Analyses Reveal Opposing Kinase Signaling Networks Underlying the Inverse Relationship Between Cancer and Alzheimer’s Disease
authors: Joyce Fang, Montgomery Blair High School, Silver Spring, MD, USA, United States; Xinkun Wang, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, IL, USA., United States
abstract: Cancer and Alzheimer's disease (AD) cause millions of deaths worldwide each year. Epidemiological studies have consistently reported an inverse relationship between these diseases, in which AD patients exhibit reduced cancer risk and vice versa. However, the molecular basis of this relationship remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that opposing kinase activities represent a network-level systems mechanism underlying this inverse relationship. We performed integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses of lung cancer, glioblastoma (GBM), and AD datasets. Differential analysis identified 37 proteins with opposing abundance patterns between cancer and AD. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) and pathway enrichment analyses showed significant connectivity and enrichment in kinase signaling and phosphorylation-related pathways, supporting a central role for kinase-mediated regulatory networks. Phosphoproteomic analysis identified 69 differentially phosphorylated sites (DPSs) with opposing phosphorylation patterns between cancer and AD. Because kinase activity is more accurately reflected by substrate phosphorylation than protein abundance, we applied kinase-substrate enrichment analysis (KSEA) to phosphoproteomic data, identifying 24 kinases with opposing activity profiles. Integration of kinase activity and phosphosite data revealed 16 kinase-substrate pairs with consistent opposing patterns, including 5 high-confidence associations, implicating diverse processes such as apoptosis, neuronal signaling, and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. A machine learning approach (random forest) was further explored to prioritize phosphosites contributing to disease classification. Together, these findings establish opposing kinase signaling networks as a central mechanism underlying this inverse cancer-AD relationship and suggest potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This study presents a novel systems-level computational framework integrating multi-omics data to investigate inverse disease relationships.

title: Sample-Specific Differential miRNA Network Rewiring Associated with Asthma Exacerbation Using LIONESS
authors: Parham Hadikhani, Department of Pediatrics, University of California San Diego, San Diego, CA, USA, United States; Shraddha Piparia, Department of Pediatrics, University of California San Diego, San Diego, CA, USA, United States; Alvin T Kho, Computational Health Informatics Program, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA, United States; Michael McGeachie, Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA, United States; Rinku Sharma, Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA, United States; Scott T. Weiss, Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA, United States; Kimberly Glass, Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital & Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA , USA, United States; Kelan Tantisira, Department of Pediatrics, University of California San Diego, San Diego, CA, USA, United States
abstract: Background: Asthma exacerbations confer considerable clinical and economic burden, and the molecular regulatory mechanisms are not well understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional modulators of immune and inflammatory pathways that may regulate exacerbations. Differential expression analysis cannot account for changes in miRNA regulatory interactions. Sample-specific network analysis may be useful for understanding the co-regulatory architecture and network rewiring within individual omics samples. Methods: We analyzed serum miRNA sequencing data from two CAMP cohorts of children with asthma (n = 491 discovery cohort and n = 485 replication cohort). Sample-specific miRNA co-expression networks were constructed using both standard LIONESS and a sparsity-aware LIONESS approach. Using both methods, differential edges were identified by comparing exacerbators (>1 exacerbation events during Year 1) and non-exacerbators (≤1 event) using ordinary least squares regression with FDR correction. Results were replicated in the second cohort and compared to standard LIONESS. Results: Analysis of networks derived using sparsity-aware LIONESS identified 18 differential edges, whereas the standard LIONESS identified 46 differential edges; one edge was identified using both approaches miR-483-5p–miR-92a-3p. Although standard LIONESS identified a larger number of differential edges, it did not replicate in the second cohort (p = 0.15). In contrast, the sparsity-aware approach identified a more constrained network topology with stronger replication (p = 0.0042). Conclusions: Sample-specific miRNA rewiring differentially identifies exacerbators and non-exacerbators and is reproducible across cohorts and can be used to understand changes in miRNA regulation with asthma exacerbation. Our comparison of standard versus sparsity-aware LIONESS demonstrated a trade-off between sensitivity and reproducibility.

title: BIRDccNEST: Interpretable single cell characterization with inferred cell networks
authors: Gizem Cicekli, Tufts University, United States; Adrita Samanta, Tufts University, United States; Hao Zhu, Tufts University, Harvard Medical School, United States; Donna Slonim, Tufts University, United States
abstract: Motivation: Trajectory inference for single cell RNA sequencing data aims to elucidate continuous biological processes like differentiation by ordering cells along a pseudo-temporal trajectory. While there are nominally-unsupervised trajectory inference algorithms, many still require designating a root node to create the directed trajectory relationship ordering amongst cell clusters. Here, we introduce BIRDccNEST (pronounced “bird’s nest”), an efficient unsupervised framework for characterizing cells and defining trajectories in scRNA-seq data by inferring directed cell-cell relationship networks. Methods: The BIRDccNEST framework infers directed cell networks by applying our RegDiffusion network inference algorithm to the transposed scRNA-seq expression matrix, learning a weighted directed adjacency matrix whose edge weights capture the similarity of expression distributions between individual cells. These networks are then transformed into cell flow networks, where the directed relationships between cell-cell communities are found with oriented maximum spanning trees, yielding interpretable trajectories and characterizing subgroups of cells. Results: We demonstrate on BEELINE datasets that BIRDccNEST finds new cell subtypes more coherent than the cell states identified in their original publications, while automatically capturing the known underlying temporal or developmental trajectories. For all datasets, we show that the BIRDccNEST cell clusters are significantly more coherent, as measured by the Davies-Bouldin Index and Silhouette Score. Availability: The full manuscript appeared in Proceedings of the 20th annual Machine Learning in Computational Biology meeting, PMLR 311:270-279, September, 2025. Code is available at: https://bcb.cs.tufts.edu/BIRDccNEST.html

title: Genetic Interaction-based Machine Learning Models for Disease Risk Prediction
authors: Mathew Fischbach, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota-Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, United States; Wen Wang, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota-Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, United States; Chad Myers, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota-Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, United States
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) aim to find associations between genotypes and phenotypes to identify specific genetic loci that affect disease risk. GWAS has been successful in discovering new risk loci for diseases, yet it is still difficult to clinically predict complex polygenic diseases. We have previously shown that genetic interactions underlying human diseases form structured networks connecting within and between biological pathways and have developed a method called BridGE for the systematic discovery of genetic interactions. BridGE has discovered many complex genetic interactions from human genotype cohort data for multiple diseases; however, these genetic interactions have not yet been used as features to predict disease risk. In this work, we created a machine-learning (ML) pipeline for predicting Parkinson's disease case-control phenotypes that leverages combinatorial (pairwise) genotype information and curated gene sets (e.g., pathways). We evaluated our pipeline with two types of genetic interaction data models: pairwise SNPs and pathway-based aggregated SNP pairs. These are compared against a data model of single SNPs with no knowledge of pathways or genetic interactions. Aggregating SNP pairs into biological pathways on average outperformed SNP-pair only data models in all but one ML model. We also found that even though the aggregated SNP-pairs are derived from the single SNPs, the two data models fundamentally predict the same individuals differently. These results demonstrate that pathway-based genetic interactions are complementary to single SNPs when predicting Parkinson's disease and these genetic interactions could be used for other genomic-based predictive tasks.

title: TENET+: a tool for reconstructing gene networks by integrating single cell expression and chromatin accessibility data
authors: Hyeonkyu Kim, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, 369Sangdo-Ro, Dongjak-Gu, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Hoebin Chung, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, 369Sangdo-Ro, Dongjak-Gu, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Hwisoo Choi, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, 369Sangdo-Ro, Dongjak-Gu, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Woo Seok Cha, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, 369Sangdo-Ro, Dongjak-Gu, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Bokim Cho, Department of Anatomy, College of Medicine, The CatholicUniversity of Korea, Seoul 06591, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Kyoung-Jae Won, Computational Biomedicine, Sedars-Sinai Medical Center, LosAngeles, CA 90069, USA, United States; Dongha Kim, Department of Anatomy, College of Medicine, The CatholicUniversity of Korea, Seoul 06591, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Junil Kim, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, 369Sangdo-Ro, Dongjak-Gu, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea
abstract: Gene expression is regulated by multiple epigenetic factors including chromatin structure. Single cell chromatin accessibility data combined with transcription factor (TF) binding motif information enhances our understanding of gene expression regulation. However, enhancer-driven gene regulation remains limited due to the lack of promoter-enhancer interaction data. Here, we developed TENET+, a tool for reconstructing enhancer-driven gene regulatory networks (eGRN) by integrating single cell transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data. By leveraging causal relationship inference based on pseudo-time-ordered gene expression and chromatin accessibility, TENET+ predicts interaction between TF expression, target gene expression, and open chromatin regions including long-range enhancer. Applying TENET+ to a paired scRNAseq and scATACseq dataset of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, we identified critical regulators and their epigenetic regulations. Interestingly, TENET+ exhibited a superior performance to predict promoter-enhancer interactions provided by cell type-specific Hi-C datasets compared with other motif-based GRN reconstruction tools. Notably, TENET+ demonstrates competitive performance in ChIP-seq validation compared to other tools, even without relying on motif information We identified key regulatory factors in CD4 T cell, and subsequent siRNA knockdown experiments confirmed that their target genes were indeed regulated by these identified factors. Overall, TENET+ provides a robust framework for reconstructing eGRN with a single-cell resolution. Giyhub : https://github.com/hg0426/TENETPLUS

title: Multi-omic Single-cell Atlas Construction to Elucidate Cellular Heterogeneity and Developmental Trajectories in Cardiovascular Disease and Aging
authors: Seungyoon Song, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Hyeonkyu Kim, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Junyoung Kim, L&C Bio 12F, 275 Gangnam-daero, Seocho-gu, Seoul 06729, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Cherin Lee, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Hun-Jun Park, Department of Biomedicine and Health Sciences, The Catholic University of Korea, Seoul 06591, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Manryul Lee, Department of Stem Cell and Regenerative Biotechnology, Konkuk University, Seoul 05029, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Junil Kim, Department of Bioinformatics, Soongsil University, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea, South Korea
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains one of the most fatal global health challenges, ranking second only to cancer. Understanding the complexities of CVD requires high-resolution analysis at the cellular level, as traditional bulk sequencing is limited to providing averaged gene expression profiles that obscure critical shifts in specific cell populations like cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts. In this study, we constructed a comprehensive multi-omic single-cell atlas to identify disease-specific gene expression patterns and chromatin structures. By integrating scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, VisiumHD, and scDNAmethylation-seq, we characterized genetic diversity within cardiac pathologies and identified specific cardiomyocyte clusters associated with cardiac aging. Notably, we pinpointed potential stem cell populations exhibiting high expression of differentiation-related genes. Pathway-based gene set scoring revealed that these progenitor-like clusters are characterized by elevated YAP signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers. Furthermore, trajectory analysis using scATAC-seq data highlighted key transcription factors, such as TRPS1, that play a pivotal role in cellular transitions. Finally, by applying the Horvath gene list, we successfully identified aging-specific cell clusters from an epigenetic perspective. These findings provide a high-resolution molecular roadmap for understanding the progression of heart disease and the mechanisms of cardiac aging.

title: Simplifying Complex Trait Analysis with QTLretrievR: An R Package for Molecular QTL Identification
authors: Hannah Dewey, The Jackson Lab and Tufts University, United States; Selcan Aydin, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Steven Munger, The Jackson Laboratory, United States
abstract: Over the past two decades, integrating -omics scale molecular profiling with genetic mapping in diverse populations termed systems genetics has proven powerful for linking complex disease phenotypes to genetic variants and their regulatory effects. Model organisms from multi-parent mapping populations further increase power by enabling linkage mapping. However, these combined genomic and genetic analyses remain computationally intensive and often inaccessible to researchers without a strong computational background, a problem compounded in studies with multiple tissues or thousands of molecular -omics phenotypes. We developed QTLretrievR, an R package designed to simplify and streamline the identification and downstream analysis of molecular quantitative trait loci in multi-parent mapping populations. QTLretrievR builds on widely used R packages such as r/qtl2 for quantitative trait locus mapping and r/intermediate for mediation analysis, and incorporates substantial parallelization features to improve computational efficiency. Benchmarking demonstrates that QTLretrievR can reproduce results from previous quantitative trait locus studies while significantly reducing the time required for quantitative trait locus peak detection and downstream analyses. Additionally, QTLretrievR includes plotting functions to visualize results of the included downstream analyses.

title: SpinMCIA improves joint embedding inference for multimodal single cell data
authors: Cemil Can Ali Marandi, La Jolla Institute for Immunology; University of California, San Diego, United States; Ferhat Ay, La Jolla Institute for Immunology; University of California, San Diego, United States
abstract: Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) maps chromatin contacts at the individual cell level, revealing architectural features that shape gene regulation. Recently, multimodal co-assays have incorporated scHi-C to jointly profile 3D genome organization alongside other epigenetic and transcriptomic modalities, providing high-resolution insights into gene regulation and cell type heterogeneity. However, integrative analysis of these datasets poses significant computational challenges due to large scale of the data (tissue atlases), extreme data sparsity and massive feature spaces (e.g., quadratic space for contact matrices). Current integration methods often require a trade-off: highly scalable spectral embedding approaches (e.g., SnapATAC2) generate accurate cell embeddings but lack feature-level interpretability, while explicit joint tensor factorization models (e.g., Muscle) provide direct biological insights but are often prohibitive for large datasets. To bridge this gap, we developed SpinMCIA, a Python framework for Multiple Co-Inertia Analysis (MCIA) optimized for sparse, high-dimensional multi-omic data. SpinMCIA utilizes a Nonlinear Iterative Partial Least Squares (NIPALS) algorithm to sequentially extract latent factors directly from on-disk sparse matrices, avoiding the need to construct dense covariance matrices. SpinMCIA does this while learning a small set of latent axes that capture shared variation across data blocks and maintaining separate projections per modality. Benchmarking across eight published multimodal scHi-C datasets comprising over 470,000 cells, we demonstrate that SpinMCIA scales to atlas-level data while maintaining robust clustering accuracy. Importantly, SpinMCIA retains explicit feature-level interpretability, allowing the derived latent space to be mapped directly back to the physical 3D chromatin loops and epigenetic loci that govern cell-type identity.

title: Pervasive multi-specificity of bZIP transcription factors revealed by biophysically interpretable machine learning
authors: Shaoxun Liu, Columbia University, United States; Chase Ende, Columbia University, United States; Paul Nieuwerburgh, Columbia University, United States; Richard Mann, Department of Systems Biology, Columbia University, United States; Harmen Bussemaker, Columbia University, United States
abstract: Basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors (TFs) are key regulators of diverse biological processes that bind DNA as homodimers or heterodimers. They are believed to be classifiable into subfamilies that bind either an odd-symmetry binding site (TGASTCA for the AP-1 subfamily) or an even-symmetry one (TGACGTCA for the CREB subfamily; TTGCGCAA for the C/EBP subfamily). However, we previously showed anecdotally that individual bZIPs can allosterically adapt to the DNA sequence and bind with either symmetry, and with relative preference that is an intrinsic property of the bZIP protein (Riley et al., eLife, 2015, PMID 26701911). To investigate how general this phenomenon is, we systematically analyzed 171 SELEX-seq datasets covering 67 bZIP homodimers from multiple species using ProBound, a biophysically interpretable machine-learning framework (Rube et al., Nature Biotechnol., 2022, PMID 35606422). We find that for approximately a quarter of bZIPs a single weight matrix does not suffice to fully capture their DNA binding behavior. Instead, it is necessary to quantify DNA sequence preference in terms of self-cooperativity between two half-sites that depends on the spacing between them. These models show greatly improved cross-platform predictive performance on ChIP-seq data over state-of-the-art static motif models. Family-level analysis of these allosteric binding models revealed specific amino-acid residue positions that govern half-site specificity, which we validated experimentally.

title: PhytoTFBS: a motif-free framework for cross-species transcription factor binding site discovery in plant genomes using fine-tuned DNA foundation models
authors: Maryam Haghani, Department of Computer Science, Virginia Tech, United States; Song Li, Computer Science; Genetics, Bioinformatics, and Computational Biology; Plant and Environmental Sciences, Virginia Tech, United States
abstract: Transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) are cis-regulatory elements controlling gene expression, yet experimental maps of TFâ€“DNA binding remain sparse across plant transcription factors, species, and conditions. We present PhytoTFBS, a fast, retrainable workflow for plant TFBS discovery that adapts pretrained DNA foundation models to practical regulatory analysis. Building on prior benchmarking in ABF-family DAP-seq datasets from Arabidopsis thaliana and Sisymbrium irio, PhytoTFBS uses HyenaDNA with a lightweight classifier to predict TFBSs directly from sequence, supports standardized positive/negative set construction, and enables balanced or imbalanced evaluation with metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, and MCC. The workflow is designed for practical downstream use, with rapid TF-specific retraining that typically completes in minutes, alongside promoter scanning, TFBS-set enrichment, and attribution-based interpretation. In the case of ABF-family, a model trained on S. irio data predicted significant enrichment of TFBSs in ABA-induced Arabidopsis genes (odds ratio = 3.8; Fisherâ€™s exact p = 3.02Ã—10âˆ’20), demonstrating recovery of biologically meaningful regulatory signal comparable to direct DAP-seq-based annotation. To extend beyond the original benchmark, we tested the pipeline on the largest multi-species DAP-seq data (Baumgart2025) spanning 10 flowering plant species and 90 TFs from 35 TF families. Although zero-shot transfer is not uniformly reliable, our lightweight retraining results showed promising predictions across species diverged more than 200 million years ago. For example, promoter scanning with a Sorghum-trained model recovered localized binding profiles in Arabidopsis promoters that aligned with experimentally defined DAP-seq peak regions. PhytoTFBS provides a fast, end-to-end framework for TFBS discovery, transfer, retraining, and interpretation across diverse plant regulatory settings.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics reveals Cell-Type and Region-specific Vulnerability in a Rodent Model of Postpartum Depression
authors: Maria Eleni Fafouti, University of Toronto, Canada; Romina Garcia De Leon, University of Toronto, Canada; Bharti Kukreja, Boston Chrildren's Hosptial, United States; Shahrzad Ghazisaeidi, Krembil Centre for Neuroinformatics (KCNI), Canada; Hugo Hudson, University of Toronto, Canada; Brian Kalish, Boston Chrildren's Hosptial, United States; Liisa Galea, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), Canada; Shreejoy Tripathy, University of Toronto, Canada
abstract: Pregnancy and the postpartum period involve remarkable neuroplasticity but also heightened vulnerability to postpartum depression (PPD). We employed two spatial transcriptomics platforms: Slide-seq and Slide-tags to chart gene expression and cellular remodeling in a corticosterone-induced rodent model of PPD, focusing on limbic regions like the hippocampus. Our results reveal differences in immature neurons: in corticosterone-treated rats, there is decreased signal for neural connectivity and maturation. We also observe disrupted intercellular communication. Specifically, we observe decreased trophic support from astrocytes to the immature neurons, through the Fgf13-Egfr pathway. We also observe decreased synaptic adhesion (Pcdh15, Astn2) in the CA3 region of the hippocampus, along with inhibition of long-term potentiation (Camk2n1). In the medial habenula, which is involved in modulating anxiety-like behaviors, we observe decreased excitability (Cacna2d1). In the neurons of the medial amygdala, we observe upregulation of stress-related receptors (Tacr1), along with elevated levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6, which is related to depression. Our study offers a uniquely detailed perspective on the spatial organization of gene expression in the maternal postpartum brain. For the first time, we capture the whole transcriptome of corticosterone-stressed dams and identify cell-type-specific mechanisms driving PPD-related dysfunction. So far, our findings imply suppressed maturation and region-specific activity that might interfere with the cognitive demands of motherhood, while many resources are used to attend to stress-related stimuli. By localizing these signals on the tissue and understanding their interactions, we can propose molecular targets that provide resilience to stress during the vulnerable peripartum period.

title: A Composite Scoring Framework for Computational CRISPR-Cas9 Guide RNA Prioritization Against Multidrug-Resistant Genes
authors: Sanghati Basu, University of Illinois Springfield, Springfield, IL, United States; Bishnu Sarker, University of North Texas, Denton, TX, United States
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) causes approximately 1.27 million deaths annually and is projected to reach 10 million per year by 2050. CRISPR-Cas9 offers programmable disruption of resistance genes, but quantitative frameworks for multi-criteria guide RNA (gRNA) prioritization across diverse strain populations remain limited. We developed a two-phase computational pipeline in Python using a weighted composite scoring mechanism to prioritize gRNAs against four resistance genes: blaKPC, blaNDM-1, mcr-1, and mecA. Phase 1 performs Photospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM) site enumeration, 20-nt spacer extraction, GC-constrained on-target scoring using positional rules proposed by Doench in 2016, and mismatch-tiered off-target penalty assessment, integrating efficiency and specificity in a 0.6/0.4 weighted model. Phase 2 extends this framework by incorporating pan-strain conservation from multi-variant FASTA alignment into a three-component model weighted as On-Target Ã— 0.4, Specificity Ã— 0.3, and Conservation Ã— 0.3. Out of 6,373 Phase 1 candidates, the best gRNAs got composite scores of 90.4 and had no predicted off-target hits across 0 to 3 mismatch classes. Phase 2 retained 145 elite gRNAs across three variants per gene, with 96.6% classified as Excellent and a best pan-strain score of 87.8. Organism-restricted BLAST analysis of top guides against Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Escherichia coli identified recurrent full-length 20/20 exact matches across 100 or more assemblies per organism, supporting cross-strain conservation of targeted loci rather than genome-wide uniqueness. The experimental result shows promise for gRNA prioritization in this preliminary study. This gene-agnostic framework is extensible to additional resistance determinants and other Cas systems. However, all results are computational; experimental validation via in vitro cleavage assays remains a planned next step.

title: HiCInterpolate: 4D Spatiotemporal Interpolation of Hi-C Data for Genome Architecture Analysis.
authors: H. M. A. Mohit Chowdhury, University of North Texas, United States; Oluwatosin Oluwadare, University of North Texas, United States
abstract: Studying the three-dimensional (3D) structure of a genome, including chromatin loops and Topologically Associating Domains (TADs), is essential for understanding how the genome is organized. Hi-C protocol enables us to study 3D genome structure and organization. Chromatin 3D structure changes dynamically over time and modeling these continuous changes is crucial for downstream analysis in various domains. The high expense and impracticality of continuous genome sequencing, particularly what evolves between two timestamps, limit the most effective genomic analysis. It is crucial to develop a straightforward and cost-efficient method for constantly generating genomic data between two timestamps to address these constraints. We propose HiCInterpolate, a novel 4D spatiotemporal interpolation architecture that accepts two timestamp Hi-C contact matrices to interpolate intermediate Hi-C contact matrices at high resolution. HiCInterpolate predicts the intermediate Hi-C contact map using a deep learning-based flow predictor, and a feature encoder and decoder architecture similar to U-Net. In addition, HiCInterpolate supports downstream analysis of multiple 3D genomic features, including A/B compartments, chromatin loops, TADs, and 3D genome structure, through an integrated analysis pipeline. Across multiple evaluation metrics, including GenomeDISCO, HiCRep, and LPIPS, HiCInterpolate achieved consistently strong performance relative to linear, distance-aware, and Farneback optical flowâ€“based interpolation methods. Biological validation further demonstrated preservation of key chromatin organization features, such as chromatin loops, A/B compartments, and TADs. Together, these results indicate that HiCInterpolate provides a robust computer visionâ€“based framework for high-resolution interpolation of intermediate Hi-C contact matrices and facilitates biologically meaningful downstream analyses.

title: Inference of Spatial Chromatin Accessibility and Gene Regulatory Network via Integration of Spatial Transcriptomics and Single Cell Multiome Data
authors: Ishita Debnath, Indiana University Indianapolis, United States; Zhana Duren, Indiana University Indianapolis, United States
abstract: Integrating spatial transcriptomics, which maps gene expression location within tissues, with single-cell multiomics data, profiling gene expression and chromatin accessibility (or other epigenomic data) for the same cell, can offer powerful insights into gene regulation. However, commercially available kits for simultaneous spatial multi-omics profiling are currently unavailable, hindering widespread data generation. Here, we present ISON (Integrated Spatial Omics Network), a unified computational method for integrative spatial multiomics analysis from single cell multiome data and spatial transcriptomics data. ISON accurately predicts chromatin accessibility profiles for spatial spots and reconstructs spatially resolved gene regulatory networks, demonstrating scalability in both time and memory. Importantly, ISON's chromatin accessibility prediction captures patterns consistent with cis- and trans- regulatory information and enables estimation of transcription factor (TF) activity at the spot level, distinguishing between TFs even within the same family, which is unique and is not present in approaches relying solely on chromatin accessibility data. The application of ISON to Alzheimer's disease data reveals disease- and age-specific spatial variable gene regulatory modules, highlighting its potential to uncover spatially organized mechanisms driving complex biological processes.

title: SEMANTIC: Systematic Discovery of Regulatory Circuits from Genomic Deep Learning Models
authors: Barry Slaff, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Nathaniel Islas, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Yoseph Barash, University of Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Deep learning models trained on DNA and RNA sequences offer significant potential for elucidating the molecular mechanisms of gene regulation, including transcription factor binding, splicing, and gene expression. While feature attribution methods such as Enhanced Integrated Gradients (EIG) and DeepSHAP effectively identify specific nucleotides or k-mers critical for model predictions, they do not inherently provide higher-level biological insights regarding regulatory logic, such as motif combinations or positional biases. To address this limitation, we developed SEMANTIC, a computational pipeline that utilizes attribution scores from deep learning models to discover networks of interrelated sequence motifs and their syntax, which we term ""regulatory circuits"". SEMANTIC employs a data-driven approach to identify a minimal set of distinct, high-information motifs along with their patterns of co-occurrence, order, and distance. The pipeline functions as an attribution compression method, translating individual importance scores into structured motif networks. We validated SEMANTIC by demonstrating its ability to recover expected motif syntax from models trained on simulated sequences. Furthermore, applying the pipeline to attributions from models trained on unperturbed genomic sequences showed that the recovered motif syntax recapitulates established biological knowledge. These results indicate that SEMANTIC can effectively bridge the gap between low-level feature importance and high-level regulatory mechanisms, facilitating the generation of new biological hypotheses for condition-specific regulation.

title: A journey into the extrasomatic spatial transcriptome in brain, with SCOUBI
authors: Bhavay Aggarwal, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Saumya Jain, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Saurabh Sinha, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics generates substantial transcript signal outside segmented cell bodies, nearly always discarded as noise. We demonstrate that this extrasomatic space is molecularly structured, encoding the subcellular organization of neuronal processes and their signaling. SCOUBI is a computational framework that classifies extrasomatic regions by neurite identity and identifies interfaces, regions where axonic and dendritic compartments converge with significant ligand-receptor colocalization. In the mouse brain, interfaces recover known neuroanatomical organization at multiple spatial scales, and their distribution mirrors established synapse density gradients. Their molecular composition reveals both a conserved synaptic core and rich regional diversity, from a dopamine-glutamate integration axis at striatal interfaces to structural remodeling programs in the hippocampus. Critically, interface transcriptomes are not simply reflections of nearby cell bodies. We identify transcripts whose enrichment at interfaces substantially exceeds what local somatic expression predicts, pointing to selective transport or stabilization at sites of intercellular communication. These signatures are reproducible across imaging platforms and independent tissue samples. SCOUBI reframes the extrasomatic compartment as an analytically tractable layer of tissue organization, adding subcellular resolution to spatial transcriptomics using only the transcriptomic data itself.

title: BEAR-GRN: Systematic Benchmarking Reveals Context-Dependent Performance of Multi-Omics Gene Regulatory Network Inference Methods
authors: Karamveer Karamveer, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Eric Moeller, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Hannah Valensi, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Ewura-Esi Manful, Penn State College of Medicine, United States; Yasin Uzun, Penn State College of Medicine, United States
abstract: Background: Single-cell multi-omics enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility, yet numerous computational methods for inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) lack standardized evaluation, hindering method selection and reproducibility. Methods: We developed BEAR-GRN, a comprehensive benchmarking framework evaluating 10 GRN inference methods across 8 datasets (4 cell types: human macrophages, K562, iPSCs, mouse ESCs). Methods spanned correlation-based (FigR, GRaNIE), regression-based (CellOracle, SCENIC+, Pando), statistical (TRIPOD), tree-based (DIRECT-NET, STREAM), and deep learning (LINGER, scGLUE) approaches. Performance was assessed using cell-type-specific ChIP-seq and perturbation ground truths across three dimensions: accuracy (AUROC, AUPRC, precision, recall, F1), stability (Jaccard index), and scalability (memory, runtime). Results: Performance varied substantially by dataset and cell type. LINGER consistently achieved top-ranked accuracy and stability through deep learning and knowledge integration but required extensive resources (>200GB RAM, >48h runtime). GRaNIE, CellOracle, and DIRECT-NET provided competitive accuracy at 10-fold lower computational cost ( Conclusions: No method excels universally. LINGER offers superior accuracy and stability for resource-rich settings; GRaNIE and CellOracle provide practical alternatives for exploratory or resource-limited analyses. BEAR-GRN delivers standardized datasets, pre-computed benchmarks, and open-source tools for reproducible evaluation. Availability: https://github.com/UzunLab/BEAR-GRN

title: Predicting Alternative Transcription Start Site (TSS) Usage: Understanding the ‘Language’ of Transcriptional Regulation
authors: Daniel Witoslawski, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Sylvia Victor Paul, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Mehdi Khanjani, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Andrew Hsu, University of Nevada - Reno, United States; Mingon Kang, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Mira Han, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, United States
abstract: Background: Alternative transcription start site (TSS) usage is a fundamental driver of transcriptomic diversity and cell-type identity. However, predicting dynamic TSS switching events and decoding the precise regulatory grammar governing them remains challenging when relying solely on static reference genomes. Method: We developed a multi-modal deep learning architecture that integrates 1D DNA sequence, epigenetic accessibility (ATAC-seq/DNase-seq), 3D chromatin conformation (Hi-C), and transcriptomic features (RNA-seq) to predict cell-type-specific TSS dominance. To interpret the underlying regulatory logic, we developed attribution-based difference maps calculating the exact epigenetic delta between cell states. We systematically compared this complete network against a baseline model encoding only sequence, accessibility, and 3D contacts, strictly isolating the specific effect of transcriptomic context. Finally, we utilized in silico saturation mutagenesis to evaluate driving enhancers and quantify the effect sizes of cell-type-exclusive transcription factor binding events. Results: Our framework successfully isolated genuine TSS switching events by filtering out shared baseline regulatory machinery. By identifying loci where the baseline model exhibited predictive blindness but the full architecture reconstructed the biological ground truth, we localized the specific ""epigenetic gates"" driving differential TSS usage. Motif extraction and saturation mutagenesis on these validated targets identified the discrete repressor and activator motifs governing both coordinated and decoupled TSS transitions. Conclusion: This approach provides a mathematically rigorous mechanism to identify and interpret cell-type-specific regulatory drivers. By pinpointing the coordinates and motifs responsible for TSS switching, this framework uncovers the physical regulatory grammar orchestrating dynamic transcriptomes.

title: Characterizing the relationship between neuropsychiatric-associated CNVs and epithelial cancer biology
authors: Enzhe Galimova, University of Ottawa, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Canada; Jacob Billingsley, University of Ottawa, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Canada; Baptiste Lacoste, University of Ottawa, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Canada; Theodore Perkins, University of Ottawa, Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology, Canada; Yannick Benoit, University of Ottawa, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Canada
abstract: BACKGROUND. Genomic rearrangements, including copy number variations (CNVs) can be associated with either increased fitness or pathological predispositions. The evolutionary period associated with the acquisition of bipedalism, increased brain size, and social behavior is also marked by the simultaneous emergence of neuropathological conditions and increased susceptibility to epithelial cancers. Diametric neuropathological disorders driven by evolutionary-genetic trade-offs and specific to modern humans include autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia, and Parkinsonâ€™s disease (PD). Previous research suggests that certain psychiatric disorders may be inversely associated with cancer development, pointing to shared but opposing biological mechanisms. We hypothesized that CNVs associated with neuropsychiatric conditions can impact cancer patient outcomes. METHODS AND RESULTS. Using gene expression and survival data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, we found that expression of genes within two loci, 16p11.2 and 22q11.2, both previously linked to ASD and schizophrenia, was significantly associated with patientâ€™s survival in melanoma and colorectal cancer. Notably, specific co-expressed gene clusters within these loci appear to drive these survival differences. Integration with digital cytometry and gene ontology analysis revealed differences in immune cell infiltration between high and low locus gene expression groups. CONCLUSION: This project establishes a new link between neuropsychiatric-associated CNVs and epithelial cancers by identifying CNVs that significantly associate with patient survival, identifying gene clusters within these loci that drive differential survival outcomes, and revealing corresponding differences in the tumor microenvironment. Future work will validate these observations.

title: Investigating the Impact of Genome Structural Rearrangements and Somatic Variants on Enhancer-Promoter Interactions and Gene Expression in K562 vs GM12878 Cell Lines
authors: Sylvia Victor Paul, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Mehdi Khanjani, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Daniel Witoslawski, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Richard Van, University of Nevada - Las Vegas, United States; Mira Han, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, United States
abstract: Gene expression in cancer is driven by structural rearrangements and somatic mutations that reshape three-dimensional chromatin architecture and cis-regulatory elements. We investigate how CTCF boundary disruptions, copy number variants (CNVs), somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), and indels alter enhancer-promoter interactions, driving expression differences between K562 (chronic myeloid leukemia) and GM12878 (lymphoblastoid) cell lines. Existing models predict enhancer-promoter interactions within single cell types, but they rely on the human reference genome, failing to capture the complex regulatory reorganization that specifically defines cancer. We address this critical gap through two complementary approaches using EPInformer, a Transformer-based deep learning framework. First, we extend EPInformer to learn from paired-cell comparisons by integrating differential features like cell-type-specific CTCF insulation, enhancer activity, Hi-C contact frequencies, CNV dosage, and histone modifications to predict how architectural differences drive expression discrepancies between K562 and GM12878. Second, we construct a personalized K562 genome by integrating somatic SNVs and indels into the reference sequence. We train EPInformer to evaluate whether modeling sequence-level somatic mutations in cis-regulatory elements improves expression predictions relative to GM12878. Our baseline paired-cell model achieved a Pearson R of 0.66. We are currently incorporating multiple histone modification tracks as additional regulatory features and transitioning to a hierarchical Transformer architecture to capture multi-scale chromatin interactions better and improve predictive performance. Parallel efforts focus on modeling the functional impact of somatic mutations within cis-regulatory elements on expression divergence. Ongoing ablation analyses will systematically quantify each feature's contribution, advancing toward a generalizable framework linking structural alterations to specific cancer dysregulation.

title: Dynamic post-transcriptional regulation during hematopoietic differentiation
authors: Chi-Lam Poon, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) must balance self-renewal and differentiation to sustain blood production, and disruption of this balance can drive clonal outgrowth and leukemogenesis. The RNA-binding protein MUSASHI2 (MSI2) regulates asymmetric division and self-renewal in normal and leukemic HSPCs, yet how its targets are dynamically controlled during differentiation remains unclear. To address this, we mapped MSI2 binding and function across HSPCs using an MSI2-HyperTRIBE mouse model and Msi2 knockout (KO), integrating short- and long-read single-cell RNA-seq for single-cell and single-molecule resolution. MSI2 bound 4,546 genes, enriched in 3â€™ UTRs and the canonical UAG motif. Long-read data revealed isoform-specific binding in 21.4% testable genes, largely explained by alternative exon and 3â€™ UTR usage. Differential transcript usage analysis also identified widespread isoform switching during hematopoiesis in 39.4% genes. Functionally, Msi2 KO accelerated differentiation and cell-cycle progression. We developed a probabilistic graphical model to infer the editing residual deviation from cluster-level editing frequency for over 2,500 cell-type-specific editing sites. These residual deviation from cluster-level editing frequency defined five MSI2 binding modules, which are lineage-specific and functionally distinct in either RNA-level and translational modes of regulation. Finally, integrating MSI2 binding, pathway activity, and isoform usage uncovered three transitional cell states at the HSPC-progenitor boundary, linking dynamic MSI2 regulation to pathway rewiring and isoform remodeling during hematopoietic differentiation.

title: FAIRification and meta-analysis of large-scale Perturb-seq data
authors: John Goertz, Boehringer Ingelheim, United States; Adele Sadat Haghighat Hoseini, Boehringer Ingelheim, United States; Christine Hajdin, Boehringer Ingelheim, United States
abstract: The landscape of single-cell perturbation transcriptomics (perturbomics) is undergoing an unprecedented expansion. Until recently, the field was anchored by a single million-cell benchmark; however, the past two years have witnessed a proliferation of public datasets scaling from tens to hundreds of millions of cells. Crucially, this data explosion is not merely expanding the breadth of explored biological contexts and perturbation spaces. It is also producing overlapping, independent experiments, presenting a powerful yet largely untapped opportunity for cross-study integration, robust validation, and meta-analysis. Here we present a FAIRification and analysis framework for Perturb-seq data that enables researchers to draw insights from both within and across studies, driving mechanistic understanding and drug target prioritization.

title: Contribution of DNA breathing to transcription factor binding
authors: Tsu-Pei Chiu, University of Southern California, United States; Wei Yu Tang, University of Southern California, United States; Xin He, University of Chicago, United States; Remo Rohs, University of Southern California, United States
abstract: Interactions between transcription factors (TFs) and DNA play a central role in regulating gene expression and are widely thought to be determined by recognition of specific DNA sequence motifs. However, this model does not fully explain why variants influencing TF binding often occur outside core motif regions. One possible explanation is that the physical properties of DNA also contribute to TFâ€“DNA interactions. In particular, DNA shape features have been shown to influence TF binding, especially in regions flanking core motifs. Beyond these static features, a key dynamic property of DNA is DNA breathing, defined as the spontaneous and transient opening of the double helix driven by thermal fluctuations. Yet, genomic-scale studies of DNA breathing in TFâ€“DNA interactions remain limited. Here, we analyze in vitro TFâ€“DNA binding data from HT-SELEX and protein binding microarrays across more than 200 TFs and find that DNA breathing features within and near core motifs are associated with TF binding affinity. We further extend our analysis to ChIP-seq data and find that breathing features near core motifs are associated with TF binding across 44 TFs. Notably, both the direction and magnitude of these associations vary across TFs. Together, our results support a potential role for DNA breathing as a biophysical determinant of TFâ€“DNA interactions and highlight the importance of dynamic DNA properties in gene regulation.

title: ArchVelo: Archetypal Velocity Modeling for Single-cell Multi-omic Trajectories
authors: Maria Avdeeva, Flatiron Institute, United States; Sarah Walker, Princeton University, United States; Joris van der Veeken, Research Institute of Molecular Pathology, Austria; Alexander Rudensky, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Yuri Pritykin, Princeton University, United States
abstract: Inferring dynamic cellular processes from static single-cell measurements remains a central challenge in genomics. Here we introduce ArchVelo, a new method for modeling gene regulation and inferring cell trajectories using single-cell simultaneous chromatin accessibility (scATAC-seq) and transcriptomic (scRNA-seq) profiling. ArchVelo represents chromatin accessibility as a set of archetypes -- shared regulatory programs -- and models their dynamic influence on transcription. Compared to previous methods, ArchVelo improves inference accuracy and gene-level latent time alignment, and enables identification of the underlying transcription factor activity. We benchmark ArchVelo on developing mouse brain and human hematopoiesis datasets and apply it to CD8 T cells responding to viral infection, revealing distinct trajectories of differentiation and proliferation. Focusing on the progenitor CD8 T cell population with key roles in sustaining immune responses and translationally linked to immunotherapy outcomes, we identify a previously uncharacterized differentiation trajectory from Ccr6âˆ’ to Ccr6+ progenitors, shared between acute and chronic infection. In sum, ArchVelo provides a principled framework for modeling dynamic gene regulation in multi-omic single-cell data across biological systems.

title: Discovering cell types and states from reference atlases with heterogeneous single-cell ATAC-seq features
authors: Yuqi Cheng, Georgia Tech, United States; Xiuwei Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Despite substantial recent advances in query mapping and cell type or cell state discovery tools, their application to single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq) data remains challenging. The heterogeneous nature of peak feature spaces across samples hinders the effectiveness of existing methods, while the absence of dedicated tools for detecting perturbed cell types and states in scATAC-seq data further limits the depth of downstream analyses. To address these limitations, we present EpiPack, an integrative computational toolkit that leverages heterogeneous transfer learning and graph-based modeling strategies to advance scATAC-seq analysis. At its core, the Peak Embedding Informed Variational Inference (PEIVI) framework within EpiPack enhances mappable reference construction, query mapping, and label transfer, demonstrating that leveraging heterogeneous features in scATAC-seq data outperforms methods relying solely on conventional homogeneous features. In addition, EpiPackâ€™s globalâ€“local out-of-reference (OOR) detection framework achieves robust and efficient detection of perturbed cell types and states, extending the utility of scATAC-seq to disease and perturbation contexts. With its modular design and transferable pre-trained references, EpiPack can be readily applied to diverse analytical tasks and is available as a Python package at https://github.com/ZhangLabGT/EpiPack.

title: Modeling the temporal evolution of regulatory relationships in the Drosophila melanogaster IMD response
authors: Tamara Hadzic, Boston University, United States; Lianne Cohen, Boston University, United States; Pawel Przytycki, Boston University, United States; Zeba Wunderlich, Boston University, United States
abstract: Studying innate immunity is crucial to elucidating how animals mount a defense against pathogens in their environments. An ideal model organism for this study is the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, that lacks an adaptive immune system yet shares many pathways with other insects and humans. Previous work has detailed the temporal dynamics of gene expression in the fly IMD immune response, but less is known about how these dynamics arise from gene regulatory networks. To survey enhancers responsive to IMD stimulation and understand enhancer-mediated regulation changes, we generated STARR-seq data over 24 hours, and paired bulk ATAC- and RNA-seq data at various post-infection timepoints. Our analysis suggests that genes associated with the early immune response may be linked to immune-specific enhancers, while the coordination of the late immune response may involve repurposing constitutively active enhancers. To distinguish between Control and IMD-responsive enhancers, we trained DeepSTARR to predict activity from sequence. The model shows moderate performance (PCC: 0.38), which suggests that sequence-based features are insufficient to explain enhancer activity over a 24 hour time course. Transcription factor (TF) footprinting in IMD-responsive enhancers shows enrichment of chromatin remodelers at late infection timepoints, while pathway analysis suggests tradeoffs between immunity and metabolic and growth pathways. These results suggest a rewiring of regulatory relationships between TFs, enhancers, and their target genes over the course of infection that may relate to differential infection-fighting strategies in Drosophila. Future work includes estimating enhancer activity changes using linear deconvolution and network modeling to study changing regulatory relationships.

title: Single-cell ATAC-seq Analysis Reveals Epigenetic Regulatory Landscapes Driving Dedifferentiation in Thyroid Carcinoma
authors: Wooseok Cha, Soongsil University, South Korea
abstract: [Background] Thyroid cancer exhibits extreme clinical and biological heterogeneity, ranging from indolent Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC) to highly aggressive and lethal Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma (ATC). While genetic mutations are well-documented, the epigenetic regulatory networks driving tumor dedifferentiation and metastasis, particularly in rare subtypes like Metastatic Oncocytic Carcinoma (OCA), remain poorly understood. [Methods] We performed high-resolution single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq) profiling of human thyroid tissues encompassing Normal, FTC, Poorly Differentiated (PDTC), ATC, and Metastatic OCA samples to map the epigenetic landscape of tumor progression. By sub-clustering the neoplastic epithelial compartment, we investigated subtype-specific chromatin accessibility, promoter peak dynamics, and downstream functional pathways. Crucially, matched single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data were utilized as an orthogonal validation cohort to confirm the transcriptomic consequences of the identified epigenetic alterations. [Results] Our scATAC-seq analysis successfully deconvoluted the tumor microenvironment and revealed profound epigenetic heterogeneity across epithelial cancer subtypes. In ATC, we observed a systemic loss of chromatin accessibility at the promoters of thyroid-specific differentiation markers (e.g., TG, PAX8, EPCAM), coupled with the opening of regulatory elements driving Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) and cell cycle pathways. Conversely, Metastatic OCA exhibited a highly distinct chromatin signature enriched for oxidative phosphorylation and metabolic pathways. Importantly, our scRNA-seq validation confirmed that these subtype-restricted promoter accessibility peaks directly translated into corresponding gene expression changes, demonstrating that the observed transcriptomic dysregulation is intrinsically governed by underlying epigenetic remodeling. [Conclusion] Our scATAC-seq-driven approach provides a comprehensive epigenetic atlas of thyroid cancer progression, successfully validated at the transcriptomic level. By pinpointing specific chromatin remodeling events that dictate tumor dedifferentiation and unique metabolic states, we uncover novel epigenetic regulatory vulnerabilities that could serve as therapeutic targets for refractory thyroid cancers.

title: Modeling Context-Specific Regulatory Effects of Genetic Variants Through Transcription Factor Activity
authors: Hui Ma, Indiana University School of Medicine, United States; Zhana Duren, Indiana University School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Noncoding genetic variants influence gene regulation in a context-specific manner. However, existing approaches face important limitations. Association-based studies such as GWAS and eQTL analyses are constrained by linkage disequilibrium and reduced statistical power for rare variants, while recent sequence-to-function foundation models often lack mechanistic interpretability and do not explicitly model interactions between genotype and context-dependent transcription factor (TF) activity. Here, we present a TF-mediated framework for modeling chromatin accessibility and context-specific regulatory variant effects. Using ENCODE chromatin accessibility data, we constructed regulatory-element-level models by integrating TF binding information with TF expression profiles. Higher-order TF interaction terms were incorporated to capture regulatory dependencies across tissues. The resulting framework accurately predicts chromatin accessibility in held-out tissues, suggesting that the model captures generalizable regulatory programs rather than tissue-specific memorization. Building on these predictions, we derived context-specific variant scores by quantifying predicted accessibility changes caused by altered TF binding at variant loci. Model-prioritized variants showed approximately five-fold enrichment for GTEx eQTLs and liver caQTLs, while higher-scoring variants were enriched for rare variants and larger regulatory effect sizes. Because the framework explicitly models both context-specific TF activity and genotype-dependent effects on chromatin accessibility, it enables in silico perturbation of either TF expression or sequence variation. This allows us to evaluate how TF perturbations influence the regulatory impact of the same genetic variant under different environmental conditions or cellular contexts. Together, our results demonstrate that mechanistically interpretable TF-based models can capture context-specific regulatory effects and provide a framework for studying how person-specific changes in TF activity influence chromatin accessibility.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Metabolic and proteomic impacts of fine particulate matter on the bronchial epithelium
authors: Sara Mosavarpour, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States; Dana Luong, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States; Juan Sepulveda, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States; Fia Stratton, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States; Simone Sidoli, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States; Lindsay LaFave, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States; Roger Chang, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, United States
abstract: Fine particulate matter (fPM) is a class of air pollutant and carcinogen known to increase risk of pulmonary diseases and lung cancer. Given the complexity and diversity of these environmental exposures, mechanisms and systemic changes that lead to lung dysfunction remain understudied. The bronchial epithelium, one of the first internal tissues to interact with fPM upon exposure, acts as an important physicochemical barrier to protect proximal and distal lung tissues and against secondary effects on other organs. Deleterious cellular phenotypes, such as metabolic reprogramming and oxidative stress have been observed with fPM exposure. We have observed increased protein oxidation in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) following fPM exposure. Oxidation not only affects protein structure and function, but also has cascading effects on cell signaling, proliferation, and metabolism. While several individual cellular pathways have been implicated after fPM exposures, these isolated effects are insufficient to account for the complexities of fPM-induced stress responses. To address these gaps in the field and perform a systematic characterization of the pathways altered following fPM exposures, we use in silico metabolic network modeling to simulate fPM exposure in BECs. Our computational models suggest dysregulated metabolism related to carbohydrate, nucleotide, and amino acid metabolism after fPM exposure in BECs. By combining in silico modeling techniques with redox proteomics, we broadly explore cellular changes as well as identify impacts of protein oxidation. Altogether, this systems-based approach will characterize changing interactions within multi-omic landscapes from fPM exposure and help uncover causal mechanisms in the development of fPM-induced pulmonary diseases.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Simulation-Guided Deep Learning for Target-Layer Oxygenation Inference from NIRS Signals
authors: Jinho Park, Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute, South Korea; Dohum Kim, Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute, South Korea; Thien Nguyen, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, National Institutes of Health, United States; Amir Gandjbakhche, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Accurate estimation of deep tissue oxygenation is essential for understanding physiological processes and assessing conditions such as placental dysfunction. However, NIRS signals consist of mixed contributions from multiple tissue layers, making it challenging to accurately infer oxygenation of a specific target tissue layer. We propose a simulation-guided deep learning framework to infer oxygen saturation in a target tissue layer from multi-wavelength, multi-distance NIRS measurements. A two-layer tissue model was constructed to represent superficial and deep biological structures, and Monte Carlo simulations were used to generate a large-scale dataset under varying tissue thicknesses and oxygenation conditions, incorporating a multi-distance sourceâ€“detector configuration (1â€“6 cm separations) and three wavelengths (730, 800, and 850 nm) to reflect realistic measurement settings. A one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) was trained to estimate target-layer oxygenation from optical measurements and superficial layer thickness. The model was trained using an adaptive optimization method and mean squared error loss, effectively capturing the nonlinear relationship between mixed optical signals and underlying physiological parameters, and demonstrating accurate and robust prediction performance across varying tissue conditions. This study shows that integrating physics-based simulation with data-driven modeling enables target-specific, depth-resolved inference of tissue oxygenation from non-invasive measurements. The proposed approach provides a scalable framework for solving inverse problems in biological signal analysis and has potential applications in non-invasive monitoring of placental oxygenation and other clinically relevant physiological processes.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Towards a Catalogue of Protein Functional States for Dynamic Regulatory Network Modeling
authors: Szabolcs Cselgő Kovács, Pázmány Péter Catholic University Information Techonology and Bionics Department, Hungary; Erzsébet Fichó, Cytocast Hungary Kft, Hungary; István Zoltán Reguly, Pázmány Péter Catholic University Information Techonology and Bionics Department, Hungary; Attila Csikász-Nagy, Cytocast Hungary Kft, Hungary
abstract: The decision-making capability of regulatory networks is embedded in the crosstalk of protein functional regions, which serve as logical switches that drive the downstream progression of cellular responses. Computational methods have demonstrated that PTM crosstalk patterns are conserved and decryptable. One of the most comprehensive databases is Reactome, which integrates multiple data sources into unified regulatory interactions. However, building genome-scale regulatory models remains challenging because data sources often provide binary interaction data, while Reactome compresses interacting entities into implicit complex assembly rules that are suitable only for qualitative modeling. Here, we propose a protein state catalogue database for Saccharomyces cerevisiae that reorients regulatory interactions from the perspective of the participating proteins and considers protein states as building blocks for model construction. We utilized Reactome V95 as a primary source to combinatorially extract complex assembly rules into a pool of explicit interactions and assigned structural annotations to each protein. The protein state catalogue contains protein state observations for 1322 yeast proteins that participate in 15 789 explicit alternative interactions across 194 regulatory pathways. Although 484 proteins have PTM site annotations, only 132 participate in interactions that lead to their state transitions. The state catalogue can serve as a valuable basis for systematically constructing regulatory models, training machine-learning models, and gaining a deeper understanding of protein functional crosstalk in broader cellular regulation mechanisms. Supported by the URSP-CDP-24 University Research Scholarship Program - Cooperative Doctoral Programme of the Ministry for Culture and Innovation from the source of National Research, Development and Innovation Fund.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Integrating single-nucleus RNA-seq with genome-scale metabolic models to predict dementia biomarkers
authors: Seo Young Kim, Graduate School of Engineering Biology, KAIST, Daejeon 34141, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Junhyeok Jeon, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon 34141, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Hyun Uk Kim, Graduate School of Engineering Biology, KAIST, Daejeon 34141, Republic of Korea, South Korea
abstract: Dementia lacks accessible biomarkers that reflect disease mechanisms and support early diagnosis. In this study, we developed a systems biology framework to predict metabolite biomarkers for dementia by integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data with genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs). Public and in-house postmortem brain datasets were analyzed to classify 1,977,975 high-quality nuclei into major brain cell types. Among the identified cell types, astrocytes, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia, and oligodendrocytes were selected for downstream analysis. Pseudo-bulk expression profiles were generated and integrated into the human generic GEM Human1 to reconstruct 3,622 patient-specific GEMs across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Lewy body dementia (LB), and normal controls. The cell-specific GEMs were simulated to quantify disease-associated metabolic activity. Significant metabolites were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Spearman correlation analysis, and log2 fold change. A total of 831 metabolites initially showed significant alterations in the AD and PD+LB cohorts, with prominent disease-associated changes observed in microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes; these metabolites were further subjected to screening. Candidate biomarkers included betaine, spermidine, N-acetylgalactosamine, and S-adenosylmethionine for AD, and agmatine, arachidonate, sphingosine, spermidine, and hypoxanthine for PD+LB. These results show that integrating snRNA-seq with GEMs can systematically identify cell type-specific metabolic alterations and support biomarker discovery in dementia.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Tissue- and system-level discovery of gero-protective perturbation candidates using transcriptomic signature enrichment
authors: Philipp Trollmann, Boston University, United States; Rocio Rodriguez Quiroz, Boston University, United States; Paul Okoro, Boston University, United States; Preshita Dave, Boston University, United States
abstract: Aging is a gradual and irreversible biological process which not only drives the decline in tissue function across organ systems, but also significantly increases the risk of various aging-related diseases. To systematically investigate interventions that may reverse tissue-specific aging signatures, we derived tissue-specific aging profiles from GTEx, Tabula Sapiens, and Tabula Senis and compared them with signatures derived from the large-scale perturbational datasets Tahoe-100M, Perturb-Seq, DrugMatrix and SciPlex. By standardizing these signatures as OmicSignature objects and applying gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), we classified perturbations as "gero-protective" or "gero-advancing" based on their similarity or anti-similarity with age-associated transcriptional changes. Candidate signatures were prioritized by computing the mean effect, the p-value weighted sum of effects, and the average directionality of effects across tissues. We identified several systemic gero-protective candidates. One of the most notable gero-protective drugs identified was fenofibrate, which exhibited a consistent effect direction across all three aging datasets and across top-contributing tissues, in agreement with prior literature. Other identified candidates, such as bezafibrate, enalapril, and pantoprazole, further support the analysis through existing or emerging evidence of protective effects. These results highlight a promising framework for the identification of systemic gero-effects across diverse aging and perturbational resources. Future work will include integrating these hits with drug mechanism annotations and cross-validating findings using GSEA leading-edge genes and Perturb-Seq knockdowns in order to prioritize consistent candidates for follow-up experimental validation. This systematic approach provides a clear strategy for identifying novel pre-clinical anti-aging therapies.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Systems Pharmacology Analysis of Off-the-Shelf Peptide Vaccine Combined with PD-1/CTLA-4 Blockade in Fibrolamellar Carcinoma
authors: Osman N. Yogurtcu, US FDA, United States; Joel Eliason, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Aleksander S. Popel, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Hong Yang, US FDA, United States
abstract: We developed a preliminary quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model of the FLC-Vac vaccine plus nivolumab/ipilimumab for fibrolamellar carcinoma (FLC), qualitatively benchmarked against clinical trial observations, to provide initial estimates of component contributions and scheduling effects. Adapted from a hepatocellular carcinoma platform, this mechanistic ordinary differential equation model was tailored to FLC biology. It incorporates FLC-Vac depots, tumor-draining lymph node antigen handling, CD4+/CD8+ T cell priming, tumor trafficking, checkpoint-antibody pharmacokinetics, suppressive circuits, and an exhausted CD8+ pool. Deterministic simulations mirroring the published protocol compared the full combination against arms missing individual components (vaccine/adjuvant, nivolumab, or ipilimumab) and evaluated concurrent ICI initiation versus a 4-week vaccine lead-in using Julia. The full combination yielded modest tumor shrinkage (-16.4% best diameter change), outperforming simulated ICI-only conditions, directionally consistent with modest historical ICI activity. Removing the vaccine/adjuvant reduced peak lymph-node pMHC-II (38.8%) and activated CD4+ cells (45.0%). Removing nivolumab increased the week-10 exhausted-to-active intratumoral CD8+ ratio 3.18-fold, worsening tumor response by 16.4 percentage points and accelerating progressive disease. Omitting ipilimumab reduced peak activated lymph-node CD4+ (43.3%) and tumor CD8+ effectors (22.5%). A 4-week vaccine lead-in before ICI worsened tumor response by 6.5 percentage points and attenuated early lymph-node CD8+ priming, qualitatively matching clinical trial observations. This model supports a mechanistic division of labor: FLC-Vac drives class-II/CD4+ priming, nivolumab restrains local CD8+ exhaustion, and ipilimumab augments CD4+/Treg control to enhance intratumoral CD8+ accumulation. Concurrent ICI initiation proved superior to a vaccine lead-in. These preliminary estimates warrant further refinement via virtual-patient analyses.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Expressed Gene Landscape (EGL) Analysis: Systems-level Evaluation of Lung Cell Phenotypes and Druggable Targets
authors: Bingfang Xu, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Ajith Pankajam, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Kumar Arvind, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Anne Deslattes-Mays, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Matthew Diller, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Raymond LeClair, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Beverly Peng, Department of Informatics, J. Craig Venter Institute, La Jolla, CA, USA, United States; Noam Rotenberg, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; William Spear, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Zhizheng Wang, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Yun Zhang, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Richard Scheuermann, Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States
abstract: A cellâ€™s phenotype, and thereby its function, is dictated by the subset of genes and proteins it expresses. Recent advances in single-cell technologies allow us to quantify cell phenotype at the resolution of individual cells. Here, we present Expressed Gene Landscape (EGL) analysis, a framework that not only profiles the gene-expression-defined phenotype of individual cell types but also systematically evaluates phenotypic variation across cell types within a tissue. EGL adopts gene-specific probabilistic base models to estimate the likelihood of gene expression in each cell type. After fine-tuning the base models and applying a data-driven probability threshold, EGL identifies all genes expressed in each cell type. To enable systems-level analysis, EGL generates a binary gene-by-cell-type matrix, with hierarchically organized cell types as columns and genes as rows. By defining input genes using Gene Ontology categories, EGL compares diverse biological functions across cell types. EGL is also integrated with an agentic AI workflow that uses large language models (LLMs) to guide input selection and aid in result interpretation.
