Applying EGL to lung single-cell datasets, we constructed gene expression landscapes for key biological processes across lung cell types, defined gene expression landscapes in healthy and diseased lungs, and generated druggable gene expression landscapes. Within each landscape, EGL revealed three patterns of expression: ubiquitously expressed genes, cell-type-selective genes, and genes enriched in specific cell-type classes. Together, EGL provides a comprehensive view of the functional characteristics of each cell type and serves as a tool for systems-level evaluation of cell phenotypes and therapeutic targets.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: DeepTaxa: A Hybrid CNN-Transformer Architecture for Hierarchical Taxonomic Classification of 16S rRNA Sequences
authors: Ahmed Moustafa, The American University in Cairo, Egypt; Rana Salah Khalel, The American University in Cairo, Egypt; Khlood Abdelaal, The American University in Cairo, Egypt; Lobna Ghonaim, The American University in Cairo, Egypt; Olaitan I. Awe, African Society for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology, South Africa
abstract: Accurate taxonomic classification of 16S rRNA gene sequences remains central to microbial ecology, yet existing methods struggle at fine-grained ranks where sequence divergence is minimal and label spaces are large. We present DeepTaxa, a deep learning framework that jointly predicts taxonomy across all seven standard ranks (domain through species) using a hybrid architecture that pairs convolutional neural networks with a BERT-style transformer. The CNN branch extracts local k-mer motifs through multi-kernel convolutions, while the transformer captures long-range contextual dependencies. Input sequences are tokenized using DNABERT-2 byte-pair encoding, which outperforms one-hot nucleotide encoding by over 6 percentage points at the species level. Trained on Greengenes2 2024.09 (277,336 training / 69,335 test sequences), the hybrid model achieves 92.9% species accuracy with tight cross-seed reproducibility (std To rigorously evaluate each component, we conducted Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization (20 trials per architecture) so that every variant receives a fair comparison at its best configuration. The optimized hybrid (92.97%) outperforms the optimized CNN-only (92.29%) and BERT-only (86.41%), confirming that both branches contribute meaningfully. The BERT-only model performs catastrophically (4.7%) with the hybrid's default hyperparameters but recovers to 86.4% with proper tuning, highlighting how sensitive transformers are to learning rate on genomic data. track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: GSFM: A Gene Set Foundation Model Pre-trained on a Massive Collection of Diverse Gene Sets Applied to Gene Set Enrichment Analysis
authors: Daniel Clarke, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Avi Ma'Ayan, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States
abstract: Foundation models have transformed scientific and commercial domains. Trained on massive datasets, foundation models can effectively capture complex patterns within these datasets and convert these patterns into embeddings that can be used for a variety of useful applications. Here we created a gene set foundation model (GSFM) that was trained on millions of unlabeled gene sets from two large gene set databases: Rummagene and RummaGEO. Rummagene automatically extracts gene sets from supplemental tables of publications deposited in PubMed Central (PMC); and RummaGEO has gene sets automatically computed from comparing groups of samples from RNA-seq studies deposited into the gene expression omnibus (GEO) and uniformly aligned by ARCHS4. Several foundation model architectures and training methodologies were benchmarked in the downstream tasks of predicting gene function, gene-disease associations, and protein-protein interactions, as well as gene set enrichment analysis. The selected best GSFM architecture is a denoising autoencoder trained on multi-hot encoded gene sets and it achieves state-of-the-art performance on gene function prediction tasks. GSFM was used to systematically augment gene sets from a collection of sources to create gene pages for all human genes. It also applied to performing gene set enrichment analysis with benchmarks demonstrating superior performance compared with other enrichment analysis algorithms and tools. The GSFM web-interface, model, and source code can be accessed from: https://gsfm.maayanlab.cloud.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: A Novel Computational Framework for Fractal Analysis of Spatial Transcriptomic Data
authors: Elijah Yu, Irvine High School, United States; Xinmin Li, University of California, Los Angeles, United States
abstract: Fractal analysis is an emerging mathematical technique able to characterize the complexity of biological systems. Traditionally used to analyze morphological imaging data, this study aims to create a computational framework applying the methods and concepts of fractal analysis to 10X Visium transcriptomic outputs. The pipeline was validated using public datasets of glioblastoma and triple-negative breast cancer samples. Given the discrete nature of Visium spots, individual spots were assigned deconvoluted topics using STDeconvolve, and subsequently categorized as “tumor” or “host” based on top genes and common tumor-associated markers. Then, Python scripts for the box-counting algorithm were used to calculate measures of monofractal tumor boundary complexity through the fractal dimension (Df), while the Chhabra-Jensen algorithm was used to calculate measures of multifractal complexity with the singularity exponent range (Δα) and singularity spectrum (f(α)). Df and Δα values were interpreted based on transcriptomic and histological profiles of the tissue sections, and cross-referenced with original findings. Our results demonstrated that higher values of Df and Δα illustrate extensive intermingling and complex interactions between host and tumor tissue, while lower values represent homogeneous tumor regions or a defined host-tumor boundary. Compared to spatial metrics like Moran’s I, which measures spatial autocorrelation, Df and Δα values can quantify boundary complexity and diversity of probability distributions, respectively. The proposed framework offers a novel perspective on the biophysical reality of tumor microenvironments, and serves as a proof-of-concept for calculation of fractal metrics across a diversity of spatial transcriptomic platforms.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Image-Based Machine Learning For Alzheimer's Detection
authors: Varun Menon, Independent, United States
abstract: In this project I examined how well Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can distinguish between the severity of Alzheimerâ€™s disease using MRI brain images. Early diagnosis of dementia is desirable as it leads to better treatment outcomes and allows for earlier intervention, and machine learning techniques provide a useful methodology for improving diagnostic processes. A CNN model was developed and trained using a labeled dataset of MRI brain images sorted into four categories of classification: Non-Demented, Very Mild Demented, Mild Demented, and Moderate Demented. Prior to training, the images were processed and formatted to ensure consistency and improve model performance. The model was trained over multiple iterations, allowing it to learn patterns and structural differences within the brain scans associated with each stage of the disease. When shown novel images during testing, the model performed with a high level of accuracy. While this indicates that the model can distinguish between the image groups, it may also be due to overfitting of the data used during training or limitations in dataset size and diversity. All in all, this project demonstrates the usefulness of deep learning algorithms in identifying patterns within neuroimaging data in order to assist in diagnosing Alzheimerâ€™s disease. However, further study would be beneficial to validate these findings and enhance the reliability and real-world applicability of this algorithm.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Identifying clinically relevant cell state interactions in the tumor microenvironment of IDH-mut glioma.
authors: Arashdeep Singh, National Institutes of Health, United States; Bharati Mehani, National Institutes of Health, United States; Vishaka Gopalan, National Institutes of Health, United States; Sushant Puri, Oregon Health & Science University, United States; Kenneth Aldape, National Institutes of Health, United States; Sridhar Hannenhalli, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Tumor microenvironment (TME) comprises a diverse milieu of cell types that occupy heterogeneous transcriptional states across tumors. Interactions among these cell states play a central role in shaping tumor progression and therapeutic response. However, systematic identification of functional cell-state interactions (CSIs) remains challenging, owing to the limited availability of scRNA-seq cohorts with clinical annotation and the lack of cellular resolution in bulk RNA-seq datasets. Here, we present CSI-TME, a computational framework that generalizes the concept of gene-level interactions, such as synthetic lethality, to the level of cell states, enabling the inference of prognostic CSIs directly from large-scale bulk transcriptomic cohorts. Applying CSI-TME to IDH-mutant gliomas, we uncover a highly reproducible cell-state interaction network (CSIN) that is predominantly pro-tumorigenic and exhibits distinct activation patterns between IDH-mutant astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma. Malignant cell states within this network recapitulate multiple neuronal lineage programs, including astrocyte-like and oligodendrocyte progenitorâ€“like states, and reveal key interactions between glioma stem-like cells and T cells. The CSIN stratifies patient response to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring its clinical relevance. Approximately 20% of identified CSIs are supported by direct ligandâ€“receptor interactions and show spatial co-localization in spatial transcriptomic data. Notably, we identify a robust pro-tumorigenic interaction between tip-like endothelial cells and hypoxic malignant cells, mediated by multiple ligandâ€“receptor pairs. In contrast, anti-tumor CSIs associated with oncogenic alterations are preferentially active in early disease stages, suggesting a transient tissue homeostatic response. Collectively, CSI-TME provides a scalable and clinically grounded framework to uncover prognostic cell-state interactions and nominate therapeutic ligandâ€“receptor targets, offering new insights into how coordinated cell-state dynamics shape the TME in IDH-mutant glioma.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Mathematical and experimental models of interactions among subclones and immunity in melanoma
authors: MG Hirsch, Intramural Research Program of National Library ofMedicine, NIH; University of Maryland, United States; Jon Ergun, Mellon College of Science and School of Computer Science,Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Sung Chin, Laboratory Animal Science Program, Frederick NationalLaboratory for Cancer Research, NIH, United States; Cari Graff, Laboratory Animal Science Program, Frederick NationalLaboratory for Cancer Research, NIH,, United States; Danielle Yee, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute, NIH;University of Maryland, United States; Eva Eugenia Perez Guijarro, nstitute for Biomedical Research Sols-Morreale, SpanishNational Research Council,17 Universidad Autonoma de Madri, Spain; Glenn Merlino, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute, NIH, United States; Chi-Ping Day, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute, NIH, United States; Teresa Przytycka, Intramural Research Program of National Library ofMedicine, NIH, United States
abstract: Melanoma tumors often contain heterogeneous subclones, typically with proliferative or invasive phenotypes. These subclones interact with each other and the immune system to shape tumor progression. Understanding these interactions between subclones and the tumor microenvironment is a fundamental challenge for optimizing melanoma treatment. To analyze such interactions, we developed dedicated in vivo melanoma mouse models and new mathematical models to study such interactions. In the experimental models, admixtures of proliferative and invasive subclones of varying proportions were implanted into immunocompromised and immunocompetent mice. Tumor growth and subclone composition were tracked over time. In parallel, we built a computational model to capture the interactions between subclones and the immune system. By estimating parameter values of our mathematical model using the experimental measurements, we found that, while the proliferative subclone outgrew the invasive subclone, T cell activities selected for the invasive subclone. The initial subclonal proportion in this dynamic system determines the overall tumor sensitivity to immune response. The key subclone-subclone and subcloneâ€“immune interactions identified in this study provide insights into how intratumor heterogeneity and immune pressure influence melanoma progression, suggesting strategies for optimizing therapeutic timing and adaptive treatment.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Han Xin Protocol (HXP): A Multi-Scale Mechanistic Framework for Engineered Bacterial Swarms in Solid Tumours
authors: Trung Kien Tran, University of Greenwich, United Kingdom; Tuan Vuong, University of Greenwich, United Kingdom
abstract: This work presents the results of modelling, simulation, and visualisation of the spatiotemporal interactions of engineered bacterial swarms within the solid tumour microenvironment (TME). Solid tumours present compounding delivery barriers: hypoxic cores, elevated interstitial fluid pressure, and metabolic immunosuppression driven by secondary bile acid accumulation that induces T-cell exhaustion. Traditional passive drug delivery fails to address these obstacles simultaneously. We propose the Han Xin Protocol (HXP), a multi-scale mechanistic framework designed to capture the dynamic behaviour of engineered Salmonella Typhimurium VNP20009. HXP couples continuous Reaction-Diffusion PDEs with discrete Agent-Based Modelling (ABM), coordinating three bacterial sub-populations governed by a Finite State Machine. Infiltrators employ aerotactic sensing to penetrate hypoxic zones and trigger quorum-sensing-mediated lysis. Besiegers form concentric rings for sFlt-1-mediated VEGF sequestration, inducing vascular blockade. Logistics agents neutralise immunosuppressive bile acids via BSH activity, characterised by Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Swarm dynamics follow Lennard-Jones potentials, with JIT-compiled spatial hashing achieving O(N) complexity for fixed-radius interactions. Gene Regulatory Network delays are approximated using Hill kinetics, and tumour decay is simulated by Gompertzian ODEs. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that HXP achieves 83.3% vascular regression, neutralises 56.7% of immunosuppressive metabolites, and delivers 73.6% of cytolytic payload. By bypassing the physical limits of unguided passive diffusion, the framework reduces overall tumour viability by 48.4%. The model predicts in situ vaccination via antigen release and incorporates an alternating magnetic field (AMF) thermal kill-switch to ensure clinical safety. HXP establishes a predictive foundation for precision oncology by bridging mathematical biology and bioinformatics to illuminate complex bio-hybrid swarm behaviours.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Leveraging Simulated Spatial Omics to Develop and Benchmark Counterfactual Prediction of Tissue Perturbation Effects
authors: Zachary Danaceau, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States; Irene Ong, University of Wisconsin Madison, United States
abstract: It is evident that spatially resolved biomolecular profiles, such as spatial â€˜omics data can provide insight into the mechanisms of disease and treatment induced changes. However, due to the heterogeneity of tissues, perturbation effects can be complex and dependent on spatial context. Here we present a strategy for evaluating computational methods for spatial â€˜omics perturbation effect prediction. Developing and comprehensively benchmarking perturbation effect prediction models for spatial omics will facilitate the study of how tissue context and perturbation distribution drive response, allowing for further mechanistic understanding and therapeutic optimization. These potential benefits come with substantial additional challenges as tissue context and spatial perturbation distribution increase the complexity of response modifying covariates and applied treatment respectively. To begin to address this problem, we devise and apply a hybrid data simulation strategy based on scDesign3, previously used to benchmark single cell perturbation models, and scCube, used to generate realistically complex spatial patterns, to benchmark the adaptation of single cell perturbation prediction methods to spatial omics. This strategy allows for the generation of simulated spatial â€˜omics data with complex response relationships modified by both spot composition and neighborhood effects to assess recovery of these new factors introduced by spatially resolved â€˜omics with counterfactual ground truth. To validate the utility of this strategy, we examine the correspondence between simulation performance and performance on spatial â€˜omics data of tumors treated with heterogenous radiation therapy and of murine Alzheimerâ€™s model brains. This serves as a foundation for further development of spatial â€˜omics perturbation prediction methods.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: PolMed-BERT: A Polish Medical-Domain LLM for Clinical EHRs Classification in Infertility Treatment
authors: Dawid Zamojski, Department of Data Science and Engineering, Silesian University of Technology, Poland; Gyncentrum Sp. z o.o., Poland, Poland; Martyna Szyszka, Faculty of Automatic Control, Electronics and Computer Science, Silesian University of Technology, Poland, Poland; Adam Pudelko, Department of Immunology, Academy of Silesia, Poland; Gyncentrum Sp. z o.o., Poland, Poland; Michal Marczyk, Department of Data Science and Engineering, Silesian University of Technology, Poland; Yale School of Medicine, USA, Poland
abstract: Medical large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved clinical text mining, but no dedicated Polish medical language model in infertility treatment has been reported so far. Existing Polish LLMs are trained mainly on general-domain corpora resulting in insufficient representation of clinical terminology. This study presents the first, to our knowledge, continued pretraining effort toward a Polish medical language model developed using a newly constructed domain-specific corpus. The goal of this project is to support clinical decision-making, including multi-label classification of electronic health records (EHRs). Polish medical corpora were constructed by aggregating thematic corpus resources, including open-access literature and translated PubMed abstracts with over 4 million words. Text preprocessing included cleaning and tokenization, followed by selected model's vocabulary expansion. Starting from a Polish-distilRoBERTa backbone with extended vocabulary size, continued pretraining was performed. The resulting PolMed-BERT was evaluated in a downstream multi-label clinical classification task included optimization of hyper-parameters under real-world class imbalance. PolMed-BERT achieved stable Masked Language Modeling convergence with a minimum validation loss of 1.01. Extensive optimization experiments demonstrated that hyper-parameters tuning and preprocessing choices had a measurable impact on downstream performance, resulting in macro balanced accuracy reaching up to 0.7 on real infertility treatment data. Compared with baseline models, the domain-specific variant provided more consistent learning behavior and improved attribution quality in explainable AI analyses. This work advances the development of Polish medical LLM by introducing a domain-adapted language model. Future work will focus on further optimization, threshold calibration for multi-label prediction, and expanded evaluation protocols on ongoing datasets. Acknowledgments: The project was conducted in cooperation with the Genetic Laboratory of the Gyncentrum Sp. z o.o. in Sosnowiec. This work was supported by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education 'Implementation Doctorate' grant number DWD/7/0396/2023.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: GlycaNER: An automated Glycan Structure Term Detection and Normalization Tool in Biomedical Literature
authors: Shovan Bhowmik, Department of Computer & Information Sciences, University of Delaware, United States; Rene Ranzinger, Complex Carbohydrate Research Center, The University of Georgia, United States; Jeet Vora, Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Medicine, The George Washington School of Medicine and Health Sciences, United States; Michael Tiemeyer, Complex Carbohydrate Research Center, The University of Georgia, United States; Raja Mazumder, Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Medicine, The George Washington School of Medicine and Health Sciences, United States; K. Vijay-Shanker, Department of Computer & Information Sciences, University of Delaware, United States
abstract: Glycosylation is a widely studied post-translational modification where complex carbohydrate molecules, known as glycans, are covalently attached to biomolecules. Glycans play essential roles in protein folding, stability, intracellular trafficking, and molecular recognition. In biomedical literature, glycans are often described using terms referring to entire structures or specific substructures, such as motifs, types, branching patterns, or terminal forms; collectively known as glycan structure terms (GSTs). To support systematic glycosylation information extraction (IE) from the literature, a glycan structure dictionary (GSD) [1] was developed, containing experimentally verified GSTs along with definitions, synonyms, and literature evidence. However, this dictionary remains incomplete. The wide variation in how GSTs are used across publications demands a more comprehensive dictionary. In this work, we present a named entity recognition tool, GlycaNER, consisting of a transformer-based model that automatically detects GSTs from text to facilitate glycosylation IE, and a standardization pipeline that maps terms to GSD entries and suggests unmatched terms for inclusion as synonyms or new entries. We applied GlycaNER to approximately 2,000 PubMed abstracts and predicted nearly 17,000 GST mentions, of which about 9,000 GSTs were successfully normalized to 150 GSD entries out of 190 entries, demonstrating GlycaNERâ€™s ability to capture diverse glycan descriptions, reduce manual curation effort, and semi-automatically expand the GSD. Overall, GlycaNER highlights the value of automated text-mining approaches for advancing glycoscience knowledge bases and enabling downstream bioinformatics applications. [1] Vora, Jeet, et al. ""The Glycan Structure Dictionaryâ€”a dictionary describing commonly used glycan structure terms."" Glycobiology 33.5 (2023): 354-357.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) for Extracting Impacts of Variants from PubMed Abstracts
authors: Pratim Ugale, University of Delaware, United States; Karen Ross, Georgetown University Medical Center, United States; Chuming Chen, University of Delaware, United States; Vijay Shanker, University of Delaware, United States; Cathy Wu, University of Delaware, United States
abstract: Studies analyzing the impacts of genetic variants are usually published in the form of unstructured text in scientific literature. Converting these into a structured format is an important task that allows consolidating results and understanding the mechanism of diseases from different papers. We explore the usage of out of the box Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task. We use a multi-stage LLM pipeline to extract the impact of variants from PubMed abstracts in the form of a 3-tuple - ([subject entity] [relation] [effect]). The pipeline first involves extracting the variants mentioned in an abstract. For each extracted variant, the next stage generates a natural language sentence containing an effect of that variant. The final LLM stage is used to break this sentence into the 3-tuple. In addition to effects of the variant, we also extract contextual information such as the number of patients involved in the study, authorâ€™s confidence in the proposed effect, and whether the effect is mentioned as a background fact, a result of the author's study, or a hypothesis. Preliminary results on a set of abstracts related to Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias show that this method is effective in extracting the effects of variants and the contextual information. Currently, we are working on a formal evaluation of all aspects of this approach. The applicability of this method extends to a wider range of extractive tasks, providing valuable insights for future approaches and other tasks.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Navigating genomes of cereal crops with agentic and open model systems
authors: Gerard Lazo, USDA ARS, United States
abstract: The rapid expansion of crop reference genomes, coupled with the advancements in artificial intelligence, is revolutionizing pangenome research. We are developing an AI Research Assistant (AIRA) platform, leveraging the GrainGenes database to facilitate comprehensive genome surveillance. AIRA employs retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in an agent-oriented workflow to identify promising genomic regions for investigation and enables AI-driven conversations about cereal genetics. RAG topics are keyed on disease-related research covering rusts, fusarium, powdery mildew, wheat blast, and bacterial leaf streak disease. Other topic-based skills are planned to expand areas of research. AIRA tools allow rapid navigation of over 100 cereal reference genomes and their annotation files via JBrowse2 comparative maps and Jalview sequence alignments, revealing key associations. Pairing GFF3 genome annotation files with the AIRA platform have enhanced genome navigation. An interface connecting genome- structured BLAST database files provide dynamic extraction of sequenced regions of interest that can included in downstream workflows. One application investigates cis-regulatory element diversity, focusing on 5' regulatory motif influence on gene expression. A natural language processing (NLP) step is being incorporated to build an atlas that can be tied to gene expression profiles. Agentic systems using Claude Code and NemoClaw are being developed around open-sourced models and air-gapped environments for independent research and secured testing. This integrated AI-driven platform promises to accelerate pangenome research, offering rapid insights into genetic diversity and facilitating targeted investigations for enhanced crop improvement.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Schema-Driven Extraction of Protocol Execution Graphs from Biomedical PDFs: Multi-Dimensional Inter-Model Concordance Evaluation on 55 Liver Organoid Publications
authors: Yanling Liu, NIH/NIAID/RTB, United States; Curtis Lisle, NIH/NIAID/RTB, United States; Suh Yeon Yoon, NIH/NIAID/RTB, United States; Jack Collins, NIH/NIAID/RTB, United States
abstract: Biomedical experimental protocols are typically reported as narrative text, limiting systematic cross-study comparison. In organoid development, where differentiation outcomes depend on precise growth factor concentrations, media change timing, and extracellular matrix composition, the absence of machine-readable representations hinders reproducibility and meta-analysis. We describe a pipeline that extracts Protocol Execution Graphs (PEGs) from PDF manuscripts: directed acyclic graphs in which each node represents a single atomic physical action annotated with controlled-vocabulary verbs, typed reagent, functional zones, and quantitative parameters. Extraction proceeds in three stages: (1) LLM-based initial extraction with JSON Schema enforcement; (2) deterministic structural validation and atomicity refinement; and (3) iterative LLM-based repair covering content accuracy, coverage gap detection, and topology correction, with regression preventing constraints. We applied this pipeline to 55 liver organoid publications using two frontier LLMs with native PDF understanding under identical configuration. To evaluate procedural agreement at the step level, each protocol is encoded as a sequence of three-base codons mapped from action verbs, and pairwise alignment is performed with semantic verb groupings. Across 55 paired comparisons, high-level semantic agreement was observed (cosine > 0.87) while step-level sequence identity remained low (median 0.33). Concordance attribution analysis decomposed non-matching alignment positions into gaps within shared zones, zone assignment disagreement, and verb disagreement. Despite raw extraction quality variations, our repair pipeline resulted comparable non-structural residual issue counts on both models. These results indicate that inter-model disagreement in structured protocol extraction is dominated by granularity differences in step decomposition rather than semantic content errors.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Enhancing Medical Knowledge in Large Language Models via Supervised Continued Pretraining on Clinical Notes
authors: Davy Weissenbacher, Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University, United States; Moizza Shabbir, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, United States; Ian M. Campbell, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Carl T. Berdahl, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, United States; Graciela Gonzalez-Hernandez, Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University, United States
abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) contain limited professional medical knowledge, as large-scale training on clinical text has not yet been possible due to restricted access. Objectives: To continue pre-training an open-access instruct LLM on de-identified medical notes and evaluate the resulting impact on real-world clinical decision-making tasks and standard benchmarks. Methods: Using 500K de-identified clinical notes from Cedars-Sinai Health System, we fine-tuned a Qwen3-4B Instruct model with supervised learning to generate medical decision-making (MDM) paragraphs from patient presentations, and evaluated it on assigned-diagnosis prediction, in-hospital cardiac-arrest mention detection, and a suite of general and biomedical benchmarks. Results: The fine-tuned model produced MDMs that closely resembled those written by physicians and outperformed the base-instruct model and larger clinically untrained models (Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-405B Instruct) on assigned-diagnosis prediction, the task most aligned with its training objective. On the task of detecting in-hospital cardiac arrest mentions, the model initially exhibited mild label collapse, but a brief task-specific fine-tuning stage resolved this issue and allowed it to surpass all competitors. The model also demonstrated global general knowledge retention on biomedical and general-domain evaluation benchmarks compared to the baseline. Conclusion: Supervised full fine-tuning on clinical notes allowed the model to incorporate medical knowledge without sacrificing general-domain abilities, and to transfer this knowledge to unseen biomedical tasks without wholesale loss of general-domain abilities, while revealing collapse-related failure modes that motivate more principled strategies for clinical specialization.

title: Anatomy of a modular toolchain for reproducible bioinformatics workflows
authors: Kelly Sovacool, Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research, United States; Samarth Mathur, Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research, United States; Vishal Koparde, Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research, United States; Parthav Jailwala, Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research, United States
abstract: The reproducibility and replicability of data-intensive biological studies depend on the quality of the software used during data analysis. Here we describe a toolchain for the development of reproducible bioinformatics workflows that follow established guidelines for high-quality scientific software. The central component is a template repository for generating new pipeline repositories, ensuring consistent structure across the whole suite of pipelines we have developed. Each pipeline step points to a container to define dependencies, with Docker recipes stored in a central repository for reuse. A Python-based command-line interface (CLI) provides user-friendly commands for initializing projects and launching the pipeline on HPC systems. The CLI uses functions from a shared package to reduce code duplication across template deployments and to streamline ongoing maintenance. Because the interface is consistent, once a biologist uses one of our pipelines, they can easily use others, regardless of which workflow language is used by the developers. The template also contains continuous integration workflows via GitHub Actions for testing, enforcing code format and quality, deploying documentation, and preparing releases. Custom GitHub Actions are defined in a standalone repository for reuse in CI workflows across our organization. Using this toolchain, we have developed multiple Nextflow pipelines for analyzing data from whole-genome sequencing, ChIP-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, and CRISPR experiments, with additional workflows in development. This approach has streamlined our development and maintenance processes by enabling faster updates and consistent improvements across pipelines while following best practices including modular design, code reuse, automated testing, clear documentation, and standardized release practices.

title: PheMINE: an open Snakemake workflow for interpretable phenome-wide modeling from EHR data
authors: Dayi Bian, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Wanying Zhu, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Alyssa C. Scartozzi, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Douglas M. Shaw, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Elena F. Evans, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Autumn R. Morrow, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Elizabeth Frankel, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Dillon G. Pruett, School of Communication Sciences & Disorders, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL 32306, USA, United States; Alexander S. Petty, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States; Jennifer E. Below, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN 37232, USA, United States
abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain longitudinal clinical information that can support large-scale biomedical discovery, but phenome-wide feature discovery and individual-level modeling are often implemented separately for specific traits. We developed PheMINE, the PHEnome-wide Modeling and INference Engine, as an open-source, Snakemake-based Python workflow for reproducible analysis of EHR-derived phenotypes. PheMINE provides a reproducible framework for feature discovery using either phenome-wide enrichment analysis or phenotype-to-phenome association testing, followed by individual-level prediction using interpretable machine-learning models. PheMINE takes in structured EHR-derived phenotypes, usually in the form of phecodes, and can be executed end to end from phenotype construction to feature discovery to predictive modeling. Feature discovery can be performed using PheWES, a permutation-based phenotype-wide enrichment test, or Phe-PheWAS, a covariate-adjusted phenotype-to-phenome association scan. Selected phecodes are then used by PheML to train a supervised classifier for risk prediction. More importantly, the workflow can calculate permutation feature importance at global level and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values at local level, providing insights into the phenotypic drivers of predictions. As a demonstration, the framework was applied to an EHR-derived stuttering cohort containing 1,122 manually reviewed cases with matched controls. PheWES tested 1,877 phecodes and identified 20 enriched phecodes, including speech and language disorder, developmental delays, and aphasia/speech disturbance. A random forest classifier was trained using the enriched phecodes as features and achieved an AUC of 0.88 on the held-out evaluation dataset. PheMINE is implemented in Python and distributed as an open-source Snakemake workflow under the MIT license. Source code, documentation, and example configurations are available at https://github.com/belowlab/PheMINE.

title: PosterSentry: a light-weight multimodal classification system for scientific poster quality assurance in open repositories
authors: James ONeill, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, San Diego, CA, United States; Parth Sarin, Graduate School of Education, Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA, United States; Adam Buttrick, California Digital Library, University of California Office of the President, Oakland, CA, United States; Bhavesh Patel, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, San Diego, CA, United States
abstract: The Posters.science project aims to build an index of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) of posters by extracting machine-actionable metadata from PDFs stored in open access repositories. During harvesting of poster records from Zenodo and Figshare, we found that many were mislabeled, containing multi-page papers, proceedings, abstract books, or presentations. Label noise at this scale severely limits the viability of automated FAIR pipelines. To mitigate this, we developed PosterSentry, a lightweight, open-source multimodal classifier that identifies whether a PDF is a true scientific poster. We fused three complementary feature streams in PosterSentry: 1) text embeddings via model2vec (512 dimensions), 2) visual features including color statistics, edge density, and spatial complexity (15 dimensions), and 3) structural PDF layout features such as page geometry, font diversity, and text density (15 dimensions). We concatenated these streams into a 542-dimensional vector and used logistic regression to classify them. PosterSentry was trained on 3,606 heuristically selected real-world examples with no synthetic augmentation. It achieved 87.3% accuracy, runs on CPU in under one second per file, and requires only a 10kb model head, which is orders of magnitude smaller than other LLM-based alternatives. PosterSentry is publicly available under an MIT license on Hugging Face alongside its training data, and is currently deployed in the Posters.science quality control pipeline. In this presentation, we will present the development of PosterSentry, results across 30,205 poster PDFs from open repositories, and discuss future work planned in collaboration with the Collaborative Metadata (COMET) initiative.

title: CTRL: A Dynamic open source e-Consent Platform
authors: Maxime Hebrard, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Ignatius Menzies, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Tim Kallady, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Peter Louk, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Rishi Israni, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Katherine Champ, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Filippo Ammazzalorso, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Leonard Goldstein, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Sarah Kummerfeld, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia
abstract: Dynamic consent represents a transformative approach to the traditional informed consent model, fostering continuous engagement between researchers and participants. Unlike static methods, this framework facilitates ongoing communication, allowing researchers to provide study updates and solicit renewed consent for amended protocols. Simultaneously, it empowers participants to proactively manage their involvement. Transitioning from paper-based systems to electronic platforms enhances research efficiency through robust audit trails, stringent access controls, and adherence to the principle of least privilege, thereby streamlining data management and institutional accountability. Initiated by Australian Genomics and developed by Garvan Institute, the open source CTRL platform (pronounced ""control"") is a component of the Australian BioCommonsâ€™ GUARDIANS program. CTRL serves as a critical module in national infrastructure for human genomic research. The platform comprises two specialized web interfaces: Researcher Portal: This administrative hub allows clinicians to manage multiple studies within a secure environment. Researchers can design bespoke consent forms featuring modular sections, embedded educational media, and ontology-integrated terms to ensure machine-readability. The portal further enables participant invitation and real-time oversight of consent statuses. Participant Portal: This interface provides a secure environment for individuals to register personal data, review consent statements, and provide authorizations. A dedicated news feed ensures participants remain informed of research milestones, while integrated communication tools facilitate direct contact with study teams. In summary, CTRL is an open source, electronic dynamic consent solution that delivers an intuitive, secure, and engaging interface for both the scientific community and the public.

title: FAIRSCAPE: Pre-model AI-Readiness and Interpretability for Biomedical Data
authors: Sadnan Al Manir, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Maxwell Adam Levinson, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Justin Niestroy, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Christopher Churas, University of California San Diego, United States; Nathan Sheffield, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Brynne Sullivan, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Karen Fairchild, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Monica Munoz-Torres, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Sarah Ratcliffe, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States; Jilliian Parker, University of California San Diego, United States; Trey Ideker, University of California San Diego, United States; Timothy Clark, University of Virginia School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Post-model and in-model AI explainability methods have recently received enormous attention. Yet equally important are interpretability methods for complex, and frequently opaque, data preparation tasks in biomedical applications. These may include ethically sensitive decision making and analytic methods such as image segmentation, embedding generation, and multi-stage feature derivation. Pre-model pipelines cannot remain opaque if post-model results are to be trusted and reliable. The FAIRSCAPE AI-readiness framework addresses this problem by operationalizing and scoring 28 AI-readiness criteria developed by the NIH Bridge2AI Standards Working Group across seven categories: FAIRness, Provenance, Characterization, Pre-model Explainability, Ethics, Sustainability, and Computability. FAIRSCAPE packages data and metadata as Research Object Crates (RO-Crates), providing machine-readable metadata in schema.org and PROV/EVI vocabularies; component-resolvable provenance graphs; and an extended Gebru-style human readable datasheet; supplemented by LinkML and Croissant metadata translations. AI-readiness evaluations are provided as multi-factorial scores associated with data packages, enabling targeted identification of quality gaps across each AI-readiness category. The framework is production-deployed and cloud-native, and has been used to packaged multiple Bridge2AI releases. In recent additional work, FAIRSCAPE provenance graphs are resolved, and used for graph-RAG across the data, software, and model provenance components and metadata to produce a layered, audience-targeted interpretation with Likert-scoring of issues such as data leakage, and potential impact on results. Interpretations are stored as annotations in the provenance graph, and provided in severity-coded visualizations to the user. These features help enable the fine-scaled attention to rigor and reliability in pre-model data transformation required for critical decision making in biomedical research.

title: Generalized linear models for clustering of RNA-seq time series experiments
authors: Jherson Medina Correa, Systems and Computing Engineering Department, Universidad de los Andes, Bogotá, Colombia, Colombia; Juan Diego Enriquez-Ramos, Systems and Computing Engineering Department, Universidad de los Andes, Bogotá, Colombia, Colombia; Jorge Duitama, Systems and Computing Engineering Department, Universidad de los Andes, Bogotá, Colombia, Colombia
abstract: RNA-seq in time series experiments is a fundamental experimental design model for identification of important changes in gene expression along a biological process. Gene clustering allows to identify groups of genes with similar expression patterns throughout the process. Clusters can be interpreted as shared regulation mechanisms, which can be related to biological functions. Most current methods for gene clustering in time series implement classical unsupervised learning techniques which do not take into account the structure of the experiment, including management of replicate samples. We present a generalized linear model (GLM) implemented in a new open source software for gene clustering in time series RNA-seq experiments. Given an input matrix of raw counts and metadata file, the model calculates log fold changes (LFC) across the time points relative to the basal expression level at time zero, according to a GLM similar to that implemented in DeSeq2 for differential expression. The LFC values can be interpreted as normalized expression values, considering the variance across replicates. Three different alternatives (K-means, Neighbor joining and DBScan) with two different distance functions (euclidean and correlation) were implemented to perform gene clustering over the LFC values. The software was implemented in Java with minimal dependencies, following an interface driven design with object oriented best practices. Benchmark experiments against Clust and WGCNA using real time series datasets shows that the new model has improved computational efficiency and provides clusters with better internal consistency than previous solutions.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Leveraging tumor microenvironment variability to explain cellular communication effects
authors: Austin Varela, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Melissa Hubisz, Institute of Biotechnology at Cornell University, United States; Ashley Laughney, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States
abstract: Inter-cell communication within the tumor microenvironment (TME) drives complex and context-dependent modulation of cellular transcriptional regulation. To unravel these effects, we previously developed ContactTracing, a tool that capitalizes on variation in receptor expression on target cells and ligand availability in the TME to identify key cell-cell interactions driving tumor progression. This framework demonstrated that chromosomal instability (CIN), reprograms STING signaling from an interferon response to an endoplasmic reticulum stress response, fostering a pro-metastatic TME (Li et al., 2023). However, the intricate nature of human patient tumors introduces additional sources of tumor heterogeneity, such as differences in genotype, treatment and environmental exposures, which demand more advanced analytical methods. To address this, we are building on the core principles of ContactTracing by incorporating variational inference into single-cell analyses, enabling us to model cell type- and context-specific responses to ligand engagement across diverse human tumors and tissue types with greater precision and explanatory power. Stochastic variational inference methods have shown a remarkable capacity to elucidate latent factors that influence cellular behavior by providing both explicit interpretability and decoupling noise within the data from true signals. We, therefore, propose a principled variational inference-based generative model to infer how conditionally-dependent cellular interaction shape the TME. This model can decouple intrinsic and extrinsic sources of cellular variation to identify specific context-dependent interaction pathways for communication and their downstream transcriptional consequences called SCULPT. Our probabilistic model exploits subtle, inter-microenvironmental variation to not only identify cell signaling, but explain the effects through a probabilistic generative modelling lens.

title: Toward domain-specific genomic AI agents: benchmarking sequencing library structure extraction
authors: Michael Goneos, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Chi-Lam Poon, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Novel single-cell sequencing technologies require fast and accurate quality control (QC) to evaluate data quality and identify protocol-level issues that limit throughput and sensitivity. AI agents powered by frontier large language models (LLMs) have the potential to automate tasks in this workflow and accelerate protocol iteration. While downstream computational QC is highly standardized, the first step, deriving the oligonucleotide library structure from heterogeneous experimental protocols, remains a manual bottleneck that requires deep domain expertise. We benchmarked nine frontier LLMs across the Gemini, Claude, GPT, Grok, and Kimi families on their ability to extract library structure from sequencing protocols, using 13 ground-truth library structures manually curated from the scg_lib_structs community resource, explicitly testing whether models understand the underlying biochemistry rather than pattern-matching variable regions. We tested three input modes: (i) raw PDF upload, (ii) text extracted from PDFs, and (iii) assay-name-only prompting with web-search tools enabled. LLM outputs were scored against ground truth using normalized Levenshtein similarity, and mean similarities are 0.801, 0.805, 0.836, respectively. All models scored substantially worse on academic protocols than on commercial 10x kits. This gap suggests that current LLM performance is mostly driven by memorized chemistry rather than document comprehension, and indicates that such domain-specific tasks requiring perfect accuracy will need dedicated agent fine-tuning and specialized training data despite the rapid progress in general-purpose LLMs.

title: Using AI to develop, maintain, and translate bioinformatics training materials
authors: Geraldine Van der Auwera, Seqera, United States; Jonathan Manning, Seqera, United Kingdom; Phil Ewels, Seqera, Sweden
abstract: Keeping training materials accurate and up-to-date for a rapidly evolving software ecosystem is a major challenge, particularly when learners must interact directly with code. As the team responsible for the nextflow-io/training repository, we have experimented with AI tools to address three key bottlenecks: (1) maintenance and version updates, (2) new content development, and (3) multilingual translation. For maintenance and content development, we developed custom Claude skills: structured, reusable prompt templates that guide Claude (Anthropic) through consulting reference documentation, identifying affected materials, implementing changes, and executing hands-on exercises in a containerised environment to validate results. This has accelerated update cycles by orders of magnitude: days to hours, hours to minutes. For new content development, results have been more mixed. Claude can produce technically accurate exercises, but lacks the pedagogical insight needed to structure learning progressions or anticipate learner confusion. Curriculum design still requires human expertise in both subject matter and instructional design. For translation, we implemented an AI-assisted system based on the FastAPI project's approach, using language-specific LLM prompts integrated into GitHub Actions. Human review focuses on improving prompts rather than edited translated files directly, ensuring that fixes propagate to all future translations. As a result, our materials are now available in ten languages besides English, and the translations are always up-to-date. All Claude skills and LLM prompts are published in the nextflow-io/training repository for the community to reuse and adapt. We hope that our experience will prove useful for others in the bioinformatics community.

title: The AOP-Wiki EMOD Tool Suite: An Open Source Foundation for Enhanced Integration Between Adverse Outcome Pathways (AOPs), New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), AOP-Supporting Evidence, and Agentic Support for AOPs
authors: Virginia Hench, Open BioData Modeling, LLC, United States; Harry Caufiled, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, United States; Rebecca Boyles, Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI), University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States; James Balhoff, Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI), University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States; Sierra Moxon, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, United States; Matthew Watson, Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI), University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States; Gaurav Vaidya, Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI), University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States; Nyssa Tucker, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States; Alex Tropsha, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill and Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI), United States; Chris Mungall, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, United States; Jason O'Brien, Environment and Climate Change Canada, United States; Kristie Sullivan, Institute for In Vitro Sciences, Inc., United States; Stephen Edwards, UL Research Institutes - Chemical Insights, United States
abstract: Adverse outcome pathways (AOPs) are logic models used to organize heterogeneous evidence for causal relationships between biomechanisms and phenotypes, characterized by upstream molecular initiating events leading to downstream adverse outcomes through intermediate key events (KEs). AOPs help contextualize New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), in vitro and in silico methods, that offer alternatives to animal testing. The AOP-Wiki Knowledge Base is the central AOP repository that serves a global community of NAMs developers, linked data system architects, toxicologists, and regulatory decision-makers. As the sole AOP authoring tool, the AOP-Wiki plays a pivotal role in defining AOP standards. Yet, further growth and evolution is limited by the AOP-Wiki's outdated infrastructure and data model. To address these limitations, we introduce three open source tools to facilitate a much needed AOP-Wiki data modernization overhaul. A CLI tool offers functions to filter and extract AOP entities from the AOP-Wiki XML into multiple formats for further analysis and curation. As the most recent AOP-Wiki evidence model (EMOD) prototype, the AOP-Wiki EMOD 3.0 web app features a seizure use case that demonstrates how new data model classes enable semantic mapping between AOPs, NAMs and biological targets, harmonization to reduce redundancies and enhance utility, and provenance tracking to source citations and contributors. We introduce an integration score for classifying KEs, which is needed for AOP-Wiki content quality improvement and agentic curation priorities. Lastly, our AOP EMOD LinkML schema defines a standard to support computational and agentic approaches to AOP development.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Small area estimation of disability prevalence in South Africa using area‑level Poisson mixed models
authors: Yegnanew A Shiferaw, Department of Statistics, University of Johannesburg, South Africa
abstract: Small-area estimation (SAE) has gained importance due to the demand for reliable statistical estimates from both the public and private sectors. Household surveys, while effective for providing estimates at national and provincial levels, often have limited sample sizes in smaller geographic units, leading to inaccuracies. This study aims to estimate disability rates at the district municipality level in South Africa by addressing the challenges of generating accurate prevalence estimates in smaller areas using linked national surveys. Employing an area-level Poisson mixed model, the research analyzed data from the 2023 Generalized Household Survey (GHS) and the 2022 Population Census. The GHS categorizes disability based on reports of "Some difficulty," "A lot of difficulty," or being "Unable to do" certain activities, with UN disability assigned to those reporting "Some difficulty" in two or more categories. The study covered all 52 districts in South Africa and provided more precise district-level estimates than those derived solely from the 2023 GHS data. The model-based estimates showed severe disability rates ranging from 0.8507% (95% CI: 0.3326% to 1.4259%) in District Code 48 (DC48) to 13.4258% (95% CI: 11.6061% to 14.7649%) in District Code 27 (DC27). Additionally, UN disability rates ranged from 1.7231% (95% CI: 0.8347% to 2.6199%) in DC48 to 14.1957% (95% CI: 12.2681% to 16.3476%) in DC27. By integrating publicly available data sources, the study highlights the importance of accurate disability estimates for local health departments and policymakers to facilitate targeted interventions and resource allocation.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Trans-Ancestry Polygenic Risk Score for White Blood Cell Count and Associated Phenotypes
authors: Seungha Um, NHGRI, United States; Sean Mooney, NHGRI, United States
abstract: White blood cell count (WBC) is a well-established inflammatory biomarker associated with numerous chronic diseases. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) for WBC hold substantial promise for precision medicine by identifying individuals at elevated genetic risk for immune dysregulation and inflammatory diseases, thereby enabling targeted screening and early prevention strategies. However, most existing PRS for blood cell traits have been developed and validated primarily in populations of European ancestry, resulting in reduced predictive performance and limited clinical applicability in non-European populations. To improve equitable clinical implementation, we developed a trans-ancestry WBC PRS using Bayesian polygenic modeling and post hoc ancestry adjustment approaches in the multi-ethnic Electronic Medical Records and Genomics (eMERGE) cohort. Using the trans-ancestry WBC PRS, we evaluated: (i) predictive performance compared with a PRS derived using European ancestry data only; (ii) WBC distributions and longitudinal trajectories across PRS quartiles, as well as their associations with body mass index (BMI) and sex; and (iii) phenotypes associated with genetically predicted WBC risk through a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS). We further propose a screening framework leveraging WBC PRS to estimate individual risk of phenotype onset and support preventive clinical interventions.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: FuseLens: Attention-Pooled Chimeric Transcripts Classification via Long-Context Genomic AI Foundation Models
authors: Udi Bahat, Msc. Computer Science Student, Israel; Milana Frenkel-Morgenstern, Scojen Institute of Synthetic Biology, Dina Recanati School of Medicine; Reichman University, Israel
abstract: Motivation: Chimeric transcripts are hybrid RNA molecules that act as functional biomarkers and actionable therapeutic targets in cancer genomics. High-throughput discovery pipelines generate noisy candidates necessitating accurate post hoc validation. Existing sequence-first deep learning models are limited by architectural bottlenecks: Convolutional Neural Networks lack a global receptive field, while standard Transformer architectures (O(n2)) mandate sequence truncation and k-mer tokenization, destroying single- nucleotide fidelity. Methods: We introduce FuseLens 2.0, a Multi-Task Learning (MTL) framework built on sub-quadratic (O(n log n)) implicit long convolutions. It scales to 32,000 bp genomic windows at single-nucleotide resolution. To prevent shortcut learning, we generated a deduplicated dataset of 187,925 samples, employing adversarial negative curation (dinucleotide shuffling, intra-gene circular permutations). We enforce spatial grounding by coupling binary classification with a differentiable soft-argmax coordinate- regression penalty. Results: Evaluated on a curated test set, FuseLens 2.0 achieves robust diagnostic sensitivity (AUC 0.944, Recall 0.920). Crucially, the explicit MTL coordinate supervision condenses the diffuse attention baseline, achieving a precise Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 61.3 bp for breakpoint localization. Conclusion: By bridging long-context foundation models with exact spatial coordinate regression, FuseLens compresses spatial ambiguity into a sub-100 bp window. This demonstrates that attention mechanisms can serve as true physical pointers to biological phenomena, establishing an automated, clinically actionable post- filter for liquid biopsy assays. Availability: The implementation and dataset generation pipelines are publicly available in Git.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Network-based optimal transport analysis of gut microbiome data in colorectal cancer
authors: Wei Wei, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Rena Elkin, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Joseph Deasy, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Jung Hun Oh, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: "Background: Metagenomic studies of the gut microbiome face challenges from high cross-study variability and conventional abundance-based methods often overlook microbial interaction structure. We developed an unsupervised network-based clustering method coupled with optimal transport to stratify colorectal cancer (CRC) and healthy cases using large-scale metagenomic data. Materials and Methods: Metagenomic gut microbiome data from 3,752 participants, including the relative abundance of 1,135 bacterial species and 603 biological pathways, were obtained from the Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis (CAMDA) challenge. After filtering low-prevalence species, a co-occurrence network was constructed using Spearman correlation coefficients. A Wasserstein distance-based K-means clustering algorithm that we developed was applied to the largest connected component of the network, enabling geometry-aware, structure-informed stratification of CRC and healthy cases. Results: Two clusters were identified; Cluster A was enriched with healthy samples (n = 991/1,630) whereas Cluster B was enriched with CRC samples (n = 291/468; chi-squared p = 1.8 Ã— 10â»Â¹â¸). Cluster B also showed significantly older age and higher body mass index (BMI) compared to Cluster A (p = 2.8 Ã— 10â»Â²Â² and p = 9.2 Ã— 10â»â¹, respectively). The proposed method outperformed traditional K-means and consensus K-means clustering in stratifying CRC from healthy samples. Pathway analysis revealed 28 pathways that differed significantly between the two clusters. Conclusion: The network-based K-means clustering method applied to gut microbiome profiles effectively distinguishes CRC from healthy samples while accounting for microbial interaction structure, demonstrating potential as a robust tool for large-scale microbiome analysis. "

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: A Unified Weighted-Distance Framework for No-Box Membership Inference Attacks on Synthetic Gene Expression Data
authors: Owen Tucker, Emory University, United States; Lily Wang, Emory University, United States; Harutoshi Okumura, Emory University, United States; Ruixuan Liu, Emory University, United States; Li Xiong, Emory University, United States
abstract: Membership Inference Attacks (MIA) assess whether individual records were used to train a generative model, and are a key tool for privacy auditing of synthetic data. We present our red-team submission to the ELSA Health 2026 Challenge, which tasks participants with inferring training membership from synthetic bulk RNA-seq gene expression data (TCGA) produced by four blue-team generators (MVN, CVAE, Noisy Diffusion, DP-PGM); we focus on CVAE and will include results of other target models in the full version. Building on prior works, we unify a family of no-box MIAs under a single weighted-distance framework: each variant is a LOGAN-style cosine score that differs only in its choice of feature weights: uniform (baseline), per-gene variance, KL divergence between synthetic and reference distributions, top-k PCA residualization (zero weight on dominant components), and biologically-informed pathway selection. We further compose this framework with two orthogonal augmentations: subtype-stratified candidate pools and a MinK-style surrogate signal. Our best variant on TCGA-COMBINED, PCA residualization, reaches AUC=0.8951, TPR@1=0.5970 (LOGAN baseline 0.8251 / 0.3842); on TCGA-BRCA, KL-weighted distance reaches AUC=0.7231 (baseline 0.7166), with {TPR@1%}=0.1853 comparable to baseline.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Computational Biology for Biologists in the Age of AI: A Course Experience Report
authors: Dan DeBlasio, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Computational biology is a crucial part of the biological sciences curriculum. Traditionally, a dedicated computational course for biology majors had two goals: (1) to teach the quantitative and computational principles underlying modern science, and (2) to provide practical skills in tools, programming, algorithmic thinking, and reproducible data pipelines. However, the rapid emergence of advanced AI agents and LLMs has drastically changed scientific computation and data analysis. This paradigm shift requires a critical re-evaluation of the traditional pedagogical approach, especially concerning the practical skill-building components. The core question for educators is how to adapt a foundational course when AI can rapidly generate code, debug scripts, and propose analysis workflows. This challenge is currently being addressed in the ""Introduction to Computational Biology"" course at Carnegie Mellon University, offered since 2012 and a mandatory requirement for BS in Biology students since at least 2014. In direct response to the implications of AI, the course is undergoing a significant systematic revision. This report details the specific modifications implemented in the Spring 2026 iteration, contrasting them with the Spring 2025 semester. Furthermore, it outlines a proposal for more fundamental structural changes planned for full implementation in Spring 2027. Our dual aim is to transparently share the rationale, process, and preliminary outcomes of these curriculum adjustments with the educational community, and to actively solicit constructive feedback on the proposed future model to ensure no critical knowledge or skill components are overlooked.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: DNA Subway 2.0: Expanding Bioinformatics, Nanopore Sequencing, and Data Science for Workforce-Oriented Biology Education
authors: Anna Feitzinger, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, United States; Jason Williams, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, United States; Daniel Jacobs, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, United States; Susan Lauter, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, United States; Skyla Robinson, Unaffiliated, United States; Maytal Dahan, Texas Advanced Computing Center, United States; Monica Trujillo, Queensborough Community College, City University of New York, United States; David Micklos, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, United States
abstract: Since its launch in 2010, DNA Subway has become one of the most widely used platforms for bioinformatics in the classroom. DNA Subway 2.0 (dnasubway.org) builds on this foundation to provide a more streamlined environment while aligning with workforce needs in biotechnology, genomics, and data science. Subway 2.0 expands classroom-friendly analysis of DNA sequence data by eliminating the need for software installations or command-line tools and providing integrated, research-grade bioinformatics software through easy-to-use workflows. The completely rebuilt platform was developed using a mobile-first design approach, emphasizing usability and accessibility. Subway 2.0 incorporates current technologies, including containerization and cloud computing, to ensure security, scalability, and alignment with evolving standards. In addition to support for DNA barcoding (e.g., species identification, comparative phylogenetics) and metabarcoding (e.g., microbial diversity and eDNA), Subway 2.0 has been refactored to use containerized workflows, scalable cloud computing, and classroom management tools. New feature releases support analysis of Oxford Nanopore sequence data, including basecalling, quality control, genome alignment, metagenomics, and small genome assembly. Developed by the DNA Learning Center at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Subway 2.0 aligns with the goals of the InnovATEBIO Genomics Hub, including course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs), technician education, and workforce preparation across high schools, community colleges, and four-year colleges. The project is developed in collaboration with the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) and Queensborough Community College and is guided by faculty and industry advisors representing biotechnology, genomics, cloud computing, and pharmaceutical research. These partnerships ensure that Subway 2.0 reflects current workforce needs and emerging career pathways. Importantly, Subway 2.0 is being designed to meet accessibility standards, with guidance from experts including Microassist and the Science Gateways Community Institute (SGX3). DNA Subway 2.0 will be disseminated through mentor networks, workshops, and open educational resources, fostering broad adoption by educators. By lowering barriers to bioinformatics, cloud computing, and genomic data analysis, Subway 2.0 helps prepare students for careers in biotechnology, genomics, health, agriculture, and bioscience data analysis.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Development and implementation of a bioinformatics research curriculum integrating AlphaFold and AlphaMissense into undergraduate biology education
authors: Raquel Meyer Nunes, Florida International University, United States; Héctor Loyola Irizarry, Caldwell University, United States; Jessica Siltberg-Liberles, Florida International University, United States
abstract: AI-based bioinformatics tools such as the protein structure predictor AlphaFold2 have catalyzed biological research. However, undergraduate life science curricula often lag in integrating bioinformatics, and faculty have postulated students' lack of motivation and preparedness to study bioinformatics as barriers. Previous research has shown that students benefit from research experiences, but available opportunities are often limited. To increase access to research experiences, improve preparation for the modern biology workforce, and stimulate motivation to learn bioinformatics, we developed a biomedical research curriculum to train students in bioinformatics, research, and other transferable skills. Here we present the curriculum and its implementation, where students investigate the relationship between AlphaMissense pathogenicity predictions and structural features of cancer-implicated proteins, using AlphaFold2 predicted models and more. Each student independently studies a protein, constructs an evolutionary context, and extracts or predicts features such as per-residue AlphaMissense pathogenicity, AlphaFold pLDDT scores, and evolutionary rates to build their dataset. Using structural visualizations, students make observations and statistically test their own hypotheses about protein features and pathogenicity. Students then apply their insights to tentatively annotate known missense Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS) in their proteins. Further, our curriculum also includes career development training, scientific article annotation modules, journal clubs, and a focus on scientific writing. We include an assessment of the impact of our curriculum and demonstrate the versatility of the course structure for different bioinformatics-driven research questions, to establish training in recent bioinformatics skills in biology education.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Positioning Peru as a Regional Hub for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology in Latin America
authors: David Requena, Sociedad Peruana de Bioinformatica y Biologia Computacional, United States
abstract: The Peruvian Society for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (SPBBC) is a non-profit organization that has served the scientific community since 2018, connecting researchers, students, and institutions across Peru and internationally. In 2019, we conducted the first census of Peruvians working in bioinformatics and computational biology, which revealed gender and ethnic inequities, unequal access to training, limited access to expert knowledge, and infrastructure gaps. Since then, SPBBC has implemented a multi-level strategy to strengthen the field through national and international alliances, collaborative networks, support for underrepresented groups, and expanded access to specialized training. Among our initiatives, we established the Regional Student Group Peru (RSG-Peru) in partnership with the International Society for Computational Biology (ISCB). This student-led initiative has fostered satellite groups in Peruvian provinces, expanding opportunities beyond Lima and promoting decentralized scientific participation. SPBBC has also built collaborations with professional and student scientific organizations, universities, and has helped support emerging graduate bioinformatics programs in Peru. Internationally, SPBBC works with ISCB, SoIBio, Latin American national bioinformatics societies, and training initiatives such as CABANAnet, BiotrAIn, RIABIO, and RIABIA-Pro. These partnerships have supported educational activities in Spanish, including journal clubs, workshops, conferences, and scientific events, reaching nearly 40,000 people. A major milestone was SPBBC's selection to co-organize the Latin American Conference in Bioinformatics 2026 with ISCB and SoIBio. For the first time, Peru will host this major conference, placing Lima in the international spotlight from November 9 to 13 and potentially creating new opportunities for collaboration, training, and regional visibility in bioinformatics.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Teaching Computational Biology with a Free Web-Based Learning Lab
authors: Derek Peng, The Pingry School, United States; Morgan D'Ausilio, The Pingry School, United States
abstract: Computational biology has become central to modern biological research, yet introductory biology education often lacks accessible tools for helping students connect biological concepts with computation, data, and molecular visualization. The Computational Biology Learning Lab is a free, browser-based educational platform designed to make computational biology more approachable for learners from middle school through introductory college courses. The platform reduces technical barriers by requiring no specialized software installation and by presenting computational biology through interactive visualizations, short tutorials, and scaffolded learning pathways. The website introduces core topics in molecular and computational biology, including DNA and RNA structure and function, PCR and genomics, biomolecular structure, ligand binding, molecular visualization, and artificial intelligence in biology. Its interactive tools include a molecule viewer, RNA secondary structure viewer, cryo-EM and PDB overlay tool, ligand binding explorer, and Python sandbox. Together, these tools support exploration of biological systems across multiple representations, from sequence and secondary structure to atomic-level molecular models. The platform is designed around the idea that computation should be introduced as a tool for biological reasoning rather than as a prerequisite technical skill. Students can use the website to interpret molecular models, analyze biological data, compare biological representations, explore structure-function relationships, and construct evidence-based explanations. The learning materials emphasize transferable scientific practices, including computational thinking, data literacy, model-based reasoning, pattern recognition, and scientific communication. The Computational Biology Learning Lab also includes instructional supports for different levels of prior knowledge, such as vocabulary scaffolds, guided exploration prompts, structured activities, and extension opportunities for more advanced learners. By offering multiple entry points into computational biology, the platform aims to broaden participation in a field that is often perceived as inaccessible to students without prior coding experience or advanced coursework. This work presents the website as an open educational resource for integrating computational biology into classrooms, outreach programs, and independent learning environments. Its goal is to help students develop intuition for how biological questions can be investigated through computation, visualization, and data-driven reasoning.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: Integrated Antigen-Processing Immuno-genomics of Kenyan Populations Exposes Systematic Blind Spots in Global Precision Medicine
authors: Sharon Nyagaka, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, United States; Catherine Waruiru, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya; Frank Onyambu, University of Nairobi, Kenya; Brian Ogoti, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya
