abstract: Background Precision medicine tools trained predominantly on European genomes produce structural errors when applied to East African populations. African populations represent fewer than 5% of IMGT/HLA records and are underrepresented in NetMHCpan and IEDB training data. No published cohort has simultaneously profiled the antigen-processing axis (HLA, ERAP1/2, KIR) alongside pharmacogenomics in East African individuals. Methods We integrate publicly available whole-genome sequences (1000 Genomes Project, HGDP, SGDP; under data-access-committee approval) into a uniformly processed 123-individual Kenyan cohort spanning six populations. Analyses include >30-locus HLA and 17-locus KIR haplotyping (T1K), phased MHC reconstruction (GATK, BEAGLE 5.4, WhatsHap), ERAP1/2 functional classification, NetMHCpan/MHCflurry peptidome prediction, pathogen-driven selection scans, and CPIC pharmacogenomics. Results In a 10-individual pilot (mean 29.6× coverage, Ti/Tv 2.04), T1K resolved >30 HLA loci per sample, yielding 68 unique alleles across six classical loci and 15 distinct HLA-B alleles, with 108,091 East-African variants enriched relative to or absent from gnomAD AFR. Pathogen-shaped variation exposes precision-medicine blind spots across immunogenomic and pharmacogenomic layers simultaneously. HLA-B53:01, a malaria-associated allele under documented pathogen-driven selection in Africa, segregates in the cohort alongside G6PD-deficiency variants — the latter independently contraindicating primaquine, malaria's only radical cure. HLA-B57:03, the African HIV elite-controller allele, occurs in a population in which CYP2B6 non-normal metabolisers reach 70% (95% CI 40–89%), so the same first-line HIV regimen that the immunogenome favours carries population-level efavirenz-toxicity risk. UGT1A1 *80+*28 approaches fixation (100%; CI 72–100%), signalling irinotecan-overdosing risk. Full-cohort results, ERAP integration, KIR haplotypes, selection signatures, and transplant metrics will be presented. Significance This is the first integrated immunogenomic and pharmacogenomic characterisation of Kenyan populations across the antigen-processing axis, demonstrating that infectious-disease selection has produced compounding precision-medicine failures across immunogenomic and pharmacogenomic layers simultaneously.

title: HiMWA: A Hierarchical Multiple-Wave Admixture Model for Inferring Complex Admixture Histories
authors: Yuhan Yang, Fudan University, China; Rui Zhang, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Lu Yang, Beijing Jiaotong University, China; Kai Yuan, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Xumin Ni, Beijing Jiaotong University, China; Shuhua Xu, Fudan University, China
abstract: Population admixture is a pivotal evolutionary process that has profoundly shaped genetic diversity and population structure in modern human populations. Most existing methods for inferring admixture history rely on overly simplified assumptions, such as ancestral populations mixing into the target population sequentially, one by one, which limiting their applicability to realistic admixture scenarios. Here, we introduce a novel computational framework, the Hierarchical Multi-Wave Admixture (HiMWA) model, which accurately reconstructs complex admixture histories by characterizing the order and pattern of ancestral population mixture. HiMWA employs a model selection strategy to identify the most plausible admixture model and estimates corresponding model parameters with high precision. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of HiMWA in both model selection and parameter estimation. Applying HiMWA to two populations with strong genetic and historical connections to Central Asiaâ€”Kazakhstanâ€™s Kazakhs and Xinjiang Uyghurs from northwestern China, we reveal a shared hierarchical admixture structure. Both populations exhibit two waves of Western ancestry (West European and South Asian) and two waves of Eastern ancestry (East Asian and Siberian), highlighting the prevalence of multi-wave admixture in Central Asia. This study provides a powerful tool for unraveling complex admixture histories and offers new insights into the genetic landscape of Central Asian populations. The manual, source code, and example data of HiMWA are publicly available at https://github.com/Shuhua-Group/HiMWA.

title: Comparative Codon Usage Bias and Volatility Reveal Regional Evolutionary Signatures in SARS‑CoV‑2
authors: Lawrence Okoror, Federal University, Oye-Ekiti, Nigeria; Mclawrence Okoror, Federal University, Oye-Ekiti, Nigeria; Feyikemi Akinsulire, Federal University, Oye-Ekiti, Nigeria

title: DrOVi: an interactive web platform for synteny-guided orthology exploration in Drosophila
authors: Wei-Sheng Wu, Dept. of Electrical Engineering, Nat'l Cheng Kung University, Taiwan
abstract: Orthologous genes, which diverge through speciation, are fundamental for understanding gene function and evolutionary relationships across species. In Drosophila, a genus characterized by extensive gene turnover and structural variation, precise ortholog identification is crucial for comparative and functional genomics studies. While sequence- and phylogeny-based methods remain standard, incorporating conserved local synteny improves resolution in gene families with complex evolutionary histories. Existing synteny-based tools are typically limited by narrow taxonomic coverage, the absence of customizable parameters, or a need for sophisticated computational skills. To address these limitations, we developed the Drosophila Orthology Viewer (DrOVi), an interactive platform for exploring orthology across 20 Drosophila species and one outgroup. DrOVi provides orthology data from public databases and de novo predictions, along with synteny-based comparisons, and allows users to adjust parameters such as sequence similarity thresholds and syntenic window sizes for exploring synteny. The platform supports visualization of conserved gene order and interactive refinement of ortholog predictions through a streamlined interface. By combining customizable orthology inference methods with genomic context, DrOVi enables scalable, accessible analysis of gene evolution, function, and conservation across Drosophila. DrOVi can be accessed through https://cosbi9.ee.ncku.edu.tw/DrOVi/

title: Haplotype-resolved methylation profiling across three generations reveals principles of human epigenetic inheritance
authors: Weixue Mu, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Epigenetic inheritance is fundamental to human development and disease, yet the mechanisms governing the transmission of DNA methylation across generations remain incompletely understood. In this study, we performed haplotype-resolved, whole-genome DNA methylation profiling in a healthy three-generation Chinese family, leveraging high-depth Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) and PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing, anchored to a proband-specific telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly. We observed globally conserved bimodal methylation landscapes across all individuals and generations. Stratified analyses revealed clear functional compartmentalization of methylation marks, characterized by distinct hypomethylation in centromeres and hypermethylation in retrotransposons and repetitive elements. Chromosome-resolved analysis of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) arrays demonstrated a domain-specific methylation pattern with hypomethylation in the transcriptional core and hypermethylation in the intergenic spacer, with evidence for age-associated epigenetic drift in the transcriptional core domain. Through de novo identification and validation, we mapped 23 high-confidence imprinting control regions (ICRs) showing robust parent-of-origin-specific methylation, all overlapping known imprinted genes and enriched for regulatory element signatures. Haplotype-resolved X chromosome analysis further uncovered sex- and allele-specific methylation patterns linked to X inactivation dynamics. Together, this pedigree-scale, high-resolution study delineates the landscape and principles of intergenerational DNA methylation inheritance, revealing both conserved and dynamic features shaping the human epigenome.

title: Pathogenic Spirochaetes Acquired Cholesterol Metabolism Enzymes via Horizontal Gene Transfer from Gut Commensals
authors: Angela Jiang, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health, United States; Maggie Grant, Department of Cellular Biology and Molecular Genetics, University of Maryland, United States; Gabriela Arp, Department of Cellular Biology and Molecular Genetics, University of Maryland, United States; Brantley Hall, Department of Cellular Biology and Molecular Genetics, University of Maryland, United States; Xiaofang Jiang, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Several Treponema species are causative agents of periodontitis. Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of pathogenic properties is thought to be a major driver of dental pathogen evolution, including cholesterol metabolism, which depletes host cells of cholesterol and disrupts inflammatory responses. In vitro, T. denticola converts cholesterol to cholestanol via a two-step pathway. However, the enzymes responsible are unknown, leaving a gap in our mechanistic and evolutionary understanding of this process. Using our previously identified gut microbial cholesterol 3Î²-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase (SpiR) as a BLAST query, we identified a homologous putative cholesterol isomerase/reductase (SciR) and a neighboring 5Î±-reductase in Treponema that together catalyze the two-step conversion of cholesterol to cholestanol via cholestenone and 5Î±-cholestan-3-one. Phylogenetic analyses of SciR homologs in the Genome Taxonomy Database reveal three independent interphylum HGT events of sciR from commensal Bacillota to Treponema, while 5Î±-reductase was acquired from Bacteroidota. HGT events were validated using the HGTphyloDetect index. Ancestral habitat reconstruction predicts that the common ancestor of oral and intestinal Treponema resided in the intestine, suggesting that oral Treponema is a derived lineage that colonized the oral cavity. Consistent with a role in pathogenesis, Pagel's test of correlated evolution shows that 5Î±-reductase acquisition is significantly associated with oral habitat occupancy across Treponematales, and shotgun metagenomics across multiple cohorts shows that sciR and 5Î±-reductase are enriched in periodontitis patients. These results improve our mechanistic and evolutionary understanding of Treponema cholesterol metabolism, highlight therapeutic targets, and exemplify HGT of a pathogenic property from gut bacteria to oral pathogens.

title: Genomic Insights into Pathogenicity in Avibacterium paragallinarum
authors: Oluwatobiloba Aminu, Iowa State University, United States; Mostafa M. S. Shelkamy, Iowa State University, United States; Eman Gadu, Iowa State University, United States; Amro Hashish, Iowa State University, United States; Yuko Sato, Iowa State Univeristy, United States; Michael Zeller, Iowa State University, United States; Tatum Mortimer, University of Georgia, United States; Mohamed El-Gazzar, Iowa State University, United States
abstract: Avibacterium paragallinarum (AP) is the causative agent of infectious coryza, a respiratory disease in chickens that leads to reduced egg production and significant economic losses worldwide. The recent identification of non-pathogenic isolates co-circulating with pathogenic strains has complicated disease diagnosis and highlighted the need to better understand the genetic basis of pathogenicity. This study aimed to identify genes associated with pathogenicity using a pan-genome-wide analysis framework. Whole-genome sequences from 87 pathogenic and 14 non-pathogenic isolates were analyzed. Pan-genome reconstruction identified 5,012 gene clusters, with approximately 66% comprising the accessory genome. Phylogenetic analysis revealed clear clustering of pathogenic and non-pathogenic isolates, indicating strong population structure. To account for this, three genome-wide association study (GWAS) methods were applied: Scoary, pyseer, and Random Forest. Two genes, hmp and nsr, were found to be unique to pathogenic isolates, while no genes were exclusive to non-pathogenic strains. Scoary initially identified 362 significant genes; however, after correction for population structure, no associations remained significant, suggesting limited independent evolutionary transitions across the phylogeny. All Scoary-identified genes were also detected by Random Forest. These results highlight a key limitation of GWAS methods when traits arise along a single phylogenetic branch. Although no genes were consistently identified by all methods, a prioritized list of candidate genes was generated. This provides a foundation for future functional validation of pathogenic mechanisms in AP.

title: traceDB: An Integrated Resource for Comparative Genomics, Phylogenomics, and Host Virus Interaction Analysis of Turkey Reoviruses
authors: Jagathiswaran Radhakrishnan, South Dakota State University, United States; Naveen Duhan, South Dakota State University, United States; Sunil K Mor, South Dakota State University, United States; Mohamed H Selim, South Dakota State University, United States; Gun Temeeyasen, South Dakota State University, United States; Tamer Sharafeldin, South Dakota State University, United States
abstract: Turkey reoviruses (TRVs) are avian orthoreoviruses in the genus Orthoreovirus and family Spinareoviridae, with genomes composed of 10 linear double stranded RNA segments. These viruses are associated with arthritis/tenosynovitis, enteric disease, hepatitis, and neurologic disease, imposing health and economic burdens on turkey production. Because TRVs frequently reassort across all 10 genomic segments, single segment typing is often insufficient for genotype assignment, variant tracking, and evolutionary analysis. To address this challenge, we developed traceDB, a resource for whole genome analysis of TRVs and related avian orthoreoviruses. traceDB combines about 500 in house TRV genomes, about 250 avian orthoreovirus genomes from NCBI, and host, pathotype, and sample metadata in a searchable environment. traceDB supports comparative analysis across all segments and enables machine learning guided genotype prediction from sequence derived features. The resource is designed to support genotype classification at both segment and whole genome levels and classification of isolates into major turkey reovirus groups, including turkey arthritis reovirus (TARV), turkey enteric reovirus (TERV), turkey hepatitis reovirus (THRV), and turkey brain reovirus (TBRV). For reproducible computational workflows and downstream applications, traceDB integrates sequence similarity search, multiple sequence alignment, phylogenetic tree construction, mutation profiling, protein structure visualization, and genotype classification within one platform. These capabilities allow users to compare internal and public datasets, identify reassortment patterns, characterize genome wide diversity, assign genotypes, and generate phylogenetic hypotheses from complete genome constellations rather than single segment markers. traceDB also incorporates predicted turkey virus interaction information to support host pathogen analysis, exploration of host virus relationships, and generation of testable hypotheses about viral mechanisms and pathogenicity. By connecting genomic, structural, phylogenetic, genotype, and host associated information in a single environment, the platform reduces fragmentation across separate resources and analytical workflows. As a unified analytical resource, traceDB is designed to support genomic surveillance, variant discovery, phylogenomic analysis, genotype classification, and data driven study of turkey reoviruses, with the broader goal of accelerating research on avian orthoreovirus evolution, disease biology, and future control strategies.

title: Comparative genomic analysis of chemosensory receptor genes in pteriomorphian bivalves
authors: Sharmistha Goswami, The Ohio State University, United States; Kyle McElroy, The Ohio State University, United States; Anna Ward, The Ohio State University, United States; Jeanne Serb, The Ohio State University, United States
abstract: Background: Most marine invertebrates are characterized with a biphasic life cycle that transitions between a pelagic larval stage and a sessile benthic adult form. These planktonic larvae get influenced by chemical and physical cues coming from the surrounding environment to settle and metamorphose into adult form. At this juncture, larvae face an extraordinary challenge: locating a suitable settlement habitat within a complex, dynamic, and often variable marine environment. Chemoreception is fundamental for the settlement and survival of these larvae. But chemosensory receptors are poorly studied among marine organisms like bivalves which are an ecological and economically important mollusk class. Here, we targeted chemosensory G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) and ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) that detect chemical cues, neurotransmitters etc. Method: We used RNA-seq data for six pteriomorphian bivalves and conducted phylogenetically informed annotations to identify candidate receptors followed by examining their expression across three larval stages (i.e., trochophore, veliger, pediveliger). Result: ML phylogeny revealed that these putative chemosensory genes have expanded significantly in pteriomorphian bivalves. Larvae express all chemoreceptor genes in these bivalves across all three developmental stages. Notably, clades include highly expressed orthologous genes from all species which reflect conservation. Conclusion: Divergence of chemosensory genes indicate more evolutionary opportunities for these species to expand into new ecological niches. And the conserved genes suggest that these are fundamental for the survival across all the larval stages of these pteriomorphian bivalves.

title: Modular Genomic Architectures Underlie Mammalian Life-History Diversity
authors: Thodoris Danis, VANDERBILT UNIVERSITY, United States
abstract: In placental mammals, life-history traits such as gestation length, brain size, and lifespan vary widely across species and reflect complex interactions among physiology and development. Although comparative studies have identified extensive correlations among these traits, the genetic mechanisms underlying their joint evolution remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate comparative life-history data with protein-coding genes to investigate the molecular basis of mammalian life-history variation using relative evolutionary rate analyses. Using a dataset of approximately 200 species spanning major eutherian clades, we analyzed nine life-history traits, including gestation length, brain mass, longevity, and along with trait residuals that account for allometric effects. Across all analyses, we identified 66 unique genes whose evolutionary rates were significantly associated with life-history variation. Strikingly, no gene was shared across all traits. Most associations were both trait- and clade-specific, indicating a highly modular genomic architecture. Only a single gene, CRYGB, was associated with more than two traits, linking brain mass, sexual maturity, and gestation length after correcting for body mass, consistent with limited and biologically structured pleiotropy. Residual traits consistently yielded fewer but stronger gene associations than raw traits, demonstrating that correcting for allometry exposes distinct evolutionary signals rather than obscuring them. Despite minimal overlap at the gene level, pathway enrichment analyses revealed strong convergence across traits and taxonomic orders, highlighting conserved regulatory programs related to PRC2- and H3K27me3-associated targets, cell-cycle and transcriptional regulation. Together, these results show that mammalian life-history evolution arises through pathway-level convergence via lineage-specific genetic routes, reconciling phenotypic convergence with genomic modularity.

title: Beyond gene length: Exon-intron architecture and isoform potential in the evolution of eukaryotic complexity
authors: Senbao Lu, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Yue Bao, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Gloria Sheynkman, University of Virginia, United States; Dmitry Korkin, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States
abstract: The emergence of introns enabled regulated alternative splicing (AS), substantially increasing the complexity of eukaryotic organisms. However, the extent to which AS contributes to such complexity increase at proteomic and phenotypic level remains unclear. A recent large-scale study showed that mean protein length stopped growing during evolution, whereas mean gene length continued to expand exponentially with respect to evolution time, implicating expansion of non-coding gene regions. We ask how the emergence of introns and the split of exons contribute to the growth of multicellular genome complexity along with the mean gene length, especially after the length of coding region stabilizes. We analyzed gene annotation from 2,683 eukaryotic genomes and examined how mean exon count scales with mean gene length. We found that mean exon count per gene continues to increase beyond the transition where protein length plateaus, rising rapidly in fungi and protists and then slowing markedly in plants, invertebrates, vertebrates, and ultimately saturating at ~10 exons per gene. Across six model organisms, isoform count scaled logarithmically with exon count in vertebrates and plants, indicating constrained use of otherwise combinatorial isoform-coding potential, with human showing the highest per-gene scaling. A simple stochastic exon-splitting model reproduced the two-phase growth pattern and estimated a minimum exon length of 138 bp, comparable to the minimum size of a protein domain. Together, these results suggest that exon-intron architecture and exonic combinatorial coding potential serve as complementary determinants of eukaryotic genome complexity after coding-sequence length has stabilized.

title: Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing reveals the cellular programs driving nematode-induced giant cell formation in tomato
authors: Sobhan Bahrami Zadegan, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Peitong Li, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Mst Shamira Sultana, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Hafiz Muhammad Khalid Abbas, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Nicole Coffey, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Cengizhan Öztürk, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Mariam Elwasif, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; John Hollis Rice, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States; Hari B Krishnan, Division of Plant Science and Technology, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA, United States; Tarek Hewezi, Department of Plant Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA, United States
abstract: Introduction: Root-knot nematodes (RKNs) are widespread parasites that infect more than 2,000 plant species. Meloidogyne incognita is the most devastating plant-parasitic nematode species. A characteristic symptom of RKN infection is the formation of giant cells, which serve as permanent feeding sites for the nematodes. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of giant cells remain poorly understood. The goal of this study was to define gene regulatory networks driving giant cell formation and characterize transcriptional trajectories in tomato. Materials and Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing was performed on galls and adjacent root tissues at two stages of infection. More than 35,000 high-quality nuclei were analyzed to identify cell-type specific transcriptional changes. Promoter-reporter assays and gene silencing experiments were performed as functional studies to validate candidate gene function. Results: Our analysis resulted in the identification of three stele-associated clusters representing young and differentiated giant cells, with 772 genes preferentially expressed. Functional assays confirmed giant cell-specific expression patterns of our selected genes and the impact of these genes on plant susceptibility to M. incognita. Trajectory analysis showed elevated expression of cell cycle related genes during early pseudotime and increased activation of cellular processes associated with more differentiated giant cells during late pseudotime. Conclusions: In conclusion, our study provides the first single-nucleus transcriptomic map of nematode-induced giant cells, including identification of specifically expressed genes in giant cells. It provides a comprehensive understanding of host cell reprogramming in plant-parasitic nematodes, enabling us to develop resistance strategies against RKNs through the identification of potential molecular targets.

title: CompBioAgent: An LLM-powered agent for single-cell RNA-seq data exploration
authors: Yu Sun, Biogen, United States; Haotian Zhang, Biogen, United States; Wenxing Hu, Biogen, United States; Xu Cui, Stanford University, United States; Zhengyu Ouyang, BioinfoRx, United States; Xinmin Zhang, BioinfoRx, United States; Derrick Cheng, BioinfoRx, United States; Baohong Zhang, Biogen, United States
abstract: Advancements in high-throughput biological technologies, particularly single-cell RNA sequencing, have generated vast amounts of complex data that provide valuable insights into gene expression, cellular behavior, and disease mechanisms. However, analyzing these data often requires specialized computational expertise, posing a challenge for researchers with limited computational backgrounds. The ability to rapidly gain insights from such data is also crucial, as timely discoveries can drive research progress and clinical applications. To address this challenge, we have developed CompBioAgent, a web-based application powered by Large Language Models and Prompt Engineering, designed to help biologists interact with single-cell RNA sequencing data through natural language queries and obtain meaningful analytical insights. By integrating with the CellDepot and Cellxgene VIP, CompBioAgent enables users to easily query and explore single-cell datasets across various diseases, cell types, and experimental conditions. The web application can be accessed at https://celldepot.bxgenomics.com/compbioagent/, and the source code, available under the MIT license, can be found at https://github.com/interactivereport/CompBioAgent. A detailed user guide is included to assist with deploying the application on a local server. Additionally, examples of how to use the tool are available in the tutorial, which provide guidance on how users can effectively interact with CompBioAgent.

title: Accurate germline variant detection in low-coverage long read sequencing with Clair-LC
authors: Zhenxian Zheng, School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Lei Chen, School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Xian Yu, School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Junzhe Li, School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Minggao He, School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Ruibang Luo, School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Variant calling, while foundational to genomic research, traditionally requires high read coverage to ensure accuracy. Achieving precise germline variant detection at minimal sequencing coverage is critical for reducing costs and broadening access to clinical diagnostics and precision medicine. The emergence of long-read sequencing technologies provides new opportunities for low-coverage variant calling by capturing comprehensive haplotype information and linking multiple variants within a single read. However, current variant callers for long-read data are primarily optimized for coverages exceeding 10Ã— and exhibit significant limitations in low-coverage scenarios. Here, we introduce Clair-LC, a new computational method in the Clair series of variant callers that enables accurate germline variant detection from low-coverage ( 20Ã—) approaches. Our methodology represents a paradigm shift from traditional, site-specific variant calling to a haplotype-aware framework. Clair-LC leverages linkage disequilibrium information from large reference panels, incorporates allele-specific methylation patterns for haplotype phasing, and implements a specialized deep learning architecture that integrates local genomic context with long-range variant linkages. Benchmarking results across GIAB HG001-HG007 and other HPRC samples demonstrate the robust capability of our approach. Specifically, on the low-coverage GIAB HG003 sample, Clair-LC outperformed Clair3 and DeepVariant by approximately 10% across various low-coverage settings, confirming its superior accuracy in resource-constrained scenarios.

title: Generating Joint Transcriptomic and Morphological Responses to Drug Perturbations via Rectified Flow
authors: Shourya Verma, Purdue University, United States; Mengbo Wang, Purdue University, United States; Luopin Wang, Purdue University, United States; Simran Kadadi, Purdue University, United States; Mario Sola, Purdue University, United States; Majid Kazemian, Purdue University, United States; Ananth Grama, Purdue University, United States; Nadia Atallah Lanman, Purdue University, United States
abstract: Motivation: Predicting cellular responses to drug perturbations requires capturing complex dependencies between transcriptomic and morphological changes. Existing approaches model these modalities in isolation, missing critical molecular-phenotypic relationships that occur simultaneously during drug treatment. No current method jointly predicts gene expression profiles and cellular morphology from chemical perturbations. Results: We introduce PertFlow, a unified computational framework that simultaneously predicts treatment gene expression (bulk RNA-seq) and generates cellular morphology (Cell Painting images) from control cellular states, conditioned on drug metadata. Evaluated on paired RNA-seq and imaging data from 3 cell lines and 40 compounds (17,242 samples), PertFlow achieves Pearson correlation of 0.780Â±0.264 for transcriptomic prediction and FID of 24.06 for morphological generation. Board-certified pathologists rated generated images with median similarity scores of 7.11-7.89/10. The model successfully recovers known drug mechanisms including microtubule disruption, DNA damage, and MAPK pathway inhibition, with gene enrichment analysis confirming activation of expected biological pathways (EMT, p53, apoptosis). Availability: Code and pretrained models will be available at https://github.com/wangmengbo/PertFlow.

title: Early Excess Methylation at Disease-Associated CpGs in Endometrial Cancer Inferred from Bulk Tissue
authors: Kefan Meng, University College London, United Kingdom; Thomas Bartlett, University College London, United Kingdom
abstract: Endometrial carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy, making the epithelial compartment central to understanding how DNA methylation change relates to disease development. However, methylation studies are typically performed in bulk tissue, where epithelial, fibroblast, and immune signals are combined. We asked whether epithelial-associated methylation change can be assessed from bulk DNA methylation data at CpG resolution, and whether disease-associated CpGs show excess methylation across the endometrial disease trajectory. We analysed matched tumour and normal-adjacent samples from TCGA UCEC using cell type deconvolution and CpG-specific linear mixed modelling. For each CpG, we derived an adjusted expected tumour methylation level from estimated cell type proportions and compared this with observed tumour methylation. This identified CpGs with higher observed methylation than expected in tumour samples, including loci in GYPC and ZSCAN12. In cancer-free hyperplasia, highlighted CpGs already showed elevated methylation relative to normal-adjacent tissue, and CpGs gaining methylation in hyperplasia tended to fall in the region of positive deviation in the tumour analysis. By contrast, metastatic comparison showed little evidence of widespread additional methylation gain beyond that expected from matched primary tumour and tissue composition. Finally, higher prognostic scores based on mean observed-minus-expected methylation across a selected CpG set were associated with poorer overall survival in TCGA UCEC. Together, these findings show that bulk tissue methylation data can be used to assess epithelial-associated methylation change at CpG resolution and detect early excess methylation at disease-associated CpGs.

title: Multi-modal data integration to quantify disease potential in models of arterial hypertrophy
authors: Bingjie Xue, Department of Genome Sciences, Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Virginia, United States; Silvia Medrano, Department of Pediatrics, University of Virginia, United States; Lucas Ferreira de Almeida, Department of Pediatrics, University of Virginia, United States; Jason Smith, Department of Pediatrics, University of Virginia, United States; Maria Luisa Sequeira-Lopez, Department of Pediatrics, University of Virginia, United States; R. Ariel Gomez, Department of Pediatrics, University of Virginia, United States; Nathan Sheffield, Department of Genome Sciences, Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Virginia, United States
abstract: Integrating heterogeneous biological data is challenging when samples have missing data modality. We address this in multi-modal data from mouse models of kidney arterial hypertrophy. In those mouse models, renin-expressing cells accumulate due to genetic or pharmacological perturbations, causing arterial hypertrophy. Here, we present a multimodal framework that handles missing modalities to classify disease states and quantify disease potential via a continuous recruitment score. We collected data from control (Ctrl), Ren1 knockout (KO), and captopril-treated (Trt) groups across age groups, spanning five modalities: scATAC-seq, scRNA-seq (kidney), plasma and urine metabolomics, and urine proteomics. We evaluated four multimodal fusion architectures, including PCA- and autoencoder-based early and late fusion models, combined with linear or shallow neural classifier heads. Each model was tested with two missing-modality imputation strategies. Performance was assessed by leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), with recruitment scores defined as cosine distance from the control centroid. PCA early fusion with mean-pooled tokens and SVM achieved 82.1% LOOCV accuracy. Mean-pooled tokens improved accuracy over zero-fill in three of four architectures, with the largest gain being 25 percentage points. Recruitment scores separated phenotypic classes: Ctrl 0.12, KO 0.69, Trt 0.45. Our framework shows that multimodal fusion with mean-pooled token can classify disease states even when samples lack of data modalities. The recruitment score provides a continuous, biologically interpretable measure that stratifies samples along a disease progression spectrum. This approach shows potential to apply broadly to combine different types of biomedical data, even when some data modalities are missing.

title: New methdology for monitoring in vitro differentiation process of stem cells
authors: Kak Ho Chris Hui, University of Sydney, Australia; Giselle Yeo, University of Sydney, Australia; Zhiyong Wang, University of Sydney, Australia; Jingjing You, University of Sydney, Australia
abstract: Background Cell therapy is a critical approach in modern medicine that requires a high level of quality control. However, there is currently no established methodology to monitor the differentiation process. The pySCENIC algorithm identifies regulon activity across cell populations but provides limited temporal context [1]. In this study, we demonstrate that combining Slingshot [2], a trajectory inference method, with pySCENIC overcomes these limitations. Methods We used human embryonic stem cell (hESC) differentiation into retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) as a model system because its regulatory networks are well characterised. We analysed a publicly available dataset (GEO: GSE164092) comprising seven differentiation time points (11,791 cells), spanning the transition from hESCs to RPE [3]. PySCENIC identified active regulons, and Slingshot inferred differentiation trajectories with hESCs as the starting cluster. Selected regulon activities were plotted against pseudotime to visualise changes during differentiation. Results Slingshot predicted four distinct lineages, each converging on a different terminal cell cluster. In the lineage terminating as RPE, key transcription factors (TFs) involved in RPE development showed distinct patterns along pseudotime. The activities of PAX6, OTX2, MITF, and MYRF increased exponentially before declining, whereas SOX9 activity remained elevated. Conclusions The combination of pySCENIC and Slingshot allows precise tracking of changes in regulon activity during cell differentiation, providing a robust framework for monitoring differentiation processes. Moreover, this approach distinguishes transcription factors involved in different developmental stages, such as differentiation and maturation. While this study focuses on RPE differentiation, the framework is readily extendable to other cell types.

title: Agentomics: An Agentic System that Autonomously Develops State-of-the-art Solutions for Biomedical Machine Learning Tasks
authors: Vlastimil Martinek, University of Malta, Malta; Andrea Gariboldi, University of Malta, Malta; Dimosthenis Tzimotoudis, University of Malta, Malta; Mark Galea, University of Malta, Malta; Elissavet Zacharopoulou, University of Malta, Malta; Aitor Alberdi Escudero, University of Malta, Malta; Edward Blake, University of Malta, Malta; David Čechák, CEITEC Masaryk University, Czechia; Luke Cassar, Centre for Molecular Medicine and Biobanking, University of Malta, Msida, Malta, Malta; Alessandro Balestrucci, University of Malta, Malta; Panagiotis Alexiou, University of Malta, Malta
abstract: Motivation: Extracting knowledge from biomedical data is crucial for advancing our understanding of biological systems and developing novel therapeutics. The quantity, quality, and resolution of biomedical data constantly evolves, requiring the automation of biomedical machine learning (ML). Existing Automated ML tools lack flexibility, while Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to consistently deliver reproducible machine learning codebases, and existing LLM Agent-powered solutions lag behind human-engineered ML models. Results: Here, we introduce Agentomics, an autonomous LLM-powered agentic system for end-to-end ML experimentation. Given a biomedical dataset, Agentomics implements various ML modeling strategies, and produces a ready-to-use ML model. Agentomics introduces strict validation checkpoints for standard ML development steps, allowing gradual development on top of working code with defined interfaces and validated artifacts. Further, it offers native support for biomedical foundation models that can be leveraged during experimentation. The generic nature of Agentomics allows the user to create ML solutions for a large variety of datasets and use various LLMs. We evaluate Agentomics across 20 datasets from the domains of Protein Engineering, Drug Discovery, and Regulatory Genomics. When benchmarked against other agentic systems, Agentomics outperformed them in all tested domains. When benchmarked against human expert solutions, Agentomics generated novel state-of-the-art models for 11/20 established benchmark datasets. Availability and Implementation: Agentomics is implemented in Python. Source code and documentation are freely available at: https://github.com/BioGeMT/Agentomics-ML

title: Improving Allergen Prediction with Protein Language Models and Reliable Evaluation
authors: Brian Shing Hei Wong, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Joshua Mincheol Kim, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Sin-Hang Fung, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Qing Xiong, Department of Health Technology and Informatics, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong SAR, Hong Kong; Kelvin Fu Kiu Ao, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Junkang Wei, Department of Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA, United States; Ran Wang, School of Biomedical Sciences, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, Hong Kong; Dan Michelle Wang, School of Biomedical Sciences, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, Hong Kong; Jingying Zhou, School of Biomedical Sciences, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, Hong Kong; Feng Bo, School of Biomedical Sciences, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, Hong Kong; Alfred Sze-Lok Cheng, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Kevin Y. Yip, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, United States; Stephen Kwok-Wing Tsui, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Qin Cao, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Allergic diseases are an expanding global health concern, affecting both children and adults at rising prevelence. Improved computational tools for identifying allergenic peptides could accelerate early-stage screening and support safety assessment of emerging food sources. In this work, we present a new machine learning framework for protein-level allergenicity prediction that delivers more reliable evaluation and stronger performance than prior approaches. Our current research introduces three critical improvements over previous studies. First, we propose a dataset partitioning strategy that explicitly controls similarity both between classes and across training and test splits. This reduces information leakage that can occur when highly similar sequences appear in multiple splits. Using this stricter setup, we show that many existing methods were likely evaluated on overly easy partitions, leading to overestimated performance. Second, we leverage recent protein language models (pLMs), including ESM-2, ProtTrans, and xTrimoPGLM, and improve their usefulness for allergen prediction via probing and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Under our robust evaluation protocol, these models outperform existing allergen detection baselines. Third, to better reflect real-world deployment scenarios, we manually curate eight biologically meaningful benchmark test sets. These include challenging cases such as allergens and non-allergens from the same protein family, as well as allergens and systematically perturbed variants derived from mutational scanning experiments. Across all curated benchmarks, our method consistently achieves superior results, indicating improved generalization in realistic settings. Overall, the combination of controlled splitting, modern pLMs, and carefully designed benchmarks represents a substantial step forward for practical allergenicity prediction.

title: Cell2Map: A Graph Attention Autoencoder Framework for Integrating Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Yanan Chen, College of Computer and Information Engineering, Tianjin Normal University, China; Ruoyu Chen, College of Arts and Sciences, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Shaoqiang Zhang, Tianjin Normal University, China; Yong Chen, Rowan University, United States
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables genome-wide gene expression profiling at single-cell resolution but loses the spatial context essential for interpreting cell identity and tissue organization. In contrast, spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) preserves spatial information but typically lacks single-cell resolution or complete transcriptome coverage. To obtain a more comprehensive view of heterogeneous spatial domains and cellular gene expression, we present Cell2Map, an unsupervised deep learning method that integrates scRNA-seq and SRT data from the same tissue region. Cell2Map assigns individual cells to SRT spots using a graph attention autoencoder equipped with a specially designed multi-term objective function that jointly optimizes expression-based, density-based and embedding-level similarity and distance constraints. On benchmark datasets from mouse cerebellum and hippocampus, Cell2Map achieves higher single-cell mapping precision and overall accuracy than three popular methods (Celloc, CytoSPACE, Tangram) across a range of noise levels and spot cell densities. In real cancer applications, Cell2Map resolves intratumoral heterogeneity by accurately localizing tumor subclones and separating normal epithelial cells from ductal carcinoma in situ regions, and more faithfully reconstructs tumor microenvironments and immune-cell localization than competing approaches. Across breast cancer and myocardial infarction datasets, Cell2Map consistently attains higher sensitivity with fewer false positives, in close agreement with histological and biological annotations.

title: Enhanced Whole Genome Analysis Framework with Genetic Variant Detection for a Large-scale Korean Genome Project
authors: Dongyoon Lee, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Yeonsu Jeon, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jimin Ahn, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Seungrin Yang, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jong-Hwan Kim, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jongbum Jeon, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jin Ok Yang, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Haeyoung Jeong, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea
abstract: Background: The analysis pipeline established through the Large-scale Korean Genome Project (2020-2022) has been effectively applied to large-scale whole genome sequencing (WGS) data. To extend variant detection capabilities, we enhanced the pipeline by incorporating modules for de novo variants, structural variations (SVs), short tandem repeats (STRs), and mobile element insertions (MEIs). De novo variant detection is particularly important for identifying genetic causes of sporadic rare diseases. Methods: We performed optimized germline and somatic variant calling, joint genotyping, and WGS-based sex and kinship inference for quality control. For comprehensive variant detection, we integrated specialized tools, including Platypus and DeNovoCNN for de novo variants, ExpansionHunter for STRs, ARC-SV for SVs, and MELT for MEIs. Results: The enhanced framework modularizes analysis by variant type and expands detectable variant classes from SNVs/INDELs and SVs to include STRs, de novo variants, and MEIs, covering five categories. This integration improved both detection accuracy and the breadth of variant discovery. Conclusion: We present an expanded WGS analysis framework incorporating rare variant detection alongside standard germline, somatic, and joint genotyping workflows. The framework includes defined computational resource specifications to support reproducibility. This approach improves scalability, accessibility, and efficiency for large-scale WGS analysis involving over 10,000 genomes.

title: Revisit Global Expression Change in Single-cell Perturbation Data
authors: Shuyue Wang, University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Global expression change (GEC), defined as coordinated transcriptome-wide shifts in single cells, provides a quantitative view of global transcriptional regulation. Although MYC-driven transcriptional amplification is well documented across cancers, the broader set of regulators that modulate global transcriptional output remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce a computational framework to identify GEC from single-cell RNA-seq perturbation data using total UMI counts as a proxy for global transcriptional activity. We quantify GEC by comparing perturbed cells to non-targeting control cells and incorporating cell cycle as a major confounder to refine estimates of global transcriptional variation. Applying this approach to multiple large-scale perturbation datasets across diverse cell lines, we identify both genetic and pharmacological perturbations that induce global transcriptional amplification or repression. We observe concordant effects between genetic and pharmacological perturbations, suggesting shared regulatory mechanisms. In addition, GEC responses can be cell type specific; for example, perturbation of KDM1A selectively reduces global transcriptional output in leukemia-derived models. Together, our results establish GEC as a robust and scalable phenotype in single-cell perturbation screens and highlight its utility for systematically identifying regulators of global transcription, with implications for therapeutic target discovery.

title: Enhancing Drug-Target Interaction Prediction through Cross-modal Alignment of Tri-modal Features
authors: Gwang Hyeon Yun, Yonsei University, South Korea; Jong Hoon Park, Yonsei University, South Korea; Young Rae Cho, Yonsei University, South Korea
abstract: Predicting drug-target interactions (DTIs) has become a promising approach for drug screening and development. Although recent studies have tried to use pharmacological multimodal information to increase prediction accuracy, information loss during integration of more than three modalities remains a critical bottleneck. We propose TriDTI, a novel framework that incorporates three modalities-structural, sequential and relational-for both drugs and proteins. Cross-modal contrastive learning is employed for semantic alignment across disparate feature spaces, preserving complementary signals that are otherwise discarded in conventional fusion pipelines. Furthermore, we introduce a two-stage adaptive fusion technique that combines soft attention to dynamically weight modality contributions with cross-attention to model interaction-aware representations. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that TriDTI achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models, consistently outperforming all baselines in both AUROC and AUPRC metrics. The model also exhibits robust generalization across three challenging cold-start scenarios: unseen drugs, unseen targets, and unseen binding pairs. Its practical utility is further substantiated through molecular docking case studies, which confirm the physical plausibility of our top-ranked predictions. These results highlight TriDTI's potential as a robust and practical tool for accelerating computational drug discovery.

title: Antibody Responses Elicited by Different SARS-CoV-2 Vaccines: Durability, Impact on Variants and HIV Infection
authors: Shannon Ramkistan, African Health Research Institute, South Africa
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic prompted the rapid development of several vaccine platforms. In Africa, where the burden of coinfections such as HIV is high and vaccine rollout lagged, comparative studies of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine immunogenicity and durability remain limited. The evaluation of immunogenicity, durability and cross variant neutralisation requires the integration of laboratory immunology with bioinformatics to analyse high-dimensional, longitudinal data generated across diverse cohorts, time points, and viral variants. The study had used bioinformatics pipelines to manage and analyse large, multidimensional immunological datasets of antibody responses by different SARS-CoV-2 vaccines against representative prototypes of major variants in 255 participants from Botswana who received Pfizer mRNA (BNT162b2), Janssen adenovirus 26 (Ad26.COV2.S), AstraZeneca chimpanzee adenovirus (ChAdOx1-S), or Sinovac whole inactivated virus. Participants were stratified by time since vaccination (â‰¤3 months vs >3 months), HIV status and variant. In the 3 months post vaccination with a pronounced decline in neutralisation compared to the other platforms. Across all vaccines, neutralising antibodies were markedly lower against the recently emergent JN.1 variant, often falling below the limit of detection compared with the ancestral D614G strain. No significant differences were observed by HIV status or sex. These findings underscore platform-specific trade-offs between peak immunogenicity and durability and demonstrate how bioinformatics is essential for resolving complex interactions between vaccine technology, viral evolution, host factors, and time.

title: SLiM identification with protein language models
authors: Jonathan Oxman, University of Western Ontario, Canada; Julia Malec, University of Western Ontario, Canada; Jonathan Peters, University of Western Ontario, Canada; Silvana Ilie, Toronto Metropolitan University, Canada; G. Brian Golding, McMaster University, Canada; Lucian Ilie, University of Western Ontario, Canada
abstract: Short Linear Motifs (SLiMs) are short (3-10 amino acids), degenerate sequence patterns, occurring usually within intrinsically disordered region, that often mediate protein-protein interactions. Because they are short and degenerate, a few mutations can create a new occurrence. This creates a major challenge of identifying the small fraction of true functional motifs among the many occurrences by chance of the same sequence pattern. We introduce a new method for SLiM identification, SLiMVal, that uses sequence similarity based on protein language models, such as ProtT5 or Ankh. These are deep learning models trained on very large unlabelled protein sequence datasets that learn context-aware representations capturing structural and functional properties from sequence alone. They produce a high dimensional vector (embedding) associated with each residue within a protein sequence that captures the properties of that particular residue. The score given by the cosine similarity of these embeddings has been shown to produce the best sequence alignments, surpassing even those produced by aligning AlphaFold structures. SLiMVal uses a pLM-based score and combines ProtT5 and Ankh to produce a method that achieves much higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art SLiMprob. The use of SLiMVal opens new opportunities for the study of the function and evolution of small linear protein motifs, including the possibility to find ancestral proteins without the characteristic motif and then search for alternate motifs that might carry out the same function.

title: Mining for Tick Blood Meal Hosts with Ematille: Initial Results
authors: Bj Stubbs, Tufts University, United States; Heidi Goethert, Tufts University, United States; Donna Slonim, Tufts University, United States
abstract: Tick-borne illnesses like Lyme disease are evolving public health concerns, requiring holistic mitigation strategies incorporating ecological, biological, and zoological approaches. Identifying host species that serve as the source of tick blood meals may improve understanding of the transmission cycle in nature, which can lead to targeted interventions. But doing so efficiently through molecular sequencing, while potentially feasible, is not straightforward. This problem requires molecular markers that are species-specific but sufficiently abundant to be detected in small, highly degraded DNA samples. Prior work has relied on laborious manual PCR primer selection. We present Ematille, a workflow for finding PCR primers for a pre-specified zoo or set of potential host species. We take advantage of long transposable elements, which occur frequently in genomes and often feature species-specific mutation patterns. Ematille uses k-mer statistics in a hierarchical fashion to rapidly find PCR primers both specific enough to be used for species identification and abundant enough for detection in severely degraded host DNA. We computationally verify Ematille on a test set of diverse genomes. Ematille finds primer sequences matching over a thousand sites in the desired genomes with no off-target hits, including in the tick itself. We compare Ematilleâ€™s results to those for mitochondrial eDNA marker genes, and we assess the value of using transposable elements for this search. Overall, Ematille offers a freely available computational approach to solving a complex search problem previously only performed by hand. Ematille is written in Python and available at https://github.com/bjstubbs/ematille data and results available at https://bcb.cs.tufts.edu/ematille/

title: One Size Does Not Fit All: The Critical Role of k-mer Size in Genomic Similarity Analysis
authors: Adrita Hossain Nakshi, Computer Science and Engineering, Penn State University, United States; David Koslicki, Computer Science and Engineering, Biology, and The Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences, Penn State University, United States
abstract: K-mers are widely used in computational genomics as the basis of many alignment-free analyses, including genome identification, clustering, classification, etc. Despite their importance, most studies rely on a single k-mer size, often chosen heuristically or inherited from prior work. In this work, we analyze datasets from prior k-merâ€“based studies to examine how varying k affects similarity structure and downstream outcomes. We compute pairwise similarities across multiple k values and analyze pairwise similarity ranking changes using swap plots. At small k ( We further analyze nearest-neighbor relationships and find that small changes in k can significantly alter top neighbors. Correlation heatmaps show strong agreement between nearby k values, while distant k values (e.g., k=14 vs. k=25) exhibit weak correlation. Beyond k â‰ˆ 19â€“20, similarity matrices become highly correlated, indicating stabilization. This suggests that nearest-neighbor applications (genome identification, taxonomic classification, and database retrieval) can be highly sensitive to k value. Finally, we examine the number of distinct k-mers as a function of k across datasets and observe a similar increasing-then-plateau trend but with dataset-specific transition points, indicating that no single k is universally â€œoptimalâ€. Overall, our results highlight k-mer size as a critical parameter and motivate considering multiple k values for robust genomic analysis.

title: NCBI Datasets: Simplified Access to NCBI Sequence Data and Metadata
authors: Nuala Oleary, NCBI, United States; Mirian Tsuchiya, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Eric Cox, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Brad Holmes, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Robert Falk, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; William R. Anderson III, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Vichet Hem, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Laurie Breen, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Steven Gaudaen, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States
abstract: Retrieving biological sequence data and metadata from NCBI has historically required navigating multiple databases and interfaces, presenting a barrier to efficient and reproducible research. NCBI Datasets addresses this by providing modern, user-friendly interfaces (including a web interface, command line tools, and an OpenAPI) designed to simplify access to NCBI's biological data holdings. Data is delivered as structured packages: ZIP archives that bundle sequence, metadata, and annotation together, ensuring researchers have full context for what they retrieve and can more easily reproduce and report on their analyses. Metadata reports are delivered in JSON format with fully documented schemas, making it straightforward to parse, validate, and integrate NCBI metadata into downstream workflows. Extensive documentation supports users across all levels of computational expertise. NCBI Datasets currently provides access to all assembled genomes, RefSeq genes, and associated data from the BioSample, BioProject, and Protein databases. In this presentation, we describe recent enhancements to gene data access, including retrieval of gene orthologs to support comparative genomics workflows, and introduce a new service for accessing data from NCBI's Nucleotide and Protein databases, substantially expanding the scope of what is available through the Datasets interface. Together, these updates reflect NCBI's ongoing commitment to making its data holdings more discoverable, accessible, and immediately usable by the research community.

title: In silico Binding of SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein with Phytochemicals in Flaxseed and Sesame Oil
authors: James Villanueva, Ross University School of Medicine, Barbados
abstract: A promising target of interventions against the COVID-19 pandemic is the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein which mediates viral attachment and cellular entry by binding to the ACE2 receptor. Within spike protein, there is a free-fatty-acid binding pocket where omega-6 fatty acid, has been shown to bind, stabilizing spike protein in a closed conformation that inhibits interaction with the ACE2 receptor. Interventions designed to exploit this mechanism may play a role in combating the virus. Lignans are phytochemicals found in flaxseed oil as well as sesame oil. We used molecular docking simulations to probe for potential interaction between prominent lignans and the SARS-Cov-2 spike protein. Our results indicate that these lignans tend to localize with high affinity to the free-fatty-acid binding site. Binding energies, docked poses and amino acid interactions indicate that these lignans may stabilize the spike protein in the closed conformation, potentially inhibiting the interaction between the spike protein and the ACE2 receptor.

title: Integrative Protein Network Analysis Identifies a Candidate Modifier Gene in X-Linked Dystonia-Parkinsonism
authors: Alejandro Nato Jr., Department of Biomedical Sciences, Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine, Marshall University, Huntington, WV 25755, USA, United States; Vinícius Magalhães Borges, Department of Biomedical Sciences, Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine, Marshall University, Huntington, WV 25755, USA, United States; Natalia Fagundes Borges Teruel, Department of Medicine, New Jersey Medical School, Rutgers University, Newark, NJ 07103, USA, United States; Alfonso Luis Gener, Department of Biology, University of the Philippines Manila, Padre Faura, Manila, 1000 Metro Manila, Philippines, Philippines; Alfred Benjamin Tierra, Department of Biology, University of the Philippines Manila, Padre Faura, Manila, 1000 Metro Manila, Philippines, Philippines; James Denvir, Department of Biomedical Sciences, Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine, Marshall University, Huntington, WV 25755, USA, United States; Josephine Agapito, Department of Biology, University of the Philippines Manila, Padre Faura, Manila, 1000 Metro Manila, Philippines, Philippines; Custer Deocaris, Biomedical Research Section, Philippine Nuclear Research Institute, Diliman, 1101 Quezon City, Philippines, Philippines
abstract: X-linked Dystonia-Parkinsonism (XDP) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder strongly associated with reduced neuronal expression of the transcription factor subunit TAF1 of TFIID complex. XDP is a condition mainly affecting males of Filipino descent, yet its selective vulnerability and phenotypic variability remain unexplained. Here, we applied an integrative systems biology framework combining protein-protein interaction network (PPIN) analysis and structural modeling to identify other genes that contribute to XDP pathogenesis. By checking the TAF1-centered network, we found 343 proteins related to chromatin regulation and neurodegeneration-related pathways. Using network topology metrics, we prioritized key genes likely to function as regulatory hubs. KAT8, a histone acetyltransferase known to interact with TAF1, emerged as the most central node. Structural modeling of KAT8-TAF1 complexes demonstrated stable interaction interfaces, while pathogenic non-synonymous SNPs in both genes were predominantly located distal to the binding interface, producing minimal effects on interaction energetics. These findings suggest that disease-relevant variants may act through allosteric mechanisms, perturbing acetyltransferase activity, complex assembly, or chromatin engagement rather than direct disruption of proteinâ€“protein binding. We propose an alternative mechanism where XDP arises not solely from TAF1 dysfunction, but from perturbations in a broader chromatin regulatory network. Our integrative network-based approach highlights KAT8 as a candidate modifier linking transcription initiation and histone acetylation, highlighting epigenetic dysregulation as a mechanism in XDP pathology. Future studies involving functional validation and investigation KAT8-TAF1 network perturbations driven by other genes may provide additional insights regarding the etiology of XDP.

title: TwInsPEctor for Twin Prime Editing Analysis
authors: Nate Masson, University of Utah, United States; Kendell Clement, University of Utah, United States
abstract: Twin prime editing (twinPE) is a genome editing approach where paired prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs) target a genomic site and direct a prime editor protein to reverse transcribe programmable templates from opposing DNA strands, generating complementary DNA flaps that hybridize and can replace intervening endogenous DNA. This architecture enables larger insertions, deletions, and replacements than single-pegRNA prime editing, but yields heterogeneous outcomes that are difficult to interpret with existing amplicon-sequencing analysis workflows. We developed TwInsPEctor, an open-source, mechanistically informed command-line tool that takes amplicon sequencing data, aligns reads using CRISPResso2, and applies an analysis framework tailored to twinPE. TwInsPEctor constructs composite reference representations of the wild-type and edited amplicons and uses alignment-based interpretation to classify allele outcomes. The tool generates visualizations and per-base editing profiles quantifying efficiency, indels, and flap incorporation. Its allele tables show the full scope of the twinPE edit, providing an in-depth look at editing outcomes. Applied to twinPE datasets, TwInsPEctor successfully resolved complex outcomes, revealing that editing performance was significantly limited by incomplete or asymmetric flap processing. In addition to unedited and perfectly edited rates, substantial fractions of reads exhibited imperfect edits, characterized by partial or absent incorporation of both flaps, or single-flap edits resulting from complete or partial incorporation of only one flap, and variable removal of the endogenous sequence. These results demonstrate that TwInsPEctor can enable systematic comparison of twinPE platforms and configurations while providing mechanistic insights that inform prime editor choices, pegRNA designs, and experimental conditions.

title: Improving Detection of Subgenomic RNAs across SARS-CoV-2 Lineages
authors: Bradley Jenner, Boston University, United States; Arden Lee, Boston University, United States; Jennette Prince, Boston University, United States; Elm Markert, Boston University, United States; Gary Benson, Boston University, United States; Jillian Petrosky, Boston University, United States; Joseline Velasquez-Reyes, Boston University, United States; John Connor, Boston University, United States
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 produces several proteins through subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs), which are short, discontinuous transcripts that allow for efficient translation of structural and accessory proteins. As SARS-CoV-2 has evolved, genomic changes have given rise to new variants such as Alpha, Delta, Gamma, and Omicron with altered virulence and transmissibility. Therefore, it is imperative to understand the effect of these mutations on the sgRNA landscape. To quantify how sgRNA production has changed across novel variants, we analyzed amplicon sequencing data from patients infected with different SARS-CoV-2 strains utilizing popular sgRNA detection tools – LeTRS and DI-tector. We found that LeTRS substantially outperforms DI-tector and successfully captures sgRNAs in early strains, yet fails to capture nucleocapsid (N) sgRNAs in more recent variants. We hypothesize that a known deletion preceding the N open reading frame in newer variants causes LeTRS to fail to detect N sgRNA reads. This highlights a limitation in rigid, junction-dependent approaches in sgRNA detection. Consequently, we developed sgRNAtor, which identifies sgRNAs through fuzzy string matching to transcription regulatory sequences without relying on additional sequence-based assumptions. Not only does sgRNAtor perform similarly to LeTRS, but also recovers N sgRNAs in more recent variants. Taken together, our results show that sgRNAtor is an evolution-tolerant method for sgRNA detection that can be used to further study how the transcriptional and translational landscapes of SARS-CoV-2 evolve.

title: BEAS: A Simple Scalable Batch Effect Assessment Score
authors: Youla Ali, University of Oklahoma, United States; Sriram Boddeda, University of Oklahoma, United States; Olajumoke Oladapo, University of Oklahoma, United States; Suryaveer Kapoor, University of Oklahoma, United States; Marmar Moussa, University of Oklahoma, United States
abstract: Batch technical variations arise from differences in sequencing platforms, reagents, or experimental conditions. Metrics such as kBET, LISI, and ASW work at the local neighborhood level and have shown variable sensitivity and dataset-dependent performance. A previous benchmark compared KBET with ASW and LISI and KBET outperformed both metrics. However, KBET gives a pass score only if local cell neighborhoods match the global batch composition. To address this limitation we developed a new metric BEAS - A simple scalable Batch Effect Assessment Score. BEAS is composed of the average product of a Parent Penalty (PP) and Weighted Similarity (WS) across all neighborhoods in an integrated dataset.â€‹ We define WS as a weighted average of centroid similarities between all subpopulation pairs found within a neighborhood.â€‹â€‹ And we define PP score as the ratio of datasets present in a local neighborhood to the total datasets in the integrated collection. We tested BEAS against KBET and found that BEAS matches and outperforms KBET in cases where the datasets to be integrated have a partial shared composition, i.e. some cell types are specific to some but not all of the datasets that otherwise match. Furthermore, BEAS is implemented and publicly available via AtlasCollect tool for single cell dataset integration. BEAS provides a simple and interpretable but powerful assessment tool for batch effect quantification that helps researchers decide on integration workflows in downstream analyses.

title: NCBI Datasets: Accessing Virus Sequence Data and Metadata
authors: Eric Cox, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Mirian Tsuchiya, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Brad Holmes, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Robert Falk, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; William R. Anderson III, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Vichet Hem, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Laurie Breen, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Steven Gaudaen, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States; Nuala O'Leary, NCBI/NLM/NIH, United States
abstract: NCBI Datasets is a resource from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) that provides easy and intuitive access to genome sequences and metadata for a broad range of taxa through a web interface, command-line tools, and API. Since its initial release, NCBI Datasets has been under constant development with the goal of meeting the data retrieval needs of the biological research community. This presentation will highlight recent updates to virus genome sequence data and related metadata and how to access it from the NCBI Datasets web and command-line interfaces. The NCBI Datasets virus data package, available from the NCBI Datasets command-line tools, brings together genomic, CDS, and protein sequences, as well as metadata, in a compressed zip archive that is available for download as a single file. In addition, highly-compressed, cached data packages are available for Alphainfluenzavirus and SARS-CoV-2. We are currently gathering feedback from the research community on whether there is a demand for cached packages for additional virus taxa. For segmented viruses, including Alphainfluenzavirus, the NCBI Virus curation team has developed a custom process that groups nucleotide sequence genome segments derived from the same biological sample into genome assembly records. We are currently in the early stages of developing new nucleotide and protein sequence record pages, including for viral genome and protein sequences, as well as the underlying services to populate these pages. We are gathering information about how the community uses these pages and the underlying data to help us plan our development.

title: Indel Fitness Prediction from Diverse Deep Mutational Scanning Data with DDGindel
authors: Aidan Horne, Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program, University of Michigan, United States; Yang Li, Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Michigan, United States
abstract: Protein engineering is a scientific discipline that seeks to design proteins that treat diseases, counteract venoms, and act in biofuels. Research in this field seeks to find proteins or protein mutations that are more stable, active, or structurally specialized than those that are currently known or exist. With the use of highly accurate machine learning models, the change in thermodynamic fold stability, or the ΔΔG (pronounced delta delta G), of a mutation can be predicted, reducing resource consumption in the creation and testing phases of protein design. A good protein folding stability is crucial, as a protein with poor folding stability will either misfold or fail to fold at all, resulting in a nonfunctional protein. Here, most machine learning models focus on predicting the ΔΔG of substitution mutations, leaving predictive methods for insertion and deletion mutations (indels) sorely deficient. This project identifies how different mutation types affect the stability of proteins differently and aims to increase the number of methods to accurately predict the ΔΔG of indels by showcasing DDGindel: a sequence-based ΔΔG-prediction model that adapts the model architecture of DDGemb to facilitate ΔΔG-prediction of indels through the implementation of pairwise sequence alignments. DDGemb, a substitution-only ΔΔG-prediction model, outperformed 24 other ΔΔG-prediction models on a set of benchmark datasets. DDGindel adapts the architecture of DDGemb to incorporate the ability to predict the ΔΔG of indels and attempts to maintain predictive performance on substitution mutations. DDGindel is trained using 1,547,092 forward and reverse single-substitution, double-substitution, single-insertion, and single-deletion mutations on 479 proteins and domains (331 natural and 148 designed) and is tested on benchmark datasets to allow comparison with other ΔΔG-prediction models.

title: Information-Theoretic Optimization of scRNA-seq Clustering
authors: Urshila Choubal, Georgetown University, United States; Sivan Leviyang, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables the study of gene expression at the level of individual cells. Identifying cell-types through clustering is a key task in downstream analysis of scRNA-seq. Common approaches, such as the Louvain algorithm and hierarchical clustering algorithms, depend on parameters that are often chosen heuristically. This can lead to over-or under-clustering and biologically artificial clusters. In hierarchical methods, which produce levels of clustering, the challenge is to choose the optimal level of clustering by using stopping conditions. However, not only are hierarchical methods computationally expensive, but they also assume underlying statistical models to define stopping criteria. In this work, we apply ideas from information theory to evaluate clustering in scRNA-seq. Specifically, we employ Rate-Distortion (RD) theory to define an optimal clustering baseline in the context of unsupervised clustering. We further demonstrate that RD theory can be used to establish a computationally efficient, model-free stopping condition for hierarchical clustering in scRNA-seq. Additionally, when ground-truth cell-type labels are available, the Information Bottleneck (IB) framework provides us with an optimal baseline for supervised clustering. Finally, we show that the IB method quantifies how closely unsupervised clustering algorithms approach optimal supervised clustering. Overall, our framework provides a principled way to evaluate hierarchical clustering in scRNA-seq that can quantify trade-offs between cluster granularity and biological relevance.

title: CADBURY: Covariate-Aware Deconvolution of BUlk Rna-seq analYsis
authors: Yixiao Wu, Dept. of Biomedical Informatics and Data Science andProgram in Comp Biol and Biomed Info, Yale University, United States; April Yang, Dept. of Biomedical Informatics and Data Science andProgram in Comp Biol and Biomed Info, Yale University, United States; Youwen Liu, Dept. of Biomedical Informatics and Data Science, YaleUniversity, United States; Jihoon Kim, Dept. of Biomedical Informatics and Data Science andProgram in Comp Biol and Biomed Info, Yale University, United States
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides high-resolution, cell-type-specific transcriptomic profiles but faces limitations including restricted tissue accessibility, dissociation-induced selection bias, loss of spatial context, and inefficient mRNA capture producing sparse, noisy measurements. Additional challenges-batch effects, protocol variability, and limited individuals-further constrain its utility for population-scale analyses. In contrast, bulk RNA-seq datasets are abundant and better capture cohort-level variation but lack cellular resolution. Deconvolution methods can estimate cell-type fractions (CTFs) from bulk data; however, existing approaches lack calibrated uncertainty estimates, do not support hierarchical modeling with sample-level covariates, and show variable performance across cell types and reference datasets. We present CADBURY (Covariate-Aware Deconvolution of BUlk Rna-seq analYsis), a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework that jointly infers CTFs and cell-type-specific expression using scRNA-seq references as informative priors. The model employs logistic-normal priors on CTFs, enabling incorporation of covariates and random effects while mitigating batch effects.
