In simulated pseudo-bulk PBMC data (N=120, 6 cell types), CADBURY achieves superior performance for rare cell types (DC: r=0.931, RMSE=0.007 vs. next-best r=0.918; B cells: r=0.961 vs. 0.955; overall RMSE=0.005 vs. NNLS 0.007) while remaining competitive overall (r=0.958 vs. BayesPrism 0.963). In Alzheimer's disease brain data (ssREAD, entorhinal cortex, 5 donors), it achieves the highest per-cell-type correlation for astrocytes (r=0.911, RMSE=0.038) and uniquely recovers covariate effects, including decreased excitatory neurons (β=−0.61) and increased microglia (β=+0.44) with advancing Braak stage. Notably, CADBURY is the only method providing calibrated posterior credible intervals (91% coverage at nominal 95%). Overall, it integrates uncertainty quantification, robust rare cell-type estimation, and covariate modeling within a unified Bayesian framework.

title: Pathway redistribution across cellular states reveals a shared signaling backbone and context-dependent regulatory modules in RNA-binding protein networks
authors: Naoki Osato, Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan; Kengo Sato, Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan
abstract: Understanding how regulatory architectures are reorganized during biological state transitions remains a central challenge in functional genomics. Here, we integrate co-expression–derived regulatory interactions with interpretable deep learning to compute gene-level contribution scores and introduce delta NES (normalized enrichment score difference) to quantify pathway redistribution across biological states. Applying this framework to neural progenitor and leukemia-associated cellular states, we identify systematic redistribution of functional modules across RNA-binding proteins, including PKM, HNRNPK, and NELFE. Neural System– and Immune System–associated modules are differentially positioned along contribution-ranked regulatory landscapes, while Signal Transduction consistently forms a conserved signaling backbone. These findings suggest that pathway redistribution reflects regulatory reorganization across biological states and provides a framework for interpreting large-scale regulatory coordination beyond expression-centric analyses.

title: Spatial Transcriptomic Dissection of the Gut-Skin Axis in Hidradenitis Suppurativa and Inflammatory Bowel Disease
authors: Amazigh Mokhtari, Sanofi, France; Anya Djafri, Sanofi, France; Clement Levin, Sanofi, France; Sandrine Longuemaux, Sanofi, France; Anne Caron, Sanofi, France; Anne-Laure Bauchet, Sanofi, France; Matteo Cesaroni, Sanofi, France; Donald Jackson, Sanofi, France; Vincent Mikol, Sanofi, France
abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) and inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, are chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disorders with growing evidence of a close biological association. Epidemiological studies support a bidirectional relationship between these conditions, with a particularly strong link between HS and Crohn's disease, while recent genetic evidence suggests that IBD may contribute causally to HS development. Together, these findings point to a shared gut-skin inflammatory axis, although the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics enable genome-scale profiling of intact tissue sections at subcellular resolution, providing a powerful framework to resolve cellular composition, phenotypic states, and intercellular communication within complex diseased tissues. In this study, we apply Xenium subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics to HS and IBD tissue samples to systematically characterize shared and disease-specific cellular architectures and signaling pathways. By integrating spatially resolved gene expression with computational analyses of cell states and cell-cell interactions, we aim to identify convergent inflammatory programs, tissue-specific features, and candidate therapeutic targets. This work provides a spatially informed framework for dissecting the pathobiology of HS and IBD and for advancing mechanistic understanding of the gut-skin axis.

title: Comprehensive analysis of pseudogene expression in human and macaque brains compared with other tissues
authors: Yunzhe Jiang, Yale University, United States; Yucheng Yang, Yale University, United States; Cristina Sisu, Brunel University of London, United Kingdom; Tianxing He, Columbia University, United States; Hyejung Won, University of North Carolina, United States; Mark Gerstein, Yale University, United States
abstract: Although gene expression in the brain has been extensively investigated and compared to other tissues, the activity of pseudogenes has not been comprehensively surveyed. Here, leveraging large-scale RNA-seq data, we construct consistent pseudogene expression profiles in human and macaque brains and compare them to 29 other tissues. We further annotate pseudogenes with potential cellular roles based on co-clustering them with protein-coding genes. Notably, the majority of the expressed pseudogenes show elevated expression in the brain relative to other tissues, and these pseudogenes show broad and consistent expression patterns across brain subregions. Furthermore, spatiotemporal analyses reveal that pseudogenes in different brain subregions have greatly varying temporal trajectories (e.g., increasing vs. decreasing), in contrast to protein-coding genes that tend to be more uniform. Finally, we identify a set of pseudogenes exhibiting significant changes in neuropsychiatric disorders, some of which overlap with known brain eGenes (genes whose expression is associated with expression quantitative trait loci, eQTLs), as well as with genes implicated by genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Together, our study provides a public resource of pseudogene expression in human and macaque brains (in comparison to other tissues) and highlights aspects of pseudogene expression in brain development and pathogenesis.

title: A Pipeline for Histone Mark Meta-Analysis and Investigation into the Heterogeneity of H4K16ac
authors: Naveen Ahuja, University of Ottawa, Canada; William Stanford, University of Ottawa, Canada; Theodore Perkins, University of Ottawa, Canada
abstract: Histone H4 lysine 16 acetylation (H4K16ac) is a dynamic histone modification that plays diverse roles across cellular contexts, including gene regulation/activation, double-strand repair, and activation of transposable elements that act as enhancers. It is the only acetylated H4 tail residue to disrupt contacts between the H4 tail and H2A-H2B acidic patch, preventing nucleosome array assembly, and thereby creating an accessible chromatin environment. It is also the single most abundant mark in the human genome, and yet it is far less studied than various H3 acetylations and methylations, which have their own strong associations with DNA accessibility and gene regulation. To clarify the various roles of H4K16ac, we developed a pipeline for histone mark meta-analysis that integrates ChIP-seq or related sequencing data from multiple studies. In analyzing H4K16ac, we found that the mark comprises both narrow and broad domains, similar to H3K27me3. We confirmed previous associations with gene expression and LINE1 elements. However, we identified three distinct binding profiles across gene promoters and bodies, each linked to different transcriptional outcomes. Moreover, we found sample-dependent variations in H4K16ac marking at coding and non-coding gene promoters. Some of these differences might be linked to the antibodies used in the ChIP, but the sequencing method and other technical factors did not appear to influence results. Our workflow enabled us to systematically evaluate the H4K16ac mark, presenting a holistic view of its variability across cell types and regulatory elements, providing a standardized framework of analysis that can be applied to other understudied marks.

title: KurtoRank: An Unsupervised Ensemble Strategy for Cell Subtype Annotation in Gene-Limited Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Chao Hui Huang, Pfizer Inc., United States; Oluwamayowa Esther Awosika, Pfizer Inc., United States; Jadwiga Bienkowska, Pfizer Inc., United States
abstract: Sub-cellular imaging platforms such as 10x Xenium deliver spatial single-cell resolution, but their targeted panels (~300 genes) leave many conventional annotation methods underpowered. No single statistical test is universally reliable across tissues, gene panels, and subtype granularities, and naive voting of multiple tests dilutes the signal of whichever test happens to be informative for a given cluster. We present KurtoRank, an unsupervised ensemble framework for cell-subtype annotation in gene-limited spatial transcriptomics. For each Leiden cluster, KurtoRank evaluates a panel of complementary per-subtype tests by utilizing various subtyping methods, e.g., permutation-based empirical p-values, DE-gene overlap (top-N and FDR-thresholded hypergeometric), geometric-mean combined DE p-values, z-score enrichment, Fisher exact, proportion tests, markerâ€“marker correlation, spatial co-occurrence, etc., producing a score vector per candidate subtype. The key innovation is a kurtosis-based weighting scheme: for each test, the excess kurtosis of its across-subtype score distribution quantifies how sharply that test discriminates within the current cluster; peaked, decisive tests receive higher weight, while flat, uninformative tests are down-weighted. The weighted ensemble is then rank-aggregated into a final subtype call, with tie-breaking by a curated lineage prior derived from a pan-tissue CELLxGENE Census atlas. We demonstrate KurtoRank on human breast, colorectal, and immune Xenium datasets, showing coherent spatial patterns and lineage-consistent subtype assignments, including for rare and malignant populations. KurtoRank is released as an open-source python package; systematic benchmarking against existing annotation methods is ongoing.

title: Novel Approach for Identifying Differentially Expressed Genes
authors: Charles Street, University of Oklahoma, School of Computer Science, United States; Suryaveer Kapoor, University of Oklahoma, Stephenson School of Biomedical Engineering, United States; Marmar Moussa, University of Oklahoma, School of Computer Science, Stephenson School of Biomedical Engineering, United States
abstract: Differential expression (DE) analysis is central to interpreting single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, as it enables the identification of genes that are over- or under-expressed across cell types, states or biological conditions. Existing methods use a variety of parametric and non-parametric tests, logistic regression, and other models to identify these genes. Here, we propose a novel algorithmic metric, Contrastive Scatter Score, as an alternative approach for evaluating changes in gene expression across cell populations. Our approach emphasizes genes that are both highly expressed and strongly different between populations while reducing the influence of low-expression noise. To improve robustness, we further apply bootstrapping techniques to filter unstable gene rankings. We compare our novel method, Contrastive Scatter Score, against the leading method in the field, DESeq2, and we recover similar marker genes with competitive performance, but most importantly, we identify marker genes that are consistently missed by DESeq2 algorithms. To assess performance across diverse biological contexts, we evaluated both methods on public datasets and a new dataset we sequenced specifically for this work. Functional enrichment analysis using g:Profiler further validates the individual strengths of both approaches in identifying consistent biological pathways. Our results demonstrate that the proposed new score can provide an interpretable and computationally efficient alternative to traditional statistical models for single-cell transcriptomic analysis.

title: BAMEN: A Biologically Associated Masked Encoder Network for Multi-omics Clustering
authors: Yashu Vashishath, University of North Texas, United States; Serdar Bozdag, University of North Texas, United States
abstract: Understanding molecular heterogeneity remains a central challenge in medical research and precision medicine. Integrative analysis of multi-omics data offers the potential to identify biologically meaningful disease subtypes; however, many existing integration methods treat omics modalities as independent feature blocks and fail to explicitly model known regulatory relationships across molecular layers. To address this limitation, we propose BAMEN (Biologically Associated Masked Encoder Network), a biologically informed deep learning framework for unsupervised multi-omics representation learning. BAMEN is designed to integrate one data modality with another by embedding prior biological knowledge directly into the network architecture through sparse masked connectivity. Unlike conventional multimodal autoencoders that concatenate omics views, BAMEN employs a structured modulation mechanism in which methylation-derived signals regulate gene-expression representations prior to latent compression. The framework further incorporates repeated training, hyperparameter optimization, and consensus embedding aggregation across multiple runs to improve embedding robustness and clustering stability. We evaluated BAMEN on paired TCGA cancer datasets and compared them with representative multi-omics integration methods.

title: A comprehensive omnibus framework integrating diverse genetic architectures for highly powered gene-based association testing using GWAS summary statistics
authors: Jungsook Yang, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), South Korea; Minji Jang, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), South Korea; Dougu Nam, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), South Korea
abstract: Gene-based association tests are instrumental in elucidating the biological mechanisms underlying genome-wide association study (GWAS) discoveries. However, the statistical power of existing methods remains highly sensitive to the underlying genetic architecture, particularly characterized by linkage disequilibrium (LD) masking, minor allele frequency (MAF)-dependent effect sizes, and varying signal sparsity. Here, we present wBAT-omni, an efficient C++ command-line tool that integrates seven summary statistics-based gene-set tests - including three novel weighting strategies - into a unified omnibus framework. By harmonizing methods tailored to distinct genetic architectures, wBAT-omni autonomously maximizes statistical power across diverse and unknown genetic landscapes. Extensive simulations using UK Biobank and 1000 Genomes data confirm that wBAT-omni yields superior power over state-of-the-art methods while strictly controlling type I error. When applied to large-scale GWAS data for diverse complex traits - including type 2 diabetes, height, lipids, and 35 blood biomarkers - wBAT-omni uncovered numerous novel, biologically relevant gene associations. These results underscore wBAT-omni as a powerful and versatile solution to accelerate post-GWAS discoveries.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: scMultiPreDICT: A single-cell predictive framework using transcriptomic and epigenetic signatures
authors: Ewura-Esi Manful, Pennsylvania State University College of Medicine, United States; Yasin Uzun, Pennsylvania State University College of Medicine, United States
abstract: Cellular responses to genetic perturbations depend on both transcriptional programs and the epigenetic landscape. While single-cell multiomics technologies enable simultaneous profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility, the relative contribution of each regulatory layer to gene expression remains unclear. Existing computational approaches focus on data integration and gene regulatory network inference but do not systematically compare the predictive performance of transcriptional versus epigenetic features on a gene-by-gene basis. We present scMultiPreDICT, a computational framework for comparative predictive modeling of gene expression using single-cell multiomics data. scMultiPreDICT benchmarks RNA-only, ATAC-only and multimodal feature sets across six machine learning models from linear regression to deep learning approach across different biological datasets. We show that RNA-derived features generally provide strong predictive power, whereas chromatin accessibility alone yields a modest performance. Surprisingly, multimodal integration does not uniformly improve prediction accuracy; instead, its benefit is gene-specific and context-dependent. Feature importance analysis reveals that transcriptional features dominate for most genes, whereas chromatin accessibility contributes meaningfully for a subset of genes in specific cellular contexts. Overall, the results demonstrate that regulatory layers contribute differently to gene expression. scMultiPreDICT provides a systematic framework for identifying the relative contributions of transcriptional and epigenetic regulation across genes and cellular contexts, guiding the design of targeted perturbation studies and the prioritization of regulatory layers for therapeutic interventions. scMultiPreDICT is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/UzunLab/scMultiPreDICT/.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Autoencoding Sequence and Expression Profiles for Context-Specific Synthetic Lethality Prediction
authors: Aneesh Singh, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, United States; Alice Berger, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Synthetic lethality in paralog pairs is highly context-dependent, varying across cell lines as expression changes alter functional redundancy. To better capture this context specificity, we developed an autoencoder-based framework that integrates protein sequence information with cell-line-specific gene expression to estimate how functionally similar two paralogs are in a given cellular background. For each gene (n = 1904) in each cell line (PC9 and HeLa), we combined a pretrained protein embedding from the amino acid sequence with log2(TPM+1) expression data from the Broad Institute Cancer Dependency Map. The joint representation was then compressed into a latent vector using an autoencoder. We then compared latent vectors for gene pairs using L2 distance, cosine similarity, and mean/max absolute difference as pairwise similarity features. This approach is designed to learn a shared â€œstateâ€ that reflects both intrinsic protein properties and cell-line-specific activity, without relying on manually engineered features or study-specific assumptions. We benchmarked these pairwise features derived from the latent vectors against 38 more traditional pairwise metrics, such as amino acid sequence identity, total number of proteinâ€“protein interactions, and gene expression correlation. Using these latent similarity metrics, we found that pairwise features derived from the learned embeddings are significant indicators of cell-line-specific synthetic lethality. Specifically, the pairwise latent matrix cosine similarity proved to be the best feature for predicting synthetic lethality, producing ROC-AUC and average precision (AP) that ranked the sixth highest amongst all of the features and produced a Kruskal-Wallis p-value of 1.69e-10, while the p-value of every other pairwise latent matrix feature was each six orders of magnitude higher. These results suggest that jointly modeling sequence and expression can produce informative features for prioritizing paralog dependencies and may improve prediction of synthetic lethal interactions across cellular contexts.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: sPotts: Soft Probabilistic modeling for de novo cellular phenotyping of complex tissue microenvironments
authors: Chris Andersen, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Shikhar Uttam, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: A foundational principle in physics, from Ising models of ferromagnetism to statistical field theory, is that emergent macroscopic behavior arises from efficient characterization of local interactions between neighboring elements. When local interaction rules are well specified, global structure reveals itself naturally, without imposing top-down assumptions. Inspired by this foundational principle, we present sPotts, a fully unsupervised clustering algorithm built from first principles, which treats cellular identity not as a hard discrete assignment but through soft probabilistic labeling. This probabilistic framing allows sPotts to flexibly identify, without any strong a priori assumptions, cellular populations in a platform-agnostic manner within highly heterogeneous tissue microenvironments, spanning inflammatory diseases, cancer, and embryonic development. Critically, by probabilistically modeling local cell-cell spatial relationships alongside gene or protein expression simultaneously, sPotts demonstrates that emergent tissue-level organization can be recovered de novo. As an immediate consequence, we show that spatially-informed sPotts identifies putative cellular niches that respect spatial constraints and local boundaries. When leveraging expression alone, however, sPotts recovers populations substantially concordant with state-of-the-art methods, however with enhanced sensitivity to rare phenotypes. sPotts requires minimal distributional assumptions, minimal preprocessing steps, and only an upper bound on the expected number of emergent cellular populations, the last of which represents a much weaker prior than the current state of the art. sPotts represents a significant methodological advance for spatially resolved single-cell biology in complex tissue microenvironments.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PRIME-Bench: A Benchmark for Pathway-Level Reasoning in Genome Language Models
authors: Taylor Le Lievre, Columbia University, United States; Noga Aharony, Columbia University, United States; Mohammed Alquraishi, Columbia University, United States
abstract: Foundation genome language models (gLMs) promise to advance genome design, accelerating metabolic engineering to produce, degrade, and transform compounds that reshape our world. Central to this vision is the ability to reason over the functional relationships among pathway genes. Recent work has demonstrated gLM-guided genome synthesis, from novel operons to whole phage genomes, yet no evaluation has tested whether models capture gene relationships across the genomic distances that pathways span. Here, we introduce PRIME-Bench, a benchmark suite for zero-shot metabolic pathway gene prediction. PRIME-Bench comprises two tasks, intra-path and inter-path, constructed from metabolic pathways mined from EcoCyc. For intra-path, we identify all pathway forks; the model is conditioned on genes along one branch, and we compare the log-likelihood it assigns to the true next gene versus a gene on the alternate branch. For inter-path, the model is conditioned on a single pathway gene, and we compare the log-likelihood of its sequential partner versus a random gene from a different pathway in the same organism. The tasks' setup allows probing both functional relations and long-range genomic encoding, as metabolic pathways are often comprised of genes spread throughout the whole genome. We find that neither Evo1 (intra-path AUROC=0.4548, inter-path AUROC=0.4484) nor gLM2 (intra-path AUROC=0.4780, inter-path AUROC=0.4660) assigns higher likelihood to true pathway genes over controls, indicating that current foundation models fail to capture functional gene relationships at pathway scale.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Stability-informed low-N learning of protein fitness landscape
authors: Shannon Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Yunan Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Predicting how protein sequence mutations affect fitness is central to protein engineering and variant effect interpretation, yet most experimental assays yield only limited labeled variants, making low-N learning a major challenge. We present PsiFit, a protein stability-informed framework for low-N protein fitness prediction. PsiFit is motivated by the biological principle that proteins must remain sufficiently stable to support function. PsiFit explicitly incorporates this constraint into learning the sequenceâ€“fitness landscape. Building on our prior work in mutation stability prediction (SPURS) and low-N fitness modeling (ConFit), PsiFit introduces a unified framework that integrates stability-aware biophysical priors with protein language model adaptation. Specifically, PsiFit leverages predicted mutation-induced stability changes as an explicit signal to guide fitness learning, while employing a contrastive fine-tuning strategy that preserves the general biological knowledge encoded during pretraining and aligns the model with experimentally measured fitness. By embedding stability constraints directly into the learning process, PsiFit improves sample efficiency and mitigates overfitting in small and noisy datasets. Across more than 100 deep mutational scanning datasets in ProteinGym, PsiFit consistently outperformed multiple state-of-the-art low-N fitness prediction methods. The gains were observed across diverse proteins and assay types, indicating that stability provides a broadly useful inductive bias for learning protein fitness landscapes from sparse data. These results show that integrating biophysical stability priors with protein language models offers an effective and general strategy for data-efficient protein fitness prediction, with implications for ML-guided protein engineering and variant effect interpretation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: EN-TEx Chat: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Interactive Exploration of Personal Epigenomics
authors: Yuhang Chen, Yale University, United States; Matthew Jensen, Yale University, United States; Jiaqi Li, Yale University, United States; Heng-Le Chen, Yale University, United States; Andy Gu, Yale University, United States; Alp Namalan, Yale University, United States; Joel Rozowsky, Yale University, United States; Timur Galeev, Yale University, United States; April Yang, Yale University, United States; Tai Michaels, Yale University, United States; Mark Gerstein, Yale University, United States
abstract: The EN-TEx personal epigenomics resource comprises joint efforts of the ENCODE and GTEx consortia to profile genomic regulatory elements in ~30 tissues of four healthy donors by mapping ~1600 functional genomics datasets onto haplotype-resolved personal genomes, identifying patterns of allele-specific activity. We recently extended EN-TEx+ Resource, incorporating new datasets, including single-cell ATAC-Seq (scATAC-Seq) for 11 aggregated cell types, aligned to higher quality, de novo assembled personal genomes. This enables identification of cell-type-specific allele-specific peaks (ASPs) and haplo-novel regulatory elementsâ€”chromatin accessible regions present in individual haplotypes but absent from the reference genome. Despite its richness, EN-TEx+ is large, multi-modality, and difficult to query interactively. Here, we present EN-TEx Chat, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system for natural-language exploration of this dataset. Genomic tables are chunked via a row-window strategy with header context, embedded with text-embedding-3-small, and indexed in a FAISS vector store. At query time, questions are parsed by variant, tissue, gene, and assay; top-K chunks are retrieved by cosine similarity and passed to an LLM for grounded answers, deployed via Gradio on Hugging Face Spaces. EN-TEx Chat supports diverse query types: identifying ASPs in specific cell clusters across donors; querying whether a genomic interval harbors haplo-novel peaks overlapping protein-binding sites or open chromatin regions; assessing whether graph genome alignments reveal regulatory elements absent from the linear reference; and linking these features to tissue and cell-type-specific eQTLs or allele-specific expression patterns. Future work will evaluate EN-TEx Chat by comparing RAG-based responses against a no-retrieval baseline on accuracy, relevance, and domain-expert scoring, using GPT as an automated evaluator. Overall, EN-TEx Chat establishes a paradigm for natural-language exploration of personalized regulatory genomics.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking single cell transcriptome matching methods for incremental growth of cell atlases
authors: Yun Zhang, National Library of Medicine, United States; Joyce Hu, J. Craig Venter Institute, United States; Beverly Peng, J. Craig Venter Institute, United States; Ajith Viswanathan Asari, National Library of Medicine, United States; Bingfang Xu, National Library of Medicine, United States; Vikrant Anil Deshpande, Indiana University, United States; Andreas Bueckle, Indiana University, United States; Bruce Herr II, Indiana University, United States; Christopher Dupont, J. Craig Venter Institute, United States; Katy Borner, Indiana University, United States; Richard Scheuermann, National Library of Medicine, United States
abstract: Background: The advancement of single cell technologies has driven significant progress in constructing a multiscale, pan-organ Human Reference Atlas for healthy human cells. Many multi-faceted cell atlases for different organs, species, and diseases now exist, though challenges remain in harmonizing cell types and unifying nomenclature among respective cell atlases. Multiple machine learning and artificial intelligence methods, including models pre-trained on large-scale cell atlas datasets, are publicly available for single cell community users to computationally map their cell clusters to the cell atlases. Results: This study benchmarks seven computational tools for cell type matching and label transfer â€“ Azimuth, CellTypist, CellHint, FR-Match, scArches, scPred, and singleR â€“ in ten organ systems. Using healthy lung as an exemplar organ, when matching the well-annotated cell types in two atlases â€“ the Human Lung Cell Atlas (HLCA) and the LungMAP Single-Cell Reference (CellRef), variations in the matching accuracy were observed, especially in rare cell types, underlining the need for a consensus strategy using a selective set of computational methods. In the meta-analysis of integrating these lung atlases, selective benchmarked methods were used to incrementally integrate 61 HLCA and 48 CellRef cell types, resulting in a meta-atlas of 41 matched, 20 HLCA-, and 7 CellRef-specific cell types. Similar approach revealed 25 matched cell types existed in two independent kidney atlases. Generalizability of the benchmarking performance was further demonstrated in a variety of organ systems. Conclusion: This study reveals the complementing strengths of the benchmarked methods and presents a framework for incremental growth of cell types in cell atlases.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A Computational Framework for Recovering Molecular Relationships from Biological Pathway Diagrams
authors: Xiwen Zhao, Northeastern University, United States; Benjamin King, University of Maine, United States; Mingyang Lu, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Biological pathways contain rich mechanistic knowledge about molecular interactions; however, much of this information exists primarily in static images rather than structured, machine-readable representations. Although some databases provide pathway annotations in structured formats, many regulatory and signaling relationships explicitly depicted in pathway diagrams are not fully captured in these representations. Existing methods for automated parsing of biological pathway diagrams largely focus on local relationship extraction rather than modeling the global structure of pathway diagrams as a whole, and therefore struggle to resolve complex topological patterns such as branching structures and feedback loops. Here, we propose a computational framework that fine-tunes visual recognition models on manually labeled KEGG pathway diagrams to recognize key visual elements, including line segments, oriented junction points, and biological symbols, and subsequently assembles these elements into a graph representation, thereby recovering molecular relationships directly from pathway image. For visual element recognition, our framework achieves a structural average precision (sAP15) of 81.4% for line segment detection, representing the best performance among the compared methods. It also achieves OKS AP50 scores of 0.95 and 1.00 for junction and symbol recognition, respectively, for which no directly comparable baseline is currently available. This work provides a scalable computational approach for extracting molecular relationships directly from pathway diagrams, with the potential to augment existing pathway resources and support downstream computational analyses.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Integrating Celltype-specific Signatures from Multi-Modal Data into an Ensemble Deep Learning framework for Clinical Outcome Prediction
authors: Shrabanti Chowdhury, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Anna Xing, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Gabriela Vasconcelos, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Pei Wang, Icahn school of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States
abstract: Predicting clinical outcomes from high-dimensional molecular data is a cornerstone of precision oncology, yet most approaches rely on bulk measurements that obscure cell-typeâ€“specific biology and spatial context. This limitation is critical, as tumor behavior and treatment response are shaped by heterogeneous cellular states and microenvironmental interactions. In this work, we introduce an ensemble learning framework that (1) specifically dissects cell-type-specific signals from bulk data; (2) integrates biologically curated pathways with cell-stateâ€“specific and spatial niche-informed gene signatures from public single-cell or spatial omics datasets; and (3) supports prediction of binary (treatment response), multiclass (molecular subtypes), and survival (time-to-event) outcomes. Specifically, to incorporate cell-type specific contributions, we first deconvolve bulk data to estimate molecular profiles of tumor, immune and other tumor microenvironmental cell compartments in each sample. In parallel, we leverage single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data to derive cell-state specific and niche-informed gene signatures (sets). These functional annotations, together with literature pathways, are incorporated into a hierarchical two-layer ensemble framework of deep learning models. The first layer constructs pathway/signature-specific prediction models within each cell compartment, capturing celltype-specific signals, while the second layer aggregates these predictions into robust and calibrated outcome predictions. Across simulations and real datasets from high-grade serous ovarian cancer studies, our framework outperforms conventional protein- and pathway-based ensemble prediction models that ignore cell-states or spatial programs. It also identifies clinically relevant, cell-type-specific signatures associated with treatment resistance, providing interpretable insights into tumor-microenvironment interactions. This approach enhances predictive accuracy and biological interpretability, offering a scalable strategy for precision oncology.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: GASTON-VI efficiently quantifies spatial gradients of gene expression from large-scale spatial transcriptomics data
authors: Zhirui Ning, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Sayuni Dharmasena, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Uthsav Chitra, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Background: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies measure gene expression at many spatial locations in a 2D tissue slice, enabling the identification and analysis of spatial gene expression patterns. For example, many genes exhibit spatial gradients of expression along an underlying 1-D spatial axis (e.g. in the liver, zonation genes vary along the portal vein-central vein (PV-CV) axis) while other genes exhibit variation independent of this axis (e.g. cell cycle). However, few computational methods identify spatial gradients along a continuous axis, and these methods do not scale to large datasets (e.g. 100,000-1,000,000s of cells) or tissues with complex geometries nor can they identify variation independent of this 1-D axis. Results: We introduce GASTON-VI, an interpretable variational inference (VI) model that learns both spatial gradients and underlying sources of variation in gene expression from ST data. GASTON-VI extends the classical variational autoencoder (VAE) framework to a spatial VAE model through a 1D spatial latent variable ("isodepth") that describes the underlying spatial axis of variation. GASTON-VI parametrizes the isodepth using a neural field model with positional encoding, and uses a novel warmup training scheme to disentangle the isodepth from other latent variables. Applied to a VisiumHD mouse liver ST dataset, GASTON-VI more efficiently and accurately recovers both the PV-CV axis and known zonation marker genes compared to existing methods. By separating spatial organization from other sources of variation, our method more accurately recovers the spatial axis and gene gradients, which informs better understanding of tissue structure and function.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Towards RNA Drug Discovery with RiboLead
authors: Charlie Wang United States
abstract: Modern drugs treat disease by binding to pockets on harmful proteins and modulating their function, but 85% of disease-relevant proteins lack these pockets and are thus undruggable. Targeting the RNA that builds these proteins could stop disease at its source, unlocking treatments for conditions long considered untreatable, like cancers and neurodegenerative disease. However, today, screening for molecule candidates that bind to RNA requires years of expensive physical experiments, leaving successful therapies rare. RiboLead is a deep learning model that predicts RNA-small molecule binding affinity to accurately screen RNA drug candidates. The model improves on three stages of the model pipeline: 1) On input, it replaces dependency on scarce 3D structures with evolutionary profiles, secondary structures, and language model embeddings to establish biological context; 2) On fusion, a co-attention mechanism with tanh gating allows RNA sequences and drug atoms to interact in a way that resembles physical binding; and 3) in training, ensemble-derived quantified uncertainty enables a self-distillation filtered by quality, tackling the paucity of known RNA-drug interactions. Tested against 10 frontier models, RiboLead shows superior generalization, with 90% accuracy in 5-fold CV and r=0.65 compared to r=0.58 prior when stratified by RNA type. We deployed RiboLead as an open-source web platform to accelerate physical screening and applied it to identify 89 candidate drug molecules as potential repurposing treatments for previously-undruggable cancers, ALS, SARS-CoV-2, and EDS.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking Cell‑Typing Algorithms for Visium HD Using Orthogonal Multiplexed Protein Ground Truth in Kaposi Sarcoma–Infected Tissues
authors: Saitheja Pucha, HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Laura Bassel, Frederick National Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Frederick, MD, USA, United States; Gil Kanfer, Laboratory of Receptor Biology and Gene Expression, NCI,National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Kathleen Noeller, Institute for Genome Sciences, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, USA, United States; Jose Mercado-Matos, HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Andrew Warner, Frederick National Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Frederick, MD, USA, United States; Baktiar Karim, Frederick National Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Frederick, MD, USA, United States; Joseph Ziegelbauer, HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Ramya Ramaswami, HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Elana Fertig, Institute for Genome Sciences, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, USA, United States; Robert Yarchoan, HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States; Daniel Naiman, Department of Applied Mathematics, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA, United States; Bahman Afsari, HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, United States
abstract: Visium HD captures transcriptomic signals at high spatial resolution, enabling precise study of tissue architecture, cell to cell interactions, and disease associated microenvironments in situ. However, accurate identification of individual cell types remains challenging due to low transcript counts, technical noise, segmentation inaccuracies, and lack of validated algorithms. To evaluate cell typing algorithms for Visium HD, we leveraged orthogonal information to establish a marker based ground truth. Because Visium HD cannot be performed simultaneously with multiplex protein imaging on the same section, we applied multiplex immunohistochemistry (IHC) on nearby serial sections from the same Kaposi Sarcoma sample. Images from both measurements were aligned using the SpatialData pipeline, with the viral protein LANA serving as a positive control for registration accuracy. Following alignment, IHC-derived intensities for CD34, CD38, and IBA1 were assigned to each segmented Visium HD cell. Otsu thresholding determined marker positivity on a per-cell basis, enabling classification into broad, marker-defined categories that served as a proxy ground truth. Using this framework, we benchmarked several cell typing algorithms, including SingleR, CellTypist, and RCTD, across multiple references and strategies (e.g., cluster-level typing for SingleR). Model performance was evaluated by comparing predicted cell types against the IHC-based classifications, revealing substantial variability across methods (from 15% to 51% accuracy for three classes). Overall, these results provide practical guidance for selecting effective cell typing strategies in Visium HD and establish a proof of concept for using orthogonal approaches to evaluate cell typing performance in high-resolution spatial transcriptomics. This approach could potentially be used with other tissues and a wider array of protein markers.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Intron-based non-coding variation as a predictor of disease stage in multiple myeloma
authors: Stephanie Kim, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, United States; Chrissy Baker, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, United States; Justin Taylor, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, United States; Benjamin Diamond, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, United States; Vanessa Aguiar-Pulido, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) is an incurable hematologic malignancy originating in the plasma cells of bone marrow. Despite advances in treatment, accurately predicting disease progression remains a major clinical challenge. While several high-risk genetic features have been defined, the role of intronic and synonymous variants in MM progression and prognosis remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate intron-based non-coding and synonymous variant burden as potential biomarkers for disease state and progression in MM. We integrate single-nucleotide variant data from the Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation (MMRF) CoMMpass study with curated intron annotations from the Minor Intron Database (MiDB). Using intronic variant and clinical features, we created machine learning models to predict each patientâ€™s International Staging System (ISS) stage, a standard prognostic score. Preliminary results show that a Random Forest (RF) model achieved the best performance, with a test accuracy of 70.4% (kappa = 0.53). A linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) model also demonstrated statistically significant performance, with an accuracy of 63.6% (kappa=0.44). Notably, the most informative predictors included creatinine levels and fraction of synonymous variants, non-canonical intronic variants, and untranslated region (UTR) variants. These results suggest that intronic variant features contribute to disease stratification in MM and may provide complementary predictive value beyond traditional clinical and coding-based genomic features. Future work will leverage high-depth whole-genome sequencing for improved resolution, alongside ongoing efforts in model refinement, feature expansion, and hyperparameter tuning to enhance predictive performance.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ChromeZoo reveals chromatin organization across mammalian evolution
authors: Anupama Jha, Department of Genetics, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, CT, United States; Xumeng Zhang, Department of Biomedical Informatics and Medical Education, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, WA, United States; Jacob Schreiber, Department of Genomics and Computational Biology, UMass Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, United States; Olga Dudchenko, Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA, United States; Georgi K. Marinov, Department of Genetics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA, United States; Annie Staker, Bio-Rad Laboratories, United States; Ghulam Murtaza, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, WA, United States; Shengqi Hang, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, United States; Tangqi Fang, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, United States; Anshul Kundaje, Stanford University, United States; William Greenleaf, Stanford University, United States; Sheng Wang, University of Washington, United States; Erez Lieberman Aiden, Baylor College of Medicine, United States; William Stafford Noble, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, WA, United States
abstract: DNA in the nucleus folds into loops, domains, and compartments. Genomes across mammalian evolution contain these higher-order chromatin structures, which are crucial for conserved and species-specific gene regulation. Sequence-to-function models for predicting chromatin organization, such as AlphaGenome and Orca, have two major limitations. First, they fail to capture species-specific effects outside their training set. Second, they can only capture interactions within 1 MB of the diagonal at 4 KB resolution, ignoring interactions at >1 MB genomic distances or capturing them at coarser resolution. To overcome these limitations, we present ChromeZoo, a chromatin foundation model that predicts whole-chromosome chromatin interactions at loop resolution from chromatin accessibility data and DNA sequences. ChromeZoo leverages Hi-C and ATAC-seq data from 18 mammalian species, outperforms the state-of-the-art AlphaGenome model in predicting chromatin organization, and excels at learning structural features such as loops, TADs, and compartments across mammalian evolution.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: MIMIC: A Generative Multimodal Foundation Model for Biomolecules
authors: Siavash Golkar, Center for Data Science, New York University, United States; Irina Espejo, Center for Data Science, New York University, United States; Jake Kovalic, Applied Physics, Yale University, United States; Samuel Sledzieski, Center for Computational Biology, Flatiron Institute, United States; Minhuan Li, Center for Computational Mathematics, Flatiron Institute, United States; Ksenia Sokolova, Princeton Precision Health, Princeton University, United States; Geraud Krawezik, Scientific Computing Core, Flatiron Institute, United States; Alberto Bietti, Center for Computational Mathematics, Flatiron Institute, United States; Claudia Skok Gibbs, Center for Data Science, New York University, United States; Shengwei Xiong, Chemistry, New York University, United States; Pilar Cossio, Center for Computational Mathematics, Flatiron Institute, United States; Sonya Hanson, Center for Computational Biology, Flatiron Institute, United States; Alisha Jones, Chemistry, New York University, United States; Olga Troyanskaya, Princeton Precision Health, Princeton University, United States; Shirley Ho, Center for Computational Astrophysics, Flatiron Institute, United States
abstract: AI models in biology remain largely fragmented: protein language models, genomic sequence models, and regulatory forward models each operate in isolation, estimating conditional distributions over a single modality rather than the full joint distribution of biological states. We introduce MIMIC, a generative multimodal foundation model that learns a unified latent representation spanning DNA, RNA, protein, and textual modalities. MIMIC is trained on LORE, a large-scale multimodal aligned dataset that we developed for this purpose. By approximating the joint distribution over modalities, MIMIC enables bidirectional translation across the genome, transcriptome, and proteome, and supports flexible conditioning on any available subset of modalities at inference time. We show that multimodal representations achieve competitive or state-of-the-art performance across PFMBench and mRNABench on diverse tasks including function, developability, localization, and interaction, positioning MIMIC as a foundation model for molecular biology. On splice site prediction, MIMIC outperforms SpliceAI and AlphaGenome at the gene level and uniquely supports transcript-conditioned inference, recovering internal splice structure given transcript boundary information. Finally, we show that MIMIC enables multimodal conditioned generative design tasks. Around the pathogenic HBB IVS-II-654 C>T variant, MIMIC generates an RNA sequence that suppresses aberrant splice-site gain, even in windows not overlapping the pathogenic mutation. For protein design targeting PD-L1 and SARS-CoV-2 Spike binders, conditioning on backbone structure and MaSIF surface features produces higher-quality sequences than backbone conditioning alone, measured by AlphaFold2 pLDDT and AlphaFold3 co-folding. Together, these results position MIMIC as a shift from variant scoring to molecular state simulation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Virtual Cell Generative AI Enables Cell-Type-Targeted Therapeutic Design
authors: Shuo Zhang, Hunter College, City University of New York, United States; Rahul Ohlan, Graduate Center, City University of New York, United States; Mohammadsadeq Mottaqi, Graduate Center, City University of New York, United States; Lei Xie, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Generative AI shows strong potential for drug discovery, but most existing methods remain focused on the target-based one-drug-one-gene paradigm, which is often inadequate for chronic and systemic diseases. Here, we introduce GEM-GPT, a transcriptomics-guided molecular generation framework for cell-type-targeted therapeutic design. Operating in a virtual cell context, GEM-GPT uses gene expression representations from a single-cell foundation model to guide molecular generation through our deep fused attention, enabling compounds that shift diseased cell states toward desired healthy phenotypes. GEM-GPT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and generalizes well to unseen cell types. In opioid use disorder (OUD) drug discovery, it identifies both novel candidate compounds and approved drugs capable of modulating cell-type-specific disease phenotypes.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CyPerPred: Learning Permeability of Cyclic Peptides via Structural and Physicochemical Representations
authors: Sohyun Chung, Korea University, South Korea
abstract: Motivation: Cyclic peptides offer significant advantages in drug design, including high binding affinity and low toxicity, making them promising candidates for next-generation therapeutics. However, their broader application has been hindered by poor cell permeability, which limits their ability to effectively target intracellular sites. Recent studies have explored the prediction of membrane permeability for cyclic peptides. However, most approaches rely on two-dimensional (2D) representations and fail to capture the underlying physical mechanisms. While some methods incorporate three-dimensional (3D) features, they often depend on conformations generated by RDKit, which may lack sufficient accuracy. Precise 3D structural information is critical, as the permeability of cyclic peptides is largely governed by their conformational states, which are factors that cannot be adequately represented by 2D features alone. Incorporating accurate 3D structures together with physics-based descriptors (e.g., solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) and polar surface area (PSA)) enables models to better reflect these mechanisms, leading to more reliable and physically grounded predictions. Results: In this study, we propose CyPerPred, a predictive model for cyclic peptide permeability that integrates three-dimensional conformational information with physicochemical descriptors within a learned representation framework. Specifically, we employ a three-dimensional equivariant graph neural network to effectively encode geometric and structural features of cyclic peptides. We evaluate CyPerPred on the CycPeptMPDB-4D dataset and demonstrate that it achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of mean squared error metrics. Our evaluation spans multiple settings, including in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and permeability cliff scenarios, highlighting the robustness of the proposed approach.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: An Agentic AI Plug-and-Play Framework for Causal Inference in Biomedical Data
authors: Xiaotong Xu, Georgetown University, United States; Ao Yuan, Georgetown University, United States; Ming Tan, Georgetown University, United States; James Li, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Causal inference is central to biomedical research but requires careful selection of statistical methods under varying study designs and data characteristics. We present a plug-and-play agentic AI framework for causal inference that combines natural language understanding with deterministic statistical estimation. Given a user's natural language query and dataset, the system maps user intent to appropriate analytical pipelines using a large language model. The LLM is used strictly for orchestration and does not participate in numerical estimation, ensuring reliability and reproducibility, while all causal effect estimation is performed by deterministic statistical modules. The framework adopts a plug-and-play architecture in which each causal inference method is implemented as an independent module with standardized interfaces, allowing new tools to be integrated without modifying the core system. Supported methods include doubly robust average treatment effect estimators, including binary eDRIP, and inverse probability weighted survival analysis. We evaluate the framework on real-world biomedical datasets and show that it achieves performance comparable to expert-specified pipelines while reducing manual effort and mis-specification. Different causal inference tasks (e.g., survival, continuous, and binary outcomes) require distinct statistical methods, motivating automated method selection via LLM-based routing. This work demonstrates how combining agentic AI-based orchestration with deterministic statistical methods enables scalable, reproducible, and extensible causal inference in biomedical research.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PerturbCausal: Can Virtual Cell Models Replace Perturb-seq for Causal Network Inference?
authors: Aayan Alwani, Independent Researcher, United States
abstract: Virtual cell models are deep neural networks that predict transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations and are proposed as in silico substitutes for laboratory CRISPR screens. Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber (2025) recently showed that current models fail to outperform simple linear baselines at per-gene prediction; we ask whether the same holds downstream when their predictions are used to recover causal gene regulatory networks. We introduce PerturbCausal, a benchmark that pushes predictions from four virtual cell models (GEARS, CPA, Geneformer, and the 2025 Arc Institute STATE foundation model) through four causal discovery algorithms (GIES, inspre, PC, NOTEARS) on the Replogle K562 and RPE1 Perturb-seq datasets and the Norman 2019 K562 dataset. Across five seeds, the three pre-2025 models do not significantly outperform a sparse linear regression trained on control cells alone. STATE appears to exceed the linear baseline at a single seed (F1 = 0.462, 320-cell embedding subset), but this does not replicate: across three seeds F1 = 0.184 with a 95 percent CI of [-0.415, 0.783] that spans zero, so even the 2025 foundation model does not robustly beat sparse linear regression, and its absolute causal F1 remains below 0.5. The conclusion is backend- and context-invariant: GEARS and CPA retrained on a second cell type (RPE1) and a second perturbation modality (Norman CRISPRa), evaluated under all four backends, never exceed the linear comparator and never reach real-data quality. Both deep models sit at or below a per-backend permutation chance floor in four of six cross-dataset cells; the two above-floor points (PC on RPE1, and GEARS under inspre on Norman by a single-seed margin) are observational co-expression or near-band, not interventional recovery, and remain an order of magnitude below substitutable quality. We reconcile two competing narratives in the recent literature, mode collapse and effect-size inflation, as two views of the same failure: deep models predict similar dense response patterns across perturbations. A model-agnostic quantile-matching calibration corrects the magnitude marginal exactly yet does not close the causal gap on held-out perturbations, locating the residual in joint-distribution structure (gene-gene covariance and edge orientation) that distributional calibration cannot reach. The benchmark, post-hoc quantile-matching calibration module, and reproducibility code are released as an open-source Python package.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Deep Learning Multi-Omics Integration Identifies New Molecular Subtypes of Lung Cancer
authors: Bianca Gonda, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States; Derek Wang, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States; Sayed Mehedi Azim, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States; Gabrielle Romano, Department of Pharmacology and Physiology, Drexel University College of Medicine, Philadelphia, PA, USA, United States; Iman Dehzangi, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States
abstract: Background: Lung cancer is a heterogeneous disease characterized by diverse molecular alterations that influence tumor behavior and clinical outcomes. While prior studies have identified molecular subtypes using single data modalities, integrative approaches remain underexplored and may better capture tumor complexity. Methods: Gene expression and somatic mutation data from TCGA (primarily LUAD and LUSC; n = 299) were processed and filtered for protein-coding genes. Separate autoencoders were applied to each data modality for dimensionality reduction, followed by concatenation of latent representations and recursive model-based unsupervised clustering of latent features to identify molecular subtypes. Downstream biological and clinical analyses were performed to characterize clusters. Results: We identified nine distinct clusters with varying biological and clinical characteristics. Several clusters were enriched for specific histological subtypes, while others demonstrated mixed composition, suggesting shared molecular programs across histological classifications. Pathway analysis revealed distinct enrichment patterns across clusters, including immune and inflammatory signaling (interferon alpha and gamma responses, IL-2/STAT5, IL-6/JAK/STAT3) and proliferative pathways (E2F signaling and MYC targets). Additionally, clustering patterns were associated with smoking status and smoking-associated mutational signatures, indicating potential links between environmental exposure and molecular subtype. Conclusion/Significance: These findings demonstrate that multi-modal integration of gene expression and mutation data can identify biologically meaningful lung cancer subtypes, capturing both histology-associated and cross-lineage molecular features.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Predicting Gene Mutations in Colon Cancer Using Deep Dependency Learning on a Directed Co-Occurrence Asymmetry Graph
authors: Collin Sumrell, University of Oklahoma, United States; Aleksandr Shishkin, University of Oklahoma, United States; Marmar Moussa, University of Oklahoma, United States
abstract: Accurate prediction of mutational dependencies to model tumor evolution can improve our understanding of cancer progression and is crucial for early diagnosis and interventions. This is especially true in colorectal tumorigenesis, which often follows stepwise mutational progression patterns. Here, we propose a graph-based approach to infer both a longest path and a global gene mutational order based on data-driven co-occurrence conditional probabilities. We train long-term deep learning models (including a dilated Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network) to predict, for each path and at each pseudo-temporal step, whether the next gene in the inferred path is mutated. We use a large gene network (23,858 genes) and a large curated cohort (2,344 samples) of publicly available human colon adenocarcinoma samples for path inference and training and validation tasks. From the proposed directed co-occurrence asymmetry graph, we inferred a longest path and global graph-derived mutational order. Both proposed long-term models achieve high prediction accuracies and dramatically improve precision and recall in mutation prediction over previous studiesâ€™ results, with a model trained on the longest weighted path configuration achieving the best results overall. In conclusion, this study highlights the potential of inferring and validating mutational order in colon cancer via a graph-deep learning combined approach.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Unified imputation of missing data modalities and features in multi-omic data through shared representation learning
authors: Ananthan Nambiar, University of Washington, United States; Carlo Melendez, University of Washington, United States; William Noble, University of Washington, United States
abstract: Multi-omic studies promise a more comprehensive view of biological systems by jointly measuring multiple molecular layers. In practice, however, such datasets are rarely complete: entire molecular modalities may be missing for many samples, and observed modalities often contain substantial feature-level missingness. Existing imputation approaches typically address only one of these two problems, relying either on feature-level imputation within a single modality or on pairwise translation models that cannot accommodate arbitrary combinations of missing modalities. As a result, there is, to our knowledge, no unified framework for reconstructing both missing data modalities and missing values within those modalities. We present MIMIR, a deep learning framework for unified multi-omic imputation that addresses both missing modalities and missing values through shared representation learning. MIMIR first learns modality-specific representations using masked autoencoders and then projects these representations into a common latent space, enabling reconstruction from any subset of observed modalities. Evaluated on pan-cancer multi-omic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, MIMIR consistently outperforms baseline methods across a range of missing-modality and missing-value scenarios, including missing completely at random and missing not at random settings. Analysis of the learned shared space reveals structured cross-modal dependencies that explain modality-specific differences in imputation accuracy, with transcriptional and epigenetic modalities forming a strongly aligned core and copy number variation contributing more distinct signal. Together, these results demonstrate that shared representation learning provides an effective and flexible foundation for multi-omic imputation under heterogeneous missingness.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: H&E to Spatial Transcriptomics Inference: Topology-Aware Encoding and Mixture of Residual Modeling with LLM Gene Semantics
authors: Yuqi Cheng, Georgia Tech, United States; Boshuai Zhang, UCSD, United States; Chandra Sekhar Reddy Edula, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Mo Sun, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Ziqi Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Xiuwei Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression while preserving tissue architecture, but its high cost and technical complexity limit routine use. In contrast, H&E whole-slide images are inexpensive and widely available, motivating computational prediction of spatial gene expression from histology. Existing methods typically rely on a single global predictor and are evaluated mainly with vector-level metrics, limiting their ability to preserve boundary-resolved spatial patterns and to generalize to genes unseen during training. We present two complementary frameworks for histology-to-ST inference. TIGEM introduces topology-aware encoding, using local geometric and topological constraints to guide attention-based representation learning and improve spatial coherence and boundary fidelity. MiraST introduces a mixture-of-residual formulation that decomposes expression into a global gene-conditioned prediction plus latent tissue-state-specific residual corrections, yielding more flexible modeling and interpretable region-of-interest maps. Both models incorporate large-language-model-derived gene semantic embeddings, enabling strict zero-shot prediction for out-of-distribution genes by directly substituting text-derived gene embeddings at inference time. Across multiple large public ST benchmarks spanning diverse tissues and pathological conditions, the proposed methods achieve consistently improved performance over existing approaches on standard metrics, including mean squared error and Pearson correlation, and on a new graph-spectral concordance metric designed to assess spatial boundary preservation. Qualitative analyses further show sharper biomarker boundaries and stronger alignment with pathology-relevant tissue compartments. In addition, MiraST demonstrates nontrivial zero-shot gene prediction and improved generalization when unseen genes are semantically related to those observed during training. These results establish topology-aware encoding and residual tissue-state modeling as effective principles for accurate, spatially faithful, and more generalizable histology-based transcriptomics inference.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Splice site classification and usage quantification across tissues
authors: Matthew Runyan, Northeastern University, United States; Saumya Gupta, Northeastern University, United States; Jennifer Dy, Northeastern University, United States; Predrag Radivojac, Northeastern University, United States; Yohannes Tesfaigzi, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Peter Castaldi, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Ayan Paul, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Alternative splicing affects over 95% of human protein-coding genes and is a major driver of disease. Sequence-based deep learning models have made substantial progress in predicting splice sites from pre-mRNA, however most models have been trained on reference annotations or aggregated data rather than splice site usage quantified from individual RNA-seq samples. We trained a dilated convolutional neural network, SPLAIRE (SPLicing in AIRway Epithelial cells), on splice site usage quantified from RNA-seq across 100 human airway epithelial cell donors to perform splice site classification and splice site usage quantification. SPLAIRE was compared against SpliceAI, Pangolin, and SpliceTransformer across five tissues. SPLAIRE outperforms these existing models on splice site usage prediction across all tissues including those held out during training. When classification performance was stratified by usage level, all models showed substantially degraded classification at low-usage sites. Variant effect prediction performance was assesed using reporter assays and fine-mapped sQTLs from 49 GTEx tissues and found that all models performed in a similar range with performance declining steadily for variants further from splice junctions. Gradient-based attribution analysis showed that the regression head distributes signal across wider regions than the classification head, that low-usage sites show more dispersed and less positive attribution, and that the model learns distinct patterns for rare non-canonical donor dinucleotides.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: EpiFold: A Multimodal Framework for Generalizable Antibody-Specific Epitope Prediction
authors: Eunha Lee, Korea University, South Korea
abstract: Antibody-specific epitope prediction is a fundamental problem in immunoinformatics with direct applications in vaccine design, therapeutic antibody development, and drug discovery. Despite recent advances, the task remains unsolved. Sequence-based approaches lack the structural context required to model conformational epitopes, which constitute the majority of antigenic sites. Structure-based methods have demonstrated stronger performance; however, prevailing methods, as evaluated on AsEP, the largest benchmark for this task, rely on experimentally determined antibody-antigen complex structures as input. This carries a critical conceptual limitation: when a bound complex structure is available, epitopes can be identified through simple distance-based criteria alone. Moreover, experimental complex structures are scarce and expensive, making such methods inapplicable to real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we present EpiFold, a sequence-driven epitope prediction framework requiring no experimental structural data. Given only antibody and antigen sequences, EpiFold utilizes monomeric structures independently predicted by AlphaFold3 and ABodyBuilder3, bypassing the need for bound complex coordinates. To explicitly account for the imperfection of predicted structures, EpiFold leverages all structures in the AF3-predicted ensemble and integrates self-confidence metrics including pLDDT, thereby modulating the influence of structurally uncertain regions. From the predicted structures and sequences, we extract complementary 1D sequence features, 2D relational representations, and 3D geometric descriptors, jointly processed through a transformer-based architecture for residue-level epitope prediction. Evaluated on the AsEP benchmark, EpiFold achieves competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines, while operating under substantially more realistic assumptions, offering a more generalizable solution to antibody-specific epitope prediction.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PUFFIN: Protein Unit Discovery via Functional Supervision
authors: Gökçe Uludoğan, Bogazici University, Turkey; Buse Giledereli, Bogazici University, Turkey; Elif Ozkirimli, Roche AG, Switzerland; Arzucan Ozgur, Bogazici University, Turkey
abstract: Motivation: Proteins carry out biological functions through the coordinated action of groups of residues organized into structural arrangements. These arrangements, which we refer to as protein units, exist at an intermediate scale, being larger than individual residues yet smaller than entire proteins. A deeper understanding of protein function can be achieved by identifying these units and their associations with function. However, existing approaches either focus on residue-level signals, rely on curated annotations, or segment protein structures without incorporating functional information, thereby limiting interpretable analysis of structure-function relationships. Results: We introduce PUFFIN, a data-driven framework for discovering protein units by jointly learning structural partitioning and functional supervision. PUFFIN represents proteins as residue-level structure graphs and applies a graph neural network with a structure-aware pooling mechanism that partitions each protein into multi-residue units, with functional supervision that shapes the partition. We show that the learned units are structurally coherent, exhibit organized associations with molecular function, and show meaningful correspondence with curated InterPro annotations. Together, these results demonstrate that PUFFIN provides an interpretable framework for analyzing structureâ€“function relationships using learned protein units and their statistical function associations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: BOSS (Beta Optimal Shrinking Score): Sparse Signal Discovery for High-Dimensional Molecular Studies
authors: Osorio Meirelles, National Institute on Aging, United States
abstract: High-dimensional studies such as GWAS and multi-omics analyses often quantify very large numbers of candidate features, although only a small subset reflects true biological signal. This creates a practical need for models that preserve predictive performance, reduce false positives, and return short, interpretable candidate lists. We developed BOSS (Beta Optimal Shrinking Score), a regression-based method that uses false-discovery-rate-informed shrinkage to account for the number of predictors tested. To validate our approach, we built a synthetic benchmark with 1,000 samples, one true signal, three noise levels, and k ranging from 10 to 1,000,000 independent predictors. We compared BOSS against LASSO using repeated simulations and evaluated prediction, precision, and recall. At lower dimensionality (k â‰¤ 10,000), both methods achieved similar predictive RÂ², but BOSS produced fewer false positives. At 100,000 to 1,000,000 predictors, BOSS typically selected about 1-2 variables, whereas LASSO selected hundreds to more than 1,000. Across 100,000 to 1,000,000 predictors, BOSS maintained predictive RÂ² of about 0.49-0.50 versus 0.33-0.34 for LASSO under moderate noise and about 0.18-0.19 versus 0.02-0.06 under high noise. These results support BOSS as a promising approach for settings where true signals are rare and validation is computationally expensive. Potential applications include GWAS fine-mapping, eQTL discovery, and multi-omics feature screening. Ongoing work extends this framework to correlated predictors in more realistic biological data structures.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Spatial phenotyping linking single cells genomics to disease pathology through joint deep representation learning
authors: Chenfeng He, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison, United States; Haotian Ma, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison, United States; Pubudu Kumarage, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison, United States; Xuerou Li, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin at Madison, United States; Kalpana Arachchilage, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA., United States; Shuang Liu, Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA., United States; Daifeng Wang, University of Wisconsin - Madison, United States
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) simultaneously captures gene expression and tissue architecture, providing unprecedented opportunities to study tissue organization and disease biology. However, identifying disease- or phenotype-associated spatial niches from multimodal ST data often requires extensive pathology annotation and substantial computational effort, particularly at near single-cell resolution. We previously developed a graph-learning framework that predicts Alzheimerâ€™s disease (AD) phenotype-associated cells (PACs) across cohorts using population-scale single-cell RNA-seq data (scRNA-seq). Here, leveraging multimodal ST and scRNA-seq data, we extend this framework to identify spatially informed PACs by learning joint representations of gene expression and spatial organization, thereby assigning a phenotype-association score (PAC-score) for each spot or cellular coordinate within ST data, termed phenoSPA. Using the phenoSPA latent space and PAC-scores, we demonstrate accurate cross-cohort prediction of disease-associated niches, subtyping of morphologically indistinguishable but biologically distinct regions in breast cancer, and dissection of pathological microenvironments related to disease markers such as amyloid plaques in AD. In addition, the cross-modality generative capability of phenoSPA highlights its potential for modeling disease progression and advancing spatially resolved studies of AD and other complex diseases.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: lncRNA Localization Prediction: Harder than it Seems
