authors: Jason Miller, Hood College, United States; Weijun Yi, West Virginia University, United States; Donald Adjeroh, West Virginia University, United States
abstract: The human genome contains about as many long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes as protein-coding genes, yet many lncRNAs have yet to be functionally characterized. Subcellular localization data can provide clues. Among the few lncRNAs with functional characterizations, some are specific to the nucleus or the cytoplasm of cells. Furthermore, abundance information has been generated for some lncRNAs by sequencing nuclear and cytoplasmic complements of human cell lines. Localization and sequence data are available from the lncATLAS and Ensembl databases, respectively. Since 2018, computer scientists have used those data sources to train and evaluate several machine learning models. Their publications claim 72â€“74% accuracy and 79-85% AUROC at the task of predicting the dominant cellular compartment of a lncRNA given its nucleotide sequence. A common feature of these experiments was a filter that excluded RNAs whose known localization signal was not entirely nuclear or cytoplasmic. We argue that excluding cases with intermediate values gives a misleading boost to the model performance metrics. This â€˜middle exclusionâ€™ filter cannot be applied to unlabeled data, for which the models are designed. Using published models and our own models, we consistently achieve 61% accuracy and 67% AUROC on unfiltered test sets. We show that filtering the training set does not boost performance, but filtering the test set does boost performance metrics. Based on those results, we claim that predicting lncRNA subcellular localization, given the nucleotide sequence alone, remains a challenging problem. We present updated comparisons using the benchmark we proposed.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Predictive models of the genetic bases underlying budding yeast fitness in multiple environments
authors: Kenia Segura Abá, Genetics and Genome Sciences Graduate Program, Michigan State University, United States; Paulo Izquierdo, Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, New Mexico State University, United States; Gustavo de Los Campos, Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Michigan State University, United States; Melissa Lehti-Shiu, Department of Plant Biology, Michigan State University, United States; Shin-Han Shiu, Department of Plant Biology, Michigan State University, United States
abstract: The ability of organisms to adapt and survive depends on the effects of genes and the environment on fitness. However, the multigenic nature of fitness and genotype-by-environment interactions hinder our understanding of the genetic basis of fitness. Here, we established fitness prediction models for 35 environments using machine learning and existing fitness data and different genetic variant types for a Saccharomyces cerevisiae population. Models revealed that the predictive ability of genetic variants varied across environments, with copy number variants explaining the majority of fitness variation in most cases. Model interpretation showed that different variant types identified distinct gene sets associated with predictive variants. These gene sets were significantly enriched in experimentally validated genes affecting fitness in only a subset of environments, indicating that many genes influencing fitness remain unexplored. Notably, non-experimentally validated genes were more important than validated ones for fitness predictions. Gene contributions to predictions were both isolate- and environment-dependent, pointing to gene-by-gene and gene-by-environment interactions. Furthermore, models uncovered experimentally validated and novel candidate genetic interactions for a well-characterized stress, the fungicide benomyl. These findings highlight the feasibility of identifying the genetic basis of fitness by using different genetic variant types and offer novel targets for future functional analysis.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Cardiomyocyte Maturation & Aging Clock (CMAC) - A Probabilistic Transcriptional Age Atlas for Murine Cardiomyocyte Maturation
authors: Kwaku Quansah, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, United States; Sean Murphy, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, United States; Esther Kwon, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, United States; Emma Anderson, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, United States; Chulan Kwon, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Background Cardiomyocyte (CM) maturation spans embryogenesis through postnatal life, encompassing coordinated transcriptional, metabolic, and structural transitions. Disruption of this program underlies congenital heart disease and limits the utility of stem cell-derived CMs in regenerative medicine. Despite numerous single-cell RNA-sequencing studies of CM development, no unified computational framework exists for estimating transcriptional maturation state in a batch-invariant, quantitative manner across datasets and conditions. Objective To build a probabilistic transcriptional age atlas of murine CM maturation (CMAC) that enables absolute biological age estimation for novel datasets including disease models. Methods We integrated 22 murine scRNA-seq datasets (75,740 cells, E7.75 to P84) using scVI, a deep generative model that represents gene expression as a negative binomial distribution, learning a 50-dimensional batch-corrected latent space across multiple sequencing platforms. An XGBoost regressor was trained on the latent representations to estimate cardiomyocyte age. Results The latent space recapitulated continuous developmental progression from E7.75 to P84. Leave One Dataset Out (LODO) achieved a pooled Pearson r=0.74, and MAE of 3.52; Leave-One-Timepoint-Out (LOTO) achieved an MAE of 3.21 days, demonstrating strong interpolation performance across developmental stages. Mapping HCN1 knockout cardiomyocytes revealed a significant maturation deficit at P14 (predicted age 27.0 vs 33.1 days in wildtype), validated by differential expression of sarcomere, metabolic, calcium handling, and ECM maturation markers. Conclusion This framework provides a generalizable tool for quantifying CM maturation state across technologies and disease conditions, with direct applications in congenital heart disease modeling and cardiac regenerative medicine

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking Spatial Transcriptomics Alignment Methods for 3D Tissue Reconstruction
authors: Jan Matthias, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Jianing Yao, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Vani Padmakumar, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Guan Gui, Johns Hopkins University, United States; An Wang, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Stephanie Hicks, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Unlike bulk or single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables mRNA quantification while preserving the spatial organization of gene expression across tissues. In a typical ST workflow, consecutive tissue slices are collected from a sample, but they are usually analysed as separate two-dimensional sections rather than being aligned into a unified three-dimensional (3D) representation. Aligning slices into a three-dimensional space enables downstream analyses, such as 3D domain clustering and spatial differential expression. Although numerous alignment algorithms have been proposed, their relative suitability for specific tasks and spatial transcriptomic technology remains unclear. In this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 14 alignment algorithms across multiple ST acquisition technologies, spanning approaches from deep learning to diffeomorphic registration and optimal transport. We consider three alignment settings: pairwise tissue alignment within a single donor, 3D reconstruction of multiple slices, and alignment across sequencing technologies. All tasks are carried out on both biologically derived and in silico generated ST data. Based on cell-type matching accuracy across slices, SPACEL and SPIRAL perform best for pairwise alignment, while SPACEL performs best for 3D reconstruction. However, runtime and compute benchmarking on in silico data shows that SPACEL requires, on average, higher computational resources. In this benchmark, we show that no single algorithm is universally optimal in terms of accuracy. Instead, we find that performance depends on the alignment objective and the ST technology, and there can be large differences in computational efficiency between algorithms.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Cell Ontology aware hierarchical single‑cell annotation in healthy and disease intestinal epithelial cell cultures
authors: Timothy Rumbell, IBM, United States; Vibha Anand, IBM, United States; Scott Espenschied, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Ryan Musich, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Joao Bettencourt, IBM, Ireland; Natasha Mulligan, IBM, Ireland; Viatcheslav Gurev, IBM, United States; James Kozloski, IBM, United States; Jianying Hu, IBM, United States; Thaddeus Stappenbeck, Cleveland Clinic, United States
abstract: Biomedical Foundation models provide high quality embeddings for single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) datasets, enabling models to classify cell types with high predictive accuracy, especially for mature cell types. This is particularly true when the model is fine-tuned with labels from comparable (in vivo) scRNA-seq dataset. However, such an approach cannot provide reliable estimates of uncertainty for maturing cells that are observed in in vitro cultures5. We have recently trained models that leverage the labeling scheme from the Cell Ontology to effectively pre-train a universal classifier. Using ontology aware Biomedical Foundation Models for RNA with 32M (masked language model (MLM)) and 47M (whole cell encoderâ€“decoder (WCED)) parameters, we annotate cell type labels across healthy and disease tissue in vitro datasets along with a matched in vivo reference dataset. We are then able to use measures of entropy along with other analyses to quantify uncertainty (or variability) of annotations at multiple hierarchical levels of the Cell Ontology, thus providing a new view into sub-populations of cells. Across datasets, the 47M model exhibits higher baseline prediction entropy and ontology path entropy, i.e. entropy of node or path activation frequencies, than the 32M model. In healthy in vitro cultures, both models show reduced entropy relative to in vivo data suggesting stable cellular states. Despite lower baseline entropy, the 32M model exhibited more variability in prediction in inflammatory perturbation dataset. Ontology aware foundation models enable hierarchical annotation at different granularities and therefore may provide valuable insights into the cellular sub-types present as clusters in datasets.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Mapping Trajectories of Cellular Fates on Single-Cell Lineage Trees
authors: Divya Koyyalagunta, Weill Cornell/MSKCC, United States; Quaid Morris, MSKCC, United States
abstract: Understanding the trajectories of cellular differentiation is central to some of the most fundamental questions in biology, from the complex orchestration underlying embryonic development to the perturbed contexts underlying disease. Recent lineage tracing technologies enable the simultaneous readout of cellular phenotypes and lineages at a single-cell level. However, current computational methods to model this data either do not make use of this lineage information or assume that cellular differentiation always follows a stereotyped, unidirectional hierarchy, therefore excluding many biological applications of interest such as cancer. In this work we present FateTrace, a method to infer ancestral cellular states along single-cell lineages using a model of cellular differentiation that captures the complexity of transitions in both normal and perturbed contexts such as cancer. Building on our recent work on gradient-based, multi-objective optimization, FateTrace efficiently samples multiple plausible fate labelings supported by the data and scores these hypotheses using two priors when available: single-cell gene expression and multiple biological replicates. We show that FateTrace outperforms baseline methods in recovering fate maps on simulated data with a known ground truth. Applied to single-cell lineage tracing data from a mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma, FateTrace reconstructs the temporal ordering of fate transitions across tumor evolution and infers which state transitions are enriched at critical transition points such as metastasis.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A constrained distance space for anti-CRISPR detection in deployment-grade phage proteomes
authors: Chan-Seok Jeong, Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, South Korea
abstract: Anti-CRISPRs (Acrs), phage proteins that disable bacterial CRISPR-Cas, are increasingly deployed as switches for programmable genome editing. Discovery is bottlenecked by an extreme prevalence skew: only a few hundred sequences survive identity-based deduplication of validated entries, while a phage proteome offers ~10^5 unannotated candidates. Conventional predictors are still benchmarked on artificially balanced 1:1 splits, and once realistic prevalence and 40% identity control are enforced, the conventional deep model collapses. We learn an embedding, not a label. A two-layer head over a non-trainable PLM projects pooled features onto a hypersphere, trained with a margin loss against semi-hard distractors and a centroid-distance focal term that converts geometry into a calibrated score. Difficult negatives are mined in two steps: a per-epoch global ranking against the centroid feeds shortlists into batches, where triplets are then refined by a semi-hard rule. Splits use 40% identity clustering nested within five-fold cross-validation. At a 1:383 prior, AUPRC moves from 0.017 (deep-classifier baseline, ESM-1b) to 0.355, and to 0.508 when the encoder scales to ESM-2 (3B). The projection space and training dynamics are also analysed. Lastly, we investigate the interpretability with an in silico alanine scan of AcrIF11 and isolate the catalytic His7. A constrained distance space, in place of a probability head, generalises to other rare-positive function-discovery problems.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A systematic benchmark of Hi-C enhancement deep learning models reveals discordance between contact-map similarity and biological feature recovery
authors: Hye-lim Mo, Soongsil University, South Korea; Je-Keun Rhee, Soongsil University, South Korea
abstract: Deep learning models for Hi-C matrix enhancement have proliferated in recent years, and are typically evaluated using contact-map similarity metrics such as Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) and structural similarity index (SSIM). Whether these metrics reflect the recovery of biologically meaningful chromatin structure has not been systematically tested. Here we benchmark eight representative Hi-C enhancement models — DeepHiC, DFHiC, HiCARN1, HiCARN2, HiCNN2, HiCPlus, iEnhance, and SRHiC. The evaluation spans eight contact-map similarity metrics covering the pixel, patch, TAD, and whole-map scales, three hierarchical biological features (A/B compartments, TADs, and chromatin loops), three cell lines (GM12878, K562, and CH12-LX), and nine sequencing depths (30M–540M reads), with five independent subsampling replicates per condition. Contact-map similarity metrics yielded inconsistent rankings. Most metrics, including PCC, HiCRep, TAD measure of concordance, and insulation score correlation, compressed all eight models into narrow ranges, whereas SSIM and directionality index correlation separated them into distinct groups. At least one model achieved a PCC above 0.87 while producing TAD directionality essentially uncorrelated with the reference. Biological feature recovery followed a clear scale-dependent pattern. A/B compartments were preserved above the unenhanced baseline by most models, TAD-scale recovery diverged across models and hierarchical levels, and loop detection separated models most sharply, with F1 scores ranging from near zero to nearly 0.5. In cross-species CH12-LX at 180M reads, every enhancement model produced TAD Jaccard scores below the unenhanced baseline at every hierarchical level. Beyond the input depths used during training, model performance plateaued or grew slowly while the unenhanced baseline continued to improve with deeper sequencing, exceeding every enhancement model in loop detection F1 at input depths of 300M reads and above in all three cell lines. Architectural complexity, training time, and GPU memory differed by orders of magnitude across models but did not predict biological feature recovery. These findings reveal a substantial discordance between contact-map similarity and biological feature recovery, and argue for evaluation protocols that report performance separately across pixel, TAD, and loop scales, alongside biological anchoring measures, when benchmarking Hi-C enhancement methods.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ViP-SegD: Virchow2-based Pixel-wise Segmentation of the Tumor Microenvironment in Breast Whole-slide Images
authors: Himangi Srivastava, Department of Medical Physics, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Leyla Seyed Ebrahimpour, Department of Medical Physics, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Jun Hun Oh, Department of Medical Physics, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Joseph Deasy, Department of Medical Physics, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Kevin Boehm, Department of Radiation Oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Fresia Pareja Zea, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Larry Norton, Department of Medicine, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Background: Spatial characterization of the tumor microenvironment (TME), including tumor epithelium, stroma, inflammatory infiltrates, and necrosis, has prognostic relevance in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). We developed ViP-SegD (Virchow2 Pixel-wise Segmentation Decoder), a scalable AI-assisted pipeline for generating pixel-level TME maps from H&E whole-slide images (WSIs). Methods: ViP-SegD begins with standardized slide preprocessing using Mussel, a computational pathology framework for whole-slide image loading, tissue tiling, coordinate tracking. Whole-slide images were tessellated into 224 Ã— 224 pixel patches, and patch-level features were extracted using a frozen Virchow2 encoder, which was pre-trained on 3.1 million histopathology slides spanning more than 40 tissue types. For pixel-level tissue classification, we used a lightweight convolutional decoder, with weights pre-trained on the Breast Cancer Semantic Segmentation (BCSS) dataset. This dataset includes 151 TCGA-TNBC whole-slide images with pixel-level annotations for five tissue types: tumor, stroma, inflammatory infiltrate, necrosis, and other. The decoder converts the Virchow2 patch-token into a full pixel prediction map. After inference, near-white background regions were removed by intensity thresholding, and we obtained reconstructed slide-level segmentation overlays with per-class GeoJSON annotations. Results: On the BCSS validation set, ViP-SegD achieved Dice scores of 0.773 for tumor, 0.705 for stroma, 0.628 for inflammatory infiltrate, and 0.743 for necrosis, with a 4-class macro-Dice of 0.712. Necrosis segmentation exceeded reported U-Net-based BCSS benchmarks. Independent pathologist review of TCGA-TNBC slides showed strong concordance, with 95 % of segmentations rated mostly correct. Conclusion: ViP-SegD enables scalable, annotation-efficient TME segmentation and supports downstream spatial biomarker analysis across TNBC.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Predicting Heat Stress-Responsive Cis-Regulatory Elements in Arabidopsis thaliana Using Machine Learning
authors: Jingyao Tang, Michigan State University, United States; Thilanka Ranaweera, Department of Plant Biology, Michigan State University, USA, United States; Rajneesh Singhal, Department of Plant Biology, Michigan State University, USA, United States; Shin-Han Shiu, CMSE, Department of Plant Biology, DOE-GLBRC, Michigan State University, USA, United States
abstract: Rising global temperatures threaten crop yields and future food security. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying heat response remains a key challenge and is critical for improving crop heat resilience. Here, we utilized classical machine learning and deep learning approaches to identify regulatory DNA sequences predictive of differential gene expression (DGE) across five heat-stress conditions (27Â°C, 30Â°C, 33Â°C, 36Â°C, and 39Â°C) in Arabidopsis thaliana. Genes were classified as significantly upregulated, downregulated, or non-responsive based on a false discovery rate Random Forest (RF) models were trained on k-mer-based features enriched within 2kb upstream and 0.5kb downstream of the transcriptional start site (TSS), and 0.5kb upstream and 2kb downstream of the transcriptional termination site (TTS). The Deep Learning model (Enformer-based architectures) was trained on open chromatin region data along with the Arabidopsis genome sequence to capture both close and long-range regulatory motifs. RF models showed moderate predictive performance for upregulated genes (F1 â‰ˆ 0.6~0.68), while the deep learning model matched the RF models in 4 temperatures and outperformed RF models at 39ÂºC. Spatial analysis of enriched k-mers revealed high frequency of regulatory motif presence in regions 200-400 bp upstream of the TSS and 0-200 bp upstream of the TTS. Higher temperatures were associated with a greater number of enriched k-mers, suggesting that heat stressâ€“responsive cis-regulatory elements exhibit increased activity under more extreme conditions. These findings provide new insights into the sequence determinants of heat stress responses and identify candidate regulatory elements for further functional investigation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Toward the identification of newborn neurons in the adult hippocampus: A machine learning framework for quantifying cell state signature from single-cell RNA-seq
authors: Inyoung Sung, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, United States; Pourya Naderi, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, United States; Isabel Castanho, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, United States; Winston Hide, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, United States
abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) is the generation of new neurons in the dentate gyrus of the adult hippocampus. The existence of AHN challenges century-old dogma that neurogenesis halts during childhood. Recent single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) studies report rare immature-like neuronal populations consistent with AHN. Detection of these populations across datasets is limited by low abundance and inconsistent marker definitions across studies. Here, we present a machine learning framework to identify immature-like cell states across human hippocampal snRNA-seq datasets. We integrated four datasets (130 individuals, ~600,000 nuclei) using a variational inference architecture followed by kernel densityâ€“based one-class learning in a shared latent space to score cells for immaturity. Unlike marker-based annotations, our method replaces discrete annotation with a continuous immaturity score across datasets. We identified 22,986 previously uncharacterized single nuclei from cells that scored as highly immature. Candidate cells were enriched in glutamatergic neurons and dentate gyrus granule cell types, consistent with known neurogenic regions. These cells were more prevalent in individuals aged 1â€“4 than in adults. They were enriched in pathways associated with synaptic signaling, neuron development, and axonogenesis. Our results suggest that large-scale integration combined with quantitative, machine learningâ€“based scoring provides a promising approach to detect rare immature-like cell states. This framework extends existing strategies for rare cell type characterization and offers opportunities to establish a systematic framework for studying neurogenesis-like processes in the adult human hippocampus. Our approach may provide insights into aging and neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimerâ€™s disease.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: scMNB: Unified Batch Integration and Gene Regulatory Network Inference through Multivariate Negative Binomial Distribution
authors: Erzhuo Wang, University of North Texas, United States; Serdar Bozdag, University of North Texas, United States
abstract: Downstream analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) involves two critical tasks: learning latent representations of individual cells and inferring global gene regulatory networks (GRNs). However, existing models often struggle to balance these objectives effectively. Here, we introduce scMNB, a novel variational autoencoder framework based on the multivariate negative binomial distribution. While learning cellular latent representations, scMNB jointly optimizes a precision matrix within the evidence lower bound(ELBO) of the multivariate negative binomial distribution, from which partial correlation coefficients are directly extracted to reconstruct the GRN. Our preliminary results on geneRNIB benchmark and OpenProblems batch integration benchmark indicate scMNB can simultaneously achieve competitive batch integration and single-omics GRN inference with strong performance on causality-related metrics, specifically TF binding recovery and Wasserstein distance on interventional data.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A Universal State Space Model for Cross-Species Splice Site Prediction
authors: Bowen Chen, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Chirag Adwani, University of Maryland, United States; Hibiki Kato, University of Maryland, United States; Brian R. Hunt, University of Maryland, United States; James A. Yorke, University of Maryland, United States; Mihaela Pertea, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Aleksey V. Zimin, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: Accurate splice site prediction is essential for ab initio gene finding and validation of transcripts assembled from RNA-seq data. However, distinguishing splice sites that yield functional transcripts from the vast number of similar sequence motifs in the genome remains a major computational challenge. Several computational approaches have been developed for this task, ranging from classical statistical models such as Markov chains and GeneSplicer to deep learning approaches, including splice-site-specific predictors such as SpliceAI, Spliceator, and Splam, as well as broader DNA foundation models such as Caduceus and AlphaGenome. We present a novel approach to the splice site prediction task across species using a bidirectional state space model (SSM). By exploiting the selective SSM dynamics, our model achieves linear time and memory complexity in sequence length, enabling efficient training on long sequence contexts. Trained on a well-curated multi-species dataset, our method matches the performance of SpliceAI on human held-out chromosomes while training substantially faster and outperforms existing predictors on other model organisms, including Arabidopsis thaliana and Drosophila melanogaster. These results suggest that selective SSMs can provide a practical and universal foundation for splice site annotation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Predicting Drug Activity across Cell Lines from Transcriptomic Profiles
authors: Léa Kaufmann, Université de Montréal, Canada; Lola Le Breton, Mila (Quebec AI Institute) ; Polytechnique Montréal, Canada; Quentin Fournier, Mila (Quebec AI Institute), Canada; Sébastien Lemieux, Université de Montréal, Canada
abstract: Nearly 90% of drug candidates fail in clinical trials, highlighting the need for better early-stage selection tools in the drug discovery pipeline. Phenotypic screening offers rich biological readouts, but its low throughput limits scalability. While machine learning holds promise for in silico drug screening, approaches relying solely on chemical structure fail to capture complex biological interactions within the cell. We hypothesize that treatment-induced changes in gene expression provide a more informative representation of compound activity than chemical descriptors, and that responses observed in one cellular context can predict responses in another. We leverage two large-scale transcriptomic perturbation datasets: Tahoe-100M and LINCS L1000. For each treatment condition, we compute a Î”-profile by subtracting the DMSO control from the treated profile. We train a multilayer perceptron that takes the Î”-profile of a reference cell line and the untreated profile of a target cell line, and predicts the target cell line's transcriptomic response to the same treatment. Compounds are split using the Butina algorithm to ensure structural dissimilarity between train and test sets. The model achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.80 on the Tahoe-100M test set, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen compounds. Performance on LINCS is lower (r = 0.12), consistent with its poor inter-plate reproducibility. Restricting evaluation to reproducible profiles recovers performance up to r = 0.80. Chemical structure embeddings from molecular foundation models provide no improvement over transcriptomic representations alone. These results suggest that Î”-profiles are effective encoders of compound activity with promise for scalable, cell-context-aware drug response prediction.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Allele-specific prediction of accessibility in F1 hybrid mice
authors: Aditya Sinha, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Qianzi Li, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Xiao Liu, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Christina Leslie, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Quaid Morris, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: The vast majority of genetic variation occurs in noncoding regions of the genome, and functional variants, while rare, are subsequently enriched in these regions and have been implicated by GWAS as playing a role in phenotypic changes in T-cells driving autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. Since the correlation with expression is indirect, we turn to an epigenetic lens to shed light on these effects. This has motivated the modeling of the relationship between sequence and chromatin accessibility using neural networks, in an effort to predict the effect of variation in silico as well as identify transcription factor (TF) binding motifs that they affect. However, importantly, these methods train only on the reference genome, relying on it as a proxy for genetic variation. Here, using bulk ATAC-seq from F1 hybrid mice and allele-aware modeling paradigms on SOTA model ChromBPNet, we show in several immune subtypes that information about natural genetic variation improves both the prediction of the effect size and identification of differential regulation patterns through TF binding motif disruption. We corroborate these with CUT&RUN occupancy data for the corresponding TFs. Furthermore, we use these trained cell-type specific mouse models to make zero-shot predictions on human caQTLs, where again we note improved predictions over models trained solely on the reference.

title: Bridging Omic Predictions and Network Biology through Subnetwork Prioritization
authors: Rodolfo Argueta-Rios, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, United States; Maricel Kann, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, United States
abstract: Precision oncology increasingly relies on machine learning classifiers to distinguish patient subtypes and predict outcomes, yet these models often function as black boxes, offering limited insight into underlying molecular mechanisms or biomarker networks. Network-based interpretation provides a powerful lens for connecting omic-level predictions to biological context, helping identify coherent molecular subnetworks that drive disease phenotypes. We present a framework that translates per-gene importance scores from an upstream omic classifier into class-weighted protein interaction graphs constructed from STRING data. By applying community detection to these weighted networks and ranking discovered subnetworks based on algorithmic quality, overlap with known disease-associated genes, and contribution to classifier performance, we surface the communities most discriminative between patient classes. Applied to TCGA lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) cohorts, this approach integrates machine learning interpretation with network biology to uncover candidate functional modules that may serve as novel biomarkers or mechanistic hypotheses in cancer subtype differentiation.

title: Multi-Resolution Interventional SEM for Gene Regulatory Network Inference from Perturb-seq Data
authors: Chandra Sekhar Reddy Edula, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Xiuwei Zhang, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Perturb-seq pairs CRISPR perturbations with single-cell RNA sequencing to directly measure how each gene responds to targeted knockouts. This interventional signal should enable gene regulatory network (GRN) recovery, yet on the CausalBench benchmark no method currently leads both the protein-complex co-regulation ground truth (CORUM) and the functional-interaction ground truth (STRING). We present a multi-resolution Interventional Structural Equation Model (I-SEM) that infers a sparse matrix W from interventional mean shifts through the resolvent (I-W)â»Â¹, and sweeps a Tikhonov parameter Î» across scales. Small Î» retains high-order path contributions and reproduces indirect functional interactions; large Î» damps those terms and reproduces near-neighbor complex co-regulation. A stability-selection ensemble aggregates the per-scale solutions by rank fusion. On Replogle K562 Perturb-seq (1,158 perturbed genes, 240,148 cells passing QC), I-SEM outperforms GRNBoost2, LASSO, and DCDI on every precision-oriented metric we examined, including AUPRC against the STRING and CORUM ground truths and a CausalBench-style statistical-precision test (Mann-Whitney U, p

title: Binding affinity perturbation informs cell-cell communication analysis
authors: Zhuyang Lin, North Carolina State University, United States; Yafan Zhang, North Carolina State University, United States
abstract: Cell-cell communication (CCC) networks vary across cellular contexts, but molecular drivers of edge-level shifts in ligand-receptor (L-R) signaling remain poorly understood. Current tools such as CellChat and COMMOT infer L-R signaling mainly from transcript abundance and spatial context, while overlooking binding affinity and its alteration by mutations. Here, we tested whether AI-predicted mutation-induced binding free-energy changes explain mutation-associated changes in CCC strength. Using the Tahoe-100M perturbation atlas, we built a mutation-mapped set of structurally evaluable L-R interactions curated from CellChatDB, predicted single-mutation absolute ddG values using AlphaFold 3 and Pythia-PPI, and quantified CellChat-style CCC strengths across 15 independent lung cell lines. Cross-cell-line permutation testing (p 2.0), although the smaller number of cell lines limited statistical power. Together, these results suggest that mutation-aware binding affinity perturbation provides a complementary, structure-informed feature for edge-level CCC analysis. As a methodological extension, we are developing affinity-aware variants of CellChat and COMMOT that incorporate binding-affinity perturbation directly into CCC scoring and spatial transport costs.

title: Deep integrative multiplex network-based analysis of rare neuromuscular disorders reveals overlapping multiscale endotypes involved in cardiac and skeletal muscle myopathies
authors: Iker Núñez Carpintero, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Philipp Friedrich, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine, Austria; Davide Cirillo, Barcelona Supercomputing Center, Spain; Alfonso Valencia, Barcelona Supercomputing Centre BSC, Spain; Jörg Menche, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria; Julia Guthrie, Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Network Medicine at the University of Vienna, Austria
abstract: "Applying these integrative methods to analyze large-scale biomedical data to rare diseases remains challenging due to limited data availability. A central difficulty is interpreting molecular relationships linking clinically overlapping conditions, knowledge that could uncover opportunities for drug repositioning. Addressing such scenarios requires strategies that combine scarce disease-specific data with biomedical knowledge databases. Here we showcase how multiplex networks can address this challenge: we introduce multiCore, a network diffusionâ€“based approach to perform endotype definition using multiplex networks. Focusing on 13 monogenic neuromuscular disease (NMD) categories, we build a biomedical multiplex network comprising 71 layers spanning phenome, tissue-specific interactome and co-expression, pathways, and drugâ€“target relationship knowledge. Disease-specific layer relevance is then used to compute NMD modules, from which molecularly and functionally coherent endotypes are derived. Overlap analysis among the resulting endotypes reveals a densely connected landscape: 97.2% share genes with endotypes from other NMD categories, with a major cluster of 11 highly overlapping endotypes being enriched for processes underlying skeletal and cardiac muscle development, providing mechanistic insight into the co-occurrence of skeletal and cadiomyopathic myopathies and highlighting therapeutically actionable bridging genetic interactors currently under study with clinical partners. We further study how multiplex-based disease module identification remains robust under systematic layer-removal perturbations, and we introduce netviz-interactive, a 3D visualization framework that enables intuitive analysis of multiplex networks, revealing strong contributions from heart and skeletal muscle proteinâ€“protein interaction and coexpression layers. Our results establish multiplex networks as a robust framework for integrating large-scale knowledge for uncovering shared rare disease pathomechanisms."

title: Traditional machine learning vs. deep learning from dynamic graph representations of proteins’ 3D folds in the task of protein structure classification
authors: Aydin Wells, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Notre Dame, United States; Francis Gatsi, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Notre Dame, United States; Aaron Striegel, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Notre Dame, United States; Tijana Milenkovic, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Notre Dame, United States
abstract: Determining protein function experimentally is resource-consuming. This has motivated computational prediction of protein function. A protein's amino acid sequence determines its 3D structure/fold, which in turn determines its function. Consequently, computational methods extract features from sequences or 3D structures to predict functions. Before such features are used for function prediction, it is desirable to first validate that they actually meaningfully reflect the proteins' folds. Protein structure classification (PSC) serves exactly this purpose. PSC is a supervised task of linking proteins' features to their CATH/SCOP/SCOPe structural classes. Historically, features for PSC have been extracted from sequences or 3D structures. More recently, features extracted from protein structure network (PSN) representations of 3D structures have emerged, which have often outperformed sequence or direct (non-network) 3D structural approaches. The earlier successes were based on static PSNs. More recently, we introduced a dynamic PSN to mimic a protein's folding dynamics. In our PSC evaluation on ~44,000 CATH/SCOPe domains, dynamic PSNs were significantly superior to static PSNs, and thus by transitivity to sequence and direct (non-network) 3D structural approaches. This existing dynamic PSN approach is a "traditional ML" approach: it uses manual, pre-engineered features with an off-the-shelf classifier. Hence, we examine whether deep learning (DL) can automatically extract additional signal from dynamic PSNs; we examine multiple DL architectures/variants. In our PSC evaluation, traditional ML holds value even in presence of the methodologically more advanced DL, i.e., traditional ML is comparable to the best of the DL variants in terms of accuracy, while also being much faster.

title: Single-Cell Multiome Analysis Links Genetic Risk to a Cell-Type–Specific Regulatory Program in L6 IT Car3 Neurons Following Opioid Exposure
authors: Fengge Chang, Inst Human Genetics & Dept Genetics/Biochem, Clemson Univ; Dept of Medical & Molecular Genetics, IU School of Medicine, United States; Alexey Kozlenkov, Friedman Brain Inst & Psychiatry, Icahn Sch Med Mt Sinai; James J. Peters VA & VISN 2 MIRECC, United States; Jinyoung Jung, Friedman Brain Inst & Psychiatry, Icahn Sch Med Mt Sinai; James J. Peters VA & VISN 2 MIRECC, United States; Gregory Rompala, Friedman Brain Inst, Dept Psychiatry & Addiction Inst, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Yasmin Hurd, Friedman Brain Inst, Dept Psychiatry & Addiction Inst, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Zhana Duren, Dept of Medical & Molecular Genetics, IU School of Medicine, United States; Stella Dracheva, Friedman Brain Inst & Psychiatry, Icahn Sch Med Mt Sinai; James J. Peters VA & VISN 2 MIRECC, United States
abstract: "Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a major public health crisis, however the mechanisms underlying its molecular pathology remain unclear. Here, we performed single-nucleus multiome profiling (snRNA-seq + snATAC-seq) of 331,015 nuclei from postmortem human orbitofrontal cortex across 14 heroin users and 12 controls. Differential expression analysis revealed most of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are observed in intratelencephalic (IT) neuron populations. Especially L6 IT Car3 and L6b neurons showed significant enriched in KEGG morphine addiction pathway (hsa05032). Co-expression analysis identified a gene program (Module 5) that is highly enriched for differentially expressed genes and morphine addiction pathways in L6 IT Car3 neurons. Notably, this module exhibits markedly stronger enrichment compared to all other detected modules in L6 IT Car3. Integration with previous GWAS study revealed significant enrichment of OUD heritability within regulatory elements linked to this module. Multiple genome-wide significant and sub-threshold risk loci overlap these regions, indicating that genetic risk preference maps to this transcriptional program. We next integrated transcription factors with Module 5 to reconstruct a hierarchical regulatory architecture underlying this gene program. This analysis defined three functional classes of regulators: (i) candidate upstream regulators, (ii) core regulators, and (iii) downstream effectors. Together, these regulators form a coordinated network that drives this gene program. Representative factors include HIF1A and ARNT (upstream), EGR family members (core), and CREB1 and NPAS2 (downstream). Together, our results identify a cell-type-specific regulatory network in L6 IT Car3 neurons that links genetic susceptibility to a cell-type-specific transcriptional program in OUD. "

title: drGT: Attention-Guided Gene Assessment of Drug Response Utilizing a Drug-Cell-Gene Heterogeneous Network
authors: Yoshitaka Inoue, University of Minnesota, United States; Hunmin Lee, University of Minnesota, United States; Tianfan Fu, Nanjing University, China; Rui Kuang, University of Minnesota, United States; Augustin Luna, National Library of Medicine/National Cancer Institute, United States
abstract: Background: For translational impact, accurate drug response prediction and biological plausibility of predictive features are needed. We present drGT, a heterogeneous graph deep learning model over drugs, genes, and cell lines that couples prediction with mechanism-oriented interpretability via attention coefficients (ACs). Results: We assess predictive generalization (random, unseen-drug, unseen-cell, and zero-shot splits) and biological plausibility (text-mined PubMed co-mentions and comparison to a structure-based DTI predictor) on GDSC, NCI60, and CTRP datasets. Across benchmarks, drGT delivers top regression performance while maintaining competitive classification accuracy for drug sensitivity. Under random 5-fold cross-validation, drGT attains an AUROC of up to 0.945 (3rd overall) and an R2 of up to 0.690, outperforming baselines on regression. In leave-one-out tests for unseen cell lines and drugs, drGT achieves AUROCs of 0.706 and 0.844, and R2 values of 0.692 and 0.022, the only model yielding positive R2 for unseen drugs. In zero-shot prediction, drGT achieves an AUROC of 0.786 and a regression R2 of 0.334, representing the highest scores among models. For interpretability, AC-derived drug-gene links recover known biology: among 976 drugs with known DTIs, 36.9% of predicted links match established DTIs, and 63.7% are supported by either PubMed abstracts or a structure-based predictive model. Enrichment analyses of AC-prioritized genes reveal drug-perturbed biological processes, providing pathway-level explanations. Conclusions: drGT advances predictive generalization and mechanism-centered interpretability, offering state-of-the-art regression accuracy and literature-supported hypotheses, leveraging graph learning from heterogeneous data for biological discovery. Code: https://github.com/sciluna/drGT.

title: stem.MAP: A mouse embryonic stem cell specific protein complex map
authors: Akshaya Rajaraman, University of Illinois at Chicago, United States; Samantha Fischer, University of Illinois at Chicago, United States; Ron Sistrunk, The University of Texas at Austin, United States; Ryan Gray, The University of Texas at Austin, United States; Kevin Drew, University of Illinois at Chicago, United States
abstract: Proteins assemble into protein complexes to coordinate all cellular processes, with each complex shaped by cell-type, diseases, and environmental conditions. Identifying context-specific protein complexes is necessary to build insight into development and diseases. Most systemic studies overlook this, instead offering a static, one-size-fits-all atlas of complexes. Current methods to identify context-specific complexes require thousands of mass spectrometry experiments, are costly and laborious. To address this, we present stem.MAP, a mouse Embryonic Stem Cell (mESC)-specific protein complex map generated using Co-Fractionation Mass Spectrometry(CF-MS) experiments and machine learning(ML). CF-MS measures protein co-elution in orthogonal separations to predict their interactions in a label-free manner. We apply three ML strategies to improve the predictive power while minimizing reliance on large orthogonal datasets. (1) We integrate prior knowledge from a cell-type agnostic map, hu.MAP 3.0, (2) refine benchmarks to be cell-type specific, and (3) introduce randomness in priors to recognize true interactions not supported by priors. We evaluated our stem-cell specific map and we observed that the prior-weighted model markedly outperforms an unweighted model. stem.MAP ultimately predicts >375,000 interactions and ~4,000 complexes. We identify stem-cell specific variants of major chromatin remodeling assemblies including the BAF-pBAF and NuRD complex. stem.MAP also predicts ~1,400 high confidence novel interactions, which we validated using AlphaFold3. Further, we used stem.MAP to prioritize candidate genes for congenital heart defects in early zebrafish development, where 66% candidate gene knockouts produced heart-related phenotypes like edema and hemorrhage. Together, our results establish stem.MAP as a validated and scalable approach for identifying context-specific interactions and prioritizing disease-relevant complexes in early development.

title: Systemic chemotherapy modulates effector T cell differentiation in metastatic TNBC
authors: Hye-Yeon Ju, Division of Life Sciences, College of Life Sciences and Bioengineering, Incheon National University, South Korea, South Korea; Hyundong Yoon, Program in Cancer Biology, Vanderbilt University, USA, United States; Seungpil Jung, Division of Breast and Endocrine Surgery, Department of Surgery, Korea University Anam Hospital, South Korea, South Korea; Serk In Park, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Korea University College of Medicine, South Korea, South Korea; Tae Kon Kim, Division of Hematology/Oncology, Department of Medicine, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, USA, United States; Mi-Ryung Han, Division of Life Sciences, College of Life Sciences and Bioengineering, Incheon National University, South Korea, South Korea
abstract: Background: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) has the poorest prognosis among the three major subtypes of breast cancer, and more than one-third of patients with TNBC experience recurrence or distant metastasis. Despite advances in diverse immunotherapy strategies for metastatic TNBC (mTNBC), multiple mechanisms underlying resistance to treatment remain unknown. Methods: In this study, the dynamic changes in the immune landscape in mTNBC were assessed and compared with healthy donors using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. By integrating internal and public scRNA-seq data, 61,149 cells extracted from East Asian patients with mTNBC and 51,448 cells extracted from East Asian healthy donors were used to landscape a comprehensive cellular profile of mTNBC. Results: Results showed that nine overexpressed genes from patients with mTNBC in effector T cells such as CTSW, PRF1, GNLY, GZMA, CCL5, KLRD1, KLRB1, B2M, and GZMB exhibited favorable survival prognoses. In addition, effector T cells enriched in patients with mTNBC were more differentiated compared with those enriched in healthy donors. Conclusion: Collectively, this study is the first to provide potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets of East Asian chemotherapy-treated mTNBC with regard to effector T cells.

title: Alternative Splicing Signatures of SSRI Response in Depression Patients: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Patrick Vo, Butler University, United States; David Cooper, Butler University, United States; Kathryn Cannaday, Butler University, United States; Victoria Gaertig, Butler University, United States; Elizabeth Durbin, Butler University, United States; Caleb Class, Butler University, United States
abstract: Despite decades of research, predicting antidepressant response remains challenging, limiting progress toward precision medicine in depression. Genomic approaches are promising, but findings across individual studies are often inconsistent. Building on our recent work examining gene expression signatures of fluoxetine response, we synthesize alternative splicing data across selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) to identify reproducible patterns associated with treatment outcomes in human patients and rodent models. Publicly available transcriptomic studies were searched and screened following PRISMA guidelines to identify relevant studies profiling SSRIs. Alternative splicing analyses were performed for each included study using RMATS, and results were synthesized across studies using Max-P meta-analysis. Results from this process were analyzed in the NetMix2 algorithm to identify protein networks associated with treatment response. Of 116 retrieved datasets, 4 RNA sequencing datasets met inclusion criteria and included comparisons of responders vs. non-responders. Analysis of the 2 human datasets via the NetMix2 Algorithm yielded a subnetwork of 227 proteins that were alternatively spliced between Responder and Nonresponder groups. Utilizing STRINGâ€™s search function, the subnetwork was identified to contain proteins within studies concerning dopaminergic disturbance of mitochondrial function, Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling, and ribosomal structure. Alternative splicing analysis of 2 mouse datasets resulted in protein subnetworks centered around chromatin binding and histone modification. These results provide further evidence that polygenetic and polyprotein signatures will guide us towards precision medicine in depression. Specific proteins and their connections to each other must be further researched to identify protein groups associated with differential response to SSRI response.

title: SYNERGIE: A mechanism-aware framework for identifying clinically actionable drug synergies via multi-layer modeling and network controllability
authors: Satoko Namba, Nagoya University, Japan; Mitsuhiro Goda, Hiroshima University, Japan; Yurika Kuniki, Tokushima University Hospital, Japan; Keisuke Ishizawa, Tokushima University, Japan; Midori Iida, Kyushu Institute of Technology, Japan; Jun-Ichi Takeshita, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Japan; Yoshihiro Yamanishi, Nagoya University, Japan
abstract: Multidrug therapies are essential for treating intractable diseases such as cancer, yet there is no mechanism-aware framework can accommodate diverse clinical needs, including intensively targeting key pathways, minimizing adverse effects, or designing combinations based on clinically approved drugs. Here, we introduce a mechanistic framework that redefines drug combination into two distinct synergy paradigms—"boost" and "complement"—and present SYNERGIE, a network-based method for predicting such combinations across diseases. For diseases lacking known therapeutic targets, we introduced network controllability analysis to estimate therapeutic pathways and target molecules. SYNERGIE integrates drug–disease and drug–drug interactions across multiomics layers using Bayesian optimization to prioritize disease-state-specific combinations, and outperforms existing methods across 14 diseases. Using SYNERGIE, we predicted novel combinations from 500,500 candidate pairs and validated top-ranked complement-type combinations in colorectal cancer through in vitro experiments. Multiple combinations involving non-antineoplastic and antineoplastic drugs exhibited clear synergistic effects despite their inherent difficulty. Notably, a triplet incorporating a first-line drug showed enhanced therapeutic effects compared to doublets, supporting its clinical relevance. Mechanistic analyses using bulk and single-cell transcriptomics revealed that coordinated regulation across pathways and cell types underlies the observed synergy. SYNERGIE provides a mechanism-aware approach for identifying clinically viable combination therapies, and supports stratified treatment of intractable diseases.

title: An Evidence-Driven Retrieval and Lightweight Agentic AI Framework for Drug Recommendation
authors: Aakash Kumaran, School of Computing Technologies, RMIT University Australia, Australia; Deval Mehta, Monash University, Australia, Australia; Sonika Tyagi, School of Computing Technologies, RMIT University Australia, Australia
abstract: Current approaches to clinical drug recommendation face three critical limitations: (1) existing models are typically designed for raw EHR data limiting cross-hospital applicability; (2) many systems compromise patient representation by focusing on single modalities or failing to effectively integrate multiple clinical data types, thereby losing critical patient signals; and (3) real-world clinical data frequently contains missing modalities, yet current methods lack robust mechanisms to handle such incompleteness during inference. We present a novel architecture for multi-label drug recommendation that addresses these challenges by combining neural network predictions with an enhanced hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline to deliver clinically verified recommendations. Our system is built on the OMOP-CDM, ensuring cross-hospital portability and standardization across diverse healthcare systems. The architecture employs a multimodal encoder that integrates multiple clinical modalities, including clinical notes, conditions, procedures, and measurements into a unified visit representation. For inference, we introduce an enhanced hybrid RAG pipeline that retrieves evidence from both internal and external sources: (1) similar patient visits from historical data using a query combining semantic embeddings, structured modality values, and neural network drug predictions, and (2) external medical guidelines such as Therapeutic Guidelines Australia to ensure adherence to established clinical standards. The hybrid retrieval strategy integrates both semantic similarity and lexical matching to ensure comprehensive evidence retrieval from both data sources. Rather than over-relying on agent-based reasoning, our system prioritizes automation: the neural network provides primary predictions, RAG supplies evidence from similar cases, and a lightweight multi-agent system (Similar Patient Evaluator, Ranker, Safety Critic, and Resolver) performs focused validation and final synthesis. This design ensures that most of the decision-making is automated and data-driven, with agents serving as targeted validators rather than primary decision-makers. We demonstrate the system on a cohort of 58,976 visits from OMOP-CDM, embedding 1.85 million clinical notes. The enhanced hybrid RAG pipeline ensures that final recommendations are both clinically sound and verified against similar patient evidence, producing interpretable, evidence-based drug recommendations that address key limitations of black-box models in high stakes medical decision-making.

title: Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals a clinically relevant aggressive subtype in primary high-grade serous ovarian cancer
authors: Dae Won Sim, CHA university, South Korea; Jong Heon Park, CHA university, South Korea; Je-Gun Joung, CHA university, South Korea; Sook-Young Kim, CHA medical center, South Korea
abstract: High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the most lethal gynecologic malignancy, frequently diagnosed at advanced stages and characterized by high rates of recurrence and chemoresistance. Intratumoral heterogeneity and complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) critically underlie these challenges, however, bulk transcriptomic approaches lack the resolution required to capture cellular diversity and intercellular communication dynamics within the TME. We conducted integrative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of 22,793 cells from primary HGSOC tissues to delineate malignant epithelial subpopulations and their interactions with the TME. Among the identified epithelial subclusters, one subtype exhibited the highest copy number variation (CNV) score and occupied a late-stage position along the differentiation trajectory, suggesting a highly malignant and potentially metastatic cell state. Functional analyses revealed markedly elevated epithelialâ€“mesenchymal transition (EMT) activity within this subtype. Ligandâ€“receptor interaction analysis demonstrated strong fibroblast-derived signaling targeting this subtype, implicating fibroblast-mediated crosstalk in invasion, immune evasion, and EMT promotion. Furthermore, SCENIC-based gene regulatory network inference identified key transcriptional regulators associated with the malignant phenotype. Finally, in silico drugâ€“target interaction analysis nominated candidate therapeutic agents for this aggressive subtype.

title: SCOPE: Revealing Hidden Mechanisms in Phenotypic Screens Through Target and Pathway Enrichment
authors: Abhijeet Kapoor, NCATS/NIH, United States; Keith Kelleher, NCATS/NIH, United States; Suzanne Underhill, NIDA/NIH, United States; Sankalp Jain, NCATS/NIH, United States; Darian Williams, NCATS/NIH, United States; Brandon K. Harvey, NIDA/NIH, United States; Mark J. Henderson, NCATS/NIH, United States
abstract: Phenotypic screening enables discovery of small molecules without requiring predefined targets, but mechanistic interpretation remains challenging due to polypharmacology and pathway complexity. We developed SCOPE (Screening Compound Ontology for Pathway Enrichment), a KNIME-based computational framework that resolves the molecular drivers of phenotypic activity by linking compound-level screening data to annotated targets and pathways. SCOPE integrates multi-source target annotations and performs statistical enrichment to identify shared mechanisms of action. Applied to a high-throughput screen for modulators of ER-stress induced secretion of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) resident proteins, a process known as exodosis, SCOPE identified calcium signaling as the most enriched KEGG pathway without prior biological context. Target enrichment revealed G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) involved in inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors (IP3Rs)-mediated signaling, with widespread antagonism among hit compounds implicating this pathway in the regulation of exodosis. Notably, SCOPE uncovered a novel role for the histamine receptor HRH1, which was validated by RNAi knockdown and pharmacological inhibition, implicating HRH1 as a potential therapeutic target in ER stress-related disorders. These results highlight SCOPEâ€™s potential to deconvolute phenotypic screens and uncover actionable mechanisms in complex cellular systems.

title: BIOS: Bio-anchored Interpretable Omics Subtyping for Cancer
authors: Utkarsh Goyal, Florida State University, United States; Pankaj Bhattarai, Florida State University, United States; Xian Mallory, Florida State University, United States
abstract: Unsupervised cancer subtyping from high-dimensional omics data is a fundamental problem in computational biology, yet existing deep clustering approaches often lack biological interpretability due to their fully data-driven nature. We present BIOS (Bio-anchored Interpretable Omics Subtyping), a weakly supervised deep clustering framework that incorporates prior biological knowledge into representation learning to improve both clustering performance and interpretability. BIOS builds upon the Subtype-DCC architecture, introducing structured constraints in the latent space by anchoring a subset of embedding dimensions to predefined biological signals. Specifically, we define a number of bio-anchors corresponding to key cancer-relevant processes, including copy number alterations (CNAs), proliferation, angiogenesis, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and enforce alignment between these anchors and selected latent dimensions during training. This design preserves the flexibility of deep clustering while guiding the model toward biologically meaningful representations. We evaluate BIOS on The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) breast cancer cohort. Compared to baseline methods, including Subtype-DCC and Subtype-GAN, BIOS achieves improved clustering accuracy and demonstrates enhanced stability across runs. Importantly, the anchored latent dimensions enable direct interpretation of subtype structure in terms of known biological processes, facilitating mechanistic insights without post hoc analysis. Overall, BIOS provides a principled approach for integrating biological priors into deep clustering models, yielding more accurate and interpretable cancer subtypes. This framework is generalizable to other omics modalities and disease settings where domain knowledge can inform representation learning.

title: CHiP-FL: A Hierarchical Federated Learning Framework for Equitable ICU Risk Modeling
authors: Rhea Zhou, Cary Academy, United States
abstract: Machine learning (ML) in healthcare is constrained by strict privacy regulations and institutional data silos, limiting the development of models that generalize effectively across hospitals. Federated learning (FL) addresses this challenge by enabling collaborative training without sharing raw data. However, clinical datasets are highly heterogeneous (non-IID), leading to unstable optimization and systematic performance disparities, where large institutions often benefit more than smaller ones. We propose CHiP-FL (Client Clustering, Hierarchical Aggregation, and Personalization), a FL framework designed to improve cross-site equity while maintaining strong predictive performance. CHiP models heterogeneity at three levels (global, cluster, local) by grouping institutions using data signature vectors and introducing hierarchical proximal regularization. Unlike prior methods such as FedProx, which constrain clients only toward a global model, CHiP incorporates both cluster-level and global alignment, enabling structured knowledge sharing while preserving institution-specific variation. We evaluate CHiP using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (200,000+ ICU stays across 200+ hospital systems) and compare it against established FL baselines including FedAvg, FedProx, hierarchical aggregation, clustered training without global fusion, and post-hoc personalization. While FedProx achieves the highest AUROC (0.933), this gain is accompanied by substantial inter-site inequality, including the highest standard deviation (0.062) and strong site-size bias (-0.032), measured as the slope of AUROC vs log(n), where n is the number of ICU stays per institution. In contrast, CHiP achieves competitive AUROC (0.903 global; 0.897 personalized) while reducing site-size bias by over 90% (-0.002), nearly eliminating the relationship between hospital size and predictive performance. CHiP also maintains a low Gini (0.028 global; 0.027 personalized) and competitive worst-decile AUROC (0.84), demonstrating balanced protection across sites without sacrificing generalization. Personalization further improves dispersion and lower-decile performance without reintroducing bias, suggesting that hierarchical regularization and local adaptation act as complementary mechanisms. These findings position equity as a core optimization objective in federated clinical AI. By enforcing structured, multi-level alignment across institutions, CHiP mitigates disparities inherent to heterogeneous healthcare systems while preserving strong overall performance. This framework provides a principled pathway toward fairer and more generalizable multi-institutional clinical ML systems.

title: A PLUM Job: Peptide modeLs for Understanding and engineering anti-Microbial therapeutics
authors: Priyanka Banerjee, Dept. of Computer Science, Iowa State University, United States; Iddo Friedberg, Iowa State University, United States; Britta Rued, Veterinary Microbiology and Preventive Medicine, Iowa State University, United States; Oliver Eulenstein, Dept. of Computer Science, Iowa State University, United States
abstract: Motivation: Antibiotic-resistant infections in humans and animals are rising, creating an urgent need for new antimicrobial strategies. This challenge extends beyond clinical settings to food production systems; the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that foodborne pathogens cause over 48 million illnesses annually in the U.S. alone. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a promising alternative, with broad activity and lower risk of resistance. However, rational design remains challenging, especially when simultaneously controlling sequence, function, and peptide length. Results: We introduce Peptide modeLs for Understanding and engineering antiMicrobial therapeutics (PLUM), a structured conditional Variational Autoencoder for controlled AMP generation. PLUM disentangles sequence, function, and length in its latent space, enabling de novo and prototype-conditioned generation of peptides 5-35 amino acids long, allowing capture of larger functional domains. Across 45,000 generated peptides, PLUM achieved the highest AMP yield (0.885, 7% higher than HydrAMP) and increased AMP diversity (14% higher than HydrAMP), while maintaining the highest non-AMP sequence yield 0.895 (19% higher than HydrAMP). For prototype-conditioned generation, PLUM produced 37% more AMPs than HydrAMP, generating sequences that closely matched real peptide compositions with low predicted toxicity. Integrated AMP classifiers enabled robust evaluation of identity and potency across diverse bacteria. These results establish PLUM as a scalable, versatile platform for designing AMPs and next-generation therapeutics. Availability: https://github.com/priyamayur/PLUM

title: Unsupervised Integration of Imbalanced Bulk Transcriptomic Datasets via Latent Subgroup Estimation
authors: Preston Raab, Brigham Young University, United States; Amanda Warren, Brigham Young University, United States; Carter Larsen, Brigham Young University, United States; Stephen Piccolo, Brigham Young University, United States
abstract: Publicly available bulk transcriptomic samples are dispersed across many datasets, hindering analyses that require large sample sizes. While dataset aggregation increases sample count, it also introduces batch effects: non-biological, technical variation between the samples. Batch effects are especially pronounced in cross-platform aggregations of microarray data, which constitute a large proportion of public human samples, and sequencing data. Integration requires the removal of distributional differences, but not all differences between datasets should be removed. Datasets may be biologically distinct; in particular, subpopulations may be represented disproportionately. Most algorithms designed for bulk transcriptomes are equipped to handle this effect only if the subpopulations are known. Given the sparsity and lack of standardization of metadata available in public repositories, methods that can account for imbalanced subpopulations without phenotypic labels are key to generating large aggregated datasets that preserve biological patterns. We propose an unsupervised algorithm to identify axes of biological variation where batch effects are limited and cross-dataset sample similarities can guide a reference-based adjustment of target datasets. We find that genes cluster into meaningful groups using graph cuts on a bimodality-driven correlation graph. After an unsupervised restriction to the gene groups most likely to indicate subpopulation status, samples across datasets cluster on principal axes of variation according to known biological labels. We use these unsupervised clustering assignments to calculate gene-specific location and scale adjustments, effectively removing batch effects while preserving cross-dataset neighbor relations.

title: OmicsGPT: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Autonomous and Interpretable Precision Oncology
authors: Patrick Roney, Department of Biostatistics, Bioinformatics, and Biomathematics, Georgetown University, United States; James Li, Department of Biostatistics, Bioinformatics, and Biomathematics, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer reasoning capabilities, but standalone models can fail in practice due to hallucinations, acronym collisions, and inability to consider biological context. To address these limitations, we developed OmicsGPT, an autonomous, agentic system built on LangGraph that transforms bulk RNA-seq datasets and free-text prompt into an actionable report for drug development or biomarker discovery. OmicsGPT begins with PyDESeq2 and gene set enrichment analysis and then passes selected genes to a multi-agent cognitive architecture. These targets first are investigated by a planner agent which autonomously selects domain-specific tools OpenTargets, OncoKB, STRING, and PubMed. Next, a molecular pathologist agent applies biological context using GTEx-informed baseline to filter lineage-mismatch artifacts and a bioinformatics auditor that resolves acronym collisions. Finally, an AI Tumor Board debates the evidence and provides a synthesis which the medical writer then reports. Benchmarked against a standalone Gemini 3.1 Pro baseline, OmicsGPT demonstrated enhanced transparency and more robust reporting. Gemini used Welch's t-test rather than PyDESeq2, did not provide supportive materials for druggability claims, and did not consider the tissue context. OmicsGPT used proper statistical approaches, verified target essentiality with APIs, and incorporated tissue-context for the user's project. By utilizing guidelines in the foundational architecture and incorporating agentic self-correction, OmicsGPT shifts discovery from a black box to a verifiable glass box. This framework significantly reduces hallucinations and establishes a safe foundation for autonomous multi-omic discovery.

title: Pathogene-on-FHIR: A flexible utility for interconversion FHIR entities and pathogenomic analysis
authors: Sonika Tyagi, RMIT University, Australia
abstract: Infectious diseases arise from the invasion and colonization of the host by pathogenic microorganisms, with the progression and severity influenced by the host and the infecting agent. It is hypothesised that a harmonised data containing both the patient and pathogen characteristics can greatly enhance modelling the clinical outcomes related to infectious diseases. In this regard, there is a need for an utility to combine the Electronic Health Records (EHRs) containing the host responses with the pathogen genomic data for better modelling of infectious diseases. However, existing solutions that can be used for this purpose lack flexibility, hindering their adaptability to diverse use cases. To address this gap, we developed a data harmonising utility using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR). Utilizing this utility, we created an integrated representation of EHR and genomic data and a case study on Staphylococcus aureus was conducted to demonstrate its analytical and modeling potential.

title: Cabana: A Deep-Learning-Assisted Framework for Extracellular Matrix Characterization in Human Cancers
authors: Astrid Magenau, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Xufeng Lin, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Tim Kallady, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Anne-Maree Haynes, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Deborah Barkauskas, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Angela Fontaine-Titley, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Anna Howell, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Aparna Raina, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Omali Pitiyarachchi, University of New South Wales, Australia; Frank Lin, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; George Sharbeen, University of New South Wales, Australia; Phoebe Philips, University of New South Wales, Australia; David Goldstein, University of New South Wales, Australia; Anthony Gill, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Shona Ritchie, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Marija Dinevska, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Kendelle Murphy, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Brooke Pereira, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Sean Porazinski, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; David Herrmann, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Renea Taylor, Monash University, Australia; Marina Pajic, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Filippo Ammazzalaorso, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; James Kench, University of Sydney, Australia; Sarah Kummerfeld, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Roger Daly, Monash University, Australia; Lisa Horvath, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Paul Timpson, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia; Leonard Goldstein, Garvan Institute of Medical Research, Australia
abstract: Collagen is a fundamental component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and plays a crucial role in cancer progression by influencing tumor growth, invasion, and metastasis. It contributes to tumor progression not only structurally but also by modulating mechanical properties of the ECM and signaling networks. Alterations in fiber density, alignment, and cross-linking have been associated with tumor aggressiveness and therapeutic resistance. To enable precise and reproducible quantification of collagen architecture, we introduce Cabana (Collagen Fiber Analyzer), an open-source software toolkit combining deep learning and image analysis for collagen segmentation and fiber detection. Applied to over 3,000 images from 158 patients with high-risk prostate cancer cohort and 15 years of follow-up, Cabana identifies distinct collagen phenotypes that correspond to clinical variables, such as disease stage, biochemical and clinical recurrence and metastatic progression. Cabana resolves maturation-specific ECM signatures that independently predict metastasis-free survival beyond established clinicopathological variables. By linking quantifiable stromal remodeling to patient outcomes, Cabana provides a robust framework for prognostic assessment, risk stratification, and potential personalized treatment strategies, validating Cabana as a machine learning tool to allow the integration of ECM architecture into future pathology workflows. Cabana is freely available at https://github.com/Garvan-Data-Science-Platform/Cabana.git. Comprehensive documentation can be accessed at https://cabana.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ including installation instructions, usage tutorials, and guidelines for interpreting results.

title: CGRRA: A Deep Learning Framework for Predicting Tumor Cell Responses to Glucocorticoids from Single-Cell Data
authors: Jiaqi Li, NIEHS, United States; Osafu Egbon, NIEHS, United States; Trevor Archer, NIEHS, United States; Benedict Anchang, NIEHS, United States
abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) are widely used in cancer therapy due to their anti-inflammatory effects. However, how tumor cells respond to GCs is still unclear. Tumor cells are highly heterogeneous in response to GCs. GR activation can suppress tumor growth or promote proliferation. The guide for the clinical use of GCs in cancer is critically needed. To systematically characterize GR-mediated responses, we developed the Cancer GR Response Atlas (CGRRA), an AI powered framework integrating GR ChIP-seq data with large scale dexamethasone (Dex) treated scRNA-seq datasets. We manually curated large Dex treated scRNA-seq datasets from diverse cancer cell lines, comprising approximately one million cells, for modeling GC response.
