We constructed a GR target gene set (GR100) using ChIP-Atlas data. UMAP analysis based on GR100 gene expression showed that cell line identity is not strongly encoded, suggesting a conserved GR regulatory module shared across cancers. Then, we trained a neural network model to predict Dex response states. The model achieved excellent performance (AUC = 0.9833) in classifying cells into non-response and response states. Consistent performance across multiple cell lines supports strong model generalizability. To further resolve functional heterogeneity within the response state, we applied a second stage model using an expanded gene set to stratify responding cells into proliferation-associated and apoptosis-associated outcomes. Cross validation demonstrated stable and reproducible performance, indicating robustness. Future validation using patient datasets will assess clinical applicability. CGRRA provides a single-cell resolved predictive framework for understanding tumor heterogeneity in glucocorticoid responsiveness and guiding GC use in cancer therapy.

title: Decoding Latent Temozolomide Resistance States in Glioblastoma through Multi-Omics Integration
authors: Justin Bokai Hsu, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Yuan Ze University, Taiwan
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by frequent recurrence and the rapid development of resistance to temozolomide (TMZ), making reliable patient stratification a persistent challenge. In this study, we developed a multi-omics framework to identify latent resistance states and to build predictive models in GBM. We first derived resistance-associated gene signatures from TMZ-sensitive and TMZ-resistant cell lines, and projected these signatures onto patient transcriptomes using single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA). This enabled stratification of patients into putative resistant (high-risk) and sensitive (low-risk) groups. The two groups showed clear differences in overall survival and were consistent with known clinical markers, including MGMT promoter methylation and gene expression. To further characterize these groups, we integrated transcriptomic, DNA methylation, mutation, immune enrichment, and metabolomic data using MOFA+. The resulting latent factors captured shared variation across data types and were used for downstream classification, yielding stable predictive performance (AUC > 0.75). Examination of factor loadings indicated that several factors were strongly associated with immunometabolic processes, particularly tryptophan metabolism. High-risk patients showed enrichment of the kynurenine pathway together with immunosuppressive features, whereas low-risk patients were more closely associated with serotonin pathway activity and increased immune infiltration. These patterns were supported by differences in the serotonin-to-tryptophan ratio between groups. Together, these results suggest that multi-omics integration can reveal biologically meaningful resistance states in GBM and highlight a potential link between immunometabolic reprogramming and treatment response.

title: A scalable dashboard for expedited genomic analysis in a clinical research setting
authors: Awtum Brashear, Shriners Children's, United States; Andrew Quitadamo, Shriners Children's, United States; Kamran Shazand, Shriners Chilren's, United States
abstract: The high-throughput bioinformatics pipelines at Shriners Children's Genomics Institute typically process hundreds of genomes per week. Resulting data are available to researchers with the correct IRB approvals, including clinical research personnel. However, managing several concurrent translational genomics projects within a large pediatric hospital system results in a variety of complex concerns bridging technical, legal, ethical, and practical needs that can delay data access and discovery. To address these challenges, we developed a scalable and governed genomics data analytics architecture that integrates cohort-level genotyping information into concise cloud-based data analysis and visualization tools. Row-level access control enables exploratory genomics analyses while maintaining institutional and regulatory compliance. Flexible data sourcing allows integration of de-identified phenotypic data from relevant sources. The infrastructure also supports a diversity of analytical approaches ranging from simple cohort visualizations to advanced machine learning applications to maximize usability for those with and without backgrounds in bioinformatics. We present the challenges and design considerations from the initial development of the Shriners Children's genomics dashboard.

title: Discovering Latent Pre-Cancer Phenotypes Through Interpretable Disease-History Embeddings
authors: Lee Mason, National Cancer Institute, United States; Inês Duarte, National Cancer Institute, United States
abstract: Background: Cancer diagnoses are often preceded by years of recorded clinical history. We hypothesize that pre-diagnostic diagnosis histories contain latent phenotypic structure associated with future cancer risk beyond established risk factors and overall morbidity burden. Interpretable embeddings may help reveal these patterns in a form that can be clinically profiled rather than treated as opaque risk scores. Methods: Using UK Biobank, we develop a temporally anchored diagnosis-history embedding framework, focusing initially on lung cancer. For each participant, diagnoses recorded before a defined index date are represented using ICD-10 disease codes. We use non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to learn additive diagnosis-history embeddings and assess the effect of embedding dimension through held-out model evaluation. Predictive models incorporating NMF-derived phenotypes are compared with baseline models containing demographic, lifestyle, and morbidity-burden variables. Robustness analyses assess whether observed signal is driven by cancer-related diagnostic codes or other potential artifacts. Results: This framework evaluates whether latent diagnosis-history phenotypes provide incremental predictive information for lung cancer beyond standard risk factors and general disease burden. Because NMF components retain loadings on the original diagnosis codes, high-risk phenotypes can be profiled by their contributing disease groups and associated patient characteristics. We characterize performance across embedding dimensions and identify components most strongly associated with future lung cancer status. Conclusion: Temporally anchored diagnosis-history embeddings provide an interpretable approach for identifying latent pre-cancer phenotypes from administrative health data and for testing whether structured patterns of prior disease contribute to cancer risk stratification.

title: Augmenting Electronic Health Records for Adverse Event Detection
authors: Gün Kaynar, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Zhaoyi You, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Richard D. Boyce, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Takahiro Yakoh, Keio University, Japan; Carl Kingsford, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Objective Adverse events (AEs) resulting from medical interventions are significant contributors to patient morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Prediction of these events using electronic health records (EHRs) can facilitate timely clinical interventions. However, effective prediction remains challenging due to severe class imbalance, missing labels, and the complexity of EHR records. Classical machine learning approaches frequently underperform due to insufficient representation of minority adverse event classes and limited capacity to capture interactions among patient demographics, administered medications, and associated complications. Methods We introduce TASER-AE, a novel data augmentation pipeline tailored for structured EHR data, coupled with transformer-based classification. TASER-AE addresses these issues through an NLP-inspired data augmentation framework adapted for EHR, enabling effective minority-class representation in sparse and imbalanced clinical datasets. The augmented records produced by TASER-AE alleviate class imbalance by enriching the representation of minority adverse event classes, which enhances the robustness and predictive performance of the classifier. Results TASER-AE yields minority-class F1 scores up to 0.70, substantially surpassing classical machine-learning baselines and prior augmentation methods across multiple adverse event tasks. Experiments conducted on two distinct EHR datasets confirm TASER-AEâ€™s ability to substantially improve adverse event detection performance. Conclusion These results demonstrate the potential of structured, NLP-inspired augmentation methods to overcome data limitations in clinical predictive modeling, ultimately contributing to improved patient safety outcomes. TASER-AE is available at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/taserae.

title: Scalable identification of rare genetic diseases from clinical notes using natural language processing and machine learning
authors: Mohammad Ghouse Syed, Institute for Genomic Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States; Tanuja Gobbur, Institute for Genomic Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States; Himanshu Sharma, Institute for Genomic Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States; Vikas Pejaver, Institute for Genomic Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States
abstract: Rare genetic diseases (RGDs) collectively impact 10% of the US population and can take an average of five years to diagnose. Due to their rarity and limited structured representation in electronic health records (EHRs), early identification remains challenging. Clinical notes, however, contain rich information that can be leveraged using natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML). We propose a scalable framework to identify multiple RGDs from clinical notes for both diagnosis and phenotyping tasks. Our dataset includes 2,183 cases (67,266 notes) and 21,821 matched controls (726,750 notes) across 41 RGDs. We extracted features using (1) vocabulary-based methods (HPO and UMLS) and (2) BERT-based models (BioBERT, ClinicalBERT, and a fine-tuned ClinicalBERT). Models are evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. We assessed performance under two definitions of diagnosis dates: the first ICD-10 occurrence (ICD FND (first noted date)) and an alternative based on earliest disease mention in notes (UMLS FND). Using ICD FND, UMLS achieves the highest AUC (84.36%), outperforming HPO (80.48%) and BERT (82%). However, with UMLS FND, the performance of UMLS and HPO declines by 3.9% and 2.5% points, respectively, while BERT remains stable with 0.6% points reduction. In longitudinal prediction up to five years prior to UMLS FND, BERT outperforms both HPO and UMLS. Phenotyping results are higher than the diagnosis (UMLS: 96.9%, HPO: 91.3%, BERT: 88.9%). These findings demonstrate that BERT-based models are more robust to uncertainty in diagnosis dates and are better suited for early disease detection, while vocabulary-based methods remain effective but sensitive to temporal assumptions.

title: A Tumor Classification Framework for Computational Pathology in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
authors: Mst Shaila Afrin, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Tyler M. Yasaka, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yu-Chiao Chiu, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Whole-slide images (WSIs) contain heterogeneous mixtures of tumor, adjacent non-tumor, stromal, and necrotic tissue, posing challenges for computational methods that assume tumor-enriched input. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a setting characterized by substantial histologic heterogeneity and underlying liver disease, this heterogeneity can degrade downstream spatial and molecular analyses. Without effective filtering, adjacent non-tumor regions introduce noise, with potential implications for molecular and prognostic modeling. We developed a tile-level classifier as an upstream gating module for computational pathology workflows. Using 31 H&E WSIs of the TCGA-LIHC project, we divided each slide into 256—256 tiles and annotated tumor versus adjacent non-tumor regions using pathologist-provided labels. Each tile was represented by a 1,536-dimensional embedding extracted from the foundation model Prov-GigaPath. We evaluated multiple classifiers under a leave-one-slide-out framework to assess generalization across slides. At the original resolution, logistic regression achieved the best overall performance (AUC = 0.95), while at lower image resolution, a support vector machine showed comparable robustness (AUC = 0.96). These results suggest that tumor gating can be integrated without additional feature extraction, even when using lower-resolution inputs to reduce computational cost. Spatial heatmap visualization demonstrated strong alignment with annotations, with errors concentrated near tumor boundaries. We further validated the generalizability of the approach using an independent in-house cohort. This framework can be readily integrated into a broad range of WSI-based computational workflows, including cancer subtyping, molecular phenotype prediction, and prognostic modeling. Future work will include systematic comparisons of alternative pathology foundation models and extension to additional cancer types beyond HCC.

title: Multi-Omics Analysis of NF1 Loss Reveals Distinct Tumor Programs in Ovarian Cancer
authors: Derek Wang, Rutgers University Camden, United States; Iman Dehzangi, Rutgers University Camden, United States; Gabriele Romano, Drexel University, United States
abstract: Neurofibromin 1 (NF1) is a key negative regulator of RAS signaling and has been implicated in multiple cancer types. Despite being among the most frequently altered genes in ovarian cancer, its functional role and downstream biological consequences in this cancer remain poorly understood. In particular, the cellular programs and tumor microenvironment features associated with NF1 loss have not been systematically characterized. To address this, we integrated large-scale public ovarian cancer datasets with multi-omic data. NF1 expression levels were used to define NF1-null tumors and stratify samples into NF1-null and NF1-wildtype groups. We then performed transcriptomic analyses and multi-omic integration to identify pathways and cellular states associated with NF1 loss. We found that NF1-null ovarian tumors exhibit significantly improved overall survival compared to NF1-wildtype tumors. At the molecular level, NF1 loss was associated with increased metabolic activity, enhanced proliferative and mitotic programs, and activation of Î²-catenin signaling. In parallel, NF1-null tumors showed upregulation of DNA repair pathways, along with reduced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and TGFÎ²-associated mesenchymal programs. Consistent with these findings, the tumor microenvironment of NF1-null tumors was characterized by a depletion of fibroblasts and stromal activity. Collectively, these features define a metabolically active, replication-driven, and more epithelial tumor state associated with NF1 loss. These findings provide new insight into the role of NF1 in ovarian cancer and establish a multi-omic framework for understanding NF1-null tumor biology. Furthermore, the identified molecular and microenvironmental features may serve as potential biomarkers to guide therapeutic strategies targeting NF1-associated vulnerabilities.

title: Biobank-scale clinical phenotype prediction through shared genetics using graph-based machine learning
authors: Aishwarya Mandava, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Jonathan Shortt, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Chris Gignoux, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Arjun Krishnan, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States
abstract: Clinical phenotype data in medical records are often incomplete, noisy, and inconsistent, thus limiting their utility for disease subtyping, comorbidity analysis, early screening, and disease management. Multiple computational approaches have been developed to address this challenge by imputing/correcting phenotype records. However, current approaches fail to scale to biobank-sized cohorts, model phenotypic co-occurrence patterns, or incorporate critical information such as the sharing of genomic segments between patients. Here, we propose a graph-based machine learning (ML) framework called ClinPhePred, that leverages shared identity-by-descent (IBD) genomic segments between individuals â€“ capturing fine-grained genetic relatedness â€“ represented as an individual-level graph, for accurate, biobank-scale phenotype prediction. ClinPhePred begins by learning two low-dimensional representations: one, of individuals in a biobank, based on their IBD-derived genetic similarity within the cohort, and another, of thousands of standardized clinical phenotypes (phecodes) based on their hierarchical relationships. Then, it trains a neural network to project individuals from the genetic latent space into the phenotypic latent space. The resulting projection is then used to predict missing and future phenotypes (and correct noisy ones). We applied ClinPhePred to the ~100,000-individuals in the biobank at the Colorado Center for Personalized Medicine (CCPM) with ~1,800 phecodes. Using the IBD-derived graph, we characterized the patient network structure using centrality measures, homophily, community structure and assessed the alignment of inferred network communities with demographic attributes. We then evaluated ClinPhePred by comparing it with baseline approaches, including existing phenotype imputation methods, identified phenotypes where ClinPhePred outperformed baseline methods, and stratified predictive performance across demographic groups.

title: dd-cfDNA Reflects Donor-Specific Antibody Strength and Class After Lung Transplant
authors: Isabella Liu, NIH/NHLBI, United States; Muhtadi Alnababteh, NIH/NHLBI, United States; Hyesik Kong, NIH/NHLBI, United States; Sean Agbor-Enoh, NIH/NHLBI, United States
abstract: Donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) are associated with increased risk for antibody-mediated rejection (AMR), chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), and reduced survival. Yet the relationship of DSA features and allograft injury remains incompletely understood. This study investigated associations between DSA features, including status, strength, and class and donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA), as an allograft injury biomarker. The multicenter study included 257 patients, 1638 paired individual DSA tests and dd-cfDNA assessments from ddPCR. An NIH committee defined DSA status (positive/negative), DSA strength as low (mean fluorescence intensity [MFI] 10,000), class as class I, or II. Comparisons across DSA positivity, strength, class and specificity were performed using bioinformatics techniques and Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis statistical tests. Incidence of DSA was 52%, detected at a median 44.5 (IQR=111.25) days post-transplant. DSA-positive samples demonstrated significantly higher dd-cfDNA compared with DSA-negative samples [166 (89-301) vs 86 (53-149) copies/mL; p DSA-positivity, strength, and class are associated with high dd-cfDNA levels, indicating greater molecular allograft injury. These findings could reflect the mechanistic link between humoral alloimmunity and allograft injury and highlight the potential of dd-cfDNA to serve as a molecular integrator of graft injury associated with DSA. Combining two non-invasive biomarkers, DSA features with cfDNA, may improve care and guide immunosuppressive therapy.

title: GutFeel: A Platform for Multimodal Personal Health Data Collection and Meal-Centered Data Curation
authors: Magdalena Nikolova, Ramapo College of New Jeresey, United States; Hristo Denev, Ramapo College of New Jersey, United States
abstract: Studying individual responses to food remains challenging because postprandial responses reflect the interaction of multiple physiological factors. Moreover, the data is often fragmented as it is collected across disconnected devices and applications, limiting analysis. Characterizing these responses requires integrating multimodal data streams. We have developed GutFeel, a platform for multimodal personal health data collection, integration, and curation. The system ingests mobile-collected and imported data from wearables (Ðµ.g. Heart rate, Heart rate variability, etc.), CGMs, food logs, sleep logs, and symptom surveys, and organizes them through a layered workflow for validation, cleaning, annotation, and standardization. These curated inputs are converted into meal-centered episodes that combine nutritional, physiological, sleep, and time-of-day context features while tracking curated representations back to the original raw records. GutFeel includes mobile and web interfaces through which participants log meals and sleep, complete post-meal surveys, and review their data visually. The platform also supports photo-based food input. The platform is designed to accommodate machine-learning-based workflows through infrastructure for model artifact storage, prediction records, and explainability-oriented outputs. The architecture is configured to route these meal episodes into predictive pipelines designed to output glucose peak predictions, classifiers indicating whether these peaks are lower-than-usual, normal, or higher-than-usual for that user, as well as predicted symptoms, energy levels, and meal satisfaction. GutFeel represents a working platform for structured data collection and standardized episode construction in pilot study settings. This system establishes a technological foundation for future evaluation of personalized postprandial modeling and broader participant-centered digital health studies.

title: PROC-DOT: Prostate Cancer Drug Pair Optimization via Transcriptomics
authors: Gargi Tawarmalani, Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, United States; Nadia Lanman, Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, United States; Yiyang Lu, Purdue IE & Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, United States; Luopin Wang, Versiti Blood Research Institute, United States
abstract: Drug resistance is associated with 90% of cancer deaths. In prostate cancer (PCa), cell heterogeneity and monotherapies drive the disease toward refractory castrate resistance and even though drug combination therapy (CT) offers a promising solution, computational methods designed to identify CT in PCa remain inadequate. Our computational model PROC-DOT is the first PCa CT screener to predict CT effects via a generalized linear model on single drug RNA-seq data and is integrated with principal component analysis (PCA) for noise reduction. Using a novel angle metric to quantify disease signature reversal, PROC-DOT pairs 419 individual drugs to rank the resulting 87,571 combinations. The top ranking combinations in PCa were validated by literature. Additionally, PROC-DOT's predictive ability was validated on a lung cancer dataset, where predicted norms and angles closely matched observed effects, achieving a strong linear correlation (R^2 = 0.9691) and angular deviations below 10 degrees. In contrast to traditional orthogonality scores derived from up and down-regulation of gene expressions, PROC-DOT utilizes magnitude of expression from robust RNA-seq data, is insensitive to drug order, and provides a more discriminative ranking, thereby identifying drug pairs capable of reversing disease signatures. By filtering vast combinatorial spaces into clinically viable candidates in minutes, this approach reduces the experimental burden associated with traditional screening. Crucially, this acceleration offers a pathway to compress the typical 10-15 year drug development timeline, representing a transformative advancement in delivering timely, effective therapies for resistant cancers.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Identified Acute Phase Drivers of Kidney Injury After Liver Transplantation
authors: Alka Rani, University of South Florida, United States; Qiang Zeng, University of South Florida, United States; Minh Tran, University of South Florida, United States; Colby Parris, University of South Florida, United States; Carlos Esquivel, University of South Florida, United States; Jinzhuang Dou, University of Alabama at Birmingham, United States; Lily Fu, Mayo Clinic Arizona, United States; Lei Wang, University of South Florida, United States
abstract: The highest incidences of kidney injury and chronic renal failure occur after liver transplantation. More than 50% of patients get affected by chronic kidney diseases within 5 years of liver transplantation, adding to the burden of kidney transplantation, for which more than 80,000 people are already waiting for a donor. Early identification and management of kidney injury after liver transplantation can increase the success rate and long-term survival of the patients. Therefore, we planned a detailed multi-omics study to understand the mechanisms behind the liver-kidney crosstalk and identify the early markers or drivers. In this study we performed orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) using inbred male C57BL/6 mice. Blood, urine, kidney tissue and liver graft samples were collected 24 hours after the liver transplantation. Liver chemistry and kidney injury markers were measured in the blood plasma samples. Unsupervised multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) integrating RNA-seq, proteomics, lipidomics and metabolomics data from a total of 20 samples identified four latent factors. Factor 1 explained the majority of shared variance and showed clear separation between liver and kidney tissue. Factor 2 had a significant correlation with the groups. Factor 2 top features were further explored for kidney specific injury markers those did not change in the liver; we found 3 markers with very high effect size in the kidney tissue. Multi-omics analysis revealed coordinated changes in liver and kidney. The results were promising and provided a foundation for understanding the mechanisms driving kidney injury after liver transplantation and for developing future screening and therapeutic strategies.

title: Language model embedding classifiers enable identification of multiple sclerosis-associated BCRs and repertoires
authors: Graham Peet, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Gregory Owens, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Jeffrey Bennett, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Arjun Krishnan, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Wendy Macklin, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease affecting over two million people worldwide. Although B cell involvement in MS pathology is well established (evidenced by the efficacy of B cell-depleting therapies and the presence of clonally expanded intrathecal immunoglobulins), a definitive adaptive immune diagnostic signature for MS remains elusive. Here we present an integrated computational framework combining a large-scale retrospective BCR dataset, a novel BCR-specific DNA language model, and sequence- and patient-level classifiers to identify MS-associated immune repertoire features. We assembled over 11.5 million IGH sequences from ~800 patients by exhaustively reanalyzing publicly available RNA sequencing data from NCBI SRA, supplemented with OPIG OAS and in-house datasets. We pre-trained BCR-Mistral, a 500M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on highly diverse BCR sequences sampled to maximize training diversity. BCR-Mistral outperformed state-of-the-art BCR and general-purpose protein language models in embedding quality. A sequence classifier trained on BCR-Mistral embeddings substantially exceeded baseline models in precision for MS-associated sequences and correctly ranked known myelin-binding antibodies above an isotype control, providing direct experimental validation. For patient classification, waypoint-based repertoire embeddings compressed variable-sized repertoires into fixed representations; combined with sequence predictions, a gradient-boosted classifier achieved ROC AUCs of 0.89â€“0.91 distinguishing MS patients from healthy, autoimmune, and infectious disease comparators across 505 repertoires. This framework and its constituent resources provide a foundation for improved MS diagnosis and for identifying pathogenic antibody candidates across autoimmune conditions.

title: Lifecourse Genetic Risk of Cardiovascular Disease in Women with Reproductive Health Conditions
authors: Tess Cherlin, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Samantha Strydesky, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Stephanie Mohammed, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Lannawill Caruth, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Aude Ikuzwe Sindikubwabo, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Ananya Rajagopalan, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Lindsay Guare, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc., Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc., United States; Penn Medicine Biobank, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Shefali Setia-Verma, University of Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Recent efforts are being made uncover the etiology of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in women and womenâ€™s health conditions (WHC) have been shown to significantly increase the risk for CVD outcomes later in life suggesting a culmination of factors contribute to cardiovascular conditions. We hypothesize that genetic factors may be underlying the increased time to CVD outcome for women with WHC. We leveraged three biobanks to address this hypothesis: Penn Medicine Biobank, the eMERGE network, and the All of Us Biobank. Phenotypes for cardiovascular conditions as well as womenâ€™s health conditions were defined by ICD codes. We did time-to-event genome-wide association (TTE GWAS) analysis to identify variants associated with disease trajectories. Two different endpoints were used: 1) onset: birth to WHC or CVD and 2) progression: WHC to first cardiovascular event. We ran ancestry-stratified TTE GWAS for the six WHCs and three cardiovascular conditions (disease onset) as well as ancestry-stratified TTE GWAS for 18 progression phenotypes. Overall, we found 9 progression associations at suggestive genome-wide significance (p-value â‰¤ 1.25E-06). In the PMBB cohort we identified one significant locus in the intronic region of CTNND2 in the PCOS onset analysis (p-value = 2.47e-09 and one significant locus upstream of ZNF385D in the PCOS to total CVD analysis (p-value = 2.50E-08). These findings provide valuable insights into the genetic basis of cardiovascular disease risk for women with reproductive health conditions. Given the high prevalence of CVD in women, longitudinal studies are needed to uncover the molecular, genetic, and pharmacogenomic pathways underlying disease progression in women.

title: Leveraging large language models to speed phenotyping of rare diseases
authors: Rachel Waymack, NIAID, United States; Yuyan Yi, NIAID, United States; Reed Shabman, NIAID, United States; Morgan Similuk, NIAID, United States; Rajarshi Ghosh, NIAID, United States; Daniel Veltri, NIAID, United States
abstract: Although individually rare, rare diseases collectively affect roughly 300 million people worldwide. The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) is a resource of standardized descriptions of clinical phenotypes often used by researchers and clinicians to aid diagnosing rare disease patients, which is often difficult and delayed. While the terms and relationships defined in the HPO are useful for determining diagnoses, extracting relevant patient phenotypes from clinical notes is a labor-intensive task. Large language models (LLMs) have shown steady improvement in their abilities to summarize and generate text over the past few years. Recent studies have leveraged LLMs to aid in diagnosing patients with rare diseases. Here we test the ability of three LLMs, Metaâ€™s Llama3, OpenAIâ€™s gpt-oss-20b and Googleâ€™s Gemini 2.0, to accurately classify HPO terms identified from biomedical text as relevant or not to the described patient. We use a previously described tool, FastHPOCR, to identify HPO terms from the text and task the LLMs with classifying each term as relevant or not based on the biomedical text. Refinement with an LLM improves precision by 1-3%, depending on the LLM used, when applied to publicly available datasets. We are also evaluating this approach in clinical notes from patients with established genetic diagnoses, which provides a clinically grounded test set for assessing whether the extracted HPO terms capture known disease-defining phenotypes. To address low precision when working with real clinical notes, we are testing numerous efforts to improve performance including prompt engineering and fine-tuning of the models.

title: Translating AI to Diabetic Foot Care: A Motion-Robust PPG Framework for Peripheral Hemodynamic Monitoring
authors: Yongwook Yoon, Yonsei University, South Korea; Erdenebayar Urtnasan, Yonsei University, South Korea
abstract: Background: Continuous monitoring of distal microvascular hemodynamics is critical for the early prevention of diabetic foot ulcers. Although photoplethysmography (PPG) provides a non-invasive, accessible alternative to painful nerve conduction velocity tests and cumbersome Doppler ultrasounds, its clinical translation is severely hindered by patient motion artifacts. Traditional rule-based PPG algorithms frequently fail to detect pulse peaks under such noise, limiting their real-world applicability. Methods: To bridge this translational gap, we propose a 1-D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) feature extraction technique for robust peripheral blood flow monitoring. Physiological time-series signals were acquired from patients' toes using a PPG sensor integrated into a foot thermal therapy device. We evaluated the 1-D CNN against a standard rule-based pipeline (band-pass filtering, baseline wandering removal, and local extrema search) using datasets with intentionally introduced patient movements (12~18 seconds) to assess algorithmic robustness. Results: During motion-free intervals, both methods accurately detected pulse peaks. However, under motion artifacts, the traditional method exhibited a simultaneous increase in false and missed peaks, causing drastic fluctuations in heart rate inference. Conversely, the 1-D CNN successfully learned non-linear morphological patterns. By generating feature maps that emphasized upstroke and template similarity, the CNN effectively suppressed noise and maintained superior continuity in pulse peak detection. Conclusion: The proposed AI-driven 1-D CNN model enables reliable, continuous monitoring of diabetic peripheral blood flow by overcoming motion-induced constraints. By providing an accessible computational method for daily point-of-care monitoring, this approach demonstrates strong translational potential for the early detection and prevention of diabetic foot complications.

title: Exploring Neoantigen–Immune Decoupling in APOBEC3-Driven Hypermutated Tumors through Multi-Omics Analysis
authors: Weiming Yang, National Institute of Health, United States; Rouf Banday, National Institute of Health, United States; Andrea Apolo, National Institutes of Health, United States; Mikhail Kolmogorov, National Institute of Health, United States; Gurram Sandeep, National Institutes of Health, United States; Salah Boudjadi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Vladimir Romero, National Institutes of Health, United States; Elias Chandran, National Institutes of Health, United States; Raju Chelluri, National Institute of Health, United States; Lisa M. Jenkins, National Institute of Health, United States; Dhanusha Yesudhas, National Institute of Health, United States; Abbas Rad, National Institute of Health, United States; Tania Aquino, National Institute of Health, United States; Kelly Butler, National Institute of Health, United States; Jaimie Ryou, National Institute of Health, United States; Ayse Keskus, National Institute of Health, United States; Arup Chakraborty, The Henry M. Jackson Foundation - Uniformed Services University, United States; Ecem Unal, National Institute of Health, United States; Bilal Lone, National Institute of Health, United States
abstract: Hypermutated tumors generate abundant neoantigens yet often fail to elicit effective T-cell immunity, revealing a central paradox in cancer biology. Elevated tumor mutational burden (TMB) frequently arises from mutational processes such as APOBEC3 activity, which drives widespread single-nucleotide variants in epithelial cancers, including bladder, lung, and breast. These tumors often display hypermutation alongside extensive copy-number alterations (CNAs). Increasing evidence links CNAs, including complex rearrangements and extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), to immunosuppressive tumor states. We hypothesized that hypermutated tumors develop intrinsic immune-evasion mechanisms that counterbalance increased neoantigen load, limiting immune recognition and therapeutic response. We integrated large-scale multi-omics data with single-cell (scRNA-seq) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) from bladder cancer cohorts. This included newly generated scRNA-seq from non-muscle-invasive tumors, snRNA-seq from high-risk and metastatic lesions, and public datasets from muscle-invasive disease. Functional in vitro and in vivo studies were conducted to define mechanistic links between genomic alterations and immune signaling. Across bladder, breast, and lung cancer types enriched for APOBEC3-mediated hypermutation, elevated NECTIN4 expression was consistently associated with reduced immune infiltration. NECTIN4 expression was largely restricted to malignant epithelial cells and was driven by recurrent 1q23 copy-number amplification, ecDNA, and hypomethylation. Mechanistically, NECTIN4 suppresses antigen presentation and inflammatory cytokine programs while reducing interferon-inducible checkpoint ligands, including PD-L1. This state is reversible with the NECTIN4-targeting antibody drug conjugate enfortumab vedotin, which restores immune-permissive signaling, providing a mechanistic rationale for combining NECTIN4 targeting with PD-1 blockade. Finally, we show that APOBEC3-mediated mutagenesis underlies recurrent NECTIN4amplification, linking hypermutation to adaptive immune escape. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which hypermutated tumors evade immune surveillance, positioning NECTIN4 as a central, targetable regulator of tumor-intrinsic immune exclusion.

title: Modeling The Evolving Phenotype of Preeclampsia: Mapping Shifts in Temporal Risk Across 3.15 Million Pregnancies
authors: Brendan Joyce, University of Wisconsin, Madison - Dept. of Biostatistics & Medical Informatics, United States; Kara Hoppe, University of Wisconsin, Madison - Dept. of Obstetrics & Gynecology, United States; Irene Ong, University of Wisconsin, Madison - Dept. of Biostatistics & Medical Informatics, United States
abstract: Purpose: Preeclampsia affects 2â€“8% of pregnancies and remains a leading cause of maternal and fetal mortality, accounting for an estimated 70,000 maternal and 500,000 fetal deaths worldwide in 2023. While early intervention significantly improves outcomes, current risk models often fail to generalize to cases arising later in pregnancy. This deterioration in predictive accuracy occurs because physiological shifts throughout gestation alter the relevance of clinical features over time; consequently, models anchored to a single ""snapshot"" lose utility as pregnancy progresses. Study Design: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 3.15 million pregnancies using the Epic Cosmos Electronic Health Records (EHR) dataset. To model preeclampsia risk longitudinally, we employed a 28-day sliding window approach utilizing a suite of classifiers, including logistic regression, decision trees, random forest, gradient boosting, and support vector machines. By calculating time-step-specific feature attribution for each model, we quantified the evolution of the preeclampsia phenotype and identified temporal shifts in predictive weight as gestation progressed. Results: Temporal mapping of feature importance revealed a crossover effect where the predictive dominance of baseline vitals (BMI, SBP) is superseded by evolving laboratory markers (urine protein, WBC) and interim clinical diagnoses as gestation progresses to the late second and early third trimesters. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that large-scale EHR data can effectively capture the dynamic clinical trajectory of pregnancy. By moving beyond static models, we provide a framework for longitudinal risk stratification. Our findings characterize late-onset preeclampsia as a dynamic clinical phenotype, highlighting a need for screening protocols that shift from fixed early-pregnancy measurements toward evolving physiological data, including real-time vitals and laboratory markers.

title: Multi-evidence prioritization of ponatinib-associated cardiotoxicity candidates from public transcriptomic signatures
authors: Joonho Kong, Department of Medicine, Yonsei University Wonju College ofMedicine, Wonju, Republic of Korea, South Korea; Jaeyeon Jang, Yonsei University Wonju College of Medicine, Wonju,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Jee Hyun Kong, Yonsei University Wonju College of Medicine, Wonju,Republic of Korea, South Korea; Taesic Lee, Yonsei University Wonju College of Medicine, Wonju,Republic of Korea, South Korea
abstract: Ponatinib, a third-generation BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor, provides potent antileukemic activity but carries clinically important cardiovascular toxicity. Public RNA-seq data were analyzed to refine transcript-level candidates linked to ponatinib-induced cardiotoxicity. In GSE186341, DMSO-treated controls were stratified by principal component analysis and k-means clustering, followed by cluster-wise differential expression analysis and fixed-effect inverse-variance meta-analysis. The meta-analysis identified 2,639 ponatinib-associated meta-DEGs. Cross-dataset comparison with ponatinib-treated hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes in GSE217421 yielded 81 overlapping candidates supported by both datasets. The 81 candidates were further ranked using four evidence layers: same-direction agreement between discovery and cardiomyocyte data, specificity against imatinib-associated responses, cardiovascular annotation, and proteinâ€“protein interaction connectivity. Candidate prioritization highlighted genes linked to ion-channel regulation, cAMP-responsive stress signaling, insulin-responsive metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis, redox regulation, apoptosis, endothelial injury, and inflammatory signaling. Candidate annotations were consistent with experimentally described mechanisms of ponatinib cardiovascular toxicity, including cardiomyocyte stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, vascular injury, thromboinflammatory activation, and impaired survival signaling. The ranking procedure reduced a broad ponatinib transcriptomic signature to a focused candidate list for follow-up qPCR, protein-level assays, and functional validation in cardiac and vascular injury models. Public drug-response transcriptomics can therefore guide experimentally testable cardiotoxicity candidate selection.

title: COMPUTATIONAL PREDICTION OF PATHOGENIC FMR1 VARIANTS IN FRAGILE X SYNDROME
authors: Vedha Tamilinian, Northview High School, United States
abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a genetic disorder characterized by reduced expression of the FMRP protein, which is essential for synaptic plasticity and neural development. FXS is most commonly caused by CGG repeat expansions (>200 repeats) in the FMR1 gene. However, recent studies have suggested that missense mutations within the KH1 and KH2 domains of FMR1 may also contribute to disease pathology. The functional impact of these variants remains poorly characterized. This limits accurate clinical interpretation, contributing to uncertainty in variant classification. This study develops a machine learning framework to improve the classification of pathogenic missense mutations in the KH1 and KH2 domains of FMR1. The model integrates protein sequence embeddings from the ESM2 protein language model, structural features predicted by NetSurfP, and evolutionary conservation features derived from multiple sequence alignment-based analysis. Variant data were collected from ClinVar and supplemented with in silico generated single amino acid substitutions across the KH1 and KH2 domains of the wild-type FMRP. Four supervised learning models including support vector machine, random forest, logistic regression, and XGBoost were trained, and evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation Among these, XGBoost achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.94, precision of 0.92, recall of 0.95, and an F1-score of 0.94. The model correctly identified the KH1 variant G266E, previously validated in experimental studies, as pathogenic when evaluated on unseen data. The proposed framework achieved a performance within the range reported for established variant effect prediction tools such as SIFT, PolyPhen-2, and AlphaMissense. Analysis of model outputs revealed amino acid substitution patterns associated with increased pathogenicity, including substitutions involving serine, proline, asparagine, glutamic acid, alanine, and valine. The model also identified mutational hotspots within KH1 (n=6) and KH2 (n=8) domains that are enriched for predicted pathogenic variants. This framework provides a scalable approach for prioritizing FMR1 missense variants of uncertain significance and may support further experimental validation of variants associated with the FXS phenotype in individuals lacking CGG repeat expansions.

title: Bayesian latent-variable modelling reveals a consistent Th17-driven inflammatory signature in Long Covid
authors: Carolina Alvarez-Garavito, Life and Medical Sciences Institute (LIMES), University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany, Germany; An Hotterbeekx, Molecular Pathology Group, Laboratory of Cell Biology Histology (CBH) and Vaccine Infectious Disease Institute (CBH), Faculty of Medicine, University of Antwerp, Antwerpen, Belgium, Belgium; Lorenzo Maria Canziani, Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Diagnostics and Public Health, University of Verona, Verona, Italy, Italy; Lenny Coppens, Molecular Pathology Group, Laboratory of Cell Biology Histology (CBH) and Vaccine Infectious Disease Institute (CBH), Faculty of Medicine, University of Antwerp, Antwerpen, Belgium, Belgium; Roy Gusinow, Life and Medical Sciences Institute (LIMES), University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany, Germany; Manuel Huth, Life and Medical Sciences Institute (LIMES), University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany, Germany; Gaia Maccarrone, Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Diagnostics and Public Health, University of Verona, Verona, Italy, Italy; Anna Górska, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland, Poland; Elisa Gentilotti, Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Diagnostics and Public Health, University of Verona, Verona, Italy, Italy; Elisa Rossi, CINECA Interuniversity Consortium, Bologna, Italy, Italy; Salvatore Cataudella, CINECA Interuniversity Consortium, Bologna, Italy, Italy; Evelina Tacconelli, Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Diagnostics and Public Health, University of Verona, Verona, Italy, Italy; Samir Kumar-Singh, Molecular Pathology Group, Laboratory of Cell Biology Histology (CBH) and Vaccine Infectious Disease Institute (CBH), Faculty of Medicine, University of Antwerp, Antwerpen, Belgium, Belgium; Jan Hasenauer, Life and Medical Sciences Institute (LIMES), University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany, Germany
abstract: Long Covid (LC) consists of symptoms persisting beyond 3 months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, with phenotypes spanning respiratory, neurosensorial, pain, and fatigue. Although its pathophysiology remains unclear, research suggests that LC may be immune-mediated, making cytokine profiling relevant. Because cytokine data are high-dimensional and strongly correlated, dimensionality reduction is often used to derive latent co-signaling clusters, whose estimated per-sample scores are entered as covariates in regression models. However, this approach ignores measurement error in the estimated scores, which can bias regression coefficients and underestimate uncertainty. Here, we apply factor analysis (FA) to derive latent immune factors from 38 serum cytokines measured in the ORCHESTRA prospective multinational study, and estimate their association with LC phenotypes using Bayesian correction for covariate measurement error. Specifically, we consider: (1) a logistic regression as the outcome model, with latent scores and clinical covariates as regressors, (2) FA as the measurement model, with loadings fixed to an initial solution, and (3) a multivariate normal prior as the conditional model for the latent scores. Under this Bayesian framework, factor scores and regression parameters are estimated simultaneously, resulting in appropriate inference. Models were fitted separately for each phenotype and follow-up period using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. Our results show clear evidence of immune-mediation in LC. Specifically, after controlling for clinical covariates, Factor 1 (IL-17F, IL-21, IL-3) and Factor 4 (Eotaxin/CCL11, CTACK/CCL27, MCP-1/CCL2, IP-10/CXCL10) were positively associated with LC during follow-up. Our findings support an immune-mediated basis for LC and suggest a persistent Th17-driven inflammatory program in its pathophysiology.

title: Harmonizing Patient-Reported Real-World Data for Drug Repurposing in Long COVID to Identify Therapeutic Signals
authors: Tahsin Farid, National Institutes of Health, United States; Keyla Tumas, National Institutes of Health, United States; Serghei Gorobet, National Institutes of Health, United States; Li Geng, National Institutes of Health, United States; Keith Kelleher, National Institutes of Health, United States; Jessica Maine, National Institutes of Health, United States; Ewy Mathe, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Long COVID is a post-infectious condition manifesting in up to 30% of SARS-CoV-2 infections. Despite substantial morbidity and an estimated global annual financial burden of $1 trillion, no FDA-approved therapies exist. Clinicians rely on repurposed drugs for symptomatic control. Systematic collection of real-world data (RWD) may enable identification of therapeutic signals and prioritization of candidates for further investigation. The CURE ID Long COVID project (https://cure.ncats.io/pilot-overview/long-covid) collects structured case reports from patients, care partners, and clinicians that include heterogeneous free-text symptom and treatment entries. This data is harmonized through AI-assisted curation and manual review to consolidate spelling variants, synonyms, and related concepts. Harmonized concepts are mapped to standard identifiers and ontologies (HPO for phenotypes and RxNorm for drugs), supporting interoperability with standard biomedical data resources, including the NIH Biomedical Translator. From 586 cases collected to date, 1,025 drug entries were consolidated into 481 unique agents and mapped to 40 pharmacologic classes. Similarly, 259 symptom entries were collapsed to 130 and organized into 18 organ systems and mechanism-informed clusters. Participants are predominantly female (70%) with a mean age in the fifth decade. A median of 7 symptoms and 3 treatments are reported per patient. The most frequent symptoms include brain fog (n=239), fatigue (n=235), and post-exertional malaise (n=220); commonly reported treatments include low-dose naltrexone (n=174), propranolol (n=79), and famotidine (n=72). Over half of symptomâ€“treatment pairs are associated with reported improvement. Further analysis can identify promising repurposing candidates. This work establishes a scalable, ontology-driven framework that enables evaluation of patient-reported RWD.

title: An ancestry-aware, cloud-native multi-omic framework for molecular heterogeneity in severe acute malnutrition
authors: Yixing Han, National Human Genome Research Institute, NationalInstitutes of Health, United States; Qing Li, National Human Genome Research Institute, NationalInstitutes of Health, United States; Emily White, National Human Genome Research Institute, NationalInstitutes of Health, United States; Neil Hanchard, National Human Genome Research Institute, NationalInstitutes of Health, United States
abstract: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) affects approximately 19 million children annually and causes substantial childhood mortality, et the mechanisms distinguishing edematous SAM (ESAM/kwashiorkor) from non-edematous SAM (NESAM/marasmus) remain unresolved. We developed an ancestry-aware, cloud-native multi-omic framework to characterize molecular heterogeneity in clinically phenotyped Jamaican and Malawian SAM cohorts. Genome-wide DNA methylation profiling of buccal cells from 309 children identified widespread ESAM-associated hypomethylation, enriched near metabolic and liver-related genes and absent in adults recovered from SAM, suggesting dynamic disease-state epigenetic remodeling. Complementary intracontinental admixture mapping and targeted genotyping of 103 one-carbon metabolism genes across 711 children identified seven ESAM-associated loci, including MTHFR, PRICKLE2, and PLD2, enriched on East African ancestral haplotypes and regions under recent positive selection. Building on these findings, we implemented reproducible AnVIL workflows integrating whole-genome sequencing, DNA methylation, RNA-seq, metabolomics, ancestry inference, variant burden testing, methylation-QTL analysis, functional annotation, and machine-learning network discovery. Current analyses include harmonized multi-omic datasets spanning 182 WGS, 374 methylation, 28 RNA-seq, and 35 metabolomic profiles, with expansion through 192 population-scale WGS and 24 cfDNA 5-base sequencing samples to improve ancestry-specific reference representation and jointly profile genetic and epigenetic variation. This framework supports a model in which inherited variation, one-carbon metabolism, and nutritional stress interact to drive ESAM pathogenesis, while providing reusable infrastructure for equitable, reproducible multi-omic discovery in complex pediatric disease and a transferable model for cloud-enabled precision health programs across diseases.

title: AI Guided Therapeutic Strategies to Combat Viral Evolution
authors: Muhammad Ali, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, United States; Gustavo Caetano-Anollés, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, United States; Elhan Ersoz, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, United States; Albert Seo, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, United States
abstract: Vaccine and binder design relies heavily on the structural stability of target proteins. Predicting mutations or identifying stable regions can help prepare for the inevitability of future pandemics. Since most mutations maintain a protein's overall fold, Inverse Folding (IF), a technique that generates sequences matching a provided structure could potentially identify stable or highly mutable regions by using positional entropies. This study investigates the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein using AlphaFold3 to generate a complete 3D model including flexible loops. We used ProteinMPNN and evaluated the minimum number of sequences needed before reaching a point of diminishing returns and observed promising results after only 1000 iterations with slight improvements from 100 iterations. The positional entropies for each amino acid were calculated using the SoftMax formula. Our analysis identified ~448 very low-entropy positions. Information on positional entropies, combined with information on surface exposure, intrinsic disorder, binding capability, epitope regions, and structure prediction confidence scores identified 37 target positions for therapeutic targeting. The entire workflow can be run in a short amount of time and help filter out key regions for binder design using tools such as BindCraft or using InverseFolding and Docking Simulations to design antibodies.

title: Conserved early transcriptional responses to experimental infection in deer, elk and bison
authors: Bruna Petry, ORISE/National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Paola M. Boggiatto, National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Alexandra Buckley, National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Kaitlyn M. Sarlo Davila, National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Eric D. Cassmann, Department of Veterinary Pathology, Iowa State University College of Veterinary Medicine, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Steven C. Olsen, National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Mitchell V. Palmer, National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States; Ellie J. Putz, National Animal Disease Center, Agricultural Research Service, USDA, Ames, IA, USA, United States
abstract: SARS-Cov-2 continues to be a threat to humans as well as domestic and wild animals. Variation in clinical severity, zoonotic potential, and host-specific immune responses contributes to the persistence and circulation of the virus across species. In wildlife, susceptibility to infection differs with some species demonstrating bigger permissiveness than others. In this study, we investigated the peripheral transcriptomic response to experimental SARS-Cov-2 infection in white-tailed deer, elk, and bison at early timepoints post-infection (pi). A substantial number of differentially expressed genes (DEG) were detected in whole blood at days 2 and 5 post-infection (pi) compared to pre-infection. Several DEGs were associated with the Coronavirus disease - COVID-19 KEGG pathway and immune system related GO terms, highlighting activation of antiviral mechanisms. All three species showed a rapid response to infection, with changes in gene expression as early as day 2 pi. Comparative analysis revealed 21 upregulated genes conserved across all species at day 2 pi. KEGG pathway enrichment of these shared genes included terms related to Coronavirus disease, Influenza A, and innate immune responses, suggesting activation of broad antiviral responses. By day 5 pi, transcriptional responses had diverged substantially among species, with only a single downregulated gene, NFACT2, conserved across all three. Together, these findings demonstrate that deer, elk, and bison initiate a rapid and partially conserved early immune response to SARS-Cov-2, but they follow species-specific transcriptional pathways. This work provides new insight into host-virus interactions in the transcriptional responses for wildlife animals and highlights potential molecular markers of early infection.

title: Recent improvements in NCBI BLAST protein searches
authors: Grzegorz Boratyn, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Preye Akuiyibo, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Christiam Camacho, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Amelia Fong, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Yuriy Merezhuk, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Yan Raytselis, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Jian Ye, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States; Irena Zaretskaya, National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, United States
abstract: Sequence database search is often an initial computational step in analysis of biological data. NCBI BLAST search programs are widely used to search large comprehensive databases, such as the Non-redundant protein database (NR), to identify similar annotated sequences and determine functional content of a biological sample. The rapid growth of the popular databases has made search time a critical computational bottleneck. We present recent improvements in NCBI BLAST protein databases and search program. ClusteredNR database was derived by clustering the NR database at 90% identity and 90% coverage, with each cluster represented by a single well annotated sequence. ClusteredNR is about half the size of nr, while maintaining broad taxonomic representation. Searching ClusteredNR takes less than half the time to search NR. The search program BLASTP was optimized to improve performance. A smaller word size enables more compact data structures and improved CPU cache utilization, yielding searches faster by about 20%. We also updated sensitivity of initial word matches improving speed-sensitivity tradeoff when finding alignment seeds reducing run time by additional 4%. Further gains (about 8%) were achieved through application of heuristics, like chaining, that discard early low-potential partial alignments. These algorithmic improvements are available in BLAST+ version 2.17.0 and through the BLAST web service.

title: Performance of whole genome and transcriptome analytics for the Applied Proteogenomics Organizational Learning and Outcomes (APOLLO) network
authors: Shiliang Wang, Martha Cancer Center Research Program, HJF, Uniformed Services University of The Health Sciences, Bethesda, MD, United States
abstract: Shiliang Wang1,3, Xijun Zhang2,3, Shaoqiu He1,3, Daniel Hupalo2,3, Liqun Jiang1,3, Craig Shriver1,4, Clifton L. Dalgard2,5, APOLLO Research Network, Matthew D. Wilkerson2,5 1. Murtha Cancer Center Research Program, Department of Surgery, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Bethesda, MD 2. Center for Military Precision Health, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Bethesda, MD 3. Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine Inc., Bethesda, MD 4. Department of Surgery, Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, Bethesda, MD 5. Department of Anatomy, Physiology and Genetics, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Bethesda, MD The Applied Proteogenomics Organizational Learning and Outcomes (APOLLO) Consortium is molecularly profiling tumors from Military members and Veterans to enable precision medicine research, including DNA whole genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA sequencing on the tumor, and WGS on the normal tissue. Key challenges include massive storage, compute requirements, analytical accuracy and data interoperability. Presently, most analysis is conducted on HPC workflows. Here, we evaluated if the Dynamic Read Analysis for GENomics (DRAGEN), consisting of specialized hardware and accelerated software, would enable high performing precision medicine research in APOLLO. Genomes and transcriptomes of cell lines and APOLLO tissues were analyzed using an HPC workflow and the DRAGEN. We compared workflow performance on reference sets. Comparing germline WGS variants, the DRAGEN showed greater precision and sensitivity than the HPC workflow. The DRAGEN was faster and produced smaller data output files interoperable with leading analytics. For somatic WGS variants, the DRAGEN had superior sensitivity and precision. Somatic copy numbers and somatic mutations had high correlation and/or concordance similar to published inter-rater agreements. RNA expression were highly similar between in quantification and differential expression. Four tumors with fusion oncogenes had identical breakpoints between workflows. DRAGEN genome data analysis has a performance advantage to HPC workflows and meets all key challenges for big data, genome analytics at scale thus enabling precision medicine research for APOLLO. title: Methylation array based imprinting disturbance analysis by imprintomeR
authors: Hongjian Jin, St Jude Children's Research Hospital, United States; Gang Wu, St Jude Children's Research Hospital, United States
abstract: Genomic imprinting is commonly assessed using discrete thresholds applied to DNA methylation data, limiting the detection of subtle, heterogeneous, and partial imprinting alterations. We present imprintomeR, an R package for quantitative analysis and visualization of imprinting using Illumina 450K, EPICv1, and EPICv2 array data. imprintomeR introduces a continuous, coordinate-based framework that models imprinting as a directional system, where deviation from the canonical hemimethylated state is captured by a radial distance (magnitude) and an angular coordinate (mechanism). This representation enables unified characterization of imprinting perturbations, including locus-specific shifts and global alterations, without reliance on arbitrary thresholds. The package integrates probe-level and locus-level analyses with a suite of visualization tools, including beeswarm violin plots, density plots for allele-specific distributions, radar fingerprints for multi-locus profiles, and annotated heatmaps for cohort-level comparisons. Together, these approaches enable multi-scale interrogation of imprinting states, revealing both subtle deviations and structured patterns across samples and genomic regions. imprintomeR provides a flexible and interpretable framework for studying imprinting dysregulation in development and disease.

title: Hood College: Cultivating Bioinformaticians in the Heart of Maryland’s Biotech Cluster
authors: Randall Johnson, Hood College, Computer Science and Information Technology Department, United States; Jason Miller, Hood College, Computer Science and Information Technology Department, United States; April Boulton, Hood College, Biology Department, United States
abstract: Hood College is located north of Washington DC in Frederick, MD along the I-270 technology corridor which is one of the densest clusters of biotech and federal research activity in the United States. Hood College is a liberal arts college with 1200 undergraduates and a growing graduate student population, including graduate programs in Bioinformatics, Health Informatics, Biomedical Science, Environmental Biology and Nursing. Our bioinformatics M.S. program, established 10 years ago, serves as a valued regional partner for workforce development in this rapidly evolving field. Students develop both a deep and broad understanding of topics such as computational genomics, machine learning and pipeline development as well as a firm grasp of the underlying biology. The Hood College motto, With Heart and Mind and Hand, informs our approach to education from start to finish as we cultivate caring, knowledgeable scientists with practical, hands-on experience. Experiential learning through independent study and capstone research allows students to solve real-world problems as part of their degree requirements. Faculty ties to industry and federal agencies enhance these learning outcomes and aligns the program with current needs of regional employers. We present data on student outcomes, showing how our practical, interdisciplinary approach enables local professionals to pivot into bioinformatics roles or advance within their current organizations. This provides a model for how such programs can bridge the gap between academic training and the specialized needs of industry and government partners.

title: The Epigenetic Role Of DNA Methylation In Gene Expression In Pseudomoans Putida with adaption To Different Conditions
authors: Siqin Li, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States; Natalie Farny, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States
abstract: DNA methylation in prokaryotes has been shown to regulate gene expression in a variety of contexts that influence functions such as cell cycle progression, biofilm formation, sporulation, host virulence, and others. Pseudomonas putida is an organism widely used in environmental and industrial applications, such as bioremediation. However, there's no research that has ever studied the role of DNA methylation in P. putida. Due to the advancement of the third generation sequencing technology, we could characterize the genome wide DNA methylation profile of P. putida under different growth condition and the regulatory effect of DNA methyltransferase in gene expression. In this study, we detected and compared the DNA methylation profile of Pseudomonas putida under lab and soil condition under different growth phases and also investigate the transcriptional control role of DNA methyltransferase HsdM with comparisons among strains of knockout DNA methyltransferases, overexpressed DNA methyltransferase (DNMTs) and widetype.

title: Democratizing single cell and spatial omics analysis with cloud infrastructure and agentic workflows
authors: Stephen Williams, 10x Genomics, United States; Govinda Kamath, 10x Genomics, United States; Stephanie Kravitz, 10x Genomics, United States; Zach Kulis, 10x Genomics, United States; Sagar Patni, 10x Genomics, United States; Guy Joseph, 10x Genomics, United States; Evan Winget, 10x Genomics, United States; Preyas Shah, 10x Genomics, United States; Dylan Webster, 10x Genomics, United States
abstract: Background: The exponential growth, scale, and resolution of single-cell and spatial omics is transforming the understanding of biology and disease. While modern pipelines process data efficiently, the diversity of analytical approaches remains a bottleneck, demanding the deep intuition and technical acumen of experienced bioinformaticians to navigate high-dimensional data. To overcome these barriers, we present a highly scalable framework designed to democratize omics analysis through autonomous, AI-driven workflows. Methods: We introduce a novel LLM-driven analytical environment that enables multi-step, agentic conversational workflows beginning with scRNA-seq data. Our multi-agent system decomposes a user-specified hypothesis into a bounded execution plan with explicit per-step success criteria, evaluates intermediate results against those criteria, and adaptively replans. To complement this, and to support emerging high-plex technologies, we deployed a cutting edge architecture. This bypasses localized infrastructure limitations, enabling low-latency, real-time visualization and interactive downstream analysis within a streamlined web interface. Results: Application of our autonomous AI agent against benchmarks demonstrates high concordance with expert-validated results across a variety of approaches. Operating strictly de novo and blinded to original source publications, the agent consistently draws conclusions consistent with those of publications. Critically, testing against a battery of null datasets confirms the agentâ€™s robustness against spurious discoveries and analytical pitfalls. Conclusion: Developing autonomous AI agents alongside advanced infrastructure resolves current analytical and scalability bottlenecks, laying the groundwork for streamlined multi-modal interpretation. By bridging biological intuition with computational execution, this framework lowers the barrier to selecting optimal analytical strategies and accelerates multi-omic discovery.

title: Integrating functional effect scores of single nucleotide variants to identify novel genes in cancer
authors: Amanda Bataycan, The University of Texas at El Paso, United States; Ming-Ying Leung, The University of Texas at El Paso, United States
abstract: We developed an integrated scoring function, iQ(G), to assess the cumulative effects of nonsynonymous single nucleotide variants (SNVs) on the protein-coding genes and applied it to find novel candidate cancer-related genes from patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), ovarian cancer (OvCa), and thyroid cancer (ThCa). Using the Genomic Data Commons as primary data source, SNV data were extracted from variant call format (VCF) files for patients diagnosed with one of these cancers. For each cancer type, iQ(G) aggregates the deleterious effects of individual SNVs across transcripts of a given gene, weighing them by the difference in occurrence frequencies between tumor and normal samples among patients, while also taking into consideration transcript lengths. Four established functional effect analyzers, FATHMM-XF, SIFT, PolyPhen, and CADD, were integrated to compute iQ(G). Genes were then ranked according to their iQ(G) scores, with top-ranking genes considered strong candidates for cancer association. Performance was evaluated using compiled lists of known cancer-related genes and measured by the standardized average rank. Results indicated that the integrated approach outperforms individual effect analyzers. Downstream pathway analysis of top-scoring genes suggests links among different cancer types and other shared diseases. A brief investigation of protein complexes in these pathways generated new hypotheses for future studies. Notably, several genes in the CACNA1 family within the type II diabetes mellitus pathway appear related to both OvCa and ThCa, highlighting additional molecular interactions that warrant further investigations in OvCa prognosis and ThCa treatment.

title: Comprehensive Benchmark for Circadian Phase Inference Tools
authors: Souparna Purohit, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Tom Brooks, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Greg Grant, University of Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Circadian phase inference from RNA-seq data is a fundamental problem in chronobiology that has received considerable attention over the past two decades, owing to its relevance in fields such as precision medicine and forensics. Numerous bioinformatics tools have been developed to address this challenge, some supervised - requiring time-stamped samples for training - and others unsupervised, inferring circadian phase without any timestamp information. In this work we focus on the latter set of tools, which include, among others, CYCLOPS, Tempo, CHIRAL, Cyclum, and COFE, which span a range of algorithmic approaches from traveling salesman-based trajectory estimation and Bayesian cosinor modeling to more recent machine learning and deep learning techniques. Despite this growing toolkit, no comprehensive benchmarking study has yet compared all of these tools simultaneously across a diverse range of datasets. This work aims to fill that gap by benchmarking these tools in a rigorous, objective, and systematic study, evaluating performance across multiple data modalities (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq), normalization strategies, seed gene selections, and dataset sizes. Simulated datasets for both modalities are developed with particular attention to ensuring they faithfully capture the statistical properties of real RNA-seq data. These simulated datasets, alongside a curated collection of real RNA-seq data, form the foundation of our evaluation framework.

title: A resource for interpreting mutations in cancer genes through protein structures
authors: Do Young Hyeon, Boston Children's Hospital, United States; Yuxiang Zhou, Boston Children's Hospital, United States; Wendy Chung, Boston Children's Hospital, United States; Felix Dietlein, Boston Children's Hospital, United States
abstract: Introduction: Interpreting somatic mutations in cancer is key in clinical genomics. Despite large-scale tumor sequencing having found hundreds of recurrently mutated genes, the functional significance of many individual mutations remains unclear. Current tools either use dichotomous ""driver vs. passenger"" labels or rely on generic scores without disease-specific context. Here, we present a proteo-genomics framework that combines disease-specific knowledge with structural information from proteomics data into an interactive web resource. Methods: We built a proteo-genomics framework integrating AlphaFold-predicted 3D protein structures with somatic mutation data across over 25 tumor types. At its core, a machine learning model dissects where mutations accumulate beyond background expectations. We aligned significant regions onto protein structures and assessed overlaps in functional domains, interaction interfaces, and post-translational modification sites. We validated against matched RNA-seq, proteomics, and clinical outcomes. Results are available at oncofold.org with 3D visualizations, per-residue overlays, mutation lookup, and downloadable datasets. Results: Significant mutation regions consistently align with functionally important protein regions, including active sites, interaction interfaces, and structural domains. Affected domains correspond with mechanisms of oncogene activation or tumor suppressor inactivation, and even truncating mutations exhibited clear positional preferences. Mutations in significant regions show stronger associations with altered expression, signaling, clonality, survival, and therapeutic response consistently. Discussion/Conclusions: Our resource offers a scalable, unbiased way to interpret somatic mutations at single-residue resolution and link them to tumorigenic mechanisms through 3D protein structures. It moves variant interpretation from binary labels toward phenotype-based assessment, supporting patient stratification, clinical response prediction, and mechanistic interpretation.

title: Annotation Query (AnnoQ): An Integrated and Interactive Platform for Comprehensive Genetic Variant Annotation on a Large Scale
authors: Bryan Queme, University of Southern Calfornia, United States; Anushya Muruganujan, University of Southern Calfornia, United States; Tremayne Mushayahama, University of Southern Calfornia, United States; Dustin Ebert, University of Southern Calfornia, United States; Huaiyu Mi, University of Southern Calfornia, United States
abstract: The Annotation Query (AnnoQ) system (https://annoq.org/)) is a comprehensive and dynamic platform that provides up-to-date functional annotations for human genetic variants. Supported by an extensive database, it includes approximately 700 million variants from the Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) program, each pre-annotated with more than 800 annotation types from diverse resources. AnnoQ distinguishes itself through its user-friendly and efficient query interface. Unlike traditional annotation tools that require users to configure and execute analyses, AnnoQ offers precomputed annotations for all variants, enabling it to function as an intuitive search engine. Its advanced search framework and API support efficient handling of large datasets, making it accessible to researchers with varying levels of computational expertise. The interactive interface also allows users to quickly query data and review results before conducting more extensive analyses. The gene model annotation came from the WGSA pipeline.
