To ensure functional annotation data currency, AnnoQ maintains close integration with leading resources such as the Gene Ontology Consortium, Reactome, and PANTHER, regularly incorporating updates from these partners. Importantly, AnnoQ extends annotation beyond coding regions. By leveraging PEREGRINE, a genome-wide enhancerâ€“gene linkage database, it associates non-coding variants with their target genes, functions, and pathways. Built on an Elasticsearch framework, AnnoQ provides robust API access for seamless integration into bioinformatics workflows. It also offers software packages in languages such as R and Python. Overall, AnnoQ serves as a powerful platform for efficient exploration and analysis of genomic data.

title: DeepFFPEClean: A Multi-Input CNN Framework for Filtering FFPE-Specific False Positives in Somatic Variant Detection
authors: Ritsuko Onuki, Saitama Cancer Center, Research Institute for Clinical Oncology, Japan; Eisaku Furukawa, National Cancer Center, Research Institute, Division of Bioinformatics, Japan; Jo Nishino, National Cancer Center, Research Institute, Division of Bioinformatics, Japan; Hanako Ono, National Cancer Center, Research Institute, Division of Bioinformatics, Japan; Momoko Nagai, National Cancer Center, Research Institute, Division of Bioinformatics, Japan; Daichi Narushima, National Cancer Center, Research Institute, Division of Bioinformatics, Japan; Mamoru Kato, National Cancer Center, Research Institute, Division of Bioinformatics, Japan
abstract: Background: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens are widely used in clinical genomic profiling, but the fixation process induces cytosine deamination and other DNA artifacts that generate false positive variant calls mimicking true somatic mutations. Conventional filtering approaches based on logic and statistics are computationally expensive and labor-intensive to make and often fail to capture the full complexity of FFPE error patterns. Methods: We developed DeepFFPEClean, a multi-input convolutional neural network (CNN) integrating two complementary inputs: PilePlus3, a matrix encoding sequence alignment information within 100 bp of each candidate variant site, and SampleQ, capturing sample-level quality features reflecting FFPE-specific DNA degradation. Five CNN architectures were evaluated across three input patterns and six batch sizes using 515 clinical cases. Performance differences were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: The optimal model, combining a custom CNN for PilePlus3 with an AlexNet-based SampleQ branch, achieved a mean F1-score of 0.899 ± 0.006 (SD) in 10-fold cross-validation (recall: 0.941, precision: 0.861). SampleQ addition significantly improved performance over the PilePlus3-only model at matched batch size (ΔF1 = 0.010, 95% CI: [0.003, 0.016]; p = 0.004). DeepFFPEClean outperformed NeuSomatic (F1 = 0.684) and VarNet (F1 = 0.096) on the same clinical dataset under tool-specific default settings. Grad-CAM analysis revealed that the model integrated local substitution patterns and sample-level quality metrics to distinguish true somatic mutations from FFPE artifacts, supporting the biological rationale of the multi-input design. Conclusion: DeepFFPEClean provides an accurate, efficient solution for FFPE artifact filtering, with potential for integration into clinical variant calling pipelines.

title: Deciphering the missing genetic matters of neuropsychiatric disorders through integrating cohort-level whole-genome sequencing with multi-omics information
authors: Jingqi Chen, Fudan University, China; Jixin Cao, Fudan University, China; Zhengyu An, The Institute of Science and Technology for Brain-inspired Intelligence, Fudan University, China; Xing-Ming Zhao, Fudan University, China
abstract: The genetics underlying neuropsychiatric disorders are far from being fully understood, which hinders the development of successful therapeutic procedures. Our recent efforts focus on deciphering the missing genetic matters of neuropsychiatric disorders, through developing omics-integration methods to identify and interpret disease-relevant rare and noncoding variants. First, for identifying rare deleterious SNVs from whole-genome sequence data when the cohort size is limited, we have designed a hybrid framework, taking advantage of the statistical power of SKAT-O while integrating it with disease-specific variant prioritization. Applying this framework to a medium size Chinese cohort for Alzheimer's disease, we have identified 11 disease-relevant genes, mostly driven by East-Asian specific rare SNVs. One of the rare SNVs, RABEP1 p.R845W, was found to induce endocytosis dysregulation and exacerbate toxic amyloid Î² accumulation, supporting its involvement in the mechanisms of Alzheimer's disease. Second, we have developed SVJudge, for scoring the pathogenicity of noncoding structural variants through integrating multi-omics regulatory information, and showed that it outperformed state-of-the-art methods. We leveraged long-read sequencing and SVJudge, identifying tandem repeat expansions as a significant genetic contributor for Schizophrenia. We dissected their regulatory impact through a whole-genome scanning of transcriptional factor (TF) binding activities, demonstrating that many of the tandem repeat expansions affect the binding of TF-target genes that are therapeutically relevant to Schizophrenia. In summary, our work has expanded the toolbox for identifying and interpreting the hidden genetic matters of neuropsychiatric disorders, especially for medium-sized cohorts. Our findings may broaden the understanding of the population-specific genetic mechanisms and promote the development of effective therapeutic interventions for these disorders.

title: Gene- and domain-aware calibration increases the clinical utility of variant effect predictors
authors: Yile Chen, yilechen@uw.edu, United States; Shawn Fayer, Department of Genome Sciences, School of Medicine, University of Washington, United States; Shantanu Jain, The Institute for Experiential AI, Northeastern University, United States; Mariam Benazouz, Molecular Engineering and Sciences Institute, University of Washington, United States; Yuriy Sverchkov, Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, University of Wisconsin, United States; Jeremy Stone, Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine, University of Washington, United States; Himanshu Sharma, Institute for Genomic Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Timothy Bergquist, Institute for Genomic Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Ross Stewart, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Northeastern University, United States; Sean Mooney, National Human Genome Research Institute, United States; Mark Craven, Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Predrag Radivojac, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Northeastern University, United States; Lea Starita, Department of Genome Sciences, School of Medicine, University of Washington, United States; Douglas Fowler, Department of Genome Sciences, School of Medicine, University of Washington, United States; Vikas Pejaver, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States
abstract: The utility of clinical genetic testing is limited because around 90% of missense variants in ClinVar remain of uncertain clinical significance. Variant effect predictors (VEPs) can score any missense variant, potentially empowering variant classification. Realizing this potential requires calibration to translate predictor scores into evidence. However, genome-wide calibration ignores predictor heterogeneity across genes, causing evidence misassignment. We developed an automated, data-adaptive framework that optimizes two complementary approaches: gene-specific calibration for genes with enough variants for calibration, and domain-aggregate calibration for other disease-associated genes, which groups variants from protein domains with similar predictor score distributions for calibration. Applied to three predictors across 2,769 genes, this framework assigned evidence to 10.6% more variants on average while generally improving evidence accuracy compared to genome-wide calibration. These calibrations and the resulting calibrated computational evidence are available through the PredictMD portal. Our framework substantially increases the clinical utility of VEPs for variant classification.

title: Structural Analysis of Missense Mutations on the Stability of the DISC1 Scaffold Protein
authors: Malcolm Anthony, Howard University, United States; Sade Olajide, Howard University, United States; Shaolei Teng, Howard University, United States
abstract: Disrupted in schizophrenia 1 (DISC1) is a multifunctional scaffold protein that supports neurite outgrowth and cortical development through a wide range of protein interactions and is a risk factor for multiple psychiatric illnesses, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, and potentially autism spectrum disorders. Although DISC1â€™s interactome has been extensively mapped, an understanding of which interactions and structural features most strongly disrupt disease-relevant neuronal phenotypes is still lacking. Here, we apply computational saturated mutagenesis, pathogenicity prediction tools, and molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate how missense mutations in specific regions of DISC1 may impact its stability. The saturated mutagenesis of DISC1 resulted in 16,226 missense mutations, with A697W (29.07 kcal/mol) and D694W (29.79 kcal/mol) as the top destabilizing mutations and G139R (-2.67 kcal/mol) and P432K (-2.33 kcal/mol) as the top stabilizing mutations, based on the folding energy (Î”Î”G) calculations. Both A697W and D694W mutations lie within DISC1â€™s interacting region with NDEL1. All three pathogenicity prediction tools (AlphaMissense, CADD, PolyPhen-2) predicted these top destabilizing mutations to be likely pathogenic, highly deleterious, and probably damaging to the DISC1 protein, respectively. In contrast, the P432K mutation was predicted to be benign across all three tools. These pathogenicity predictors allowed us to prioritize destabilizing variants most likely to contribute to disease. Molecular dynamics simulations of the DISC1 variant monomers in physiological conditions further characterize their structural and dynamical consequences. Overall, this work aims to pinpoint DISC1 residues of psychological importance and analyze how specific protein mutations may modulate DISC1 stability and potentially its function.

title: Artemis: An AI-Enabled, Web-Based Platform for Variant Review and Interpretation
authors: Xijun Zhang, Henry Jackson Foundation, United States; Joaquin Villar, Henry Jackson Foundation, United States; Shiliang Wang, Henry Jackson Foundation, United States; Juvianee Estrada-Veras, Henry Jackson Foundation, United States; Lydia Hellwig, Department of Pediatrics, Department of Medicine, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, United States; Craig Shriver, Murtha Cancer Center Research Program, Uniformed Services University, United States; Clifton Dalgard, Center for Military Precision Health, Department of Anatomy, Physiology and Genetics, Uniformed Services University, United States; Matthew Wilkerson, Center for Military Precision Health, Department of Anatomy, Physiology and Genetics, Uniformed Services University, United States
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing and whole-exome sequencing have become essential tools to identify clinically actionable genetic variations. However, due to the high volume of data being produced, the task of efficiently filtering, annotating, visualizing and interpreting variants remains a bottleneck for precision medicine. Existing tools often fail to seamlessly integrate with sequence analysis pipelines such as Illumina DRAGEN, lack the capacity to evaluate structural variations and copy number variations alongside single nucleotide variations and indels, and do not fully utilize the power of recent LLM models. To address these needs, we developed Artemis, an open-source, light-weight, AI-enabled and web-based variant interpretation platform. Artemis parses Illumina DRAGEN Nirvana annotations into a SQLite3 database and thoughtfully displays these data through a Python Dash based web application including dashboards and detailed variant metadata. To facilitate variant review and interpretation by clinical geneticists, Artemis presents variant annotation, predictions by in-silico tools, sequence alignment visualization using the Integrative Genomics Viewer and an â€œAI Assistantâ€ enabled by LLM models. Benchmarking Artemis against four Coriell cell lines with known germline mutations yielded 100% classification concordance. Deployed within the pan-cancer APOLLO5 cohort, the platform facilitated the expert review of 11,998 WGS variants, successfully identifying 137 Pathogenic (P) and 82 Likely Pathogenic (LP) secondary findings. Artemis provides a comprehensive framework that streamlines the operational burden of genomic variant interpretation and delivers a lightweight solution for distributed precision medicine initiatives, accelerating the translation of whole-genome sequencing into actionable clinical insights.

title: Single-Nucleotide Variants in IGF2R Are Associated with Cardiovascular Disease Risk and Blood Pressure
authors: Prisha Dani, Department of Quantitative Health Sciences, Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, United States; Noah Daniels, Department of Quantitative Health Sciences, Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, United States; Anukriti Sharma, Department of Quantitative Health Sciences, Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, United States; Kevin Pantalone, Endocrinology and Metabolism Institute, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, United States; Daniel Rotroff, Department of Quantitative Health Sciences, Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, United States
abstract: Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) in MAS1 and IGF2R are in close proximity, and each gene has been proposed as potentially implicated in cardiovascular disease (CVD). However, their specific genetic contributions to cardiovascular phenotypes remain underexplored. Mas1 regulates angiotensin-(1â€“7) and has been shown in mice to mediate protective effects in cardiovascular and renal systems. Circulating IGF2R levels have been shown to be elevated in individuals with coronary heart disease. In this study, we aimed to investigate the associations between SNVs in MAS1 and IGF2R and cardiovascular disease and blood pressure. We analyzed genetic and clinical data from the NIH All of Us Research Program and focused on SNVs within +/- 100 kb of MAS1 and IGF2R, respectively. CVD was defined using ICD codes, yielding 127,422 cases and 287,408 control individuals. Individuals were included in in the blood pressure cohort if they had at least one recorded blood pressure measurement, resulting in 389,701 individuals. Linear and logistic association analyses were performed using PLINK. Bonferroni correction was performed based on the number of independent variants within the locus. Here, rs3777420 was associated with elevated risk of CVD (OR = 1.03; P = 2.16 x 10-4), and rs144174270, rs408889, and rs56017621 were associated with systolic blood pressure (P 0.05). These findings help clarify evidence for MAS1 and IGF2R as relevant loci in cardiometabolic genetics, supporting efforts to understand the molecular basis of cardiovascular risk.

title: A systems-level analysis of cancer mutations in intrinsically disordered protein regions
authors: Kivilcim Ozturk, UC San Diego, United States; Hannah Carter, UC San Diego, United States
abstract: Cellular functions emerge from complex interactions among proteins and other biomolecules, and cancers frequently aim to disrupt these interactions, leading to disease phenotypes. While many proteins adopt stable structures to perform their biological functions, a substantial portion of eukaryotic proteomes contains intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). These regions lack a fixed three-dimensional structure yet actively participate in diverse protein functions involved in many cellular processes. Although IDRs in several cancer driver proteins have been shown to mediate oncogenic signaling and post-translational regulation, their role in facilitating protein-protein interactions (PPI) remains less understood. In this study, we investigate the mutational landscape of IDRs and their role in perturbing protein interaction networks in cancer. A comprehensive analysis of our structurally resolved PPI network reveals that IDRs involved in mediating protein interactions are significantly enriched for cancer-associated missense mutations. Moreover, proteins containing IDRs occupy more central positions within the protein interaction network, particularly cancer driver proteins, where disordered drivers exhibit significantly higher network centrality than ordered ones. These findings suggest that the structural flexibility of IDRs may enable interactions with a broader set of molecular partners, facilitating signal propagation within the cell and amplifying the functional impact of mutations that target them. Overall, our results highlight the importance of characterizing the systems-level mutational landscape of IDRs to better understand mechanisms underlying cancer development and progression, and to support improved identification of therapeutic targets.

title: CRISPRme+: expanding variant-aware off-target analysis for diverse and personal genomes
authors: Ann Cirincione, Department of Pathology, Massachusetts General Hospital, United States; Manuel Tognon, Department of Computer Science, University of Verona, Italy; Benjamin Vyshedskiy, Department of Pathology, Massachusetts General Hospital, United States; Linda Lin, Division of Hematology/Oncology, Boston Children’s Hospital, United States; Hufeng Zhou, Department of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, United States; Daniel Bauer, Division of Hematology/Oncology, Boston Children’s Hospital, United States; Rosalba Giugno, Department of Computer Science, University of Verona, Italy; Luca Pinello, Department of Pathology, Massachusetts General Hospital, United States
abstract: CRISPR-based genome editing has rapidly advanced toward clinical therapeutics, making comprehensive off-target prediction an essential step in the design and evaluation of therapeutic editing strategies. Off-target risk depends on guide RNA sequence, tolerated mismatches, and crucially, the genetic background of the individual being treated. CRISPRme was developed to address this need, providing an exhaustive, haplotype-aware framework for off-target prediction that incorporates population-level genetic variants alongside the human reference genome (hg38). Since its initial release, several large-scale sequencing initiatives have expanded the catalog of human genetic variation. Here we present CRISPRme+, which has been extended to accommodate updated VCF datasets from the 1000 Genomes Project (1KG), TOPMed, AllofUs, and gnomAD. Running CRISPRme+ with this expanded variant set nominates >8,000 additional off-target sites for BCL11A sg1617 when considering a maximum of four mismatches and DNA/RNA bulge sizes of two, compared to previous results using the 2019 1KG and Human Genome Diversity Project (HGDP). This suggests that larger, more diverse cohorts meaningfully expand the predicted off-target landscape. Beyond variant-based approaches, we also extend CRISPRme+ to support full personal genome assemblies as an alternative to hg38. Using the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) individual HG01255 as a benchmarking example, we identify an exact-match off-target site unique to that individual's assembly, providing a proof-of-concept for personalized risk assessment. Because personal assemblies use independent coordinate systems, we develop a standardized pipeline for cross-coordinate comparison, generalizable beyond CRISPRme+. Together, these advances move toward a more diverse and patient-aware off-target assessment.

title: Calibration of in-frame indel variant effect predictors for clinical variant classification
authors: Haneen Abderrazzaq, Northeastern University, United States; Mugdha Singh, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Larry Babb, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Timothy Bergquist, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Steven Brenner, University of California, Berkeley, United States; Vikas Pejaver, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Anne O'Donnell-Luria, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, United States; Predrag Radivojac, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Insertions and deletions (indels) represent a substantial source of human genetic variation, yet they are difficult to interpret clinically and remain critically understudied compared to single nucleotide variants. While computational predictors for missense variants have been rigorously evaluated and calibrated for clinical use, equivalent benchmarking for in-frame indel tools has yet to be performed, limiting their adoption in clinical workflows for variant interpretation. Here, we present a calibration framework for eight in-frame indel prediction tools, ranging from traditional methods to protein language models, enabling their direct integration into clinical variant classification under ACMG/AMP guidelines. We constructed a high-confidence variant dataset of in-frame indels from ClinVar and gnomAD, and estimated the prior probability of pathogenicity for rare in-frame indels in disease-associated genes, as well as for insertions and deletions separately. Applying a likelihood ratio framework based on local posterior probabilities, we established score thresholds for each tool corresponding to distinct pathogenic and benign evidence strengths. All eight tools achieved multiple calibrated evidence levels, demonstrating that existing indel predictors carry measurable clinical utility. Notably, indel predictors consistently underperformed relative to missense predictors, regardless of method type. These results provide the first systematic calibration of in-frame indel predictors for clinical use and motivate the development of improved computational methods for this variant class.

title: Agent-driven development of a validated open-source statistical genetics toolkit on genotype representation graphs
authors: Seyed Alireza Rasoulzadeh Hosseini, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Richard Border, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Statistical genetics relies on dozens of specialized tools, each with its own formats and numerical quirks, none able to exploit the compressed genealogical structure that genotype representation graphs (GRGs) make available. We present glink, an open-source toolkit that reimplements and extends PLINK, GCTA, BOLT-LMM, SAIGE, and RHE-mc on GRG backends, built in 34 days with AI agent assistance and validated by a three-tier automated testing framework. Agents generate candidate implementations from method specifications, and an automated test harness validates each implementation against reference tools through oracle agreement tests, unit tests, and integration tests before acceptance. An orchestrator spawns parallel agent sessions, each gated by two requirements: correctness, then competitive performance. A human domain expert designs benchmarking specifications to ensure that measured speedups translate to real-world gains, and sets passing thresholds for each test, since stochastic and algorithmically distinct methods require different standards of agreement. The framework currently covers 84 oracle and 37 sanity specifications across 38 analysis categories. Because every analysis reduces to forward and adjoint products on a GenotypeOperator interface, GRG traversals at O(|V|+|E|) replace O(nm) matrix operations. On linear GWAS with 20 covariates, glink runs 327x faster than PLINK2 at n=200,000 (10 seconds vs. 55 minutes) with 8.6x lower memory. For heritability estimation, glink achieves 79x speedup and 42x memory reduction over existing tools. Speedups grow superlinearly with sample size. All benchmarked implementations pass their correctness tests. This methodology generalizes to any domain where established open-source tools can serve as validation oracles for AI-generated successors.

title: A Machine Learning-Guided Genome-Wide Association Study Reveals Genetic Architectures for MASLD for Overweight and Lean Individuals in the All of Us Cohort
authors: Kaushik Karambelkar, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, United States; Ananthan Nambiar, University of Washington, United States; Arjun Athreya, Mayo Clinic Rochester, United States; Alina Allen, Mayo Clinic Rochester, United States; Konstantinos Lazaridis, Mayo Clinic Rochester, United States; Sharon Donovan, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, United States; Sergei Maslov, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, United States
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) arises from excessive hepatic fat accumulation that triggers inflammation and liver injury. It is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide, affecting more than one quarter of adults. Despite this, MASLD is often underdiagnosed, making it more difficult to perform genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Here, we implemented a machine learning (ML)-guided GWAS framework to identify genetic risk factors for MASLD across lean and overweight individuals in the All of Us Research Program. We trained a random forest model on laboratory measurements, vital signs, and demographic features to predict an in silico MASLD (I-MASLD) score, a continuous risk score for MASLD, which was validated to accurately represent clinical MASLD diagnosis. The I-MASLD score, providing a continuous measure of disease likelihood and capturing gradations of risk that are often missed in case/control definitions, was then used as the phenotype in a GWAS of whole-exome sequencing variants. The resultant GWAS discovered a novel variant in the ANGPTL4 gene to be significantly associated with MASLD risk and recapitulated known variants in various genes involved in lipid metabolism and insulin signaling. Our results also suggest a potential role of APOA5 in MASLD onset or progression in lean patients. These findings demonstrate that ML-derived quantitative phenotypes can enhance genetic discovery in large, heterogeneous cohorts where conventional case/control labels are limited or imprecise.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Correcting cell count bias improves perturbation effect estimates and virtual cell models
authors: Gerold Csendes, Turbine, Hungary; Bence Czakó, Turbine, Hungary; Gema Sanz, Turbine, Spain; Zsolt Gyüre, Turbine, Hungary; Milán Sztilkovics, Turbine, Hungary; László Mérő, Turbine, Hungary; Gábor Kovács, Turbine, Hungary; Kristóf Szalay, Turbine, Hungary; Bence Szalai, Turbine, Hungary
abstract: Artificial intelligence-based virtual cell (AIVC) models aim to predict post-perturbation cellular states, such as gene expression changes following genetic or chemical perturbations. A key challenge for these models is generalization to new biological contexts, including unseen cell types and perturbations. Since generalization critically depends on the consistency of perturbation effect estimates across datasets, we analyzed seven recent Perturb-seq datasets, commonly used benchmark datasets in the AIVC field. While the direction of pseudo-bulk differential expression (PB-DE) profiles showed moderate agreement across studies (median Pearson correlation > 0.4 for strong perturbations), the magnitude of perturbation effects (L1 norm of PB-DE vectors, effect size) varied substantially. We observed a strong inverse relationship between the number of cells per perturbation (n_cell) and effect size, indicating systematic inflation of effect sizes at low cell counts. Importantly, PB-DE magnitude and n_cell did not correlate with independent biological measures such as gene essentiality from DepMap, and the same relationship was recapitulated by downsampling control cells, supporting a technical rather than biological origin. We therefore introduce a simple scaling approach based on the empirical relationship between n_cell and PB-DE magnitude. This correction substantially improves cross-study agreement of perturbation effects and their association with biological readouts. Furthermore, using the scaling approach significantly improves the cross-context prediction performance of AIVC models. These results demonstrate that cell count-dependent bias in training data directly limits model generalization, and that correcting this bias leads to more accurate and transferable predictions.

title: A Blueprint for FAIR Data Sharing Across a Distributed Biomedical Data Ecosystem
authors: Lisa Mayer, NIH/NIAID, United States; Darya Pokutnaya, NIH/NIAID, United States; Julianne Christopher-Ohlin, GO FAIR US, San Diego Supercomputer Center, United States; Chris Erdmann, GO FAIR US, San Diego Supercomputer Center, United States; Doug Fils, GO FAIR US, San Diego Supercomputer Center, United States; Sydney Foote, NIH/NIAID, United States; Ismael Kherroubi Garcia, GO FAIR US, Kairoi, Ltd., United Kingdom; John Graybeal, GO FAIR US, San Diego Supercomputer Center, United States; Meghan Hartwick, NIH/NIAID, United States; Nancy Hoebelheinrich, GO FAIR US, Knowledge Motifs, LLC, United States; Barbara Magagna , GO FAIR US, GO FAIR Foundation,; Bert Meerman, GO FAIR US, GO FAIR Foundation,; Keith Maull, GO FAIR US, University Corporation for Atmospheric Research, United States; Matthew Mayernik , GO FAIR US, University Corporation for Atmospheric Research, United States; Rachel Waymack, NIH/NIAID, United States; Wilbert Van Panhuis, NIH/NIAID, United States; Christine Kirkpatrick, GO FAIR US, San Diego Supercomputer Center, United States; Reed Shabman, NIH/NIAID, United States
abstract: The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) has a long history of data sharing, but the absence of requirements for data standards or repositories has led to a fragmented data landscape. To reduce barriers to discovery, reuse, and interoperability of publicly available NIAID-funded datasets, NIAID's Office of Data Science and Emerging Technologies (ODSET) developed A Blueprint for Including Digital Objects in the NIAID Data Ecosystem (NIAID Blueprint; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17161562, CC BY-NC), the first unified framework for sharing NIAID research data, in collaboration with 11 NIAID-funded repositories and GO FAIR US (GFU). The NIAID Blueprint spans five focus areas: Minimal Metadata Schema, Persistent Identifiers, Minimal API Specifications for Metadata, Minimal Citation Requirements, and Point of Contact for Outreach and Training. These recommendations aim to streamline data discovery and reuse, including connection to the NIAID Data Ecosystem Discovery Portal, a metadata catalog indexing over 4 million records. Since its launch in March 2025, ODSET and GFU have conducted public webinars and regularly met with representatives from the 11 pilot repositories, fostering a community of practice around the NIAID Blueprint. Repository adoption typically takes one of two forms: applying the NIAID Blueprint to new tools or methodologies, or mapping existing practices to NIAID Blueprint recommendations. Representatives share their findings, informing iterative improvements to the specification. We present this model as a replicable approach for enhancing FAIRness in a complex, interdisciplinary biomedical research environment through community engagement.

title: Bridging the Metadata Gap: A Two-Stage Federated Learning Architecture and Visual Audit Tool (FedViz) for Global Biobank Consortia
authors: Aditya Karna, Springfield College, United States; Hieu Ngo, Yeshiva University, United States; Yuan-Ting Hsieh, Nvidia, United States
abstract: The harmonization of heterogeneous biomedical data remains a critical bottleneck for global collaborative research. During the 2026 CMU-NVIDIA Hackathon, a global consortium collaborated to build prototype software for federated learning (FL) across biobanks using NVIDIA FLARE. Across various prototype tracksâ€”including federated GWAS meta-analysisâ€”a universal challenge emerged: deploying FL at scale requires strict feature alignment across institutional nodes before training can safely execute. To operationalize this alignment, we developed FedViz, an open-source visual architecture designed to audit federated readiness prior to model execution. Built with a React/TypeScript frontend and an Elasticsearch backend, FedViz executes a two-stage approach: Consortium-Wide Discovery and Targeted Model Execution. As a demonstration, we used FedViz to audit metadata across 14 simulated international biobank cohorts (e.g., CANPATH, CHoP). Out of 11,511 unique clinical variables detected, the visual dashboard revealed a baseline Readiness Index of just 1.04%, mapping the severe fragmentation of genomic and imaging metadata. We then filtered for this high-quality harmonized subset (120 variables), so targeted federated models could be safely executed. After users conduct auditing and associated filtering, the FedViz Evaluation Layer integrates post-training metrics from NVIDIA FLARE, utilizing site-specific ROC curves and confusion matrix distributions to enable researchers to visually detect local domain drift. This prototype demonstrates that combining robust FL infrastructure with rigorous, visual data-readiness auditing (FedViz) provides a scalable blueprint for leveraging open biomedical data across global biobanks.

title: Posters.science: Building Open Infrastructure for FAIR and AI-ready Scientific Posters
authors: Bhavesh Patel, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, United States; Jamey O'Neill, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, United States; Dorian Portillo, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, United States; Sanjay Soundarajan, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical Innovations Institute, United States
abstract: Every year, millions of scientific posters are presented at conferences. They are particularly relevant to biomedical research, where conference posters often represent the earliest public glimpse of ideas and findings that will eventually shape clinical guidelines and drug targets. Yet, most posters disappear by the end of conferences, rolled up under chairs or stuffed into recycling bins. Through our investigation of poster-sharing practices, we found only ~150,000 posters online across 86 platforms, and even those lacked basic metadata, like author identifiers, funding sources, and conference information, making them hard to find and reuse. To address this, we are developing Posters.science, a free and open-source platform that simplifies poster sharing. User only need to upload a PDF of their poster, review auto-extracted metadata, and publish to a repository of their choice, like Zenodo. We developed a custom LLM pipeline that handles the metadata extraction and generates a poster.json file, which is a structured, machine-readable version of the poster that makes it interoperable and AI-ready. The platform also works as a registry, currently indexing over 1,500 posters from Zenodo and Figshare, with more on the way. For the biomedical community specifically, this could open new possibilities for systematically mining early-stage findings on a disease or gene across thousands of posters. In this talk, we will present our analysis of current poster-sharing practices, introduce the poster.json schema design, and give a live demonstration of Posters.science.

title: Evaluating the Performance of LLMs in Drafting Data Management Plans
authors: Nahid Zeinali, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical InnovationsInstitute, United States; Xuebin Dong, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical InnovationsInstitute, United States; Rebecca Hofstein Grady, California Digital Library, University of California Officeof the President, United States; Maria Praetzellis, California Digital Library, University of California Officeof the President, United States; Brian Riley, California Digital Library, University of California Officeof the President, United States; Bhavesh Patel, FAIR Data Innovations Hub, California Medical InnovationsInstitute, United States
abstract: Data Management Plans (DMPs) are now required by most funders for grant proposals to ensure researchers plan in advance for effective data management and sharing. Preparing a DMP is usually difficult for researchers because they often lack training and knowledge in data management practices. Moreover, funding organizations have different policies that require adherence to specific data management strategies and DMP formats. In this work, we evaluated the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in drafting DMPs compliant with the National Institutes of Health (NIH)™s 2023 guidelines. The goal was to investigate whether LLMs were ready, off-the-shelf, to assist biomedical researchers in preparing their DMPs. We evaluated the performance of an open-source LLM, Llama 3.3, and a commercial LLM, GPT 4, in drafting NIH-compliant DMPs. We used comparisons to NIH-provided human-written DMP samples to quantify the performance of Llama and GPT models. We also asked domain experts to evaluate LLM-generated DMPs. Overall, we found that LLMs can accelerate initial draft creation, but would still require expert review before submission to ensure full correctness and compliance. Moreover, open-source LLMs may not be as ready off-the-shelf as commercial ones for drafting funding-compliant DMPs.

title: MEDFORD in a Box: Demonstrating the Improvements and Future Directions for a Metadata Description Language
authors: Benjamin Stubbs, Tufts University, United States; Polina Shpilker, Tufts University, United States; Michael Sayers, University of Rhode Island, United States; Yumin Lee, Tufts University, United States; Yaman Bosnali, Tufts University, United States; Gabriel Songerwala, Tufts University, United States; Lenore Cowen, Tufts University, United States; Donna Slonim, Tufts University, United States; Alva Couch, Tufts University, United States; Noah Daniels, The University of Rhode Island, United States; Shaun Wallace, University of Rhode Island, United States
abstract: Scientific research metadata is vital to ensure the validity, reusability, and cost-effectiveness of research efforts. The MEDFORD metadata language was previously introduced to simplify the process of writing and maintaining metadata for non-programmers. Here we introduce MEDFORD-in-a-Box (MiaB) to lower even further barriers to entry and usability for the MEDFORD system. MiaB contains many improvements, including an updated MEDFORD parser with expanded reference capabilities. MiaB also includes an improved VS Code extension that supports these changes through a visual IDE, as well as a new macro syntax to ameliorate repetition. By simplifying metadata entry while ameliorating some difficulties of data transport and metadata duplication, MiaB supports the creation of correct, consistent, and reusable metadata improving research reproducibility.

title: Large-scale Reference-Guided Cell Type Re-annotation of Single-Cell Brain Data
authors: Rachel Schwartz, University of British Columbia, Canada; Paul Pavlidis, University of British Columbia, Canada
abstract: Cell type annotation is a critical but poorly standardized step in single-cell transcriptomics. Across publicly available human and mouse brain datasets, cell-type specific meta-analysis is impeded by diverse annotation strategies, inconsistent cell type nomenclature, and varied granularity of annotation. To address these inconsistencies in a reproducibile manner and enable large-scale re-analysis of single-cell brain datasets, we developed a reference-guided Nextflow pipeline for hierarchical cell type annotation, now deployed in the Gemma gene expression database. In developing the pipeline, we benchmarked deep learning (scVI) and PCA-based (Seurat) label transfer across 9 human cortex and 7 mouse brain single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq cohorts, varying reference atlas, confidence threshold, and other parameters. A Random Forest classifier trained on scVI embeddings typically achieves higher macro-F1 scores than Seurat and is more computationally efficient, though Random Forest confidence scores are poorly calibrated for filtering. Study of origin accounts for more variance in annotation accuracy than method, reference, disease or experimental perturbation status. Some cell types fail systematically across all configurations; we mitigate this by grouping poorly discriminated cell types into higher-level categories for re-analysis. The recommended pipeline configuration achieves macro-F1 = 0.940 for human and 0.770 for mouse. In a reanalysis of PsychENCODE, differential expression (DE) concordance with author labels was high overall, but as expected, cell types with annotation failures and/or label harmonization issues showed poorer reproducibility. The framework presented here, deployed in Gemma for over 200 brain experiments, provides a reusable alternative to per-study annotation with documented caveats tied to annotation quality.

title: The Common Fund Data Ecosystem (CFDE) Incubator for Pan-NIH Resources: Enhancing Interoperability
authors: Julie Jurgens, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Mackenzie Brandes, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Jason Flannick, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States; Noel Burtt, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, United States
abstract: Authors Julie A. Jurgens1, MacKenzie Brandes1, Jason Flannick1, NoÃ«l P. Burtt1 Affiliations 1Programs in Metabolism and Medical & Population Genetics, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA Abstract The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) has funded a collection of repositories and knowledgebases for housing and disseminating biomedical data. Because these resources are often created in isolation, they often lack interoperability, thus posing challenges to interoperability, integration, and sustainability. To address these challenges, the Common Fund Data Ecosystem (CFDE) Knowledge Center will launch the CFDE Incubator for Pan-NIH Resources, scheduled to occur on July 9-10, 2026, in Bethesda, MD. This first-of-its-kind event aims to facilitate identification of common goals, hurdles, and opportunities for collaboration across NIH-funded resources. Focusing on knowledge graphs and gene-based representations, the session will identify means for attendees to connect their resources through shared standards, embeddings, and protocols. Participants will pinpoint gaps, best practices for overcoming them, and future cross-resource pilot projects leveraging these standards and best practices. At ISMB, we will share the outputs of the CFDE Incubator event, recommendations for future efforts around integrated knowledge graphs, and plans for future collaborations across knowledgebases and repositories. By uniting leaders from the NIH and many of its funded resources, we hope this event will create a collaborative forum for improved connection and sustainability among resources.

title: A FAIR Framework for Structured Biomarker Representation, Discovery, and Hypothesis Generation
authors: Maria Kim, George Washington University, United States; Jeet Vora, George Washington University, United States; Cyrus Chun Hong Au Yeung, George Washington University, United States; Rene Ranzinger, University of Georgia, United States; Raja Mazumder, George Washington University, United States
abstract: Biomarker data is dispersed across data sources, impeding discovery and hypothesis generation. Moreover, existing biomedical knowledge graphs record biomarker associations, such as gene X relates to disease Y, but not the measurable change that defines a biomarker according to the NIH-FDA definition. This omission limits both machine reasoning and clinical interpretability. Here we present Biomarker Knowledge Graph, a comprehensive knowledge graph incorporating biomarker information from multiple sources, which represents each biomarker as a structured triple: a change type (e.g., increased), an entity (e.g., IL6), and an assessed aspect (e.g., level). It unifies fragmented biomarker data in a standardized data model and terminology (Biomarker Ontology). Additionally, Biomarker Knowledge Graph enables discovery and design in a complex, interconnected system of biomarkers, entities, diseases, exposure agents, specimens, terminology of health measurements, and publications, by allowing users to identify patterns, and shortest paths between entities. Finally, Biomarker Knowledge Graph allows the user to deduce new facts from existing relationships rather than just recalling stored data. A controlled vocabulary was developed to avoid duplication of biomarker data, and we used our standardized data as nodes and edges to construct the knowledge graph, thus enabling the data to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). Thanks to Biomarker Knowledge Graph (https://github.com/clinical-biomarkers/Knowledge-Graph), clinicians and researchers can identify biological patterns of biomarkers (freely available at data.biomarkerkb.org), their interconnections, and use this knowledge in clinical and research practices, and generate new hypotheses. Contributions of the open-source community could include visualization tools, e.g. neo4j implementations, and LLM-based CYPHER query construction.

title: Curating Gene Symbol Relationships for the Resolution of Gene Symbol Ambiguity
authors: Anastasia Bratulin, Ohio State University/ Nationwide Children's Hospital, United States; James S. Stevenson, Nationwide Children's Hospital, United States; Kori Kuzma, Nationwide Children's Hospital, United States; Wesley Goar, Nationwide Children's Hospital, United States; Matthew Cannon, Nationwide Children's Hospital, United States; Alex Wagner, Nationwide Children's Hospital, United States
abstract: Although gene symbols are used ubiquitously, community guidelines on their use in the literature and genomic data resources are not commonly followed or enforced. As a result, it is often necessary to disambiguate gene symbols when linking knowledge in genomic research and clinical applications. A common source of ambiguity is when a single gene symbol represents multiple genes, known as a gene alias collision. For example, the symbol â€œBCRâ€, is the primary gene symbol for one gene but also the alias symbol of another, RN7SL263P. These are distinct genes with BCR being implicated in two gene fusion events with clinical significance in cancer while RN7SL263P lacks functional characterization in literature. Such ambiguity limits the effectiveness of data aggregation and linking tools. In Ensembl, 3,784 (7.8%) records share an alias with another gene, compared to 2,482 (5.6%) in HGNC and 5,964 (13.4%) in NCBI Gene. Additionally, 767 (1.6%) Ensembl records share a primary gene symbol as an alias with another gene, along with 546 (1.2%) in HGNC and 1,613 (3.6%) in NCBI Gene. To address this, we developed Gene Harmony, a resource for resolving ambiguous gene symbols in biomedical literature and genomic knowledgebases. We curated relationships between gene symbols and gene concepts using manual, programmatic, and automated methods to assign relationship labels. This structured semantic data supports automated symbol disambiguation and lays the foundation for evidence-driven protocols to improve gene harmonization workflows in knowledge aggregation resources such as DGIdb and MetaKB.

title: MuSAlS: Fast Multiple Sequence Alignment Using Hierarchical Clustering
authors: Emily Light, Department of Computer Science and Statistics at University of Rhode Island, United States; Noah Daniels, The University of Rhode Island, United States; Najib Ishaq, Department of Computer Science and Statistics at University of Rhode Island, United States
abstract: Motivation: The multiple sequence alignment (MSA) problem has been extensively studied, with numerous approaches developed over recent years. With the rapid growth of sequence data, there is an increasing need for fast and accurate MSA tools that scale effectively to large datasets. Building on our previous work on CLAM, we are able to use exact dynamic programming (Needleman-Wunsch) while scaling to large datasets. We introduce MuSAlS (Multiple Sequence Alignment at Scale), a fast and scalable de novo MSA aligner. MuSAlS uses hierarchical clustering to construct a guide tree based on the Levenshtein distance metric, enabling efficient and accurate alignment through a bottom-up approach. Results: MuSAlS achieves competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while significantly improving runtime performance. This makes it a valuable tool for researchers analyzing large-scale genomic and metagenomic datasets, addressing the growing demand for scalable bioinformatics solutions. Availability and Implementation: MuSAlS is implemented in the Rust programming language, and available at https://github.com/URI-ABD/clam.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Multi-scale k-mer Modeling and Feature Selection for Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction
authors: Priyanka Singh, University of Iowa, United States; Phuong Nguyen, University of Iowa, United States; Shri Vishalini Rajaram, University of Iowa, United States; Erliang Zeng, University of Iowa, United States
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prediction using genomic data remains challenging due to the diversity and complexity of underlying resistance mechanisms. In this study, we present a systematic machine learning framework for predicting resistant and susceptible phenotypes across multiple bacteria-antibiotic combinations using k-mer based genomic representations. For each bacteria–antibiotic pair, we generated multi-scale feature representation using 4-mer, 5-mer, and 6-mer frequencies, along with a merged k-mer (k = 4, 5, and 6) representation to capture sequence patterns across multiple genome resolutions. Baseline machine learning models, including linear Support Vector Machines (SVM), logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost, were evaluated using nested cross-validation to reduce model selection bias. To enhance performance and interpretability, we integrated BEAR (Bootstrap Ensemble Attribute Ranking), an in-house feature selection framework that combines multiple ranking strategies and bootstrap-based evaluation to identify compact and robust feature subsets. To assess whether non-linear models capture additional AMR signal beyond linear classifiers, we also benchmarked a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for each bacteria-antibiotic pair. The best-performing model for each dataset was selected based on cross-validated performance, retrained on the full training data, and applied to CAMDA test datasets with strict feature alignment. Our results demonstrate that multi-scale k-mer representations combined with systematic model selection and BEAR-based feature optimization enable adaptive AMR prediction across diverse bacterial pathogens.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
authors: Buse Giledereli, Bogazici University, Turkey; Başar Temiz, Bogazici University, Turkey; Amirreza Sattarzadeh Khanehbargh, Bogazici University, Turkey
abstract: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that invariant gene handling is a central determinant of privacy severe leakage, where a Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing privacy-conscious design choices throughout data generation.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: From Graphical Models to Foundation Models: Synthetic Bulk RNA-seq Data Generation
authors: Daniil Filienko, University of Washington Tacoma, United States; Elias Chaibub Neto, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Sikha Pentyala, University of Washington Tacoma, United States; Jineta Banerjee, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Luca Foschini, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Martine De Cock, University of Washington Tacoma, United States
abstract: Genomic data remains heavily siloed due to privacy regulations, limiting reproducibility and collaboration in biomedical research. Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) offers a promising alternative, yet new tabular SDG methods remain largely unevaluated on high-dimensional biological data. We assess two recent state of the art SDG methods, namely MIAV, a deep learning approach extending TabPFN via in-context learning, and TabSDS, a lightweight non-parametric shuffle-based alternative. We evaluate them on bulk RNA-seq datasets from the CAMDA'26 Health Privacy Challenge, with differentially private Private-PGM as a baseline. We measure the performance of the methods across utility, fidelity, and empirical privacy metrics on two TCGA datasets. We find that both MIAV-TabPFN and TabSDS achieve significantly higher fidelity compared to the baseline.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Metabolite-centric functional annotation with context-specific starting points
authors: Ivory Blakley, UNC Charlotte, United States
abstract: "(Not yet implemented - in progress) Although this approach was born out of the Gut Microbiome Interaction Network Challenge, it requires starting from sequences, and the approach is therefore not suitable for the challenge data. A poster could facilitate discussion of the merits and challenges of the approach. Abstract: Human fecal WGS captures information from gut microbes, the human host, dietary organisms, and foodborne microbes. Misidentifying non-microbial reads as gut community members introduces error; correctly separating them offers multiple insights from one data source. Removing human reads is already standard. FooDB and MEDI extend this by identifying food-derived reads â€” enabling their removal from community tabulations while informing which metabolites are available as gut inputs. Host-derived enzymes (e.g., released into the lumen) should similarly be treated as present reactions, even when not microbiome-derived. Functional assessment should shift from pathway abundance tables to per-metabolite probability estimates. For each metabolite, we model both sides: production (relevant genes present and required inputs available; chained in series until reaching either an available input or an impasse) and consumption (consuming reactions and any required co-reactants present). This frames function around a specific metabolite endpoint with context-defined starting points â€” e.g., ""a host who recently ate a banana"" â€” rather than universally defined pathways that lack environmental grounding. Datasets with joint metabolomics and WGS provide an avenue to refine and validate the model, identifying metabolites that fit the model well and those that do not. Diet- and microbiome-associated plasma metabolites should be the highest priority for model validation and refinement. Direct taxa-to-outcome relationships remain important. But the complex interplay of host, diet, and microbiome â€” and its effect on health â€” is most powerfully modeled through the metabolite environment the host actually experiences. "

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: A Flipped-Classroom Model for Engaging Health Professions Students in Data Analysis and Bioinformatics
authors: Caleb Class, Butler University, United States
abstract: As big data becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare, students in the health professions must be trained to evaluate and appropriately apply AI tools and data analysis. To address this need, we designed a two course sequence that introduces nonâ€“data science students to core concepts in data analytics, statistical reasoning, and bioinformatics. The first course, â€œIntroduction to Healthcare Analyticsâ€, provides hands-on experience with multiple computational tools including the R programming language, as well as introductory statistical modeling and machine learning. The second course, â€œGenetics, Genomics, and Biotechnologyâ€, extends these skills by introducing foundational genomics concepts and bioinformatics tools with clear links to real-world biomedical applications, including drug development and precision medicine. Both courses are delivered in a flipped-classroom format, where lecture time focuses on games (with learning objectives) and collaborative analysis activities. Despite many students entering with low confidence in quantitative work, anonymous course evaluations indicate that our approach has been effective and well received. Few students questioned the courseâ€™s relevance while many more commented positively, with some noting that they have become more confident in approaching unfamiliar challenges. Explicit connections between course activities and traditional or emerging pharmacy roles were also noted as helpful. Our experience demonstrates that non-specialist learners can successfully engage with analytics and bioinformatics through a reproducible model integrating analytics tools and applied team-based learning. Ongoing refinement will address student feedback and technological advances.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Addressing Computational Skills Gap: A Scalable Workshop Model for Teaching Reproducible Research Practices in a Biomedical Community
authors: Sofia Fertuzinhos, Yale University, United States; Max Wegener, Yale University, United States; Justin De Mayo, Yale University, United States; Levi Dolan, Yale University, United States
abstract: Background: The revelation of a reproducibility crisis in 2016 prompted the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to identify computational reproducibility as an attainable priority. Consequently, funding and publishing agencies introduced reproducibility requirements that researchers are now expected to meet â€” yet most lack the computational knowledge and skills to do so effectively. Methods: We developed and implemented the ""Advancing Reproducibility with Computational Skills (ARCS)"" workshop series at the Cushing/Whitney Medical Library. Drawing on our library's expertise in data management, manipulation, and analysis, ARCS guides researchers through the preparation of publicly available sequencing data for reanalysis. ARCS harnesses researchers' appetite for coding instruction as a vehicle to teach them embedded programmatic best practices essential to reproducible science. The first edition of the series, ""Introduction to Programming in R,"" comprised three sequential two-hour sessions covering: coding in base R vs Tidyverse; project setup in RStudio; reporting with Quarto; and version control with Git/GitHub. Results: All three sessions filled (35 seats each), with waiting lists for every session, confirming an unmet need. The audience was diverse, composed by postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, faculty, and staff from departments across the Schools of Medicine and Public Health. Conclusion: The overwhelming demand for the ARCS workshop series demonstrates a pressing need for accessible, hands-on computational training. Our modular, progressive curriculum provides an effective and scalable model for equipping biomedical researchers with the fundamental skills in R and Git required to conduct more robust and reproducible science. This framework can be readily adopted by other institutions to empower their research communities.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Target, Characterize, Screen: A Scalable Computational Framework for Introducing Drug Discovery in Medical Education.
authors: Christopher Campbell, Orlando College of Osteopathic Medicine, United States
abstract: As precision medicine becomes foundational to clinical practice, medical curricula must evolve to include accessible training in bioinformatics and computational biology. This project presents a scalable, step-by-step pedagogical framework designed to introduce medical students to the drug discovery pipeline through high-impact, small-scale computational projects. Utilizing Plasmodium falciparum as a model organism, the research project guides students through the practical application of online genomic databases to identify and characterize genes critical to pathogenesis. The methodology transitions from sequence to structure, teaching students to utilize bioinformatics tools for gene characterization, followed by advanced protein modeling techniques including homology modeling and structural assessment. Students utilize platforms such as AlphaFold and SwissDock, to evaluate protein architectures and simulate binding interactions with small molecules curated from the PubChem and ChEMBL-NTD databases. By integrating these virtual screening protocols, the projects demystify the complexities of computational biology, providing medical students with tangible insights into how molecular inhibitors are identified and translated into potential therapeutic leads. This modular approach demonstrates that sophisticated drug discovery concepts can be made accessible and relevant to future clinicians, fostering the data literacy required to navigate the future of genomic medicine and infectious disease management.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: An Intensive in AI for Molecular Biology
authors: Tsu-Pei Chiu, University of Southern California, United States
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping biology and medicine, but training often leaves students in one of three incomplete positions: methods without domain depth, applications without foundations, or predictions without mechanism. To address this problem, we designed the Dornsife Intensive AI for Molecular Biology, a three-course upper-division curriculum that integrates foundational machine learning, modern AI methods, and mechanistic structural reasoning. QBIO 460 addresses applications without foundations by teaching students to formulate biological questions as modeling problems and to evaluate core machine-learning approaches in Python on real biological datasets. QBIO 465 addresses methods without domain depth by placing contemporary approachesâ€”including transformers, generative models such as diffusion models, and large language modelsâ€”into the major data modalities of biology and medicine, so students learn not just the names of current methods, but when they are appropriate and what their limitations are. QBIO 481 addresses predictions without mechanism by grounding AI in structural bioinformatics, molecular interactions, molecular simulation, and AlphaFold-era modeling, enabling students to interpret outputs in terms of structure, dynamics, and biological function rather than as black-box predictions. Together, the three courses move students beyond black-box model use toward critical, mechanism-aware reasoning across data, structure, and function. Designed for students from computing, natural science, and quantitative biology backgrounds, the intensive is implemented through three existing 4-unit courses already taught at our institution. Current enrollments are about 20â€“30 students per course, with clear capacity to scale beyond 50 students. This curricular model offers a practical and scalable framework for preparing students for AI-driven biology, medicine, and interdisciplinary scientific careers.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Embedding bioinformatics in biology courses: Using artificial intelligence to design teaching activities for life science instructors
authors: Aida T. Miro-Herrans, University of Florida, United States
abstract: There is a growing need for improving bioinformatic skills in biology undergraduates. Exposing students to bioinformatics early in their biology education makes it easier for them to consider future training for bioinformatics careers. A major barrier to capacity-building at scale is often life science instructors' limited bioinformatics knowledge and time for lesson planning. Generative AI, including large language models, can help lower these barriers by synthesizing information on rapidly evolving methods and generating new educational content. To address these barriers to bioinformatics instruction, a bioinformatics librarian facilitated a workshop for life science instructors on how to use generative AI to develop bioinformatics lessons that were tailored for individual curriculums. The workshop showed how to develop prompts (sentences or paragraphs that describe the task to be completed) for AI chatbots that generated open-source bioinformatics exercises aligned with the NIBLSE bioinformatics core competencies for the life sciences. The prompt results stated the required software and datasets, instructions on how to perform the exercises, and the learning objectives and bioinformatics competencies addressed. Likert-scale pre and post-workshop surveys were implemented to assess the learning gains in bioinformatics skills and bioinformatics lesson development after participating in the workshop. Pre and post-workshop comparisons showed statistically significant increases in participants' perceived ability to develop bioinformatics lessons and in confidence in integrating bioinformatics topics into biology instruction. While mastering the prompting strategies may take some time and effort, the results demonstrate that AI can provide time-saving assistance and can be used to increase inclusion of bioinformatics in life science courses.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: Kenya Reference Genome Initiative pilot: from audit to action in East African population genomics
authors: Sharon Nyagaka, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya; Mitchel Motari, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya; Sarah Pollock, Ultima Genomics, Inc. Fremont, CA, USA,, United States; Francisco M. De La Vega, Ultima Genomics, Inc. Fremont, CA, USA,, United States; Brian Ogoti, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya; Frank Onyambu, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya; Catherine Waruiru, Centre for Molecular Biosciences and Genomics, Kenya
abstract: Background. Kenya is repeatedly named a priority for African precision medicine, yet an audit of public whole-genome sequencing (WGS) found that all Kenya-attributed data resolve, after de-duplication, to 123 individuals, 86% from one community (Luhya). These data support research but cannot serve as national precision-medicine infrastructure. We launched the Kenya Reference Genome Initiative (KRGI) to close this gap and report its first pilot. Methods. Fifteen deeply phenotyped participants from nine communities spanning the Bantu, Nilotic and Cushitic language families were sequenced on the Ultima Genomics UG200 platform (Solaris 2.0) and aligned to GRCh38 (no-alt). Calling used EfficientDV (short variants), GRIDSS with cnMops and cnvpytor (structural and copy-number), Parascopy (segmental duplications), HLA-LA (HLA) and PyPGx (CPIC pharmacogenes). Results. Coverage averaged 39.6× (99.8% of reads mapped; Ti/Tv 1.98), giving 5.59 million SNVs/indels and ~25,000 structural/copy-number calls per genome, plus 81 two-field HLA alleles across six classical loci (17 at HLA-B), mostly African-common. About 1.7% of cohort SNVs (~259,000) were absent from dbSNP. Every participant carried at least one actionable CPIC diplotype (mean 4.6), including reduced-function UGT1A1 in 93%, altered CYP2B6 in 67%, and the African G6PD A- deficiency allele in two men. Parascopy and PyPGx resolved CYP2D6, the hardest short-read pharmacogene, in 14 of 15 genomes. Conclusion. A 15-genome pilot already recovers actionable pharmacogenomic and immunogenomic variation, much of it in genes governing the antiretroviral, antimalarial and antitubercular drugs central to Kenyan care and under-represented in panels used to guide African prescribing. Full-cohort sequencing is under way.

title: Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K (J.2.4.1) viruses associated with a surge at a university health clinic, Arizona, the United States, November to early December 2025
authors: Matthew Scotch, Arizona State University, United States; Temitope O.C. Faleye, Arizona State University, United States; Angelica Urquidez-Negrete, Arizona State University, United States; Bradley Bobbett, Arizona State University, United States; Veronica Boyle, Arizona State University, United States; Kelly Conard, Arizona State University, United States; Lucy Sublasky-Rodriguez, Arizona State University, United States; Vel Murugan, Arizona State University, United States
abstract: From November to early December 2025, a marked rise in influenza diagnoses was observed at a university student health clinic on a large urban campus in Tempe, Arizona, United States. We investigated whether the surge was associated with influenza A(H3N2) subclade K (J.2.4.1) and assessed antigenic and transmission implications. Nasopharyngeal swabs from students with influenza-like illness were confirmed and subtyped by RT-qPCR. Twenty-seven A(H3N2)-positive specimens collected 5 November–2 December 2025 underwent whole-genome sequencing at CDC. Haemagglutinin (HA) sequences were classified with Nextclade, amino acid changes were characterized with FluSurver, predicted vaccine protection was estimated using an epitope-based pEpitope model relative to the 2025/26 cell-based vaccine reference strain, and Bayesian phylodynamic analyses evaluated campus-based community diffusion using residence metadata. All 27 HA sequences belonged to subclade K and were highly similar. Ten HA substitutions were common, including T135K, S144N, N145S, N158D, I160K and K189R, with seven mapping to antigenic sites A/B/D and the receptor-binding domain. The epitope model predicted reduced vaccine protection (mean 0.13; 26/27 sequences), with one sequence showing lower predicted protection (0.02) and HA1 T127A, consistent with a potential glycosylation change. Phylodynamics suggested multiple introductions, early campus predominance, and onward spread to offâ€‘campus and outside-Tempe locations; phylogeny was significantly structured by residence (p A(H3N2) subclade K viruses with antigenically relevant HA changes were associated with a university surge, and campus mixing likely facilitated rapid amplification and spillover, underscoring the value of genomic surveillance in semi-closed settings for early characterization of emerging lineages.

title: Cultivated sunflower (Helianthus annuus) pangenome to identify agricultural breeding targets
authors: Esme Padgett, University of British Columbia (Michael Smith Laboratories), Canada; Marco Todesco, University of British Columbia (Michael Smith Laboratories), Canada
abstract: At current rates of crop innovation, future growing seasons are projected to fall short of 2025 production demands. Next-generation technologies could rescue current farm ecosystems by allowing us to harness more diverse genomic variation for data-driven agriculture. Crop breeding previously integrated short genetic regions into breeding regimes; new pangenome technologies contain complete genome architectures from multi-species and genus groups. Pangenome graphs are a more efficient and diverse portfolio of variation, cataloguing genetic regions of interest from wild relatives, and under-utilized landrace and Indigenous varieties. To inform breeding, for sunflowers (Helianthus annuus), the worldâ€™s third largest oilseed crop, we constructed a graph-based pangenome using the high-quality, long-read assemblies of 11 cultivated and wild varietals and the nascent telomere-to-telomere reference genome of H. annuus (var. HA412). Critical attention has been drawn to large structural variants (SV) within H. annuus, where genes controlling agronomic traits are concentrated within inverted regions of the genome, earning them the moniker of â€œsupergenesâ€ and creating novel targets of interest for oilseed and confectionary sunflower breeders. Evolutionary comparisons can be drawn across the domestication timeline of Helianthus from the pangenome. Flowering time, coloration, and architectural phenotypes can also be interrogated for selective sweeps and gene flow that emerge from large, non-recombining structural variants (SV). Given the effects of linkage draft and recalcitrance towards genetic engineering in sunflowers, breeding programs stand to benefit from the pangenome investigation here, which aims to offer future breeding targets to improve disease/pest resistance and drought tolerance without compromising seed quality or yield.

title: Population Genomics and Co-evolutionary Analysis of H. majoris and its Host the Blue Tit (Cyanistes caeruleus) Over a Quarter of a Century
authors: Esther Weyer, Center for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology & Department of Entomology and Wildlife Ecology, University of Delaware, United States; Olof Hellgren, Department of Biology, Evolutionary Ecology and Infection Biology, Lund University, Sweden; Dag Ahrén, Department of Biology, NBIS, SciLifeLab, Lund University, Sweden; Diana Ekman, Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, NBIS,SciLifeLab, Stockholm University, Sweden; Jan-Åke Nilsson, Department of Biology, Evolutionary Ecology and Infection Biology & Ecological and Evolutionary Physiology, Lund University, Sweden; Vincenzo Ellis, Department of Entomology and Wildlife Ecology, Universityof Delaware, United States
abstract: Determining pathogen and host dynamics at the genomic level is essential for understanding underlying mechanisms for infectivity and fitness. A valuable study system to investigate host-pathogen evolution and ecology exists in a population of Eurasian blue tits (Cyanistes caeruleus) around KrankesjÃ¶n in Southern Sweden. Infections of these birds with the avian malaria pathogen Haemoproteus majoris have been monitored over decades, with sample collections covering multiple generations of the host species. By applying a newly developed selective whole genome amplification (SWGA) method, we are able to utilize these historically collected samples to study genomic fluctuations in the host and pathogen populations over time. This study incorporates approximately 200 samples of positive infections spanning a 28-year period from the same geographic region experiencing an increase in pathogen prevalence from ~40% to ~90% among the adult birds. We have identified pathogen variants of interest by calculating the difference in allele presence over the study period and by estimating phenotypic changes with snpEff, focusing on annotations with moderate effects. We used presence and absence of these pathogen variants as phenotypes for a Genome Wide Association Study (GWAS) against the host to find associated SNPs as potential co-evolutionary effects. Preliminary results reveal significant associations between pathogen membrane protein phenotype and SNPs in host protein-binding gene WDFY4. Ongoing work focuses on enrichment analysis of associated host genes to understand the pathways and functions linked to the changes in pathogen phenotypes, aiming to provide insight into co-evolutionary dynamics of vector-transmitted haemosporidian parasites and their hosts.

title: Development of a Practical Haplotype Graph for Tepary Bean
authors: John Hamilton, Center for Applied Genetic Technologies, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, United States; Yi-Wen Wang, Center for Applied Genetic Technologies, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, United States; Joshua Wood, Institute of Plant Breeding, Genetics, & Genomics, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, United States; Kathrine Mailloux, Institute of Plant Breeding, Genetics, & Genomics, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, United States; Leah Tomey, Institute of Plant Breeding, Genetics, & Genomics, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, United States; Consuelo Estévez de Jensen, Department of Agro-Environmental Sciences, University of Puerto Rico at Mayagüez, Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, United States; Tim Porch, USDA-ARS Tropical Agricultural Research Station, Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, United States; C. Robin Buell, Center for Applied Genetic Technologies, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, United States
abstract: Tepary bean (Phaseolus acutifolius A. Gray) is a sister species of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.), a globally important source of dietary protein. While common bean is heat and drought sensitive, tepary bean is both heat and drought tolerant. Further, tepary has a broad array of disease resistance for use in breeding new resilient common bean varieties. To understand genetic diversity in tepary bean, we generated 13 new tepary bean genome sequences and resequenced 435 accessions from the Tepary Diversity Panel (TDP). Population structure was determined using k-mers confirming previous estimates of subpopulation structure within wild and cultivated TDP members. Currently, we are constructing a Practical Haplotype Graph (PHG) to identify the haplotypes in our tepary bean founder population and to understand the overall haplotype diversity in the TDP. Using the PHG, we will impute haplotypes for the 435 TDP samples to provide a resource for the bean breeding community and subsample the TDP to determine the imputation capabilities of the PHG.

title: A new method for evaluating evolutionary stability for flexible genomic segments
authors: Caiqi Liu, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, China; Maggie Wang, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: The rate of molecular evolution refers to the number of fixed mutations per nucleotide site per unit time, which is conceptually distinct from the mutation rate.
