The current approaches of estimating evolutionary rate are mainly based on molecular phylogenetics, which includes the root-to tip linear regression, the estimation of rate as a parameter in maximum likelihood tree, and Bayesian inference with Markov chain Monte Carlo. However, these methods are computationally demanding and difficult to estimate evolutionary rates for an extremely small genomic segment. Here, we introduce a novel bioinformatics approach that enables the estimation of evolutionary rate for genomic segment of arbitrary length even down to single nucleotide precision. For benchmark of rate estimation for the whole genome of virus, the results calculated by our method are consistent with those estimated based on the reconstruction of phylogenetic trees. We next evaluate position-based evolutionary rates for the influenza A pH1N1 and H3N2 viruses as well as SARS-CoV-2 based on sliding windows, highlighting genomic hotspots under high evolutionary pressure and conserved regions. In addition to nucleotide sequences, we evaluate the evolutionary stability of T-cell epitopes in the influenza A viruses and SARS-CoV-2 based on our method and select several conserved T-cell epitopes as the potential targets for the development of T-cell-directed vaccines. Overall, our method provides novel statistical framework to efficiently estimate evolutionary rates of genomic segments of any length and can also be used for screening conserved T-cell epitopes.

title: Comprehensive Multi-Omics Characterization and Evolutionary Analysis of the Scylla serrata Allergome
authors: Fu Kiu Ao, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Stephen Kwok-Wing Tsui, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Introduction: Scylla serrata (giant mud crab) is a major dietary allergen source in Asia. Building upon preliminary allergen identification, this study presents a finalized, integrative multi-omics framework to provide a chromosome-level resolution of the S. serrata allergome and its evolutionary context within Decapoda. Methods: We utilized hybrid sequencing (PacBio/Nanopore) to establish a high-quality chromosome-level genome assembly. Integrated transcriptomic and mass spectrometric workflows were employed to quantify and validate the allergen profile. Comparative genomic analysis was performed to trace the orthologous relationships of these allergens across taxonomically related crustacean species. Results: The integrative pipeline identified 18 high-confidence allergens (13 genomic-led, 5 proteomic-led). Immunoassays using recombinant proteins and patient sera confirmed the clinical relevance of key candidates, including those previously uncharacterized in mud crab hepatopancreas and eggs. Evolutionarily, these allergens show high conservation across Decapoda, suggesting a common ancestral origin for shellfish hypersensitivity. Discussion and Conclusion: This completed study provides the most detailed allergen map of S. serrata to date. By bridging the gap between genomic architecture and clinical allergenicity, these findings facilitate the development of precision component-resolved diagnostics (CRD) and provide a benchmark for future allergen studies in other commercially important shellfish.

title: Machine learning predicts molecular signatures of antimicrobial resistance in bacterial pathogens
authors: Abhirupa Ghosh, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Evan Brenner, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Charmie Vang, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Ethan Wolfe, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Emily Boyer, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States; Janani Ravi, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, United States
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacteria is a rising global health concern impeding treatments with increasing morbidity and mortality. While AMR in many bacteria is well-studied, novel resistance mechanisms are constantly evolving. Our goal is to develop a computational approach to predict a bacterial isolateâ€™s resistance or susceptibility to antibiotics and the underlying molecular mechanisms. We download bacterial genomes and their metadata (e.g., geographical location, host, isolation source, collection date) with paired AMR phenotypes. We extract molecular features (genes/proteins/domains) from bacterial genomes that serve as inputs for supervised machine learning (ML) models per bacteria-antibiotic (or antibiotic class) combination. The features are annotated to Clusters of Orthologous Genes for species-agnostic interpretation and comparison. To evaluate robustness of the models, we shuffle AMR labels to generate baseline random models. To assess the generalizability and context-specificity of the models, we implemented temporal and geographical holdouts. We tested the framework on infection-causing ESKAPE group of pathogens and obtained performant models, with median MCC>0.8 and predictive features including well-known genes like tetK for tetracycline; mecA for methicillin-resistance and lesser-known features like N-acetyltransferase domain for levofloxacin. The temporal and geographical holdouts highlighted both conserved and evolving resistance mechanisms over different periods and regions. The curated metadata, model performances, and predictive features across ESKAPE are available via our Shiny dashboard https://jravilab.cuanschutz.edu/amr/. We present our framework as an R package suite (JRaviLab/amR). In summary, the framework is broadly adaptable to other bacteria and capable of identifying AMR mechanisms.

title: Machine learning identifies the fingerprints of host adaptation in bacterial genomes
authors: Evan Brenner, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO, United States; Landon Buskirk, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO, United States; Katerina Terwelp, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO, United States; Clay Griffin-Derr, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO, United States; Sarah Mentzer, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO, United States; Janani Ravi, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO, United States
abstract: Emerging and expanding infectious diseases threaten human and animal health worldwide, but different bacterial species and strains pose different risks. As exposures to novel microbes continue to rise at the wildland-urban interface and animal agriculture increases cross-species exposures and spillover risks, how can we classify whether a bacterial isolate is likely to affect different hosts? Benchside microbiology cannot alone keep pace with the expanding scale of the challenge. We apply comparative genomics and machine learning approaches to identify predictors of host specificity. Using publicly available microbial genomics data and metadata, we extract features across molecular scales (genes, k-mers, virulence factors), train machine learning models that classify the host of origin, and extract the features driving model performance. At the whole genome sequence level, we find strong predictive performance (F1 scores > 0.9) in multiple bacterial species (e.g., Staphylococci, Streptococci), and that these models are underpinned by biological features with known involvement in host adaptation and host cell tropism. We also find predictive power in individual proteins using basic amino acid composition properties or ESM-2-based protein language model embeddings, supporting the use of multiple approaches for bacterial host specificity. Finally, errors and inconsistency in available metadata for hosts and isolation sources, and potentially confounding bacterial population structures motivate our additional work to harmonize and normalize metadata values, and test how phylogenetic relatedness affects ML model robustness. Collectively, I find that bacterial host specificity can be predicted across molecular feature scales, and that the driving motifs shed biological insights into pathogenesis.

title: Analysis of Gene Tree Heterogeneity with Applications to Incomplete lineage Sorting and Introgression
authors: Yuting Xiao, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Tanjeem Zaman, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Maureen Stolzer, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Dannie Durand, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: Incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) and introgression drive gene tree heterogeneity, leaving characteristic signatures in gene tree topology distributions. These patterns make gene tree sampling a compelling approach for inferring ancestral population processes among species. For species trees with k=3 leaves, gene tree heterogeneity can be assessed simply by counting tree topologies. Comparing the empirical distribution with theoretical models allows for hypothesis testing and parameter estimation. For larger gene trees, current approaches subsample rooted triplets targeting species tree branches of interest, because the number of unique gene tree topologies scales super-exponentially with k. However, accurate assessment requires sampling several rooted triplets for each species tree branch. Counting and combining results from multiple triplets is computationally expensive and becomes intractable when extended to whole-clade analyses. Here, we present a scalable, topology-based algorithm that characterizes gene tree heterogeneity at each species tree internode without triplet subsampling. Given a species tree and a set of gene trees, the method maps gene tree internodes to species tree internodes and tabulates the gene tree heterogeneity statistics for each species tree branch in a single, unified calculation. The algorithm automatically excludes uninformative cases arising from paralogy, gene loss, or reconstruction error. It runs in time linear in the total number of gene tree internodes. Applied to simulated and genuine datasets, the algorithm recovers topology frequency distributions consistent with theoretical predictions under ILS, even in the presence of paralogy and missing data.

title: Deducing the Evolution of Allorecognition and Primordial Immunity in Cnidarians
authors: Alberto Rivera, NIH, United States
abstract: The allorecognition system of the hydroid Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus plays an essential role in mediating self vs. non-self recognition in cnidarian colonies, which is analogous to the role of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) in bilaterian immune systems. Both complexes have contiguous stretches of similar, highly duplicated genes, suggesting a homologous relationship between the ARC and MHC. Protein structural prediction methods, such as AlphaFold2 also indicate structural similarity between the proteins encoded within the Hydractinia ARC and the MHC. We have deduced the structure of the ARC in the related hydrozoan Podocoryna to determine the conservation of the cnidarian allorecognition complex. Genome annotation software and protein structural prediction methods have revealed a number of candidate Podocoryna allorecognition proteins that form a long contiguous complex. Phylogenies suggest homology between cnidarian allorecognition genes, as well as syntenic conservation of this gene complex across Hydrozoans. We are currently applying these methods to analyze the high-quality whole-genome sequence of the basal bilaterians Branchiostoma and Ciona to identify potential ALR orthologs. We have also begun identifying homologous regions in other bilaterian species to determine likely ALR homologs. Future comparative genomics work with other basal chordates and vertebrates will be focused on determining the relationship between the ARC and the bilaterian MHC, to help elucidate the evolution of the immune system in early vertebrate history.

title: Reconstruction of Tumor Clonal Trees with Multi-Sample Bulk Sequencing Data by Integrative Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Salem Malikic, Cancer Data Science Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States; Hamza Iseric, Department of Computer Science, University of Maryland, United States; Chih Hao Wu, University of Maryland, College Park, United States; Edward Michael Gertz, Cancer Data Science Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States; Erin Molloy, Department of Computer Science, University of Maryland, United States; Cenk Sahinalp, Cancer Data Science Laboratory, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Multi-sample bulk DNA sequencing enables reconstruction of a tumorâ€™s clonal history, but scalable methods often rely on heuristic search and provide no optimality guarantees. We present CITUP2, an integrative combinatorial optimization framework that reconstructs clonal trees from descendant cell fractions (DCFs) of mutational clusters. CITUP2 formulates tree inference as a mixed-integer quadratic program (MIQP) that jointly determines the tree topology and clone prevalences across samples. It minimizes a weighted discrepancy between observed and inferred DCFs, with options to prioritize trees exhibiting consistency in the presence-absence patterns of parent-child clones. Under this formulation, CITUP2 returns provably optimal solutions (with respect to the model) and avoids the combinatorial explosion of exhaustive topology enumeration used by existing methods with optimality guarantees. In addition, CITUP2 can report a user-specified number of best trees. In simulations and analyses of a large, recently published multi-sample TRACERx cohort, CITUP2 scales to trees with tens of clones (approximately 30) and matches or improves on the fit attained by state-of-the-art approaches, while providing clear optimality certificates.

title: Improving gene annotation lift over using integer linear programming to solve a generalized weighted bipartite matching problem
authors: Hyun Joo Ji, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Tomoya Furutani, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Steven Salzberg, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: As gapless assemblies become increasingly common, the next challenge is to produce accurate gene annotations for these genomes. While annotations can be generated using de novo pipelines, for species with well-curated reference annotations, projecting annotations from one genome to another is often more efficient and accurate. Existing annotation lift over methods prioritize sequence identity while paying little attention to gene order. Explicit modeling of syntenic order is necessary to prevent lift over artifacts from being misinterpreted as structural rearrangements. Here we present Liftoff2, an updated annotation lift over method that models the process as a generalized weighted bipartite matching problem between source and target genomes. Unlike Liftoff, which selects the best mapping for each gene independently, Liftoff2 jointly evaluates candidate mappings, enabling globally optimal gene placement with respect to sequence identity and syntenic order. We incorporate syntenic constraints into the optimization objective by assigning bonuses to mappings consistent with source gene order, a framework naturally expressed and solved using integer linear programming. In preliminary experiments lifting the MANE annotation onto the Han1 assembly, Liftoff2 preserved more syntenic structure than Liftoff, reducing break distance by approximately 20% relative to the source annotation. These improvements were achieved with minimal reduction in annotated genes or overall feature coverage. Despite a modest reduction in exon coverage (~8 kbp), Liftoff2 increased CDS coverage by more than 6 kbp, suggesting improved placement of protein-coding regions. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating global syntenic constraints improves annotation lift over accuracy while maintaining high coverage and sequence fidelity.

title: A Spatial Single-cell Atlas of the Adult Mouse Spinal Cord with Multi-dimensional Annotation
authors: Qimeng Wang, Vanderbilt University, United States; Yunfei Hu, Vanderbilt University, United States; Yuling Zhu, Vanderbilt University, United States; Jing Peng, Harvard Medical School, United States; Emmanuella Osei-Asante, Harvard Medical School, United States; Gautham Chelliah, Vanderbilt University, United States; Melissa Sobanko, Vanderbilt University, United States; Brianna Sanchez, Harvard Medical School, United States; David Ginty, Harvard Medical School, United States; Xin Maizie Zhou, Vanderbilt University, United States; Shan Meltzer, Vanderbilt University, United States
abstract: The spinal cord integrates diverse somatosensory inputs and executes motor outputs through anatomically and functionally distinct circuits. Here, we employed spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the adult mouse spinal cord to gain insights into the organizational logic of the spinal cord. Our results reveal distinct spatial and laminar distributions of neuronal subtypes, including axial level and sex-specific differences. Many neuronal subtypes exhibit close spatial proximity, implicating regionally specific patterns of connectivity and circuit functions. Additionally, neuronal subtypes within the dorsal horn exhibit a wide range of predicted cell-cell communication motifs, as assessed by the spatial distribution of neuropeptide- and other ligand-receptor pairs. Finally, we identified several neuronal subtypes with altered transcriptomic and predicted cell-cell communications in a model of neuropathic pain. This spatially resolved cellular and molecular map of the spinal cord will facilitate the decoding of circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory and motor functions in health and disease.

title: Multi-omics integration and pseudotime trajectory inference reveal different molecular signatures that may lead to Parkinson's disease pathology
authors: Katia Lopes, Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA, United States; Ricardo A. Vialle, Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA, United States; Nili Tickotsky, Ben Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva, Israel, Israel; Caio M. P. F Batalha, Institute of Medical Assistance to State Civil Servants, Sao Paulo, SP, Brazil, Brazil; Shahram Oveisgharan, Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA, United States; Hans Ulrich Klein, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY, USA, United States; Yasser Iturria-Medina, Neurology and Neurosurgery Department, Montreal Neurological Institute, Montreal, Canada, Canada; Shinya Tasaki, Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA, United States; David A Bennett, Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA, United States; Aron S Buchman, Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA, United States
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a synucleinopathy defined by Lewy body accumulation and nigral neuronal loss, which begin years before clinical diagnosis. The molecular mechanisms driving PD pathology remain poorly understood, particularly in older adults with co-pathologies. We hypothesized that applying novel bioinformatic tools to high-dimensional molecular data could identify distinct molecular signatures underlying the accumulation of pathological PD and co-pathologies in aging brains. We analyzed post-mortem multi-omic data from the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP), including six modalities: DNA methylation, bulk RNA-seq, proteomics, histone acetylation, metabolomics, and single-nucleus RNA-seq cell fractions from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Differential abundance analysis using pathological PD as the outcome identified 224 genes and 1,692 proteins (5% FDR). To model disease progression, we applied Multimodal Contrastive Trajectories Inference to 1,080 participants with at least two omics layers, generating a pseudotime axis from no PD pathology to pathological PD. Top contributors included acetylation markers, metabolomics, and single-nucleus features, led by stress-response astrocytes (Ast.10), an acetylation peak near VPS13D gene. Using pseudotime as the outcome, we identified 307 proteins, 193 acetylation markers, 15 genes, 4 metabolites, and one oligodendrocyte subpopulation (Oli.6). Correlation coefficients of t-values between the two analyses ranged from 0.58 to 0.75, confirming broadly concordant signatures. Functional enrichment analysis revealed dysregulation of dopaminergic neuron differentiation, olfactory perception, alongside inflammatory response, synapse organization, and mitochondrial pathways, with stronger signals using pseudotime. This multimodal analytic approach reveals distinct trajectories leading to pathologic PD and highlights novel molecular candidates for early disease detection.

title: Joint Modeling of Transcriptomic and Morphological Phenotypes for Generative Molecular Design
authors: Mengbo Wang, Purdue University, United States; Shourya Verma, Purdue University, United States; Shyaman Jayasundara, Purdue University, United States; Aditya Malusare, Purdue University, United States; Luopin Wang, Purdue University, United States; Simran Kadadi, Purdue University, United States; Ananth Grama, Purdue University, United States; Majid Kazemian, Purdue University, United States; Nadia Atallah Lanman, Purdue University, United States
abstract: Motivation: Phenotypic drug discovery generates rich multi-modal biological data from transcriptomic and morphological measurements, yet translating complex cellular responses into molecular design remains a computational bottleneck. Existing generative methods operate on single modalities and condition on post-treatment measurements without leveraging paired control-treatment dynamics to capture perturbation effects. Results: We present Pert2Mol, the first framework for multi-modal phenotype-to-structure generation that integrates transcriptomic and morphological features from paired control-treatment experiments. Pert2Mol employs bidirectional cross-attention between control and treatment states to capture perturbation dynamics, conditioning a rectified flow transformer that generates molecular structures along straight-line trajectories. We introduce Student-Teacher Self-Representation (SERE) learning to stabilize training in high-dimensional multi-modal spaces. On the GDP dataset, Pert2Mol achieves FrÂ´echet ChemNet Distance of 4.996 compared to 7.343 for diffusion baselines and 59.114 for transcriptomics-only methods, while maintaining perfect molecular validity and appropriate physicochemical property distributions. The model demonstrates 84.7% scaffold diversity and 12.4 times faster generation than diffusion approaches with deterministic sampling suitable for hypothesis-driven validation. Availability: Code and pretrained models will be available at https://github.com/wangmengbo/Pert2Mol.

title: “Novel RNAseq”, a scalable and reproducible bioinformatics workflow for novel gene discovery
authors: Mohamad Elian, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Carleton University, Canada; Elroy Cober, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Canada; Ashkan Golshani, Carleton University, Canada; Bahram Samanfar, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Carleton University, Canada
abstract: The advent of next generation sequencing (NGS) has greatly increased the capacity for generating multi-omic data. Consequently, improved methods of data processing have become key in reliably extracting meaningful conclusions from these large datasets. However, computational requirements for big data processing increases the barrier to entry for downstream analyses as sequence file sizes reach terabyte scales requiring massive investment in computational resources beyond what most computers can feasibly accomplish. Bioinformatics pipelines which are scalable in high performance computing (HPC) environments are critical for addressing these technical bottlenecks. RNAseq data in particular has several potential uses including for novel gene discovery and functional annotation. Here, we present â€œNovel RNAseqâ€, a user friendly, parallelizable nextflow based bioinformatics workflow that was designed as part of the Omicsflow platform for RNAseq analysis focusing specifically (but not limited to) on identification of novel genes. The workflow was applied to a preliminary case study using Glycine max (soybean) and identified 203 potential novel candidate genes; however the inclusion of user-customizable parameter files allows for applicability to any other organism. The results are easily interpretable by users through a custom Quarto report that is produced with key pipeline results. â€œNovel RNAseqâ€ is also designed as a reproducible workflow with compatibility for apptainer containers and can be run using either local or HPC systems. Future additions to the pipeline will include underexplored methods of downstream RNAseq analysis such as â€œWeighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysisâ€ (WGCNA) to help with functional annotation of the novel genes in question.

title: Genetic alterations of HLA class I genes in keratinocyte cancers
authors: Harsh Sharma, University of California, San Francisco, United States; Barbara Rentroia-Pacheco, Erasmus MC, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, Netherlands; Chirag Krishna, Broad Institute, Cambridge, MA, United States; Kairi Tanaka, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, United States; Eric Wilson, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, United States; Carlos A. Garcia-Prieto, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, United States; Mikio Tada, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, United States; Yuying Qin, University of California, San Francisco, United States; Joleen Traets, SkylineDx BV, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, Netherlands; Bishal Tandukar, University of California San Francisco, United States; Harmen van de Werken, Erasmus MC, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, Netherlands; Domenico Bellomo, SkylineDx BV, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, Netherlands; Loes Hollestein, Erasmus MC, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, Netherlands; Marlies Wakkee, Erasmus MC, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands, Netherlands; Iwei Yeh, University of California San Francisco, United States; Boris C. Bastian, University of California San Francisco, United States; Diego Chowell, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, United States; A. Hunter Shain, University of California San Francisco, United States
abstract: Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) class I genes mediate antigen presentation to cytotoxic T cells and are among the most polymorphic loci in the human genome. This extreme polymorphism has historically hindered the detection of genetic alterations at the HLA locus using standard sequencing pipelines. Keratinocyte cancers exhibit exceptionally high mutation burdens and are highly immunogenic; however, alterations affecting antigen presentation have not been systematically characterized. To address this gap in knowledge, we developed HLAkit - a specialized software to detect both somatic point mutations and loss of heterozygosity affecting HLA class I genes. Using this approach, we analyzed whole-exome sequencing data from 263 keratinocyte cancers, with matched RNA-sequencing data available for a subset of tumors. We found that 30% of tumors harbor somatic alterations in HLA class I genes, with point mutation frequencies markedly higher than those in other cancer types. Nearly half of these mutations were truncating (i.e., nonsense, splice-site, or frameshift), indicating positive selection for loss of HLA function during tumorigenesis. Somatic HLA alterations were enriched in histopathologic subtypes characterized by prominent inflammation. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed distinct immune microenvironments: HLA wild-type tumors contained resident T cells embedded within a fibrotic stroma, whereas HLA-mutant tumors exhibited immune activation patterns consistent with non MHC-restricted responses. Together, these findings suggest that a reduced baseline capacity for antigen presentation, inherited by germline HLA alleles, and/or the acquired loss of antigen presentation, through somatic alterations, promote keratinocyte carcinogenesis.

title: Decoding Organ Morphology and Disease Mechanisms via AI-Driven Pan-Organ Imaging and Multi-Omics Integration
authors: Fengyuan Hu, AstraZeneca, United Kingdom; Boxing Liu, University of Dundee, United Kingdom; Chao Li, University of Cambridge, United Kingdom; Quanli Wang, AstraZeneca, United States; Slavé Petrovski, Astrazeneca, United Kingdom
abstract: Background: The impact of rare variants on organ morphology and systemic disease pathways remains largely unexplored. We leverage UK Biobank's whole-genome sequencing, multi-organ imaging, and multi-omics data with advanced AI methodologies to: 1) identify rare variant effects across organ systems, 2) characterize functional noncoding variants, 3) reveal shared genetic architecture underlying disease mechanisms, and 4) develop AI-driven tools to enhance imaging phenotype extraction and disease classification, advancing precision medicine through novel biomarker and therapeutic target discovery. Methods: We perform gene-level collapsing analyses of rare variants in coding and noncoding regions (prioritized using MAF, CADD, and JARVIS scores), testing associations with 4,384 UKB imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) across brain, heart, and abdominal organs, plus 2,923 plasma proteins and 325 metabolites. We developed OG-SAM (Organogenesis SAM), an advanced segmentation model incorporating biologically inspired hierarchical adaptation (OrganAdapt) and multi-scale organ feature fusion, benchmarked against state-of-the-art models. We enhanced MILTON (MachIne Learning with phenoType associatIONs) by incorporating IDPs to identify misclassified individuals in case-control studies and enhance statistical power. Results: Our analyses uncovered 648 significant associations between coding sequences and IDPs, 97,810 between proteomics and IDPs, and 14,025 between metabolomics and IDPs. We identified 23 genes associated with brain structures, including novel associations: PTEN with cortical area, RICTOR with brain morphology, and CELSR1 with white matter integrity. OG-SAM demonstrates superior boundary delineation and generalizability across organ systems. MILTON with IDP integration shows enhanced disease classification, with substantial improvements for Multiple Sclerosis using brain MRI features and Osteoporosis using bone mineral density, BMI, and vitamin D measures. Conclusions: This study represents the largest-scale analysis of rare variant effects on multi-organ imaging phenotypes enhanced by AI. Our dual AI strategyâ€”OG-SAM for robust organ segmentation and MILTON enhancement with imaging featuresâ€”creates a comprehensive pipeline from image acquisition to disease prediction. These findings validate known associations, reveal novel genetic-morphology connections, and demonstrate how AI amplifies genetic association study power.

title: Efficient Virtual Screening of Ultra-Large Chemical Libraries via Ranking-Based Learning, Hashing, and Bayesian Optimization
authors: Jonghyeon Bae, Pusan National University, South Korea; Jeonghoon Choi, Pusan National University, South Korea; Juseong Kim, Pusan NationalUniversity, South Korea; Giltae Song, Pusan National University, South Korea
abstract: Efficient virtual screeningâ€”the task of identifying small molecules that can bind to a given target protein while avoiding structurally redundant candidatesâ€”remains a major bottleneck in drug discovery pipelines. In practical settings, the chemical space is only sparsely observed due to the high cost of evaluating candidate compounds through simulation (e.g., docking) or experimental assays, resulting in a budget-constrained optimization problem. In practice, effective screening requires prioritizing high-affinity ligands while ensuring sufficient structural diversity across chemical scaffolds, as selecting similar compounds yields limited value for downstream validation. Existing AI-driven approaches, including active learning and Bayesian optimization, have demonstrated strong retrieval performance but often suffer from exploitation bias, leading to suboptimal exploration and reduced diversity. To address this limitation, we propose a Bayesian optimizationâ€“based virtual screening framework that leverages LSH to structure the chemical space for improved exploration under sparse observations, together with a ranking-based surrogate model. The proposed approach maintains high retrieval performance through ranking-based learning, while benefiting from improved early-stage exploration enabled by the structured representation. In addition, acquisition functions are incorporated to guide efficient sample selection under sparse observations and constrained budgets. Experiments on the ZINC 138M dataset demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves over 30Ã— improvement in top-1% retrieval performance compared to random sampling (brute force), while improving structural diversity by approximately 15%, as measured by the number of unique scaffolds. These results indicate that the proposed method effectively balances retrieval performance and exploration, enabling scalable and robust ligand discovery in ultra-large chemical libraries.

title: NanOrigin: Single-Read Tissue-of-Origin Inference from Native DNA Methylation via Oxford Nanopore Sequencing
authors: Noah Bigelow, University of Utah, United States; Balazs Murnyak, Clement Lab, United States; Kendell Clement, Clement Lab, United States
abstract: Oxford Nanopore sequencing enables direct, bisulfite-free detection of native DNA methylation at single-read resolution, yet there exists a need for effective computational methods capable of leveraging read-level methylation for tissue-of-origin assignment. Epigenetic reference databases such as ENCODE chart the methylation patterns of different tissues, including sites with tissue-specific methylation signals which could theoretically be used to predict the tissue of origin of individual reads using methylation marks on those reads. Unlike bisulfite sequencing, which degrades DNA and introduces PCR amplification biases, nanopore sequencing directly reveals methylation signals for individual reads. We propose NanOrigin, a single-read classifier that scores individual reads against ENCODE reference methylomes to infer tissue-of-origin. Where bulk deconvolution methods obscure tissue contributions by averaging across millions of reads, NanOrigin infers tissue at single-read resolution. We evaluated the impact of nanopore read length on tissue assignment accuracy and found that reads longer than 2.5 kb could be consistently and accurately assigned to their tissue-of-origin, independent of genomic context. In contrast, reads shorter than 2.5 kb exhibited reduced reliability overall, but retained predictive power at loci with strong tissue-specific methylation signatures. We further assessed feature selection strategies and observed that excluding CpG sites with low variance across reference tissues improved classification performance, increasing the mean top-2 correlation margin without affecting overall tissue assignment rates. NanOrigin addresses the lack of single-read tissue classifiers for nanopore methylation data, enabling tissue-of-origin inference at a resolution beyond existing bulk deconvolution methods.

title: Differences in geneset signature scoring in immune-related prostate cancer genesets
authors: Ryan M. Putney, Moffitt Cancer Center, United States; Sean Yoder, Moffitt Cancer Center, United States; Brooke L. Fridley, Children's Mercy Kansas City, United States; Esther Katende, Moffitt Cancer Center, United States; Jong Park, Moffitt Cancer Center, United States; Kosj Yamoah, Moffitt Cancer Center, United States; Anders E. Berglund, Mayo Clinic Jacksonville, United States; Steven A. Eschrich, Moffitt Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Gene signatures are used in cancer-related transcriptomics studies as biomarkers of tumor activity. Curated genesets are summarized using approaches including principal component analysis (PCA) and single-sample geneset enrichment analysis (ssGSEA). Decipher GRID has profiled ~200,000 samples from prostate cancer patients using the Affymetrix Human Exon 1.0ST Array. We evaluated signature techniques among immune- related genesets within prostate cancer (GSE209954, N=113): INFG (N=198), 12CK-GES (N=12), ICS (N=259), and Macrophages (N=33). Scores were calculated using mean, z-score, PC1 (first component of geneset PCA), PC1_scaled (first component of scaled geneset PCA), ssGSEA (GSVA R/Bioconductor) and GSVA. Scores from different methods showed variation as measured by correlation coefficient from R=0.99 (e.g., PC1/PC1_scaled, PC1_scaled/Mean) to R=0.58 (PC1_scaled/GSVA). The ICS scores were least correlated and ICS was the largest geneset. Within the ICS geneset, the mean correlation among genes is lowest (R = 0.05) with 3.82% of gene pairings correlated (R>0.5) compared to 12CK-GES (n=12, 9.09% correlated), INFG (n=198, 10.74% correlated), and Macrophages (n=33, 16.67% correlated). Using the 12CK-GES (9% correlated), we evaluated gene-gene correlations in fresh-frozen RNA sequencing including TCGA PRAD (26% correlated) and TCGA LUAD (53% correlated). Geneset summarization techniques can lead to diverging gene scores within FFPE-based prostate cancer transcriptomics. The number of genes, correlation of genes within a geneset, and platform can lead to differences. Additionally, LUAD (immune-rich tumor environment) had more correlated pairs (53%) compared to the prostate cancer cohort (9%). Gene-gene correlations and empirical evaluation of gene covariance in a given disease/technology platform may be required for applicability of geneset summarization.

title: Assessing sex-based differential gene expression in placenta as a function of gestational age and cell type in single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data
authors: Kunal Kathuria, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), National Institutes of Health, United States; Guisong Wang, The Prospective Group, contractor for NICHD, National Institutes of Health, United States; Prabhavi Wijesiriwardhana, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), National Institutes of Health, United States; Tesfa Habtewold, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), National Institutes of Health, United States; Fasil Tekola-Ayele, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Sex differences in human traits are abundant and assessing these differences in the placenta is crucial to understanding early origins of later-life health outcomes. Our study maps gene expression as a function of sex for each placental cell type over the course of pregnancy to reveal patterns relevant to future health outcomes. We assembled 34 (19 male, 15 female) placenta samples from 5 different data providers totaling 79,257 single cells from early to late gestational age (GA) of pregnancy. Samples were processed in Seurat and differential gene expression (DGE) analysis was performed in edgeR in R from which we identify GA, cell and sex-dependent transcriptomic signatures. We found subpopulations within the cytotrophoblast (CTB)/syncytiotrophoblast (STB) and stromal cell types specific to late gestation and early gestation, and significant sex-based differences in these cell types in late pregnancy.
