title: MitoOmics: Subject-Level Mitochondrial Health Scoring from single-cell and circulating vesicle datasets
authors: Medha Bhattacharya, University of California, Irvine, United States; Seema Chandrakant Parte, Stanford University, United States; Hirenkumar Rajendra Patel, Stanford University, United States; Ankitkumar Maisuriya, Northeastern University, United States; Saion Chatterjee, Stanford University, United States; Bishnu Sarker, University of North Texas, United States; Sayane Shome, University of California San Francisco, United States
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction, including impaired energy production, altered mitophagy, disrupted mitochondrial dynamics, and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) instability, is a shared mechanism across cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders. However, integrative computational frameworks quantifying mitochondrial health at single-cell resolution across modalities (gene expression and protein abundance data) remain limited. We present MitoOmics, an open-source modular Python pipeline for computation at the subject-level Mitochondrial Health Index (MHI) from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and extracellular vesicle (EV)/mitochondria-derived vesicle (MDV) proteomics, using a modality-agnostic scoring architecture. MHI integrates four biologically interpretable components: transcriptional substitute for mtDNA abundance, fusion-fission balance (DNM1L, MFN1/2, OPA1), mitophagy activity (PINK1/PRKN/FUNDC1), and mitochondrial-state (Shannon entropy), annotated using MitoCarta 3.0. MitoOmics was evaluated in two independent datasets: a 73-subject breast cancer (BC) scRNA-seq cohort comprising 30,000 single cells, and a 491-sample multi-cancer EV proteomics dataset (PRIDE: PXD018301; 8,714 proteins). MHI captured subtype-specific mitochondrial differences, fusion-fission balance, and mitophagy as the strongest predictors (Pearson r = 0.936 and 0.926, respectively) of variance. Triple-negative BC exhibited the lowest mitochondrial fitness (median MHI = 0.255) versus invasive lobular carcinoma (median MHI = 0.497; padj MitoOmics quantifies MHI across diseases from scRNAseq, EV/MDV proteomics, enabling multi-omics integration, disease/patient stratification, and biomarker discovery for oncology, tumor immunology, and precision medicine.

title: Large-Scale Whole-Genome Landscape of Rare Diseases in 15K Koreans
authors: Yeonsu Jeon, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Dongyoon Lee, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jimin Ahn, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Seungrin Yang, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jong-Hwan Kim, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jongbum Jeon, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Jin Ok Yang, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea; Haeyoung Jeong, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, South Korea
abstract: Background: Rare diseases collectively affect millions worldwide, yet their genetic heterogeneity makes molecular diagnosis challenging. As the pilot phase of the National Genome Project in Korea, we performed large-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) on 15,004 individuals (6,868 rare disease probands and 8,136 family members) between 2020 and 2022 to build a comprehensive genomic resource and evaluate the clinical utility of WGS for rare disease diagnosis in Korea. Methods: After excluding consent-withdrawn participants, 14,905 samples (6,785 probands; 8,120 family members) were analyzed. Family-based trio analysis enabled systematic identification of de novo, compound heterozygous, and inherited variants. Variant pathogenicity was assessed by integrating multiple predictive frameworks, such as PolyPhen-2, SIFT, CADD, AlphaMissense, and InterVar, with population allele frequency filtering and ACMG/AMP classification. Results: A total of 460,582,345 variants were cataloged across the cohort, encompassing SNVs, indels, and structural variants. Neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders were the most prevalent disease categories, followed by tumor syndromes and cardiovascular diseases. Trio-based analysis identified a substantial number of de novo variants in probands, highlighting the critical value of family-based sequencing design. As an illustrative case, a proband presenting with global developmental delay (HP:0001263) received a precise molecular diagnosis through identification of a causative de novo variant, informing clinical management. Conclusion: This pilot phase of the National Genome Project demonstrates that large-scale, family-based WGS provides a powerful framework for rare disease variant discovery and molecular characterization. The 15K genome dataset constitutes a foundational resource for genomic medicine in Korea and addresses the underrepresentation of East Asian genomes in global databases. Subsequent phases will enroll an additional 30,000 patients, expanding precision medicine infrastructure in Korea.

title: GlyGen: Enabling Bidirectional Data Integration and Harmonization in Glycoscience
authors: Urnisha Bhuiyan, George Washington University, United States; Raja Mazumder, George Washington University, United States; Michael Tiemeyer, The University of Georgia, United States; Rene Ranzinger, The University of Georgia, United States
abstract: Glycosylation is one of the most prevalent forms of post-translational modification, which plays a critical role in diverse biological processes. As glycoscience advances, knowledge accumulates across the literature yet remains dispersed, limiting its accessibility and systematic analysis. Multiple specialized resources have captured complementary aspects of glycobiology, including standardized glycan identification (e.g., GlyTouCan), chemical composition and properties (e.g., PubChem and ChEBI), and glycan associations with proteins and disease (e.g., UniProtKB). GlyGen integrates data from these resources to harmonize knowledge on glycans and glycoconjugates and actively feeds curated and harmonized glycoscience data back to these platforms, creating an ecosystem based on bidirectional data exchange. Standardized glycan identifiers, glycoprotein associations, and glycosylation sites aggregated within GlyGen are shared with partner databases, enabling them to enhance their own records and web interfaces with enriched glycosylation content. GlyGen is also a member of the GlySpace Alliance, a partnership of major glycoscience data resources, including Glyco@Expasy (Switzerland) and GlyCosmos (Japan). This international effort aims to further harmonize glycoscience data by promoting standardized representation and shared frameworks for glycan and glycoconjugate data. With coordinated data integration and dissemination across all three platforms, the alliance enhances data interoperability and accessibility. Through partnerships such as the GlySpace Alliance and continued engagement with external resources and research groups, GlyGen not only aggregates and harmonizes complementary data but also returns curated, standardized annotations to its collaborators. This bidirectional exchange enables GlyGen to expand both the breadth and depth of its knowledgebase while simultaneously enriching partner resources with enhanced glycosylation-related information.

title: SlideCNA: spatial copy number alteration detection from Slide‑seq‑like spatial transcriptomics data
authors: Diane Zhang, Duke University, United States
abstract: Solid tumors are spatially heterogeneous in their genetic, molecular, and cellular composition, but recent spatial profiling studies have mostly charted genetic and RNA variation in tumors separately. To leverage the potential of RNA to identify copy number alterations (CNAs), we develop SlideCNA, a computational tool to extract CNA signals from sparse spatial transcriptomics data with near single cellular resolution. SlideCNA uses expression-aware spatial binning to overcome sparsity limitations while maintaining spatial signal to recover CNA patterns. We test SlideCNA on simulated and real Slide-seq data of (metastatic) breast cancer and demonstrate its potential for spatial subclone detection.

title: Glycan Image Extractor - A Tool for Semantic Extraction of Glycans from Manuscript Figures
authors: Nicole Mathias, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Campbell Ross, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Xinyu Hu, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Michelle Vesser, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Wenjin Zhang, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Nhat Duong, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Nathan Edwards, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: A significant amount of published glycobiology knowledge appears as glycan structure cartoons annotating experimental data, such as mass-spectra and chromatograms, in manuscript figures. This knowledge is inaccessible to text-mining, and is rarely recapitulated in tables or supplementary data. Furthermore, while stable accessions for glycan structures, based on the GlyTouCan registry, have been available for many years, these rarely appear in manuscripts. The Glycan Image Extractor (extractor.glyomics.org) finds and extracts semantic glycan structures from manuscript figures, providing IUPAC sequences with a GlyTouCan accession, if previously been registered, or a link to the GNOme structure browser (gnome.glyomics.org) to explore similar structures, if not. The Extractor automatically extracts figures from PDFs and subjects them to a YOLO-based deep-learning object registration pipeline that identifies glycans in each figure, and extracts semantic details of each cartoon - monosaccharides, glycosidic links, and reducing-end - in order to reconstruct the IUPAC sequence. The IUPAC sequence is then matched with registered structures (glylookup.glyomics.org) for the GlyTouCan accession. Despite a push to standardize glycan cartoons (SNFG), manuscript figures contain a substantial amount of variability in how glycan structure cartoons are drawn, something the fine-tuned YOLO-based deep-learning models cope with quite well. The Extractor also supports community annotation of glycobiology manuscripts to improve the tool by producing annotated PDFs readily corrected and fed back into the training infrastructure. We hope that the Glycan Image Extractor will ultimately be able to provide glycobiology knowledgebases such as GlyGen a reliable way to capture otherwise inaccessible glycan knowledge.

title: The ELITE Portal: Multi-omic Data Resources for Studying Exceptional Longevity and Healthy Aging
authors: Milan Vu, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Melissa Klein, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Jonathan Liaw-Gray, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Tanveer Talukdar, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Amelia Kallaher, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Christine Suver, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Susheel Varma, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United Kingdom; Solveig Sieberts, Sage Bionetworks, United States
abstract: Exceptional longevity (EL) is a rare phenotype characterized by an extended healthspan and sustained physiological function. Understanding the biological pathways and mechanisms underpinning protective genomic variants in EL can reveal therapeutic strategies for maintaining lifespan and healthspan, however this often requires the generation of large scale -omics data in rare EL populations. To empower the aging research community, we present the Exceptional Longevity Translational Resources (ELITE) Portal (eliteportal.synapse.org). The ELITE Portal is a centralized, National Institute on Aging (NIA)-funded open-access ecosystem designed to provide researchers with access to harmonized data from large-scale, longitudinal studies of healthy aging and longevity. Key datasets include integrated multi-omic profiling of deeply phenotyped human longitudinal cohorts such as the Long Life Family Study, the New England Centenarian Study and the Arivale Wellness Study; cross-species references enabling comparative biology approaches which can be used to understand conserved mechanisms contributing to species-related lifespan; and longevity-intervention models (mouse and cell lines/systems) which allow researchers to validate molecular response to longevity interventions. Tools include in-browser analytical explorers and chemoinformatics tools for real-time pathway visualisation; computational tools for data analysis; and interoperability with multiple cloud-based Trusted Research Environments. By adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles, the ELITE Portal lowers the barrier to complex translational research. We invite attendees to utilize these resources to uncover the molecular drivers of healthy aging and catalyze the translation of longevity discoveries into the next generation of geroscience interventions. Funded by NIA 5U24AG078753 and 2U24AG061340.

title: AI strategies for GlyGen
authors: Sujeet Kulkarni, The University of Georgia, United States; Michael Tiemeyer, The University of Georgia, United States; Raja Mazumder, The George Washington University, United States; Rene Ranzinger, The University of Georgia, United States
abstract: GlyGen is a glycoscience knowledgebase that integrates curated data on glycans, glycoproteins, diseases, and biomarkers, providing a unified platform to support discovery, analysis, and data-driven research in glycobiology. To enhance search capabilities, improve data availability, and support user interactions in glycoscience, GlyGen uses a variety of artificial intelligence based strategies: (1) To lower the barrier to searching for data in GlyGen, the AI Query Assistant uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to translate natural-language queries into JSON and retrieve relevant glycan and protein data. (2) GlyGen has also developed GlycoSiteMiner and GlycaNER, which use text-mining approaches to extract glycosylation site data from PubMed abstracts, thereby enriching the knowledgebase with additional data that was previously inaccessible. (3) To support the standardization and use of glycan names in literature-mining approaches, GlyGen has incorporated AI methods to extract glycan structure terms from publications and build the Glycan Structure Dictionary. (4) The Glycan Image Extractor uses deep learning models to extract and identify glycan structures from images and publications, facilitating knowledge extraction. (5) To support interoperability, reduce hallucinations, and improve the quality of LLM responses in interactions involving GlyGen data, a GlyGen Model Context Protocol (MCP) server has been implemented. (6) GlyGen is also developing a chatbot to support basic glycoscience research and answer related user queries. Together, these AI tools and features facilitate glycoscience data extraction, improve user interactions, and enhance data availability. Overall, GlyGen is successfully applying AI to further democratize glycoscience research and expand access to glycoscience data.

title: A Pareto-optimal framework for dissecting transcriptional heterogeneity across inflammatory bowel disease trajectories
authors: Danielle Pitlor, University of Pittsburgh, Department of Cellular andSystems Biology, United States; Rhonda Brand, University of Pittsburgh, Department of Medicine, United States; Beverley Moore, University of Pittsburgh, Department of Medicine, United States; Marc Schwartz, University of Pittsburgh, Department of Medicine, United States; Shikhar Uttam, University of Pittsburgh, Department of Cellular andSystems Biology, United States
abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) presents significant challenges for relapse prediction due to biological heterogeneity. Its remission also remains poorly characterized at gene and pathway levels, and its definition as a biologically distinct state, rather than partial restoration of healthy physiology or a reduced state of inflammation, is not fully established. To address these gaps, we have developed a pareto-optimal framework that leverages bulk RNA-seq data from Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's Disease patients across inflamed and remissive states, alongside healthy controls, to identify distinct biological mechanisms underlying IBD trajectory. We performed differential gene expression analysis stratified by disease subtype: Inflamed vs. Remission, Inflamed vs. Healthy Control, and Remission vs. Healthy Control. Candidate genes were filtered by stringent significance (âˆ’logâ‚â‚€(PADJ) â‰¥ 5) and effect size (logâ‚‚FC â‰¥ 5) and ranked by fold-change magnitude. Gene subsets were constructed through pareto-optimal scoring that jointly maximized sensitivity and specificity of predicting patient disease status via a diagonal dominance metric. Pareto-optimal framework was then extended to the pathway level by employing pathifier and paired significance testing. Key findings were validated at the protein level through cyclic immunofluorescence imaging. Our key results include identification of: 1. Novel IBD-associated genes and pathways that are sensitive and specific to IBD remission state as distinct from inflamed and healthy, 2. A hierarchical set of gene and pathway signatures that underlie relapse, and 3. How they are spatially organized. Details of our modeling and results will be discussed in our presentation.

title: Paired Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics to Dissect the Tumor Microenvironment Architecture of Cutaneous Melanoma
authors: Susanne Ibing, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Reta Birhanu Kitata, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Hyeyoon Kim, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Weiping Ma , Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Azra Krek, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Chelsea Newton, Van Andel Research Institute, United States; Meredith Freeman, Washington University School of Medicine, United States; Kristin Beaumont, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Tujin Shi, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Galen Hostetter, Van Andel Research Institute, United States; Paul Harms, University of Michigan-Ann Arbor, United States; Marcin P. Cieslik, University of Michigan-Ann Arbor, United States; Tao Liu, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, United States; Pei Wang, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Francesca Petralia, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States
abstract: Despite high tumor mutational burden and immune checkpoint inhibitor treatments improving outcomes in cutaneous melanoma, many patients exhibit primary or acquired resistance that cannot be explained by genomic features alone. Since bulk approaches lack spatial context of the tumor microenvironment (TME) architecture, we present an integrative analysis of paired spatial transcriptomics (ST) and unbiased spatial proteomics (SP) data from 10 melanoma samples. We used the 10x Genomics Visium HD platform and laser-capture microdissection (100 x 100 Âµm) coupled with mass spectrometry on closely spaced 10-Âµm thick FFPE slides. ST and SP were aligned by manual region of interest (ROI) mapping followed by correlation-based optimization. We performed Bayesian cellular deconvolution of proteomics spots using BayesDeBulk, incorporating ST-derived estimates as informative priors on cell type proportions. We then conducted differential abundance analyses across ROIs to characterize tumor cell-specific changes associated with the TME. Based on both ST and SP data, we focused on characterizing tumor-specific changes associated with cancer-associated fibroblast proximity. The median number of detected proteins was 3359 in immune regions, 3806 in stroma regions, and 3174 in tumor regions, enabling untargeted proteomic analysis across TME regions. By integrating spatial transcriptomics and proteomics data, we identified tumor-specific programs at both the gene and protein levels that are modulated by the TME. To our knowledge, this represents the first melanoma study to jointly analyze spatial transcriptomic and proteomic data, providing a framework to uncover spatially resolved tumor microenvironment interactions and tumor cell states not accessible through single modality or bulk analyses.

title: A Cross-Species Framework for Translating Human Addiction GWAS to Mouse Models
authors: Alyssa Klein, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Robyn L. Ball, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Ashley A. Auth, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Matthew W. Gerring, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Matthew J. Kim, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Vivek M. Philip, The Jackson Laboratory, United States; Elissa J. Chesler, The Jackson Laboratory, United States
abstract: Human genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified a growing number of risk variants for addiction-related behavioral processes, yet critical questions remain about what a variant does, where it acts, and how it influences biology. Mouse genetic studies offer a powerful complementary resource to functionally characterize these effects. We present a framework that harmonizes mouse genetic studies with human disease data to inform preclinical experimental design including strain background and assay choices. We developed a data-driven algorithm that ranks 657 inbred mouse strains by comparing imputed transcriptomes to disease-associated gene set scores, identifying strains as more vulnerable or resistant to a given disease. In global validation, the approach correctly predicted strain effects for 94.7% of diseases and 93.3% of rare diseases. Applying this to substance use disorder, we derived a candidate gene set from All of Us RVAS summary statistics using variant-to-gene mapping, then predicted vulnerability scores for Collaborative Cross strains. Predicted vulnerable strains exhibited significantly higher cocaine preference, locomotor reactivity, anxiety-related behavior, and impulsivity, confirming biological relevance. We developed a mouse-human GWAS meta-analysis approach that functionally characterizes human variant effects using mouse genetic and phenotypic data. Human and mouse GWAS meta-analyses converged on 30 orthologous addiction-associated genes, including PDE4B/Pde4b. Variants affecting Pde4b expression mediate withdrawal-related effects across multiple substances in mice, implicating it as a promising drug target. Integrated with thousands of mouse phenotypic studies in the Mouse Phenome Database, this framework moves beyond association to understand what a variant does, where it acts, and how it can be targeted.

title: Mutational Signature Activity at Non-canonical DNA Structures Across Cancer Types
authors: Damian Wojtowicz, University of Warsaw, Faculty of Mathematics, Informatics, and Mechanics, Poland; Zuzanna Milczarska, University of Warsaw, Faculty of Mathematics, Informatics, and Mechanics, Poland; Teresa Przytycka, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Cancer genomes accumulate a large number of somatic mutations over time from exposures to carcinogenic agents, cancer-related aberrations of DNA maintenance machinery, as well as imperfections of DNA processing during the normal cell cycle. Each of these processes leaves a distinctive footprint of mutations called a mutational signature. Computational methods such as non-negative matrix factorization have successfully identified numerous signatures from large-scale sequencing data, yet the mechanistic understanding of how genomic context shapes these mutational processes remains incomplete. Recent evidence suggests that both large-scale genomic features (GC content, chromatin structure, replication timing) and local elements (transcription factor binding sites, nucleosomes, DNA motifs) significantly modulate mutation rates and patterns. Non-canonical DNA conformations, such as Z-DNA (a left-handed helix), cruciforms, H-DNA (triplex structures), and G-quadruplexes, represent mutation-prone regions that may selectively interact with specific mutagenic processes. For example, APOBEC-induced mutations have been found to occur preferentially within cruciform loops â€“ suggesting that the relationship between non-canonical DNA structures and mutational signatures is both real and mechanistically informative. In this work, we interrogated whole-genome mutational profiles across several cancer types to systematically analyze the mutagenicity of potential non-B DNA motifs and their associations with mutational signatures. Using a statistical framework that controls for local sequence composition, we quantified signature-specific mutation enrichment at predicted non-canonical DNA loci and examined position-specific mutation patterns to better understand the implications of non-B DNA structures in cancer mutagenesis.

title: SigMatch: a transcriptome-based regression method for cross-disease drug repurposing
authors: Kewalin Samart, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Landon Buskirk, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Arjun Krishnan, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, United States; Janani Ravi, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University ofColorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States
abstract: Due to the rise of antibiotic resistance, infectious disease (InfD) treatment strategies are shifting toward host-directed therapeutics (HDTs) that complement antibiotics by modulating host responses. While computational drug repurposing has shown promise, these methods typically consider each disease in isolation and often overlook shared molecular mechanisms across diseases, such as the NF-ÎºB pathway, which plays a role in active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), autoimmune disorders, and cancer. This limitation hinders the discovery of potential HDT strategies for less-studied InfDs by leveraging evidence from better-studied non-infectious diseases (NInfDs). We present SigMatch, a novel regression method that leverages disease gene expression signatures to transfer mechanistic insights from NInfDs to InfDs through shared differential expression patterns. SigMatch selects a combination of disease signatures that best recapitulates a target disease signature using regression-based optimization. We evaluated SigMatch on ~2,400 disease signatures across ~550 diseases using a leave-one-disease-out framework and compared it to a disease ontology-based similarity baseline. Our analysis reveals key limitations in cross-disease modeling where tissue gene signatures are stronger predictors than disease. Moreover, performance varied substantially across diseases and disease systems in recovering known disease-disease associations, highlighting the modelâ€™s difficulty in extracting complex disease structures from heterogeneous differential expression data. To address this issue, we are now developing a tissue-aware model to better isolate disease-specific signals and improve interpretability. Together, this work provides a systematic analysis toward developing a regression method for understanding cross-disease relationships from transcriptional signatures, and outlines key directions for improving computational approaches to HDT discovery.

title: Multiomic analysis of therapeutic effects of HDAC inhibitors in DMD muscles
authors: Monica Nicolau, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, United States; Aimilia Skafida, Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca, Italy; Martina Sandonà, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Italy; Valentina Saccone, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Italy; Chiara Nicoletti, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, United States; Pier Lorenzo Puri, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, United States; Lucia Latella, Institute of Translational Pharmacology - Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, Italy
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a X-linked recessive genetic neuromuscular disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. Recently, the FDA-approved a histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi, Givinostat/Duvyzat) as the first non-steroidal pharmacological treatment for DMD patients. While the anti-fibrotic, anti-adipogenic, and anti-inflammatory effects have been demonstrated by previous studies, whether HDACi exert therapeutic effects on dystrophic myofibers and muscle stem cell (MuSC)-mediated regeneration remain currently unknown. In addition, previous studies revealed that beneficial effects are limited to early stages of disease progression in the DMD mouse model â€“ the mdx mice. To investigate the cell type-specific effects of HDACi on gene expression and chromatin accessibility at early and late stages of disease progression, we performed snRNA/snATAC multiomic sequencing. Integrated analysis of the multiomic data revealed pro-regenerative effects of HDACi on fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs), a muscle-resident mesenchymal cell population that can either support or hinder muscle regeneration. Furthermore, our analysis showed an HDACi-mediated increase in MuSCs and committed muscle progenitors, with a coherent increase in regenerating myonuclei in both young and old mdx mice. Interestingly, snATAC-seq analysis showed intermediate signatures of chromatin accessibility that could be amenable for future therapeutic interventions. Overall, this study reveals pro-regenerative properties of HDACi in DMD that support the long-term efficacy of HDACi-based treatments for DMD.

title: SurvStudio: a unified survival analysis platform integrating classical, machine learning, and deep learning models for right-censored data
authors: Jihye Park, Dankook university, South Korea; Seoyeon Youn, Dankook university, South Korea; Keunsoo Kang, Dankook university, South Korea
abstract: Survival analysis in translational and clinical research typically requires multiple disconnected tools — Kaplan-Meier estimation, Cox regression, machine learning model fitting, and result export are rarely integrated into a single reproducible environment. This fragmentation increases the risk of analytical inconsistency and limits throughput in research settings where reproducibility is critical. We developed SurvStudio, a local-first, GUI-based platform implemented in Python and JavaScript, designed to consolidate the full survival analysis workflow into a single executable environment. SurvStudio supports Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox proportional hazards regression, cohort summary tables, tree-based survival models, and representative deep learning models within one unified interface. The platform further provides exploratory biomarker grouping, approximate time-dependent variable importance summaries, partial dependence plots, and model-based counterfactual exploration. Bundled public cohorts, including TCGA LUAD and GBSG2, enable immediate demonstration and reproducible benchmarking without external data dependencies. SurvStudio runs locally on macOS and Linux (Ubuntu), with Windows support via WSL2, and is freely available at https://github.com/kangk1204/SurvStudio. SurvStudio delivers a reproducible, end-to-end workflow for exploratory and comparative survival analysis of single-event right-censored tabular cohorts. By unifying heterogeneous analytical steps — from descriptive statistics to interpretable deep learning — within a single local platform, SurvStudio reduces workflow fragmentation and supports manuscript-ready output, lowering the barrier to rigorous and reproducible survival analysis across biomedical research communities.

title: Discovering Genetic Biomarkers of Neuronal Vulnerability Using Post-Mortem Brain Datasets
authors: Xiaolin Zhou, University of Toronto, Canada; Daniel Kiss, University of Toronto; Centre for Addiction and MentalHealth, Canada; Isabel Kerrebijn, University of Toronto; Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute, Sinai Health, Canada; Shahrzad Ghazisaeidi, University of Toronto; Centre for Addiction and MentalHealth, Canada; Nicole Endresz, University of Toronto, Canada; Vanessa Gonçalves, University of Toronto; Centre for Addiction and MentalHealth, Canada; Yuliya Nikolova, University of Toronto; Centre for Addiction and MentalHealth, Canada; Shreejoy Tripathy, University of Toronto; Centre for Addiction and MentalHealth, Canada
abstract: Background Neuropsychiatric disorders are associated with brain cellular composition changes, including cortical neuron loss, such as somatostatin (SST) and parvalbumin (PVALB), in late-onset Alzheimerâ€™s disease (AD). This study aims to identify genetic factors influencing neuronal vulnerability and their links to neuropsychiatric traits. We hypothesize that different neuronal subtypes exhibit distinct genetic susceptibilities. Methods Using bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from the ROSMAP cohort (n=1,168), we estimated cell type proportions (CTPs) with the MarkerGeneProfile (MGP) method. We validated these CTP estimates against single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) data from the same individuals (n=334). We identified SNPs linked to variation in CTPs using genome-wide association study (GWAS) and meta-analysis across AMP-AD cohorts (n=1,501). Subsequently, we integrated significant SNPs into polygenic risk scores (PRS) to quantify individual genetic liability for neuronal susceptibility, followed by the validation with the ROSMAP and CommonMind (n=475) cohorts. Results GWAS meta-analysis identified 56 SNPs robustly associated with SST-CTP variability with the suggestive threshold of p Conclusion These findings highlight the genetic regulation of neuronal CTPs and show that SST interneurons, in particular, harbor distinct vulnerabilities partly governed by genetic factors. Further elucidating these genetic factors governing cell typesâ€“specific vulnerability may clarify disease onset and progression, guiding precision interventions.

title: DTWarp: Dynamic Time Warping Alignment for RNA and Protein Identifies Protein-Level Effectors of Epithelial-to-Mesenchymal Transition
authors: Ruohong Wang, Bioinformatics Program, Boston University, United States; Pawel Przytycki, Faculty of Computing & Data Sciences, Boston University; Bioinformatics Program, Boston University, United States
abstract: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a fundamental process in development and cancer metastasis, yet the protein-level effectors that execute this transition remain poorly characterized. Although transcriptomic profiling has identified gene expression programs associated with EMT, mRNA abundance is a limited predictor of protein levels, as studies report modest mRNA-protein correlations driven by variation in translation rates and protein turnover. Moreover, prior multi-omic analyses of EMT have not accounted for the temporal lag between transcript and protein accumulation, making it difficult to distinguish transcriptional responders from downstream protein effectors. To address this gap, we developed DTWarp, which uses soft-DTW to model the mRNA-to-protein temporal lag by aligning single-cell transcriptomic data to bulk proteomic time series, then applies quadratic programming to estimate per-cluster proteomic contributions. Soft-DTW considers multiple alignment paths rather than committing to a single optimal warp, accommodating timing uncertainty between modalities. We applied DTWarp to TGFb-stimulated MCF-10A epithelial cells profiled with bulk time-series transcriptomics, proteomics, and single-cell RNA-seq collected at shared timepoints but not paired at the cellular level. Across ten transcriptionally defined clusters, DTWarp nominated cluster-specific genes as candidate protein actuators. These candidates capture protein-level behavior rather than transcriptional timing, since the lag correction shifts the frame of reference from transcription to protein accumulation. We validated these candidates against an independent single-cell proteomics dataset from the same EMT system, confirming enrichment of candidate proteins in their predicted transition stages. These results suggest that modeling the mRNA-to-protein temporal lag reveals protein-level regulators of EMT otherwise invisible to temporally naive multi-omic analyses.

title: MARBLE: Multi-Agent Autonomous Refinement of Bioinformatics Models via Literature-Guided Exploration
authors: Sunghyun Kim, Department of AI Convergence, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Youngseo Yun, Department of AI Convergence, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Youngrak Lee, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Dongguk University,Seoul, South Korea; Sangsoo Lim, Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence,Dongguk University, Seoul,, South Korea
abstract: Developing high-performing bioinformatics models remains a labor-intensive process that requires iterative cycles of error analysis, literature review, and manual redesign. Although recent advances in AI-assisted coding have improved development efficiency, there is still a lack of principled frameworks that systematically link model-specific deficiencies to targeted methodological improvements grounded in scientific literature. We present MARBLE, an autonomous framework for iterative model refinement that integrates model diagnosis, literature-guided solution search, and structured memory. MARBLE identifies performance bottlenecks through explicit analysis of model behavior and formulates refinement as a sequential decision-making problem. It employs the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm to balance exploration of novel methodological directions with exploitation of previously successful refinement strategies. To enable efficient and non-redundant refinement, MARBLE maintains a graph-based memory that captures relationships among model deficiencies, applied modifications, and resulting performance changes. We evaluate MARBLE across diverse bioinformatics tasks, including spatial transcriptomics domain segmentation, cell type annotation, and drug response prediction. Across all tasks, MARBLE consistently improves model performance while maintaining stable and reproducible refinement trajectories. These results demonstrate that integrating architecture-aware reasoning, literature-guided exploration, and structured memory enables a systematic approach to the autonomous refinement of bioinformatics models.

title: CellposeCellCounter: A Fast and Free Automated Cell Counting and Viability Assessment Platform based on Cellpose-SAM segmentation models
authors: Matthew Yang, University of Maryland School of Medicine, United States; Yajie Liang, University of Maryland School of Medicine, United States
abstract: Accurate cell quantification underpins fundamental assays in biomedical research, including viability testing, proliferation analysis, and confluency measurement. Existing approaches â€” manual hemocytometry and commercial automated counters â€” remain either labor-intensive and subject to human variability, or financially inaccessible for resource-limited laboratories. We present CellposeCellCounter, an open-source, GPU-accelerated web platform hosted on Hugging Face Spaces that addresses these barriers through AI-driven image segmentation. The platform integrates custom segmentation models trained via human-in-the-loop machine learning, enabling iterative refinement on imaging conditions. User-adjustable thresholding provides automated cell counting alongside quantitative viability and confluency measurements without requiring local computational infrastructure. Model performance was rigorously evaluated using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing default Cellpose models against custom-trained counterparts across three segmentation metrics â€” Intersection over Union (IoU), Dice coefficient, and F1 score â€” on ten cell line datasets. Custom models demonstrated statistically significant improvements in 9 of 10 evaluated metrics. Automatic cell counts achieved near-perfect agreement with manual ground truth counts (RÂ² = 0.99), comparable to existing commercial and ML-based methods. CellposeCellCounter lowers technical and financial barriers to high-quality cell analysis by being entirely free, browser-accessible, and adaptable to diverse imaging modalities. Its modular architecture supports straightforward extension to new cell types, promoting reproducibility and scalability across the research community. These results establish CellposeCellCounter as a broadly applicable tool for any laboratory conducting cell-based research, with direct relevance to high-throughput screening, drug discovery, and clinical cell biology workflows.

title: A Public Genomic Resource of 8,266 SARS-CoV-2 Assemblies from Asymptomatic Carriers in Japan
authors: Hajime Ohyanagi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Junko S. Takeuchi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Yuichi Kawanishi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Saya Ohi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Teiichiro Shiino, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Moto Kimura, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Yusuke Takahashi, Health Sciences University of Hokkaido, Japan; Shigeru Yoshida, Health Sciences University of Hokkaido, Japan; Minoru Kato, SB Coronavirus Inspection Center Corp., Japan; Yukumasa Kazuyama, SB Coronavirus Inspection Center Corp., Japan; Masato Ikeda, SB Coronavirus Inspection Center Corp., Japan; Wataru Sugiura, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan
abstract: Asymptomatic carriers are a hidden but important source of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, yet genomic resources derived specifically from asymptomatic populations remain limited. We generated and released a large-scale SARS-CoV-2 genomic dataset from asymptomatic individuals tested at the SB Coronavirus Inspection Center Corp., a commercial screening facility in Japan. Between July 27, 2020 and January 16, 2023, 4,573,575 saliva samples from individuals without reported symptoms were screened by RT-qPCR, yielding 18,475 SARS-CoV-2-positive cases. Residual positive saliva specimens were subjected to whole-genome sequencing using the Illumina COVIDSeq workflow, followed by consensus assembly and lineage analysis. In total, 8,266 SARS-CoV-2 genome assemblies were successfully generated, including 2,917 near-complete genomes of at least 29,000 nucleotides. These assemblies captured major epidemic waves in Japan, including periods dominated by Alpha, Delta, and Omicron sublineages BA.1, BA.2, and BA.5. The lineage distribution in the asymptomatic dataset was broadly comparable to that of domestic Japanese sequences deposited in GISAID, supporting the representativeness of the sampling and sequencing workflow. Technical validation further confirmed the utility of the dataset for allele-level analysis, including assessment of the co-occurring nucleocapsid mutations R203K/G204R. All raw sequencing reads and consensus genome assemblies have been deposited in public repositories through DDBJ/INSDC, with assemblies also submitted to GISAID. By focusing on individuals without reported symptoms, this study complements conventional surveillance datasets. It provides a unique public resource for investigating SARS-CoV-2 genomic diversity in asymptomatic infections and for future studies on viral epidemiology, fitness, and symptom-associated genomic features.

title: Mining higher-order protein oligomers from super-resolution microscopy data using optimal transport
authors: Luis Wyss, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Germany; Till Schulz, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Germany; Rafal Kowalewski, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Germany; Luciano Masullo, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, IBYME, Argentina; Megan Joseph, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Germany; Ralf Jungmann, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Germany; Karsten Borgwardt, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Germany
abstract: Super-resolution microscopy methods image cell surfaces down to the resolution of individual membrane proteins. These data hold enormous promise for the discovery of novel spatial biomarkers and for our understanding of immune and disease signalling. However, the interpretation of these data is hampered by a lack of suitable algorithms. Notably, both the reliable detection and discovery of protein oligomers beyond dimerisation remain largely unsolved. We propose the first pattern mining approach identifying protein complexes in super-resolution microscopy data. Our method operates directly on the protein point clouds and consists of three steps, starting with frequent-multiset mining to detect frequent protein colocalisations. This is followed by a pairwise distance computation step, where we follow an optimal transport approach to compute adapted Gromov-Wasserstein distances, thereby comparing the spatial arrangement of compositionally similar protein colocalisation events. Lastly, we perform distance based clustering to identify common spatial arrangements in our data, which we hypothesize to represent frequently observed oligomeric states. We validate our method on both in silico generations and microscopy data from DNA-origami and cellular samples. Our method successfully recovers known protein oligomers in different settings and we show that it is able to recover larger oligomers up to hexamers. Unlike existing models, it does not require knowledge about expected protein oligomerisation states. Our method opens up the spatial dimension of proteomics data to biomarker discovery.

title: Improving kinase enrichment analysis with predicted kinases of phosphorylation sites and an interactive kinase centric network explorer
authors: Manju Anandakrishnan, University of Delaware, United States; Chuming Chen, University of Delaware, United States; Karen Ross, Georgetown University Medical Center, United States; Vijay-Shanker K, University of Delaware, United States; Cathy Wu, University of Delaware, United States
abstract: Protein kinases regulate many signaling cascades and crucial cellular processes via phosphorylation. To infer aberrant kinase activities from phosphoproteomics data, kinase enrichment analysis methods use kinase-substrate associations. However, less than 7% of human phosphorylation sites have annotated kinases, thereby significantly limiting the available data for kinase enrichment. Therefore, we investigate the capability of kinase-substrate associations derived from computational tools and in vitro studies to improve the ability to accurately infer enriched kinases. We compile kinase-substrate libraries by supplementing the curated kinases of substrates with computationally predicted associations and evaluate the libraries using a previously compiled benchmark kinase perturbation dataset. Our results indicate that supplementing the available knowledge with high quality kinase-substrate predictions improves the ability to identify the perturbed kinase(s). Particularly, accurate inference of certain serine/threonine kinase families improve with predictions based on both cellular context of proteins and sequence context of phosphorylation sites. Further, we present a web application to conduct kinase enrichment analysis with a novel feature that enables exploration of common biological links between (1) the enriched kinase(s) and differentially phosphorylated proteins in an experiment, and (2) a predicted kinase and its substrate protein. Besides quantitative measures, the kinase-centric network exploration feature will allow researchers to gain insights into the biological mechanisms affecting condition states of interest. The application allows use of one of the compiled kinase-substrate libraries or userâ€™s custom library.

title: Principal Genes: A PCA-based approach to highly variable genes selection for scRNA-Seq analysis
authors: Enos Kakwambi, University of Oklahoma, United States; Tuan Nguyen, University of Oklahoma, United States; Suryaveer Kapoor, University of Oklahoma, United States; Marmar Moussa, University of Oklahoma, United States
abstract: Motivation: Single Cell RNA-Seq workflows have a gene selection step prior to clustering which helps remove low variability genes and reduce high-dimensional gene space. A de-facto method for selection of highly variable genes (HVG) uses dispersion and mean expression scores to evaluate individual gene variability. However, methods based on mean- to-variance for gene selection suffer from susceptibility to variance instability and arbitrary determination of optimal number of genes to use. Results: Here, we propose an innovative method for selecting highly variable genes not based on mean-to-variance approach: â€Principal Genes (PG)â€; utilizing rotations (loadings) from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to calculate a novel variability gene score: â€Gene Principal Score (GPS)â€. GPS evaluates genes based on their contribution in PCA rotations and hence ranks genes according to their variability from highest to lowest. For efficient implementation we utilize Augmented Implicitly Restarted Lanczos Bidiagonalization to obtain Principal Components (PCs) associated with the largest variance. Genes with highest GPS, i.e. Principal Genes, can then be used downstream, especially for clustering. We use several validation strategies, including clustering of labeled data (i.e. data with known â€™ground truthâ€™ cell types). Furthermore, we measure our performance against dispersion-based highly variable gene (HVG) approach using sensitivity and adjusted rand index for clustering based on genes selected using PG vs. HVG; our validation datasets include five real labeled scRNA-Seq datasets. Our findings show Principal Genes is often superior in selecting highly variable genes, furthermore achieves ultra-fast gene selection from PCA results. Availability:https://github.com/moussa-lab/PrincipalGenes Contact: marmar.moussa@ou.edu.

title: Alignment Metadata Leakage Enables Re-identification and Variant Calling in Secure Read Mapping Pipelines
authors: Navid Bin Hasan, Computational Biology Department, Carnegie Mellon University, United States; Yun William Yu, Computational Biology Department, Carnegie Mellon University, United States
abstract: As increasing amounts of genomic data are collected, more data analyses have been outsourced to the cloud. However, this raises severe privacy concerns, as genomic data are inherently sensitive, immutable, and uniquely identifying. Thus, a nascent but promising line of research is the development of cryptographic methods for secure genomic computation, but implementation is tricky to get right, and even seemingly small metadata leaks can be harmful. To wit, Zhao et al. (2018) proposed a hybrid-cloud solution to securely align short reads to a reference genome. Their bespoke alignment pipeline operates on encrypted representations of read and reference sequences. The public cloud server, which is deemed the adversary, accesses only these encrypted representations and returns CIGAR-like alignment results with encrypted supporting metadata, while underlying sequence and positional information remain hidden. However, despite these measures, we demonstrate that their method remains vulnerable. In particular, we show that the output CIGARs leak sufficient donor-specific information to enable inference attacks under realistic sequencing settings, across varying read lengths and coverages. We construct distinctive signatures from informative patterns within the CIGARs and compare them using set-similarity and containment measures. Across short reads ranging from 100 to 250 bp, our method achieves perfect re-identification in 78% of cases, reaching 100% perfect re-identification for 250 bp reads. Moreover, a substantial degree of variant calling is possible from the leaked information. Our results suggest that hiding sequence information alone is insufficient for secure read mapping and that alignment-derived metadata must also be considered sensitive.

title: SynFit: Synergistic Contrastive Learning for Multi-Objective Protein Fitness Prediction and Optimization
authors: Tony Tu, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Wei Huang, University of California Santa Barbara, United States; Ziang Li, Georgia Institute Of Technology, United States; Kerr Ding, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Yang Yang, University of California Santa Barbara, United States; Yunan Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Proteins function through a complex interplay of structural and biochemical properties, and mutations can reshape these properties to generate fitness landscapes spanning multiple functional objectives. A central challenge in protein engineering is the need to simultaneously optimize multiple properties. In biocatalysis, for example, practical enzyme development routinely requires the concurrent optimization of catalytic activity, selectivity, stability, and substrate generality. However, despite recent advances in computational protein design and fitness prediction, most existing approaches treat these properties independently and do not explicitly capture the dependencies and trade-offs that govern real-world protein performance. We present SynFit, a multi-objective learning framework that integrates pretrained protein language models with experimental fitness measurements for protein fitness prediction and engineering. SynFit learns both shared and property-specific protein sequence representations through a synergistic contrastive learning strategy, enabling the identification of variants that simultaneously optimize multiple functional properties. Across a large-scale multi-fitness deep mutational scanning benchmark, SynFit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised models trained on individual objectives and more accurately identifies variants that balance competing functional constraints. We further applied SynFit to multi-objective enzyme design for a new-to-nature biocatalytic enantioselective borylation reaction, providing a diverse array of novel cytochrome c sextuple variants in a single round of design with simultaneously improved catalytic activity and enantioselectivity that rival the best variants obtained through directed evolution. Together, these results establish SynFit as a general framework for multidimensional protein fitness prediction and highlight its potential to enable efficient multi-objective optimization in protein engineering, particularly in biocatalysis.

title: Accurate inversion-aware alignment reveals increased divergence between closely-related human haplotypes
authors: Harun Mustafa, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Hyun Joo Ji, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Celine Hoh, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Nika Mansouri Ghiasi, ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Steven Salzberg, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: A commonly-cited statistic is that human genomes are, on average, 99.6% identical, or 99.923% when only considering single-nucleotide variants. These are traditionally estimated by measuring average distances between variant calls from mapped high-throughput sequencing reads. However, standard read mapping approaches overestimate these values since they discard large segments or entire reads of DNA fragments originating from structurally-complex genomic regions. For complete genome assemblies, optimal global alignment of whole chromosomes can be more precise and comprehensive, but can potentially underestimate identity because it does not model inversion mutations. Incorporating inversions into optimal algorithms results in a worst-case O(dn^3) time complexity (where d is the sequence dissimilarity), necessitating approximate seed-chain-extend approaches that find long exact matches and connect them using global alignment. However, existing inversion-aware approximate tools do not compute alignments between seeds of opposite orientation, and thus fail to compute precise inversion breakpoints. We introduce a seed-chain-extend approach featuring a novel bi-directional global alignment algorithm that incorporates inversions, computing nucleotide-level inversion breakpoints. Our algorithm finds the optimal breakpoint between seeds of opposite orientation via alternating iterative alignment steps that traverse inwards from opposite ends. Using our algorithm, we determined that the two closely-related haplotypes from the recently-completed HG002 diploid assembly are >1% more divergent than previous reports, 98.42% identity compared to 99.6%. When only considering single-nucleotide or short (

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Comprehensive Assessment of Sequence-Derived Features for Predicting SUMOylation Sites
authors: Junyan Li, Howard University, United States; Shaolei Teng, Howard University, United States
abstract: SUMOylation is a common post-translational modification that can change protein stability, localization, and interaction networks. However, predicting SUMOylation sites from sequence remains challenging because many true sites do not follow a strict consensus motif and local context can strongly influence modification. In this study, we systematically evaluated sequence-derived physicochemical features for SUMOylation-site prediction using AAindex-based descriptors. We constructed a dataset comprising 5,888 experimentally verified SUMOylated lysines and 415,918 non-SUMOylated lysines from 176 human proteins collected from dbPTM and UniProt. For each candidate lysine in SUMOylated proteins, we generated lysine-centered windows of multiple lengths and encoded each window with 566 AAindex properties. We first ranked individual AAindex features using single-feature XGBoost performance on the full dataset, then assembled top-N feature subsets and benchmarked several classifiers (logistic regression, SVM, random forest, and XGBoost) across window sizes. Based on these results, we trained a XGBoost model and a stacked ensemble (XGBoost + random forest + logistic regression with a logistic regression meta-learner) using a balanced training subset and evaluated both models on an external independent dataset (EMSID: EMS60105). The best setting used an 11 (Â±5 from center lysines)-residue window and ~350 top-ranked features. Under this configuration, the stacked ensemble achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9426 on the test set, substantially outperforming the best single model. Motif-level analysis confirmed the presence of the canonical Î¨-K-x-E consensus, but the strongest predictive signals arose from flexible, coil-promoting sequence regions flanking the lysine. Overall, our results show that rich physicochemical encoding combined with stacking can markedly improve SUMOylation-site prediction and helps highlight property patterns that are most informative around SUMOlyated lysines.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Inferring Compartment-Level Gene Expression from Histology via Adaptive Spatial Graph Neural Networks
authors: Tianci Song, Yale University, United States; Jonathan Warrell, Yale University; NEC Labs America, United States; Eric Cosatto, NEC Labs America, United States; Lajos Pusztai, Yale University, United States; David Klimstra, Yale University, United States; David Rimm, Yale University, United States; Mark Gerstein, Yale University, United States; Thazin Aung, Yale University, United States
abstract: Characterizing gene expression at the cell-type compartment level is critical for understanding tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental organization in cancer, where distinct regions exhibit different molecular programs that drive disease progression and therapeutic response. However, obtaining compartment-specific expression remains costly and technically challenging. We present the Adaptive Spatial Compartment Graph Neural Network (ascGNN), an extension of our prior Adaptive Spatial Graph Neural Network (asGNN), that infers compartment-level gene expression from histological images using spatial transcriptomics (ST) data generated by Digital Spatial Profiling (DSP). We formulate this task within a graph neural network framework, where nodes correspond to cell-type compartments within randomly cropped hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) image patches. Our compartment-aware architecture incorporates nuclei-level information to infer compartment identity and learn compartment-specific adaptive spatial graphs. In a neoadjuvant breast cancer cohort treated with anti-PD-L1, we built a three-compartment model, including lymphocyte, macrophage, and neoplastic compartments. Despite the absence of direct DSP supervision, ascGNN achieves better agreement with ground truth on ST data (average PCC = 0.363 vs. 0.307) and improves treatment outcome prediction (AUC = 0.75 vs. 0.67, p-value = 0.01). With the increasing availability of ST data at the compartment and single-cell levels, we further extend the framework to leverage paired H&E images and ST data, using nodes within defined regions of interest (ROIs) as supervision anchors. Associated bulk expression can also be incorporated as complementary supervision to regularize the learning. We perform cross-validation on ST datasets and conduct downstream analyses to systematically evaluate the benefits of the proposed training strategy.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Alignment of Spatial Multiomics with Riemannian Metric Learning
authors: Peter Halmos, Princeton University, United States; Yufan Xia, Princeton University, United States; Benjamin Raphael, Princeton University, United States
abstract: Recent spatial technologies measure the transcriptome, epigenome, proteome, metabolome, and other modalities from thousands of cells across a tissue. Most assays typically profile only one modality from a tissue slice, raising the question of how to align spatial data from heterogeneous feature spaces. While multiple approaches have been developed for multi-modal integration of single-cell datasets, few existing techniques perform spatial alignment across arbitrary modalities incorporating both spatial and feature information. We introduce Manifold Gromov-Wasserstein (MGW), a metric-learning framework that exploits the product structure of spatial multiomics to infer modality-specific Riemannian pull-back metrics with neural fields. MGW aligns Riemannian distances induced by these metrics via Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, yielding a hyperparameter-free cost across arbitrary modalities sharing a spatial base. The formulation enjoys theoretical invariances including orthogonal transformations of the spatial and feature domains as well as global feature scalings. We demonstrate the advantages of MGW on multiple alignment tasks, including Stereo-Seq spatiotemporal transcriptomics of mouse embryo, Xenium and Visium spatial transcriptomics of colorectal cancer, and spatial metabolomics-transcriptomics from human striatum and kidney cancer. MGW recovers biologically meaningful correspondences and spatially coherent tissue structures, outperforming existing OT and non-OT based multi-modal baselines.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: From gene expression to disease mechanisms: the largest atlas of genetically-integrated transcriptomic programs
authors: Marc Subirana Granés, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Haoyu Zhang, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Sutanu Nandi, Department of Pharmacology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States; Maria Chikina, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA, United States; Milton Pividori, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA, United States
abstract: Current mechanistic, multigenic models of complex diseases, such as the omnigenic and stratagenic models, suggest that genetic risk propagates through interconnected regulatory networks spanning multiple molecular levels. This multi-layered architecture motivates 1) a shift beyond single-gene associations toward coordinated gene modules that capture gene-gene interactions and 2) the integration of omics data to understand complex phenotypes. Gene modules, groups of co-expressed genes, address both needs by capturing gene-gene interactions while enabling integration across omics modalities. However, no existing method learns interpretable modules at the scale of modern bulk RNA-seq compendia while jointly integrating genetic association data. Here we present CLAMP (Curated Latent-variable Analysis with Molecular Priors), a semi-NMF framework comprising an unsupervised baseline (CLAMPbase) and a prior-informed variant (CLAMPfull) that incorporates pathway knowledge, designed to construct the largest genetically-integrated atlas of transcriptomic programs from bulk RNA-seq. We evaluated CLAMP on two contrasting datasets: GTEx, a small homogeneous cohort, and ARCHS4, the largest public bulk RNA-seq resource (~600,000 samples). On GTEx, CLAMPfull achieved the highest tissue separability across state-of-the-art methods, with pathway priors improving performance over CLAMPbase. To test whether gene modules captured disease-relevant biology, we trained random forests that identified tissue-discriminating modules enriched for pathways and UK Biobank traits consistent with the tissues they separated. We then tested whether CLAMP could scale to nearly all publicly available bulk RNA-seq data while still yielding disease-relevant mechanisms. Integrating learned modules with GWAS and drug-induced transcriptional profiles from LINCS L1000, we found clear convergence between tissue, trait, and drug signatures at the module level. Orthogonal validation confirmed recovery of CRISPR-validated lipid regulatory programs and known drug-disease relationships. Together, these results establish CLAMP as a scalable framework for bridging gene expression, genetic risk, and therapeutic mechanisms.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking DNA Foundation Models for Sequence-Based DNA Methylation Prediction
authors: Nishan Khatri, Old Dominion University, United States; Jiangwen Sun, Old Dominion University, United States
abstract: DNA methylation is a fundamental epigenetic mechanism that regulates gene expression and cellular identity, with broad implications in development and disease. Because DNA methylation is influenced by genomic sequence context, machine learning models can, in principle, predict methylation directly from sequence. Several approaches have been proposed, including supervised convolutional neural networkâ€“based models such as CpGenie and DeepCpG. However, predictive performance remains limited, likely due to complex regulatory dependencies spanning long genomic distances. Recent advances in large-scale DNA foundation models have shown strong potential across functional genomic tasks. Despite this progress, a comprehensive evaluation of these models for DNA methylation prediction is still lacking. In this study, we address this gap by benchmarking recently developed DNA foundation models using methylation datasets from NCBI GEO and ENCODE, with DeepCpG as a baseline. The evaluated models include Caduceus, JanusDNA, Nucleotide Transformer (v2/v3), DNABERT-2, GENA-LM, and Evo2. We adopt a zero-shot framework, extracting sequence embeddings from pre-trained models and using them as input to a multi-layer perceptron for methylation prediction. We also examine the impact of sequence context length, varying inputs from 1,001 to 16,001 bp. Our results show that embedding-based approaches achieve strong performance and consistently outperform DeepCpG. The best-performing model, Caduceus, achieves a mean ROC-AUC of 0.9474 Â± 0.0070 and an F1 score of 0.7729 Â± 0.0202 at 16,001 bp. Performance improves with longer context, highlighting the importance of long-range regulatory information. Overall, these findings demonstrate the effectiveness of DNA foundation models for methylation prediction and their potential in epigenomic analysis.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: mRNABench: A curated benchmark for mature mRNA property and function prediction
authors: Ruian Shi, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Taykhoom Dalal, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Philip Fradkin, University of Toronto, Canada; Divya Koyyalagunta, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Simran Chhabria, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Andrew Jung, University of Toronto, Canada; Cyrus Tam, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Defne Ceyhan, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Jessica Lin, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Kaitlin Laverty, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Canada; Ilyes Baali, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Bo Wang, University of Toronto, Canada; Quaid Morris, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is central to gene expression, and its half-life, localization, and translation efficiency drive phenotypic diversity in eukaryotic cells. While supervised learning has been used to study the mRNA regulatory code, self-supervised foundation models support a wider range of transfer learning tasks. However, the dearth of standardized benchmarks limits efforts to pinpoint the strengths of various models. Here, we present mRNABench, a benchmarking suite for mature mRNA biology, focused on human transcripts, that evaluates the representational quality of mature mRNA embeddings from self-supervised nucleotide foundation models. We curate 11 datasets and 79 prediction tasks that broadly capture salient properties of mature mRNA, and assess the performance of 24 families of nucleotide foundation models for a total of 259k experiments. Using these experiments, we study parameter scaling, correlations between sequence compressibility and performance, and data-splitting strategies. We identify synergies between two self-supervised learning objectives, and pre-train a new Mamba-based model that achieves state-of-the-art performance using ~700 fewer parameters. mRNABench can be found at: https://github.com/morrislab/mRNABench.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Investigating Host-Range Determinants of Flaviviruses Using Foundation Model Embeddings: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation Framework
authors: Brhanu Fentaw Znabu, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, United States; Nicole Sexton, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, United States; Qiuming Yao, University of Nebraska Lincoln, United States
abstract: Arboviruses in the genus Orthoflavivirus cause substantial global morbidity, yet insect-specific flaviviruses (ISFVs) within the same genus cannot infect vertebrates. Machine learning approaches to viral host prediction have been developed, but whether previous models reflect true biological signal or evaluation leakage from closely related genomes in training and test sets has not been tested. We developed a leakage-aware evaluation framework and applied it to three feature representations (DNABERT-2 foundation model embeddings, k-mer TF-IDF, and nucleotide composition) to quantify how much evaluation leakage contributes to reported accuracy in orthoflavivirus host prediction. Complete genomes (n = 3,031; 2,816 arboviruses, 215 ISFVs) were segmented into overlapping 1-kb windows (n = 59,980) and classified under progressively stringent grouped cross-validation. All methods achieved high average precision (AP) under accession-grouped evaluation (AP = 0.981, 0.997, and 0.928, respectively) but showed consistent decline under species-grouped evaluation (AP = 0.819, 0.858, and 0.834), confirming that evaluation leakage inflates accuracy regardless of feature type. track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Batch-aware integrative analysis of transcriptomic data from a rare disease
authors: Orion Banks, Sage Bionetworks, United States; Jineta Banerjee, Sage Bionetworks, 2901 3rd Ave #330, Seattle, WA 98121, United States
abstract: High dimensional data analysis often relies on integrating multiple datasets to derive enough power for sophisticated computational methods. While several tools are available to correct for systematic variation between independent sample sets, traditional batch correction methods can mask real variation. In the study of rare disease, where low prevalence and small patient cohort sizes necessitate data integration, batch-aware analysis may allow researchers to preserve biological signals and identify biomarkers more readily. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a rare disease that predisposes individuals to developing several tumor types, including plexiform neurofibroma and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. While genomics data from NF1 patients has identified relevant biomarkers for different manifestations, the processes underlying disease trajectory are not fully understood. A well-defined mechanism of how NF1 leads to distinct, potentially aggressive tumors may reveal novel therapeutic targets. To assist in our processing of bulk RNA-seq data from patients with manifestations of NF1, we designed a batch-aware computational pipeline that accepts gene expression counts and converts them to lower-dimensional embeddings. We applied the tensor decomposition technique PARAFAC2 to normalized and scaled counts from four sample batches. PARAFAC2 embeddings were compared to PCA of the uncorrected as well as traditionally batch corrected dataset. We found that PARAFAC2 embeddings produced resolved sample clusters across several pre-processing strategies and showed similar levels of explained variability as same-rank PCA. Importantly, while PCA applied to data without batch correction shows non-biological clustering, PARAFAC2 embeddings for data that was not batch corrected produce clusters aligned with diagnosis labels.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Region-Guided Adversarial Learning for Anatomically Consistent Segmentation of Hippocampal Subregions
authors: Sayed Mehedi Azim, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States; Brian Corbett, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States; Iman Dehzangi, Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Rutgers University, Camden, NJ, USA, United States
abstract: Accurate delineation of anatomically distinct regions from hippocampal tissue images is essential for enabling large-scale quantitative analysis in neuroscience and advancing our understanding of disease mechanisms, developmental dynamics, and therapeutic interventions. The hippocampus, comprising the dentate gyrus (DG), Cornu Ammonis 1 (CA1), and Cornu Ammonis 3 (CA3) subregions, presents significant challenges for automated segmentation due to irregular morphology, diffuse boundaries, and variability across staining modalities in immunohistochemistry (IHC) imaging. Despite the importance of region-specific analysis of the hippocampus, no publicly available datasets or established benchmarks exist for automated segmentation of hippocampal subregions from fluorescent IHC images. To address these limitations, we introduce ROIsGAN, a region-guided generative adversarial framework for anatomically consistent segmentation of hippocampal subregions. The proposed method employs a U-Net-based generator and a spatially aware discriminator that produces pixel-wise realism maps, enabling dense structural feedback. A region-guided adversarial objective integrates Dice-based overlap supervision with binary cross-entropy, explicitly enforcing spatial alignment and improving boundary delineation during training. In addition, we curate a murine hippocampal IHC dataset comprising 1,558 images with expert-annotated subregion masks across multiple staining protocols, including cFos, NeuN, and multiplexed combinations with Î”FosB or GAD67, capturing complementary structural and functional signals. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that ROIsGAN consistently outperforms established architectures, achieving up to 10% gains in Dice and substantial reductions in boundary error metrics, including Hausdorff distance and average symmetric surface distance. These results highlight the importance of region-guided adversarial supervision for anatomically consistent segmentation and establish a foundation for structure-aware analysis of complex biomedical imaging data.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Systematic discovery of robust gene expression marker sets for endothelial cell subtypes
authors: Daniel Pintard, National Library of Medicine/National Institutes of Health, United States; Ajith Viswanathan Asari Pankajam, National Library of Medicine/ National Institutes of Health, United States; Bingfang Xu, National Library of Medicine/ National Institutes of Health, United States; Yun Zhang, National Library of Medicine/ National Institutes of Health, United States; Richard Scheuermann, National Library of Medicine/ National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Endothelial cells compose the lining of blood vessels and lymphatics in the lung and other tissues, playing important roles in homeostasis and repair of these systems following injury or disease. Endothelial cells display considerable heterogeneity in function and gene expression profiles, which is reflected by the variety of diseases and complications associated with this population of cells, such as pulmonary hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and more. Many single cell transcriptomic studies focused on endothelial cell types within the lung have been published, with the aim of grasping an understanding of the heterogeneity of these cell type populations. A common challenge in single cell transcriptomic data analysis is identifying marker gene sets that can robustly identify cell types across different studies with high specificity. Here we present a method for systematic evaluation of gene marker sets applied to endothelial cell types. Using NS-Forest v4.1, we define global, local, class, and combined markers and assessed their performance in identifying endothelial cell types across an array of studies. Global markers are obtained from the entire (â€˜globalâ€™) dataset. Local markers are sourced from a subset of the data, in this case, closely related endothelial subtypes. Class markers are obtained from the local data being grouped into an individual class amongst all other cell types in the global data.
