When class-level and local markers are combined, improved precision in delineating endothelial cell types within their class and delineating them from all other cell types in the global data was obtained.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Predicting Accessible Chromatin Regions in Plants using Co-linear Chaining and Machine Learning
authors: Madelyn Warr, University of Utah, United States; Trung Dinh, University of North Florida, United States; Bella Root, National Center for Genome Resources, United States; Elyse Onstott, National Center for Genome Resources, United States; Kevin Yu, Tufts University, United States; Joann Mudge, National Center for Genome Resources, United States; Thiruvarangan Ramaraj, DePaul University, United States; Indika Kahanda, University of North Florida, United States; Brendan Mumey, Montana State University, United States
abstract: Accessible Chromatin Regions (ACRs) are DNA regions accessible to regulatory proteins. Identifying ACRs is an important problem in bioinformatics because many genetic variants associated with phenotypes fall within them. However, determining ACR regions in the wet lab can be quite expensive. In this work, we investigate whether conserved short patterns of DNA sequences (motifs) can be used to computationally predict ACRs in a genome. We focus on plants because of their agricultural and ecological importance and because their complex genomes provide important stress tests for our algorithm. We show that regulatory motif sequence similarity can be efficiently detected using co-linear chaining, a method that forms a chain between two sequences, where each link corresponds to a motif present in both sequences in the order of appearance. The resulting similarity scores from co-linear chaining are used as input features for machine learning models to explore the feasibility of effectively predicting ACRs in genome assemblies. Here, we formulate the ACR prediction as a binary classification task and train traditional machine learning models such as multi-layer perceptrons. Our experimental results on 23,516 curated ACR regions from Arabidopsis thaliana (A. thaliana), a model plant organism, indicate that colinear-chaining features are promising for distinguishing ACR from non-ACR regions (AUROC values of 0.7+). In the future, we plan to expand to other plant species and use predicted ACRs to identify phenotypes. This study has implications for plant biologists, computational biologists, and bioinformaticians.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: DistillMD: Cancer drug response prediction using teacher-student models
authors: Aniruddh Saxena, Department of Human Genetics, University of Utah, United States; Casey Sederman, Department of Human Genetics, University of Utah, United States; Gabor Marth, Department of Human Genetics, University of Utah, United States
abstract: Precision oncology aims to match patients with treatments that will be most effective for their given cancer. Yet, current approaches based on tumor alterations often fall short as they are often not actionable and do not accurately predict drug response. Additionally, the heterogeneity of tumors makes it challenging to discern relationships between molecular features and treatment outcomes. Despite recent advances, these challenges persist, highlighting the need for methods that can integrate complex tumor data and generalize to unseen tumors. Here, we present DistillMD, a machine learning (ML) algorithm that uses a teacher-student approach to achieve superior performance compared to previous multi-drug models. DistillMD first trains separate teacher single-drug linear regression models for each therapy. Afterward, the true response values and teacher model outputs are used together to train a student, multi-drug model. This approach harnesses the strong generalization capabilities of regularized linear baselines (teachers) to train a unified multi-drug predictor with enhanced generalization to unseen tumors. DistillMD achieved superior response-prediction performance and enhanced treatment-selection capabilities on unseen tumors compared to the same architecture trained solely on raw drug response data. We see improvements in response rate from 64% to 76%, in per-drug Pearson correlation (PCC) from 0.48 to 0.51, and in residual drug sensitivity (PCC per tumor) from 0.30 to 0.37. Further, DistillMD can be finetuned to an individual tumor using a small drug screen for that tumor, which can substantially improve predictions for untested drugs, providing a promising path toward more effective precision oncology.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Motif2Gene: Interpreting Model-Identified Important Regions via Motifs, Transcription Factors, and Nearest Genes
authors: Tejaswi Vemuri, University of north florida, United States; Indika Kahanda, University of North Florida, United States; Joann Mudge, National Center for Genome Resources, United States; Trung Dinh, University of north florida, United States; Zonglin Yang, DePaul University, United States; Thiruvarangan Ramaraj, DePaul University, United States; Brendan Mumey, Computer Science, Montana State University, United States; Bella Root, National Center for Genome Resources, United States; Elyse Onstott, National Center for Genome Resources, United States
abstract: Predicting phenotype (observable traits or conditions) from genotype (DNA sequences) is an important problem in bioinformatics. Modern machine learning (ML) models can accurately predict phenotypes from genomic data. Still, it is often unclear why a model makes a prediction or whether the genomic regions it highlights are biologically meaningful. We developed Motif2Gene, a containerized, web-based pipeline that interprets model-identified important regions (DNA segments most influential for predictions). Motif2Gene aligns regions to a reference genome, identifies nearby genes, discovers enriched DNA motifs (recurring sequence patterns), and matches motifs to known transcription factors (TFs, or proteins that regulate gene expression) using curated motif libraries. It maps intervals to the nearest or overlapping genes as candidate regulatory targets and produces ranked TF-gene reports and interactive visualizations to assess regulatory plausibility. Established alignment and motif tools are integrated with automated reporting in one Docker deployment, lowering installation barriers and aiding reproducibility for non-specialist users. An optional LLM-assisted literature summary contextualizes top TF-gene findings with citation-verification guardrails in an extensible design. We applied Motif2Gene to 35 yeast phenotypes using regions prioritized by Enformer Bio-LLM, analyzing the top 200 important regions per phenotype with shared reference. In aggregate, most intervals mapped unambiguously to the genome assembly and received gene context, with motif and TF annotations produced for each phenotype. Currently, biologists are assisting with manual validation of these observations. By linking ML-derived important regions to motifs, transcription factors, and nearest genes, Motif2Gene helps researchers judge model plausibility and generate testable hypotheses across organisms and model types.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: An Agentic AI Framework for Generative Molecular Workflows
authors: Bum Chul Kwon, IBM Research, United States; Leili Zhang, IBM Research, United States; Elif Eyigoz, IBM Research, United States
abstract: While biomedical foundation models promise to accelerate drug discovery, researchers remain hindered by the fragmentation of public databases and open-source tools, making it difficult to compose reproducible, end-to-end workflows. A critical bottleneck in this landscape is the lack of seamless integration of *de novo* molecular generation, particularly for specific protein targets. To address this, we present an agentic AI system designed for small molecule generation. Unlike static pipelines that constrain tool selection, our system uses dynamic agent coordination to iteratively compose workflows that adapt to user-defined molecular generation goals. The system integrates generative AI models with bioinformatics tools, interactive visualizations, databases, and a natural language interface, enabling hypothesis-driven exploration. We provide the system's architectural design, including LLM agents, MCP servers, and a chat interface, which streamlines complex tasks ranging from protein sequence retrieval to small molecule generation. Furthermore, we share key lessons learned during development, offering a roadmap for building next-generation multi-agent systems that enhance human-guided scientific discovery.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PerTurbo enables scalable and robust Bayesian differential expression analysis of genome-wide Perturb-seq data
authors: Logan Blaine, Harvard Medical school, United States; Jiaqi Lu, Helmholtz Munich, Germany; Martin Jankowiak, Basis Research, United States; Jayoung Ryu, New York University, United States; Matthias Heinig, Helmholtz Munich, Germany; Luca Pinello, Massachusetts General Hospital & Harvard University, United States
abstract: Identifying differentially expressed genes upon perturbation is a key task in the analysis of Perturb-seq data. However, despite the abundance of differential expression analysis tools for observational single-cell data, suitable methods for Perturb-seq remain lacking: pseudobulk methods are generally inapplicable due to a lack of replicates in current datasets, generic statistical tests can exhibit poor calibration and accuracy, and robust resampling-based approaches are often prohibitively slow for genome-scale Perturb-seq analysis. To address these challenges, we developed PerTurbo: a Bayesian framework for differential expression analysis in large-scale Perturb-seq studies. PerTurbo is based on a hierarchical Bayesian model that accounts for single-cell sparsity and sources of technical variability such as CRISPR guide efficiency and library size. Using GPU-accelerated stochastic variational inference, PerTurbo performs robust Bayesian differential expression analyses across thousands of perturbations and millions of cells within hours on a single machine. We demonstrate that PerTurbo outperforms other methods in identifying differentially expressed genes on simulated and real data while running in a fraction of the time. In our reanalysis of several previously published genome-wide Perturb-seq datasets, we observed stronger enrichment for known protein complexes and pathways compared to previous analyses. Finally, we leverage PerTurbo to perform power analyses to identify optimal sequencing depth and sample size requirements for Perturb-seq experiments. We anticipate that PerTurbo can also aid in the benchmarking of models for perturbation response prediction, where overlap of differentially expressed gene sets has frequently been used as a primary evaluation metric.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Meta-Framework for Interpretability in Precision Oncology
authors: Charvi Gangwani, University of Maryland Baltimore County, United States; Maricel G. Kann, University of Maryland Baltimore County, United States
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) is a leading cause of male mortality in the United States. With 36,320 deaths projected in 2026, nearly all metastatic patients develop resistance to standard therapies or face therapeutic failure due to complex resistance mechanisms. The genomic alterations underlying cancer progression remain poorly characterized and hinder effective intervention. Explainable AI (XAI) models trained on multi-omic data offer a solution for identifying signatures associated with distinct disease-states. However, while there are standardized metrics to measure predictive performance, no standards exist to evaluate the consistency and biological relevance of model explanations. To identify genomic drivers of cancer lethality, we developed an ensemble interpretability framework utilizing a suite of machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, SVM, AdaBoost) alongside P-NET, a biologically-informed deep learning architecture. Our approach directly addresses the black-box nature of these models, while introducing a novel framework for evaluating and comparing interpretability performance. We extract feature importance through a multi-modal attribution approach, aggregating SHAP, LIME, and Gradient-based saliency maps on the classifiers. From these attribution signals, we computed a Consensus Priority Score (CPS) for each gene that integrates feature importance rankings, and prior evidence from established oncogenic literature. The resulting ranked gene set and associated CPS values can be used to benchmark feature sets identified by other machine learning models, compared against established multi-gene prognostic panels, and prioritize candidate targets for clinical validation for early and accurate risk stratification.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Graph attention networks reveal stage-resolved rewiring of hepatic cell-cell communication across steatosis-to-fibrosis progression in human liver
authors: Imran Shah, LiverLogic, United States
abstract: Background. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) reflects rewiring of signalling between hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, sinusoidal endothelial cells, and cholangiocytes. Existing ligand-receptor workflows score communication within cohorts but do not directly learn which donor-level patterns distinguish multi-stage disease progression. Methods. We analyzed three liver scRNA-seq atlases (GSE136103, GSE189600, GSE192742). Rather than using one pooled matrix, we kept datasets independent, built donor-level communication graphs, and aligned node features with a frozen 2,000-gene vocabulary derived from 20,638 shared candidates. LIANA rank-aggregate ligand-receptor scores yielded 36 internal donor graphs, split into 24 training, 6 validation, and 6 test graphs. Wang 2023 (GSE212837; 12 donors) was withheld as a holdout. A graph attention network (GAT) was trained for multi-class stage prediction, and steatosis-to-fibrosis rewiring was ranked using attention deltas. Results. On held-out internal donors, the GAT achieved macro-F1 = 0.40 versus 0.19 for the ligand-receptor baseline across multiple MASH stages. Steatosis-versus-fibrosis analysis identified 5,758 rewired edges. The strongest positive shift was hepatocyte-to-hepatocyte ALB->B2M_FCGRT, with additional fibrosis-enriched interactions including DLL1->NOTCH3 and GSTP1->EGFR. In independent bulk validation with GSE135251, leading rewired ligands associated with disease severity, including PLAU (Spearman r = 0.388), CXCL8 (0.341), ANXA1 (0.319), and CXCL12 (0.264). Performance did not transfer to the withheld snRNA-Seq Wang cohort, indicating substantial cross-cohort domain shift. Conclusions. Donor-level GNN learning on liver communication graphs recovers stage-associated rewiring patterns not captured by static per-cohort scoring alone, while highlighting the need for stronger domain adaptation before cross-study deployment.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: SynTex: Leveraging Large Language Model Embeddings and Multimodal Integration for Drug Synergy Prediction
authors: Juyeon Kim, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Minzhe Zhang, PromptBio Inc., United States; Melisa McCoy, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Bruce Posner, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Chaoying Liang, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Peifeng Ruan, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States; Yang Xie, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, United States
abstract: Identifying synergistic drug combinations is essential for effective cancer therapy but remains challenging due to the vast combinatorial space and complex biological interactions. Recent work has shown the utility of large language model (LLM)-derived text embeddings for drug synergy prediction, yet it remains unclear how these compare to structured molecular and transcriptomic features, and whether more expressive integration strategies can improve generalization to unseen combinations. We present SynTex, a framework that systematically evaluates text-only models, simple multimodal concatenation, and transformer-based fusion for drug synergy prediction. SynTex leverages structured textual descriptions of drugs and cell lines to capture prior biological knowledge and integrates them with chemical structure and gene expression data. Across three benchmark datasets (O'Neil, DrugComb, and GDSC²), text embeddings alone provided a competitive baseline, matching established methods. However, on the more challenging GDSC² dataset, models using structured molecular and genomic features exhibited stronger performance, suggesting that text embeddings may be less reliable for underrepresented data. Naïve concatenation of additional modalities yielded only marginal gains (ΔPearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) ≤ 0.02), indicating limited cross-modal complementarity from simple fusion. Motivated by this, we developed a transformer-based architecture that models cross-modal interactions at the token level. Evaluated under a zero-shot setting on an independently constructed dataset, SynTex outperformed representative approaches based on either molecular and transcriptomic features (DeepSynergy) or text embeddings (BAITSAO). These results suggest that effective drug synergy prediction for novel combinations depends not only on the choice of modalities, but also on how interactions between modalities are modeled.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ChromCodes: interpretable discrete representations enable controllable design of cell-type-specific regulatory DNA sequences
authors: Luca Pinello, MGH/Harvard University/BROAD, United States
abstract: Deep learning models for regulatory DNA either achieve interpretability or enable sequence generation, but rarely both. Discriminative models like ChromBPNet and Enformer predict chromatin accessibility from sequence but cannot generate sequences with specified properties. Generative methods like DNA-Diffusion enable cell-type-conditional design but operate as black boxes whose outputs cannot be decomposed into interpretable features. We present ChromCodes, an architecture unifying these capabilities through three components: motif-detecting convolutional filters, vector quantization into a discrete codebook, and a cross-attention decoder. ChromCodes encodes 200 bp DNA using 512 reverse-complement-equivariant filters, quantizes embeddings through a 512-entry codebook, and reconstructs via cross-attention with no skip connectionsâ€”forcing all information through an interpretable bottleneck. Trained on 48,000 chromatin accessible peaks across four human cell types (GM12878, hESCT0, K562, HepG2), the model recovers known TF motifs in 48% of filters (GATA1, HNF4A, NANOG, SPI1) and predicts accessibility from a bag-of-codes representation (Pearson r=0.780). This creates a traceable chain from nucleotides through motifs and discrete codes to cell-type identity. We introduce CodeProp, a gradient-based method that designs DNA sequences with target activity by optimizing the input sequence directly through the frozen ChromCodes pipeline. CodeProp achieves high tunability while generating genuinely novel sequences. Cell-type transformations recover expected master regulators: stem cell to erythroid transformations gain GATA1/GATA2/TAL1 while losing SOX2/FOXH1. External validation with ChromBPNet, an independent accessibility model, confirms generated sequences match endogenous profiles. ChromCodes unifies interpretation, representation, regression, and generation of regulatory DNA in a single differentiable framework, enabling controllable design without sacrificing transparency.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: OncoVec: A Fitness-Aware Tumor Representation Model Encoding Oncogenic and Immunogenic Selection
authors: Ko-Han Lee, University of California San Diego, United States; Hannah Carter, University of California San Diego, United States
abstract: Somatic mutation is not a stochastic process. The mutational landscape of a tumor is the observable consequence of a multi-layered selection process shaped by tissue-specific chromatin accessibility, carcinogen exposure, proliferative fitness, and host immunosurveillance. Current models capture only subsets of these factors and have been predominantly evaluated on cancer typing alone. Here, we present OncoVec, a mechanistic model that sequentially encodes mutation-level fitness, clonal interactions, and global mutational landscape into a unified tumor representation. Each mutation is embedded by integrating gene context, oncogenic fitness, and immunogenic visibility, and aggregated through a clonality-aware transformer architecture that enforces the directional structure of tumor evolution. A parallel landscape arm encodes regional mutation distributions, trinucleotide signatures, and copy number alterations via a convolutional neural network. Mutation embeddings are pretrained on gene similarity and feature density, and the full model is trained in a self-supervised manner using a masked language modeling approach. OncoVec is evaluated across cancer typing, genomic indices, transcriptomics-derived immune features, and immunoediting metrics on the TCGA pan-cancer cohort. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component, and the sensitivity of immunoediting metrics to the immunogenicity module suggests that OncoVec successfully captures the selective pressure of host immunosurveillance within its latent space.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: LLM-Guided Literature Mining for Large-Scale Discovery of Cell-Type Marker Genes Across Plant Species
authors: Sajib Acharjee Dip, Virginia Tech, United States; Song Li, Virginia Tech, United States; Liqing Zhang, Virginia Tech, United States
abstract: High-throughput sequencing has enabled large-scale identification of cell-typeâ€“specific marker genes; however, existing resources are predominantly derived from transcriptomic data and often lack mechanistic and functional context. In contrast, decades of low-throughput literature contain rich, experimentally validated evidence for geneâ€“cell-type relationships across diverse plant species, but this information remains unstructured and inaccessible for systematic analysis. We present a scalable language modelâ€“based framework for extracting and aggregating marker gene evidence directly from full-text scientific literature. Our approach consists of three stages: (i) high-recall retrieval of candidate geneâ€“cell-type pairs from PDFs using domain-specific entity matching; (ii) large language modelâ€“based evidence grading to classify evidence type (expression, function, localization, indirect, or noise), assign confidence, and determine validity; and (iii) evidence-aware aggregation to integrate signals across sentences and documents, producing ranked geneâ€“cell associations. As a proof of concept, we apply the framework to Arabidopsis root-related literature spanning multiple cell types (including endodermis, xylem, and root hair), processing dozens of papers to generate over 100 candidate evidence instances and identifying a high-confidence set of marker genes. The system recovers well-established regulators such as LKS4 (endodermis), PHB and MIR165A (xylem patterning), and CKX7 (xylem differentiation), demonstrating biologically meaningful prioritization and effective noise filtering. Importantly, this framework is designed to scale to hundreds of papers, multiple plant species, and comprehensive cell-type atlases, enabling automated construction of literature-driven marker gene resources. Integration with existing databases will further support validation and benchmarking.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Evolutionary Multi-Objective Optimization for De Novo Design of Multi-Epitope Vaccine Antigens
authors: Lucas Wu, The Harker School, United States
abstract: Rapid viral evolution continues to outpace conventional vaccine development, particularly for highly variable pathogens such as Influenza A, Norovirus, and HIV. Existing epitope-based vaccine approaches rely on heuristic filtering or sequential scoring pipelines that fail to jointly optimize immunogenicity, evolutionary conservation, and population-level HLA coverage. We present a fully automated end-to-end framework for de novo epitope-based antigen design that enables scalable construction of multi-epitope immunogens. We formulate epitope and antigen design as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem over sequence space, jointly optimizing immunogenicity, evolutionary conservation, and population-level HLA coverage. To solve this problem, we introduce an evolutionary optimization framework based on Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) that efficiently explores high-dimensional epitope combination space and constructs optimized antigen assemblies. The resulting constructs are further assessed using C-ImmSim to quantify antibody kinetics, cellular activation, and memory formation. We apply the framework to Influenza A, HIV, and Norovirus, generating antigen designs with high conservation (mean Shannon entropy By reformulating vaccine antigen design as an optimization problem, this framework decouples immunogen quality from the bottlenecks of manual curation and sequential heuristics. Applied across three divergent pathogen classes, it demonstrates that conservation, HLA coverage, and immunogenicity can be jointly achieved at scale, suggesting a generalizable computational strategy for accelerating antigen development in outbreaks and pandemics.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Resolving cellular origins of bulk molecular aging signatures
authors: Katarina Vlajic, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA, United States; Alison Luciano, The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME, 04609, USA, United States; Gennifer Merrihew, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA, United States; Michael Riffle, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA, United States; Michael MacCoss, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA, United States; Gary Churchill, The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME, 04609, USA, United States; Devin Schweppe, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA, United States
abstract: Aging is characterized by gradual decline of organ function at systemic, cellular and molecular molecular levels. Multi-omics approaches advanced the aging field, however the challenge in aging biology is poor correlation between mRNA and protein abundances; however, tools identifying cell type-specific vs global expressed programs are required. To investigate age-dependent molecular shifts in the immune system, we profiled matched proteomes and transcriptomes from murine spleens across eight timepoints spanning 6-30 months, yielding 8,528 genes after cross-modality alignment. Linear regression and generalized additive models per gene, and linear mixed models per protein complex, revealed linear and nonlinear age-associated changes. Protein-RNA correlation increased significantly at 24 and 30 months. Analysis of protein-RNA discordance identified 419 significantly discordant genes. To map the cellular origins of bulk molecular changes, we developed Celestial, a random forest-based framework that assigns genes to cell types using expression features derived from single cell reference data. Celestial outperformed Seurat for bulk-level cell type assignment (mean AUPRC: Celestial = 0.841 vs. Seurat = 0.395). Cell type-specific genes showed higher protein-RNA correlation than globally expressed genes (median r = 0.519 vs. 0.219). Celestial performed origin-of-change analysis that distinguishes age-related shifts in cell type abundance from cell-intrinsic expression changes using single-cell aging data. Lef1 RNA decline originated from loss of Lef1+ T cells, consistent with its protein-RNA discordance in bulk. For the first time, this study has assigned age-related changes in RNA processing and ubiquitin-proteasomal system components as globally expressed programs across all splenic cell types using single cell-informed analysis.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: 3R-Fold: Retrieval-Augmented RNA Secondary Structure Prediction via Deep Self-Representation and RNA Foundation Models
authors: Chaimae Toubali, Sherbrooke university, Canada; Kunpeng Xu, McGill, Canada; Shengrui Wang, Sherbrooke university, Canada; Aida Ouangraoua, Sherbrooke university, Canada
abstract: RNA secondary structure is a key determinant of RNA function, governing processes such as gene regulation, catalysis, and RNAâ€“protein interactions. Despite decades of research, accurate computational prediction of RNA secondary structure remains challenging. Classical thermodynamic methods such as ViennaRNA rely on minimum free-energy optimization and often struggle to capture complex structural motifs and long-range interactions. Recently, pretrained RNA foundation models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to encode structural information directly from sequence data. However, how to effectively leverage these representations for retrieval-guided RNA folding remains largely unexplored. We introduce 3R-Fold, a retrieval-augmented framework for RNA secondary structure prediction that integrates RNA foundation model embeddings with representation learning and structural similarity search. In the first stage, RNA sequences are encoded using RNA-FM together with a Deep Self-Representation (DSR) model to learn structure-aware embeddings capturing global relationships between RNA sequences. In the second stage, FAISS similarity search retrieves structurally related RNAs from a knowledge base, and their secondary structures are aggregated to produce a consensus structural signal that guides folding prediction. Experiments across multiple RNA families and sequence lengths show that retrieval-based guidance substantially improves prediction accuracy compared with classical thermodynamic folding. The proposed 3R-Fold framework achieves the strongest overall performance among evaluated approaches and does not require prior knowledge of RNA family annotations. More broadly, 3R-Fold can be viewed as a modular retrieval layer that augments existing RNA folding algorithms and provides a promising direction toward scalable, data-driven RNA structure prediction.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: OncoGAT: A Multimodal Graph Attention Network for Breast Cancer Molecular Subtype Classification and Survival Prediction
authors: Srikar Karri, Bridgeland High School, United States
abstract: Breast cancer is a molecularly heterogeneous disease requiring precise subtype classification for optimal treatment selection. Current approaches rely predominantly on single-omics data, capturing only a fraction of the molecular landscape. We present OncoGAT, a multimodal Graph Attention Network integrating six omics modalities â€” genomic mutations, gene panel sequencing, mRNA expression, DNA methylation, copy number alterations, and clinical features â€” for simultaneous PAM50 subtype classification, survival prediction, and treatment personalization. OncoGAT constructs a patient similarity graph from the METABRIC cohort (n=1,411) using cosine similarity across multi-omics profiles. LASSO-based feature selection reduces dimensionality from over 27,000 features to 500 informative biomarkers. A three-layer GAT architecture with eight attention heads and 256 hidden dimensions learns patient-level embeddings by propagating information across molecularly similar patients, with multi-head attention capturing distinct biological signal patterns analogous to specialist perspectives in a molecular tumor board. OncoGAT achieved 92.13% accuracy for PAM50 subtype classification and a C-index of 0.713 for survival prediction, outperforming baselines by 15-20%. Risk stratification into low-, medium-, and high-risk groups demonstrated statistically significant survival differences (p By unifying subtype classification, survival prediction, and treatment personalization in a single interpretable framework, OncoGAT advances precision medicine in routine oncology practice. Published in IEEE UEMCON 2025 proceedings; Best Paper Presentation Award.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: SpliceCOV: Accurate Identification of Transcriptional Features from RNA Sequencing
authors: Celine Hoh, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Ida Shinder, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Kuan-Hao Chao, Johns Hopkins University, United States; Ales Varabyou, Johns Hopkins University, United States
abstract: High-throughput RNA sequencing enables transcript discovery and quantification, but the resulting coverage profiles often contain substantial transcriptional noise, making it difficult to distinguish genuine transcript features from spurious signals. We present SpliceCOV, a two-stage framework for identifying splice sites and transcript boundaries from RNA sequencing coverage and junction data. SpliceCOV first identifies candidate splice sites from junction evidence and candidate transcript boundaries from coverage transitions, then applies supervised machine learning with coverage-derived features to classify high-confidence sites. Across human tissue datasets, SpliceCOV consistently outperformed two widely used changepoint detection methods in recovering annotated splice sites while removing a larger fraction of likely false positives. For transcript start and end sites, SpliceCOV achieved the best balance between recovering annotated boundaries and limiting excess predictions. When incorporated into transcriptome assembly, SpliceCOV-guided predictions increased assembly precision without reducing sensitivity, with larger gains observed in tissues with greater sample depth. A model trained on human data also generalized well to mouse RNA sequencing, improving splice site detection and transcriptome assembly without retraining. These results show that coverage-based classification can effectively separate biological transcriptional features from noise and provide a scalable approach for improving transcriptome analysis.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Contrastive Learning to Enrich Rare non-B DNA Signals for Structure Prediction from Nanopore Translocation Time Data
authors: Qianying Ren, School of Computing, University of Connecticut, United States; Marjan Hosseini, School of Computing, University of Connecticut, United States; Aaron Palmer, School of Computing, University of Connecticut, United States; Rachel J. O'Neill, Institute for Systems Genomics and Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of Connecticut, United States; Derek Aguiar, School of Computing and Institute for Systems Genomics, University of Connecticut, United States
abstract: Motivation: Non-canonical (non-B) DNA structures account for roughly 13% of the human genome and play a critical role in gene regulation, but their computational detection remains challenging due to a lack of reliable ground-truth annotations, and the difficulty of resolving rare non-B signatures against a noisy B-DNA background. Most existing non-B detection methods depend primarily on sequence motif information, which are insufficient for predicting structure, or they do not explicitly account for sequencing noise. Results: We address these challenges by introducing a noise-resilient contrastive learning framework that leverages nanopore translocation time signals to predict non-B DNA structure. To prevent the model from overfitting to mislabeled sequences, we first dynamically isolate confident negative samples based on their distances to a canonical B-DNA centroid in an embedding space and then incorporate an early-learning regularization term that anchors representation learning to early-stage memorization of clean labels. We address the lack of ground-truth labels by developing a non-B DNA structure prediction algorithm that uses embedding-based statistics in a large-scale multiple hypothesis testing framework with false discovery rate control. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves a 17% improvement in F1-score over competing approaches on simulated data. Furthermore, application to whole-genome nanopore sequencing data (NA12878) shows significantly divergent mutation rates in non-B DNA regions detected by our model compared to those of undetected regions and control signals.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Interpretable Genomic Language Models for SARS-CoV-2: Comparing Unsupervised and Supervised Transformer-VAE Approaches
authors: Saya Ohi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Junko S. Takeuchi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Yuichi Kawanishi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Moto Kimura, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Masato Ikeda, SB Coronavirus Inspection Center Corp., Japan; Wataru Sugiura, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan; Hajime Ohyanagi, Japan Institute for Health Security, Japan
abstract: Background: Asymptomatic infections contribute substantially to SARS-CoV-2 transmission, yet the viral genomic basis of asymptomatic versus symptomatic presentation remains unclear. While single-variant analyses (GWAS) have found no significant genomic differences between asymptomatic and symptomatic infections, whether deep learning models trained on genome-wide SNP profiles can reveal latent structure â€” and what that structure represents â€” remains unexplored. Methods: We applied a Transformer-based Variational Autoencoder (Transformer-VAE) to 5,834 SARS-CoV-2 genomes (2,917 asymptomatic; 2,917 symptomatic) from a large-scale Japanese surveillance cohort, using 211 SNP positions (MAF â‰¥ 0.01, missingness â‰¤ 0.10). Three model variants are compared: (1) an unsupervised VAE with no labels, (2) a supervised model trained on Pangolin lineage labels, and (3) a supervised model trained on clinical phenotype. Self-attention weights are extracted from each model and mapped to known functional variants via CoV-GLUE. Latent spaces are visualized using UMAP. Results: Analysis is currently underway. To date, unsupervised k-means clustering on the VAE latent space has yielded three genomic groups (k=3; Silhouette=0.47) with no clear correspondence to clinical phenotype. Cross-model comparison of attention maps, UMAP visualizations, and CoV-GLUE-based functional variant mapping are currently in progress. Conclusions: This three-way comparison is expected to demonstrate the utility of Transformer-VAEs for interpreting genomic language models and may offer a partial answer to the open question of whether symptom status in COVID-19 is primarily governed by viral genomic variation or by host-side determinants.

title: Ancestry-specific performance of variant effect predictors in clinical variant classification
authors: Predrag Radivojac, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic variants and assessing prediction performance are key computational tasks in genomic medicine. It has been shown that well-calibrated variant effect predictors can be reliably used as evidence towards establishing pathogenicity (or benignity) of missense variants, thereby rendering these variants suitable for use in (or exclusion from) the genetic diagnosis of rare Mendelian conditions. However, most predictors have been trained or calibrated on data that may not be sufficiently representative to lead to similar performance across all genetic ancestries. This raises questions about the responsible deployment of these tools to improve human health. To better understand the utility of computational predictors, we set out to assess their ancestry-specific performance in terms of accuracy and evidence strength according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines. First, we determined that the expected count of rare variants in an individual's genome and the allele frequency distribution of these variants are the key confounders when evaluating a predictor's performance across different genetic ancestries. Second, we found that a predictor's accuracy itself inversely correlates with the allele frequency of the rare variant. After stratifying according to allele frequency, we show that established methods for predicting the pathogenicity of missense variants have comparable performance levels across major ancestry groups. Our results therefore support the wide deployment of such models in the context of genetic diagnosis and related applications.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Less Uncertainty, More Information: Combining Deep Learning Exploration with Experimental Design for Active Learning in Sequence-to-Function Models
authors: Michael Kleyman, Moderna Inc, United States; Eric Ma, Moderna Inc, United States
abstract: Advances in massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) technologies combined with deep learning have led to large improvements in sequence-to-function modeling, deep learning architectures leading in performance. However, sequence space remains exponentially large, and achieving robust model generalizability beyond the training distribution is still a difficult problem. Acquiring additional labeled data through MPRA experiments is costly, making principled strategies for selecting maximally informative sequences essential. Two complementary paradigms address this challenge. Black-box active learning exploits neural network uncertainty estimates to explore under sampled regions of sequence space, while optimal experimental design leverages interpretable models to select sequences that maximize information gain. Both aim to improve models with minimal additional data, but from fundamentally different theoretical perspectives. However, the best methodology remains unclear, and benchmarking is difficult due to the inherent cost of iterative MPRA experiments, since each round of wet-lab characterization limits practical evaluation of competing strategies. The Random Promoter DREAM Challenge, a previous effort by the DREAM consortium , comprising approximately 6 million yeast promoter sequences with measured expression levels, provides an unprecedented in-silico testbed to benchmark and compare these strategies without wet-lab cost. This poster details our experiments on the DREAM Challenge data across a spectrum of active learning and optimal experimental design strategies, using multiple sequence-to-function models including a deep CNN and an interpretable motif-based regression. We systematically vary the balance between neural uncertainty-based exploration and information-theoretic design to determine what methodological differences actually lead to robust model improvement.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ProInterVal-BioXtal: A Web Server to Distinguish Biological from Crystallographic Interfaces Using Representation Learning and Graph Neural Networks
authors: Defne Alnigenis, Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, KoçUniversity, Istanbul, Turkey, Turkey; Damla Ovek Baydar, Dept. of Computer Eng., Koç Univ., Istanbul, Turkey &NCMBM, Univ. of Oslo, Norway, Norway; Ozlem Keskin, Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, KoçUniversity, Istanbul, 34450, Turkey, Turkey; Attila Gursoy, Department of Computer Engineering, Koç University,Istanbul, 34450, Turkey, Turkey
abstract: Accurate discrimination between biologically relevant proteinâ€“protein interfaces (PPIs) and crystallographic contacts is essential for reliable interpretation of macromolecular assemblies and their cellular functions. While X-ray crystallography remains a primary method for determining protein complex structures, crystallographic interfaces may be formed as a byproduct of the crystal packing. Therefore, robust computational approaches for interface annotation are needed. This study introduces ProInterVal-BioXtal, a web server that predicts class scores for PPIs, differentiating between biologically relevant and crystallographic interfaces. The method leverages protein representation learning and graph-based deep learning to capture structural and physicochemical features. Interface graphs derived from input complexes are processed by our novel graph-based contrastive model to learn interface representations which are used by a graph neural network for classification. The model is trained and validated on the MANY benchmark dataset comprising 5739 dimers with a balanced distribution of biological and crystal interfaces and evaluated on the DC benchmark dataset with curated interfaces of similar interface areas. On the DC test set, ProInterVal-BioXtal achieves 88% accuracy, 88% precision, and 85% F1 score, outperforming state-of-the-art methods including DeepRank-GNN, PRODIGY-CRYSTAL, EPPIC 3, PISA, and QSAlign. On an independent benchmark, the method achieves 83% accuracy and 0.91 AUC, surpassing DeepRank-GNN (AUC = 0.85). Through a user-friendly web interface, ProInterVal-BioXtal enables rapid predictions from PDB files or IDs, returning probabilistic classification scores. Our tool addresses a fundamental challenge in structural biology by utilizing graph-based protein representation which can detect complex interactions and dependencies. ProInterVal-BioXtal server is freely available at https://3dpath.ku.edu.tr/prointerval-bioxtal/

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Building a staged cell-free DNA methylation and fragmentomics workflow for cancer screening and tumor tissue-of-origin prediction using EM-seq datasets
authors: Katie Farney, National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States; Sara Bang-Christensen, National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Denmark; Peter Kilfeather, The Bioinformatics CRO, United Kingdom; Brian Bennett, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, National Institutes of Health, United States; Sabina Pathan, National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States; Sara Grimm, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, National Institutes of Health, United States; Jian-Liang Li, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, National Institutes of Health, United States; Adam Sowalsky, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States; Laura Elnitski, National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: Background: Blood-based cancer screening using plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) could reduce reliance on invasive biopsies, but low tumor fraction and heterogeneous signals limit sensitivity and tissue-of-origin (TOO) assignment. Fragmentation patterns reflect nucleosome positioning and chromatin structure, while DNA methylation encodes cell identity. We evaluated whole-genome enzymatic methyl sequencing (EM-seq) as a single-assay approach for fragmentomic and methylation analysis of plasma cfDNA. Methods: Plasma cfDNA from healthy donors (n=48) and patients with colon, liver, pancreas, prostate, stomach, and ovary cancers (n=150) was analyzed using a staged workflow: (1) targeted methylation capture to screen for cancer signal, followed by (2) EM-seq on the same converted libraries. Multimodal features were derived, including fragment lengths, methylation across tissue-informative regions, 5â€² 4bp end motifs, end-density profiles, and copy-number summaries. Multiclass TOO models were evaluated by repeated stratified cross-validation. Results: Cancer samples showed more short cfDNA fragments than healthy plasma, with enrichment around ~145bp versus the canonical ~166bp peak. Fragment-end motifs differed by cancer type, with CC-starting motifs depleted in multiple cancers. Although individual features showed modest TOO signal alone, methylation and fragmentomic features together improved discrimination over any single modality. The best 7-class classifier (healthy plus six cancer types) achieved a macro-F1 of 0.720. Performance was variable, with strongest results for stomach (F1 0.88), liver (0.86), and colon (0.80). In cancer-only classification, pancreas improved from 0.60 to 0.73 after removal of healthy samples. Conclusions: A staged EM-seq workflow can support scalable cancer screening with tumor DNA burden and TOO profiling from the same library preparation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Tumor Type Classification from Circulating Tumor DNA via Cross-Domain Ensemble Learning
authors: Simran Chhabria, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Madison Darmofal, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Quaid Morris, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Michael F. Berger, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Cancer type classification from circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is challenging due to sparse signal and tumor heterogeneity, limiting reliable tumor origin prediction in liquid biopsy settings. We introduce a large-scale cross-domain learning framework that leverages ctDNA and tissue-derived targeted sequencing data to improve generalization for cancer type classification from liquid biopsies. Our approach integrates genomic features from 15,000 ctDNA samples and 90,000 solid tumor samples generated using clinically targeted cancer gene panels. We train a hyperparameter-optimized ensemble model combining deep neural networks over somatic mutations, copy number alterations, and additional panel-derived genomic features. To evaluate generalization, ctDNA samples were partitioned such that half were used in training alongside tissue samples, while the remainder served as an independent test cohort. The model achieves 90.2% accuracy among high-confidence predictions across 31 cancer types. The proposed framework demonstrates that cross-domain training between ctDNA and tissue-derived sequencing data significantly improves liquid biopsy classification performance compared to single-modality training. Together, these results establish a scalable cross-domain genomic learning framework for cancer type classification from ctDNA and demonstrate the value of leveraging large-scale clinical sequencing datasets for robust liquid biopsy interpretation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: The COMPARATOR workflow for single cell transcriptomics: Leveraging Biomedical Foundation Models for cell type classification and benchmarking
authors: Joao Bettencourt-Silva, IBM, Ireland; Natasha Mulligan, IBM, Ireland; Scott Espenschied, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Mallory Zammataro, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Vibha Anand, IBM, United States; Ryan Musich, Cleveland Clinic, United States; Timothy Rumbell, IBM, United States; Jianying Hu, IBM, United States; James Kozloski, IBM, United States; Thaddeus Stappenbeck, Cleveland Clinic, United States
abstract: Background: The process of quantitatively comparing single cell transcriptomic studies lacks standardization and reproducible benchmarks, limiting the rigorous assessment of model fidelity across experimental platforms. To address these challenges, we developed a workflow to systematically assess and assign cell type labels across datasets. Methods: The COMPARATOR workflow leverages a fineâ€‘tuned transcriptomics foundation model to perform label transfer from a wellâ€‘annotated reference dataset to an unlabelled query dataset, yielding concordance metrics that serve as a benchmark for biological fidelity[1]. Here, we introduce a novel tool and workflow that standardizes and streamlines this process, removing the need for computationally intensive model fine-tuning, and provides a standardized scorecard. The workflow involves steps: (1) dataset preprocessing, (2) embedding generation for each dataset using selected BMFMs, (3) training and applying multiple classifiers on the reference dataset embeddings, (4) computing concordance metrics, (5) generating interactive dashboards and scorecard for visualisation of label assignments. We assessed three state-of-the-art BMFMs[2,3,4] and six different classifiers. Results: We compared label assignment results with previously reported results from a BMFM-RNA model fine-tuned model on human epithelial cell datasets[1,5]. Concordance metrics were computed to measure the distribution imbalance of all label assignment predictions. Across all label assignments previously reported, our method was able to correctly assign the same labels, with comparable precision/recall/F1(dataset[1] 0.85Â±0.11 vs 0.88Â±0.01, dataset[5] 0.71Â±0.14 vs 0.84Â±0.01). Conclusion: COMPARATOR enables the assignment of cell type labels, provides additional insights, does not require fine-tuning, and is generalizable to pairwise comparisons (e.g., benchmarking in-vitro systems vs in-vivo, evaluation of disease vs non-disease).

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: TIE-GPT: Accelerating target discovery with immunoscience-centric AI agents
authors: Arnau Arnau, Scaled Data Science Models, Digital R&D, Sanofi, Spain; Emanuele de Rinaldis, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Shameer Khader, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Peyman Passban, Scaled Data Science Models, Digital R&D, Sanofi, Canada; Hamid Mattoo, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Clément Chatelain, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Mario Pandolfi, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Jose Prieto, Scaled Data Science Models, Digital R&D, Sanofi, Spain; Nicolas Barrero, Scaled Data Science Models, Digital R&D, Sanofi, Spain; Dongyu Liu, Sanofi, United States; Sachin Mathur, Scaled Data Science Models, Digital R&D, Sanofi, United States; Mathieu Beauvais, Scaled Data Science Models, Digital R&D, Sanofi, France; Cristina Zamora, Digital In-Silico Research, Digital R&D,Sanofi, United States; Johanna Harrison, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Mahasweta Bhattacharya, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Cora Ames, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States; Franck Rapaport, Target, Disease and System Biology, Sanofi, United States
abstract: Over the past few years, computational biologists and data scientists in our organization have built and organized an extensive Disease Data Ecosystem, encompassing trillions of data points from public and private sources, including multiple omics measurements (single cell and bulk transcriptomics, proteomics, genetics), clinical trials and scientific literature, with a focus on immunoscience, under common ontologies that allow complex analyses across multiple modalities. However, this large repository is only operable by experts, as interrogating it requires understanding a complex documentation as well as the capability to understand, write and operate computer code. In order to accelerate adoption and data-driven decisions at every transition decision across our portfolio, we have developed TIE-GPT. TIE-GPT is a conversational assistant that every scientist from our organization can use to ask immunoscience questions in plain English language. This research partner is equipped with agentic AI capabilities through an orchestration mechanism, where a dedicated agent engages the right partner at the right time, including agents that pull relevant information from proprietary and internalized data repositories via code generation or intermediary tools. It finally triggers a fusion mechanism, where needed, to synthetize and merge individual answers from different sources (or agents) into a coherent and human understandable answer. TIE-GPT is a no-code solution that enables scientists to ask complex scientific questions and make data-driven decisions based on an integrated view of internally curated scientific information and external knowledge. It improves confidence in our decision-making, which leads to targets with a higher probability of success in the clinics.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking the Generalization of Chemical Language Models​
authors: Venkata Prasanth Kumar Gummadi, University of Cincinnati, United States; Dhurba Baral, University of Cincinnati, United States; Jarek Meller, University of Cincinnati, United States
abstract: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pre-trained on large molecular corpora, producing vector embeddings that capture chemically meaningful features and reflect similarity between small molecules without task-specific supervision. A key open question is how well these embeddings generalize to drug-discovery-related tasks. When actives already cluster in embedding space, a classifier trained on top may simply trace pre-existing structure rather than learn new discriminative signals, making accuracy difficult to interpret. Rather than training a classifier on top of embeddings, we directly evaluated separability of actives and decoys in embedding space across all 102 protein targets in the DUD-E benchmark. For each target, we projected MolFormer and ChemBERTa embeddings (CLS and mean pooling) alongside Morgan fingerprints onto a 2D UMAP, computed pairwise similarities within and between actives and decoys, and aggregated results across targets. We additionally analyzed whether individual Morgan fingerprint bits alone could separate actives from decoys per target. For most targets, actives form clusters visually separable from decoys, though some targets (e.g., MK01, HS90A) remain difficult. MolFormer produced better separation than ChemBERTa, and both outperformed Morgan fingerprints. Mean pooling consistently outperformed CLS representations within each model family. Individual Morgan bits alone separated large fractions of actives from decoys for several targets, revealing exploitable atomic-composition biases in DUD-E decoys. While the DUD-E benchmark remains useful for evaluating docking approaches, it should not be used as a basis for training and evaluating machine learning classifiers for actives vs. inactives discrimination, as it conflates what the embedding already encodes and extrapolates from decoy biases.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Cis-regulatory mechanisms driving tomato trichome-specific gene expression
authors: Thilanka Ranaweera, Department of Plant Biology, Michigan State University, East Lansing, United States; Rachel Kerwin, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Michigan State University, East Lansing, United States; Melissa Lehti-Shiu, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Michigan State University, East Lansing, United States; Shin-Han Shiu, CMSE, Department of Plant Biology, DOE-GLBRC, Michigan State University, USA, United States
abstract: Plant glandular trichomes produce a wide array of specialized metabolites that help protect plants from biotic and abiotic stressors and attract beneficial pollinators. These metabolites have also been used in a wide range of pharmacological and industrial applications. Specialized metabolites such as acylsugars are typically produced in a trichome-specific manner achieved through tight regulation of biosynthetic gene expression. However, the regulatory mechanisms, particularly the transcription factor binding sites, i.e., cis-regulatory elements (CREs), that determine trichome-specific gene expression are not well understood. In this study, we aim to decipher the CREs that regulate the trichome specific expression in cultivated tomato. We compared the expression differences between isolated trichomes and 21 trichome-less tissue types in tomato to find the trichome-specific genes. Next, we uncovered putative CREs (pCREs) that regulate trichome-specific expression by establishing machine learning models predicting trichome-specific gene sets. The top predictor pCREs resemble the binding sites of transcription factors, including MYB, HD-ZIP and WRKY, that were also co-expressed with trichome specific genes. CRISPR mutants were created to validate the function of an HD-ZIP gene (Solyc03g098200) whose binding sites possess significant similarity to the top pCREs. These mutants exhibited a stunted trichome phenotype at the 10-day seedling stage and altered acylsugar production relative to the wild type. These results provide experimental validation that the machine learning-predicted pCREs are functionally relevant regulators of trichome development and specialized metabolism. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into trichome-specific expression in cultivated tomato and more broadly how spatially specific gene expression in plants is regulated.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Brain-wide In Vivo Perturbation Mapping of Neurological Disorder Risk Genes
authors: Seoyeon Kim, The Scripps Research Institute, United States; Tuo Shi, The Scripps Research Institute, United States; Maria Korshunova, NVIDIA, United States; David DeTomaso, PerturbAI, United States; Grace Xy Zheng, PerturbAI, United States; Stephan J. Sanders, University of Oxford, United Kingdom; Laksshman Sundaram, NVIDIA, United States; Xin Jin, The Scripps Research Institute, United States
abstract: Human genetics has identified a growing list of high-confidence risk genes associated with neurological disorders, yet how they impact brain function remains poorly understood. Recent advances in CRISPR perturbation screening enable the interrogation of gene function at scale, but most studies remain confined to in vitro systems, limiting our ability to capture cellular diversity and context-specific effects of these mutations. We performed genome-scale in vivo CRISPR perturbation screening of 1,947 genes associated with neurological disorders across the whole mouse brain and profiled their effects with snRNA-seq. This dataset spans ~7.7 million cells across all major brain regions and cell types, providing a high-resolution, context-aware map of functional responses to genetic perturbations. Systematic analysis of ~28,000 perturbation-cell type pairs reveals that perturbations targeting genes involved in protein homeostasis and chromatin regulation drive the largest transcriptional effects. Transcriptional programs converge across functionally related genes, exemplified by coordinated stress-response activation following perturbation of proteasome components, while divergent responses are observed as reflected by anticorrelated transcriptional responses following Grin2a and Grin2b perturbations. Transcriptional disruption scales with genetic constraint and disease relevance, with enrichment for disease-associated gene sets, recapitulating key properties of neurological risk genes. To enable scalable interpretation of perturbation effects, we propose a brain-specific multimodal AI framework that learns joint embeddings of transcriptomic profiles and natural language, enabling systematic interpretation of perturbation responses and prioritization of shared therapeutic targets. Together, this work establishes a systematic map of gene function across the brain and suggests AI-guided discovery of therapeutic strategies.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Rewiring Protein Sequence and Structure Generative Models to Enhance Protein Stability Prediction
authors: Ziang Li, Georgia Institute Of Technology, United States; Yunan Luo, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States; Kerr Ding, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
abstract: Predicting how amino acid substitutions change protein thermostability is essential for understanding disease mechanisms and engineering robust proteins. Recent protein generative models achieve strong zero-shot performance across mutation-related tasks without task-specific supervision, yet this unsupervised capability remains underused for supervised stability learning. We present SPURS, a deep learning framework that rewires and integrates two complementary protein generative models, a protein language model and an inverse folding model, and reprograms the unified architecture for thermostability prediction using mega-scale $\Delta \Delta G$ data. SPURS injects structure-derived information into sequence-derived representations through lightweight cross-attention adapters and performs parameter-efficient fine-tuning, reducing trainable parameters by 98.5\% relative to full language-model tuning. The model is also computationally scalable: it predicts $\Delta \Delta G$ for all single substitutions of a protein in one forward pass, enabling proteome-scale site-saturation analyses. As a concrete example, SPURS can scan the human proteome (19,652 proteins, about $10^9$ variants) in about 30 minutes on one GPU. In benchmarking, SPURS improves over baselines on identity-controlled and external datasets, including better recovery of stabilizing mutations and generalization to unseen proteins and mutation contexts. Beyond stability prediction, SPURS supports broad protein-informatics applications, including unsupervised functional-site identification, improved low-N protein fitness prediction, and systematic analysis of stability-pathogenicity relationships in human variants. Together, these results establish SPURS as an accurate, efficient, and generalizable framework for protein stability modeling and as a tool for large-scale protein engineering and disease-variant interpretation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking and Integrating Multiple Modalities for Generalizable Gene Perturbation Prediction in Virtual Cell Modeling
authors: Dongmin Bang, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, South Korea
abstract: The virtual cell (VC) paradigm aims to model how cellular states transition in response to genetic or chemical interventions. While substantial effort has focused on modeling cell state, representation of the perturbation itself is equally critical, because the perturbation directly determines the transition between cellular states. In the context of CRISPR knockdown or â€˜gene perturbationâ€™ prediction, current perturbation representations are often restricted to simple one-hot perturbation identifiers or single modality, including sequence embeddings, biological network representations, or text description-based embeddings. Critically, one-hot representations cannot generalize to unseen perturbations, and single-modality embeddings may capture only a limited view of gene function. In this study, we systematically benchmark perturbation representations across sequence, graph, and text modalities for VC modeling of CRISPR knockdown responses. We find that different modalities contribute complementary strengths: some better preserve biological consistency, as mainly measured by differential expression, whereas others provide stronger technical predictive accuracy according to mean absolute error. Motivated by these modality-specific tradeoffs, we propose a low-complexity multi-modal integration framework that fuses graph, sequence, and text-derived gene information using graph and contrastive learning. Rather than applying all-pairwise contrasts across modalities, our graph-guided formulation reduces the integration objective to two loss terms while preserving cross-modal alignment. The proposed multi-modal representation achieves balanced performance for perturbation response prediction across both biological and technical metrics and shows advantages in few-shot and zero-shot settings. These results suggest that multi-modal perturbation representations improve the generalization capacity of VC models, especially when predicting cellular responses to previously unseen genetic perturbations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: The limits of transformers for transcriptomic representation learning
authors: Serena Chan, Université de Montréal, Canada; Sébastien Lemieux, Université de Montréal, Canada
abstract: Large-scale pre-training, popularized by its success in natural language processing (NLP), has been increasingly adopted for RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data, resulting in foundation models trained to learn representations of a cell's transcriptomic state, reducing the need for additional experiments. The quality of representation depends on two factors: input encoding and model architecture. Two main representations have emerged: a continuous vector of expression, and a rank-based ordering of genes by expression. While transformers excel at capturing hierarchical relationships, they are computationally intensive. Furthermore, preliminary findings suggest that simpler models can achieve unexpectedly strong performances, raising questions about how different strategies interpret RNA-seq data and shape the learned representation. We compare three models using the LINCS-L1000 dataset: (i) an MLP trained on raw expression; (ii) a rank-based transformer; and (iii) a hybrid transformer that sums a PCA projection of expression element-wise to the rank embeddings. The transformers are pre-trained using a masked token prediction task. Each model is evaluated on cell line identification (236 classes) and compound perturbation identification (79 classes). Both transformers struggle at the pretraining objective itself, collapsing onto a subset of highly expressed genes with low Shannon entropy across predictions. Downstream performance is comparable across all three models, demonstrating that the transformers fail to learn a transcriptomic representation beyond what a baseline MLP can achieve. This is seen in both feature extraction and fine-tuning, suggesting that the pre-trained embeddings themselves are not sufficient. Ongoing work focuses on re-aligning the pre-training objective to cell-level applications to potentially improve learned representations.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Morphology-Guided Spatial Transcriptomic Upscaling via Pathway-Encoded Intermediate Representations in Colorectal Cancer
authors: Sayed Asaduzzaman, Graduate Research Assistant, University of North Dakota, United States; Hasin Rehana, University of North Dakota, United States; Brett McGregor, University of North Dakota, United States; Junguk Hur, University of North Dakota, United States
abstract: Standard Visium imaging enables transcriptome-wide spatial profiling alongside tissue morphology analysis, but each 55 μm spot captures mixtures of heterogeneous cell populations. Although higher-resolution spatial transcriptomic assays are available, they remain costly and less accessible. To address this limitation, we developed a morphology-guided deep learning framework that infers spatial gene expression from Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) images using biologically structured pathway representations. Rather than directly predicting gene expression, the model first encodes transcriptomic information into pathway-level representations derived from curated gene sets, which are subsequently decoded into gene-level predictions. The framework was trained using co-registered Visium HD colorectal cancer datasets at 2 μm, 8 μm, and 16 μm resolutions and applied to standard Visium v2 data through weighted aggregation of predicted 16 μm bins within each 55 μm spot. Across 3,000 highly variable genes, our pathway-guided framework achieved mean spot-level Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.44 and 0.49, respectively. Gene-level evaluation yielded mean Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.51 and 0.53, outperforming direct image-to-gene prediction (Pearson = 0.32, Spearman = 0.30). Image registration between Visium HD and the Visium v2 datasets further demonstrated concordance between predicted and reference spatial expression patterns (Pearson = 0.55, Spearman = 0.51). These results demonstrate that pathway-structured representations improve the biological coherence and gene-level accuracy of histology-to-expression inference in colorectal cancer tissues.

title: MOSAIC: A Novel Method for Knowledge Graph Embedding with Applications to Systems Biology
authors: Dave D. Hill, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Deanne M. Taylor, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Jonathan C. Silverstein, The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, United States; Sharon Diskin, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Jo Lynne Rokita, Children's National Hospital and George Washington University, United States; Elizabeth Goldmuntz, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Adam Resnick, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Sarah Tasian, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Matthew Roth, Baylor College of Medicine, United States; Asif Chinwalla, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Christopher Nemarich, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Taha Mohseni Ahooyi, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; James Terry, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Varduhi Petrosyan, Baylor College of Medicine, United States; Patricia J. Sullivan, Children's National Hospital, United States; Ryan Corbett, Children's National Hospital, United States; Alan Simmons, The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, United States; Shiping Zhang, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Aditya Lahiri, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Yuanchao Zhang, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Benjamin J. Stear, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States
abstract: As Knowledge Graph (KG) databases become the backbone for aggregating increasingly complex biological data, they offer a unique opportunity to uncover hidden interactions and "unrelated" entities in biomedical research. However, the sheer scale and structural complexity of these graphs create significant barriers to direct analysis. To overcome this, transforming graph structures into low-dimensional numerical vectors, known as node embeddings, is essential. When performed effectively, these embeddings act as computable counterparts to the graph, enabling the use of diverse machine learning applications for discovery. In this work, we present MOSAIC (Multi-scale Ontology-driven Semantic Analysis and Inference over Contexts), an unsupervised and label-free method for knowledge graph embedding that combines random-walk diffusion and nonlinear manifold learning in a closed-form, interpretable, and scalable framework. The approach captures multi-hop diffusion without explicit sampling, performs spectral Eigen-decomposition to extract global structure, refines embeddings via UMAP to preserve topological and manifold features, and introduces random projection for enhanced diversity in downstream tasks. Unlike sampling-based or deep diffusion methods, MOSAIC leverages iterative sparse multiplications for efficiency while maintaining higher-order and geometric relationships without training. This design achieves strong representational quality with low computational cost, and future extensions aim to integrate probabilistic, adaptive, and Euclidean-space variants for broader applicability.

title: Deciphering Gene Regulatory Programs Within and Across Plant Species Using Network-based Machine Learning Tools and Single cell omics
authors: Chandrani Kumari, Wisconsin Institute for Discovery, University of Wisconsin, Madison, United States; Marina Kotvanova, Wisconsin Institute for Discovery, University of Wisconsin, Madison, United States; Rafael E. Venado, Department of Bacteriology, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, United States; Prakriti Garg, Wisconsin Institute for Discovery, University of Wisconsin, Madison, United States; Ryan Moreno, Wisconsin Institute for Discovery, University of Wisconsin, Madison, United States; Christopher Dervinis, School of Forest, Fisheries and Geomatic Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, United States; Wendell J. Pereira, School of Forest, Fisheries and Geomatic Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, United States; Matias Kirst, School of Forest, Fisheries and Geomatic Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, United States; Jean-Michel Ané, Department of Bacteriology, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, United States; Sushmita Roy, Wisconsin Institute for Discovery, University of Wisconsin, Madison, United States
abstract: Some cereals like maize and sorghum fix atmospheric nitrogen using mucilage secreted by root cap border cells (BC), which host nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Despite its importance, the genetic mechanisms governing mucilage production and BC development remain poorly understood. To explore the molecular and cellular basis of mucilage production and BC formation, we employed single-nuclei RNA sequencing in three plant species: maize, sorghum, and Medicago, with Medicago serving as a model for experimental validation. We developed an integrated computational pipeline to systematically analyze these single cell datasets. Using single-task and a new multi-task non-negative matrix factorization method (TIMBER), we identified 10â€“15 distinct clusters further annotated using known cellular markers. We inferred a cell lineage tree using a minimum spanning tree and later refined it based on prior biological knowledge. To infer gene regulatory networks from single-cell expression matrices, we applied computational methods scMTNI, independently to each species' dataset. scMTNI infer cell cluster specific GRN for each cell cluster in the lineage tree. Key regulators associated with BC clusters, obtained from intersection of these two methods, were experimentally validated through RNA interference in Medicago. We also performed a multi-species comparative genomics analysis at the level of modules and GRNs using Arboretum and MRTLE, respectively. Arboretum integrates gene expression data, species and gene phylogenies to identify modules of co-expressed genes and reconstruct their evolutionary trajectories across species.
