MRTLE is a multi-species GRN inference algorithm for a matched cell type across species. By integrating multi-species snRNAseq analysis, GRN inference, and functional validation, our approach provides key insights into the regulation of mucilage production and BC development.

title: Stratified Modeling to Reduce Bias in Kinase-Substrate Association Prediction
authors: Salvador Leon-Lopez, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, United States; Marzieh Ayati, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, United States
abstract: Background Protein phosphorylation is central to cancer signaling, yet more than 90% of experimentally identified phosphosites lack annotation of their upstream kinases. Existing computational methods for kinase-substrate association (KSA) prediction are biased towards well-studied kinases, limiting discovery of understudied kinases that may play important roles in diseases. This imbalance, often described as the â€œstreetlight effect,â€ is particularly problematic for cancers, where kinase signaling is highly transient and context dependent. The purpose of this study is to quantify and mitigate bias in KSA prediction by developing and evaluating a stratified, network-based framework that provides fairer prioritization of understudied kinases. Methods Publicly available KSA data, phosphatase-substrate associations, pathway information, protein-protein interactions, and phosphosite coevolution relationships were integrated into a heterogeneous protein-phosphosite network. Liver-specific proteins and phosphosites were added to the generic graph, and liver context was incorporated through tumor fold-change phosphosite correlations relative to healthy controls. Node2vec embeddings and embedding-derived kinase-site pair features were used to train a logistic regression model, evaluated using edge-level leave-one-out kinase ranking on phosphosites observed in the liver data. Results Comparison of the generic and liver-specific models showed that adding liver context changed kinase prioritization in several evaluated cases and improved the ranking of known kinases consistently. Conclusions These results suggest that liver-specific graph augmentation can shift KSA prediction toward associations that may be more relevant to liver cancer biology and provide a practical basis for comparing generic and disease-specific kinase ranking.

title: Joint Embedding Spaces Mine Cancer Precision Medicine Knowledge
authors: Natasa Przulj, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, United Arab Emirates
abstract: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide. It is a multifactorial disease that results from multiple alterations, which are only partially captured by any biological data type studied in isolation. Hence, novel multi-omics data-fusion and analytics methods are needed to holistically mine the wealth of all available clinical and molecular data for new cancer precision medicine discovery. Network embedding is a cornerstone of modelling and analysis of such complex, biological datasets. In the field of NLP, it was observed that the embeddings of words capture semantic relationships linearly, allowing for efficient mining using simple linear vector operations rather than by using computationally intensive, black-box downstream analysis methods. Then, this observation has been made in other fields, yielding the so-called linear representation hypothesis in vision language models. The question is whether this observation holds and can be exploited in the context of multi-omics data-fusion for cancer precision medicine. To assess this, we propose a Non-Negative Matrix Tri-Factorization based framework to jointly embed the multi-omics datasets of all cancer patients from TCGA (SMPs and gene expression profiles of 9,134 cancer patients from 33 TCGA projects), the protein interactions from BioGRID and the drug data from DrugBank into the same embedding spaces. By comparing the performances of linear and non-linear methods for downstream classification and clustering tasks, we demonstrate that our joint embedding spaces are linearly organized. Then, we define linear vector operations that enable prioritizing new pan-cancer or cancer-specific genes and drug repurposing, paving the way to new cancer therapies.

title: Multi-omics data-fusion uncovers distinct molecular signatures of intra-articular micro-fragmented adipose tissue versus hyaluronic acid treatments in inflammatory knee osteoarthritis
authors: Noel Malod-Dognin, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, United Arab Emirates; Vilim Molnar, St. Catherine Specialty Hospital, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Petar Brlek, St. Catherine Specialty Hospital, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Luka Bulić, St. Catherine Specialty Hospital, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Željko Jeleč, St. Catherine Specialty Hospital, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Uršula Prosenc Zmrzljak, Molecular Biology Laboratory, BIA Separations CRO, Labena Ltd., 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia, Slovenia; Thomas Klarić, Genos Glycoscience Research Laboratory, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Gordan Lauc, Faculty of Pharmacy and Biochemistry, University of Zagreb, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Dragan Primorac, St. Catherine Specialty Hospital, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia, Croatia; Natasa Przulj, Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), United Arab Emirates
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a multifactorial condition in which intra-articular micro-fragmented adipose tissue (MFAT) has demonstrated greater clinical benefit than the standard treatment with hyaluronic acid (HA). However, the molecular basis for this difference remains poorly understood. To characterize the systems-level molecular responses of MFAT and HA treatments in patients with the inflammatory KOA phenotype, independent of clinical outcome scores, 53 patients were treated with either MFAT (n = 35) or HA (n = 18) at St. Catherine Specialty Hospital and were followed longitudinally at baseline (T0), 1 month (T1), and 6 months (T6) post-treatment. Plasma-derived multi-omics datasets were generated, encompassing copy number variations, coding SNPs/InDels, proteomics, plasma N-glycomics, and miRNA transcriptomics. Then, to characterize the molecular differences between the two treatment groups, we integrated the patient-derived, multi-omics datasets together with publicly available proteinâ€“protein and miRNAâ€“gene interaction networks using an interpretable AI-based multi-omics data-fusion framework based on Non-negative Matrix Tri-Factorization, yielding patientâ€“gene and patientâ€“miRNA association scores and identifying gene and miRNA functional modules whose associations differed significantly between the two treatments. Our newly identified functional modules captured biologically coherent processes enriched in GO and Reactome annotations. Importantly, our results suggest that after treatments (at T6), MFAT-treated patients were preferentially associated with gene modules involving tissue regeneration and resolution of inflammation: canonical WNT and IL-10 signaling, positive regulation of bone mineralization and osteoblast differentiation, negative regulation of type I interferon production, and chondroprotective effectors including SIRT7, TNIP2 and NDUFC1. On the other hand, HA-treated patients remained preferentially associated with gene modules driving OA pathogenesis, including protein O-linked glycosylation, serotonin and TOR signaling, histamine secretion, and cartilage-degrading effectors such as MMP13, LIMK2, PPEF1 and UBR3. Our results using miRNA modules showed similar patterns, with the MFAT-treated patients being associated with regenerative and cell-adhesion processes and the HA-treated patients being associated with pseudopodium organization (linked to inflammatory OA invasiveness). To conclude, our AI-driven multi-omics data fusion framework discriminates the molecular signature of MFAT from HA at six months, highlighting that MFAT shifts the molecular landscape toward chondroprotection, anti-inflammatory and regenerative pathways, which supports a disease-modifying mechanism of action for MFAT.

title: Brain Glycoproteomics Links Synaptic and Lysosomal Glycoproteins to Amyloid Pathology and Reveals Mitochondrial Glycation as Independent Contributor to Cognitive Decline
authors: Aparajita Pranjal, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; Sheema Sameen, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States; David Morgenstern, Weizmann Institute of Science, Israel; Hila Levy, Weizmann Institute of Science, Israel; Yishai Levin, Weizmann Institute of Science, Israel; David A Bennett, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Michal Schnaider Beeri, Brain Health Institute Rutgers, United States; Aron S Buchman, Rush University Medical Center, United States; Hans-Ulrich Klein, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, United States
abstract: Altered brain glycoproteins have been implicated in key pathological processes in Alzheimerâ€™s disease (AD), arising from post-translational modifications such as glycosylation and glycation. These modifications generate unique glycopeptiforms, in which sugar moieties are covalently attached to peptides. Unlike conventional approaches that analyze glycans and peptides independently, our method simultaneously characterizes glycan composition and site-specific peptide attachment. Using this novel approach, we identified 9,098 unique glycopeptiforms across 361 dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) samples from the ROSMAP cohort. Co-expression analysis grouped these glycopeptiforms into 62 modules, revealing glycan composition-specific clusters with shared biological functions and cell-type associations. Among these, 34 modules were enriched for glycosylated peptiforms, many involving synaptic and lysosomal proteins, suggesting roles in neural development and signaling. Eighteen modules were significantly associated with at least one AD-related trait, strikingly none were linked to tau pathology. Bayesian network analysis highlighted distinct pathways: two glycosylated modules influenced rate of change in cognition through amyloid burden, while two glycated modules were directly associated with cognition. Notably, six glycated modules strongly correlated with ante-mortem hemoglobin A1c, implicating mitochondrial protein glycation in brain metabolic dysfunction. Stratification by clinical A1c thresholds showed these modules accelerated cognitive decline in both prediabetic and diabetic individuals, suggesting early vulnerability prior to overt disease. Integration with metabolomics further revealed disruptions in amino acid metabolism, sugar metabolism, and mitochondrial electron transport pathways. Together, these findings demonstrate that glycosylation- and glycation-driven networks in the brain contribute to synaptic dysfunction and metabolic impairment in AD, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for mitigating cognitive decline.

title: Enhancing causal network-based perturbation inference through literature-derived knowledge
authors: Zheng Liu, Northeastern University, United States; Benjamin Gyori, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Inferring active regulators from experimental readouts upon perturbation is a central problem in systems biology. Network propagation methods such as MOON (Meta-fOOtprint aNalysis) address this by propagating activity signals through a directed prior knowledge network (PKN) to score candidate regulators, but their performance is constrained by the coverage and quality of the underlying network. Most PKNs such as OmniPath or Pathway Commons aggregate manually curated databases, which are high-confidence but miss a substantial portion of literature-reported findings. To address this, we benchmarked an OmniPath-based PKN using machine reading of biomedical literature via INDRA, an automated system that extracts and assembles mechanistically resolved molecular interaction and regulation statements with associated confidence scores. We ranked candidate literature-derived edges for PKN expansion by confidence and benchmarked PKN expansions at multiple inclusion thresholds spanning the top 0.1% to the top 10% of edges. We evaluated upstream perturbation inference on two benchmark datasets: CytoSig and CellSig (both consisting of cytokine or growth-factor-induced transcriptional response signatures), and found that integrating literature-derived edges significantly improved performance with the top 0.3% highest-confidence edges resulting in the largest improvement. Baseline AUCs increased from 0.553 to 0.706 (+27.7%) on CytoSig, and from 0.609 to 0.717 on CellSig. However, AUC declined monotonically beyond a 0.5% threshold as low-confidence edges introduced contradictory signals. These results indicate that selective integration of literature-derived causal knowledge enhances network-based perturbation inference, and that edge confidence is more important than coverage when augmenting curated networks with automated extraction.

title: A Biological Information Flow Ontology for Reproducible Knowledge Graph-Based Cohort Analysis
authors: Christopher Nemarich, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Jonathan C. Silverstein, The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, United States; Kristina Cole, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the Universityof Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Sarah Tasian, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the Universityof Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Adam Resnick, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the Universityof Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Elizabeth Goldmuntz, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the Universityof Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Ryan Corbett, Children's National Hospital, United States; Patricia J. Sullivan, Children's National Hospital, United States; Jo Lynne Rokita, Children's National Hospital and George WashingtonUniversity, United States; Sharon Diskin, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the Universityof Pennsylvania Perelman Medical School, United States; Deanne M. Taylor, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Asif Chinwalla, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; James Terry, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Tiffany Callahan, Manas AI, United States; Alan Simmons, The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, United States; Aditya Lahiri, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Yuanchao Zhang, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Taha Mohseni Ahooyi, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States; Benjamin J. Stear, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, United States
abstract: Background. Pathway enrichment analysis of rare-variant cohorts typically uses hypergeometric tests against curated gene sets, treating pathway membership as a binary annotation and ignoring biomedical knowledge graph (KG) structure. We present BIFO (Biological Information Flow Ontology), a formal ontology specifying entity classes, flow classes, admissibility constraints, and conditioning protocols for graph-based cohort analysis, alongside BIFO-PPR, a reference implementation using personalized PageRank. Method. BIFO-PPR represents per-gene rare-variant burden as personalized PageRank seeds on the Data Distillery Knowledge Graph (DDKG, UBKG-derived; ~817,000 nodes spanning 20+ entity classes). A four-arm conditioning protocol restricts propagation to BIFO-admissible edge classes (gene-protein, regulatory, disease-mechanism, ontology) and recombines arms additively. Pathway scores are evaluated against a 10,000-permutation membership-rewiring null preserving degree distribution. We compare to Fisher's exact one-sided test against MSigDB v7.4 across four minor-allele-frequency thresholds. Results. In Kids First CHD (697 probands, 1,276 resolved seeds), BIFO-PPR recovers WikiPathways WP_CILIOPATHIES at rank 1 of 1,988 calibrated pathways (null_z = 13.24); Fisher recovers it at rank 1 of 2,619 across all four MAF tiers. Methods correlate (Spearman Ï = 0.75, top-10 Jaccard = 0.25) but are not equivalent: Fisher amplifies small overlap-driven hits (kâ‰¤3) that BIFO-PPR calibrates as chance-consistent. Beyond pathway ranking, BIFO-PPR scores all substrate node classes; top non-gene drivers in CHD include compounds with documented cardiac teratogenicity or developmental cardiotoxicity (valproic acid, sirolimus, LY294002, trichostatin A, 17Î²-estradiol benzoate) â€” mechanistic context unavailable from pathway-membership testing. A joint MAF Ã— restart-probability sweep confirms rank-1 stability across 20 parameter cells. Conclusion. BIFO provides a principled, reproducible framework for KG-based cohort analysis. BIFO-PPR matches Fisher on known-biology recovery while contributing a topology-aware mechanistic explanation absent from standard pathway tests. Both publicly released.

title: Optical Properties of Titanium dioxide Nanotubes for Structural-based Biosensor
authors: Wen-Yang Chang, National Formosa University, Taiwan; Te-Hua Fang, National Kaohsiung University of Applied Sciences, Taiwan; Bo-Yan Lin, National Kaohsiung University of Applied Sciences, Taiwan
abstract: Titanium dioxide (TiOâ‚‚) is well known for its high biocompatibility, non-toxicity, and chemical stability, making it a promising material for medical implant applications in structural bioinformatics. In addition, TiOâ‚‚ promotes cell proliferation, enhances surface osseointegration, and exhibits antibacterial properties, particularly when engineered at the nanoscale for biological systems. Therefore, TiOâ‚‚ nanotube arrays fabricated by electrochemical anodization were investigated with respect to their photoluminescence and optical characteristics. The investigated parameters included anodization time, anodization voltage, annealing temperature, photoluminescence spectra, and photocurrent responsivity. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), photoluminescence spectroscopy, and a precision semiconductor parameter analyzer were employed to characterize the morphology, crystal structure, and optoelectronic properties of the TiOâ‚‚ nanotube arrays for biological applications. Furthermore, an optical current sensor based on TiOâ‚‚ nanotubes was fabricated using interdigitated transducer (IDT) electrodes for applications in network pharmacology. The results indicate that well-ordered TiOâ‚‚ nanotube structures are obtained when grown in an electrolyte consisting of NHâ‚„F mixed with glycerol and deionized water. The average length and diameter of the TiOâ‚‚ nanotubes increase with increasing anodization time and voltage. Amorphous TiOâ‚‚ transforms into the crystalline anatase phase after annealing at approximately 450 Â°C. The photoluminescence peak intensity in the wavelength range of 370â€“400 nm increases with increasing anodization voltage. The photoresponsivity remains relatively flat across the bandgap region and exhibits a cutoff wavelength of approximately 400 nm under all applied bias voltages. A pronounced photoresponse is observed when the photodetectors are exposed to ultraviolet light.

title: Pan-cancer human brain metastases atlas at single-cell resolution
authors: Xudong Xing, Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (China National Center for Bioinformation), China
abstract: Brain metastases (BrMs) remain a major clinical and therapeutic challenge in patients with metastatic cancers. However, advances in our understanding of BrM have been hampered by the constrained sample size and resolution of BrM profiling studies. Here, we perform integrative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis on 108 BrM samples and 111 primary tumor (PTs) samples to investigate the characteristics and remodeling of cell states and composition across cancer lineages and subsets. Recurring and enriched features of malignant cells are increased chromosomal instability, marked proliferative and angiogenic hallmarks, and adoption of a neural-like BrM-associated metaprogram. Immunosuppressive myeloid and stromal subsets dominate the BrM tumor microenvironment, which are associated with poor prognosis and resistance to immunotherapy. Furthermore, five distinct BrM ecotypes are identified, correlating with specific histopathological patterns and clinical characteristics. This work defines hallmarks of BrM biology across cancer types and suggests that shared dependencies may exist, which may be exploited clinically.

title: PGCC Explorer: An Interactive Web Platform for Integrative Analysis of Drug Responses in Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells
authors: Li-Ju Wang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Hsiao-Chun Chen, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Chien-Hung Shih, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yuan Zhang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Huikang Ye, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Ying-Ju Lai, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yushu Ma, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Tiffany Habib, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Hsi-Chun Wang, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yu-Chih Chen, University of Pittsburgh, United States; Yu-Chiao Chiu, University of Pittsburgh, United States
abstract: Polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs), typically arising from whole-genome duplication, are major drivers of therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence. Building on our recently published high-throughput single-cell drug screening platform and ongoing efforts to profile PGCC responses across multiple cell lines representing diverse cancer lineages, we developed an interactive web-based platform that enables integrative analysis and visualization of these data. The platform integrates high-throughput PGCC drug screening results with multi-omic features curated from public cancer data resources, including somatic mutations, copy number alterations, gene expression profiles, and pathway activity scores. It supports two primary analysis modules: (1) a gene- or pathway-centric module that identifies compounds whose anti-PGCC activity is associated with specific molecular features, and (2) a compound-centric module that identifies genes or pathways linked to the activity of a selected compound. Statistical comparisons, interactive visualizations, and annotations from external knowledge bases enable users to explore drug-feature relationships and generate new hypotheses. The platform facilitates systematic investigation of PGCC vulnerabilities through data-driven exploration. Example analyses demonstrate that compounds targeting oxidative stress response and cytoskeletal remodeling pathways preferentially suppress PGCC-enriched populations, consistent with their structural plasticity and adaptive signaling. Integration with baseline pharmacogenomic datasets further distinguishes PGCC-selective inhibitors from nonselective cytotoxic agents, supporting the prioritization of therapeutic candidates. In summary, this interactive web resource provides an accessible and scalable framework for analyzing the molecular and pharmacologic landscape of polyploid giant cancer cells. By integrating our existing and ongoing high-throughput datasets with multi-omic data, it accelerates the discovery of biomarkers and therapeutic strategies to overcome treatment resistance driven by genome-doubled tumor populations.

title: CT-Derived Body Composition Combined with Tumor Metabolic Programs Identifies High-Risk Cancer Subgroups
authors: Nari Kim, Ulsan University College of Medicine, South Korea; Seongwon Na, Ulsan University College of Medicine, South Korea; Kyung Won Kim, Ulsan University College of Medicine, South Korea
abstract: Cancer prognosis is determined not only by tumor-intrinsic characteristics but also by host physiological status. Although CT-derived body composition and tumor transcriptomic data are routinely acquired in clinical practice, their integrative prognostic value has not been fully established. In this study, skeletal muscle area (SMA) derived from CT imaging was integrated with transcriptomic profiles from pan-cancer cohorts (TCGA, n=495; CPTAC-3, n=179) to investigate tumorâ€“host interactions associated with survival. Patients were initially stratified based on SMA and a tumor immune activity score (GEP). SMA was not correlated with tumor immune activity (GEP) in either cohort (TCGA: r=0.061, p=0.178; CPTAC-3: r=âˆ’0.042, p=0.577), indicating that host physiological status is not captured by conventional immune metrics. Nevertheless, combined stratification demonstrated significant differences in survival, suggesting the presence of additional tumor-intrinsic determinants. To identify such factors, an unsupervised autoencoder was applied to extract latent transcriptional programs from transcriptomic data. Among ten latent components, PC6 showed consistent and significant associations with survival across both cohorts (TCGA: HR=1.191, p=0.032; CPTAC-3: HR=1.404, p=0.012). Pathway enrichment analyses indicated that PC6 represents a Warburg-like metabolic program associated with glycolysis, hypoxia, and lactate transport. Integration of SMA and PC6 identified a high-risk subgroup characterized by low muscle mass and elevated metabolic activity, consistent with an aggressive tumorâ€“host metabolic phenotype. These findings define a tumorâ€“host metabolic axis that refines prognostic stratification beyond conventional approaches. This framework, based on routinely available clinical data, provides a scalable and clinically translatable strategy for identifying high-risk patients and supporting personalized treatment planning.

title: Mechanism-based CSF Proteomics Subtyping for Precision Medicine in Parkinson’s Disease
authors: Yonghun Son, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea; Manyoung Han, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea; Doheon Lee, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea
abstract: Parkinsonâ€™s disease (PD) is a heterogeneous disorder with diverse underlying biological mechanisms, challenging diagnosis and treatment. Although precision medicine approaches are needed, fully individualized modeling remains costly, and existing PD subtyping often lacks mechanistic interpretability. To address these limitations, we propose a biologically interpretable subtyping framework based on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomics, reflecting the molecular landscape of the CNS. Using CSF proteomic data from 843 individuals in the PPMI cohort (4,083 proteins), we mapped proteins to biological processes (BPs) via a knowledge-based annotation framework and constructed a patient-by-BP score matrix. Differentially expressed BPs between PD and controls (n = 456) were selected, and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) was applied to derive latent biological axes. Patients were then clustered into four subtypes in this reduced space. Each subtype was characterized through CSF biomarkers, clinical measures (MoCA, MDS-UPDRS, SCOPA-AUT), and pathway-level interpretation. One subtype exhibited elevated Î±-synuclein and tau levels, an atypical pattern in PD, enriched for protein transport and processing programs. An inflammation-associated subtype exhibited the poorest clinical outcomes and showed the highest proximity to levodopa-related drugs, suggesting increased reliance on dopaminergic pathways. A third subtype was enriched for proteostasis-related processes, including chaperone activity and proteasome regulation, and showed high proximity to MT101, a drug targeting proteostasis-related mechanism. The fourth subtype showed enrichment of coagulation and hemostasis regulatory processes, indicating potential vascularâ€“coagulation dysregulation. In summary, our BP-based stratification provides a mechanistically interpretable and clinically relevant disease taxonomy, representing a vital intermediate step toward patient-specific precision medicine in PD.

title: Single-cell Multiome Analysis of Pten-driven Metastatic Prostate Cancer Mouse Model Reveals Alterations in Tumor Microenvironment
authors: Savannah Washburn, Center for Prostate Disease Research, Henry M Jackson Foundation, United States; Daniel R. Schmidt, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, United States; Elise G. DeArment, Center for Prostate Disease Research, Henry M Jackson Foundation, United States; Aditi Shirke, Center for Prostate Disease Research, Henry M Jackson Foundation, United States; Kathryn Echandia-Monroe, Center for Prostate Disease Research, Henry M Jackson Foundation, United States; Chloe Springer, Center for Prostate Disease Research, Henry M Jackson Foundation, United States; Matthew G. Vander Heiden, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, United States; Xiaofeng A. Su, Center for Prostate Disease Research, Henry M Jackson Foundation, MIT, NCI, United States
abstract: Background: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common form of cancer in men and affects over one million men globally every year. The complete interplay of transcriptional and epigenomic reprograming promoting metastasis of PCa with loss of PTEN remains understudied. Single-nuclear (sn) Multiome technology, combining snRNA and snATAC sequencing, provides a unique opportunity to dissect the transcriptional and epigenetic drivers of aggressive PCa. Methods: An in house established Pten-/- PCa genetically engineered mouse model cohort with end-point primary tumor samples and metastatic cancer samples were subjected to 10XGenomics Multiome analysis. A comparative and systematic framework was developed to evaluate the effect of how different methods, approaches, and parameters cluster the data. The top clustering parameters based on the highest median Adjusted Rand Index were evaluated and annotated. The final set of clusters were determined for each modality, the primary prostate tumors, and the combined primary prostate tumor and metastatic samples. Results: The snRNA-seq clustering results revealed heterogenous immune cell proportions across primary tumors. Cell-cell communication analysis confirmed enrichment of immune system engagement, extracellular matrix remodeling, and plasticity-related pathway enrichment across various cell populations in the mice with metastatic cancer. Furthermore, transitional cell types with stem-like signatures were also identified with the high-confident clustering under this framework confirmed by snATAC-seq and histopathological evaluation. Conclusions: Future work to evaluate the effect of different clustering parameters/approaches and integration between snRNA- and snATAC-seq data will be performed to identify robust drivers for metastatic progression.

title: Transfer Learning–Enabled Prediction of Drug–Target Interactions for Data-Scarce Mitochondrial One-Carbon Pathway Enzymes
authors: Alperen Dalkiran, The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom; Takugo Cho, University of Chicago, United States; Volkan Atalay, Loyola University Chicago, United States; Kun Woo D Shin, University of Chicago, United States; Robert Hamanaka, University of Chicago, United States; Gokhan M Mutlu, University of Chicago, United States; Rengul Cetin Atalay, University of Chicago, United States
abstract: Predicting drugâ€“target interactions (DTIs) for understudied enzymes remains a fundamental challenge in computational drug discovery. Mitochondrial one-carbon (1C) metabolism which supplies glycine, reducing equivalents, and 1C units essential for nucleotide biosynthesis, is a therapeutically relevant pathway in cancer and fibrosis, yet its key enzymes SHMT2 and MTHFD2 lack sufficient DTI data for standard deep learning approaches. We present a transfer learning framework for DTI prediction on these two pharmacologically understudied enzymes. DTI was formulated as binary classification using deep feedforward neural networks (DFNNs) with Chemprop-derived molecular representations. Source models were pretrained on ChEMBL-derived, EC-matched enzyme families (EC 2.1.-.- for SHMT1/2; EC 1.5.1.- and EC 3.5.4.- for MTHFD2), achieving strong baseline performance (MCC = 0.713 and 0.902, respectively). Models were then fine-tuned on minimal target-specific data: 6 SHMT1-derived actives as a SHMT2 proxy and 29 MTHFD2 actives, each balanced with inactives, evaluating both full fine-tuning and frozen-feature-extractor modes. Transfer learning substantially outperformed de novo training. For SHMT1/2, training from scratch (10 compounds) yielded MCC = 0.0, while transfer learning reached MCC = 0.2â€“0.308. For MTHFD2, de novo training (50 compounds) achieved MCC = 0.775, versus MCC = 1.0 under both transfer modes. Virtual screening of approved DrugBank compounds identified six candidates for experimental validation. In vitro validation confirmed that three candidates significantly reduced TGF-Î²â€“induced glycine accumulation and collagen synthesis in human lung fibroblasts. This work establishes transfer learning as a strategy for DTI prediction in data-scarce metabolic enzymes and demonstrates a computational-to-experimental strategy.

title: Network-guided assessment of outpatient healthcare utilization among Explosive Ordnance Disposal Veterans.
authors: Jeffrey Page, Complex Exposures Threats Center of Excellence (VA), United States; Drew Delp, Complex Exposures Threats Center of Excellence (VA), United States
abstract: Background. Healthcare decision support systems have yet to effectively describe the relationship between Veterans Affairs (VA) healthcare utilization (HCU) and prior military occupational exposures. This work applied novel methods to predict healthcare demands to support proactive case screening and targeted research recruitment for a high-exposure Veteran cohort. Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) technicians are a unique population with specialized operational demands and a broad spectrum of potential hazards. Methods. Records from 4,100 male EOD Veterans were analyzed using scale-invariant deployment metrics and clinical encounter identifiers (VA Stop Codes). Branch-stratified, multivariate linear regressions assessed five deployment metrics as predictors of all stop code HCU. Results. Among Air Force EOD Veterans, average dwell time (i.e., time between deployments) was the strongest predictor of total HCU, whereas mean deployment duration was the major driver for Army EOD Veterans. Varimax rotated principal component analysis produced two components explaining the variance in the cohortâ€™s deployment profiles. K-means clustering defined three deployment-based subgroups. A Spearman cooccurrence network was used to identify these Veteransâ€™ most prominent HCU pattern, resulting in a 43-node module centered around primary care and mental health services. HCU differences between clusters were tested via Tukeyâ€™s test, finding Veterans in cluster one had lower outpatient HCU than cluster two (p Conclusion. These methods highlighted the healthcare needs of EOD Veterans and found relationships between their individual deployment history and downstream outpatient utilization. This approach may be applied to other cohorts with unique exposure profiles to forecast and prioritize healthcare resources.

title: Modeling large longitudinal image data to predict treatment response in the eye
authors: Meha Patel, The Lowy Medical Research Institute, La Jolla, CA, United States, United States; Kristin Raming, University of Bonn, University Hospital Bonn, Department of Ophthalmology, Bonn, Germany, Germany; Lea Scheppke, The Lowy Medical Research Institute, La Jolla, CA, United States, United States; Thomas Aaberg, Neurotech Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Cumberland, RI, United States, United States; Martin Friedlander, The Lowy Medical Research Institute, La Jolla, CA, United States, United States; Simone Tzaridis, The Lowy Medical Research Institute, La Jolla, CA, United States, United States; Roberto Bonelli, The Lowy Medical Research Institute, La Jolla, CA, United States, United States
abstract: Macular telangiectasia type 2 (MacTel) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that leads to progressive loss of central vision. Recently, a phase 3 clinical trial showed that ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) results in a slowed progression rate on loss of the retinal photoreceptor Ellipsoid Zone (EZ). We present a study where we evaluate whether additional structural and functional outcomes and phenotypic characteristics could be used to determine which patients respond best to CNTF treatment. We included 32 clinically graded phenotypic variables on 456 eyes (117 CNTF-treated, 111 sham, and 228 fellow eyes), including longitudinal observations with a mean follow-up of 30 months. Analysis of treatment response was conducted on the 117 CNTF-treated eyes. Response was defined as the difference between the observed and predicted progression rate. We calculated the observed progression rate by fitting a linear model to the EZ-loss area over time. A model was trained to obtain the predicted progression rate from the initial EZ-loss area. Effect of clinical features at baseline on treatment response was assessed by fitting a linear model. We observe structural features such as macular pigment presence in the fellow eye as well as functional characteristics such as difficulty reading and mean reading speed, to be predictive of patientsâ€™ future CNTF response. Future work will involve calculating an in-silico global severity score to determine patient global response beyond simple EZ loss areas, as well as finding features able to be used for patient-tailored clinical recommendations of CNTF effectiveness.

title: What Makes a Clinical Feature Matter? Evaluating Diagnostic Influence via Controlled Perturbations
authors: Xiao Yu Zhang, University of British Columbia, Canada; Jian Zhu, University of British Columbia , Canada; Wyeth Wasserman, University of British Columbia , Canada
abstract: Biomedical text mining has made substantial progress in extracting structured clinical information from narratives and scientific literature. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to how extracted phenotypic evidence influences downstream diagnostic retrieval, particularly in incomplete, evolving, or uncertain clinical presentations. This limits the interpretability and auditability of phenotype-driven diagnostic systems in real-world clinical settings. In this work, we present an interaction-aware evaluation framework for analyzing phenotype contribution and diagnostic hypothesis stability in phenotype-based retrieval systems derived from clinical text. Building on structured representations of rare disease case reports aligned to standardized biomedical ontologies, we investigate how subsets of phenotypic evidence support or destabilize retrieved diagnostic hypotheses under controlled perturbations. We introduce a suite of clinically motivated perturbation strategies to evaluate retrieval robustness under incomplete or ambiguous evidence. We further analyze how perturbations alter support for leading diagnostic hypotheses and characterize patterns of diagnostic drift across related disorders. Our results suggest that retrieval stability often depends on a limited subset of interacting phenotypes, while some highly weighted features may reflect retrieval shortcuts or redundancy rather than clinically distinctive evidence. This work bridges biomedical text mining, interpretable retrieval, and clinical decision support by providing a framework to audit how structured phenotypic evidence is used in downstream diagnostic systems. We argue that evaluating diagnostic hypothesis stability under phenotype perturbation is an important step toward more reliable and clinically interpretable AI-assisted rare disease diagnosis.

title: Dementia Risk Prediction using Electronic Health Records Data from the Hong Kong Hospital Authority
authors: Muhammad Danish, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Lihua Huang, GenomeLytix, LTD, Hong Kong; Tung Wai Auyueng, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Jenny Lee, Hospital Authority, Hong Kong; Timothy Kwok, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Jill Abrigo, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Yingying Wei, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Cecilia Lo, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Erik Fung, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, China
abstract: Dementia is the most common neurological degenerative disease among the elderly and severely impacts life quality. However, the mechanism of dementia is complicated and unclear. In this project, we leverage the rich electronic health records data collected by the Hong Kong Hospital Authority from 2000 to 2020 to systematically survey the risk factors of dementia. The Hong Kong Hospital Authority covers over 90% of the healthcare services in Hong Kong, thus providing an unprecedented opportunity for studying the dementia risk at a population level. Nevertheless, despite the unified health care system, the data provided by the Hong Kong Hospital Authority face various challenges of missing data as electronic health data always do. By taking four birth cohorts separated by 10 years, we use landmark analysis to investigate how the age-dependent associations between the onset of dementia and cardiovascular-related comorbidities and prescriptions vary across cohorts. Moreover, for different landmark ages, we built cox and survival random forest models to dynamically predict the dementia risk according to the evolving disease histories for the Chinese population.

title: A powerful multi-omic AI framework for Blood-Based Cancer Screening and Tissue-of-Origin Prediction
authors: Sayak Dhar, Strand Life Sciences, India; Lavanya Nemani, Strand Life Sciences, India; Shekhar Nath, Strand Life Sciences, India; Keshav Agarwal, Strand Life Sciences, India; Advika Lakshman, Strand Life Sciences, India; Shardul Kamble, Strand Life Sciences, India; Swaraj Basu, Strand Life Sciences, India; Prakash Hiremath, Strand Life Sciences, India; Nihesh Rathod, Strand Life Sciences, India; Stan Iyer, Strand Life Sciences, India; Radhakrishna Bettadapura, Strand Life Sciences, United States; Ramesh Hariharan, Strand Life Sciences, India; Badri Padhukasahasram, Strand Life Sciences, India
abstract: Early cancer detection from cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is inherently difficult because circulating tumor-derived DNA is typically present at very low abundance, especially in early-stage malignancy. While methylation patterns carry powerful tissue-specific regulatory signals, fragmentomics provides complementary information reflecting the effects of chromatin re-organization and altered nuclease activity in tumors. Existing approaches often rely on task-specific models and individual â€œomicsâ€ classes and fail to capture the complex, hierarchical dependencies across CpG sites, genomic regions and cross-modal relationships. We pre-trained a Bert-based foundation model on large-scale tissue methylation data using a self-supervised objective designed to capture co-methylation structure. It predicts CpG methylation states at nearby and distal sites using self-attention within local contexts and cross-attention over CpG query indices. Here, we present a comprehensive multi-omic computational framework for early cancer screening and tissue of origin (TOO) prediction that integrates embeddings from this model with fragmentomics. Our approach aims to unify a wide range of features including CpG site-level embeddings, fragment-level methylation summaries, methylation haplotype frequencies, global fragment size distribution, fragment breakpoint motifs, fragment end motifs, and fragment size coverage etc using a tabular data foundation model classifier (tabPFN) to maximize classification accuracy. For early cancer detection in an Indian cohort (~688 cases, 326 controls), the integrated method achieved 92.2% sensitivity at 95% specificity with a tissue-of-origin classification accuracy of 75.5%. Comparisons demonstrated significant performance improvements relative to published fragmentomics only methods such as DELFI as well as methylation only baselines (~15-20% boost in cancer classification F1 scores, ~10-30% increase in TOO accuracy).

title: Spatial Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Tumor–Immune Landscape Associated with Response to Proton Radiotherapy and Atezolizumab-Bevacizumab in Advanced Liver Cancer: a Pilot Study
authors: Hendrick Gao-Min Lim, Department of Medical Imaging and Radiological Sciences, Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Taiwan; Chen-Yang Huang, Division of Hematology-Oncology, Department of Internal Medicine, Linkou Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Taiwan; Rodney Cheng-En Hsieh, Department of Radiation Oncology, Chang Gung Memorial Hospital at Linkou and Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan, Taiwan
abstract: Advanced liver cancer exhibits substantial immune heterogeneity in response to combined Atezolizumab (anti-programmed death-ligand 1; anti-PD-L1) and Bevacizumab (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor; anti-VEGF) therapy. While proton radiotherapy (PRT) effectively treats localized tumors and potentially modulates the immune landscape, the spatially resolved characterizations that differentiate complete response (CR) from partial response (PR) are inadequately defined. In this pilot study, we conducted high-resolution (2 µm) spatial transcriptomic profiling with image-based cell segmentation on CR and PR biopsy sample from a patient treated with PRT and Atezolizumab-Bevacizumab. Following quality control and batch correction, identified cell clusters were automatically annotated based on specific marker genes to explore preliminary cell-type proportions and spatial proximity analysis. We observed a higher T-cell proportion and a depleted tumor fraction in CR, potentially indicating that PD-L1 inhibition by Atezolizumab may facilitate T-cell-mediated tumor clearance. CR also featured a difference of progenitor-VEGF-associated cells proportion, suggesting that localized VEGF modulation by Bevacizumab may contribute to suppressed angiogenesis. Notably, spatial analysis exposed high proximity between tumor cells, T cells, and progenitor-VEGF-associated cells in PR, representing early indication of active immune-tumor engagement, whereas CR exhibited increased spatial distance, reflecting a possible tumor eradication and tissue restoration. Our initial observations suggest that therapeutic success is characterized by a transition from high proximity immune engagement (PR) to a state of clearance and vascular normalization (CR). While further validation in larger cohorts is required, this pilot study provides valuable spatial insights into the potential mechanisms underlying combined treatment efficacy in advanced liver cancer.

title: Investigating the diagnostic potential of 14 pan-cancer DNA-methylation biomarkers for early detection of cancer in RUNX1 FPD patients with CHIP
authors: Chandra Mani Kafle, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States; Sara R. Bang-Christensen, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States; Sabina Pathan, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States; Sara A. Grimm, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, National Institutes of Health, Research Triangle Park, NC, United States; Brian D. Bennett, National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, National Institutes of Health, Research Triangle Park, NC, United States; Ana Catarina Menezes, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States; Erica Bresciani, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States; Paul P. Liu, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States; Laura Elnitski, The National Human Genome Research Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States
abstract: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP), a condition characterized by increased clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells, affects approximately 10% of people over age 70 and is associated with increased risk for cardiovascular disease, inflammation, and hematologic malignancies. The presence of CHIP in individuals with preexisting conditions, such as RUNX1 familial platelet disorder (FPD), further increases the risk of developing hematologic malignancies, most commonly myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia. Molecular hallmarks of CHIP include somatic mutations in genes involved in DNA methylation. We hypothesize that FPD patients with CHIP harbor differential methylation patterns compared with FPD patients without CHIP in CpG loci previously associated with multiple cancer types. With the goal of developing a non-invasive diagnostic panel for early detection of cancer in FPD patients with CHIP, we performed targeted methylation sequencing of 14 CpG loci in DNA isolated from PBMCs of healthy controls (n=23), RUNX1 FPD patients with (n=24) or without CHIP (n=30). We developed a computational pipeline to assess the methylation density at these pan-cancer biomarker CpG loci and evaluate probe performance using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Our pilot study of 8 patients with CHIP has identified 7 distinctively methylated CpG loci compared to healthy controls. We will further investigate whether biomarker methylation results vary across all cases, and whether the pathological heterogeneity contributes to methylation differences. Findings from this study will evaluate the potential of the targeted DNA methylation assay for non-invasive approach for early detection of cancer in high-risk FPD patients with CHIP.

title: Integrative model explains drug indications and side effects by learning connections from drugs to disease genes
authors: Panagiotis Nikolaos Lalagkas, University of Massachusetts Lowell, United States; Rachel Melamed, University of Massachusetts Lowell, United States
abstract: Most clinical trials fail due to efficacy and safety concerns. Human genetics can address both failure modes: disease-associated genes are promising therapeutic targets and predict drug side effects. However, because the same genetic signal underlies both outcomes, there is a need for methods that can distinguish which genes, when targeted, contribute to therapeutic benefit versus adverse effects on disease. We build upon DraphNet, our previously developed model that maps drug molecular effects onto disease genes to generate two gene sets per drug: one linked to its therapeutic effects (IND genes) and one linked to its side effects (SE genes). We show that IND and SE genes overlap for 76% of the drugs (231/304; compared to random genes), suggesting that efficacy and toxicity frequently stem from common genetic mechanisms. Moreover, we show that drugs with more similar IND genes also have more similar SE genes (Ï=0.57, p

title: A Network Control Framework for Brain-Based Drug Discovery
authors: Vena Martinez, The University of Texas Medical Branch, United States; Nathan Smith, Baylor College of Medicine, United States; Sierra Miller, Texas A&M University, United States; Jennifer Schwarz, Syracuse University, United States; Kathryn Cunningham, The University of Texas Medical Branch, United States; Ardavan Borzou, Compu-Flair, United States; Jonathan Hommel, The University of Texas Medical Branch, United States
abstract: Background Despite decades of scientific advances, effective drug development for brain disorders remains limited, leaving a substantial unmet clinical need across conditions such as neurodegenerative diseases, mental illnesses, and substance use disorders. Recent advances in computational modeling, large-scale data integration, and network control theory (NCT) offer a powerful framework to address these challenges by enabling the identification of key nodes and control points within brain circuits that govern behavior and disease states. By leveraging these approaches to predict and modulate system-level dynamics, there is a growing opportunity to develop more precise, mechanism-based interventions and fundamentally transform how we uncover treatments for brain disorders. Here, we applied NCT to predict pharmacotherapeutic targets in the brain that will decrease unhealthy, palatable food consumption in mice. Our goal was to identify the controllable network hubs in the brain involved in consuming palatable food and to apply an external input or stimulus that drives the network to reduce palatable food consumption in mice. We hypothesized that the application of this computationally derived external input would drive the network state during palatable food consumption back to baseline to decrease palatable food consumption in mice. Methods First, we established a brain-wide network connectome using the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (ABA), which mapped brain regions (217 total regions) and their connectivity. Next, we incorporated brain-wide expression of cFos as a surrogate measure of neuronal activation in mice consuming a standard lean diet versus mice consuming palatable food. This enabled us to establish the state of the networkâ€™s nodes at baseline and with palatable food, respectively. In order to precisely define the necessary external input, we applied the NCT framework to identify brain regions that need significant computationally inputs to drive the states of the nodes of the network from the palatable food state to the baseline state. We rank brain regions based on this potential controllability. Then we assessed the brain region expression pattern of 7,764 genes from ABA to identify those highly expressed in our top controllable brain regions and computationally derived which genes were predicted to most effectively return the palatable food network state to the baseline. Lastly, we empirically tested the computationally predicted gene stimulation on the network state using cFos immunofluorescence and the targeted behavioral outcome, palatable food consumption. We used a pharmacological agent that has not yet been tested in palatable food consumption and already in unrelated clinical trials, providing translational relevance. Results The top ten identified controllability brain regions are, in order, caudoputamen, olfactory bulb, nucleus accumbens, periaqueductal gray, interpeduncular nucleus, intermediate reticular nucleus, lateral septal nucleus, lateral geniculate complex, infralimbic area, and supraoptic nucleus. Data show that the gene with the greatest probability of driving the palatable food network state back to baseline is Pde10a and would require inhibition. Empirically, Pde10a inhibitor TAK-063 (0.3 mg/kg, i.p.) blocked palatable food-induced cFos expression in the caudoputamen, dorsal lateral and medial striatum, and the nucleus accumbens of mice (two-way ANOVA, p Conclusions The application of network control theory provided accurate parameters for pharmacological intervention, driving the palatable food network state towards baseline and effectively modulating the targeted behavior. This methodology can be applied to virtually any brain disorder, granting a broad application of this framework. This work provides theoretical and empirical evidence of the efficacy of network control theory in brain drug discovery, laying a foundation for rapid functionally based and translationally relevant drug development for a wide range brain disorders.

title: Proteomic Analysis of Human Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Brain Implicates Proteasome and Ribosome Dysfunction in Disease Progression
authors: Helen E. Pennington, Boston University, United States; Dillon Shapiro, Boston University, United States; Jenny Empawi, Boston University, United States; Nurgul Aytan, VA Boston Healthcare System, VA Bedford Healthcare System, and Boston University, United States; Victor Alvarez, VA Boston Healthcare System, VA Bedford Healthcare System, and Boston University, United States; Jesse Mez, Boston University, United States; Michael L. Alosco, Boston University, United States; Xiaoling Zhang, Boston University, United States; Ann C. McKee, VA Bedford Healthcare System and Boston University, United States; Thor D. Stein, VA Boston Healthcare System, VA Bedford Healthcare System, and Boston University, United States; Jonathan D. Cherry, VA Boston Healthcare System and Boston University, United States; Adam Labadorf, VA Boston Healthcare System and Boston University, United States
abstract: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease associated with repeated head impacts (RHI) commonly experienced by contact sport athletes, military personnel, and domestic abuse victims. Despite growing recognition of CTE, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression remain poorly understood. This study aims to identify proteomic alterations associated with CTE pathology and clinical features to elucidate key biological pathways involved in disease pathogenesis. SomaScan 7k high-throughput proteomics was performed on 204 dorsolateral prefrontal cortex samples from the Boston University CTE Center Brain Bank. We identified differentially expressed proteins associated with CTE, hyperphosphorylated tau (ptau) pathology, duration of contact sports play, dementia status, and Cognitive Difficulty Scale (CDS) scores. Gene set enrichment analysis revealed that proteasome subunit proteins and related pathways were strongly associated with CTE progression and correlated with years of contact sports play. Reduction in ribosomal proteins and pathways was closely associated with ptau burden. Additionally, multiple models demonstrated significant alterations in MAPK-related cell signaling pathways. These findings advance our understanding of CTE progression and identify biological and molecular processes correlated with key pathological features of the disease. Validation of these results could inform the development of diagnostics and treatments for CTE.

title: Pharmacogenomics-Guided Therapy for Complex Diseases: Applications in Cardiovascular Disease, Breast Cancer, and Mental Health
authors: Sara Munir, Faculty of Pharmacy ,university of the Punjab, lahore 54000, Pakistan, Pakistan
abstract: Introduction: Pharmacogenomics-based therapy is a revolutionary perspective of precision medicine, as it allows clinicians to personalize drug therapy based on patient genetic characteristics. The paper assessed the clinical and economic outcomes of the application of genotype-based therapy in three conditions of complex diseases, including cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and mental health disorders, based on primary patient data in tertiary hospitals in Pakistan. Methods Four hundred and fifty patients were recruited and put into a pharmacogenomics-guided (PGx) cohort or a standard therapy cohort. The influence of genetic variations on the drug metabolite and response to the treatment was studied on CYP2C19, SLCO1B1, VKORC1, CYP2D6, UGT1A1, and SLC6A4. Results The group directed by the PGx showed much more therapeutic efficacy, lower adverse drug reactions, and better cost-effectiveness in comparison with conventional care ( p. 0.05). Regression analysis was used to confirm that certain variations CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 among others were good predictors of clinical outcomes. Conclusion These developments underscore the utility of pharmacogenomics in the improvement of drug safety and efficacy, minimization of the healthcare costs and sealing the outlook of the gap between genomic science and clinical practice. The paper highlights the need to ensure the incorporation of pharmacogenomic testing into the healthcare systems particularly in developing nations as a way of encouraging evidence-based and customized therapeutics of complicated diseases.

title: Cellular Mechanisms Underlying Melanoma Brain Metastasis
authors: Bengi Ruken Yavuz, NCI, NIH, United States; Hyunbum Jang, NCI, NIH, United States; Ruth Nussinov, NCI, NIH, United States
abstract: Brain metastasis is a major contributor to melanoma-related mortality, arising from both genomic alterations and dynamic adaptations to the brain microenvironment. Tumor cells must cross the bloodâ€“brain barrier and exploit brain-specific signaling and metabolic landscapes to establish metastases. Brain metastases display molecular and phenotypic programs distinct from other organs, reflecting pre-existing and acquired mutations during progression. We analyzed primary melanoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic brain tumors genomic datasets to identify mutated proteins and signaling pathways that are common to or distinct among these tumor types. Our comprehensive computational analyses uncovered key pathways and proteins associated with brain metastasis. Brain metastases exhibit unique mutational landscapes and convergent alterations in neurotrophin, MAPK, and PI3K/AKT signaling compared with primary and metastatic melanoma. Proteins especially frequent in brain metastases pathways support survival, proliferation, and adaptation in the brain microenvironment. Pharmacology-wise, rational strategies such as combining c-KIT and VEGFR inhibitors can suppress converging oncogenic pathways and mitigate resistance in advanced melanoma. Co-targeting neurotrophin receptors with MAPK pathway members, particularly in combination with BRAF inhibitors, appears a promising approach for treating melanoma brain metastases. Our findings underscore the molecular heterogeneity of melanoma brain metastases, shaped by interconnected signaling networks, and reveal therapeutic targets that may diverge from those in other metastatic sites.

title: Quantifying Drug Combination Efficacy with Dose-Response Surface Metrics in Precision Oncology
authors: Taeho Kim, Department of Human Genetics and Utah Center for Genetic Discovery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA, South Korea; Gabor Marth, Department of Human Genetics and Utah Center for Genetic Discovery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA, United States
abstract: Quantifying drug combinations remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Most existing metrics focus on drug interaction (synergistic, additive, or antagonistic effects), but do not capture combination efficacy or potency. To address this limitation, we propose two dose-response surface-based metrics for evaluating drug pairs. First, analogous to IC50/EC50 for single agents, we define the minimum normalized dose sum required to achieve 50% tumor viability reduction. This is computed as: sum = dose(drug1)/IC50(drug1) + dose(drug2)/IC50(drug2), where IC50 values are derived from dose-response curves of single drugs (with the counterpart drug at zero dose). This metric captures the combined potency of two agents on a shared scale. Second, analogous to the area under the curve (AUC), we adopt the volume under the surface (VUC) to quantify overall efficacy across the full dose-response landscape. Together, these metrics provide complementary views of drug pair evaluation. We further developed dose-aware deep learning models to predict tumor viability and derive these metrics using the DrugComb datasets, employing drug-pair-blind splits to evaluate generalization to never-before-seen pairs. Drug pairs in the test set were ranked using median metric values. Although the top-ranked pairs differed between metrics, both metrics prioritized drug combinations based on potency and efficacy rather than interaction effects alone. Notably, rankings based on observed versus predicted metrics were not fully consistent, despite strong overall agreement (Pearson r > 0.9). This discrepancy highlights limitations in metric stability and motivates future work to refine metric definitions and improve predictive modeling.

title: Generalist large language models complement tailor-made predictors for tumor genomics interpretation
authors: Jennifer Yu, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center/Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Madison Darmofal, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Michele Waters, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; January Choy, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Thinh Tran, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Chenlian Fu, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center/Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Leah Morales, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center/Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Kaicheng U, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center/Weill Cornell Medicine, United States; Ross Levine, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Nikolaus Schultz, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Michael Berger, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Quaid Morris, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Justin Jee, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Tumor genomic profiling guides cancer treatment, but specialized bioinformatics algorithms are often required to interpret these data. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) are trained on large, heterogeneous corpora to acquire broad knowledge and perform a wide range of tasks. However, the degree to which LLMs can interpret tumor genomic data or improve the generalizability of supervised algorithms remains unclear. We benchmarked multiple LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, Claude 4.5 Opus, DeepSeek-Distill-32B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-235B-vl, MedGemma-27B) in zero-shot settings against state-of-the-art supervised models across three clinically important, real-world genomics tasks: (i) tumor vs non-tumor mutations classification (n=34,415 variants; 16,383 samples), (ii) driver vs. passenger mutation classification (n=13,470 variants; 10,752 samples), and (iii) cancer type inference from genomic profiles (n=102,791 samples across 19 institutions and 34 cancer types). The best LLMs achieved performance approaching specialized models: Qwen3-30B reached 0.926 F1 score for tumor mutations classification (vs. 0.927 for MetaCH), GPT-5 reached 0.804 F1 score for driver classification (vs. 0.897 for AlphaMissense), and GPT-5 reached 0.488 overall weighted F1 score for cancer type prediction (vs. 0.570 for GDD-ENS). Ensemble models combining LLM and specialized model outputs consistently outperformed specialized models alone across all tasks in 10-fold cross-validation. In leave-one-center-out cross-validation for cancer type prediction, ensemble models improved accuracy by an average of 20.4% across institutions, although additional supervised learning for GDD-ENS using institution-specific datasets abrogated the benefits of an ensemble model including LLM outputs. Overall, general purpose LLMs show surprisingly strong performance and can improve supervised models for clinical tumor genomic interpretation.

title: Ancient Viral Fossils as Biological Clocks: Multi-Modal Retroelement-Based Biological Age Acceleration in Myasthenia Gravis
authors: Aram Ghulijanyan, George Washington University, Milken Institute School of Public Health (PhD student), United States; Karli Gilbert, George Washington University, Laboratory for Myasthenia Gravis Research, United States; Ali Taheriyoun, The George Washington University, Milken Institute School of Public Health (Postdoctoral Research Associate), United States; Keith Crandall, George Washington University, Milken Institute School of Public Health (Professor), United States; Linda Kusner, George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, United States; Ali Rahnavard, George Washington University, Milken Institute School of Public Health (Associate Professor), United States; Henry Kaminski, George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, Department of Neurology, United States
abstract: Retroelements - ancient mobile DNA sequences constituting nearly half the human genome - are epigenetically silenced from birth and progressively derepressed with age, making them a molecular substrate for biological aging clocks. Methylation-based epigenetic clocks were applied to 90 myasthenia gravis (MG) patients at baseline, consistently detecting biological age acceleration: the pan-tissue Horvath clock showed +2.5 years (p To capture dynamic retroelement activity beyond stable CpG erosion, we trained an independent transcriptomic clock measuring HERV and LINE RNA expression - a direct readout of transcriptional derepression at retroelement loci - in 159 healthy donors (r=0.585, MAE ≈ 10 years). In MG patients at baseline (n=58), this clock revealed a substantially larger acceleration of +15.1 years (p Longitudinally, transcriptomic age acceleration declined from ~15 to ~10 years by 12 months in both the thymectomy+prednisone and prednisone-alone arms (p=0.031), with a partial rebound by 36 months; thymectomy offered no additional benefit over prednisone alone (interaction p=0.51). These findings establish retroelement-based biological aging as a robust, treatment-responsive, multi-modal molecular phenotype in MG, with potential as a prognostic and treatment-monitoring biomarker.

title: Host transcriptomic signatures of viable infection and post-treatment lesion conversion in a porcine model of neurocysticercosis
authors: Carla Apaza Quiroz, Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, Peru; Cielo Rojas Portocarrero, Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, Peru
abstract: Neurocysticercosis (NCC), caused by Taenia solium infection of the central nervous system, is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic low- and middle-income regions and is increasingly identified in non-endemic countries through migration. Clinical expression is variable, reflecting cyst location, lesion stage, and host immune response. Thus, NCC-associated pathology arises from both parasite presence and host inflammatory responses triggered during lesion degeneration or after antiparasitic therapy. However, the molecular programs underlying these transitions remain poorly defined. We performed the first bulk RNA-seq analysis on pericystic brain tissue from naturally infected pigs, a physiologically relevant model of human NCC, to characterize responses during viable infection and post-treatment lesion conversion. We compared uninfected controls (n=3), infected untreated individuals with viable cysts (n=3), and infected individuals treated with praziquantel plus albendazole (n=3). Transcript abundance was quantified with Salmon, followed by differential expression and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses. Infection was associated with transcriptional changes, including 461 upregulated and 175 downregulated genes, with enrichment of immune-associated pathways and reduced vascular and endothelial signaling. In contrast, treatment induced a more focused response, with 160 upregulated and 57 downregulated genes, marked by inflammatory activation, endothelial adhesion programs, and features consistent with blood-brain barrier remodelling. Integrated pathway analysis suggests that NCC progression is better understood as a shift between distinct lesion states rather than a linear progression from infection to recovery. These findings provide a molecular framework for understanding treatment-associated inflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and host responses that may influence neurological outcomes in NCC.

title: Multimodal Health State Modeling for Occurence Prediction of Multiple Diseases
authors: Tianhong Zhou, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China; Zhe Zhao, BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., China; Ningxuan Zhang, Department of Biochemistry, University of Oxford, China; Yuran Wang, School of Medicine, Tsinghua Medicine, Tsinghua University, China; Yin Xu, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China; Mo Chen, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China; Lungang Liang, BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., China; Sicheng Guo, BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., China; Shaojie Li, BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., China; Xi Su, BGI Genomics Co., Ltd., China; Jinmeng Jia, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China; Yilong Wang, Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University, China; Lei Wei, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China; Xuegong Zhang, Department of Automation, Tsinghua University; School of Life Sciences and School of Medicine, Tsinghua University, China
abstract: 准确描述个人健康状况需要整合多种类型的数据，包括遗传数据、分子测量和临床记录。在现实世界的队列中，这些数据往往是异质性的，仅部分观察到，收集时间不同，并在长时间随访中积累。这些特性使得联合建模多模态信息和预测未来疾病事件及其时间点难以，基于异质的遗传、分子和纵向临床数据。 我们提出了StateLM，一种用于健康状态建模和疾病预测的多模态模型。StateLM利用遗传数据（WES/PRS）、蛋白质组学和核磁共振代谢组学，以及纵向电子健康记录（EHR）来建模个体健康状态，遗传数据捕捉易感性和长期风险，蛋白质组学和代谢组学反映当前生理和分子状态，电子健康记录记录追踪临床进展。对于每个模态，StateLM 首先构建一个模态特有的表示，然后将其投影到大型语言模型的输入嵌入空间中。这些对齐的表示被组合并输入语言模型，用于联合建模和预测。基于该设计，StateLM建模了跨模态关系和时间信息，预测719个疾病事件及其发生时间，并支持部分模态缺失。 实验结果表明，StateLM在多病预测任务中表现出竞争力，并揭示了不同病态对疾病特异性的依赖性。不同疾病在多模态整合中受益程度不同，表明它们由不同的主导信号源驱动。这些发现表明，StateLM能够支持针对多种疾病的健康状态评估、疾病风险排名和随访规划。

title: FlowER: A Gate-Free, Reference-Based Framework for Detecting Phenotypic Aberrancy in Flow Cytometry Without Per-Cell Supervision
authors: Ansh Kumar, Invivoscribe, Inc., United States; Jake Silberg, Invivoscribe, Inc., United States; Meindert Niemeijer, Invivoscribe, Inc., United States; Jeffrey Miller, Invivoscribe, Inc., United States
abstract: Multiparametric flow cytometry (MFC) is widely used for measurable residual disease (MRD) assessment in hematologic malignancies, but interpretation still depends heavily on manual gating and expert-defined population boundaries. We developed FlowER, a gate-free, reference-based computational framework that quantifies single-cell phenotypic deviation from normal without predefined gates or per-cell supervision. After standard preprocessing, FlowER generates repeated low-dimensional embeddings using complementary manifold-learning methods and varied initializations, aggregates them into a consensus representation, and constructs local phenotypic fingerprints summarizing neighborhood marker expression, density, and heterogeneity. Each cell is then scored against a curated healthy reference library to produce a continuous aberrancy metric. We evaluated FlowER on 116 bone marrow specimens, including 28 normal controls, processed with a 12-color AML panel. FlowER significantly separated clinically gated MRD cells from CD45-dim background cells (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 6.288 Ã— 10^-15, Cohenâ€™s d = 1.126), with higher aberrancy scores in 90% of evaluable specimens and a median elevation of 34%; median per-sample AUC against clinically gated labels was 0.924. To assess cross-assay and cross-disease transfer, we applied the same pipeline without parameter adjustment to 58 CLL specimens, including 21 normal controls, collected with a distinct 11-color panel. FlowER again significantly separated MRD+ cells from B-cell background cells (p = 3.044 Ã— 10^-7, Cohenâ€™s d = 1.058), with higher scores in 85% of evaluable specimens and a median elevation of 57%. These results support reference-based continuous aberrancy scoring as a broadly applicable strategy for analyzing rare and heterogeneous cell populations in flow cytometry in practice.

title: Scalable Manifold Alignment of MSI and IMC data to Map Architectural Deviations in Prostate Cancer Progression
authors: Richard Dzeng, Department of Computer Science, Tufts University, United States; Divya Mirgh, Vaccine and Immunotherapy Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02129, USA., United States; Benjamin Garcia, Vaccine and Immunotherapy Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02129, USA., United States; John Nam, Vaccine and Immunotherapy Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02129, USA., United States; Erin Seeley, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, 1515 Holcombe Blvd, Unit 1471, Houston, TX 77030, United States; Chin-Lee Wu, Department of Pathology, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States; Patrick Reeves, Vaccine and Immunotherapy Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02129, USA., United States
abstract: In 2025, the American Cancer Society estimated 313,780 new cases and 35,770 deaths attributable to prostate cancer (PC). While histopathological scoring of glandular architecture remains the diagnostic standard, it fails to capture the detailed cellular and biochemical information required to distinguish between indolent and aggressive disease. This creates a significant clinical challenge in accurately assessing patient risk and therefore selecting the appropriate interventions. Together with clinical information and data from additional assays, high-dimensional imaging data can generate comprehensive patient profiles that may better assess disease progression risk and therapeutic response. In this study, we present a multi-modal imaging workflow designed to characterize the cellular and biochemical states of 300 prostate cores across four tissue microarrays (TMAs). Our approach integrates single-cell information from Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) with Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization (MALDI) Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) of N-glycans, trypsin-digested peptides, and metabolites. To unify these modalities, which differ significantly in spatial resolution and data density, we utilized the Multi-modal Image Alignment and Analysis by Information Manifolds (MIAAIM) framework. This manifold-based method enabled the compression of high-dimensional data into representative manifolds, allowing for precise, non-rigid registration of cellular and biochemical maps across the cohort. Application of MIAAIM enabled mapping of molecular signatures across histopathological scores. We identified conserved cellular and molecular niches that correlate with the transitions from healthy tissue through to high-grade de-differentiated states. Our findings demonstrate that the MIAAIM pipeline offers a scalable, high-resolution solution for quantifying the architectural and molecular deviations of aggressive prostate cancer.

title: A Modular, Mapping-Driven Pipeline for Cross-Consortium Clinical Trial Data Harmonization
authors: Kyle Rodrigues, The George Washington University, United States; Bao Duong, The George Washington University, United States; Heather Wopat, The George Washington University, United States; Kim Robien, The George Washington University, United States; Ashley Tjaden, The George Washington University, United States; Scott Evans, The George Washington University, United States
abstract: The National Cancer Institute-funded â€œExercise and Nutrition Interventions to Improve Cancer Treatment-Related Outcomesâ€ (ENICTO) Consortium is comprised of a Coordinating Center and four individual clinical trials with common research questions and goals.
