Pooling data across multi-site clinical trials such as ENICTO offers substantial statistical power for answering complex research questions, but heterogeneous data collection practices across the four individual trials (including inconsistent variable naming and measurement units, differing coding conventions and visit schedules, and incompatible instrument-level responses) present significant barriers to analysis-ready dataset construction. We present a modular, mapping-driven R pipeline designed to harmonize data across the four trials, which span eleven clinical sites and currently include >400 randomized participants. An external mapping file serves as the benchmark for all harmonization logic, enabling transparent, auditable transformations without modifying core functions. A two-pass architecture ensures correct dependency ordering: a primary pass handles value remapping and computed transformations on raw source variables, while a secondary pass resolves variables whose computation depends on harmonized outputs. This design generalizes to any harmonization context requiring derived variable computation. Across approximately 5,000 trial-specific variables, the pipeline produces a harmonized, analysis-ready dataset enabling calculation of the Consortiumâ€™s primary end point, as well as a broad set of secondary endpoints. The pipeline is intentionally modular and reusable, with a clear path toward packaging as a formal researcher-friendly R package for broader dissemination to the research community. Rigorous, reproducible data harmonization across heterogeneous clinical trials is achievable with lightweight infrastructure, thereby lowering the barrier for future consortium-level research.

title: Translational Analysis of Artemisinin as a Repurposed Therapeutic for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Utilizing MDA-MB-231 Spheroid Models
authors: Jiaa Parikh, Hunterdon Central Regional High school, United States
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer remains a clinically challenging malignancy due to limited targeted therapies and high metastasis rate. This study evaluates the translational potential of artemisinin, a repurposed antimalarial drug, as a cytotoxic agent against MDA-MB-231 breast cancer spheroids. Utilizing a quantitative in vitro model, tumor spheroids were treated with varying concentrations of artemisinin (0-25 ÂµM) to analyze dose-response relationships relevant to preclinical development. Cell viability was measured using fluorescence live/dead imaging. Statistical analysis demonstrated a significant negative correlation between artemisinin concentration and cell viability (r = -0.769, p = 0.001), indicating that increasing drug concentration enhances cytotoxicity. A critical effective range between 6.25 ÂµM and 25 ÂµM was identified, establishing a therapeutic range for further investigation. While variability was observed due to known limitations of spheroid models, including drug penetration, the overall trend remained consistent across replicated trials. This study proposes an effective concentration range that may inform future in vivo studies and nanoparticle-based delivery systems aimed at improving treatment precision. Although nanoparticle conjugation was not completed due to experimental limitations, the framework developed here supports its integration. These findings suggest artemisinin as a potential candidate for drug repurposing in oncology. Future work will focus on in vivo validation and nanoparticle-mediated delivery to improve tumor penetration and therapeutic precision. Additionally, alongside the implementation of technology, such as nanotechnology based systems, an alternative relationship to furthering the clinical capabilities of artemisinin utilized for breast cancer treatment will be shown.

title: KRAS Mutation-Driven Differences in Tumor Immunity in Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
authors: Kawther Abdilleh, Pancreatic Cancer Action Network, United States; Radu Tanasa, Inflexa AI, Romania; Despina Siolas, Weill Cornell Medicine, United States
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest malignancies, with limited effective treatment options. Over 90% of PDACs harbor activating mutations in KRAS, most commonly at codon 12. Historically, all KRAS codon-12 mutations were assumed to be biologically equivalent. However, accumulating studies indicate this is not true. Notably, patients with KRASG12R mutations (~20% of PDAC cases) have the most favorable prognosis among all KRAS-mutant patients, whereas KRASG12D (~40%) is associated with the worst outcomes, suggesting the presence of biologically distinct tumor subtypes. To investigate this phenomenon, we analyzed RNAseq data for over 1,400 patients deriving from the Pancreatic Cancer Action Networkâ€™s (PanCAN) real-world and clinical trial datasets. We performed differential gene expression analysis to identify genes significantly differentially expressed between the KRAS G12R and G12D tumors. We identified a significant enrichment of immune-related pathways in KRASG12R tumors. To mechanistically dissect this result, we generated mutation-specific PDAC organoid models expressing either the KRASG12R mutation or the well-studied immunosuppressive KRASG12D mutation. While these models proliferate similarly in vitro, orthotopic implantation into immunocompetent mice revealed that KRASG12R tumors grow more slowly and exhibit an immune-active TME consisting of increased dendritic-cell and T-cell infiltration, compared to KRASG12D tumors.Spatial single-cell profiling of human PDAC specimens confirmed enrichment of antigen presenting cells and immune activation markers in KRASG12R tumors. Collectively, these data link the KRASG12R mutation to an unique immunogenic role.

title: TracMyAir: Smartphone-enabled spatiotemporal estimates for inhaled doses of particulate matter and ozone to personalize health outcomes
authors: Nicholas Lahens, Institute for Translational Medicine and Therapeutics,University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, United States; Vlad Isakov, Center for Environmental Measurement and Modeling, U.S.Environmental Protection Agency, United States; Caroline Chivily, Center of Excellence in Environmental Toxicology,University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, United States; Nadim El Jamal, Institute for Translational Medicine and Therapeutics,University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, United States; Antonijo Mrčela, Institute for Translational Medicine and Therapeutics,University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, United States; Garret FitzGerald, Institute for Translational Medicine and Therapeutics,University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, United States; Carsten Skarke, Institute for Translational Medicine and Therapeutics,University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, United States; Gregory Grant, Department of Genetics, University of Pennsylvania PerelmanSchool of Medicine, United States
abstract: Accurate quantification of individual exposure to air pollutants remains a major challenge in environmental health. Traditional fixed-site monitoring fails to account for physiological variability between individuals or their movements between different indoor/outdoor environments. We deployed TracMyAir, a smartphone-based digital health platform designed to generate time-resolved, personalized exposure and inhaled dose estimates for PM2.5 and ozone under real-world conditions. In an exploratory study of 18 adults contributing more than 1,500 participant-hours, the platform integrated smartphone geolocation data, regulatory (AirNow) and community-based (PurpleAir) air quality measures, building infiltration modeling, microenvironment classification, and wearable-derived physical activity metrics to compute eight tiers of hourly exposure estimates, culminating in individualized inhaled doses. Within individuals, we observed strong concordance between dosage estimates derived from phone- and smartwatch-based step counts, while heart rate-derived dosage estimates showed more modest concordance and higher variability both within and between participants, likely reflecting the greater diversity of physiological inputs into heart rate. We also observed substantial inter- and intra-individual variability in exposure over time, reflecting dynamic transitions between microenvironments and activity patterns. Modeled doses based on regulatory and community sensor networks were strongly correlated. Community sensors were located closer to participants on average, supporting the feasibility of integrating dense, low-cost monitoring stations into existing networks. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of a scalable, smartphone-centered digital health approach for hyperlocal exposure and inhaled dose modeling. By leveraging ubiquitous consumer devices and existing air quality networks, TracMyAir enables personalized environmental exposure assessment with potential applications in epidemiology, population health, and precision environmental medicine.

title: CURE ID: A Platform to Collect Real World Data of Drug Repurposing for Rare Diseases
authors: Keyla C. Tumas, National Institutes of Health, United States; Tahsin Farid, National Institutes of Health, United States; Hyun Cho, National Institutes of Health, United States; Ruby Li, National Institutes of Health, United States; Serghei Gorobet, National Institutes of Health, United States; Ewy A. Mathé, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: There is a high unmet need to find treatments for 10,000+ known rare diseases with only five percent currently having approved therapies. Physicians often utilize drug repurposing, off-label use, where an approved drug is used to treat a new condition. While off-label use is ubiquitous, there are few resources that capture these clinical uses and outcomes in a standardized way. This repurposing data is invaluable as it could inform clinical care for other patients. In 2019, FDA and NCATS/NIH launched the CURE ID platform, a website (https://cure.ncats.io/home) and mobile app collecting data on clinical uses of repurposed drugs. Case report forms (CRFs) were developed to collect de-identified patient information: disease, symptoms, demographics, drug(s), and treatment outcome(s). CRFs are submitted by physicians and patients or curated from published literature. Currently, CURE ID houses over 5300 cases for 350 diseases, including 694 treatment outcomes for rare cancers, 17 outcomes for rare genetic disorders, and 9700+ outcomes for rare infectious diseases. Notably, patient-submitted data is a significant resource often overlooked in research and not available through broader real-world data capture, such as electronic health records. Rare disease patients often experience many symptoms treated by multiple drugs, each with distinct outcomes (deterioration to improvement). These symptom-level treatment outcomes are captured in patient-reported CURE ID cases. For example, a patient with Costello Syndrome reported improvement for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and complete recovery of hypoglycemia when treated with trametinib. All data in CURE ID is public, enabling users to potentially identify repurposed treatments for rare diseases.

title: Leveraging off-target reads from clinical panel sequencing enables mutational signature profiling across cancer types
authors: Leah Morales, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Harshit Sahay, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Jian Carrot-Zhang, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States; Quaid Morris, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, United States
abstract: Mutational signatures encode the history of mutagenic processes in tumor genomes and growing evidence supports their use as clinical biomarkers. However, clinical sequencing platforms typically rely on targeted panel assays, yielding too few mutations for robust signature detection. We sought to leverage off-target reads to expand mutation detection from existing clinical sequencing data. In our analysis of 16,865 tumor-normal sample pairs from the MSK-IMPACT cohort, a median 19.3 megabases (Mb) of the genome was covered at >=5x in both tumor and normal samples, compared to ~2.0 Mb targeted by the panel. While the assay reported a median of 2-19 mutations depending on tumor type, including off-target reads increased median mutation counts by 11-27-fold. We performed de novo signature extraction using mSigHdp and fit signatures with SigProfilerAssignment on the 60% of samples harboring >=50 SNVs (up from 3% using only panel-reported mutations). Signature activities were consistent with known tissue-specific biology and recapitulated previously identified clinical correlations. UV mutagenesis (SBS7a/b/c) was present in 93% of melanomas, tobacco exposure (SBS4) in 60% of lung cancers, and APOBEC activity (SBS2, SBS13) in 80% of bladder cancers. Germline BRCA1/2 carriers had significantly greater homologous recombination deficiency signature activity (SBS3, p=3.14x10-56), and PD-L1+ tumors exhibited elevated APOBEC activity (SBS2, p=7.4E-12; SBS13, p=1.06x10-11). In pancreatic adenocarcinomas, SBS10b was associated with longer overall survival (HR=0.86, 95%CI=0.74-0.98, p=0.03). These results demonstrate that clinically relevant mutational signatures can be extracted from routine panel sequencing data, with ongoing work aimed at further characterizing the relationships between mutational processes and patient outcomes.

title: Enhancing User Engagement in mHealth via Multimodal Data Integration and Iterative Dashboard Refinement
authors: Younghee Lee, Penguinpoint, South Korea; Arok Choi, Seoul National University, South Korea; Rokdam Choi, Penguinpoint, South Korea
abstract: Background:The effective delivery of complex health information remains a bottleneck in mHealth adoption. While general users generate vast amounts of medical and lifelog data, few platforms provide the necessary ""intuitive synthesis"" for informed self-management. This study aimed to develop and refine a dashboard-driven application that integrates medical, lifelog, and environmental data for non-expert users. Methods:We adopted a two-phase user evaluation system to iteratively improve the appâ€™s quality. 58 users participated in the assessment using the uMARS framework. The study specifically focused on transforming raw, multidimensional data into actionable insights through visual dashboards. Statistical validation (paired t-tests) was performed to correlate user feedback with improvements in engagement and information delivery. Results:Post-refinement, the overall uMARS quality score rose significantly from 3.36 to 3.45 (p Conclusion:Our findings highlight the necessity of iterative user-centered design in health informatics. By refining the visual and interactive components of mHealth dashboards, we can bridge the gap between complex data acquisition and intuitive user understanding, fostering higher engagement in personal health management.

title: RCSB Protein Data Bank: A Living Digital Data Resource That Enables Scientific Breakthroughs Across The Biological Sciences
authors: Stephen K Burley, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, United States; RCSB PDB Team, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, United States
abstract: The Protein Data Bank (PDB) was established in 1971 as the first open-access digital data resource in biology with just seven X-ray crystallographic structures of proteins. Today, the single global PDB archive houses >250,000 experimentally-determined 3D structures of biological macromolecules that are made freely available to many millions of users worldwide with no limitations on usage. This rigorously validate and carefully curated 3D biostructure information facilitates basic and applied research and education across the sciences, impacting fundamental biology, biomedicine, biotechnology, and the energy sciences. RCSB PDB (Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics PDB) operates the US data center for the global PDB archive, and makes PDB data available at no charge to all data consumers without limitations on usage. RCSB PDB supports PDB Data Consumers in the US and around the world through our open-access web portal RCSB.org that provides tools and powerful APIs for structure visualization and analysis. PDB data are available alongside >1 million predicted Computed Structure Models. RCSB PDB Core Operations are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (DBI-2321666), the US Department of Energy (DE-SC0019749), and the National Cancer Institute, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, and National Institute of General Medical Sciences of the National Institutes of Health under grant R01GM157729. RCSB PDB uses resources of the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a Department of Energy User Facility.

title: The GlyGen Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server
authors: Robel Kahsay, The George Washington University, United States; Raja Mazumder, The George Washington University, United States; Michael Tiemeyer, The University of Georgia, United States; Rene Ranzinger, The University of Georgia, United States
abstract: GlyGen is a comprehensive glycoscience data resource that integrates and harmonizes data on glycans, glycoproteins, and glycosylation-related entities from multiple sources. Background: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting and generating biomedical text, but their ability to accurately answer glycoscience-related queries is limited by restricted access to structured, up-to-date datasets. Methods: We developed a GlyGen Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to provide LLMs with structured, real-time access to glycoscience data. The server is implemented as a remote, containerized service interfacing directly with GlyGen APIs. Functionality is organized into concept-centric tools, including protein-, glycan-, site-, disease-, and biomarker-focused operations. These tools are exposed as callable Python functions that encapsulate API requests and return standardized outputs. The production server is publicly available at https://mcp.glygen.org. Results: The MCP server enables LLMs to translate natural language queries into precise tool invocations, facilitating retrieval of glycosylation data and associated metadata. The system supports diverse query types, including glycosylation sites, disease associations, variants, glycans, and biomarkers. Its modular architecture supports extensibility as new datasets and tools are incorporated. Conclusions: The GlyGen MCP server provides a scalable framework for equipping LLMs with direct access to curated glycoscience data, improving the accuracy, reliability, and depth of AI-generated responses, and enhancing the utility of glycoscience resources in research and discovery.

title: Building the Human Tumor Atlas Network: A Foundational Multi-omic Data Resource for Cancer Research
authors: Aditi Gopalan, Sage Bionetworks, United States
abstract: The Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN) maps the cellular and molecular architecture of human tumors to advance precision oncology. The HTAN Data Coordinating Center (DCC) standardizes, integrates, and distributes multimodal data emerging from contributing centers to ensure lasting community impact. The DCC built a scalable cloud ecosystem (Synapse.org, Google BigQuery, custom portal) for data ingestion, governance, validation, and dissemination. For phase 2, a modular LinkML metadata schema, organized into per-assay domains with a strict class inheritance hierarchy across >25 assay types, ensures interoperability across clinical, biospecimen, and molecular data modalities; schema changes auto-generate Python dataclasses and JSON schemas enabling reproducible cross-platform validation. Data are disseminated via a tiered model: imaging and dbGaP-controlled sequencing via NCI CRDC, and open-access processed data via Synapse.org. Phase 2 built the modular LinkML schema with broader assay coverage, an AI-assisted curation interface, and enhanced validation. Phase 1 (v7.0) provides 334 TB of multimodal data (0.23M files) from 2,372 cases and 11,378 biospecimens spanning >60 disease types and >25 assays. The platform supports 2,573 global users annually, generating 1.9 million downloads. Most accessed modalities include scRNA-seq spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex imaging. Analysis of dbGaP requests (N=127) shows broad academic (75%) and industry use focused on genome instability, immune evasion, and metastasis, often with multi-omic and AI-driven approaches. HTAN Phase 1 establishes a globally used, integrated foundation for spatially resolved, multimodal cancer research. Phase 2 deepens spatial and clinical data integration, expands AI-readiness, and strengthens reproducibility. Explore the resource at humantumoratlas.org. ChatGPT 5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, & Claude Sonnet 4.5 were used to summarize usage metrics, conduct thematic analysis of dbGaP applications, and initial abstract drafting. All content was evaluated and approved by the authors.

title: Proteogenomic discordance uncovers pan-cancer tumor microenvironment complexity and influences biomarker efficacy
authors: Joseph LaMorte, Uniformed Services University, United States; Xijun Zhang, Uniformed Services University, United States; Nicholas Bateman, Uniformed Services University, United States; Thomas Conrads, Uniformed Services University, United States; Robert Browning, Uniformed Services University, United States; Craig Shriver, Uniformed Services University, United States; Robert Kortum, Uniformed Services University, United States; Matthew Wilkerson, Uniformed Services University, United States
abstract: Accurate quantification of RNA and protein expression in tumors can uncover novel disease mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities. Cross-tumor comparisons of gene-specific RNA and protein levels have revealed correlations that are partly attributable to pathway-level regulatory control. Beyond gene-level relationships, prior work has identified sample-level variation influencing RNA-protein concordance, termed sample-wise RNA to protein correlation (SRPC). In this study, we present the first pan-cancer analysis of SRPC using proteogenomic data from 7,872 tumors across 32 cancer types. SRPC stratified tumors according to microenvironment composition: tumors with high SRPC were enriched for cancer cells and cell proliferation pathway activity, whereas those with low SRPC showed greater immune and stromal infiltration, along with increased angiogenesis and inflammatory pathway activity. SRPC also distinguished tumors by clinical characteristics, including patient outcomes and mutational profiles. In breast cancer, SRPC was linked to discordance in PAM50 and IHC-based subtype classification, particularly among triple-negative and hormone receptor positive tumors, providing opportunities for breast cancer subtyping improvement. Additionally, drug targets in low SRPC tumors exhibited discordant RNA and protein expression, indicating that RNA augmentation to protein expression may increase biomarker performance. To support further investigation, we provide these pan-cancer proteogenomic data as a resource for precision oncology. Overall, variability in RNA-protein correlation across tumors reflects differences in microenvironment and genomic alterations, contributing to distinct biological pathways, clinical outcomes, and biomarker performance.

title: Perineural Invasion Initiates Locoregional Prostate Cancer Bone Metastasis.
authors: Joseph Patacsil, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Markus Hoffmann, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States; Joanna Kitlinska, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular & Cellular Biology, Georgetown University, United States
abstract: Prostate cancer frequently progresses from localized disease to metastatic stages characterized by bone involvement and poor clinical outcomes. Early skeletal metastases often arise near the primary tumor within the axial skeleton, suggesting that dissemination may occur through mechanisms beyond hematogenous spread. Perineural invasion has been associated with increased tumor aggressiveness and bone metastasis risk. Here, we investigate transcriptomic differences associated with progression from primary tumors (PT) to paravertebral tumors (PVT). Raw count data were processed to combine counts for genes with the same gene symbol and remove genes with zero counts. Differential expression (DE) analysis was performed using DESeq2. Log2 fold changes (L2FC) were calculated in relation to the PT, and p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. Significantly DE genes were identified with p-adj 1. We used the clusterProfiler package to perform gene ontology overrepresentation analysis and gene set enrichment analysis, applying the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Primary component analysis showed a significant difference between the PT and their PVT counterparts. DE analysis revealed 53 genes were significantly up-regulated and 100 genes were significantly down-regulated. Pathway analysis revealed significant enrichment across numerous pathways, including growth factor signaling, ossification,, and dendrite development. The transcriptomic shift between epithelial to neural-like cells was characterized by the dramatic down-regulation of the epithelial gatekeeper GRHL2 (L2FC=âˆ’7.46) and the developmental regulator HAND2 (LFC=âˆ’5.50). Conversely, the upregulation of SDK1 and IGF2BP1 (L2FC=3.25/2.22, respectively) suggests that metastatic cells in the paravertebral niche adopt a neurotropic phenotype.

title: Resolving Modality Imbalance in Single-Cell Multiomics via Poisson-Laplace Generative Modeling
authors: Sihong Li, Department of Biostatistics, Indiana University School of Medicine, Indianapolis, IN 46202, United States; Jie Zhang, Department of Medical and Molecular Genetics, Indiana University School of Medicine, Indianapolis, IN 46202, United States; Kun Huang, Department of Biostatistics, Indiana University School of Medicine, Indianapolis, IN 46202, United States; Travis Johnson, Department of Biostatistics, Indiana University School of Medicine, Indianapolis, IN 46202, United States
abstract: Integrating single-cell transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility data is important for understanding gene regulatory networks driving disease, but current models often struggle with modality imbalance. This can be caused by the lower-variance in ATAC-seq signal, which can cause posterior collapse and RNA-seq dominated representations. To address this, we performed an ablation study using myeloma single-cell multiomics to improve multimodal representations. We explored different likelihood functions (Gaussian, Poisson, Negative Binomial) and sparsity priors (automatic relevance determination (ARD), Laplace) within multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA). To evaluate these configurations, we used an imputation benchmark by randomly masking 10% of observed non-zero entries across both modalities. Model robustness and predictive accuracy were assessed using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) between the reconstructed and true hidden values. Applying a Gaussian likelihood to LSI-transformed ATAC data, especially with strong sparsity constraints, caused near-complete collapse of the ATAC signal (PCC â‰ˆ 0.00). In contrast, modeling raw ATAC and RNA counts with a Poisson likelihood substantially improved recovery of epigenetic signals (PCC â‰ˆ 0.80) while maintaining RNA predictivity. Pairing this with a Laplace (L1) prior promoted strong feature-level sparsity without the numerical instability observed with Negative Binomial models. This combination improved the interpretability of multimodal latent factors and helped reveal cell-type-specific genes and regulatory regions. The Poissonâ€“Laplace formulation provides a more robust and interpretable approach for integrating high-dimensional single-cell multiomics data. Our methodology represents an improvement upon current methodologies that will only further our understanding of gene regulatory networks in a variety of diseases.

title: Standardizing Spatial Biology Workflows at Scale with Databricks
authors: Jairaj Mathur, Boehringer Ingelheim, United States
abstract: Spatial biology technologies are rapidly expanding in both throughput and complexity, creating a growing need for scalable, reproducible, and standardized analysis frameworks that can support multiple assay types across teams. Here, we present a collaborative spatial biology workflow built on Databricks that enables end to end analysis, visualization, and operationalization of diverse spatial transcriptomics platforms within a unified environment. Our framework supports 10x Genomics Visium, Visium HD, Xenium, and NanoString CosMx, allowing harmonized processing across imaging based and sequencing based modalities. A central feature of this workflow is the use of Declarative Automation Bundles (DABS) to define, version, deploy, and maintain reusable analysis pipelines in a consistent and scalable manner. This enables standardized execution across projects while improving reproducibility, portability, and team collaboration. The workflow integrates data ingestion, preprocessing, quality control, downstream analysis, and interactive visualization, providing a structured yet flexible foundation for spatial biology applications in research settings. To support data exploration and communication of results, we incorporate Vitessce as a Databricks app, enabling interactive visualization of large spatial datasets directly within the Databricks ecosystem. This creates a seamless bridge between large-scale compute, data engineering, and biological interpretation. By combining scalable infrastructure, modular pipeline design, and interactive visualization, this platform provides a practical solution for standardizing spatial biology analyses at scale. Our work demonstrates how Databricks can serve as a unifying computational layer for enterprise-grade spatial omics, accelerating adoption of robust and reproducible workflows across technologies and teams.

title: AlphaFold 3–enhanced graph neural network repurposing of FDA-approved drugs against neglected tropical disease proteins
authors: Daniel Korkin, Student, Westborough High School, United States; Dmitry Korkin, Jurist Dean's Professor, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, United States
abstract: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) disproportionately affect populations in low-income regions, where limited funding and infrastructure have constrained traditional drug discovery, slowing development of effective therapies. Advances in machine learning (ML), particularly recent progress in protein foundation models such as AlphaFold-3, RoseTTAFold3, and Chai-1, are creating scalable and cost-efficient opportunities for drug discovery. Here, we developed a high-throughput deep learning (DL) pipeline to identify druggable protein targets across a broad range of NTDs and FDA-approved drugs that may be repurposed against them. The pipeline builds on a graph neural network (GNN)-long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture for predicting protein-ligand binding affinity, combined with AlphaFold-3 (AF3) to model target structures and Chai-1 to model protein-ligand complexes. We trained two independent GNN-LSTM models on gold-standard experimental datasets using protein targets modeled with AF3. In both cases, training on AF3-derived structures improved binding affinity prediction accuracy relative to previous predictors, making it among the most accurate models to date. We then carried out large-scale virtual screening of ~3,000 druggable NTD-related proteins against ~2,900 FDA-approved compounds, yielding ~8.4 million protein-ligand pairs. Rankings from the two models were then integrated using Borda rank aggregation. Top-ranked FDA-approved compounds were frequently predicted to bind NTD targets with higher affinity than their known native targets structurally resolved in PDB. Many top candidates were antifungal or antimicrobial compounds not previously used for NTDs. Together, these results highlight the potential of DL-driven drug repurposing as a scalable and economically efficient strategy for accelerating therapeutic discovery for NTDs.

title: The Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center: Latest Advancements
authors: Indresh Singh, J. Craig Venter Institute, United States; Elliot Lefkowitz, Department of Microbiology, University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL 35294, USA, United States; Maulik Shukla, Consortium for Advanced Science and Engineering, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637, USA, United States
abstract: The Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC; https://www.bv-brc.org) is a comprehensive resource supporting research on bacterial and viral pathogens. It currently hosts over 16 million publicly available genomes and 35 high-throughput bioinformatic analysis services with numerous visual analytic tools allowing researchers to analyze their private data, generate comparisons with public data, and share data and results with colleagues. In 2019, the BV-BRC was established by merging three longstanding BRCs: the PAThosystems Resource Integration Center (PATRIC), the Influenza Research Database (IRD) and the Virus Pathogen Database and Analysis Resource (ViPR). Over the past year, BV-BRC has continued to enhance the available resources for our user community that includes researchers, clinicians, public health practitioners, and educators. Here, we present several new and updated features and services that support rapid comparative genomics and epidemiological analysis including viral genome assembly and annotation, viral subspecies classification enabling more precise identification and analysis of evolving lineages, antimicrobial resistance analysis, whole genome SNP analysis to track and characterize pathogen outbreaks, metagenomic read mapping, wastewater analysis, influenza reassortment analysis, phylogenomics, and molecular docking for molecular modeling to study protein-ligand interactions. We have also developed a new tool, called BV-BRC Copilot, that provides an AI-powered natural-language interface combining large language models with retrieval-augmented generation to guide users through data exploration, analysis workflows, and knowledge integration. We will highlight specific analysis examples and present areas of continuing development. These improvements, combined with many other user-friendly tools and web-based interfaces, provide the community with powerful resources for genomic exploration, drug discovery, epidemiological studies, and bioinformatics analysis. The Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC; https://www.bv-brc.org) is a comprehensive, open-access resource for bacterial and viral infectious disease research. BV-BRC provides integrated data, advanced bioinformatics tools, and end-to-end analysis workflows to support the scientific community in understanding, monitoring, and responding to infectious diseases.

title: Multimodal Type 2 Diabetes Subtyping in the All of Us Dataset: Leveraging Clinical, Genomic, and Social Determinants of Health Data
authors: Shaika Chowdhury, University of North Texas, United States; Yashu Vashishath, University of North Texas, United States; Serdar Bozdag, University of North Texas, United States
abstract: Motivation: Although type 2 diabetes (T2D) is the most common form of diabetes, its underlying etiologic and pathogenic mechanisms remain incompletely understood due to substantial heterogeneity. However, prior studies have not fully leveraged multimodal sources of heterogeneity to identify distinct and clinically meaningful subtypes of T2D. Methods: For 47,292 T2D participants in the All of Us database, we collected data from three sources in the All of Us database - electronic health records (EHRs), microarray genotyping array data, and social determinants of health (SDOH) surveys - and constructed multimodal feature vectors by concatenating the clinical, SNP contribution, pathway contribution, and SDOH features. We then employed autoencoder to learn representations and applied K-means clustering to identify distinct subtypes of Type 2 Diabetes. Results: Cluster evaluation metrics indicated that the optimal number of K-means clusters was five. Visualization of these clusters in two-dimensional space using t-SNE demonstrated clear separation between clusters. Comparison of Polygenic Risk Score (PRS) distributions across clusters using one-way ANOVA and Kruskal's Wallis tests revealed clear differences in genetic susceptibility. We conducted 5-fold cross-validation using logistic regression models on the test dataset for mortality prediction, where incorporating the cluster labels improved mortality prediction in AUC performance, demonstrating the potential of clustering to provide additional predictive information. Conclusion: In this study, we leveraged multimodal features in the All of Us dataset to identify clinically meaningful subtypes of T2D, which were validated through genetic risk analysis and downstream predictive tasks. Future work will focus on modeling the longitudinal dynamics and cross-modality interactions.

title: Gene-based calibration of high-throughput functional assays for clinical variant classification
authors: Ross Stewart, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, NortheasternUniversity, Boston, MA, United States; Daniel Zeiberg, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, NortheasternUniversity, Boston, MA, United States; Shantanu Jain, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, NortheasternUniversity, Boston, MA, United States; Malvika Tejura, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington,Seattle, WA, United States; Abbye McEwen, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington,Seattle, WA, United States; Shawn Fayer, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington,Seattle, WA, United States; Yuriy Sverchkov, Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics,University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, United States; Mark Craven, Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics,University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, United States; Vikas Pejaver, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States; Alan Rubin, Bioinformatics Division, The Walter and Eliza HallInstitute of Medical Research, Parkville, VIC, Australia; Lea Starita, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington,Seattle, WA, United States; Douglas Fowler, Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington,Seattle, WA, United States; Anne O'Donnell-Luria, Program in Medical and Population Genetics, Broad Instituteof MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, United States; Predrag Radivojac, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, NortheasternUniversity, Boston, MA, United States
abstract: High-throughput assays measure a broad range of variant effects on gene function and hold promise for supporting genomic medicine. Current clinical guidelines for rare Mendelian diseases rely on establishing gene-specific score thresholds for each assay that separate pathogenic from benign variants. This introduces inconsistencies and subjectivity, ultimately lacking the rigor of calibration; i.e., mapping a variant score to a probability of pathogenicity. To address this problem, we introduce a semi-supervised framework for calibrating experimental assay data and propose Experimental score CALIBRator (ExCALIBR), a method that jointly models pathogenic, benign, synonymous, and population variants using skew normal mixtures to produce variant-specific probabilities of pathogenicity. Evaluated across 80 datasets from 39 genes, all meeting fit quality criteria, ExCALIBR substantially outperformed existing field standards and was further validated on the All of Us biobank data. Our results demonstrate that calibrated experimental assays generate indispensable evidence that will dramatically reduce variants of uncertain significance.

title: Computational and experimental identification of potential neutralizing peptides derived from human ACE2 against SARS-CoV-2 infection
authors: Qiaobin Yao, Howard University, United States; Vidhyanand Mahase, Howard University, United States; Wangheng Hou, Howard University College of Medicine, United States; Ruth Cruz-Cosme, Howard University College of Medicine, United States; Qiyi Tang, Howard University College of Medicine, United States; Shaolei Teng, Howard University, United States
abstract: The human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) is the primary receptor for the entry of SARS-CoV-2. Some human alleles of ACE2 exhibit an improved affinity for the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein. However, the impact of ACE2 polymorphisms on SARS-CoV-2 infection remains unclear. Our previous study predicted that G431 and S514 in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of SARS-CoV-2 S1 domain are important for S protein stability, and that S protein residues G496 and F497 and ACE2 residues D355 and Y41 are critical for the RBD-ACE2 interaction. In this study, we explored the potential of hACE2-derived neutralizing peptides as a therapeutic strategy against SARS-CoV-2 and investigated how ACE2 polymorphisms affect RBD-ACE2 binding affinity. We applied computational saturation mutagenesis to systematically screen the binding affinity changes among all possible ACE2 missense mutations within the ACE2â€“Wuhan-S1 complex. Mutations at ACE2 residues D355 and Y41 were predicted to weaken binding affinity, whereas those at N330 and D30 enhanced it. We identified six ACE2 regions (19-49, 65-102, 320-333, 348-359, 378-395, 552-563) to be vital for ACE2â€“RBD interaction. We synthesized peptides corresponding to these six regions and tested them using a pseudotyped viral particle system and dot blot assay. Three peptides were confirmed to bind with S protein, and four exhibited inhibitory effects. We aligned ACE2 - Wuhan-S1 and ACE2 - Omicron-S1 complexes, conducted correlation analysis, and observed similar binding patterns, suggesting that these peptides also have potential to neutralize Omicron strains.

title: Differential performance of AlphaMissense and REVEL on gain-of-function variants in monogenic diabetes genes with implications for ACMG/AMP variant classification
authors: Agasthya Metpally, Raleigh Charter High School, United States; Abhishek Kumar, Heidelberg University, Germany; Sarath Babu Krishna Murthy, Columbia University, United States
abstract: Purpose: AlphaMissense (AM) is increasingly applied as PP3 in-silico evidence under ACMG/AMP guidelines, but performance across variant molecular mechanisms has not been systematically evaluated. We compared AM and REVEL for gain-of-function (GOF) and loss-of-function (LOF) variant discrimination in monogenic-diabetes genes. Methods: We analyzed 131 ABCC8/KCNJ11/GCK variants from Hopkins et al. (2023; LOF n=66, GOF n=65) and four independent datasets: De Franco et al. (2020; n=555), GCK deep mutational scanning (n=6,016), ClinVar expert panel (LOF n=201, GOF n=44, benign n=13), and 27 curated GOF variants from GoFCards. PP3 evidence tiers were applied using likelihood ratio (LR+) calibrated thresholds (AM: â‰¥0.564, â‰¥0.740, â‰¥0.890; REVEL: â‰¥0.644, â‰¥0.773, â‰¥0.932). Random-effects meta-analysis was performed across datasets. Results: In the Hopkins cohort, AM showed a larger LOF-GOF sensitivity gap at the strong threshold (60.6% vs 29.2%; Î”31.4 pp, p=0.0004; OR=3.72) than REVEL (54.5% vs 35.4%; Î”19.2 pp, p=0.035; OR=2.19). Across five datasets, the pooled LOF-GOF gap was +35.1 pp (95% CI +31.0 to +39.3) for AM and +20.2 pp (+15.1 to +25.3) for REVEL. In the ClinVar-dataset, the AM strong threshold achieved LR+ values of 5.0-6.7, below the â‰¥18.7 threshold required for strong evidence. In externally curated GOF variants, REVEL detected 69.2% versus 38.5% for AM at â‰¥Supporting. Conclusion: AlphaMissense consistently shows reduced GOF variant detection in ABCC8/ KCNJ11/GCK genes at ACMG/AMP-calibrated thresholds. The AM strong threshold does not achieve strong-level LR+ in these genes, supporting moderate rather than strong evidence strength for clinical interpretation. Gene-specific calibration of computational evidence is warranted when applying PP3 criteria.

title: Improving Missense Variant Effects Predictors using Tissue Context and Splicing Isoform Expression
authors: Tulika Kakati, University of California, San Diego, United States; Karna Mendonca, Northeastern University, United States; Shantanu Jain, Northeastern University, United States; Himanshu Sharma, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Vikas Pejaver, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States; Predrag Radivojac, Northeastern University, United States; Lilia Iakoucheva, University of California, San Diego, United States
abstract: Accurate variant interpretation remains a major challenge in human genetics, particularly because most computational predictors overlook tissue- and isoform-specific biology. Here, we present expression-based Tissue Specific Pathogenicity (exTSP), a framework that integrates transcript-level expression profiles with pathogenicity scores to improve missense variant prioritization in a tissue-aware manner. exTSP combines splicing isoform expression from GTEx and BrainSpan with likelihood-calibrated MutPred2 scores to prioritize variants predicted to disrupt functionally important isoforms in disease-relevant tissues. We validated exTSP across five representative disorders including autism spectrum disorder, cardiomyopathy, primary ciliary dyskinesia, pulmonary hypertension, and kidney disease, and observed 10-20 percentage-point gains in variant classification performance relative to MutPred2. When evaluated on MANE Select transcripts commonly used in clinical annotation, exTSP outperformed AlphaMissense in distinguishing pathogenic from benign ClinVar variants, demonstrating enhanced generalizability through transcript-aware modeling. Applied to Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS), exTSP provided additional, transcript-specific evidence toward pathogenicity or benignity for 16â€“39% of VUS across diseases. Moreover, tissues relevant to each disorder showed an enrichment of high-scoring exTSP variants, underscoring the biological importance of tissue context in variant interpretation. By linking pathogenicity prediction with tissue-specific isoform usage, exTSP offers a scalable, biologically grounded approach for transcript-aware and tissue-informed variant classification, advancing both clinical and research applications. exTSP will be available as a web server (URL forthcoming).

title: Annotation inconsistencies impact the clinical use of variant effect predictors
authors: Timothy Bergquist, Icahn School of Medicine at Mt Sinai, United States; Vikas Pejaver, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, United States
abstract: Bioinformatics resources (e.g., Ensembl, Uniprot, RefSeq) and variant annotation tools and resources (e.g., VEP, ANNOVAR, dbNSFP) are continually updated with the most current genetic and molecular information. These updates may involve changes to the mappings between nucleotide variant coordinates and amino acid variant positions, the protein sequence, the designation of â€œcanonicalâ€ status to an isoform, among others. Missense variant pathogenicity predictors (e.g., REVEL, MutPred2, AlphaMissense) typically use such protein-level information to calculate pathogenicity scores. For scalability and convenience, it is common practice for missense variant pathogenicity predictions to be precomputed exome-wide and made available to end-users, often through variant annotation tools. However, such static pathogenicity predictions are not expected to be in synchrony with updates to bioinformatics databases and may give discordant predictions if the predictors were run using the latest information. Here, we quantify the extent to which this occurs by systematically predicting pathogenicity on the same genetic variants annotated across multiple releases of the Ensembl database. We find that among missense variants from clinically relevant genes in ClinVar (n=258,262), 34,084 (13%) are directly impacted by changes in Ensembl between release 90 and release 115. Furthermore, when MutPred2 predictions are grouped into evidential strength categories as per clinical variant classification guidelines, database changes shift the strength of evidence of 16,225 (6%) variants (i.e. move from one strength category to another). These results have implications for the use of precomputed variant effect predictor scores in clinical variant classification.

title: Causal Path Inference on a Literature-Derived Knowledge Graph for Variant Effect Interpretation
authors: Jici Jiang, Northeastern University, United States; Predrag Radivojac, Northeastern University, United States; Benjamin Gyori, Northeastern University, United States
abstract: Current computational approaches to variant effect prediction integrate diverse genomic annotation and protein-level features, yet model direct variant-to-gene or gene-to-phenotype mappings without explicitly reasoning over the mechanistic chain of events. We present a framework to generate interpretable, multi-hop causal paths that link variants to phenotypes corresponding to curated variant-phenotype evidence. These paths connect genetic variants to phenotypes through intermediate signaling, protein-interaction and regulatory events. The underlying knowledge graph is built using our INDRA system which integrates causal mechanism extraction from all available biomedical literature with the content of key pathway databases. The proposed framework accommodates a broad spectrum of genetic variation. Coding variants (missense, stop, indel) are represented through ESM2 protein language model embeddings capturing wild-type and mutant residue-level context, while non-coding variants are encoded using Nucleotide Transformer embeddings of reference and alternate alleles. Variants lacking annotated gene links are additionally mapped to candidate effector genes via Open Targets Locus-to-Gene (L2G) predictions. In total, the model is trained and evaluated on 128,220 variants across 15,781 genes. We formulate variant-effect prediction as stepwise path generation on a variant-relevant subgraph extracted from the full event network via constrained pathfinding. A variant-conditioned message-passing neural network initializes traversal from the associated gene, and a sequential path decoder scores candidate next nodes and edge polarities at each hop. This approach moves beyond the current paradigm of single-score pathogenicity prediction by producing interpretable causal paths that explain the biological mechanism from variant to phenotype, providing mechanistic evidence for variant interpretation and downstream functional investigation.

title: Population-driven discovery of tumor driving genefusion variants
authors: Jacob Krol, University of Colorado Boulder, United States; Ryan Layer, University of Colorado Boulder, United States
abstract: Structural variations (SV)s are large (>50bp) mutations in sample genomes that deviate from a reference genome sequence. In human cancer studies, SVs are prioritized by filtering out SVs common in the general population. Intuitively, common SVs are unlikely to be driving cancer progression. For example, population SV databases, such as gnomAD and the 1000 Genomes Project, are used to filter out SVs from disease association studies. Here, we show population SV databases can be used for direct discovery of SV-disease association. Using the Pan Cancer Analysis Whole Genomes (PCAWG) cohort, we discovered a high confidence genefusion SV (GSV) in liver cancer that was absent from the primary PCAWG analysis. Briefly, we designed a frequency-based score to collapse GSV evidence across multiple samples, conditions, and technologies into a single metric. We integrated GSV evidence, using STIX, from 2143 PCAWG samples across tumor/normal conditions and WGS/RNA-seq technologies plus 2535 samples from 1000 Genomes projects totaling 4678 samples. Evaluation experiments showed GSV score separated reported PCAWG fusions from random gene combinations and recurrent GSVs reported in normal samples. To discover overlooked GSVs potentially driving cancer progression, we visualized PCAWG RNA-seq sample evidence, using Samplot, for high ranking GSV scores and found a high confidence novel fusion in liver cancer: POLR3GL-LIX1L. LIX1L was reported as an oncogene in liver cancer while POLR3GL is known to have high expression in liver cancers. Overall, we showed integrating samples across conditions and technologies is useful for SV-disease association discovery.

title: Evaluating Aggregated Gene Level eQTL Scores
authors: Douglas Meyer, Bioinformatics and Systems Biology Program, UC San Diego, United States; Noa Popko, Bioinformatics and Systems Biology Program, UC San Diego, United States; David Laub, Bioinformatics and Systems Biology Program, UC San Diego, United States; Phil Schofield, School of Medicine, UC San Diego, United States; Ludmil Alexandrov, Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego, United States; Hannah Carter, Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego, United States
abstract: Existing methods for transcriptome-wide association study perform gene expression imputation followed by trait association testing. This framework has successfully nominated causal genes in a variety of human traits. Association testing on imputed scores presumes imputed scores are an accurate representation of gene function or activity. Here we examine contributing factors to imputation accuracy: imputation model type, linkage disequilibrium (LD) filter strictness and variant prioritization methods. To evaluate the impact of different parameter choices on imputed expression quality, we trained over 1.2 million models spanning 6 tissue types and 21708 genes and evaluated their performance in independent data sets. We considered 4 model types, and generally found superior performance from elasticnet models (in whole blood, all pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank test p-values Here, we demonstrated the consequences of different chosen variant prioritization methods, LD filtering strictness and model types on expression imputation quality. We benchmarked these parameter choices in held-out and independent validation samples. Finally, through the EAGLES tool, we make our model training and scoring pipelines available, along with our pre-trained models, to facilitate applications in additional cohorts.

title: Context-dependent separation of germline and somatic mutations in cancer driver genes
authors: Anastasia Lucas, University of Pennsylvania, United States; Tiffany Chang, The Wistar Institute, United States; Andrew Patterson, The Wistar Institute, United States; Pearl Zhou, The Wistar Institute, United States; Bryant Duong, The Wistar Institute, United States; McKenna Reale, The Wistar Institute, United States; Noam Auslander, The Wistar Institute, United States
abstract: Cancer arises from both inherited germline variation and acquired somatic mutations, yet evolutionary processes driving selection of protein-coding variation in cancer patients remains unresolved. Here, we harmonized germline and somatic variants in cancer driver genes from >10,000 patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas to quantify the germline and somatic origins of mutations at each cancer driver residue. We found that residues mutated in germline of cancer drivers are almost never somatically mutated, and conversely, residues with somatic mutations are largely absent from germline. Moreover, 58% of cancer drivers exhibit a statistically significant bias towards either germline or somatic mutations. Further, germline-dominant genes are enriched for tumor suppressors and inactivation effects, while somatic-dominant genes are associated with oncogenic, activating mutations (odds ratio=4.7, p=0.0045). We additionally found that amino acid context can differentiate between somatic and germline occurring mutations. We trained a long short-term memory classifier using a 21 amino acid context window, i.e. 10 amino acids upstream and downstream, surrounding each mutated cancer driver residue, to predict whether a variant is germline or somatic occurring (validation AUROC=0.78). Further, using ESM-2 embeddings of the full protein sequences, we observed that we could accurately distinguish between genes harboring predominantly germline variants and those harboring predominantly somatic variants (AUROC=0.99). This is the first study to systematically compare germline and somatic mutated protein residues in cancer driver genes, revealing a clear separation between inherited and acquired cancer mutagenesis driven by distinct selective pressures.

title: A Large-Scale Workflow for Extracting and Visualizing Genetic Variant Impacts from Alzheimer’s Disease Literature
authors: Gunjan Rajgure, University of Delaware, United States; Samir Gupta, University of Delaware, United States; Chuming Chen, University of Delaware, United States; Karen Ross, Georgetown University, United States; K Vijay-Shanker, University of Delaware, United States; Cathy Wu, University of Delaware, United States
abstract: Alzheimerâ€™s disease and related dementias represent a major public health burden, yet effective treatments remain limited. Understanding how genetic variants affect molecular functions and disease-related outcomes is therefore important for clarifying disease mechanisms. Although this evidence is widely reported in the scientific literature, it is dispersed across a large and continuously expanding body of publications, is typically embedded in unstructured text. As a result, it is difficult to determine which variants have been reported, what effects they have, and what evidence supports those findings. In addition, while the published eMIND (extraction mutation impact in neurodegenerative diseases) tool had already shown promising results on curated evaluation abstracts, broader adoption required a scalable workflow capable of moving beyond small, selected abstract sets and supporting repeated analysis on much larger collections of articles. To address this need, we developed a large-scale workflow for collecting, organizing, and presenting mutation-impact evidence from the biomedical literature. The workflow identifies relevant articles from PubMed using targeted search queries, processes abstracts against a local copy of Medline Database to get noun phrase and relations, and applies the published eMIND system to extract mutation-related effects into structured records. Each record links a paper and evidence sentence to a mutation, associated gene, disease context, reported impact, and supporting identifiers. Post-processing further standardizes names and identifiers, maps results to external resources such as UniProt and disease ontologies, and adds metadata including normalized mutation identifiers, mutation inference status, negation flags, and study-sentence indicators. To make the resulting data more accessible and interpretable, we developed eMIND Visuals, a web interface built on the final processed dataset. Users can search by gene, mutation, UniProt accession, or PubMed ID and view structured result tables alongside a linked abstract view that highlights genes, mutations, diseases, and impact phrases in distinct colors. Together, these features transform large-scale extraction output into a searchable and interpretable resource for literature-based variant analysis.

title: Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation, Edition 7 (CAGI 7) Nonsense & Frameshift Annotation Accumulation Accuracy Assessment Challenge
authors: Yaqi Su, UC Berkeley, United States; Steven Brenner, UC Berkeley, United States
abstract: The Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation (CAGI) is a community experiment that objectively evaluates computational methods for predicting the impact of genomic variation on phenotype. CAGI 7 introduced a new challenge to assess predictions of clinical significance for nonsense and frameshift variants. Nonsense variants constitute approximately a quarter of pathogenic variants in ClinVar and are central to applying PVS1, the only ""Very Strong"" pathogenic evidence criterion in ACMG/AMP guidelines. Despite their importance, most predictors ignore nonsense variants or treat them as uniformly deleterious. However, their consequences are varied and context-dependent, ranging from loss of function through NMD transcript degradation, to dominant-negative or partially functional truncated proteins, to retained function through stop-codon readthrough. This challenge was designed as an Annotation Accumulation Accuracy Assessment (A4): predictors submit predictions for all possible variants, and performance is evaluated against annotations that accumulate in repositories such as ClinVar following the submission deadline. We constructed a prediction dataset of all 1,398,617 possible stop-gain SNVs across 4,623 disease-associated genes. Because the number of potential frameshift variants is unlimited, we developed a collapsing strategy, retaining only the most 5â€² frameshift producing each distinct premature termination codon. A limitation is that aberrant peptides preceding an induced nonsense codon may independently affect protein stability. Five models from three groups participated. The top group achieved strong performance on accumulated ClinVar nonsense variants, but the available data were extremely imbalanced. These findings underscore dual challenges of modeling diverse nonsense variant consequences and the scarcity of balanced datasets for method development and evaluation.

title: Modeling gene regulatory perturbations via deep learning from high-throughput reporter assays
authors: Revathy Venukuttan, Duke University, United States
abstract: Assessing likely variant effects on phenotypes is of critical importance in diagnostic settings. While much progress has been made in interpreting genic mutations based on our understanding of coding sequence, noncoding variants remain far more difficult to evaluate using DNA sequence alone. High-throughput reporter assays such as STARR-seq and MPRA have proven useful for experimentally measuring regulatory effects of noncoding variants present in a sample. However, these methods cannot but provide information about variants that are not included in the assay input. Whole-genome reporter assays, by contrast, generate large volumes of data that can be used to train predictive models for prioritizing variants not directly observed in the experiment. Here, we describe BlueSTARR, a retrainable predictive modeling framework designed for this purpose. We present results from several models trained on whole-genome STARR-seq data collected from two cell lines and one drug treatment. Using these models, we identify a genome-wide signature consistent with purifying selection against both loss-of-function and gain-of-function regulatory variants. Notably, gain-of-function variants show a bias suggesting selection against increased cis regulatory activity in closed chromatin near genes. We also test the model on synthetic enhancers containing GR and AP-1 transcription factors binding motifs. When trained on drug perturbation data, the model captured distance-dependent and treatment specific binding patterns and their effects on reporter gene activation. Overall, our results demonstrate that lightweight, retrainable models can effectively uncover latent biological signals.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Interaction-aware multitask deep learning reveals cross-species receptor compatibility landscapes across sarbecoviruses
authors: Kritika Prasai, Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Missouri Columbia, United States; Jeffrey C. Chandler, USDA APHIS Wildlife Services, Wildlife Disease Diagnostic Laboratory, Fort Collins, CO, USA, United States; Constanza Espada, Center for Influenza and Emerging Infectious Diseases, University of Missouri, Columbia, United States; Riley Wiese, Center for Influenza and Emerging Infectious Diseases, University of Missouri, Columbia, United States; Yingyi Long, Center for Influenza and Emerging Infectious Diseases, University of Missouri, Columbia, United States; Sean P. Streich, USDA APHIS Wildlife Services, Wildlife Disease Diagnostic Laboratory, Fort Collins, United States; Jonathon Heale, USDA APHIS Wildlife Services, Fort Collins, CO, USA, United States; Nathan Roberts, College of the Ozarks, Point Lookout, Missouri, United States; Yizhi Jane Tao, Department of BioSciences, Rice University, Houston, Texas, United States; Thomas J. DeLiberto, Department of Pathobiology and Integrative Biomedical Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, United States; Xiu-Feng Wan, Center for Influenza and Emerging Infectious Diseases, University of Missouri, Columbia, United States
abstract: Predicting compatibility between interacting proteins across diverse hosts and rapidly evolving viral variants remains a fundamental challenge in computational biology, particularly when binding function diverges a lot from sequence similarity. In the context of SARS-CoV-2 and related sarbecoviruses, the receptor binding domain (RBD)â€“ACE2 interaction exemplifies this challenge, even the closely related sequences exhibit divergent binding affinities, making classical homology-based approaches unreliable. Here, we present CompatNet, a multitask deep learning framework that jointly predicts categorical binding strength and quantitative dissociation constant (KD) from paired ACE2â€“RBD. CompatNet encodes paired RBD and ACE2 sequences using LoRA-adapted ESM-2 embeddings, refines them through a dual-branch localâ€“global encoder (CNN + self-attention), and learns residue-level interaction patterns via gated multi-head cross-attention. The multi-task objective jointly optimizes regression (pKD) and classification (four binding strength categories) over a shared representation, enabling both continuous affinity prediction and interpretable risk classification. We train and evaluate on a curated experimental dataset using 17 wildlife ACE2 orthologs, 16 sarbecovirus RBDs, and additional public dataset of 414(ACE-RBD paired data) and 20,000 deep mutational scanning variants. CompatNet outperforms classical and deep learning baselines and identifies key interface determinants and generalizes well to held-out Omicron sub lineages (Pearson correlation R = 0.95). This framework maps receptor compatibility landscapes across peri-domestic U.S. wildlife and provides a scalable platform for prioritizing receptor-compatible hostâ€“virus pairs for surveillance and experimental evaluation.

title: Design and validation of a Xenium spatial transcriptomics viral panel for virome profiling in Sjögren’s Syndrome
authors: Federica Bichicchi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Natalie Atyeo, National Institutes of Health, United States; Danny Yi, National Institutes of Health, United States; Jay Chiorini, National Institutes of Health, United States
abstract: glands, leading to severe dryness and systemic complications. While its exact cause remains unknown, genetic predisposition and environmental triggers are thought to contribute to disease onset and progression. Several viruses are known to infect salivary gland cells, and emerging evidence suggests that persistent infections may drive immune dysregulation and chronic inflammation in SjD. However, the specific viruses involved and their impact on disease pathology remain unclear. To address this, we developed and validated a spatial transcriptomics viral probe panel. We implemented a computational pipeline to retrieve viral genomes, perform multiple sequence alignment, and quantify sequence conservation using normalized Shannon entropy. Conserved regions were selected to guide probe design across genomes with varying variability, resulting in a panel of 258 viral targets. For experimental validation, representative viral fragments were cloned into plasmids and embedded in tissue microarrays (TMAs) enabling controlled benchmarking of probe performance within a Xenium spatial transcriptomics framework. Control experiments demonstrated robust detection of viral and host transcripts with consistent signal across replicated cores. Integration of probe-level expression with known ground truth enabled quantitative assessment of sensitivity and specificity, revealing strong performance for targets and identifying potential cross-reactivity in variable genomes. This study establishes a scalable framework for the design and validation of spatial viral panels, supporting accurate virome profiling in salivary gland tissues. Future work will apply this approach to SjD patient samples to investigate virusâ€“host interactions and their role in disease pathogenesis

title: Computational Analysis of K-Ras Gene Expression in Dendritic Mouse Cells (DC2.4)
authors: K'Yana Edwards, University of South Florida, United States; Dr Michael Shamblott, University of South Florida, United States
abstract: The K-Ras oncogene drives immune evasion in cancers, but its role in dendritic cells (DCs) remains underexplored. This study investigated K-Ras expression in the murine DC line DC2.4 using PCR, gel electrophoresis, DNA sequencing, and BLAST alignment. The findings confirmed robust K-Ras expression in DC2.4 cells, with high sequence homology to reference transcripts (Mus musculus KRAS variant 8). These results establish DC2.4 as a relevant model for studying K-Ras-mediated immune modulation in cancer. Further research should assess how oncogenic K-Ras mutations alter DC function, potentially revealing new immunotherapy targets.

title: Spatial Profiling Reveals Significant Tumor-Border Immune Differences Across Multiple Cancer Types
authors: Leia Huang, Rancho Bernardo High School, United States
abstract: The tumor-border is an invasive belt which defines the boundary between malignant and adjacent healthy tissue; understanding the location of the tumor-border is important for defining patient prognosis, recurrence rate, achieving maximal survival and quality-of-life. Although the tumor-border is essential for understanding the tumor microenvironment, definitions of the tumor boundary remain unclear, requiring further study using quantitative approaches. H-Plot, a novel graph-based spatial-profiling plot, allows researchers to analyze immune-cell infiltration using an empirically defined tumor-border. H-Plot assigns each cell a spatial layer index relative to the tumor boundary using k-hop traversal of a Delaunay cell graph constructed from H&E WSIs, without requiring manual annotation. The algorithm compares the proportion of immune-cell infiltration with distance from the tumor border. A dataset of 1,500+ pretreatment cases was obtained from TCGA, including BRCA, STAD, UCEC, CESC, and CRC repositories. Using an image analysis platform, researchers classified cells into various cell subtypes. This study revealed that immune-cell tumor stromal infiltration differs most significantly near the tumor-border across multiple cancer types. We observed that group-level differences reached peak statistical significance within approximately 0 to 275 Î¼m toward the tumor core, with p-values as low as 10^-33 across multiple cancer types. These findings support the tumor-border as a key spatial compartment for the evaluation of different immune microenvironment states across various cancer types. Furthermore, this study may lead to a biologically driven method for tumor-border identification, leading to a better understanding of oncological studies for future developments of cancer immunotherapies.

title: FunGI, Functional Genomics Interpreter, and Computational Chemical Genomics
authors: Abolfazl Arab, UCSF, United States; Thomas O'loughlin, Mount Sinai, United States; Nick Youngblut, Arc Institute, United States; Nianzhen Li, Arc Institute, United States; Luke Gilbert, Arc Institute / UCSF, United States; Kevan Shokat, UCSF, United States
abstract: Advances in CRISPR technology have greatly enhanced our capacity for precise genetic modifications and large-scale functional genomics screening. Beyond single-guide approaches, multiplexed genetic perturbations are essential for studying interactions among coding and non-coding elements. An adaptable screen design and data processing framework is critical and computational tasks varying based on platform and research goals. This study introduces several genome-scale CRISPRi loss-of-function drug screens using chemical compounds activating or inhibiting their target proteins. First, we introduce a database of screens performed using inhibitors targeting DNA methylation enzyme DNMT1 and core constituents of the DNA damage response (DDR) machinery PARP, ATR, ATM, DNAPK, and WEE1. Then, we introduce a screen using small molecule targeting the p53-Y220C mutant to restore wild-type conformation and rescue tumor-suppressor activity. These experiments identify >1000 genes whose perturbation modifies the targeted treatment effects and provides a rich resource to the cancer therapeutics community. In addition, this compendium of functional genomics data reveals opens computational challenges to query specific chemical-genetic interaction for further studies. “Computational Chemical Genomics” approaches can integrate high-resolution functional genomics, sequence-informed predictive modeling, and rational chemical probe design to find novel therapeutic strategies in cancer.

title: Hypothesis-Driven Analysis of Gut Microbiome in Subclinical ASCVD
authors: Shreya Chindepalli, Duke University, United States; Anita Shlesinger, Duke University, United States; Joshua Granek, Duke University, United States; Francois Haddad, Stanford University, United States; Jessilyn Dunn, Duke University, United States
abstract: Host-microbe interactions contribute to pathways relevant to atherosclerosis pathogenesis, including lipid metabolism, bile acid metabolism, and vascular inflammation. Alterations in human gut microbial composition have been reported in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), though evidence in early, subclinical stages remains limited. Subclinical ASCVD is characterized by measurable plaque burden prior to onset of symptomatic cardiovascular disease. Studying this stage enables investigation of biological processes associated with disease development. This study examines associations between gut microbiome taxonomic composition and subclinical ASCVD. Stool metagenomic sequencing data from 485 samples across 136 participants (68 with subclinical ASCVD, defined as coronary artery calcium score > 100; 68 matched controls with no coronary artery calcium) was obtained from the Project Baseline Health Study. Participants were propensity-matched on age, sex, race, ethnicity, BMI, hypertension, ASCVD risk score, and type 2 diabetes status. Species-level taxonomic profiles were generated using MetaPhlAn v4. Based on published findings linking specific gut taxa to ASCVD, four genera were selected for prespecified hypothesis-testing: Collinsella, Roseburia, Eubacterium, and Streptococcus. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with multiple testing correction identified higher relative abundance of genera Collinsella and Roseburia in the subclinical ASCVD group. Species-level tests identified three taxa, Eubacterium ventriosum, Eubacterium ramulus, and Streptococcus gordonii, as significantly associated with subclinical ASCVD status after multiple testing correction. These findings suggest that some microbial associations with ASCVD reported in the literature are also detectable in subclinical ASCVD. This work represents an initial hypothesis-testing analysis within an ongoing investigation of this longitudinal data from the Project Baseline Health Study cohort.

title: Discovering Biological Signals in the Noise
authors: Sophia Cheng, University of Michigan, United States
abstract: Like astronomers who have only ever known a star by its light, biologists studying individual cells face a fundamental observational constraint - they cannot directly witness a cell's decisions, only interpret its signals. Single-cell RNA sequencing provides researchers with a snapshot of individual cells from which they can infer what the cell is, what it is doing, and what it might do next. This research focuses on the preprocessing that occurs before analysis begins. Current standards flag cells as noise to be filtered out if they fall outside any single quality control threshold. From a data quality standpoint, this is sound practice. However, the thresholds are often defined using the same set of assumptions that are being analyzed, introducing causal ambiguity. To investigate this further, I performed my own analysis on the discarded noise data from a high-impact 2021 paper (Pal et al., 2021). Using their provided supplementary data, I separated the samples into cells that would be discarded (noise) or analyzed (real). I identified 3 potential biological signals (PBS) when analyzing the latent space of the noise. Using these signals, I then built a decision tree classifier on the noise cells. The classifier has a high sensitivity to ER+ tumors (94.5%) with a moderate overall accuracy (69.3%). This research provides preliminary evidence that there are signals in what is discarded. Investigating these cells more carefully may matter most in cancers where heterogeneity is highest and treatment resistance is hardest to explain, such as breast cancer.

title: Therapeutic Target Discovery for Rare Diseases via Machine Learning Integrating GWAS and TWAS
authors: Satoko Namba, Nagoya University, Japan; Michio Iwata, Kyushu Institute of Technology, Japan; Shin-Ichi Nureki, Oita University, Japan; Noriko Otani, Nagoya University, Japan; Yoshihiro Yamanishi, Nagoya University, Japan
abstract: Identifying therapeutic targets for diseases is important in drug discovery. However, the depletion of viable therapeutic targets has a major bottleneck, contributing to the recent stagnation in drug development, especially for rare and orphan diseases. Here, we propose a disease signature, TRESOR, which characterizes the functional mechanisms of each disease through genome-wide association study (GWAS) and transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) data. Based on TRESOR and target perturbation signatures (TGPs)—i.e., gene knockdown and overexpression profiles of target-coding genes—we develop machine learning methods for predicting inhibitory and activatory therapeutic targets for various diseases. TRESOR enables highly accurate identification of target candidate proteins based on inverse correlations between TRESOR and TGPs. Furthermore, Bayesian integrative method combines TRESOR-based inverse correlations and omics-based disease similarities, providing more reliable predictions for rare and orphan diseases with few or no known targets. We make comprehensive predictions for 284 diseases with 4,345 inhibitory target candidates and 151 diseases with 4,040 activatory target candidates.
